summary: This skill guides an agent through finding installable agent skills when a person asks how to do a task or whether a capability exists. It points the agent to the skills.sh leaderboard, then to the npx skills find command, and gives a checklist for judging popularity and source before recommending anything. It also covers offering to install a chosen skill and what to say when nothing matches.
tasks: find a skill for a specific task
check whether a skill exists for a framework
recommend and install a vetted agent skill
search skills by keyword and owner
qualityWhy: The steps, commands and example reply are clear and usable, but the quality checks are thin and cannot be verified with the CLI as described, and it does not tell the agent to read a skill before installing it.
why: It helps an agent on a node find extra skills now and then, but it depends on an outside registry and the CLI rather than local data. Its install example uses -g, which differs from the node's rule that skills go into one element's folder, so the agent must install locally instead.

summary: This skill tells an agent to run a relentless question-and-answer session that tests a plan or design before work starts. The SKILL.md file contains only one instruction, which hands off to a separate skill named "grilling" that is not part of this bundle. It is aimed at people who want their plans challenged before they build.
tasks: grill me on this feature plan before I build it
stress-test my system design with hard questions
find the gaps in my product spec
qualityWhy: The skill is a wrapper that only points to another skill ("grilling") and contains no steps, examples or checks of its own.
why: A planning-critique habit is useful now and then for a node's builders, but the skill only works if the separate "grilling" skill is also installed, and that skill is not in this bundle. The skill is stack-free, so it fits the node as written, with no risk found in its files.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive the HyperFrames command-line tool for video projects: scaffolding a project, linting and checking it, taking snapshots to inspect frames, editing the timeline, previewing, and rendering locally or in the cloud. It also covers reading the tool's JSON output and recovering from build or render failures. It is aimed at people producing motion video from HTML-based compositions.
tasks: render a 30 second promo video locally
check a video project for layout and contrast errors
snapshot frames to review a composition
trim or move clips on a video timeline
recover from a failed Chrome or render step
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with a clear command table, a step-by-step loop, and failure-recovery rules, though many details are delegated to reference files not included here.
needs: HyperFrames paid cloud plan (only for cloud render)
AWS or GCP account (only for lambda and cloudrun commands)
why: It is a local-first video rendering tool that fits making video content, so value is some rather than high because it is a narrow tool for one kind of output and not for building the app itself. It is marked install-with-service because cloud render, lambda and cloudrun call outside hosted services the person must choose and pay for.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to make videos as HTML: each scene is a timed composition that renders frame by frame from a paused timeline, so the output is repeatable. It covers the rules that keep the files editable in a preview app, a work loop from story and spec through checks and review, and how to choose the right pattern for launch films, explainers, music videos, charts, vertical clips, captions and overlays. It is aimed at people who make promo videos, explainers and social clips.
tasks: make a 15-second product launch video
build an explainer video with captions and overlays
turn a website into a short animated video
make a vertical social clip with title cards
animate a data chart as a video
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is concrete, with a numbered contract, check commands and a clear work loop, but many details sit in referenced files and the scripts could not be read, so the instruction's completeness can't be fully confirmed.
needs: HeyGen account for presenter, avatar or voice media when the person chooses it
HyperFrames plan for the usage command
why: Making video for products, social posts and landing pages is directly what nodes are for, and the video renders from local HTML files. It needs a HeyGen account only for presenter or avatar media and reports plan usage, and the scripts it ships could not be read to confirm their behaviour.

summary: This is a discovery stub for a browser automation command-line tool. It tells an agent to load the real instructions from the installed CLI before driving a Chrome or Chromium browser, and lists specialized guides for Electron apps, Slack, QA testing and cloud browsers. The file contains no workflow of its own. Its use depends entirely on the content the CLI serves at runtime.
tasks: test a web app's forms and flows in a real browser
take screenshots of a page for review
extract data from a website
run an exploratory QA pass on a site
qualityWhy: The file is only a stub that points to other commands, with no steps, examples or checks of its own.
why: A local browser automation tool is useful for testing and capturing pages on a node, but the stub gives no usable instructions and the real guide must be fetched from the CLI after a global npm install (npm i -g), which differs from the node's per-element install. Specialized guides for cloud browsers and Slack are outside what a node is for, so they should not be loaded without a closer look.

summary: This skill is a short wrapper that tells the agent to invoke two other skills, one for relentless questioning of a plan and one for domain modeling. The interview is meant to sharpen a plan or design while it records decisions as architecture decision records and a glossary. It is aimed at people planning a product or feature before building it.
tasks: sharpen a feature plan through questions
record design decisions as ADRs
build a project glossary while planning
qualityWhy: The file is only a two-line pointer to two other skills, so it gives no steps, examples or checks of its own.
why: Planning and documenting design decisions serves building a product, but the actual method lives in the "grilling" and "domain-modeling" skills, which are not in this package, so installing this alone would do nothing useful. Its disable-model-invocation setting means it only runs when the person asks for it.

summary: This skill lets an agent find or create media for a HyperFrames video project: music, sound effects, images, icons, logos, voiceovers, presenter clips, transcripts, cutouts and colour grades. Each result is saved as a local file in the project's assets folder with a record of where it came from. It is aimed at people making short videos and social or landing-page content, and it also covers reshaping footage that looks dark, flat or dull.
tasks: make a 15-second promo video with a voiceover and background music
find a royalty-free sound effect for a transition
generate images or icons for a landing-page video
transcribe a clip and add captions
colour-grade dark or flat footage to look cinematic
mix music under a voiceover with ducking
tools: HyperFrames CLI (npx hyperframes media-use, media-treatment, transcribe, tts, remove-background)
qualityWhy: SKILL.md gives concrete commands, a source table, sign-in and credit rules and a reference index, but the referenced files and scripts could not be read, so the depth of the steps is unverified.
needs: HyperFrames sign-in (free, unlocks HeyGen voices, music catalog and asset search)
HeyGen CLI for direct recipes and helpers
Optional local tools: Kokoro, Parakeet or whisper, MusicGen, mflux, LTX
Optional: Gemini API key for Gemini TTS
why: It directly serves making video and social content for a product, and its media lands in local files as the node expects. It calls the HeyGen service and needs a sign-in, and billed credits apply, so this is a paid service the person chooses. Many scripts (audio, grading, transcription) were unreadable, so I could not check what they do beyond the description.

summary: The skill guides an agent through finding Reddit threads where people openly ask for a product's kind of help, then drafting short, honest replies that disclose any affiliation. It works in two phases: scanning target subreddits and ranking a few threads, then writing peer-style replies for a human to review and post by hand. It is aimed at founders and marketers who want to engage on Reddit without spamming.
tasks: find reddit opportunities for my product this week
draft a disclosed reply to a reddit recommendation request
pick the best threads to engage with on target subreddits
review reddit replies before I post them
qualityWhy: The instructions give clear phases, ranking criteria, a register check, a product-naming gate and ethical rules, though they lack a concrete scanning method and example outputs.
why: It is a stack-free marketing playbook, useful occasionally for promoting a product on Reddit, but it does not build or run anything on the node. It has no install-time risks, and the only thing an agent would do is draft text for a human to post.

summary: This skill has an agent look through a codebase's recent commit history and modules for places where small, shallow pieces of code make understanding and testing harder. It then writes a standalone HTML report with before-and-after diagrams for each candidate refactor and opens it for the person. Once the person picks one, the agent works through the design decisions with them and keeps the project's domain glossary and decision records up to date.
tasks: find refactoring opportunities in a codebase
review the architecture of a module before changing it
plan how to make shallow modules deeper for easier testing
produce a visual architecture review report
qualityWhy: The steps, report structure, card contents and decision rules are concrete and followable, though it depends on three companion skills and an HTML-REPORT.md scaffold whose content was not provided.
why: It is a stack-free review habit for keeping a codebase maintainable, so it is useful now and then rather than for everyday building or selling. Its report loads Tailwind and Mermaid from public CDNs when opened, and it calls the codebase-design, grilling and domain-modeling skills, which were not included in the files reviewed.

summary: This skill lets an agent drive the Sleek design service over its REST API: it creates a project, sends a written brief, and gets back mobile screen designs as renders and HTML. It then guides the agent to turn those designs into working React Native or HTML code, with checks along the way. It is aimed at people who want a mobile app interface designed quickly and then built. Authentication uses a device-approval flow or a pasted API key.
tasks: design a mobile app screen set from a brief
turn a Sleek design into HTML or React Native code
make a review screenshot of a mobile screen
create a style direction for an app's look
qualityWhy: SKILL.md gives a clear auth flow, endpoint table, error contract and parsing advice, though the referenced detail files were not included in the material I was given, so the workflow beyond the overview is only partly verified.
needs: Sleek Pro plan or higher for sustained use
why: It directly serves designing app screens and producing HTML that runs on a node, but the design step depends on the outside Sleek service and its paid credits, so the person must choose that. The React Native target is outside the node's Next.js stack, so only the HTML path fits the node as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through test-driven development in red-green-refactor cycles, focusing on tests that check behavior through public interfaces rather than internals. It asks the agent to agree on test seams with the user before writing any test, and to work in vertical slices instead of writing all tests first. It also lists anti-patterns to avoid, such as implementation-coupled and tautological tests. It is aimed at developers building features or fixing bugs test-first.
tasks: build a feature test-first
fix a bug with a failing test first
write integration tests for a module
review which seams to test before coding
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear rules, anti-patterns and a loop structure, with links to supporting examples, though it has few concrete steps or commands for a given test framework.
why: It is a stack-free testing method that fits building and fixing features in any node-hosted app, so it can be installed as written. Its one reference to another skill, codebase-design, is optional. I only read SKILL.md; the other three files (tests.md, mocking.md, agents/openai.yaml) were not provided, so their content is unverified.

summary: The skill gives an agent a local catalogue of about 450 ready-made HyperFrames blocks and components, installed as editable source. An agent searches the catalogue by describing the visual effect it needs, then installs the matching item with the hyperframes CLI and wires it into a video composition. It is aimed at people producing motion graphics and video content with HyperFrames.
tasks: add a glitch or CRT scanline effect to a video
find a lower third or title card for a scene
add animated captions to a clip
insert an animated chart into a video
apply a camera move or transition between scenes
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete commands, install and wiring rules, and pointers to reference files, though much of the detail sits in linked files and some steps are only summarised.
why: It is useful for video and motion-graphics content made with HyperFrames, and it is a local-first workflow; it is not a core part of building web apps or sites, so it is only occasionally useful on a Fractera node. Search is local by default, and the optional on-device model is a one-time ~33 MB download that the person must approve. The install command is the standard npx hyperframes add with no differences from the node's own setup.

summary: This skill prepares a code repository for a set of engineering helper skills. The agent inspects the repo, asks the person to choose an issue tracker (GitHub, GitLab, local markdown, or another system), and optionally sets up a triage label scheme. It then writes the configuration into the agent instruction file and into docs under docs/agents. The setup is aimed at developers who run agent-driven workflows on their own codebase.
tasks: set up issue tracking for this repo before using agent skills
configure triage labels for incoming bug reports
create a glossary and ADR layout for a codebase
make a repo ready for agent-driven ticket writing
qualityWhy: The steps are concrete, with explicit branches, file templates, and a verification check for the repo connection, though the GitHub-first default leaves some gaps for other trackers.
needs: GitHub account with gh CLI (for the GitHub tracker option)
GitLab account with glab CLI (for the GitLab tracker option)
why: It is a developer-workflow setup rather than a tool for building or selling a product, so its value is occasional; the local-markdown option needs no account, but the default path uses GitHub Issues and its label commands, so it is marked as needing a service.

summary: This skill tells an agent to condense the current conversation into a handoff document saved in the system temp folder, so a fresh agent can pick up the work. The document should point to existing specs, plans, issues and commits by path or URL rather than repeating them, and it should list which skills the next agent should invoke. Sensitive details such as keys, passwords and personal data must be removed, and any user-supplied focus for the next session shapes the document. It is aimed at people running long multi-session work who need continuity between agent sessions.
tasks: hand off a half-finished site build to a new agent session
write a handoff note before ending a long coding session
summarise progress and next steps for a fresh agent
prepare a continuation document for the next session's focus
qualityWhy: It gives a clear purpose and a few sensible rules (temp location, referencing rather than duplicating, redaction, argument handling), but it lacks a template, examples and checks for what the document should contain.
why: It is a stack-free workflow habit that helps when long work on a node spans several agent sessions, but it has nothing specific to Fractera's elements, so its value is occasional rather than central. Saving to the temp folder means the document may be lost on reboot, which the person should be aware of.

summary: This skill guides an agent through designing distinctive, intentional user interfaces rather than generic templated ones. It asks the agent to ground visuals in the product's subject, plan a small token system for color, type and layout, check that plan against cliché patterns, then build and self-critique. It also gives copywriting rules so interface text stays plain, active and consistent. It is aimed at designers and builders making new or reshaped screens.
tasks: redesign the landing page so it doesn't look templated
pick a typeface and color palette for a new app
plan the layout and visual direction before building a page
review a finished UI for generic AI-style design tells
write clearer button labels and error messages for a screen
qualityWhy: It gives a clear multi-step process with concrete anti-patterns and checks, though it leans on abstract taste guidance and has no code examples.
why: It is a stack-free design guidance skill that directly serves building and polishing the node's web UI, so it fits as written. Its reliance on taste judgement means output quality still depends on the agent and the person's brief.

summary: This skill turns an agent into a relentless interviewer that stress-tests a plan, decision or idea. It maps the topic as a design tree and asks questions in numbered rounds, each with a recommended answer the user can accept. An agent using it would reach a shared understanding with the person before acting, and it fits planning and product-decision work.
tasks: stress-test my product plan
grill me on this architecture decision
challenge my startup idea before I build it
walk through open questions for a launch
qualityWhy: The instructions give a clear round-based method, an exact output format and a stop condition, though they leave the question-writing style and the sub-agent usage loosely specified.
why: It is a stack-free thinking habit that helps a builder plan sites, apps and content, but it is not specific to Fractera. The skill has no risks in its files.

summary: This skill turns a maintainer's issue tracker into a triage workflow: it sorts open issues and external pull requests into buckets, recommends a category and state, checks whether a claim is real by reproducing it or reviewing the diff, and then writes either an agent brief, human handoff notes, needs-info questions, or a close comment. It is aimed at open-source project maintainers who handle incoming reports. It depends on the repo having a configured label mapping and a glossary/ADR setup, and it instructs the agent to post disclaimers on every comment.
tasks: triage new issues in a repo
decide whether an external PR is ready for an agent or a human
write an agent brief for a bug report
ask a reporter for specific missing information
close an already-implemented or rejected feature request
qualityWhy: The state machine, roles, buckets and templates are concrete and followable, though the agent-brief and out-of-scope details live in referenced files and the label mapping depends on an external setup command.
needs: an issue tracker account with write access to the repo
why: It serves maintaining open-source project issue queues, not building, running, selling or making content with a Fractera node, so value is none; it also posts to an external issue tracker, which the node's local-first design does not cover.

summary: This skill guides an agent to build a throwaway prototype that answers one design question. For questions about logic or state, it produces a single HTML file with buttons and guided walkthroughs that a non-developer can drive. For questions about appearance, it generates several contrasting UI variants on one route, switched by a URL parameter and a floating bar. It is aimed at product builders who want to learn something quickly before committing to production code.
tasks: check whether a state model or workflow logic feels right
explore what a page or screen should look like
compare several UI variations on one route
capture a validated prototype decision without polluting main
qualityWhy: The rules and branch selection are clear and actionable, but the actual steps for each branch are delegated to LOGIC.md and UI.md, which were not part of what I read, so the instruction is thin on its own.
why: It directly supports building UI and product logic, and it is mostly stack-free process guidance that fits a Next.js node. I only read SKILL.md, so the referenced LOGIC.md and UI.md files, and the agents/openai.yaml file, are unverified; the UI branch's routing advice needs checking against the node's own App Router conventions.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to create short AI videos by calling hosted video models through the inference.sh command-line tool. It covers text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-based video, talking-head avatars and lipsync, video editing, upscaling, sound effects and merging clips. It is aimed at people making social media posts, ads, explainers and product demos.
tasks: make a 15-second promo video from a text prompt
animate a product photo into a short video
create a talking-head avatar video from a portrait and audio
add sound effects to a silent video
merge several clips into one video with transitions
upscale an existing video
qualityWhy: It is a clear catalogue of models and runnable commands, but it gives no steps for checking output, polling for results, downloading files or handling errors.
needs: inference.sh credits or API access to run the hosted models
publicly reachable URLs for input images, video or audio
why: Video generation directly serves making content for a product, but every model runs on the inference.sh cloud, so the person must accept that their prompts and media go to that service. The linked CLI install instructions were not in the files, so their contents are unknown and should be checked before installing.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to generate, edit, and upscale images by running hosted AI models through the inference.sh belt CLI. It covers choosing among about 15 models (GPT-Image-2, FLUX, Gemini, Grok, Seedream and others) and gives example commands for text-to-image, image-to-image editing, upscaling and stitching. It is aimed at people making product mockups, social graphics, marketing visuals and illustrations.
tasks: generate a product photo mockup
create social media graphics with AI
edit an existing image with a text prompt
upscale an image to higher resolution
make concept art or illustrations
qualityWhy: It gives concrete, copy-ready commands and a model table, but it has no steps for saving or checking outputs and no error handling.
needs: inference.sh API access for hosted image models
why: Directly useful for making images for products and social posts, but the images are produced by a paid outside service, so the person must accept that prompts and image URLs go to inference.sh. The skill's prerequisite points to a raw GitHub install guide that I could not inspect, so what that guide runs is unverified.

summary: This skill lets an agent post tweets and posts with media to X, reply-free engagement such as likes and retweets, send direct messages, follow accounts, and read profiles or posts. It runs each action through the inference.sh command-line tool, so the agent calls hosted apps rather than the X API directly. It suits someone who wants to publish or schedule social content, or grow an audience, from a script or agent.
tasks: post a tweet with an image or video
schedule social media content
like or retweet a post
send a direct message to a follower
look up a user's X profile
qualityWhy: The commands are concrete and easy to follow, but the skill is a list of app calls with no input schema, error handling, rate-limit guidance or verification steps.
why: It directly serves publishing and promoting content for a product, but posting runs through a hosted third-party service and the person's X account must be linked to it, so the person should accept that before use. The install instructions point to a remote file, which the agent should check before running. Automated likes, follows and DMs may breach X's terms, and that is worth weighing before use.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to produce talking-head and avatar videos by running hosted models through the belt command-line tool. It covers choosing between a portrait-plus-script model with built-in voices and models that need separate audio. It also gives recipes for batch UGC-style ads, multi-presenter variants and dubbing a video into another language. The intended users are marketers, course makers and product teams who want presenter videos without filming.
tasks: make an AI presenter video from a portrait and a script
create a UGC-style ad with a virtual presenter
generate several presenter variants of one product message
dub a video into another language with lipsync
qualityWhy: The examples are concrete and runnable, but the skill is mostly command lists with no steps for checking results, polling output, or handling errors.
needs: pay-per-use fees for the hosted video, image and voice models
why: It directly serves making video content for a product, but every generation runs on a paid outside service, so the person's portraits and audio are uploaded to third parties. The belt CLI itself is installed from another source (npx skills add belt-sh/cli), which the person should check before installing.

summary: This skill gives a coding agent a set of design playbooks for building, redesigning, polishing, and reviewing web and iOS interfaces. It routes each request to a matching workflow, such as new work, product dashboards, simplification, read-only audits, or native iOS checks. It asks the agent to study the existing product and comparable screens first, to build from a realistic target image, and to render and inspect the result at real device sizes. It can optionally pull references and assets from a paid Uizze service.
tasks: design a new landing page or app screen
redesign a dashboard for clarity
polish spacing, hierarchy and details of a screen
audit a web or iOS interface visually
simplify a cluttered settings or product page
qualityWhy: The router and workflow rules are clear and detailed, but most of the actual playbooks (reference/*.md, references/*.md) are linked and not included in the package, so an agent cannot follow many of the steps as shipped.
why: It directly helps build and polish product UI for web and iOS, and it works without an account, though its fullest form uses a paid Uizze MCP and an image tool. Many linked playbook files are missing from this package, so agents will have gaps until those files are supplied.

summary: This skill guides an agent through shaping a project's domain model while the design is still in progress. It has the agent question vague or conflicting terms, propose precise names, test relationships with concrete edge-case scenarios, and check the code against what the person says. It also tells the agent when to record a term in a GLOSSARY.md file and when a decision is significant enough for an architecture decision record (ADR). It is written for developers and product builders working on a codebase.
tasks: design the domain model for a new app
write or update a GLOSSARY.md of project terms
record an architecture decision as an ADR
resolve conflicting terminology between the code and the team
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear, ordered behaviours, file layouts and explicit criteria for when to write an ADR, but the referenced format files and the agent config were not included for review.
why: It is a stack-free design discipline that directly supports building a product's model and its documentation, so it works on a node as written. Only SKILL.md was reviewed in full; the ADR-FORMAT.md, GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md and agents/openai.yaml files were listed but not shown, so their contents are unverified.

summary: This skill turns the agent into a multi-session tutor for a topic the user wants to learn. It keeps a local workspace with a mission statement, reference sheets, a resource list, learning records and short HTML lessons, so each session builds on the last. It suits a person who wants to pick up a new subject step by step, grounded in their own goals.
tasks: teach me a new programming concept over several sessions
build a learning plan tied to my goal
make a short interactive HTML lesson with a quiz
create a glossary and cheat sheet for a topic I'm studying
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear, detailed workflow with file roles, lesson rules, quiz rules and a learning-record model, though the actual format details live in linked files that were not reviewed.
why: It is a general learning workflow rather than a tool for building, running or selling a product, so it is useful now and then rather than core to a node. It is stack-free and local-first, writing its files into the workspace, and it needs no keys or outside accounts; its only outside help is the web resources it asks the agent to find.

summary: This skill gives an agent a shared design vocabulary for deep modules: a small interface hiding a lot of behaviour, placed at a deliberate seam and tested through that interface. It tells the agent to use fixed terms such as module, interface, seam, depth, leverage and locality, and to avoid words like component or boundary. It also points to two companion guides, one on deepening a cluster given its dependencies and one on comparing several radically different interface designs through parallel sub-agents. It is written for developers who want to design or restructure code so it is easier to test and to navigate.
tasks: design a simpler interface for this module
find where to add a seam for testing
review a codebase for shallow modules to deepen
compare several interface designs before choosing one
qualityWhy: The principles, glossary and worked examples are concrete and consistent, though the main file gives few step-by-step checks and leans on the two linked files for process.
why: It is a stack-free design habit guide, useful now and then when restructuring code on a node, but it does not build or serve anything directly. The companion files were not provided for review, so their contents are unknown.

summary: This skill teaches an agent a disciplined method for hard bugs and performance regressions. The agent first builds a fast, deterministic, red-capable feedback loop (test, curl script, CLI diff, headless browser, replay, bisection, or a human-in-the-loop bash script), then reproduces and minimises the failure, ranks falsifiable hypotheses, instruments one variable at a time, fixes with a regression test, and cleans up debug code. It is aimed at developers debugging code that is broken, throwing, failing or slow.
tasks: debug this failing test
diagnose a slow page regression
reproduce an intermittent crash
find the cause of a wrong output
qualityWhy: The phases, completion checklist and examples are concrete and followable, though the bash template script could not be read so its helper is unverified.
why: It is a stack-free debugging discipline that helps a developer building a product on the node fix bugs in its own code, but it only helps now and then rather than directly building or selling content. The bundled hitl-loop script could not be read, so its contents are unchecked.

summary: The skill gives an agent a catalogue of 70 React and Next.js performance rules grouped into eight categories, from eliminating request waterfalls and bundle size to re-render control and server-side caching. When writing, reviewing or refactoring components, pages and data fetching, the agent checks code against these rules and applies the matching fix. It is aimed at developers who build web frontends and want faster load times and smoother interaction.
tasks: review a React component for performance problems
remove request waterfalls in a Next.js data fetch
reduce bundle size of a Next.js page
optimize re-renders in a React form
refactor a server component to parallelize fetches
qualityWhy: Each rule has a short explanation with incorrect and correct code examples and a priority ranking, which an agent can follow directly, though the files were not all read here and some rules may be thin.
why: Its rules target the exact stack a node runs (Next.js 16, React 19), so it is directly useful for building and reviewing site code. It is marked "ideas" rather than "install" because it is generic guidance and some rules (for example around data fetching and caching) should be adapted to the node's own SQLite element and Fractera conventions rather than applied verbatim. Its popularity figure was ignored in this judgement.

summary: This skill lets an agent read, create, edit and summarise Feishu (Lark) cloud documents and wikis through the lark-cli command-line tool. It can also insert or download images and attachments, handle version history, and work with whiteboards and mind notes inside those documents. It is aimed at office workers and teams who keep their writing in Feishu. The SKILL.md is a router that sends each task to a separate reference file, so the detailed steps sit in those files.
tasks: summarise a Feishu document
create a Feishu doc from an outline
polish or rewrite an existing Feishu wiki page
insert a local image into a Feishu doc
qualityWhy: The routing and command rules are clear and specific, but most of the working detail lives in reference files that were not included for review.
why: Feishu cloud documents are a company's cloud place to keep text, so the content would live in the cloud rather than on the person's own computer, which makes it a poor fit for a local-first node. The skill also depends on a workplace platform the node does not serve for building, running, selling or making content. I could only review SKILL.md, not the 43 reference files, so the full instructions are unverified.

summary: This skill lets an agent operate Feishu (Lark) Base, a spreadsheet-style database with tables, fields, records, views, forms, dashboards, workflows, permissions and BaseApp pages. It routes requests to dozens of lark-cli commands and points to detailed reference files for each area. It is aimed at teams working inside the Feishu/Lark ecosystem, not at building a local product.
tasks: create a table with fields in a Feishu Base
add or update records in a Base table
build a dashboard with charts from Base data
set up a Base form to collect submissions
configure a workflow that runs on record changes
qualityWhy: It gives a clear resource model, concrete command routes, JSON examples and a per-area reference index, though much of the detail lives in external reference files that were not included.
why: Feishu Base is a cloud database and spreadsheet service, so under the local-first rule it counts as a cloud place to keep data and is value none; it is not meant for a node's local SQLite-based data.

summary: This skill points an agent to the Mediabunny browser library for reading basic media facts from audio and video files. Mediabunny is a local, in-browser library that fits a Next.js node without a cloud service. I did not read the full text of the three reference notes, so their exact code is unverified.

summary: The skill gives an agent a set of map-animation techniques for Remotion videos: a static satellite image, Mapbox, MapLibre, MapTiler, and CesiumJS flythroughs. The skill is written for Remotion, which fits the node's video-making use, and the scripts read and write local files only.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to handle incoming code review feedback: read it fully, restate the requirement, verify each claim against the actual codebase, and push back with technical reasoning when a suggestion is wrong. why: It is a stack-free habit skill for handling code review, useful to a team building a product but not specific to building or selling content on a node; the only tool reference is the GitHub CLI for replying to threads, which needs no outside account beyond the person's own repository access.

summary: This skill lets an agent run the higgsfield command-line tool to create images, videos, 3D models and audio from text prompts or reference files. Without that risk it would be install-with-service, since the generation service is outside and the person chooses to use it.

summary: This skill tells an agent to sweep an existing interface for places that should animate and to reject most candidates, keeping only a short list of high-value motion ideas. Each surviving idea gets exact easing, duration and property values, and the agent must justify it against a frequency, purpose, speed and function gate. suggest motion for a dashboard without over-animating it
audit a React app for missing press feedback and transitions
make this feel more alive without slowing it down

The node's own stack is Next.js with Tailwind and shadcn/ui, so the recipes need adapting to that stack and its existing tokens before use.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to split several unrelated failures or problems into independent domains and hand each one to its own sub-agent with a tightly scoped, self-contained prompt. The agents run concurrently, and the main agent then reviews their summaries, checks for conflicts, and runs the full suite. why: It is a stack-free workflow habit useful for a developer building on a node when several independent fixes exist, but it is not a product-facing feature. It does not depend on any outside service, and its guidance applies directly without adaptation.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write and revise other agent skills using a test-first routine: run a task without the skill to see where the agent goes wrong, write the smallest skill that fixes those failures, then retest and close loopholes. edit an existing SKILL.md without breaking it
draw a process flowchart for a skill

why: It is stack-free process guidance, so it fits a node that builds agent skills, but it does not directly help build, run or sell a product. Its paths point to a personal ~/.claude/skills directory and mention other runtimes, which the node's per-element installation will not match exactly; this should be checked, not treated as a blocker. The bundled render-graphs.js only runs the local dot binary on SKILL.md and writes into a diagrams folder, so it raises no safety concern.

summary: This skill tells an agent to first check whether it is already inside an isolated git workspace, and if not, to create one, preferring any native worktree tool the harness offers and falling back to a manual git worktree in a project-local directory that is verified as git-ignored. After setup it installs dependencies by project type and runs the test suite to confirm a clean baseline before implementation. create a git worktree before implementing a plan
check whether I am already in a worktree
verify a clean test baseline before coding

summary: This skill tells an agent to start Remotion Studio, the local preview server for Remotion video projects, as soon as the project can run, and to keep it open while the composition is built and edited. It explains when to omit the --no-open flag so the browser opens by itself, and when to open the printed URL in an in-app browser instead. check that a video composition renders in the browser

why: Remotion makes videos from React code on the person's own computer, which fits making video content for social networks and landing pages, and the skill runs a local preview with no outside service. It is a short launch note rather than full video guidance, and it assumes Remotion is already set up in the project.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to work with PDF files locally using Python libraries and command-line tools. It covers reading text and tables, merging, splitting, rotating and watermarking pages, creating new PDFs, OCR for scanned files, encryption, image extraction, and filling forms by reading their field structure. The Tesseract OCR binary and the other command-line tools must be installed separately, and the license is custom, so its terms in LICENSE.txt should be read before use.

summary: The skill guides an agent through closing out a finished feature branch: it runs the full test suite, detects whether the work sits in a normal repo, a named-branch worktree, or a detached HEAD, and then offers a fixed menu of choices. Those choices are merging locally into the base branch, pushing and opening a pull request, or keeping the branch as it is. decide how to integrate completed work safely

why: Useful for git-based development workflows and any node project under version control, but it is a generic git habit rather than something tied to Fractera's stack. It stays in the local repository and makes no outside calls, and its destructive paths require explicit confirmation.

summary: This skill guides an agent through creating, reading, editing and reviewing Word .docx and .dotx files. The skill relies on the node having docx, pandoc, LibreOffice and poppler available, which the agent should check before use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing a pull request description with a fixed layout: a visual summary, evidence of the change working, and a merge-risk section. summary: This skill lets an agent produce brand product photos, lifestyle scenes, ad variants, carousels and banners by calling a Higgsfield CLI command that runs a remote prompt enhancer and then the gpt_image_2 image model. It sorts requests into ten modes, asks a few labeled questions before generating, and returns only the image links. Higgsfield backend prompt enhancer and gpt_image_2 access

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive a real browser from the command line: open pages, read an accessibility snapshot with element refs, click, type, and inspect the DOM. summary: This skill trains a personal face model, called a Soul Character, from 5 to 20 photos of one person through the Higgsfield command-line tool. Uploads people's face photos to the Higgsfield cloud service; the skill does not warn the person about biometric data leaving their machine.

summary: Guides an agent through a design exploration for one described UI piece: it scopes the request to a single component, maps the project's stack and tokens, and builds three or more genuinely different variants on named axes such as layout, density, or motion. Its PICKER.md companion was not supplied in full, so the picker markup is unverified.

summary: This skill makes an agent turn a system, process, schema, timeline or code repository into a checked, standalone HTML diagram with an interactive viewer. summary: Teaches an agent to drive the Sentry command-line tool: list and inspect issues, events and traces, stream logs, run a local Spotlight server, query Sentry docs, browse the API schema, manage releases and sourcemaps, and make raw authenticated API calls. summary: This skill walks an agent through setting up the Firebase command-line tool, logging in to a Google account, choosing or creating a Firebase project, and downloading Android and iOS app config files. summary: This skill tells an agent how to put a project online on Vercel, a cloud hosting service. It checks whether the project is already linked to Vercel and has a git remote, then picks a route: push to git, deploy with the CLI, link first, or make a temporary no-login deployment. It always deploys as a preview unless the person asks for production, and it returns the URL to the person.

summary: This skill guides an agent through adding user sign-in to an app using Google's hosted Firebase Authentication service. It covers enabling providers such as Google, email/password, phone and anonymous accounts, then wiring up the web, Flutter, Android and iOS clients. It also explains how to restrict Firestore and Storage data to signed-in users. It is aimed at developers whose apps depend on the Firebase cloud backend.

summary: This skill lets an agent drive a headless browser through the inference.sh cloud service. The agent opens pages, reads numbered element references, clicks and fills fields, takes screenshots, runs JavaScript, and can record video of a session. It is aimed at people who want web scraping, form filling, login flows or browser testing done by an agent.

summary: Guides an agent through deploying static sites and single-page apps to classic Firebase Hosting, including custom domains, firebase.json settings for redirects, rewrites and headers, multi-site setups, preview channels and local emulation. It is aimed at developers who want to publish front-end builds to Google's hosting service via the CLI. The skill explicitly routes SSR apps to App Hosting and excludes Auth, Firestore, and similar products.
tasks: deploy a static website to Firebase Hosting
set up a custom domain for a web app
add redirects and rewrites in firebase.json
create a preview channel to test changes before going live
qualityWhy: The main SKILL.md is clear and well scoped, but the two reference files were not included in the excerpt I can judge against, and the instructions are mostly pointers rather than step-by-step procedures.
why: Firebase Hosting is a cloud hosting service, which the node's local-first rule classes as value none and use skip, regardless of how clean the instructions are.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to deploy Next.js or Angular apps that use server-side rendering to Google's Firebase App Hosting. It covers the firebase.json and apphosting.yaml setup, creating a backend, storing secrets, and connecting a GitHub repository for push-based rollouts. It is aimed at developers who want a managed hosting pipeline for full-stack web apps.
tasks: deploy a Next.js app to Firebase App Hosting
configure apphosting.yaml for a backend
store and grant access to app secrets
set up GitHub-connected automatic deployments
choose between Firebase Hosting and App Hosting
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete steps, command examples, config snippets and reference files, but it leaves gaps such as error handling and rollback guidance.
needs: Firebase project on the Blaze billing plan
Google account with Firebase console access
GitHub account and repository for CI/CD
why: Firebase App Hosting is a cloud hosting and backend service that runs the app on Google Cloud, so it falls outside what a local-first node is for. It also requires a paid Blaze billing plan, and the commands fetch the latest firebase-tools package at run time, which is worth knowing even though it is not a risk in itself.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building a relational backend on Google's hosted SQL Connect service, which runs on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The agent writes a GraphQL schema, authorized queries and mutations, and real-time refresh rules, then generates type-safe client SDKs for web, Android, iOS and Flutter. It is aimed at developers who want a Firebase-managed relational database for an app.
tasks: design a relational schema for a web app
write authorized queries and mutations for user-owned data
set up real-time updates on a Postgres-backed backend
generate a type-safe SDK for a mobile app
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete workflow steps, file layouts, validation commands and pointers to detailed references, though much of the substance sits in linked files.
why: The database is a cloud service hosted by Google (Firebase SQL Connect on Cloud SQL), which a local-first node should not depend on, and deployment runs with `firebase deploy` to that cloud. Its stack is also not the node's own SQLite element.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to apply psychology and mental models to marketing: explaining why people buy, naming relevant biases or frameworks, and suggesting ethical ways to use them in messaging, pricing and funnels. It is aimed at marketers and founders deciding how to influence customer behavior. It is a broad reference of models rather than a step-by-step procedure, and it points to other skills for page, pricing and copy work.
tasks: explain why customers hesitate to buy
pick psychological principles for a landing page
suggest ethical persuasion tactics for a pricing page
map cognitive biases to a retention problem
qualityWhy: It is well organised and gives a clear model, principle and marketing application for each entry, but it is a list of concepts with no worked examples, checks or concrete procedure for an agent to follow.
why: It is a stack-free thinking aid that helps with messaging and conversion decisions, so it is useful now and then rather than core to building a product. It contains no code or outside services, and its advice is generic, so it needs judgment from the person using it.

summary: This skill guides an agent to plan what content a business should produce, not to write it. It covers searchable versus shareable content, topic pillars and clusters, buyer-stage keyword mapping, scoring ideas from customer research and keyword data, and a 60/30/10 editorial calendar split. It is aimed at marketers and founders who need to decide what to publish next.
tasks: plan a content strategy for my product
decide what blog topics to cover next
build a topic cluster map and editorial calendar
score and prioritize content ideas from customer research
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with scoring templates, output formats, keyword modifiers and a clear checklist, though some sections point to other skills and the references are not shown.
why: It serves building and running a product's content, since blogs and landing pages are what the node is for, and it is a stack-free planning skill that works as written. Its one open point is that it leans on web search for competitor and forum research, which the agent must have available.

summary: This skill is a multi-phase orchestrator that takes a business idea or an existing app through discovery, architecture planning, infrastructure-as-code scaffolding, and deployment to Microsoft Azure, with cost estimates and approval gates at each stage. It is aimed at developers who want their app running on Azure without knowing which services to choose. It delegates to many sub-phases and reference files, and it leans heavily on Azure CLI, Bicep and azd-style deployment.
tasks: deploy my existing app to Azure
estimate the monthly cost of running my app on Azure
generate Bicep infrastructure for my app
plan which Azure services my app needs
qualityWhy: The skill is detailed, with ordered steps, references, schemas and conformance scripts, though much of its guidance depends on other skills and reference files that were not all shown.
needs: Azure CLI login with RBAC permissions
why: Its whole purpose is to deploy and run apps on Azure cloud services, which a local-first Fractera node does not use for its own data, files or hosting, so the value is none. It is skipped under the cloud-hosting rule, not because of any single risk.

summary: This skill makes an agent evaluate a repository before any Azure infrastructure work. It checks build health, app completeness, dependency compatibility and deployment feasibility, then reports per-component PASS/WARN/FAIL verdicts and blockers. It is aimed at developers who want to know whether their code can ship to Azure and what must change first.
tasks: check if my app is ready to deploy to Azure
find deployment blockers in my repo
check whether my dependencies are compatible with Azure
tell me what my app needs before deploying
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a numbered workflow, explicit gates, routing tables and schemas, though many steps depend on the referenced files and the Azure-specific MCP tools.
needs: Azure subscription and az CLI login
why: The skill is built around deploying to Azure, a cloud hosting target, so for a local-first Fractera node it is a cloud deployment tool and it is marked skip under the value rules. It also routes into Azure infrastructure, subscription and resource-group setup, which a node does not use.

summary: Explains how to install and configure Sonner, a React toast notification library, including mounting a single Toaster at the app root, choosing between toast variants, promise and loading toasts, updating and dismissing them, and styling through a ladder from defaults to headless custom JSX. It also covers theming, icons, multiple toasters and a troubleshooting table for common symptoms such as duplicate or missing toasts and stacking problems. The guide is aimed at developers building React or Next.js front ends who use toast messages.
tasks: set up toast notifications in a Next.js app
show a loading toast that becomes success or error
fix toasts appearing behind a modal
style toasts to match a design system
make toasts follow dark mode
qualityWhy: Concrete and well organised, with a decision table, recipes, a styling escalation ladder and a symptom-cause-fix table, though it leans on the API.md file for exact props.
why: It is a frontend UI library guide, useful for building a node's interface, but it is written for a generic React app rather than the node's own stack, and the node already has its own UI kit (shadcn/ui), so it should be read for ideas and adapted to shadcn/sonner conventions. No outside service or key is needed, and nothing in the files is risky.

summary: This skill guides an agent through making a site's pages easier for AI answer engines such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude and Google AI Overviews to find, read and cite. It covers an audit of current AI visibility, checks on page structure and extractable answer blocks, bot access policy by crawler purpose, and machine-readable files like llms.txt and a pricing file. It is aimed at marketers and site owners who publish product pages, blogs, docs or comparison content.
tasks: audit our site for AI search visibility
make our product pages citable by ChatGPT and Perplexity
add llms.txt and a machine-readable pricing file
check whether AI crawlers can access our pages
plan content that AI answer engines will cite
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete checklists, templates and per-platform guidance, but relies on drifting vendor statistics and sends the reader to many reference files and outside tools without a single implementation path for a web stack.
why: It directly serves making and marketing a product's site and content for AI answer engines, and it is stack-free advice that needs no account. Its monitoring tools (Semrush, Ahrefs, Otterly and similar) are optional paid services the person may choose, not requirements, and some cited statistics will need re-checking before use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through planning and building many search-targeted pages from one template and a data source. It covers choosing a pattern such as locations, comparisons, integrations or directories, checking search demand, designing unique content per page, linking pages together, controlling indexation, and picking a build platform. It is written for marketers and site owners who want to capture long-tail search traffic at scale.
tasks: plan location pages for a local service business
build comparison pages against competitor products
design a directory of integration pages
decide which pages to index and which to noindex
check whether a site's CMS can generate hundreds of SEO pages
qualityWhy: The instructions are well structured with a playbook table, a clear framework and pre-launch checks, but they stay high-level and give no concrete template or code examples in the SKILL.md itself.
why: It directly serves a node's purpose of building and growing sites and content, and it is stack-free, so an agent can follow it as written on a local-first node. Only SKILL.md was provided in full; the reference files were listed but not read, so their depth is unknown.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building React Native and Expo animations in a disciplined order: first deciding whether motion is warranted at all, then choosing the cheapest tool, the right properties, spring or timing curves, and keeping work on the UI thread. It targets mobile app developers who need gesture-driven motion, sheets, screen transitions, press feedback and haptics that hold up on real devices. It is a rigorous, opinionated construction guide built around Reanimated, Gesture Handler and Expo Router.
tasks: add a drag-to-dismiss bottom sheet to an Expo app
make press feedback on buttons feel physical
fix an animation that stutters on Android
animate a list row swipe-to-delete
add haptics to a picker or slider
qualityWhy: It gives concrete decision gates, exact spring and easing configs, dependency install commands, a never-ship table and a companion recipes file, so an agent can follow it step by step.
why: It directly serves building polished motion for Expo apps, which is central to what Fractera nodes are for, and it uses the node's own stack of Expo, Reanimated and Gesture Handler with no cloud service. Its guidance is opinionated, and feel can only be verified on a real device, which the skill itself states.

summary: The skill guides an agent through editing existing marketing copy in focused passes: clarity, voice, so-what benefits, proof, specificity, emotion, and risk reduction. It also flags common AI-written tells such as contrast reveals and negation lists, and it covers refreshing outdated pages. It is aimed at marketers and content writers who already have a draft they want improved.

refresh an outdated product page
review email copy before sending
sharpen the messaging on a sales page

why: Editing and refreshing marketing copy is directly useful for building and selling through a product or site, and it is stack-free writing guidance that needs no outside service. The evals and reference files were not reviewed in full, so their completeness is unverified.

summary: The skill gives an agent a catalogue of 139 marketing ideas for software products, grouped by category such as content and SEO, paid ads, communities, partnerships, launches and product-led growth. When someone is stuck, it helps the agent narrow the list to a few ideas that fit the product's stage, budget and team, then lay out how to start each one. It points to deeper reference files for a few ideas, such as guerrilla marketing. It is aimed at founders and marketers of SaaS or software products.
tasks: suggest marketing ideas for my SaaS product
brainstorm ways to grow my app's user base
pick low-budget marketing tactics for a small team
plan the first steps for a chosen growth idea
qualityWhy: It is a well-organised index with clear output format and checks, but most of the 139 ideas are only named in a table, and the implementation guidance is generic rather than step-by-step.
why: It is a stack-free strategy aid that helps a node's owner plan growth for a product they build, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. The skill text itself contains no stack-specific or outside-service requirements.

summary: This skill is a product-selection guide for Cloudflare: it maps a user's stated need (uploads, background jobs, search, agents, security, deployment) to the right Cloudflare product and points to a sibling skill or reference for implementation. It tells agents to choose between the cf CLI and Wrangler depending on the project's configuration. It is aimed at developers who build on Cloudflare's hosted platform.
tasks: choose Cloudflare products for a file upload app
pick storage for an AI document search feature
decide between Workers and Pages for a new site
find the right Cloudflare product for background jobs
qualityWhy: It is a broad, well-organised routing table, but it gives no concrete steps, examples or checks of its own and mostly defers to links and other skills.
why: Its whole purpose is to steer work onto Cloudflare's hosted services (R2, D1, KV, Queues, Workers hosting), which the node's local-first rule treats as value none and use skip. It would send the person's data and apps to a cloud platform rather than keeping them on their own computer.

summary: Launches Chromium through standard Playwright calls with a frozen real-device fingerprint, a persistent isolated profile per identity, and a per-profile proxy that sets timezone and WebRTC. It is aimed at people who run their own accounts, test their own bot detection, or check ads and pricing from another region. It also covers Android phone profiles, temporary profiles for automation, and an MCP mode for AI agents. The skill relies on an outside SDK and a closed-source browser kernel that is downloaded at runtime and tied to an API key.
tasks: keep several of my own accounts logged in separately
check how my site looks to a phone visitor
test my bot detection against a realistic browser
check ads or prices as seen from another country
qualityWhy: Very detailed with concrete code, options and limits, but it is mostly a product description, and its own scope and authorization rules are not enforced by the instructions themselves.
why: It is useful for testing and multi-account work on a local machine, but the browser kernel is closed-source and downloaded at runtime, and every launch needs a key and a licence token from a remote server, so it does not run offline. Its scope is limited to authorized use, and the skill itself is written as a sales pitch that treats its own product as the answer to detection.
risks: Downloads a closed-source browser kernel at runtime, and launches need a network licence token; code from a third party runs on the machine.

summary: This skill lets an agent create, edit, and deploy websites, web apps, and browser games through Higgsfield's hosted platform, using its command-line tool. It asks the person to choose between a plain website, an app that signs in with Higgsfield and generates media, or a multiplayer game, then follows a matching step-by-step workflow. The output is a React and TanStack Start app running on Cloudflare Workers with hosted databases and storage. It also covers game art and audio such as spritesheets, textures, and 3D animation.
tasks: build a landing page for my product
make a portfolio website
create a web app that generates images
deploy my site live
make a 2D arcade game with multiplayer rooms
qualityWhy: The files give concrete steps, rules, examples, and deploy gates an agent can follow, though several scripts are cut off and the workflow is long and tightly tied to one platform.
needs: Meshy API key for 3D game assets
why: Sites are deployed to Higgsfield's cloud on Cloudflare Workers, D1, R2 and KV, which are hosted services rather than the node's local files and SQLite element, so this is a cloud-hosting skill and is skipped. It also depends on an outside account and credits for every generation step.
risks: Installs the Higgsfield CLI by downloading a shell script from the internet and piping it straight into sh without review.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to run the Vercel command-line tool with an access token instead of an interactive login. It covers finding the token and team scope, linking a project, deploying previews or production builds, managing environment variables and domains, and reading build logs. It is written for developers who host their web projects on Vercel.

add an environment variable to a vercel project
link a local repo to an existing vercel project
check the build logs of a failed deployment
add a custom domain to a vercel project

why: Vercel is a cloud hosting and deployment platform, so this skill serves cloud hosting rather than a local-first node, and the rules place it at value none and use skip. The skill also reads .env files to locate tokens, which is a secrets-handling risk.
risks: Reads .env files and greps for any vercel-named variable to find an access token, which exposes secrets to the agent's context.

summary: The skill makes an agent act as a red-team security auditor for Firestore and Cloud Storage security rules. It walks through a checklist covering update bypasses, trust in user-supplied fields, type checks, size limits, and ownership checks, then returns a scored JSON report. It is aimed at developers and reviewers who want their Firebase rules checked for holes.

review storage rules for missing size limits
check create versus update rule inconsistencies
score my rules against a security checklist
qualityWhy: The skill gives a concrete six-item checklist, a 1-5 severity scale, a bootstrap-admin exception, and a required JSON output format, though it has no worked examples.
needs: Firebase project with Firestore or Cloud Storage rules files
why: Auditing rules is useful when building apps, but the skill is built around Firebase, a cloud backend, and this node's own data lives in its SQLite element, so Firestore rules rarely apply here. It would be installed only for a project that actually uses Firebase.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to wire Google's Gemini models into mobile and web apps through the Firebase AI Logic client SDKs, so the app calls the model directly without a custom backend. It covers provisioning the service with the Firebase CLI, initializing the SDK on Android, iOS, Web or Flutter, and features such as chat, streaming, multimodal input, structured JSON output, text-to-speech and image generation. It also explains App Check protection and switching model names through Remote Config. The audience is app developers who want generative AI features in a Firebase-hosted product.
tasks: add a Gemini chatbot to my Android or iOS app
generate speech audio from text in a web app
protect Gemini API calls with App Check
switch the AI model without redeploying the app
provision Firebase AI Logic for an existing Firebase project
qualityWhy: The platform reference files give concrete setup and code steps, but SKILL.md has empty sections such as Text-Only Generation and Search Grounding and relies on links for much of its detail.
needs: Blaze pay-as-you-go billing plan for image generation and Agent Platform
why: Firebase is a cloud backend, and this skill routes every Gemini call through Firebase cloud services and a Firebase project instead of local files, so it does not fit a local-first node. The skill also needs a paid Blaze plan for some features and sends user prompts and media to Google's cloud.

summary: This skill guides an agent to write ad copy and build ad creative for paid platforms such as Google, Meta, LinkedIn, TikTok and X. It works from grounded inputs like winning ads, customer reviews and comments, and checks headlines and copy against each platform's character limits. It also covers static ad layouts, short-form and faceless video workflows, and a creative strategy loop that iterates on performance data. It is aimed at marketers and product teams who make and test ads.
tasks: write Google RSA headlines and descriptions for a new campaign
generate a batch of static Meta ad concepts from customer reviews
plan a monthly creative roadmap and retro from ad performance
make a 15-second faceless explainer video ad

qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete platform limits, templates, checklists and output formats, but a promotional block for a third-party product and many links to an external repo make parts of it read as an advertisement.
needs: image generation service key (for example Nano Banana Pro, Flux or Ideogram)
video generation service key (for example Veo, Kling or Runway)
voice service key (for example ElevenLabs or OpenAI TTS)
ad platform accounts and API access (Google Ads, Meta, LinkedIn, TikTok) for pulling performance data
why: It directly serves making ad and social content for a product, and its file-based output stays on the node. Image, video and voice generation depend on paid outside services the person chooses, and performance pulls need ad-platform credentials. The skill also promotes a third-party marketing agent that would take ad account access, so the person should decide that for themselves.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up and managing Google Cloud Firestore databases, choosing between Standard and Enterprise editions, and writing data models, queries, and indexes. It also covers SDK integration for Web, Python, iOS, Android and Flutter, and points to a separate skill for security rules. It is aimed at developers who build apps on Firebase.
tasks: create a Firestore database for a web app
define a data model and indexes for queries
write Firestore queries with the Web SDK
integrate Firestore into an Android or iOS app
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear, ordered steps for edition detection, provisioning and reference selection, and the per-platform guides are listed, though I only saw the main file.
why: Firestore is a cloud database, and the node is local-first with its own SQLite element as the only door to data, so this skill would push the person's data into a cloud service they do not control. The skill also runs npx firebase-tools@latest, which pulls a package at run time, though that is ordinary CLI use and not a stated risk.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to run and troubleshoot the Wrangler command-line tool in projects that already have a Cloudflare Wrangler configuration file. It covers local development, preview environments, deployments, secrets, bindings and rollbacks, and it sends new projects to the separate cf CLI instead. The guidance is written for developers who host and run their code on Cloudflare's network.
tasks: deploy a Worker to Cloudflare
set a secret on a deployed Worker
create a preview environment for a pull request
add a binding and regenerate types
roll back a bad deployment
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with clear decision tables, validation steps and documentation links, though they depend heavily on external pages the agent must fetch.
why: Wrangler deploys and runs code on Cloudflare's cloud hosting, which the node's local-first design rules out, so it is not useful for building or running a product here. I did not read the skill's feedback reference file, so that part is unchecked.

summary: This skill guides an agent through designing and building an MCP server, which is a small program that exposes an external API or service to LLM clients as tools. It covers planning tool coverage and naming, choosing TypeScript or Python SDKs, writing input and output schemas, testing with the MCP Inspector, and writing read-only evaluation questions with a Python harness. It is aimed at developers who want agents to reach a third-party service.
tasks: build an MCP server for a REST API
let an agent call a third-party service through tools
test an MCP server with the MCP Inspector
write evaluation questions to check an MCP server
qualityWhy: The guide gives concrete phases, schema and annotation rules, build and test commands, and a complete evaluation workflow, though much of the SDK detail is fetched from external URLs at run time.

why: It is stack-free guidance for writing integration servers, so an agent on a node can follow it directly, but it is not central to building sites, content or the node's own data flow. Its TypeScript path uses the MCP SDK rather than the node's stack, and it fetches SDK docs live from GitHub and modelcontextprotocol.io. The optional npx codemod and inspector commands are official maintainer tools run only when requested.

summary: The skill gives an agent a long, opinionated guide to writing modern Swift, covering value-type modeling, Swift 6 concurrency and data-race safety, protocols and generics, API design, performance, ARC, Swift Testing, macros and logging. It is aimed at developers building native Apple-platform apps and libraries, not at web or Fractera node stacks. It is a single SKILL.md with no scripts or other files.

migrate a Swift project to Swift 6 language mode
fix a retain cycle or slow Swift performance
write Swift Testing tests for a Swift module
qualityWhy: It is concrete and detailed, with clear rules, examples and decision tables, though it is long and its Swift 6.4 items are unreleased.
why: Swift and Apple-platform native development is outside what a Fractera node is for (web, Next.js apps, sites, content), so the skill is not useful on a node. The skill is also a general language guide without any node-specific stack, so it would not fit the node even if it were usable.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up Google's Firebase Crashlytics in Android or iOS apps, including provisioning a Firebase project and app. It also covers adding custom keys, logs, user identifiers and non-fatal error reports, and points to per-platform reference files. It is aimed at mobile app developers who want to see why their apps crash. Crash data is collected by the SDK and read back through the Firebase CLI's MCP server.
tasks: set up crash reporting in an Android app
add crash reporting to an iOS app
report non-fatal exceptions from mobile code
add custom logs and keys to crash reports
read crash data through the Firebase CLI
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is a short overview that mostly points to platform reference files, so it is useful but thin on steps within the file itself.

why: Crashlytics is a Google cloud service for native Android and iOS apps, which is outside the Next.js web stack and local-first data that a node is for, and its crash data is sent to Google's servers. Use would also require a Firebase project and Google account.

summary: The skill tells an agent how to add Swift Package Manager dependencies, such as the Firebase iOS SDK or Alamofire, to an existing Xcode project without hand-editing the project file. It runs a bundled Swift command-line tool that writes the package reference, links the chosen product modules to the app target, and optionally adds a GoogleService-Info.plist. It is aimed at native iOS developers working on macOS.

install Alamofire in an Xcode project
link Swift packages to an app target
add GoogleService-Info.plist to an Xcode project

summary: This skill guides an agent writing, reviewing or configuring Cloudflare Workers code. It covers compatibility dates, Workers Logs and Traces, placing compute near regional databases, streaming bodies, promise lifetimes, secrets, and a table of common anti-patterns with their fixes. It is aimed at developers shipping production applications on Cloudflare's edge runtime.
tasks: review a Cloudflare Worker for production readiness
configure wrangler.toml bindings and compatibility date
fix async and streaming bugs in a Worker
enable logs and traces for a Worker
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with a clear reference index, an anti-pattern table with fixes and validation steps, but many details are delegated to external docs and reference files.
why: Cloudflare Workers is a cloud compute platform, which conflicts with the node's local-first design, so it is not useful for building on a node. The guidance is well written but would only help with a cloud-hosted Worker.

summary: This skill guides an agent through creating a minimal Next.js web app backed by Convex, a hosted reactive database and backend, and starting it on a local dev server with an anonymous dev deployment. It runs a remote scaffolding recipe, then asks the person to confirm before adding features. It also sets out coding rules for Convex functions, schema, imports, HTTP routes and verification, aimed at developers building a small backend.
tasks: start a new Next.js and Convex app from an idea
scaffold a minimal backend with Convex functions
check that Convex backend code compiles and deploys

network access to fetch the quickstart-recipe
why: Convex is a cloud backend, and the node's data must stay in its own local SQLite element, so this skill is outside what nodes are for. It also relies on a remotely fetched recipe and can rebind a signed-in user's cloud deployment configuration.

Can rebind the project's .env.local to an anonymous deployment, which may break a signed-in user's cloud deployment settings.

summary: This skill guides an agent through adding, finding, fixing and styling shadcn/ui components in a project, using the project's own config to pick the right imports and primitives. It also covers forms, chat interfaces, icons, and building a themed design system from a DESIGN.md brand spec. It is written for developers and designers building web apps and sites.

build a chat interface with streaming replies

Its load-time command runs the latest shadcn package from npm, and community registries it mentions would pull third-party code, so the agent should keep to the registries the person names.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building a reusable Convex component: a folder with its own tables, backend functions and config, wired into the app and called through a small app-side wrapper. It covers choosing between local, packaged and hybrid shapes, the boundary rules for auth, environment variables and IDs, and how to validate with Convex codegen. It is written for developers who build backend features on Convex.

extract backend logic into its own component

package Convex functionality for other apps
