why: Convex is a cloud backend and database, which the node's local-first design excludes, so the skill is not useful for building on a node and should be skipped. Its guidance is otherwise well written, but it depends on a hosted Convex deployment.

summary: This is a compatibility redirect for an older video explainer skill. It tells an agent to hand the request to a newer Higgsfield skill, higgsfield-faceless-video, and to keep the user's topic, duration, language and aspect ratio. It does no work itself, so an agent needs the newer skill installed before it can produce anything. It is meant for people who already use the older workflow.
tasks: make an illustrated explainer video from a topic
continue an existing explainer video workflow
turn source files into a narrated explainer clip
qualityWhy: The file is only a pointer to another skill with no steps, examples or checks of its own.
needs: higgsfield-faceless-video skill from the Higgsfield skills package
why: It is a video-making redirect, which can help a node's content work, but it is a wrapper and the real workflow lives in a different skill that must also be installed. Generation uses the Higgsfield cloud service, which the person would choose and pay for; the result comes back to local files.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing B2B cold outreach emails that read like a thoughtful colleague wrote them, with short copy, one low-friction ask, and follow-ups that each add something new. It also covers the setup that keeps those emails out of spam folders, such as secondary sending domains, list verification, and tracking choices. Further guidance covers LinkedIn steps, multichannel cadences, outbound plays, and how to classify and answer replies. It is aimed at founders, sales reps, and marketers who run outbound sales.
tasks: write a cold email to a prospect
build a three-to-five step follow-up sequence
set up sending domains and deliverability
write a LinkedIn connection request message
triage and answer replies to outbound emails
qualityWhy: The skill is detailed and structured, with frameworks, checklists, a quality check, and linked reference files, though several key details live in external links and some references are summarized only briefly in SKILL.md.
needs: optional outbound sending platform such as Instantly or lemlist
optional lead verification service such as Truelist or Hunter
optional CRM and booking tools such as HubSpot, Attio, Close, Calendly or SavvyCal
why: It is useful for sales and marketing outreach on a product, but it is not about building or running the node itself, so its value is occasional. Its core writing advice needs no outside service, but its sending, verification and reply-logging steps depend on third-party tools the person would choose and pay for.

summary: This skill guides an agent to visit a public website with a headless browser and pull out its visual building blocks, such as colours, fonts, spacing, radius and shadow scales. It then turns those findings into starter token files (JSON and CSS variables) inside the user's project. The skill is aimed at developers who want a quick starting point for a new project's styling, not a finished design system. It also tells the agent to ask before touching existing app code or styles and to treat the output as something to review.
tasks: extract the colours and fonts from a reference website
generate starter design token files for a new project
turn a public site's spacing and radius scales into CSS variables
qualityWhy: The steps and safety boundaries are clear, but the skill is short, gives no detail on how the token files are structured, and the referenced output and workflow files were not included for review.
why: It runs locally and writes token files into the project, so it helps when starting a site or app, but it only covers the initial styling step and is situational. The npx command runs an unpinned third-party npm package, so the person should check that package before relying on it, and extracted results need review before use.

summary: This guide walks an agent through setting up the Better Auth library in a TypeScript project, covering the server config, client, database adapters, environment variables and migrations. It also explains how sessions are stored, how cookie caching works, and which plugins add features like two-factor login or passkeys. It is aimed at developers who need to add sign-in and account handling to an app.
tasks: add email and password sign-in to a web app
set up Google or GitHub login
configure session expiry and cookie caching
add two-factor login with a plugin
qualityWhy: It gives concrete setup steps, config tables, CLI commands and a list of gotchas, though much of the detail is pointed at external docs.
why: Better Auth is a local library, so it is not a cloud service, but a node already ships its own sign-in element built on next-auth 5, so this skill should be read for ideas and built the node's way. Its Drizzle and Prisma instructions do not match the node's SQLite element, and the docs lookup relies on an optional MCP.

summary: This skill guides an agent through planning a website's page hierarchy, navigation menus, URL patterns, and internal linking. It covers site-type templates, a three-click depth rule, header and footer rules, breadcrumb alignment, and Mermaid or ASCII sitemap outputs. It is aimed at people planning a new site or restructuring an existing one, including marketers and founders who need to decide what pages to build.
tasks: plan the page structure for a new website
restructure navigation and URL patterns on an existing site
draw a visual sitemap with Mermaid
design an internal linking plan for a blog or docs section
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with rules, tables, URL patterns, output formats and a checklist, though some reference files were not reviewed.
why: It is a stack-free planning skill that helps design the structure of sites built on a node, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. It mentions platform choice and migration, but that is advice only and does not force any cloud service.

summary: This skill tells an agent to design a static poster or artwork as a PNG or PDF. It starts by writing a short visual design philosophy as a Markdown file, then turns that philosophy into a single-page composition. The agent picks typefaces from a bundled font folder and checks margins and spacing so nothing overlaps or runs off the page. It suits people who need striking static graphics for posters, social images or landing-page visuals.
tasks: make a poster for an event
design a social media image
create a one-page visual art piece as PNG or PDF
make a minimalist cover or banner design
qualityWhy: The instructions give a clear two-step process and useful checks for spacing and overlap, but they stay heavy on aesthetic language and give no concrete rendering steps or tool commands.
why: It directly serves making visual content such as posters and social images, and it is stack-free with bundled fonts and no outside service. The skill does not name a rendering tool, so the agent will need to choose one for producing PNG and PDF output.

summary: The skill guides an agent through Firebase Remote Config: downloading, editing and deploying the config template JSON, checking version history, and setting up the SDK on Android or iOS. It explains fetch-and-activate loading patterns, in-app defaults and real-time listeners for apps that change behaviour without a store release. It is written for developers who run their app on Google's cloud configuration service.
tasks: deploy a Remote Config template change
set up Remote Config in an Android app
add feature flags with fetchAndActivate
roll out a value to a user segment
qualityWhy: Concrete commands, a mandatory review step and error handling are present, but the platform references were not checked in full and the editing guidance is brief.
why: Remote Config is a cloud configuration service, which the node's local-first rule classes as none, and the skill's whole workflow depends on deploying to Firebase's cloud. It is built for the Firebase stack, not for the node's own SQLite element and settings.

summary: This skill guides an agent through reducing customer churn in a subscription business: designing cancel flows with an exit survey and matched save offers, spotting at-risk users with health scores and usage signals, and recovering failed payments through smart retries and dunning emails. It is aimed at founders, growth and retention teams running paid software or subscription products. The files are documentation and playbooks, with no executable scripts in the listed files.
tasks: design a cancel flow with a save offer
recover failed subscription payments
build a customer health score
set up dunning email sequences
analyze why customers are cancelling
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is concrete, with flow structures, offer-to-reason tables, retry timings, metrics and cautions, and it points to reference playbooks, though it leans on generic benchmarks and its examples are not tied to any stack.
needs: Stripe or another billing provider account
Optional retention tools such as Churnkey or ProsperStack
why: A subscription product built on a Fractera node needs exactly this kind of cancel flow and dunning logic, so it serves the node's purpose. It is marked install-with-service because the practical setup relies on a billing provider and optional retention platforms the person chooses, and its tool guidance names several external services. Its benchmarks and health-score weights are illustrative and must be checked against the person's own data before use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building sales collateral for B2B teams: slide decks, one-pagers, objection-handling docs, demo scripts, battle cards, win-loss reviews, ROI calculators, proposals and playbooks. It asks for product context and sales motion first, then produces each asset in a set format with scannable structure. The audience is sales reps, AEs, SDRs and the marketers who support them.
tasks: write a pitch deck outline for a CTO buyer
draft a one-pager for post-meeting follow-up
answer a price objection from a live deal
build a battle card for a named competitor
analyse why we lose deals to a competitor
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed and actionable, with frameworks, checklists, output formats and clear rules on evidence, though the reference files were not included in the review so their depth is unverified.
why: Sales collateral is directly useful to a node that sells products and content, and the skill is stack-free writing and planning guidance. It depends on the reference files and on the node's product-marketing context file for best results; the skill's claims-discipline rules are a good fit for a node's own sales material.

summary: The skill guides an agent through customer research in three modes: analysing existing transcripts, surveys, tickets and reviews; mining public communities and review sites for unprompted customer language; and running interviews and surveys directly. It produces themes with confidence levels, verbatim quote banks, personas built only from enough evidence, and jobs-to-be-done maps. It is aimed at marketers and founders who want messaging and product choices grounded in what customers actually say.
tasks: analyze customer interview transcripts for pains and language
mine G2 and Reddit reviews for competitor weaknesses
build customer personas from research data
write a PMF survey and interview outreach
create a VOC quote bank for landing page copy
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear structure, extraction framework, confidence rules and templates, though its reference files were not shown to me and some steps are generic.
why: It is useful for building and marketing a product, but it is a marketing-methodology skill written for a marketing toolkit that uses other skills (copywriting, cro, marketing-plan) rather than node elements, so an agent would need to adapt the handoffs to the node's own skill set; there is no code, so it is not a stack conflict. Only SKILL.md was provided; the three reference files were listed but not included, so I could not check them.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a Vercel cost and performance audit of a deployed project, starting from production metrics and usage data and only then reading source files tied to flagged routes. It produces ranked, cited recommendations for Next.js, SvelteKit, Nuxt and limited Astro apps. It is aimed at developers and teams who want to cut a Vercel bill or speed up slow routes.
tasks: audit Vercel bill and find cost reductions
find slow or expensive routes on a deployed app
suggest caching improvements for route responses
review Vercel function invocations and build minutes usage
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a concrete, staged pipeline with commands, blockers and output rules, though many referenced scripts and files are not shown in full, so some steps cannot be checked from the files alone.
needs: Vercel CLI login and linked project
why: It is built around Vercel's cloud hosting and metrics, which the node is not meant to depend on, so the cloud-administration rule makes it value none and skip. Its advice would also target Vercel-hosted deployments rather than a local-first node.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to run web searches and pull page text through the inference.sh belt command-line tool, using the Tavily and Exa search apps. It covers quick search, direct factual answers, extracting content from given URLs, and chaining a search result into an LLM step for summaries or research. It is aimed at people building research features, fact-checking flows, or RAG pipelines on top of live web data.
tasks: search the web for recent news on a topic
extract the text of a list of article URLs
get a direct factual answer with sources
gather sources for a research summary
feed search results into a RAG pipeline
qualityWhy: It gives working command examples for each app, but it has no output format details, no error handling, and its research workflow passes a placeholder instead of the saved search results.
needs: Tavily and Exa apps on inference.sh
why: Live web search and extraction is useful for research, content and RAG work, but it only works through an outside service and needs an inference.sh login, so the person must choose to use it. The quick start points to a remote install guide that I could not check from these files, so the install step should be read before running it.

summary: This skill lets an agent turn React/Remotion TSX component code into an MP4 video by sending the code to the inference.sh cloud service through the belt CLI or its Python SDK. It covers the Remotion APIs (frames, springs, interpolation, sequences), configurable size, frame rate, duration and codec, and includes runnable examples for titles, counters, spring motion and props. It is aimed at people making programmatic motion graphics and data-driven videos for social posts, landing pages or product content.
tasks: make a 15-second animated title video from React code
render a data-driven motion graphic as MP4
create a square spring-animated promo clip for social media
turn a TSX component into a video with props
qualityWhy: It gives a clear input schema and several working examples, but it has no error handling, no output checks, and leaves parameters such as composition_id and codec undocumented.
why: Rendering React-based videos for social posts, landing pages and product content directly serves what a node is for, but the render itself runs on the inference.sh cloud, so the TSX code and output pass through that outside service and need the person's account. The skill also suggests installing several other skills, which the person should review first.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive the inference.sh command-line tool, which runs hosted AI models for images, video, language models, web search, 3D generation and X/Twitter actions. It gives example commands for running an app with JSON input, uploading local files automatically, checking task status, and browsing the app store. It is aimed at developers and creators who want generated media or AI calls without running their own GPU.
tasks: generate an image with FLUX
create a short video from a text prompt
call Claude or another LLM through OpenRouter
run a web search with Tavily or Exa
post a tweet with local media
qualityWhy: The commands and examples are clear and usable, but the skill is mostly a catalogue of apps with little error handling, verification or step-by-step workflow.
why: The skill offers useful hosted generation, so value is high, but its install step pipes a remote script into sh, which is a risk, so it is skipped. Local files are uploaded to the inference.sh cloud, which the skill states openly; provider and account keys sit with that service.
risks: Install step runs `curl -fsSL https://cli.inference.sh | sh`, downloading and executing a remote script and binary.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive the inference.sh belt command-line tool, which runs hosted AI apps for image generation, video creation, LLM calls, web search, 3D models and Twitter/X actions. It gives install steps, sample commands for each category, how to pass local files that the CLI uploads automatically, and commands for listing, searching and checking task status. It is aimed at people who want generative AI output without their own GPU.
tasks: generate an image with FLUX from a text prompt
make a short video from a prompt or a local image
call Claude or another LLM from a script
search the web with Tavily or Exa
post a tweet with local media
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete commands, example inputs, a command table and an explained installer, though error handling and output formats are thin and the reference files were not provided.
needs: inference.sh credits for the hosted models it calls
X/Twitter account authorised through inference.sh for the posting commands
why: It directly serves making images, video, voice-free media and social posts, and all output returns to local files, but every run executes on inference.sh's cloud, so it is a service the person must choose. It is skipped because the recommended install pipes a remote script into sh, which is a risk.
risks: The recommended installer runs `curl -fsSL https://cli.inference.sh | sh`, downloading and executing remote code without review; a manual path is offered but still depends on remote binaries.

summary: This skill lets an agent send Python code to a remote sandbox run by inference.sh, using the belt command-line tool, and collect any files the script writes back. The agent can then run data analysis, scraping, image or video edits, 3D file conversion, PDF generation, or API calls without installing those libraries locally. It is aimed at people who want quick throwaway scripts rather than a local development setup.
tasks: scrape a web page and extract its data
make a chart from a dataset
resize or composite images
generate a short text-overlay video
convert or export a 3D model file
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete run commands, a library list and examples, but it is mostly a thin wrapper around an external CLI with no error handling or verification steps.

why: The code runs on inference.sh's cloud servers, and the outputs are returned from there, so it is a cloud place to run things, which the node's local-first rule excludes. The node could run the same libraries locally, so this skill adds an external dependency without serving the node's needs.

summary: This skill guides an agent through designing the processes that link marketing to sales: lifecycle stages, MQL and SQL definitions, lead scoring, routing rules, pipeline stages and handoff SLAs. It is aimed at founders and revenue teams who want their leads to reach sales faster and convert better. The agent can produce standalone specs for each part, and it asks about the business first (GTM motion, ACV, sales cycle, current stack).
tasks: set up lead scoring for a sales team
decide when marketing should hand leads to sales
design pipeline stages and required fields
route inbound leads to the right rep
audit CRM data hygiene each quarter
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with tables, numeric thresholds, decision steps and checklists, but they have no scripts or worked examples inside SKILL.md and lean on linked reference files.
why: It is a stack-free process methodology that helps a product's sales pipeline, but it is not about building or running a site or app, so its value is occasional. CRM and scheduling tools are only optional links, so no account or key is required.

summary: The skill guides an agent through planning lead magnets, the free downloadable or gated offers that capture emails and generate leads. It covers choosing a format by buyer stage, gating and form design, landing page structure, delivery methods, distribution, and success metrics. It also points to references for format creation, benchmarks, and packaging owned course or content material as an installable agent skill. It is aimed at marketers and founders planning email capture.
tasks: plan a lead magnet for email capture
choose a gating strategy for a free guide
outline a checklist or cheat sheet offer
structure a lead magnet landing page
package a course as an agent skill
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is well organised with tables, decision rules and output format, though its core content is strategic and the referenced files were not provided for review.
why: It is a planning and marketing strategy skill with no stack dependency, so it is useful for designing offers on a node, but it produces plans rather than building anything in the node's code, and its agent-skill packaging section is only a pointer to other files. Its install is stack-free but its value for building product code is limited, so it is marked as ideas.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building, debugging and reviewing Cloudflare Durable Objects, which hold per-entity state and coordinate work such as chat rooms, bookings or scheduled timeouts. It covers wrangler configuration and migrations, SQLite storage, RPC methods, alarms, WebSocket handlers and sharding, and points to Cloudflare docs and a Vitest testing reference. It is written for developers who run their backend on Cloudflare Workers.
tasks: build a chat room with Durable Objects
configure wrangler bindings and SQLite migrations
add alarms for scheduled work per entity
review existing Durable Object code
write Vitest tests for a Durable Object
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with code patterns, critical rules, anti-patterns and checks, though much detail is delegated to external reference pages.
why: Durable Objects are a cloud coordination and storage service that runs on Cloudflare's edge, not on the person's computer, so it falls under the cloud backend exclusion for a local-first node. The skill also assumes the Workers stack rather than the node's Next.js and SQLite elements.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a web performance audit: recording a cold-load trace in Chrome, reading Core Web Vitals such as LCP, CLS and INP, and checking network requests and an accessibility snapshot. When the agent has access to the code, it also inspects the bundler, tree-shaking, polyfills and compression. The skill is aimed at developers and site owners who want to find and fix slow pages.
tasks: audit my site's loading speed
find out why the LCP is slow
reduce layout shift on the landing page
check page performance before launch
qualityWhy: The steps, tool calls, metric thresholds and output format are concrete and checkable, but it depends on MCP tools that may be missing and leaves insight-name variations to the agent to work out.
needs: Chrome DevTools MCP (installed locally through npx)
why: It directly serves building and running sites and is stack-free, since the codebase phase covers general bundlers and frameworks rather than one stack. It needs the local Chrome DevTools MCP, which the skill says to install only within the user's authorized scope; the npx entry it suggests uses @latest and is unpinned, so the person should confirm it before use.

summary: Turns the agent into a 'lazy senior developer' that aims for the smallest change fully solving a coding task, reusing existing helpers, platform features and installed dependencies before writing new code. It also asks for a short closing note naming what was skipped or unchecked and any risk. It is aimed at developers who want terse, minimal-diff coding work.
tasks: make the smallest change that fixes a bug
implement a feature without adding dependencies
review a diff for unnecessary code
reply with a short summary of skipped checks and risks
qualityWhy: The rules are clear and actionable, but the file is a behavioural style guide with no concrete examples, checks or commands, so it is useful yet somewhat generic.
why: It is a stack-free working-style instruction that can help any coding task in a node, but it adds no node-specific knowledge and its usefulness depends on the agent's judgement. It does not conflict with the node's stack, so it can be installed as written.

summary: The skill gives an agent a checklist for confirming that several browser profiles on one machine are truly separate: timezone matching the exit IP, WebRTC leaking only the proxy, stable canvas and WebGL hashes, and no shared persona, address or cookie jar. It is written for people running multiple accounts or test identities through the antibrow anti-detect browser. Its main use is checking and assembling setups that avoid linking accounts across sites.
tasks: check that browser profiles are isolated from each other
verify timezone and WebRTC match the proxy exit IP
audit a fleet of profiles for shared fingerprints or addresses
wire isolation checks into CI
qualityWhy: The steps, check table, failure-triage order and configuration examples are concrete and followable, though the skill is broad and some points rely on an external closed-source kernel.
why: The skill serves evading account association across sites, not building, running, selling or making content for a product, and it relies on a cloud license service and optional cloud profile sync, which the node's local-first design excludes. The stated legitimate uses are narrow and the skill itself mainly serves identity masking.

summary: This skill lets an AI agent run a fingerprinted browser through MCP tool calls, so it can open pages, click, fill forms, read text and take screenshots without the person writing Playwright code. Logins are kept in named profiles, so later runs stay signed in. It is aimed at developers and operators who want an agent to work on a site they own or are allowed to use. The browser kernel it relies on is a closed-source binary from a vendor.
tasks: let an AI agent log into my dashboard and report figures
have an agent click through a site flow and extract results
take screenshots of a web page for an agent to review
keep an agent's browser session signed in between runs
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete setup steps, a tool list, supply-chain notes and clear safety rules, though parts read like marketing and some claims cannot be checked from the file.
needs: antibrow browser kernel download from the vendor CDN
why: It is useful for agent-driven browsing, but it is not core to building or running a site on a local node, and it depends on a vendor account and a closed binary that checks licence online. Because the risk below is present, the skill should not be installed.
risks: Downloads and runs a closed-source browser binary from a vendor CDN on first launch, with licence checks that phone home and no offline mode.

summary: This skill turns the agent into a read-only explorer subagent that finds where relevant code lives in a repository. It fans out several Glob, Grep and Read calls at once, then returns only a short list of file paths with line ranges for a solver agent to use. It suits a developer or coding agent who is new to a codebase or whose direct search has failed.
tasks: find where the login logic lives in this repo
locate the function that handles checkout
orient in an unfamiliar codebase before making changes
list the files that cover a feature across the project
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with a parallel-search procedure, a strict citation output format, an example and an honest empty-result fallback, plus a test file that checks them, though it says little about large or monorepo edge cases.
why: It is generic developer tooling rather than something that builds, runs or sells a site, app or content, but a coding agent on a node may use it now and then while working in a project's code. It is stack-free and read-only, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill reviews documentation or prose files against a remote Writing Guidelines handbook. Before each review it fetches the latest rules from a GitHub URL, reads the files the person names, and reports violations in a terse file:line format. It is aimed at people who write docs, pages or copy and want a style check.
tasks: review my docs for writing style
audit this page against the writing handbook
check the voice and tone of my prose
list style violations with file and line
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is short and mostly points to a remote file for all the actual rules and output format, so the skill itself gives an agent little concrete guidance.
why: Prose review is useful now and then for docs and copy on a node, and the skill needs no key or stack, but its rules live entirely in an external file that can change at any time and was not reviewed here. Each review depends on fetching that remote content.

summary: This skill guides an agent through scaffolding a small React and TypeScript project with Tailwind and shadcn/ui components, then bundling it into one self-contained HTML file. It is meant for interactive tools, dashboards and multi-part mini-apps that need state or routing and would be too complex for a single-file artifact. The intended audience is someone who wants a shareable interactive page rather than a full production site. The skill's own design advice steers away from generic AI-looking layouts.
tasks: build an interactive dashboard as a single shareable HTML file
make a multi-component React mini-app with shadcn/ui
bundle a React project into one self-contained HTML page
prototype an interactive tool with state and routing
qualityWhy: The steps and scripts are concrete, but the referenced 'Common Development Tasks' section is missing, the testing guidance is thin, and one error message in the init script names the wrong file.
why: It targets claude.ai artifacts and a React 18, Vite, Parcel and Tailwind 3 stack, while a node uses Next.js 16, React 19 and Tailwind 4, so it must be rebuilt on the node's stack and not installed as written. Its scripts install global pnpm and project packages, which is normal for this kind of setup. The bundled shadcn tarball is binary and was not inspected, which is an unknown worth checking before anyone relies on it.

summary: The skill tells an agent to apply Anthropic's official brand palette and typography to documents and presentations: dark and light neutrals, orange, blue and green accents, Poppins for headings and Lora for body text, with Arial and Georgia as fallbacks. It is aimed at people who want their artifacts to match Anthropic's look. The instructions are short and mostly descriptive, with a python-pptx mention but no step-by-step workflow. The licence text is in a separate LICENSE.txt that was not reviewed here.
tasks: make a slide deck in Anthropic's brand style
apply brand colors and fonts to a document
style a PowerPoint presentation with brand typography
qualityWhy: It lists colors and fonts clearly but gives no concrete steps, examples or checks for applying them, and the description is generic.
why: Brand styling helps only for artifacts that should look like Anthropic, which is a narrow need for a product node. The skill targets python-pptx and PowerPoint, not the node's Next.js and Tailwind stack, so its values would have to be rebuilt as Tailwind tokens and CSS rather than installed as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through the output of a caveman learn report, which measures where Claude Code token spend goes. The agent shows the ranked cost sinks and then proposes one edit at a time, such as trimming an oversized CLAUDE.md, removing duplicated rules, or moving repeated context into cavemem. Each edit is applied only after the person says yes, re-measured, and reverted if tokens per turn do not drop. It is aimed at people running Claude Code agents on their own machine who want cheaper sessions.
tasks: lower an agent's token cost
trim a heavy CLAUDE.md
show what caveman has saved
move re-pasted context into cavemem
remove duplicate rules from memory files
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and gated, with explicit commands, verification steps, revert rules and reporting limits, though the caveman CLI and cavemem behaviour are not documented in the files.
why: It helps when building and running Claude Code agents on a node, but it does not serve product content or the site stack directly. It is stack-free and needs only the local caveman CLI; the files do not show what cavemem stores or where, so that remains unverified.

summary: This skill guides an agent through restructuring code without changing what it does, such as extracting functions, merging duplicates, or moving code to a different owner. It asks the agent to set up a way to verify behavior before touching the structure and to keep feature work out of the same change. It also asks the agent to keep public interfaces, error handling, and ordering stable, and to keep each intermediate step buildable. It is written for developers who want cleanup that cannot quietly break the product.
tasks: refactor a module without changing behavior
extract shared logic into a helper
move code to a new owner one step at a time
clean up duplicated code safely
qualityWhy: The rules are sensible and specific to refactoring, but the file gives no steps, checklist, or example of how to set up the verification it requires.
why: It is a stack-free engineering discipline that applies to any code a node builds, so it directly supports building and maintaining a product. Because it is short, an agent will need to work out the verification steps itself.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing a landing page, sales page, opt-in page or checkout flow for conversion leaks. It checks ad-to-page message match, mobile above-the-fold clarity, offer clarity, form friction, trust near the payment button, the post-purchase path and conversion tracking. The output is a short ranked fix list, a set of A/B test ideas, and a note on what could not be verified. It is aimed at marketers and founders whose paid traffic is not converting.
tasks: review my landing page for conversion problems
find out why my checkout is losing buyers
rank fixes for a low-converting sales page
audit paid-traffic landing page message match
qualityWhy: The audit procedure is concrete, with ordered checks, input requirements, a fixed report format and sensible caps on claims, but the closing section is a promotional pitch for one product and some referenced skills are not described.
why: The audit method serves anyone building or selling through a page, and it is stack-free, so it would normally be installed as written. It is skipped because the closing section tells the agent to clone a third-party repository and run its containers with docker compose up on the person's machine, based on promotional text rather than the person's request.
risks: Tells the agent to fetch a third-party repository and run docker compose up on the person's computer to install a funnel builder, promoted inside the skill, without asking the person first.

summary: This skill guides an agent through evaluating a Caveman CLI optimization observation for a repository. The agent reads only the supported report-only observations, asks the operator to choose one, proposes a minimal code candidate with a paired baseline/candidate eval, and reports results without claiming savings. It is aimed at developers optimizing token or byte cost in their own code-driven AI workflows.
tasks: evaluate a caveman optimization observation
design a paired baseline and candidate eval
apply an approved minimal code change and measure it
report an optimization result without claiming savings
qualityWhy: The steps, forbidden ids, approval gates and a report template are concrete and followable, though it depends on a CLI and output format it does not show.
needs: Caveman CLI with a logged-in session
why: It is useful only for teams measuring LLM token cost in code, not for building or running a Fractera site or content, so value is some. It needs a Caveman account and CLI login, a paid or external service the person chooses, so use is install-with-service rather than install.

summary: This skill tells an agent to investigate a failure or odd behaviour before touching any code. The agent separates what was observed from what it guesses is the cause, traces inputs, state changes and ownership boundaries, and ranks candidate explanations by evidence. It edits nothing until one mechanism clearly explains the evidence, and then reports the cause with proof. It suits developers facing unknown bugs, intermittent failures or performance drops.
tasks: find the cause of an intermittent bug
diagnose a performance regression before fixing it
explain why a page or API fails without changing code
rank possible causes of a failure by evidence
qualityWhy: The method is clear and actionable, but it is short and generic, with no concrete steps, commands or checks for tracing a particular stack.
why: It is a stack-free debugging habit that an agent on a node can use while building or fixing a site or app, so its value is useful now and then rather than central. The files were read as text only and no scripts were included, so nothing was executed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building, debugging, and reviewing applications with the Cloudflare Agents SDK. It covers agent classes with persistent state, callable RPC methods, scheduling, workflows, chat streaming, MCP, email, webhooks, and voice. It points the agent to Cloudflare's current docs for each topic, since the SDK changes often. The audience is developers who run agents on Cloudflare's platform.
tasks: build a chat agent on Cloudflare Workers
debug a Durable Object agent's state sync
review an agent's scheduling and retry logic
connect an MCP server to an agent
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md and its references give concrete code, wrangler config, API tables, gotchas and a verify step, though much detail is deferred to external URLs.
why: The agents run on Cloudflare's cloud runtime through Workers and Durable Objects, which is cloud hosting, not local-first work on the person's computer. Because the value is none, the skill should be skipped on a Fractera node.

summary: This skill tells an agent to confirm that existing work already meets its acceptance conditions, using the smallest set of checks that proves it. The agent reuses results that are still current, runs focused checks before broader ones, and reports pass, fail, unavailable and blocked separately. It stops once the proof is complete and does not edit product code or add extra tests unless the request asks for fixes.
tasks: check that a feature meets its acceptance criteria
run the focused tests before the release gate
confirm a last fix is verified and stop
report which checks passed, failed or were blocked
qualityWhy: The instructions are clear and short but thin: they give no concrete commands, examples or report format beyond a few bullet points.
why: It is a stack-free habit for validation-only work that a node agent can use when checking its own builds, though it offers little detail to act on. Nothing in the file asks for secrets or runs code, and the other file (agents/openai.yaml) was not included, so it was not reviewed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through fixing a bug or making a small behavior change. It asks the agent to reproduce the failure first, or collect the best available evidence if reproducing is costly, and to trace the symptom to the code that causes it. The fix should go in the narrowest layer that owns the wrong behavior, leaving unrelated code and the user's own edits alone. The agent should add only the regression check the task needs, then run that check plus the nearest related test gate before stopping.
tasks: fix a bug without changing unrelated code
add a regression test for a small fix
make a small behavior change safely
trace a failing behavior to its cause
qualityWhy: The principles are clear and actionable, but the skill is short and generic, with no worked example, concrete commands or explicit checks for each step.
why: It is a stack-free set of debugging habits that helps when building or maintaining any product on the node, so it is useful now and then rather than central. Only SKILL.md was provided in full; the agents/openai.yaml file was listed but its contents were not shown, so I could not check it.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building a feature with a narrow, complete outcome that fits the existing system. It asks the agent to derive acceptance criteria and non-goals from the request and repository, trace the entry point through the layers that own invariants, and reuse existing seams rather than patching around them. It avoids extra modes, providers, config, or polish unless acceptance needs them, and stops once acceptance passes. It is aimed at developers who want to limit overbuilding in feature work.
tasks: build a narrow feature slice end to end
add new behavior without overbuilding
integrate a feature into an existing codebase with minimal scope
define acceptance criteria and non-goals before coding
qualityWhy: The instructions are coherent and principled but abstract and terse, giving no concrete steps, examples, or checks an agent can directly follow, and they reference an undefined 'Native Core' architecture.
why: It is a stack-free engineering habit useful now and then, but its wording depends on a 'Native Core' architecture and Core safety rules that are not defined in the skill, so an agent on a Fractera node would need to adapt it to the node's own stack (Next.js, SQLite element, Blocks) before using it, which makes 'ideas' the right choice rather than 'install'.

summary: This skill makes an agent act as a read-only reviewer of Caveman Cloud evidence, examining LLM spend, cost reports, workflow and trace data, latency, errors and savings for a selected project. It works by loading the project context, pulling aggregate reports, testing a leading explanation against bounded trace cohorts, and inspecting a few representative traces by metadata only. The audience is an operator who wants to know where LLM spend goes and what the tool found, with conclusions kept separate by cost basis.
tasks: explain where our LLM spend goes this week
find which workflow is driving cost increases
review Caveman savings and daily headroom
compare a suspect trace cohort against a control window
qualityWhy: The steps, hard rules, CLI fallbacks and report template are concrete and checkable, though it depends on an external service whose data shapes are not shown.
why: It is a review tool for a third-party LLM cost service rather than something that builds or runs a Fractera node's own site, data or content, so its use on a node is occasional; it needs the Caveman Cloud account and is read-only with no payload fetching by default.

summary: This skill tells an agent to find every LLM workflow in a repository, such as a support reply handler, a nightly digest job or an eval suite, and give each one a clear slug label. Labels let the Caveman Cloud gateway split LLM spend by job instead of one bucket. It is written for developers who run LLM code and want per-workflow cost tracking. The agent proposes a labeling table first, waits for approval, then adds headers or flags and verifies that requests still succeed.
tasks: label LLM workflows for spend tracking
break down LLM costs by workflow
discover workflows in a repository
wire workflow labels into API clients
qualityWhy: The steps, slug grammar, labeling mechanisms per SDK, verification and report format are concrete and followable, with a clear propose-then-apply gate.
needs: Caveman Cloud gateway account and API key
why: It helps a team that routes LLM traffic through the Caveman gateway track spend, but it only serves a node if the node's LLM calls go through that gateway, and it is a narrow cost-analytics task. It needs a Caveman Cloud service the person chooses to use, and its labeling mechanisms target provider SDKs rather than Fractera's own stack, so it would need checking against how the node calls models.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing a multi-step online sales funnel before any building starts. It first pins down the offer, price, traffic source, audience awareness, fulfilment and existing assets, then picks a funnel shape and writes a page-by-page spec with goals, copy outlines, proof, objections, metrics, a price ladder and launch tracking requirements. It is aimed at founders and marketers selling products or services online, and at the builders who will implement the spec.

write a page-by-page spec for a landing page and checkout

decide which tracking to set up before launching a funnel

Cloudflare account (optional, only for Autonnel production hosting)
why: The planning method directly serves building and selling products on a node, but the skill tells the agent to clone a third-party repository and run `docker compose up` on the person's machine, which executes downloaded code and is an advertisement for a competing funnel builder, so it should not be installed.
risks: Instructs the agent to clone a third-party repository and run `docker compose up`, which downloads and executes remote code on the person's computer.

summary: This skill guides an agent through reviewing experiments on Caveman Cloud, a hosted service that tests LLM traffic changes against control groups. The agent reads an experiment's state, sample sizes, quality and cost guardrails, and evidence gaps, then reports one recommendation. It is built to block any start, approve, cancel or rollback action, so it only supports read-only inspection for a person who runs AI traffic experiments.
tasks: review the results of an AI traffic experiment
check whether a model change is safe to promote
list running experiments and their evidence gaps

needs: Caveman project access with server RBAC
why: It manages a hosted cloud control plane for LLM experiments, not local site, app or content work, so it does not fit a local-first node. It is also cloud-based by design, which makes it a skip under the node's rules even though it is safe and read-only in practice.

summary: This guide teaches an agent to set up server-side conversion reporting so that sales from paid ads reach Facebook, TikTok, Google and Bing even when browsers block cookies or tracking. It lays out a required build order: capture click IDs and UTMs on the first visit, store them on the server, carry them through cross-domain checkout, attach them to each order, send purchase events server-to-server, deduplicate against the browser pixel, and reconcile against the order table. It is written for marketers and store owners who run paid campaigns and see platform numbers that don't match their real orders.

fix purchases under-reported by ad platforms
pass fbclid and gclid through checkout

check click id coverage for paid orders

TikTok pixel code and access token
Google Ads conversion action and OAuth credentials
Microsoft UET tag ID and CAPI token
why: Accurate purchase reporting directly serves selling products through paid ads, and the method is stack-independent. However, the install section points to a different self-hosted platform that a Fractera node replaces, so the node should build the pipeline on its own SQLite and Stripe elements rather than deploy that product.

summary: This skill guides an agent through adding a post-checkout upsell and downsell to a store, so that buyers can add a complementary item with one tap while the base order stays intact. It explains how to pick the offer, write the page, and handle the technical parts: off-session charges, merged orders, deferred store sync, per-charge refunds and idempotent accepts. It also says which metrics to watch, including take rate, refund rate and chargebacks, and it ends with a promotional section for one self-hosted funnel product.

raise average order value without hurting conversion
design a downsell after a declined upsell
track upsell take rate and refunds

Shopify or WooCommerce account if the store syncs orders
Cloudflare account and PostgreSQL only if deploying the referenced product

summary: This skill guides an agent to choose a landing page or sales funnel platform by calculating total cost and lock-in for a specific business, rather than comparing feature lists. It walks through the inputs that matter, such as revenue through the funnel, contact list size and who will maintain the system, then matches those to hosted, WordPress, Shopify or self-hosted options. check whether an open-source funnel tool's licence allows agency client work
pick a landing page builder for a Shopify or WooCommerce store

why: It is a stack-free decision aid that serves the node's sales page and shop work only occasionally, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. It contains a promotional section for Autonnel and mentions outside hosted services, so an agent should treat that part as advertising and check current prices itself.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to set up a self-hosted sales funnel builder, Autonnel, and take a funnel from an empty install to a published landing page, checkout, upsell and thank-you page. ad platform accounts for conversion tracking

The Docker route is local but is presented only as an evaluation step, so the skill as a whole is built around cloud hosting.

summary: This skill guides an agent through changing a schema, stored data, API, protocol, configuration or dependency without breaking existing users. roll out a config change with a rollback path
migrate stored data without losing records
check that old and new code work during a rolling deploy

why: It is stack-free and applies to the schema and API changes a node's data layer and sites will need, though it is general advice rather than a procedure. The companion agents/openai.yaml was not reviewed in detail, so its contents are unknown.

summary: This skill has an agent route a repository's LLM requests through a hosted Caveman gateway so that spend and usage are measured without changing the app's behavior. risks: Routes all prompts and responses, and in byok mode the provider key, through a third-party cloud gateway.

summary: This skill guides an agent through making YouTube thumbnails, Shorts covers and Instagram video covers by generating images with the Higgsfield CLI. summary: This skill tells an agent to run the liarjs command-line scanner against a throwaway Chrome profile. The result is a score with a list of contradictions. It is aimed at people who want to know whether a browser profile looks self-consistent or whether an automation setup leaves detectable traces.

check whether a spoofed browser profile is self-consistent
compare a fingerprint against a real browser
find out why an automated browser is flagged

outbound access to liarjs.dev unless --offline is used

summary: The skill lets an agent measure how an automated browser (Playwright, Puppeteer, Selenium or a CDP-driven Chromium) looks from the inside, using the liarjs library against an existing page or by attaching to a running browser. By default it sends a request to the third-party liarjs.dev endpoint, which is a paid-free external service the person can avoid with --offline or a self-hosted endpoint.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to add a browser fingerprint check to a CI pipeline using the liarjs command-line tool. By default the scanned browser fetches https://liarjs.dev/api/net.json, so the skill calls an outside service that the person should be aware of; the --offline and --endpoint options avoid it. The npx invocation runs a pinned npm package, which is normal for this kind of tool.

Google Fonts or supplied font files
Google Slides export URL for the brandbook template
