why: It directly serves building sites and landing pages on a Next.js node, and its image generation and photo library are optional paid or outside services the person chooses. It also installs an edit-time hook into the user's .claude/settings.json, which the person should know about. Its scripts use puppeteer and a Together AI call, which only send prompts and image requests out, not the person's data.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a browser session on a target website to find the internal endpoints or page-level steps that deliver data or trigger an action. It then wraps the verified method in Python scripts and a SKILL.md, so later runs skip the exploration. It is aimed at people who need recurring or bulk data collection, or who want to copy what an existing tool does on a site they can already use.
tasks: collect all listings from a website into a file
build a reusable scraper for a site
find the API endpoint a page uses to load its data
monitor a site and pull new items every day
replicate a scraping tool's behaviour on a chosen site
qualityWhy: The phases, verification steps, selector rules, failure handling and delivery checklist are concrete and followable, though some rules are long and a few references to other files are only summarised.
why: It is useful for collecting data from websites, which fits building and running products, but it is not a direct tool for building a Fractera node and it works on third-party sites rather than the node's own data. It depends on the outside BrowserAct service and key, and it explicitly targets reproducing other products and scraping at scale, so the person should check the target site's terms before running it.

summary: This skill guides an agent to find and score partners whose audience overlaps with a SaaS company's customers without competing for the same budget. It then helps brainstorm joint campaigns such as co-authored content, webinars, integration launches and bundles, and outlines how to approach partners and structure a co-marketing agreement. It is aimed at founders and marketing teams planning partnerships for a product.
tasks: find co-marketing partners for our product
brainstorm a joint campaign with another company
score potential partners against our ideal customer
draft a cold outreach email to a partner
outline terms for a co-marketing agreement
qualityWhy: It gives a clear scoring table, campaign-format tables, an outreach template, a call-prep list, an agreement outline and a checklist, though it leaves some steps to judgement and points to external guides for tooling.
needs: Optional: Crossbeam, Reveal, Introw or PartnerStack accounts for account-overlap and partner-program data
why: It is a stack-free planning skill for marketing a product, so it fits the node's selling and content uses and can be installed as written. The listed tools are optional and only mentioned, not required, and the detailed partnership reference file was not reviewed in full.

summary: The skill guides an agent through pricing decisions for software and other products: choosing a value metric, structuring good-better-best tiers, running willingness-to-pay research such as Van Westendorp, and rolling out price increases to existing customers. It also covers auditing a pricing page for both human clarity and whether AI agents can read and quote the prices. It is aimed at founders and product or marketing people deciding what to charge.
tasks: decide how much to charge for a new SaaS product
restructure pricing tiers and plan packaging
plan a price increase for existing customers
audit a pricing page for clarity and AI readability
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete frameworks, a rollout sequence, a checklist and a paste test, with pointers to reference files; it lacks worked examples inside the main file and some heuristics are stated without evidence.
why: Pricing strategy is useful for a node that sells products, but it is advice rather than code, so it is used now and then rather than daily. It is stack-free and needs no outside service, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up Prisma ORM in an application, connecting it to a database, or repairing an existing connection in a Prisma 6, 7, or 8 project. New projects default to Prisma 8 and are pointed to a separate versioned Prisma 8 guide; existing Prisma 6 and 7 apps stay on their version with per-database reference notes. It is aimed at developers wiring a database layer into their app.
tasks: set up Prisma ORM in a new app
connect an existing app to a PostgreSQL or MySQL database
troubleshoot a Prisma connection error
repair the setup of a Prisma 6 or 7 project without upgrading it
qualityWhy: Gives a clear decision flow, concrete commands and per-provider references with verification steps, though several parts depend on external docs and the separate prisma-8 skill.
needs: a database for the chosen provider
a Prisma 8 or earlier package release from npm
why: Prisma ORM is a database layer that suits a local-first node, but the skill's stack is Prisma's own CLI and adapters, not the node's SQLite element, so it must be adapted to route all data through the node's SQLite element rather than a standalone database connection. The skill also points to external guides and a sibling skill that may not be installed.

summary: This skill makes an agent act as a deliberately annoying user who feeds a UI component realistic worst-case data, such as very long names, unbreakable emails, one-letter names, zero items, and huge counts. It wires those fixtures behind a dev-only Demo/Worst case toggle, checks layouts at narrow widths, zoom and RTL, and reports each break with a severity, cause and fix. It is aimed at front-end developers who want to find edge cases in components or screens before users do.
tasks: stress-test a member list with long names and emails
find edge cases in a dashboard card
try the worst case on a settings screen
report what breaks in a table at 320px
qualityWhy: The skill has a clear workflow, a concrete failure-signature table with CSS fixes, a report format and hard rules, though its catalog file is referenced but was not included in the files given to me.
why: It is a stack-free UI testing method that suits any component built on a React or web stack, and it directly serves building and checking product screens on a node. It does not depend on a cloud service, and its only dependency, CATALOG.md, was not in the supplied files, which is a gap to note rather than a risk.

summary: This skill is an index for the gws command-line tool's Gmail commands. It lists helper actions for sending, reading, triaging, replying, forwarding and watching mail, plus raw Gmail API resources such as messages, drafts, labels and threads. It tells the agent to check auth rules in a shared file and to use the schema command before calling any method. It is aimed at someone who wants an agent to manage their own mailbox.
tasks: send an email from the command line
summarise unread messages in the inbox
reply to or forward a specific email
watch the inbox for new mail
qualityWhy: It is mostly an index that points to other skill files for every helper, with only a command list and a discovery hint of its own.
why: Gmail is a cloud mail service that holds the person's messages outside their computer, and managing a mailbox is not building, running, selling or making content for a product, so value is none and use is skip. The skill also depends on a remote account and on other skills it does not contain.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to add schema.org structured data, written as JSON-LD, to a website so search engines can understand its pages and show enhanced results. It covers choosing the right type for a page (organization, article, product, breadcrumbs and so on), checking whether Google still supports a requested rich result, and validating the markup before release. It is aimed at site owners, marketers and developers who want better search appearance for their pages.
tasks: add JSON-LD structured data to a product page
fix schema markup errors flagged by a validator
add breadcrumb and article markup to a blog
check whether a rich result type is still supported by Google
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, a type table with required properties, a current-support warning for retired Google features, a testing checklist and implementation notes, with fuller JSON-LD examples in a reference file.
why: Structured data directly improves how pages built on a node appear in search, which suits sites, shops and blogs. The examples are generic JSON-LD, so an agent must place them into the node's Next.js App Router pages itself, but no outside service or stack swap is required. The reference examples and evals were not fully reviewed.

summary: This skill is a small set of writing guides that tells an agent how to draft internal company communications such as 3P (progress, plans, problems) updates, newsletters, FAQ answers, status and leadership reports, and incident reports. It has the agent pick the right guide file for the request and follow its format and tone rules. It is written for a specific company's house style, so it is mostly useful for teams who want the same format.
tasks: write a 3P progress, plans and problems update
draft a company newsletter
answer a common employee question as an FAQ
write a leadership or project status report
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is clear about routing to example guides, but the guides themselves hold the actual detail and the routing step has no checks, and the description refers to 'my company' without defining its formats here.
why: Internal company writing is not something a Fractera node is built for: it does not build sites, apps, agents or public content, and the skill's formats belong to one company's internal processes. It has no stack dependency and no risks, but the value is none, so skip.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building competitor comparison and alternative pages for SEO and buyer evaluation, covering four formats: singular alternative, plural alternatives, you-vs-competitor, and competitor-vs-competitor. It requires centralized, dated competitor data, honest strengths-and-weaknesses framing, and a structured audit process that re-verifies existing competitive claims. It is written for marketers and founders who publish public comparison content about rival products.
tasks: write a 'you vs competitor' comparison page
create a competitor alternatives landing page
audit our comparison pages for outdated claims
build a centralized competitor data file
qualityWhy: Concrete page structures, keyword patterns, evidence-discipline rules and an audit procedure give an agent clear steps, though it leans on referenced files and has no worked examples inside SKILL.md itself.
why: It directly serves a product's marketing and sales pages, producing written comparison content that lives in local files with no outside service required. It is a stack-free content skill, so it fits a node as written; the referenced templates and data-structure files were not inspected in full.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to explore an Nx monorepo read-only: listing projects, filtering them by tag, target or directory, inspecting resolved project and target configuration, reading nx.json, and tracing dependencies through the project graph. It also covers troubleshooting failed task lookups and out-of-sync workspaces. It is aimed at developers working inside an Nx workspace who need to understand how it is set up before running tasks.
tasks: list the projects in this workspace
check how a project is configured
find what depends on a library
debug a missing target error
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete commands, JSON output examples and troubleshooting steps an agent can follow, with a small gap in the dependency-query example that filters only direct dependents.
why: It is useful for understanding an Nx monorepo, but Fractera nodes run on Next.js with their own structure and Nx is not part of the node's stack, so the skill would need adapting to the node's own layout before use. It is read-only and carries no security risk.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing automated email sequences: welcome flows, lead nurture, re-engagement, onboarding, post-purchase and win-back series. It sets timing, email order, subject and preview rules, length targets, and a list of AI-sounding phrasing to avoid. It also routes the agent to reference files for templates, lifecycle email types and copy rules. It is aimed at marketers and founders who need a multi-email flow written for their product.
tasks: design a welcome email sequence for new signups
write a re-engagement flow for inactive users
plan a lifecycle email program for onboarding and billing
audit an existing email drip campaign
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with sequence templates, timing, output formats and a clear reference routing table, though the sequence-specific detail lives in the reference files and the SKILL.md itself mostly lists rather than walks through steps.
why: Writing automated email flows for a product or its content is a direct use case for a node, and the skill names several hosted email tools only as optional integration pointers, which the agent does not need to use. It is a stack-free writing skill, so it can be installed as written.

summary: The skill guides an agent through planning a product launch, feature announcement or release, from a readiness check through phased rollout to post-launch follow-up. It covers owned, rented and borrowed channels, a Product Hunt playbook, and a launch-day checklist. It is written for founders and product teams getting ready to release something publicly. It also points to a reference for turning merged code changes into changelogs and announcement drafts, which is only usable if the agent can read the product repository.
tasks: plan a product launch with phased rollout
build a pre-launch and launch-day checklist
prepare a Product Hunt launch
turn merged changes into release notes and a changelog
qualityWhy: The instructions are structured and actionable, with checklists, a readiness gate and concrete case examples, though much of the advice stays general strategy.
why: It is a stack-free marketing playbook that directly serves selling and releasing a product on a node. The named tools (Introw, Navattic, SparkToro, Listen Notes) are optional suggestions, not requirements. Its two referenced files (shipped-changes.md, site-launch-qa.md) were not included in what I reviewed, so I judged only SKILL.md.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive a running Obsidian desktop app through its command-line interface. It can read, create, append, search and tag notes, manage tasks and properties, and query backlinks, including daily notes. It also covers plugin and theme development, such as reloading a plugin, checking errors and console output, taking screenshots, and inspecting the DOM. It is aimed at people who keep their notes in an Obsidian vault and want an agent to work with them.
tasks: search my Obsidian vault for notes on a topic
append a task to today's daily note
set a property on a note from the command line
reload my Obsidian plugin and check for errors
qualityWhy: The instructions are short and clear with real command examples, but they defer almost all detail to `obsidian help` and give no error handling or verification steps for ordinary note operations.
needs: Obsidian desktop app running locally with the obsidian CLI available
why: The skill works on a local vault and calls no outside service, so it is safe to install. Its direct use for building sites, apps, agents or shop content is limited, so it helps mainly for note-keeping and drafting alongside a node's work, and plugin debugging applies only to Obsidian itself.

summary: This skill is labelled as a user-authored audit skill, but its SKILL.md holds only a one-line description and the text "Not pinned." Nothing in it tells an agent what to audit, how to check the work, or what to report. It cannot guide an agent through any task yet. The author's name in the source path is not evidence of content, so the judgment rests on the file alone.
tasks: review a project for quality problems
run an audit of site code
check a build before release
qualityWhy: The file is a stub: a generic description and the words "Not pinned." with no steps, examples or checks.
why: The file has no instructions, so an agent would gain nothing from installing it, and no link to building, running or selling a product can be shown. Its value could only be judged once real audit content exists.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing, running and analysing A/B and multivariate tests, covering hypotheses, sample sizes, metric choice, variant design and result interpretation. It also covers building an ongoing growth experimentation program with hypothesis backlogs, ICE prioritisation, velocity tracking and a playbook of winning patterns. It is aimed at marketers and product teams who want to know which version performs better. It is a methodology guide with no code or tool integration beyond naming calculators and platforms.
tasks: plan an A/B test for a landing page
calculate sample size for a test
decide whether a test result is significant
prioritise experiment ideas with ICE scoring
set up a growth experimentation program
qualityWhy: Thorough and concrete, with a hypothesis template, sample-size table, checklists, statistical caveats and cadence guidance, though it has no executable steps for implementing tests in the node's own stack.
why: It directly serves a product's growth work by helping an agent plan and judge experiments on the node's pages and flows. It is stack-free methodology, so it can be installed as written, but it names PostHog, Optimizely and other external tools only as options, and the implementation advice is generic rather than tied to Fractera's SQLite data layer.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to write Obsidian Bases files (.base), which are YAML definitions that turn a vault's notes into table, card, list or map views. It covers global and per-view filters, computed formula properties, display names, summaries, and embedding views in notes. It is aimed at people who keep notes in Obsidian and want database-like views over them.
tasks: create a table view of notes filtered by tag
build a reading list base with cards and a table
add a formula for days until a due date
embed a base view in a daily notes page
qualityWhy: The instructions give a workflow, a full schema, filter and formula syntax, worked examples, and a troubleshooting section with wrong and right YAML, though there is no explicit validation script.
why: Obsidian Bases works on a local vault, but the node's data lives in its own SQLite element and nodes do not use Obsidian vaults as a data store, so the skill does not serve building, running or selling a product. The skill is safe and well written, so the skip is about fit, not risk.

summary: This skill teaches an agent the GSAP core JavaScript API: single tweens with to, from, fromTo and set, plus eases, stagger, defaults, transform aliases, CustomEase and responsive or reduced-motion handling via matchMedia. It is aimed at developers adding DOM or SVG animation in React, Vue or vanilla JS. The file is a documentation-style guide with concrete code examples and do/don't lists.
tasks: add a fade-in animation to page elements
make a staggered list entrance animation
respect reduced-motion preferences in animations
animate an SVG shape with GSAP
choose easing and duration for a UI transition
qualityWhy: Clear, complete reference with runnable examples, property tables and explicit best-practice and pitfall lists, though it lacks setup steps and a few gaps (e.g. no install instructions).
why: Animating UI for web apps and landing pages is directly useful for building products on a Next.js/React node, and GSAP runs locally in the browser with no outside service or key. The skill is stack-free for core tweens, and the SKILL.md gives no install command or external calls to worry about.

summary: The skill guides an agent through auditing an App Store or Google Play listing: it fetches the page, classifies the app's brand maturity, scores six weighted dimensions (titles, descriptions, visuals, ratings, metadata, conversion signals), and writes a prioritized report with concrete copy changes. It is aimed at app developers and marketers who want more downloads or better search visibility. The skill relies on web fetching and screenshots and is written only as instructions with reference files.
tasks: audit my App Store listing
optimize app store keywords and title
compare my app to competitors
improve app conversion rate on Google Play
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with a phased workflow, explicit scoring weights, platform spec references, and a report structure, though some checks depend on data the agent cannot access.
why: It directly serves a product's growth by improving app store listings, which is a marketing task for what nodes are for. It is a stack-free marketing skill, so it installs as written; it fetches only public store pages and needs no keys, though it cannot measure search volume or rankings without paid tools.

summary: The skill guides an agent through a multi-axis code review before merging: checking correctness, readability, architecture, security and performance, then labelling each finding by severity. It also covers test-first review, change sizing, commit descriptions, dead-code hygiene and a careful process for reviewing dependency upgrades. It is aimed at engineers and agents reviewing diffs or pull requests.
tasks: review this pull request before merging
review a diff pasted inline
check code written by another agent
review a dependency upgrade and its lockfile diff
qualityWhy: The file is concrete and complete, with a step-by-step process, a severity-label table, a review checklist, rationalization and red-flag lists, and verification steps an agent can follow directly.
why: A Fractera node builds products, so a review discipline applies to every change the node's agents make; it is stack-free and needs no outside service. It only cross-references two other skills and two reference files that are not in the bundle, which is a small gap.

summary: The skill guides an agent through researching whether a physical product is worth selling on Amazon. It walks through demand checks via web search and Google Trends, competitor and price-range mapping, a margin calculation including FBA fees, entry barriers, and a weighted 1-10 opportunity score with a formatted report. It is written for Amazon sellers evaluating product ideas, not for building software on a node.
tasks: research a product idea for Amazon
compare two products to sell on Amazon
estimate profit margin for an Amazon product
analyze competition for a product category
qualityWhy: The steps and scoring rubrics are clear and usable, but the data gathering relies on generic web searches and manual checks, and it gives no concrete fee tables or verifiable sources.
why: It serves Amazon sellers doing market research, which is not what a Fractera node is for: building, running, or selling products on the node itself. The skill also promotes a paid Nexscope platform inside its own output, and its subject is cloud marketplace selling, so under the rules it is skipped.

summary: This skill guides an agent through planning whether a free web tool, such as a calculator, grader, or generator, should be built to attract leads, search traffic, or brand awareness. It covers choosing a tool type, judging demand and fit with the paid product, deciding how much to gate it, and choosing between building custom, using a no-code platform, or embedding an existing tool. It also gives a scorecard for ranking ideas and lists common failure modes. The audience is founders and marketers deciding what to build and how to measure it.
tasks: decide whether to build a free calculator for lead generation
score free tool ideas against search demand and product fit
plan the MVP scope and lead capture for a free grader tool
choose between building custom and using a no-code tool
qualityWhy: It gives a clear structure, a scoring rubric, and pitfalls with sourced references, but it stays at strategy level and has no concrete build steps or checks.
why: It is a stack-free planning skill, so it fits a node for planning marketing tools for a product, but it produces no code or content itself and is useful only now and then. Its examples and benchmarks are not verified here.

summary: This skill guides an agent through improving what new users experience right after signing up, aiming to get them to their first real benefit quickly. It covers choosing an activation model, finding the early action that predicts retention, designing checklists, empty states and tours, and coordinating follow-up emails for stalled users. It is written for product owners and growth teams who see people sign up but not stick around.
tasks: optimize the post-signup onboarding flow
find the aha moment from user activity data
design an onboarding checklist for a new app
write empty state copy that guides a first action
plan re-engagement for users who stall during setup
qualityWhy: The instructions are structured and actionable, with a clear cohort method for finding activation signals and concrete checklists, but some claims such as the +40% completion figure are unsourced and the depth of the reference files varies.
why: It directly serves running and growing a product built on a node, and it is stack-free so it fits the node as written. Its guidance is product-marketing advice rather than code, so an agent still needs to apply it to the actual app, and some benchmark figures are not sourced.

summary: The skill gives an agent guidance and small Python helpers for making animated GIFs that meet Slack size and dimension limits. It covers recommended sizes, frame rates, colour counts, drawing with PIL primitives, common motion patterns such as bounce, pulse and shake, and checks that a finished GIF passes validation. It is aimed at people who want a short animated graphic for a Slack message or emoji.
tasks: make an animated GIF for Slack
create a 128x128 emoji GIF
animate a shape with easing
check a GIF against Slack size limits
reduce GIF file size
qualityWhy: It gives clear dimensions, parameters, runnable code snippets, a full set of motion concepts and a working validator, though some helper functions are thin and the optimisation advice is brief.
why: Making short animated graphics for social posts is useful now and then on a node, and the GIF is built locally from PIL frames with no outside service. The helper draw_text uses Pillow's default font and the skill notes emoji fonts are unreliable, so text work is limited. The GIF output and validation run on local files only.

summary: The skill teaches an agent how to add scroll-driven animation with GSAP's ScrollTrigger plugin: tying tweens and timelines to scroll position, scrubbing progress, pinning sections, and building fake horizontal scroll. It also covers batching triggers, proxying third-party smooth scrollers, refreshing after layout changes, and cleaning up triggers. It is aimed at front-end developers and designers building animated landing pages or sites.
tasks: add a scroll-linked animation to a landing page
pin a section while content scrolls
build a fake horizontal scroll gallery
animate elements as they enter the viewport
fix ScrollTrigger positions after dynamic content loads
qualityWhy: Concrete and well organised, with config tables, code examples, caveats and a do-not list, though it has some repetition and no full working project example.
why: Scroll animation is a direct need for sites and landing pages built on a node, and the skill is a stack-free-enough GSAP guide that runs locally with no outside service. It assumes the GSAP npm package or script is available, which the agent must install itself.

summary: This skill lets an agent run inside a Herdr terminal session and drive its layout: it can open sibling panes, start a named coding agent in one, send it prompts, wait for it to become idle or ask for input, and read the output back. It also covers running ordinary shell commands in another pane and waiting for specific output. The skill is aimed at developers who already work in Herdr and want one agent to coordinate others in parallel.
tasks: start a second coding agent in a split pane
run the test suite in a sibling pane and read the results
check what another agent in Herdr is doing
send a follow-up prompt to a named agent and wait for its reply
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands, ID-handling rules, wait semantics and safety checks an agent can follow, though it assumes a Herdr install and has no worked end-to-end example.
why: It is a local terminal-coordination tool, not a cloud service, so it fits a local-first node, but it only helps build or run products indirectly by managing parallel agents and shells. It works only when the agent runs inside a Herdr pane (HERDR_ENV=1) with the herdr binary installed, and it is not a content or site-building skill.

summary: This skill turns an agent into a manager of a remote team of AI workers hosted on the Agentix platform. It registers the person, creates roles and tasks, spawns short-lived workers on Modal, and watches their progress through an activity feed. It is aimed at people who want autonomous multi-agent project runs, not at building a local site or app.
tasks: spawn workers to build a feature
plan and track tasks for a team of AI agents
monitor worker progress and review results
set up a team of roles for a software project
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete endpoints, request bodies, status flow and setup steps, but it is an API reference for a hosted service rather than a self-contained method.
why: The workers, tasks and team data live on a cloud platform (agentix.cloud and Modal), not on the node's own computer, so it falls under the cloud-hosting rule and is not useful for a local-first node. The skill also tells the agent to pass the person's Anthropic key and GitHub token to that remote service.
risks: Sends the person's Anthropic API key and GitHub token to a third-party service (agentix.cloud) and stores them there.
Writes API keys to ~/.agentix/credentials on the local computer.
The autopilot mode loops continuously and spawns remote workers without the person's approval.

summary: This skill gives an agent a detailed reference for building LLM features on the Claude API and Anthropic SDKs. It covers picking a model and its price, streaming, tool use, the managed agent option, prompt caching, token counting, and moving code to newer models. It also includes guided workflows for auditing old prompts, upgrading SDK versions, cutting API costs, building evals, and tuning prompts. It is aimed at developers who want to add Claude to their own apps, sites or agents.

stream Claude responses into a web page
build a tool-using agent with Claude
migrate existing code to a newer Claude model
reduce the cost of Claude API calls
build an eval set for a Claude-powered feature
tools: Anthropic Java, Go, Ruby, C# and PHP SDKs
qualityWhy: It is very concrete, with model IDs, parameter rules, language-specific file pointers, step-by-step subcommands and explicit checks, though its size makes it heavy to read.
needs: paid Anthropic API account (or Claude on AWS, Bedrock, Vertex AI or Microsoft Foundry)
why: It directly serves building AI features into products, and the node's TypeScript stack matches its @anthropic-ai/sdk guidance without adaptation. It calls a paid outside API, so the person must choose and fund it. I reviewed the main SKILL.md and the start of the bundled scripts, not every reference file, and some script contents were cut off.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a security review of web code: threat modelling each trust boundary with STRIDE, validating input, parameterizing queries, handling auth and sessions, locking down headers and CORS, guarding server-side fetches against SSRF, and auditing dependencies and supply-chain risk. It also covers personal-data minimization for GDPR/CCPA and OWASP LLM concerns. It is written for developers and agents building or auditing web applications.
tasks: audit an input handler for vulnerabilities
check a login flow against the OWASP Top Ten
triage package-manager audit findings before a release
review a feature that accepts file uploads or webhooks
harden session cookies and security headers
assess privacy and retention for stored personal data
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed and organized into clear tiers and checklists, but much of the concrete code lives in referenced files that were not included, so some steps depend on those missing details.
why: It is a stack-free security checklist that directly serves building and running web apps on a Fractera node, so it can be installed as written. Its examples name Node-style tools (helmet, npm audit) that fit the node's Next.js stack, and the referenced hardening-patterns file was not part of the review, so its exact code is unverified.

summary: This skill guides an agent through designing, tuning and measuring referral and affiliate programs, turning existing customers and outside partners into a source of new buyers. It covers when to build sharing into the product itself, how to pick triggers, share methods and reward structures, and which metrics to track. It also includes playbooks for affiliate recruitment and commissions, and for review campaigns and handling reviews on platforms such as G2 and Trustpilot. It is aimed at founders and marketers who run a product or shop and want word of mouth to bring in customers.
tasks: design a customer referral program with rewards
set up an affiliate program with commission tiers
plan a review request campaign for G2 or Google
respond to a negative online review
choose a referral tracking tool for a Stripe shop
qualityWhy: The instructions are structured, with checklists, metrics, email templates and reference files that cover affiliate operations and review platform rules, though much of the tool detail is delegated to external links.
why: It is stack-free marketing guidance that directly serves selling and growing a product, so an agent on a node can apply it as written. The tool integrations are optional third-party services the person would choose and pay for, and the skill does not require them. Review campaigns depend on each platform's rules, which the skill itself says to check first.

summary: This skill guides an agent through security review of codebases, APIs, services, CLI tools, libraries and daemons. It separates quick security questions from full audits that run a six-phase workflow with sandboxed local tests, structured findings JSON, coverage ledgers and a final report. It is written for security reviewers and owners who want evidence-based vulnerability findings with minimal fixes.
tasks: audit this repository for security vulnerabilities
review an API for authorization and trust boundary flaws
write a structured security findings report
triage a suspected vulnerability with source evidence
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is detailed and concrete, with explicit modes, severity anchors, validation scripts and phase ordering, though the full workflow depends on many companion files and its sandbox rules are demanding.

summary: Guides an agent through creating, running, and maintaining Momentic browser end-to-end tests and reusable modules stored as YAML files. It covers the v2 file format, environment and base URL resolution, AI Action steps versus granular steps, caching behavior, preview-splice-validate workflows over an MCP session, and troubleshooting. It is written for QA engineers and developers who test web apps with Momentic.
tasks: write an end-to-end test for a checkout flow
fix a failing browser test after a UI change
reuse a login module across several tests
add an assertion that checks a stable page state
qualityWhy: Detailed and actionable with concrete rules for v2 YAML, workflows, caching, and troubleshooting, though it leans on external docs and a monorepo path for the format reference.
needs: Momentic account or local Momentic installation
a configured Momentic project with test environments and a base URL
why: Momentic is a cloud-hosted test platform with its own browser runner, and its tests and recordings are kept on its service rather than in the node's local SQLite and file elements, so it does not serve building or running a product on a local-first node; the skill is an instruction set for an external testing tool, not an element of the node.

summary: This skill guides an agent through classifying why a Momentic end-to-end test run failed. The agent walks the run's attempts and steps through the Momentic MCP tools, finds the earliest step where the run went wrong, and assigns one category, a recoverability value and a confidence level. It is written for QA engineers and test owners who triage browser test results.
tasks: explain why a Momentic test run failed
categorize a failing browser test result
compare this run with past runs of the same test
triage the failures of a test run group
qualityWhy: The skill gives a detailed step-by-step investigation workflow, evidence standards, category definitions and an output format, though it is written for the Momentic MCP and has no runnable examples of its own.
why: The skill serves testing of web products, not building, running or selling a product on a local-first node, and it depends on the Momentic cloud service for run data, so it is value none and skip.

summary: Gives an agent a process for simplifying working code without changing its behavior: check why the code exists first, find concrete complexity signals like deep nesting, nested ternaries and duplication, then apply one small change at a time with tests run after each. It is aimed at developers who want readable, maintainable code and at reviewers who flag accumulated complexity.
tasks: simplify this function without changing its behavior
reduce the nesting in this module
clean up duplicated logic before the code review
refactor this working code for readability
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear process, concrete before-and-after examples in TypeScript, Python and React, a verification checklist and red flags, though it has no examples for other languages and no guidance on tooling.
why: It is a stack-free refactoring method that directly helps build and maintain a product's code on a node, and it does not depend on any outside service. It asks the agent to keep behavior identical and run tests after each change, which fits the node's own stack.

summary: The skill guides an agent through a structured debugging process: reproduce the failure, localize the failing layer, reduce to a minimal case, fix the root cause, add a regression test, and verify end-to-end. It covers test failures, build breaks, runtime errors and regressions, and it tells the agent to stop adding features until the failure is resolved. It is written for developers fixing bugs in any codebase.
tasks: debug a failing test suite
fix a build that broke after a change
track down a regression with git bisect
find the root cause of a runtime error
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear ordered checklist, decision trees, a regression test example and a verification list, though its commands assume npm and it lacks worked examples for many stacks.
why: Debugging discipline is useful on a node for building and running apps, but it is generic and not tied to the node's stack, so it serves only occasionally; it is stack-free and can be installed as written.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to design interfaces that are hard to misuse: API contracts, consistent error formats, validation at system edges, and additive changes that don't break existing callers. It covers REST resource layout, pagination, filtering, and TypeScript types such as discriminated unions and branded IDs. It also explains how to make state-changing requests safe to retry, with atomic key claims, payload checks, and clear handling of duplicate in-flight requests. It is aimed at developers building endpoints, module boundaries, or component props for a product.
tasks: design REST endpoints for a shop or blog
define typed contracts between frontend and backend
add pagination and consistent error responses to an API
make order or payment endpoints safe to retry
qualityWhy: It gives concrete rules, code examples, a rationalizations table, red flags and a verification checklist that an agent can follow step by step.
why: It is a stack-free design guide that directly serves building and running APIs on a node, and its examples can be applied to Next.js route handlers and the node's SQLite element with the same principles. The examples use Express-style handlers and generic db calls, so the agent should translate them to the node's own route handlers and data layer rather than copy them literally.

summary: This skill guides an agent through planning and running SMS, MMS and WhatsApp marketing for direct-to-consumer brands, apps and SaaS products. It covers compliance first (TCPA, A2P 10DLC, GDPR, CASL), then sequence design such as welcome, abandoned cart, post-purchase and win-back flows, plus copy length, platform choice and metrics. It is written for marketers and product owners who need a concrete SMS program plan. Its checklists and templates are detailed, but the skill is a planning guide, not code for a node's own stack.
tasks: plan an abandoned cart SMS sequence
check TCPA and A2P 10DLC compliance for SMS
write welcome and win-back text messages
choose an SMS platform for a Shopify store
set up a WhatsApp template campaign outside the US
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete sequence timings, copy examples with character counts, compliance rules and a clear output format, though it leans on reference files and external registry links for depth.
needs: an SMS provider account such as Klaviyo, Postscript, Attentive, Twilio or Brevo
A2P 10DLC registration through The Campaign Registry for US sending
a Meta WhatsApp Business account for WhatsApp flows
why: It serves marketing for products that build and sell, but its work is mostly planning and copy, and it assumes an outside SMS platform that the node does not host, so the value is moderate. Installing it is safe, but using it means connecting a paid messaging service the person chooses, and the file references point to an external GitHub registry the agent would need to fetch.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to answer questions about the Vercel AI SDK and add AI features to an app. It directs the agent to check the installed `ai` package's bundled docs and source before writing code, since the SDK's APIs change often. It also covers picking a current model through the AI Gateway, building agents with the SDK's agent abstraction, debugging with DevTools, and checking whether the installed version is out of date. It is aimed at developers building chatbots, agents, RAG and text features.
tasks: add a chatbot to a Next.js app
build a tool-calling AI agent
generate structured JSON output from a model
check which AI models are currently available
upgrade an outdated AI SDK install
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands and a verify-against-installed-docs workflow, but most of the actual API guidance is deferred to external docs and it contains almost no code examples of its own.
needs: Vercel AI Gateway API key or OIDC auth
internet access to ai-sdk.dev and ai-gateway.vercel.sh
why: Building AI features is central to what a node is for, and the skill fits the Next.js and TypeScript stack. It needs an AI Gateway key or provider keys, and it relies on outside model services, which the person chooses. Its guidance is mostly pointers to docs, so an agent will still need to read the bundled docs to write correct code.

summary: The skill guides an agent to build features and fix bugs by writing a failing test first, then the minimal code to pass it, then refactoring while tests stay green. It stresses discovering the repository's own test commands, reproducing bugs with a test before fixing, favoring real implementations over mocks, and running the full suite before declaring work done. It also covers browser verification through Chrome DevTools for front-end changes. It is written for developers and AI coding agents who change behavior in existing code.
tasks: add tests to a function before changing it
fix a reported bug by first reproducing it in a test
verify a web page change in the browser with DevTools
refactor a module while keeping the test suite green
qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, worked examples, a decision guide, anti-patterns, a checklist and a clear way to adapt to any language's test tooling.
why: It is a stack-free engineering habit that helps any code the node builds, including Next.js and TypeScript apps, but it is not specific to Fractera and only applies when someone writes or changes code. The optional Chrome DevTools part needs that MCP server, which the person would set up themselves.

summary: This skill is a shared reference for the gws command-line tool, which lets an agent work with Google Workspace services from a terminal. It explains how to sign in with browser OAuth or a service account key, the common global and method flags, and the command syntax. It also lists safety habits such as confirming before write or delete actions and using dry runs. It is aimed at people who automate Google Workspace tasks.
tasks: sign in to Google Workspace from the command line
list files in a Google Drive folder
read a range of rows from a Google Sheet
export command output as a table or CSV
qualityWhy: It gives accurate flags, auth options and safety rules, but it is a thin reference that points to the README and gives few worked examples for the agent to follow.
needs: Google account with OAuth consent, or a Google service account key
why: Its purpose is to drive cloud Google Workspace services such as Drive, Sheets and Gmail, which the node's local-first design does not cover. The file contains no harmful instructions, but the value for building, running or selling products on a node is none.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to use GSAP animations inside Vue 3, Nuxt 4 and Svelte components, tying tween and ScrollTrigger creation to mount and unmount lifecycle hooks. It covers scoping selectors to the component root with gsap.context and reverting everything on teardown. It is aimed at front-end developers building animated interfaces in these frameworks.
tasks: add GSAP animations to a Vue component
animate a Nuxt 4 page with lazy-loaded plugins
set up GSAP cleanup in a Svelte component
add scroll-triggered animation in SvelteKit
qualityWhy: Gives concrete, runnable code for Vue, Nuxt and Svelte with clear lifecycle and cleanup rules, though it leans on referenced example folders that are not included and has a few loose notes.
why: Directly serves building animated front-end pages and components, which is central to what nodes are for, and it needs no outside service or key. It is a stack-free-in-spirit instruction set for frameworks the node uses (Next.js is not covered, so React-side guidance belongs to a different skill), and it runs entirely locally.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to organise what it reads before and during a coding session. It covers a persistent rules file such as CLAUDE.md, loading only the spec sections and source files a task needs, trimming stale output from long sessions, and handing work over cleanly to a fresh session. It is aimed at developers who use AI agents to write and change software, and it asks the agent to surface ambiguity rather than guess.
tasks: set up a CLAUDE.md rules file for a new project
reduce agent mistakes when switching between features
plan a clean handoff before starting a fresh session
keep a long coding session focused by trimming old output
qualityWhy: It gives concrete templates, checklists, anti-patterns and verification steps, though it is mostly principles with few runnable steps.
why: It is a stack-free working method that helps any agent-built site or app, but it does not build or ship content directly, so its value is occasional. It names MCP servers only as optional suggestions and needs no account or key.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to build changes in small, testable steps instead of one large pass. Each slice is implemented, tested, verified, committed, and then the next slice begins. It covers vertical, contract-first and risk-first slicing, plus simplicity, scope discipline, feature flags and rollback-friendly commits. It is aimed at developers and the agents working on their code.
tasks: implement a multi-file feature in small slices
pick up the next task from a plan safely
roll out a change behind a feature flag
refactor code without mixing concerns
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with slicing examples, rules, a checklist and rationalization tables, though they lean on other skills and a reference file for some details.
why: It is a stack-free engineering discipline that helps when building features on a Fractera node, so it is useful now and then rather than a direct product feature. It needs no outside service and works as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing a web page for accessibility against WCAG 2.2 and turning the findings into code fixes. It covers alt text, icon button names, color contrast, focus visibility, keyboard access, target size, form labels, error handling, ARIA usage and live regions, with HTML, CSS and JavaScript examples. It is aimed at developers who need to make a site or app usable by people with disabilities.
tasks: run an accessibility audit on my site
fix keyboard navigation problems in my web app
check color contrast and focus styles for WCAG compliance
add alt text and accessible labels to forms and buttons
make my landing page screen-reader friendly
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete before-and-after code, a repeatable audit workflow and a manual checklist, but it has no framework-specific guidance for React or Next.js and leans on an optional MCP tool.
why: Accessibility work on any site or app the node builds is directly useful, and the skill is mostly plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript that fits a Next.js and React stack without outside services. The automated steps use Lighthouse and axe through npx or a global npm install, and the skill itself says that passing automated checks is not WCAG conformance.

summary: This skill tells an agent to pull a design out of a Google Stitch project: it lists the project and screen through the Stitch MCP server, downloads the screen's HTML and screenshot, and reads the project's theme. From that it writes a DESIGN.md that describes the mood, colour palette with hex codes, shapes, shadows, typography and layout in plain design language. The file is meant to guide Stitch when it generates new screens that match the existing look. It is aimed at designers and developers who make landing pages or app screens.
tasks: write a DESIGN.md from an existing Stitch screen
keep new landing page screens consistent with the current design
extract the colour palette and component styles from a Stitch project
describe a site's visual language for a designer or AI prompt
qualityWhy: The retrieval steps are concrete, but the synthesis rules are generic, the output template is loosely specified, and it names read_url_content, which is missing from its allowed tools.
needs: Google Stitch account with at least one designed project
why: It helps a site or app builder keep new screens on-brand, but it works only through Google's hosted Stitch service, so it is useful only for people who already design in Stitch; the DESIGN.md it writes stays as a local file. Its usefulness depends on Stitch access, which I could not verify from the files.

summary: The skill guides an agent through git practices for every code change: small atomic commits, descriptive messages, short-lived trunk-based branches, worktrees for parallel agent work, pre-commit checks for secrets and tests, and splitting messy working trees. It also covers semantic versioning, tagging releases and writing human-facing changelogs. It is aimed at developers and agents who write and ship code.
tasks: split uncommitted changes into atomic commits
write a commit message for this diff
cut a release with a semver bump and changelog entry
run parallel feature work using git worktrees
review pre-commit hygiene before committing
qualityWhy: Concrete and well-structured with commands, templates, checklists and rationalization tables, though some sections are generic process advice and a few tool steps assume a Node project.
why: Git workflow and versioning serve directly every node that builds and ships code, and the skill is stack-free apart from optional npm examples. No cloud service or secret is required, and the commands are local git operations.

summary: This skill gives an agent a reference set for building terminal user interfaces with OpenTUI, covering the Core imperative API plus React and Solid reconcilers. It routes the agent to the right framework, components, layout, keyboard and keymap handling, animations, and testing guides. It is aimed at developers building terminal apps, not web apps.
tasks: build a terminal dashboard with OpenTUI
add keyboard shortcuts to a TUI app
create a scrollable list or input form in the terminal
write snapshot tests for a terminal interface
qualityWhy: The entry file is well structured with decision trees, critical rules and a reading order, and the 27 reference files are detailed, though the SKILL.md itself gives little code.
why: OpenTUI builds terminal user interfaces, which is not what Fractera nodes are for: sites, web apps, AI agents and content for social networks, shops and blogs. Its value to a node is therefore none, and the skill is skipped.

summary: The skill walks an agent through a three-phase ideation session: restating a vague idea as a problem statement, asking a few sharpening questions, generating and stress-testing variations, and ending with a markdown one-pager that includes a Not Doing list. It is aimed at founders, product people and developers who need to shape an idea before planning it. A small shell script creates a docs/ideas folder in the project.
tasks: refine a vague product idea into a clear direction
stress-test assumptions before committing to a plan
write a one-page idea brief with a not-doing list
explore alternative variations of a feature concept
qualityWhy: The phases, criteria, output template, anti-patterns and verification checklist are concrete and followable, with supporting reference files, though some guidance stays general.
why: It is a stack-free thinking habit that helps a builder shape a product or content idea before building, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. The only file action is creating docs/ideas inside the project, which is harmless.

summary: This meta-skill tells an agent how to pick the right workflow skill for a given piece of software work, mapping task phases such as defining requirements, planning, building, testing, reviewing and shipping to named sub-skills. It also sets standing habits: state assumptions, stop on confusion, push back on bad ideas, keep changes narrow, and verify with evidence before calling work done. It is aimed at developers who run an agent on a coding project.
tasks: decide which skill applies to a new feature
pick the right workflow when starting a coding session
follow a phased process from spec to shipping
check that work is verified before it is called done
qualityWhy: It gives a clear routing table and behavioural rules, but it is a directory of other skills with no concrete commands, examples or checks of its own.
why: It is a routing guide for a coding-agent workflow rather than a tool for building or running a node's product, so it is useful now and then. It is written for a generic development process and points to many sibling skills that are not in this package, so the node should adapt its habits rather than install it as-is.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive a real Chrome browser through the Chrome DevTools MCP server, so it can look at a running page the way a user sees it. It covers reproducing UI bugs, reading the DOM, styles, console and network traffic, recording performance traces, checking accessibility, and comparing screenshots before and after a change. It is aimed at developers who build or debug anything that runs in a browser, and it sets firm limits on how the agent may treat page content and run JavaScript.
tasks: debug a layout or styling bug in the browser
check a local page for console errors
trace why a form submit sends the wrong request
measure page load and layout shift with a performance trace
verify a fix with before and after screenshots
qualityWhy: The skill gives a concrete MCP config, a tool table, step-by-step debugging workflows, a test-plan template and a clear checklist, though it does not show exact tool call syntax.
why: It directly serves building and debugging web apps on a node, and it runs against a local dev server with a local Chrome, so no cloud service or account is needed. The setup line uses npx with -y and @latest, which fetches the npm package at run time, so the person should pin a version if they want stable behaviour; the optional --autoConnect mode touches the person's logged-in browser, which the skill itself warns against by default.

summary: This skill is a pre-launch and release guide for production deployments. It gives the agent a checklist covering code quality, security, performance, accessibility, infrastructure and docs, plus a staged rollout with feature flags, canary percentages, and go/hold/rollback thresholds. It also covers post-deploy monitoring, error budget gates and a rollback plan template. It is aimed at engineers shipping any web product.
tasks: prepare a production launch checklist
plan a staged canary rollout with feature flags
set up error monitoring before deploy
write a rollback plan for a release
qualityWhy: It is concrete, with checklists, rollout thresholds, a rollback template and verification steps, though it is generic and leans on referenced files that are not included.
why: It is a stack-free process guide that directly serves shipping a product, and a node can use it as written. Some references point to files outside this skill that are not provided, so those links will not resolve.

summary: The skill makes an agent check framework and library versions in the project's dependency file, fetch only the relevant official documentation page, and write code that follows the documented, current API rather than memory. It cites every framework-specific decision with full URLs and flags anything it could not verify. It is aimed at developers who need correct, up-to-date code for frameworks where version matters.
tasks: verify the React form pattern against current docs before coding
write auth code with citations to the official framework docs
check that a feature uses no deprecated APIs for this version
review existing framework code against the documentation
qualityWhy: The process, source hierarchy, citation rules, conflict handling and checklist are concrete and followable, though it names no specific fetch tool or example for non-JavaScript stacks.
why: It is a stack-free workflow that directly improves how an agent writes Next.js, React and other framework code for a node, so it fits the node's purpose. It does not depend on any outside service, and its only risk-relevant instruction is to ignore directives inside fetched docs, which it already handles.

summary: The skill tells an agent to review a code change the way a senior developer would before it ships. The agent reads the diff, follows callers and data flow, and reports bugs, security holes, load problems, missing tests, speed issues and code that can be deleted, each with a concrete case and a small fix. It is written for a person who may not know the code well, using plain language.
tasks: review my uncommitted changes before I ship
check this pull request for bugs and security holes
find code I can delete or simplify
tell me if this change will break under heavy load
list which changes need tests
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and complete, with a clear order of checks, a required finding format and a verification step, though they give no examples of the grep or test commands to run.
why: A review step for any product built on the node, and it works with the node's own code without any stack change. It is a stack-free habit skill, so it installs as written and needs no outside service.

summary: This guide walks an agent through building a continuous integration pipeline for a web project. It sets up ordered quality checks covering linting, type checking, unit and integration tests, builds, end-to-end tests and dependency audits, mostly as GitHub Actions workflows. It also covers preview and staged deployments, feature flags, rollback workflows, secret handling and speeding up slow pipelines. The intended readers are developers and their coding agents who want every change verified before it merges.
tasks: set up a GitHub Actions CI pipeline for a Next.js project
add lint, type check and test gates before merge
configure a rollback workflow for a deployment
speed up a slow CI pipeline
feed CI failure output back to a coding agent to fix
qualityWhy: It gives concrete, runnable YAML for each gate, a clear failure-feedback loop and a verification checklist, though a few sections (feature flags, staged rollout) stay high-level.
needs: Vercel token (only if preview or deploy steps are used)
PostgreSQL test database (only for the integration example)
why: Pipeline discipline is useful for any product a Fractera node builds, but the examples assume GitHub-hosted runners, Vercel deployments and a Postgres/Prisma database, while the node uses its own SQLite element and its own tooling, so an agent should adapt the gates rather than copy the steps as written.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write app code against the InsForge hosted backend using the @insforge/sdk package. It covers database queries, user sign-in and sessions, file uploads with storage access rules, edge functions, OpenRouter AI calls, realtime events, transactional email, and Stripe or Razorpay checkout. It is aimed at developers building web apps on InsForge's cloud platform.
tasks: add sign-up and login to a web app
fetch and filter rows from a database table
upload user files to a storage bucket
add a Stripe subscription checkout
send a welcome email to new users
stream AI chat responses in an app
qualityWhy: It gives concrete setup steps, code samples per module, and clear rules, though it depends heavily on linked references and on CLI commands the agent must run.
needs: InsForge cloud project with URL and anon key
InsForge API key for server admin code
why: InsForge is a hosted cloud backend (its own cloud database, auth, storage and deployments), which a local-first node does not use, and the node already provides its own SQLite, sign-in, storage and Stripe elements. The skill is therefore not useful here and should be skipped.
risks: The feedback command sends bug reports and details to a third-party service (InsForge) on the agent's own initiative, without asking the person first.

summary: This skill gives an agent a planning playbook for selling a product in other countries. It scores candidate markets on eight weighted factors, compares fulfillment options with rough cost and transit figures, and outlines tax and duty steps for several major regions. It also covers local payment methods, localization, and a phased rollout plan with KPIs. The intended users are online sellers who are moving beyond their home market.
tasks: score candidate countries for expansion
compare fulfillment options for cross-border orders
explain VAT, GST, and customs steps for a target market
build a phased international rollout plan
estimate landed cost and margin for a foreign sale
qualityWhy: It is concrete and well structured, with scoring weights, comparison tables, a readiness checklist, a landed-cost example and an output template, though some figures are unsourced and tax thresholds may be outdated.
why: It is strategy and planning text with no code, so it suits a seller's occasional decisions rather than building or running the node itself. Several tax thresholds and rates are stated as current facts and may be out of date, and the file carries promotional links to Nexscope, which an agent should not treat as neutral advice.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to operate the InsForge cloud backend entirely through its command-line tool: creating or linking projects, running SQL and migrations, setting row-level security, managing storage, functions, deployments, secrets, payments, schedules, branches and diagnostics. It is aimed at developers who need a hosted backend and want an agent to set it up and run it. The skill is a large routing guide that points to many sub-references for specific areas.
tasks: set up a new backend project and link it
write and apply a database migration with row-level security
deploy a frontend or edge function to the backend
configure Stripe payments and webhooks
check backend health and advisor findings
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is concrete, with commands, flags, exit codes and clear rules, though the full set of sub-references was cut off and not checked.
why: The skill is built around InsForge's hosted cloud database, storage, compute and deployment services, which the node's local-first design excludes, so value is none and it should be skipped.

summary: The skill guides an agent through retiring old systems, APIs, libraries or features: deciding whether code still earns its keep, announcing a deprecation, migrating consumers incrementally, and removing the old code once nothing depends on it. It also covers zero-downtime database schema changes using an expand/contract approach. It is written for engineers maintaining a product's codebase.
tasks: plan removing an old API safely
migrate users from one library to another
rename a database column without downtime
decide whether to keep or sunset legacy code
qualityWhy: It gives a clear decision framework, a step-by-step migration process, concrete patterns with code, a worked schema example and verification checklists, though it stays fairly general beyond the schema section.
why: It is a stack-free engineering discipline that fits building and maintaining a node's own sites and apps, and it needs no outside service. The database section speaks generally of SQL and Postgres, so an agent must apply it to the node's SQLite element with care, since CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY is Postgres-only.

summary: The skill makes an agent interview the user one question at a time, attaching a guessed answer to each, until the agent is confident about the underlying intent behind a vague request. It then restates the intent as outcome, user, timing, success, constraint and out-of-scope items, and waits for an explicit yes before any spec, plan or code. It is aimed at people who ask for something conventional like 'build me a dashboard' without saying who it's for or why.
tasks: clarify a vague feature request before building
stress-test my thinking before starting a project
turn an underspecified ask into a confirmed statement of intent
interview me about what I actually need
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear step-by-step process, a restate template, a stop rule, example, red flags and a verification checklist, though it has no scripts and some judgement is left to the agent.
why: It is a stack-free thinking habit that helps an agent scope work for any product a node builds, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. It suits interactive sessions only, and the skill itself says not to run it in unattended loops.

summary: This skill guides an agent to add Firecrawl's single-page scrape endpoint to application code, so the app can pull a page's content from a URL it already has. It covers choosing output formats such as markdown, HTML, links, screenshots and metadata, trimming page chrome, and deciding how fresh a cached copy may be. It is aimed at developers building features like knowledge ingestion, enrichment, or page monitoring.
tasks: extract the main text of a known article URL as markdown
ingest product or docs pages into a knowledge base
monitor a pricing or changelog page for changes
pull company details from a website for enrichment
tools: Firecrawl SDKs (Node, Python, Rust, Java, Elixir)
qualityWhy: It is clear and sensible about options and freshness, but it contains no code examples or concrete request shapes and defers the actual integration steps to external docs.
why: Turning a known URL into markdown for an agent's knowledge store or for enrichment directly serves products built on a node. It needs a Firecrawl key, and the hosted service is a paid choice the person makes; the skill's freshness advice is useful but its code guidance is thin.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to work with Google Calendar through the gws command-line tool: listing, creating, updating and deleting calendars, events, access rules and settings, plus checking free/busy times. It is a reference index that points to a few helper commands and tells the agent to inspect each method with gws schema before calling it. It is aimed at people who manage their own or their team's schedules.
tasks: list upcoming calendar events
create a new calendar event
check free and busy times for people
update or delete a calendar event
qualityWhy: It is mostly an API method listing with little step-by-step guidance, examples or checks, and it depends on another skill for auth and flags.
why: Google Calendar is a cloud service, and the skill's whole purpose is managing a hosted calendar, which the node's local-first rules place outside what nodes are for. It is not a build, run, sell or content tool for a product.

summary: This guide tells an agent how to add Firecrawl's search endpoint to an app or agent workflow when the process begins with a text query rather than a known web address. It covers when to run discovery first, how to keep search separate from page extraction, and when to use a follow-up scrape or interaction step. It also points to the right alternative skills for research-paper and developer-content searches. It is written for developers building search-driven products and agents.
tasks: find current web sources to answer a user question with citations
build a query-to-URL shortlist for later scraping
discover competitor or company websites from a topic
add web search to an agent workflow
tools: Firecrawl SDKs (Node, Python, Rust, Java, Elixir)
qualityWhy: It gives clear routing rules and useful caveats, but it has no concrete code steps, request examples, or checks, and most of its substance is links to other docs.
why: Web search that feeds product features and agents is directly useful for building products on a node, and the results come back into local code. It depends on the hosted Firecrawl service and its key, which the person chooses to pay for, so it is install-with-service rather than install. The skill's own files contain no risky instructions, and the main unknown is how much of the work the agent must still do from the linked docs.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building or repairing the offer a business actually sells, not just the copy around it.
