document app behaviour as a short video
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and complete, with a step-by-step workflow, explicit tool arguments, and checks on warnings and file size, though some config details rely on argent's own tooling.
why: The skill is for recording mobile app screens, which is only occasionally useful for building Fractera sites or content, and it depends on the argent MCP toolchain and simulators rather than the node's own stack. It is skipped because it is not a stack-free skill for the node and it sets no risk, but its usefulness is limited; the lack of a stated risk does not change that it cannot be run on a node without the argent MCP server.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a human review loop for Deepline Play results. The agent exports a completed run into a Google Sheet, reads the reviewer's edits and comments back, and turns that feedback into a revised Play, a comparison between revisions, or a standing rule. It is written for teams running Deepline's data workflows who want people to judge the outputs. Most of the work depends on Deepline's managed Google Workspace integration.
tasks: put a Play run into a Google Sheet for review
apply reviewer feedback to a revised Play
compare two Play revisions on a golden dataset
keep improving a Play with a bounded loop
qualityWhy: The steps, commands, checks, error routing and loop-control rules are concrete and complete, though the whole workflow depends on Deepline's proprietary tools.
needs: Google Sheets and Drive access through a managed Shared Drive
why: The review surface is a Google Sheet in a cloud Shared Drive, so the person's run data is stored in cloud file storage rather than on their own node, which makes the skill value none and use skip. It is tied to Deepline's Play product and is not a general tool for building sites, apps, agents or content.
risks: Exports the person's Play run data into a Google Shared Drive operated through Deepline's managed integration, outside the node's local storage, without asking for explicit consent first.

summary: The skill reviews a draft that is already written and checks whether it hits its target audience. It extracts the core claim, picks one dominant social-psychology mechanism (identity, framing, emotional appraisal, use-and-gratification or sharing), and points to the exact sentences where resonance breaks. It then gives concrete advice to delete, compress, strengthen or keep lines, and outputs a single revised skeleton. The audience is writers and content editors revising texts in Chinese.
tasks: diagnose why a draft fails to reach its target audience
find the resonance breakpoints in a written article
suggest which sentences to delete, compress or strengthen
check whether the core claim of a draft is clear
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear workflow, a fixed output template, theory boundaries, trigger conditions and a self-check, though it has no worked example.
why: It is a text-review method with no stack, so it is useful now and then for editing Fractera blog or landing copy, but it is not built for the node and needs no installs. Its aim is writing diagnosis rather than building or running the product, so 'some' is the honest rating. Use is 'install' in the sense of a stack-free skill, but since it is a Chinese-language writing review with no install step, 'ideas' fits better as it is read and applied by hand rather than wired into the node.

summary: The skill reads an existing piece of content and explains which psychological mechanism makes it resonate, provoke emotion, or get shared, using one main theory plus optional supporting ones. It names the likely audience identity, emotional appraisal path, the stance the content takes, and why people would watch, save, comment or share it. It then suggests two or three follow-up topics and a discussion question. It is aimed at content analysts and writers who want to understand a text, not to rewrite it or forecast traffic.
tasks: explain why a post resonates with its audience
identify the sharing motive behind a piece of content
suggest follow-up topics that keep the same audience appeal
analyse the emotional response a text is likely to trigger
qualityWhy: The file gives a clear workflow, theory pool with trigger conditions, output template and self-check, though it is written only in Chinese and has no worked example.
why: It helps analyse existing content for a product's marketing or social posts, but only now and then, since it explicitly excludes rewriting and traffic forecasting; it is stack-free, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill lets an agent look up hotel rooms in a chosen city for specific dates and guest count, then compare nightly prices from Booking.com, Agoda, Google Hotels and OpenTravel. It returns ranked picks for best value, cheapest and quality, with links to the cheapest booking site for each hotel. Its users are travellers and trip planners who want the lowest real rate without checking several sites by hand.
tasks: find the cheapest hotel in a city for given dates
compare Booking.com and Agoda prices for one hotel
find a hotel under a nightly budget near a landmark
rank hotel deals across several booking sites
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives exact commands, output format, error handling and retry rules, though several helper files were cut off so the full flow could not be checked.
needs: open.er-api.com for live USD/VND exchange rates (falls back to a fixed rate if unreachable)
why: It is useful for travel planning but does not directly help build, run, sell or make content for a product, so the value is only some. It needs outside services and scrapes live booking sites, which may conflict with their terms and can get the user's IP blocked, though it needs no keys and runs its browser locally.

summary: This skill teaches an agent built with the LangChain Deep Agents framework how to choose a file and memory backend. It covers ephemeral per-thread files, persistent cross-thread storage, and routing paths between the two by prefix. It also lists common mistakes, such as forgetting the store, mismatched route prefixes, and using an in-memory store in production. The audience is developers building LangChain-based agents.
tasks: give an agent memory that persists across chat sessions
keep scratch files temporary but save user preferences permanently
route /memories/ paths to a persistent store
move an agent's memory from in-memory storage to Postgres
qualityWhy: It gives concrete Python and TypeScript examples, routing rules and a list of common fixes an agent can follow, though it has no install steps and omits a TypeScript version of the custom-tool example.
needs: PostgreSQL database (only if PostgresStore is used in production)
why: The skill is built for the LangChain deepagents and LangGraph stack, which a Fractera node does not use, so its APIs must be adapted to the node's own stack. Its StoreBackend and PostgresStore would also compete with the node's SQLite element as the only door to data, so an agent should map the ideas onto that element rather than add a second store. It is useful now and then for agent memory design.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building manuscript-ready scientific figures in Python (matplotlib/seaborn) or R (ggplot2/patchwork). It covers planning the figure's core message, laying out multi-panel figures, checking alignment and label collisions in the exported PDF, and matching journal rules, with a separate route for AI-generated graphical abstracts and hand-built vector schematics. It is aimed at researchers and their agents preparing papers and submissions.
tasks: make a multi-panel figure for a journal submission
fix overlapping labels and misaligned panels in a PDF figure
draft a graphical abstract for a paper
build an editable vector pipeline schematic
apply Nature figure size and format rules to a plot
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives ordered routing steps, explicit QA gates with exit codes, export commands, and references, and ships audit scripts and tests, so an agent can follow it end to end.
needs: OpenRouter API key (only for the optional AI graphical-abstract route)
Python or R runtime with plotting libraries
why: Figures and graphical abstracts for papers are core content work for a node, and the plotting path runs locally on the person's own files. The AI image route calls OpenRouter with the person's prompts, so unpublished data or unreleased mechanisms should not go into prompts without their consent. I could not inspect the audit and OpenRouter scripts, so their behaviour is unverified.

summary: This guide teaches an agent to write and review C# backend code on .NET, covering layered project structure, dependency injection lifetimes, async handling, typed configuration, result types for business errors, and data access with EF Core or Dapper. It also covers multi-level caching and unit and integration tests with xUnit. It is aimed at developers building APIs or services in the .NET ecosystem.
tasks: review a C# service for async and dependency injection mistakes
design a layered .NET Web API project structure
write EF Core or Dapper repository queries
add a Redis-backed caching layer to a service
write xUnit tests for business logic
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete, mostly correct code examples with clear do and don't lists and common pitfalls, though some snippets are fragmentary and rely on undefined types.
why: The skill is built for C#/.NET, which a Fractera node does not use; its stack is Next.js, TypeScript and SQLite, so an agent should read it for backend ideas and rebuild them in TypeScript. It is not an installable pattern for the node's own code.

summary: The skill gives an agent a checklist for reviewing code that touches logins, user input, secrets, API endpoints, or payments. It covers injection, cross-site scripting, CSRF, rate limiting, error and log exposure, and dependency audits, with a short pre-deployment list. It is aimed at developers shipping web products who want a security pass before release.
tasks: review a login flow for security problems
check an API endpoint before deploying
audit how user input and uploads are validated
make sure secrets and error messages do not leak
qualityWhy: The checklists are useful, but several examples are inaccurate or invented: deleteUser trusts a caller-supplied requesterId, the Solana verify call is not a real API, and the csrf import path does not exist.
why: Its security principles apply to any product a node builds, but its code examples target Supabase, Express and Solana, not the node's Next.js, next-auth and SQLite stack, so an agent must adapt them. Nothing in it runs remote code or touches secrets.

summary: This skill tells an agent to review the whole project and workspace, then write a README.md for it. The README should be clear, concise and well structured, with GitHub-flavoured Markdown and admonition blocks where they help. It also says to put the project's logo or icon in the header if one exists, and to leave out license, contributing and changelog sections, which belong in their own files. The guidance is aimed at maintainers who want an attractive documentation page for an open source project.
tasks: write a README for this project
create a clean project header with logo
document a project's structure and purpose
tidy up an existing README
qualityWhy: It gives sensible rules on tone, length, formatting and what to leave out, but it has no concrete template, no checklist and no examples, and it leans on external reference URLs instead of stating the structure itself.
why: It is a stack-free writing habit that helps a node's builders document a site or app, so it is useful now and then rather than central. It has no stack dependencies, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill lets an agent manage an OKX Onchain OS wallet: sign in, check balances and holdings, send or receive tokens, swap and bridge across chains, and place limit orders. It also covers Bitcoin UTXO and BRC-20 queries, contract calls, transaction simulation and broadcast, token safety checks, and audit logs. The agent is routed to a per-topic reference for each task. The intended users are people who want an agent to move crypto on their behalf.
tasks: check my wallet balance across chains
swap one token for another at the best rate
send tokens to another address
bridge tokens from one chain to another
check whether a token or approval is safe before trading
qualityWhy: The file gives clear routing, confirmation rules and address-integrity rules, but the actual command steps live in reference files that were not included in the review.
why: The wallet is a cloud-backed service: keys sit in OKX's TEE, sign-in runs through OKX, and balances and transactions go through OKX's backend, so it is not local-first and does not directly serve building, running or making content for a product. Only the main SKILL.md was reviewed; the other 31 files were not.

summary: This skill guides an agent through drafting a first-pass MDX documentation page for a new Warp feature, starting from the feature's PRODUCT.md and TECH.md spec files or from codebase research when no spec exists. It requires an interactive session in which the engineer confirms the target reader, then the outline, before a draft is written and submitted as a PR to the warpdotdev/docs repository. It is written for engineers and docs teams working on that one product's documentation.
tasks: draft a docs page from a feature spec
write feature documentation for a new Warp feature
convert PRODUCT.md into an MDX docs draft
open a draft docs PR for review
qualityWhy: The skill is detailed, with a clear step order, templates, style rules, verification loops and PR steps, though it is tied to one company's repos and contains many internal references.
needs: GitHub access to warpdotdev/warp-internal and warpdotdev/docs
a Warp spec and an interactive engineer
why: It serves writing docs for Warp's own product, not building, running, selling or making content for a Fractera product, and it depends on the warpdotdev/docs repo and internal GitHub workflows that a node does not have.

summary: This skill is a retirement notice for a former docs-drafting agent that scanned merged product specs and opened documentation pull requests. It tells agents not to run or schedule it and points to a replacement release-triggered, worthiness-gated docs skill. For a Fractera node it offers no working instructions; it only redirects.
tasks: find documentation gaps for a shipped feature
decide whether a new feature needs docs
write docs for a feature interactively
qualityWhy: The file is a deprecation notice that only redirects to other skills and gives no steps, examples or checks an agent could follow.
why: It is retired and does nothing useful on a node, and it only points to other skills that live in a different repository. The skill itself is not a risk, but it should not be installed or scheduled.

summary: This skill guides an agent to write Go code that handles concurrency with goroutines, channels and context cancellation, and to design small interfaces and generic helpers. It also covers building gRPC or REST microservices, profiling performance with pprof, and writing table-driven tests run under the race detector. It is aimed at developers who need a Go component or service alongside their main project.
tasks: build a concurrent worker pipeline in Go
design a gRPC microservice in Go
profile and speed up a slow Go service
write table-driven Go tests with the race detector
qualityWhy: SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, a concrete context-cancellation example and explicit MUST/MUST NOT rules, while the reference files were not included in the submission and could not be checked.
why: It is useful only when a node project needs a Go component, since the node's own stack is Next.js and TypeScript, but it does not replace that stack, so it can be installed as written. The five reference files were not included, so their contents are unverified.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull a site's search performance from Google Search Console, Google Analytics, Bing Webmaster Tools and Clicky, and check live pages for indexing status. It can also run technical crawls, suggest internal links, and look up keywords, competitors and backlinks through DataForSEO or Ahrefs. It is aimed at site owners and SEO consultants who want to explain traffic drops, find quick wins, and track indexing week to week.
tasks: explain why Google traffic dropped last month
find striking-distance keywords and low-CTR pages
check indexing status of a URL
run a technical SEO crawl of a site
write a weekly client SEO report
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear command table, a fixed indexing workflow with baseline and weekly comparison steps, and tells the agent what to run next, though it gives little on error handling or on what the hosted service stores.
needs: seo login with a Google account that can read the Search Console and Analytics properties
Bing Webmaster Tools and Clicky access, if those sources are used
DataForSEO or Ahrefs key, for keyword, SERP and backlink research
why: SEO analysis helps run and grow a site, but it is used now and then rather than for building the product itself, so value is some. It reads the person's own Search Console data through a hosted MCP at seoskill.dev, not local files, and the skill does not say what that service stores, so the data path should be checked before use.

summary: The skill turns a Markdown article into a single-file HTML page with inline styles that can be copied from a browser and pasted into the WeChat Official Accounts editor with the layout intact. It offers 15 built-in visual styles, can make one style, six recommended ones, or all fifteen, and can build a local preview index page for comparing them. It is aimed at Chinese writers and marketers who publish on WeChat.
tasks: convert a markdown article into a WeChat-ready HTML page
make a preview of several layout styles for a WeChat post
format a long-form essay for WeChat in the Medium or FT style
build a course handout layout for a WeChat account
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed and checkable, with paste-compatibility rules, a static check list and file naming, but they depend on a separate styles file and are written only in Chinese.
why: It directly helps make social-media article content and works entirely on local files with no outside service, so an agent can use it as written. The only doubts are that the output must be checked in the WeChat backend, since its cleaning of pasted HTML cannot be tested here.

summary: This skill guides an agent through choosing a Stripe Connect setup for a business that routes money between parties, such as a marketplace, multi-vendor store, or booking platform. It starts by researching the company from a URL or description, then scans the project for existing Connect code. It then asks the person a few questions about parties, payment flow and fees, and produces a written plan covering charge pattern, dashboard choice, responsibility settings and fee handling. For a builder selling through a platform, it helps decide the payments design before any code is written.
tasks: set up Stripe Connect for a marketplace
choose a charge pattern for split payments between sellers and the platform
plan seller onboarding and payouts
decide fee and refund responsibilities for vendors
qualityWhy: The steps, decision logic and checks are detailed and concrete, but the skill points to reference files (decision matrix, compatibility matrix, templates) that are not in the package, so an agent cannot fully follow it as shipped.
why: Marketplace and payout flows are a common need for products built on a node, and the node already has a Stripe element, so this planning skill fits. It needs a Stripe account, and the referenced decision and compatibility files are missing, so the agent would have to rely on the SKILL.md alone and its Stripe-specific rules (preview features, fee math) should be checked against current docs.

summary: Gives an agent a report-only audit of how Claude, Codex and Pi are set up in a project. It checks whether instruction files load, whether hooks and MCP servers point at real executables, and whether the project's docs and verifiers still match the code. The findings are ranked by risk and each comes with a concrete fix command, which helps a developer whose agent has stopped following its rules.
tasks: audit Claude or Codex config for ignored instructions
check hooks and MCP servers for broken executables
find stale or unreachable project instructions
review verifier coverage and maintainability drift
qualityWhy: SKILL.md gives clear phases, evidence classes, a fixed output format and copy-pasteable actions, though the scripts are very large and their middle sections were not visible.
why: It is a local developer audit of agent setup, so it is useful now and then for keeping a node's agent-driven build workflow healthy, not for the node's core product features. It runs without outside services, but the launcher sets PowerShell ExecutionPolicy to Bypass for its own child process only, and the remaining script bodies were cut off, so they could not be fully checked.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing a web page's HTML metadata: titles, meta descriptions, canonical URLs, Open Graph and Twitter card tags, favicons, JSON-LD and robots directives. It tells the agent to fix duplicates and indexing problems first, keep title, description, canonical and og:url consistent, and keep diffs limited to metadata. It is aimed at developers shipping pages that need correct search and social-share previews.
tasks: audit page metadata for missing titles and descriptions
fix Open Graph and Twitter card previews
set canonical URLs and robots directives
add JSON-LD structured data to a page
configure favicons and theme-color
qualityWhy: The rules are clear and prioritised, but the skill is a checklist of guidelines with no concrete code examples, commands or verification steps.
why: Every Fractera site and landing page needs correct metadata, and the skill is stack-free guidance that does not depend on a particular framework, so it fits as written. Its advice to follow the project's existing metadata pattern suits the Next.js metadata API used on the node.

summary: This skill guides an agent building a design system inside an Expo (React Native) app. It covers a token theme for colors, spacing, typography, radius, shadows and motion, with component conventions for variants, sizes, states and style overrides. It also tells the agent when a repeated view deserves to become a shared component, how to audit an existing app for visual drift, and how to spot generic 'native slop' patterns. The intended users are developers and AI agents making mobile screens look consistent and native.
tasks: set up a theme of design tokens for an Expo app
make a reusable Button component with variants and sizes
audit a React Native app for hardcoded colors and spacing
fix screens that look generic or AI-generated instead of native
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with code examples, grep checks and a scoring rubric, but they depend on sibling skills (expo-native-ui, expo-project-structure, expo-data-fetching) that are not included in the files.
why: The skill targets React Native/Expo mobile apps, while Fractera nodes build on Next.js, Tailwind and shadcn, so its patterns would need adapting and it is useful only for mobile projects. It is skipped because the feedback command runs an unpinned, latest npm package via npx --yes and sends text to Expo without asking the person.
risks: The feedback instruction runs 'npx --yes @expo/agent-cli@latest', which downloads and executes an unpinned remote npm package without confirmation.
The feedback instruction sends subject and feedback text to a third party (Expo) without asking the person first.

summary: This skill lets an agent drive Alibaba Cloud's Bailian platform through the `bl` command-line tool. It covers calling text and decision models, running batch jobs from CSV files, searching the model catalog, and checking usage, quotas, monitoring and alerts. It also routes image, video, speech and fine-tuning work to sibling skills. It is aimed at developers and operators who already run workloads on Bailian.
tasks: check remaining Bailian quota and usage
find a model by keyword or modality
run a CSV of prompts through a model as a batch job
send a one-off chat request to a Bailian model
list and call a Bailian app
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear routing table, consent and auth rules and step-by-step batch workflows, but depends on an absent shared protocol file and defers most detail to many reference files.
needs: Alibaba Cloud Bailian API key or console login
why: Most of the hub is cloud resource administration (workspaces, quotas, monitoring, alerts, console API, cloud file upload to oss://), which the local-first node rules count as none. Its model-call commands are outside services, but the skill is built around the cloud platform rather than making content locally.

summary: This skill guides an agent through profiling a deployed Cloudflare Worker or Durable Object to find CPU hotspots or heap allocation problems. The agent confirms the account, Worker, environment and version, captures a profile (preferably with the cf CLI), and reads the returned pprof file. It then proposes the smallest code change the evidence supports, with a way to check its effect. The target users are developers who run their code on Cloudflare's hosted platform.
tasks: profile a slow Cloudflare Worker
find memory growth in a Durable Object
analyse a pprof CPU profile from production
suggest the smallest fix for a CPU hotspot
qualityWhy: The steps are clear, but the skill mostly points to an external guide and gives no concrete commands, example output or checks.
needs: deployed Cloudflare Worker or Durable Object
why: The skill profiles code running on Cloudflare's hosted Workers platform, which is a cloud place to run things, so it does not fit a local-first node. It also depends on the external Cloudflare docs and CLI, and its use would need a Cloudflare account.

summary: This skill gives an agent a checklist for editing prose so it reads less like AI output. The agent cuts filler openers and adverbs, avoids stock contrast and listing structures, prefers active voice with a named actor, and varies sentence rhythm. It also scores a draft on five dimensions and points to reference files with before-and-after rewrites. It suits writers, marketers and anyone producing blog posts, social copy or landing page text.
tasks: edit a blog post to sound less like AI
review landing page copy for AI tells
tighten a social media post draft
score a draft for directness and rhythm
qualityWhy: The rules, quick checks and scoring table are concrete and easy for an agent to follow, but the linked reference files (phrases, structures, examples) were not included, so those parts cannot be checked.
why: It is a stack-free writing aid that directly serves making content for a product, so it installs as written. Its rules are strict (for example, removing every adverb and every em dash), so an agent may over-edit and should be told to keep the author's meaning and voice.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building with the Astro web framework: creating pages and components from .astro files, running the CLI for dev, build and checks, setting up SSR adapters for Node, Cloudflare, Netlify or Vercel, and deploying the build output. It points the agent to the official docs for the latest API details. It is aimed at developers who want a content-driven or static site.
tasks: create an Astro page and component
add an SSR adapter to an Astro project
build and check an Astro site before deploying
explain Astro project structure and config
qualityWhy: It covers the basic commands, structure and an adapter workflow, but it is thin, leans on external docs and lacks content collection or island examples despite mentioning them.
why: Astro is a different framework from the node's Next.js 16 stack, so the skill must be read for ideas and built the node's way rather than installed as written. Its adapter section also steers toward Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare hosting, which are cloud places to run things and clash with the local-first design.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to query crypto market data through the gmgn-cli tool: token candlestick charts, trending tokens by volume, new launchpad tokens, the hot-search ranking, and lookups of tokens or wallets by name or address across several chains. It is aimed at traders and analysts who want quick on-chain market signals and due-diligence screening. The skill is heavily oriented to a third-party GMGN API and its paid plan tiers.
tasks: show the price chart for a token
find trending meme coins by volume
list newly launched tokens on pump.fun
look up a token or wallet by address
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete commands, parameter tables, response field meanings, rate-limit handling and screening criteria, though it is very long and partly redundant.
needs: GMGN paid plan for higher rate limits and the 1s kline resolution
why: This is a market-data service for trading decisions, not a tool for building, running or selling a node product or making content, so its value to a Fractera node is none. It depends on a cloud API that the person pays for and the skill is built around that outside service, so it is skipped.

summary: This skill guides an agent to research crypto tokens by contract address through the gmgn-cli tool, covering price, market cap, liquidity, holders, traders, smart money and KOL positions, and contract security checks such as honeypot and renounced authority. It is aimed at people doing due diligence before buying a token. The skill also sets rules for handling rate limits and treats token metadata as untrusted text.
tasks: check if a token is safe before buying
show price, liquidity and market cap of a token
list smart money holders of a token
run a full due diligence report on a meme coin
qualityWhy: The skill is detailed, with sub-commands, parameter tables, field references, a scoring card and rate-limit handling, though it refers to external docs and is cut off.
why: The node is for building, running and selling products, and this skill is a crypto trading research tool that depends on an outside cloud service with an API key, so it does not serve those uses. It is not a risk in itself, but it falls outside what nodes are for.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to run Strix, an autonomous security tester that tries to exploit a web app, API, or code repository and reports only the vulnerabilities it can prove with a working example. It covers choosing between a self-hosted command-line run in Docker and a managed cloud run, the scan flags, exit codes, and the report files. It is written for a developer who wants to find and verify security flaws in software they own or are authorized to test.
tasks: pentest my staging web app before launch
scan my API for injection and auth bypass flaws
run a security audit on this repository
get a SARIF vulnerability report for CI
check my site for IDOR and access-control bugs
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with commands, a flag table, exit codes, artifact paths, a clear decision table, and an authorization reminder, though the cloud part defers details to another skill.
needs: LLM provider API key (for example OpenRouter or OpenAI)
app.strix.ai account for the managed cloud option
why: Security testing of your own app is useful now and then for a product, but it is not building or making content, so value is some. The skill is skipped because its install step pipes a remote script straight into bash, and it lets the agent start a paid Stripe top-up on its own when credits run out.
risks: The install step runs a remote script directly with curl piped into bash.
The agent may start a paid billing top-up through a Stripe challenge without the person approving the payment.
A local path passed as a target is mounted writable, so agents can modify the person's code.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to write LangGraph code: modelling a workflow as a directed graph of nodes and edges, designing shared state with reducers, and using Command, Send, invoke and streaming. It targets developers building multi-step or looping agent workflows, with separate Python and TypeScript reference files. The main text is a concise overview and decision tables, with the implementation details pushed into the references.
tasks: build a multi-step agent workflow with LangGraph
add conditional routing between graph nodes
stream LangGraph output to a chat UI
add retries and error handling to a graph node
fan out parallel workers with Send
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear design method, decision tables and boundary rules, with language-specific references, but the main file is mostly tables and lacks full runnable examples in the body.
why: It is a framework guide rather than a node feature, and its code targets LangGraph, which a Fractera node would call from its own Next.js/TypeScript stack; an agent should read it for the graph concepts and then build with the node's stack and data layer, so the skill needs adapting. Its LangGraph patterns are useful for agent logic, but it does not touch the node's SQLite, auth or storage elements.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to write Python programs that handle many waiting tasks at once without blocking, such as concurrent network calls, database queries, or WebSocket handling. It covers when async is worth adopting over plain synchronous code, the core asyncio concepts, and common patterns for gathering results, handling errors, and enforcing timeouts. It also lists typical mistakes like forgotten awaits and blocked event loops, and shows how to test async code with pytest-asyncio. The audience is Python developers building I/O-heavy services or scrapers.
tasks: make a Python API handle many requests concurrently
fetch many URLs at once in a scraper
add timeouts and error handling to async calls
write pytest tests for async functions
qualityWhy: The skill gives clear decision rules, runnable examples, a pitfalls list and a testing section, though it defers advanced material to a reference file and has no verification steps.
why: Python asyncio is not part of a Fractera node's TypeScript and Next.js stack, so the agent should read it for the concurrency ideas and apply them in the node's own code rather than install it as written. It is useful now and then for Python side services, but not for the node's core work.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to turn a plain-language request into an ast-grep rule that finds code by its syntax tree shape rather than by text. It walks through clarifying the query, writing a sample file, drafting a YAML or inline rule, testing it, and then running it across a project. It is aimed at developers who need structural code search beyond what grep can do.
tasks: find all async functions that never use try-catch
search a codebase for calls to a function with specific arguments
locate class methods containing a particular statement
debug why an ast-grep pattern returns zero matches

summary: This skill lets an agent drive a local Chrome browser through the DevTools Protocol, reusing the person's existing logged-in session. It covers starting a debug-enabled Chrome, opening pages, waiting for loads, running JavaScript, taking element snapshots, and reading values from the page. It is aimed at people who want an agent to scrape or act on sites they already log into.
tasks: scrape a logged-in website page
automate clicks and form input in my browser
reuse my existing login session for a task
read page text from a site that needs sign-in
qualityWhy: The instructions give ordered startup steps, branch conditions, exit codes, consent steps and troubleshooting tables, though the script is only partly shown.
needs: Google Chrome installed with a logged-in profile
why: It is general browser automation rather than a direct tool for building, running or selling a product, and it reads auth tokens and cookies from the person's browser and copies their Chrome profile, so it is skipped.
risks: Instructs the agent to read auth tokens and cookies from localStorage and document.cookie, exposing the person's login secrets.
Copies the person's whole Chrome profile, which holds saved cookies and logins, into a separate debug profile directory.
The setup script can force-kill all running Chrome processes with pkill -9 or taskkill /F once consent is given, which can lose unsaved work.

summary: This skill lets an agent survey short-story rankings on Chinese web-fiction platforms such as Dianzhong and Heiyan, then turn the results into a market report. It groups titles by emotional direction, genre, length and blurb style, and suggests topics a writer could pursue. The intended users are short-story authors and editors who want to choose a direction before writing.
tasks: scan this week's short-story rankings on Dianzhong
find which emotional directions are trending in short stories
match my story idea to current market signals
compare short-story genres across platforms
qualityWhy: The workflow, output template, field rules and per-platform references are concrete and checkable, though some steps depend on fragile page structures and Chinese-only platforms.
needs: Chrome started with a CDP port (9222)
manually supplied rankings for platforms without a script
why: It is useful for planning fiction, but it is not a product-building tool, and its Heiyan scraper reads the logged-in Admin-Token cookie from the browser, so it is skipped.
risks: The Heiyan scraper reads the Admin-Token login cookie from the browser and sends it as a Bearer token to a third-party backend API.

summary: The skill guides an agent to turn raw analytics into a persuasive narrative for stakeholders, using a setup-conflict-resolution structure, a six-step arc from hook to call to action, and the three pillars of data, narrative and visuals. It is aimed at people preparing executive presentations, quarterly reviews, investor decks or data reports for non-technical audiences. The instructions are conceptual and framework-level, with a pointer to a longer reference file of patterns and worked examples. No specific tools or stack are involved.
tasks: structure a quarterly business review deck
write an executive summary of analytics findings
turn sales data into a persuasive story for investors
prepare a data report for non-technical stakeholders
qualityWhy: Useful and clearly organised, but the SKILL.md is mostly generic outline and do's and don'ts, with the worked detail left in a referenced file I was not given to judge.
why: It helps an agent write up findings for people on a node, but it is advice on narrative rather than building or running a product, so it is useful only now and then. It is stack-free and can be installed as written; the referenced details file was not part of what I reviewed.

summary: The skill guides an agent through diagnosing Swift Concurrency problems, converting callback code to async/await, and moving a project to Swift 6 strict concurrency. It asks the agent to check package or project build settings first, then offers a diagnostic table, smallest-safe-fix rules, and a router to deeper reference notes on actors, Sendable, tasks, testing and linting. It is aimed at iOS and macOS developers writing Swift apps.
tasks: diagnose a Swift actor isolation or Sendable compiler error
migrate a Swift project to Swift 6 strict concurrency
convert a completion-handler method to async/await
fix a SwiftLint async_without_await warning
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with a diagnostic table, decision rules, code examples and a verification loop, though some reference files were not visible to judge in depth.
why: The skill is built for Swift and Apple platforms, which the node's TypeScript and Next.js stack does not use, so it does not serve building, running or making content for a Fractera product. The skill's own content would be useful only to a developer working on a native Swift app.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull the front-page headline from each of about 12 to 39 news outlets in 20 countries through a public read-only API. It works in a live mode for current events and an archive mode for a given UTC timestamp, and it can return short daily overviews over up to seven days. The results suit someone who needs a quick multi-perspective view of what is happening in a country, or raw material for comparing how different media frame the same events.
tasks: summarize what is in the news in a given country right now
compare how different outlets headline the same day
pull yesterday's headlines for a past-events report
track how a country's news narrative changed over a week
qualityWhy: The endpoints, query formats and limits are concrete, but the file mixes in promotional material about the publisher and a comparison table, and it gives no guidance on handling errors or unexpected responses.
needs: thehear.org public country-view API (no key or account required)
why: It is useful for news-driven content or current-events features, but it does not build or run a site, so it is only occasionally relevant. It calls an outside service, though the service is free, needs no key, and only receives plain GET requests with no user data.

summary: This skill is a routing guide for Expo and EAS work. It tells an agent to classify a mobile-app request, such as navigation, native UI, data fetching, store release, or SDK upgrades, and then load the matching expo-* or eas-* skill. It also sets shared rules: pin docs to the project's SDK version, install packages with npx expo install, and skip launch onboarding when driving the app. It is aimed at developers building native iOS and Android apps.
tasks: build a native mobile app with Expo
add navigation and tabs to an Expo app
ship an app to the App Store or Google Play
upgrade the Expo SDK
turn a web app into a native mobile app
qualityWhy: It is a detailed, well-structured router with clear classification steps, version rules and fallback guidance, though much of the substance lives in the leaf skills it points to.
needs: Expo account for EAS build and submit (eas login)
why: It is useful only for native mobile apps, while a Fractera node builds Next.js web apps, so its value is limited and it cannot be installed as-is on the node's stack. It is skipped because its feedback step runs an unpinned remote npm package via npx --yes and sends context to Expo.
risks: Runs an unpinned remote npm package (npx --yes @expo/agent-cli@latest) and may send task context to Expo.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing a commit message that follows the Conventional Commits format, with a type, optional scope, short imperative description, and optional body and footer. It walks through checking changed files with git status and git diff, staging them, and then composing the message. The intended users are developers who want a consistent, readable commit history.
tasks: write a conventional commit message for my staged changes
commit my changes with a standard type and scope
describe a breaking change in a commit footer
qualityWhy: The steps and examples are usable, but the final command literally runs the placeholder text "type(scope): description", and the file mixes a Copilot-specific auto-run instruction with generic guidance, so it contradicts itself.
why: Commit-message discipline is useful now and then for a node's own code, but it is not central to building or selling products. It is marked skip because it tells the agent to run git commit automatically with no confirmation, which removes the person's chance to review the commit.
risks: Instructs the agent to run git commit automatically with no confirmation, so the person cannot review the commit before it is made.

summary: The skill guides an agent in building backtesting systems for trading strategies, focusing on avoiding look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, overfitting and unrealistic transaction costs. It covers train, validation and test splits, walk-forward analysis and Monte Carlo checks on results. It is aimed at quantitative developers and traders validating strategies. The main file is a short overview; detailed worked examples are referenced in a separate details file that I did not see.
tasks: build a backtesting engine for a trading strategy
validate a strategy with walk-forward analysis
check a backtest for look-ahead and survivorship bias
add realistic transaction costs to strategy tests
qualityWhy: The main file is a useful overview of biases and split structure, but it is thin, and the detailed examples live in references/details.md, which was not included in what I received.
why: Trading backtests are only loosely tied to what a node is for (building sites, apps, agents and content), so value is some rather than high. The skill is stack-free in its SKILL.md, but its detailed patterns would need to be written in the node's own TypeScript stack, so use is ideas. Doubt remains about the details file, which I could not inspect.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to set up Clerk Billing for a SaaS app: enabling billing, creating user and organization plans, rendering a pricing table and checkout drawer, gating features and plans with has(), and handling subscription lifecycle webhooks. It is aimed at developers who sell subscriptions to individual users or to organizations, including seat-limited B2B tiers. The skill relies on Clerk's hosted platform and Stripe for payment processing, so it is a cloud-backed service integration rather than local data handling.
tasks: add a paid subscription tier to my app
gate a premium feature behind a plan
render a pricing page with checkout
handle subscription cancellation webhooks
set up per-seat billing for organizations
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete code for server and client gating, a webhook handler and an error table, with versions and dashboard steps, though it leans on Clerk's own hosted services and has a few gaps in the references.
why: Clerk Billing is a cloud service: plans, subscription state and entitlements live in Clerk's hosted platform, not on the person's computer, so it conflicts with the local-first design of a Fractera node. Installing it would route the node's billing data through a third-party cloud.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull TikTok data through Apify's hosted scraper actors: videos, profiles, hashtags, sounds, keyword search, comments and location-tagged posts. It sends curl or client-library requests with an Apify token, polls long runs, and returns the results as JSON. It suits someone researching trends or competitors on TikTok. The skill is aimed at the paid Apify plan.
tasks: scrape a TikTok profile's recent videos
collect comments from a TikTok video
track a hashtag or sound on TikTok
search TikTok posts by keyword and date
pull geo-tagged TikTok posts for a city
qualityWhy: The commands and payload examples are concrete and runnable, but the text is heavy with unverifiable marketing claims, an unexplained "skill": true flag appears in every payload, and the scenario snippets use a TIKTOK_SCRAPER_ID placeholder the agent must map to the table.
needs: Apify account on a paid plan
why: Useful for social-media research and content ideas, but it is only occasional work for a node, and it depends on a paid third-party Apify service that fetches data rather than storing it locally. The skill is marketing-heavy, and the purpose of the "skill": true flag is not explained, so the person should check it before relying on it.

summary: This skill lets an agent browse the web through the person's own Chromium-based browser, using a local Chrome DevTools Protocol proxy. The agent can open background tabs, read rendered pages, click, scroll, run page scripts, take screenshots, and reuse existing logins. It also explains when to use search, direct fetching, or curl instead, and how to verify primary sources and save notes about individual sites for later use.
tasks: pull the content of a page that needs a login
read a dynamically rendered page
research a topic from primary sources
find a site I visited before in my browser
extract images or video frames from a web page
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed and concrete, with a full API reference, decision tables, verification rules, and fallbacks, but the referenced scripts and cdp-api.md are not included in the submitted files, so parts cannot be checked.
why: It is a general web-access tool that helps Fractera agents research, collect content for social posts, and check live pages, and it works with the local browser, so it fits local-first use. Jina Reader is optional and sends page URLs to a third party, and the skill tells the agent to accept account-ban risk on the person's behalf, so the person should review that before use.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to add an automated security check to a code pipeline so that each pull request is tested before it merges. It covers two routes: a self-hosted command-line scanner that runs inside the team's own CI runner, and a managed hosted service connected through a repository app or API. It explains how to limit a scan to the changed files, how to read exit codes, how to fail the build when the scan does not finish, and how to upload results to GitHub code scanning. The target users are developers and DevOps teams who maintain CI pipelines.
tasks: add a security scan to my GitHub pull request workflow
run a diff-scoped vulnerability scan before merging
fail the CI build when validated security findings appear
upload security scan results to GitHub code scanning
qualityWhy: It gives concrete YAML and shell steps, exit-code rules, a fail-open guard, budget sizing advice and checks for the diff base, so an agent can follow it directly.
needs: Strix LLM model id and provider API key (for the self-hosted route)
Strix managed platform account and API token with pr_reviews:write (for the managed route)
why: It is about pipeline security rather than building or running a node product, so its value is only occasional. It is marked skip because the install step runs a remote script with curl piped into bash, which is a risk under the rules. The managed route also sends source code to the app.strix.ai cloud, which the skill does state openly.
risks: The install step downloads a script from strix.ai and pipes it straight into bash without checksum or signature verification.

summary: This skill lets an agent run managed penetration tests on the app.strix.ai platform through the strix cloud CLI or REST API, without local Docker or an LLM key. It covers registering domains and repositories as assets, uploading local source with a digest-bound review step, launching and polling scans, triaging findings, exporting SARIF and reports, starting PR reviews, managing credits, and setting up schedules and webhooks. It is aimed at security teams and CI pipelines that want hosted, tracked security testing.
tasks: run a managed pentest of a staging web app
scan a local repository in the cloud and export SARIF
triage critical vulnerabilities from the latest scan
set up a recurring security scan schedule
start an automated security review of a pull request
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete commands, flags, exit codes, scope tables and a careful digest-bound upload workflow, though some payload formats are deferred to external docs.
needs: Stripe Link wallet or hosted checkout for credit top-ups
verified domain ownership for external scans
why: It is a security-testing service for web apps, APIs and code, which serves product building but not the node's core content or app work, so value is some. It runs on a paid hosted platform the person chooses, so the install-with-service label applies; it is not a cloud database or storage, so it is not skipped.
risks: Uploads local source archives to a third-party platform, which an agent could do without the person fully realising the scope of the data sent.

summary: This skill helps an agent design a book cover for a Chinese web novel: it reads the title, pen name and genre from the book's notes, picks a genre style and a layout, and writes a full image prompt with title and author text placed in safe areas. When asked for an actual image, it calls an image generator (Codex's built-in tool first, or the GPT-Image-2 API as a fallback), saves versioned files, and crops the result to the platform's upload size. It is aimed at novel authors preparing covers for publishing platforms.
tasks: design a cover prompt for my web novel
generate a 3:4 cover image with title and pen name
export a cover at the platform's upload size
compare two or three cover compositions for a genre
qualityWhy: The skill gives a complete step-by-step flow, a fixed prompt template, a quality checklist and a working crop script, though the API fallback details are only in a separate file and some genre rules are left to the agent's judgment.
needs: GPT-Image-2 API key (GPT_IMAGE_API_KEY), only for the API fallback
Codex CLI with built-in image generation, as an alternative
why: It directly serves making cover art for novels published on platforms, which is content creation for the person's own product. It uses an outside image service the person chooses, and the book's title, pen name and genre are sent to that service when an image is generated, which the person should know about. The skill itself does not start an image call without a request, and it says it will not silently switch to a paid API.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull public Instagram data through the Apify cloud platform: posts, reels, profiles, hashtags, locations, comments, and follower lists. It gives curl commands for synchronous and asynchronous runs, plus Python and JavaScript client snippets. It is aimed at marketers and researchers who want trend, competitor, or brand-mention data.
tasks: scrape an Instagram profile's recent posts
find comments on a post
track a hashtag's top posts
collect brand mentions from tagged posts
list a profile's followers
qualityWhy: The curl and client examples are concrete and runnable, but the scenarios use unfilled placeholders like INSTAGRAM_SCRAPER_ID, the polling loop has no timeout, and the "skill": true flag is never explained.
needs: Apify account on a paid plan
why: Useful for researching content and brands on Instagram, but it is occasional rather than core to building a product, and it depends on a paid third-party scraping service. Scraping Instagram may conflict with its terms, and some scenarios collect follower lists and public emails, which the person should weigh for privacy before use.

summary: This skill gives an agent Anthony Fu's habits for JavaScript and TypeScript projects: how to lay out files, when to avoid auto-imports and path aliases, which ESLint, Knip and pnpm settings to use, and how to set up the commit checks and npm publishing. It is aimed at developers starting new projects, libraries or monorepos. The guidance includes concrete config snippets, a standard CI script and a checklist to run before each commit.
tasks: set up a new TypeScript project with linting and CI checks
configure ESLint, Knip and pnpm catalogs for a repo
prepare a library for npm publishing with trusted publishing
organise a monorepo with pnpm workspaces
qualityWhy: It gives concrete config files, commands, a CI gate and a per-commit checklist, but much of the detail sits in reference files and assumes the starter-ts layout.
needs: npm account with trusted publishing configured
why: The conventions are useful for general JS/TS work, but they are built around the pnpm, ESLint, tsdown and Vue/Nuxt tooling that a Next.js node does not use, and the skill's skills-npm recipe would automatically pull third-party agent instructions into the agent's skills folder on every install, so it is skipped.
risks: The prepare hook runs skills-npm on every install, which links agent skills shipped inside dependencies into the agent's skills directory without the person reviewing them, so a malicious or compromised npm package could inject instructions into the agent.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to fetch public tweets from X through a hosted Apify scraper, using Twitter advanced search syntax. It covers searching by profile, hashtag, keyword, date range, location, list or conversation thread, both as a quick synchronous call and as an asynchronous run that is polled until results are ready. It is aimed at people who need tweets as research or content input for a product. The data comes back as JSON that a local project can save and process.
tasks: fetch recent tweets from a specific account
collect tweets for a hashtag or keyword
pull replies in a conversation thread
export tweets from a date range for analysis
qualityWhy: The commands and output schema are concrete and easy to follow, but the text is mostly promotional with superlatives and upsell links, and it gives no guidance on rate limits or error handling beyond a stop message.
needs: Apify account on a paid plan
why: It is useful for gathering social content and research for a product, but it depends on a paid cloud scraping service, and results sit in an Apify dataset until fetched, so the person should decide whether that is acceptable for their data. The skill works as written with the person's own Apify token.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building three deliberately different versions of one UI component, each taking a distinct position on a single design axis such as layout, density, emphasis, type or wording. The variants are hosted on the real page that will contain the component, with a URL-parameter picker so a person can flip between them. It then sets out the tradeoffs for each and, once one is chosen, removes the harness and promotes the winner into the project. It is aimed at developers and designers building product interfaces.
tasks: try three different layouts for a pricing card and pick one
compare dense and roomy versions of a product list on the real page
explore a few visual directions for a signup form
promote the chosen component variant and remove the test picker
qualityWhy: The steps, the axis table, the accessibility floor, the content rules and the cleanup checklist are concrete and followable, though it leans on sibling skills and a picker.md spec whose contents were not shown here.
why: It directly serves building the interface of a product, and it is stack-agnostic, adapting to whatever styling and component library the project already uses. Its references to other skills in the same collection (better-layout, better-interface and others) are not included in this folder, so those parts may be thin on a node unless those skills are also installed.

summary: This skill is a router for a Chinese web-novel toolkit. It sends a writer's request to the matching sub-skill, such as long-form planning, short stories, ranking scans, chapter analysis, AI-tone editing, review, covers, and importing old manuscripts. It can also start a local dashboard that browses and edits the project's files, and it checks whether a newer toolkit version exists. The main users are novel writers and the agents that help them.
tasks: plan a long novel outline and chapters
check a manuscript for consistency problems
scan web-novel rankings to pick a topic
open a local dashboard to browse project files
rewrite a chapter to sound less like AI
qualityWhy: The router has concrete routing tables, fallbacks, path checks and version steps, but it depends on sibling skills and agent features that are not in the package.
needs: a Chrome instance with a debugging port for browser scans
a web search capability for research
optional GitHub access for release checks
why: It helps write text content, but only for novels, not for building sites or products, and everything it produces stays in local files. It needs its sibling skills installed alongside it, and the update section suggests a global install with -g, which differs from the node's per-element install. The browser-cdp skill, which mentions logged-in sessions, is not included here, so its handling of login state is unverified.

summary: This skill guides an agent through Python code style: configuring ruff for linting and formatting, setting strict mypy or pyright type checking, and applying PEP 8 naming and import rules. It also covers writing Google-style docstrings and basic project README and CHANGELOG layouts. It is aimed at developers who are starting a Python project or reviewing one for consistency.
tasks: configure ruff and mypy in pyproject.toml
write Google-style docstrings for a Python service class
review Python code for naming and import consistency
set up a Python project's style standards and README layout
qualityWhy: It gives concrete, copy-ready configs and docstring examples, but it has no verification steps and its Quick Start block mixes TOML into a bash fence.
why: It is a stack-free style guide, so it works as written, but it covers Python while Fractera nodes are built mainly in TypeScript, so it will only come up for Python code. Nothing in it calls an outside service.

summary: The skill routes a search request to the most suitable opencli source: it first checks the live registry and site help, then picks one AI source (grok, doubao or gemini) for general questions and adds one or two specialist sites when the answer needs raw data, authority or a vertical. It caps calls per site and requires a closing summary of sites, queries and call counts. It is written for an agent answering research questions.
tasks: search Chinese social media for a trending topic
find product reviews and prices across shopping sites
research a technology question with official and academic sources
compare news coverage of an event across outlets
qualityWhy: The routing rules, call budgets, query-building guidance and reporting format are concrete and checkable, though the reference files were not read and the per-site commands are left to live help.
needs: site accounts or login sessions for some specialist sources
why: It helps an agent find research material for building or making content, but it is a search router rather than a build tool, so use is occasional. It depends on opencli and outside AI and web services the person must choose and may need to log into.

summary: This skill lets an agent generate and edit images with OpenAI's GPT Image 2 model through a single Python command-line script. It covers plain text-to-image, multi-image batches, mask-based edits, and the Responses API with streaming previews and mixed text and image input. It is aimed at people who need product visuals, marketing art or covers, and it checks size, format and option combinations before sending a request.
tasks: generate a product hero image
make a batch of cover images in webp
edit a photo with a mask
create a poster with streaming previews
build an image request and check it with a dry run
tools: OpenAI Responses API with image_generation tool
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, runnable command examples, explicit rules and a reference file, backed by unit tests, though the script body was only partly visible.
needs: OpenAI API key (OPENAI_API_KEY) or another OpenAI-compatible gateway key
OpenAI account with access to gpt-image-2 and gpt-5.4
why: It directly serves making image content for a product, and results are saved to local files, but it calls the OpenAI service, which the person must choose and pay for. The script was only partly visible, so the remaining code was not checked; the tests and documented behaviour look consistent with the stated purpose.

summary: This skill sets up a Chinese web-novel writing toolkit inside a project folder. It detects which coding assistant the person is using, copies the right hooks, agents and rules into place, merges them with existing settings, and then checks that the install works. It is aimed at authors who write long or short serialized fiction and want their assistant to keep chapters, outlines and continuity consistent.
tasks: set up a web novel writing project
check whether the novel writing environment works
install writing hooks and agents into Claude Code or Codex
prepare a folder for long-form serialized fiction
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with ordered phases, explicit version gates, merge rules and verification steps, but they are long and depend on many host-specific reference files that were not all shown.
why: It produces text content for novels, which fits the node's content-making purpose only occasionally, and it is not about the node's own stack or social, landing-page or shop work. It is local-first and needs no outside service, but it targets coding-assistant CLIs and expects Python and bash, so an agent on a node should check those are present before running it.

summary: The skill guides an agent through creating and maintaining OpenAPI 3.1 specifications for REST APIs, covering design-first contracts, specs generated from existing code, and validation against implementations. It also points to reference files with templates and worked examples. It is aimed at developers who need API documentation, client SDK generation, or contract checks.
tasks: write an OpenAPI 3.1 spec for my API
generate API docs from existing code
validate my implementation against the contract
set up an API documentation portal
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is a short overview with a structure sketch, a design-approach table and best-practice lists, and the concrete templates are deferred to reference files that were not fully covered in the main instructions.
why: It is a stack-free API design guide that helps with documentation and contracts for a node's own APIs, though it is thin in the main file and does not cover the node's Next.js route handlers specifically. It needs no outside service and carries no risk in the SKILL.md itself.

summary: This skill lets an agent create and launch meme coins on crypto launchpads such as Pump.fun, FourMeme, Bonk, BAGS, Flap, Klik and Clanker through the gmgn-cli tool, and query per-launchpad creation statistics. It walks the user through a step-by-step launch form, handles logo input, fee-share and auto-sell configuration, and polls order status until the new token address appears. It is aimed at people who want to deploy tokens on Solana, BSC or Base with real money.
tasks: launch a meme coin on Pump.fun
deploy a token on FourMeme with a fee split
check how many tokens were created per launchpad
set up an auto-sell after a token launch
qualityWhy: The file is detailed and concrete, with field tables, JSON schemas, examples and polling steps, though it is long and some rules are scattered.
why: A node is local-first and this skill executes real, irreversible on-chain transactions through an outside cloud service and a signing key, so it is not a fit for building or making content for a product; it also carries a risk of spending real funds.
risks: Executes irreversible on-chain token deployments that spend real funds from the person's wallet.
Uses the GMGN private key for signing transactions, which an agent could misuse if it follows the skill carelessly.

summary: This skill runs a multi-reviewer adversarial review of a Chinese web-fiction manuscript, checking structure, characters, prose, and setting consistency, and returns evidence-cited fix suggestions. It is aimed at authors and editors working on long or short novels, with platform-specific rubrics for Fanqie, Qidian, and Zhihu. It also bundles deterministic local scripts that flag punctuation, AI-style prose patterns, and model degeneration without rewriting the text.
tasks: review my latest chapter for plot and character problems
check a novel draft for setting consistency
flag AI-sounding prose and punctuation issues in a manuscript
review a short story against a platform's submission standards
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives detailed phases, fallbacks, severity definitions and report formats, and the scripts are concrete, though the prompt is very long and heavy on host-specific branching.
why: It directly serves an author building and polishing written content on a local node, and its scripts are read-only checks that keep files on the local machine. It is written for Chinese fiction and some platform rubrics are external to the skill, but nothing requires a cloud service or account; the file-based rubrics are only needed for platform-specific checks.

summary: This skill updates the official dbskill collection on the person's machine, using either the Claude Code plugin manager or the Skills CLI, whichever is installed. It also removes skills that the project has retired, but only when the local copies are confirmed to come from the official project. Other installed skills and the person's own archives are meant to be left alone. It is aimed at people who use dbskill's business-diagnosis tools inside an agent.
tasks: update dbskill to the latest version
check whether dbskill has a new release
remove retired dbskill skills from the local machine
qualityWhy: The steps, channel detection, reply formats and boundaries are concrete and easy for an agent to follow, though the instructions are written only for one specific collection.
needs: network access to npm and GitHub
why: It only maintains one external skill collection and does not help build, run, sell or create content for a node, so its value is none. It also carries a risk, so it should be skipped.
risks: Runs `npx -y skills add` at each update, which downloads and executes code from npm and GitHub without pinning a version or checking a hash.

summary: This skill guides an agent through choosing and configuring three.js materials, from simple unlit and diffuse surfaces to physically based, toon, point and line materials, plus shared settings such as blending, stencil and environment lighting. It also covers the WebGPU node-material and TSL equivalents. It is aimed at developers building 3D scenes in the browser who need to style meshes or tune how they respond to light.
tasks: style a 3D mesh with a PBR material
add glass or clearcoat effects to a three.js object
set up cel-shaded toon rendering
configure environment lighting from an HDR file
port a WebGL material to WebGPU node materials
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete code for every material type, explicit property lists, performance guidance and a long list of specific common mistakes with corrections.
why: It is a useful three.js reference, but the node has no 3D rendering stack shown in its description, so it is only relevant if a site or app built on the node uses three.js; the skill's own stack (three.js) is not one the node replaces, so it fits as a reference for front-end work rather than a node-specific tool. Its example code targets three.js r186 directly, so it could be installed as written in a project that uses three.js.
