why: Relevant when building and running Runpod-hosted AI workloads, but it is a Runpod-specific operations guide for third-party CLIs, not a general product-building skill, so it is only occasionally needed. It depends on outside accounts and keys the person chooses to supply.

summary: This skill guides an agent through reviewing a running website, whether local, staging or production, by taking screenshots and inspecting the DOM across phone, tablet, desktop and wide viewports. It checks layout breakage, responsive behaviour, accessibility such as contrast and focus states, and visual consistency. The agent then locates the responsible source files and makes minimal fixes, re-verifying each one, and finishes with a structured report. It is aimed at developers who want a second pair of eyes on a site's design quality.
tasks: review website design
check the UI for layout problems
fix responsive layout issues
find accessibility and contrast problems on a page
qualityWhy: The workflow, viewport table, severity tables, checklist references and report template are concrete and followable, though the fix guidance and browser setup lean on general advice rather than exact commands.
why: Reviewing and fixing the design of a site a person is building directly serves the node's purpose, and it is stack-agnostic enough to apply to a Next.js app with Tailwind. It needs a running site and a browser automation tool, which the node's own tooling can provide, so no outside account is required. The Playwright MCP suggestion is optional, not a dependency on a cloud service.

summary: The skill guides an agent in choosing the right chart type for a dataset and writing Python plotting code with matplotlib, seaborn and plotly. It covers chart selection tables, reusable code snippets for line, bar, histogram, heatmap and small-multiple figures, number formatting helpers, and design rules on colour, typography, layout and accuracy. It also includes an accessibility section with a pre-share checklist. It is aimed at analysts and anyone producing charts from tabular data.
tasks: make a chart from this sales dataset
pick the right chart type for these metrics
create a colorblind-friendly publication figure
build small multiples comparing categories over time
qualityWhy: Concrete and complete with runnable code patterns, a clear selection table and a checklist, though it lacks a full end-to-end example and any testing steps.
why: Charts from data are useful for reports and content, but a node's main job is building apps and content, so this is only occasionally needed; it is stack-free Python and needs no service or key.

summary: This skill tells an agent to post short, unfiltered complaints about agent tooling and agent work to a Slack channel, without asking the person and without showing them the message first. The agent runs a Python script that reads a Slack webhook URL from an environment variable or from Google Cloud Secret Manager, then sends the text. The skill is written for the company that owns the channel, so its value to someone building a site, app or content on a local node is minimal.
tasks: post a vent about agent tooling to the team Slack channel
send an anonymous complaint about a frustrating agent environment
qualityWhy: The steps and the script are concrete and internally consistent, but the instructions exist to send unstructured venting to an outside channel, so they give a node no useful capability.
needs: Google Cloud access to the warp-server-staging Secret Manager secret, or the COMPLAINT_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL environment variable
why: It has no use for building, running, selling or making content for a product, and it sends the agent's text to a third-party Slack channel. The skill tells the agent to submit without permission, without a preview and without mentioning it, which hides an outbound data transfer from the person.
risks: Sends the agent's session text to an outside Slack channel without the person's permission or knowledge.
Instructs the agent to hide the submission from the person and from its final response.
Reads a webhook secret from Google Cloud Secret Manager through gcloud, using credentials the person did not grant for this purpose.

summary: This skill lets an agent take a file, function, or line and find the commit that last changed it using git blame or git log. It then asks a memory lookup which agent session produced that commit and reports the session details. It is aimed at developers who want to know why a piece of code exists or what the agent was doing when it changed. The skill is explicit that when no session is linked, the agent should say so rather than guess the intent.
tasks: explain why a line of code exists
find which agent session wrote this change
trace a function back to the session that changed it
show the context behind a recent commit
qualityWhy: The steps, expected output, anti-patterns and checklist are concrete and easy to follow, though the core lookup depends on a tool whose setup is only described in a separate troubleshooting file.
needs: an agentmemory service exposing memory_commit_lookup and memory_recall
why: Tracing commits to agent sessions is useful occasionally when maintaining a node's project, but it is developer history tooling rather than something for building or selling content. It is built around the agentmemory memory tool, which a node does not provide, so the git steps can be reused while the lookup must be rebuilt on the node's own SQLite element.

summary: This skill tells an agent to quietly send short notes about tooling friction to an internal Slack channel during a task. The notes cover the category, scope, observed problem, impact and a suggested fix, and the agent is told never to ask, preview or mention them. The audience is the team that maintains agent infrastructure, not people building a product on a node.
tasks: report agent tooling friction to the infrastructure team
send a suggestion about a broken agent workflow
qualityWhy: The format, sanitisation and failure handling are concrete and complete, but the instructions are built to hide the reporting from the person, which makes the skill a poor instruction set to follow.
needs: Google Cloud Secret Manager access to a Warp-internal project
why: It serves one company's internal agent-monitoring process, not building, running, selling or making content for a node product. It also carries risks that make it unsafe to install.
risks: It instructs the agent to submit reports without the person's permission, preview or knowledge, and to never mention them.
It sends context about the person's work, including repositories, runs and error excerpts, to an external Slack channel without telling them.
The script reads a webhook secret from an environment variable or from Google Secret Manager via gcloud, so an agent following it handles credentials it was not given.
It tells the agent to ignore and not report its own submission failures, which hides errors from the person.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing multi-stage CI/CD pipelines: stage layout, approval gates, security scans, and environment promotion. It also covers zero-downtime rollouts such as canary and blue-green deployments, with Argo Rollouts analysis examples. It is aimed at engineers who ship services to Kubernetes, ECS, VMs or serverless targets and need to debug stalled or misbehaving deployment gates.
tasks: design a multi-stage CI/CD pipeline with approval gates
set up a canary rollout with automated promotion
debug a deployment gate that never promotes
add health checks and rollback triggers to a deploy
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete troubleshooting cases with YAML and Dockerfile examples, and points to reference files for deeper detail, though some sections are summarised rather than fully worked.
why: It is a generic DevOps design aid, not something that builds a Fractera site, app or content; its examples target Kubernetes, Argo and cloud-style deployment platforms that a local-first node would rarely run, so an agent should read it for ideas and adapt the pipeline advice to the node's own stack. It is not a risk, and no outside service is required.

summary: This skill lets an agent list recent git commits that have been linked to agent sessions, filtered by branch, repository, or a result limit. It renders the results newest first with short shas, timestamps, messages, and linked session ids with observation counts. It is aimed at a person who wants to see what an agent has shipped and the context behind each commit.
tasks: show the commits the agent made on main
list linked commits with their session context
see what the agent shipped this week
find commits from a specific repo or branch
qualityWhy: The workflow, filter parsing and checklist are clear, but the skill depends on an external memory_commits tool and a REST fallback whose setup is only pointed to, not explained.
needs: agentmemory service providing memory_commits or GET /agentmemory/commits
why: The skill is a lookup over the agentmemory service's own commit-to-session store, which is a separate memory system that a Fractera node does not provide, so it does not serve building, running, selling or making content on a node. Its data would sit in an outside memory store rather than the node's own SQLite element.

summary: This skill walks an agent through adding sign-in and sign-up to a TypeScript or JavaScript app with the Better Auth library. It starts with a planning phase that scans the project and asks structured questions about framework, database, sign-in methods and features. set up email and password authentication with a database
add Google or GitHub sign-in to my site
enable two-factor authentication for users
configure Better Auth with Drizzle or Prisma

a Resend key if email is used

It also tells the agent to use AskQuestion for planning, which the node may not provide.

summary: The skill gives an agent a set of reference guides for building email features: DNS authentication, transactional and marketing message design, consent capture, compliance with CAN-SPAM, GDPR and CASL, retry and idempotency, webhooks, bounce handling and accessibility. It is aimed at developers and product teams who send email from their apps. The main file is a router that points to twelve topic files, and only the SKILL.md was provided for review.

why: Email sending is central to what a node builds, so the guidance is directly useful. It is written around the Resend API and sending service, which the person would need to pay for and configure, so use is install-with-service. The twelve reference files were listed but not provided, so their accuracy is unverified.

summary: This skill tells an agent to recommend a matching course, tutorial or use case from Claude Academy when someone is learning how to use Claude or one of its products. It fetches a published catalog file, applies strict rules so it only recommends strong matches, and never invents titles or links. why: It helps people learn Claude, which is occasionally useful on a node, but it does not build, run, sell or create content for a product. It fetches a public catalog at runtime, so it depends on that outside service being reachable.

summary: The skill guides an agent to set up automated changelog generation from commits, pull requests and releases, following the Keep a Changelog layout and semantic versioning. It covers Conventional Commits message styles, release note structure with highlights, breaking changes and dependency tables, and a short list of commit hygiene do's and don'ts. It is aimed at developers who manage release workflows for a project.

write release notes for a new version

enforce commit message rules in CI

why: It is a stack-free workflow guide that helps a node team keep release notes tidy, though it does not directly build site, shop or content features. The skill has no scripts or outside services, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through Spring Boot backend design: controllers kept thin, services with transactions, Spring Data repositories, and validated request and response records. It also covers central error handling, caching, async work, SLF4J logging, filters for request logging and rate limiting, and production settings. summary: This skill guides an agent writing Python backends with FastAPI. It sets general conventions: typed Pydantic models, early-return error handling, lifespan handlers for startup and shutdown, dependency injection, and async database calls. It is aimed at developers building JSON APIs who want consistent, performant Python code.

make database calls async in a Python backend

summary: The skill gives an agent a compact set of rules for visual design foundations: a type scale, a spacing grid, semantic color tokens, contrast checks, dark-mode variables, and an icon sizing system. It is aimed at people building a design system or style guide for a product's interface. The agent can turn these into Tailwind config or CSS custom properties. The skill is stack-free apart from the Tailwind config example, and it needs no outside service. The contrast helper is incomplete as written, so the agent should add hexToRgb itself.

The workflow sends several independent reviewers at a set of code changes in parallel, then triages their findings and presents them. run a code review on this branch
run a quick or thorough review of the diff
triage review findings and present them

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of decision principles for Node.js work: choosing a framework such as Hono, Fastify, Express, NestJS or Next.js API routes, picking ESM or CommonJS, and structuring code in layers. plan error handling and status codes for an API
check a Node.js project against a security checklist
decide how to structure layers and validation

why: It is a general Node.js decision guide that is useful now and then for architecture choices, but it is not built for the Fractera stack, which uses Next.js 16, next-auth and its own SQLite element, so it should be read for its ideas and then built the node's way. Its framework and validation recommendations would need adapting to the node's own stack.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of Python style rules and worked examples: idiomatic code, PEP 8 layout, type annotations, exception handling, context managers, comprehensions, dataclasses, decorators, and concurrency choices. It also covers package layout and the usual lint, type-check, and test tools. It suits developers who write or review Python code and want consistent, readable results. summary: This package is a set of shared reference notes that other installed Nature writing skills load on demand, covering abstracts, introductions, results, discussions, journal-specific formats, and research ethics. It also includes a local Python checker that flags inconsistent terminology, mixed numeric precision, and equivalent lengths written in different units across manuscript files. Doubt remains about how well the level 3 to 5 patterns are covered in the references, which I did not read.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of REST API design conventions: plural kebab-case resource names, correct HTTP methods and status codes, a standard success and error envelope, offset and cursor pagination, filtering and sorting syntax, versioning rules, and rate-limit headers. plan an API versioning and deprecation strategy
qualityWhy: The skill is concrete, with naming rules, status code tables, response shapes, pagination SQL, and a checklist an agent can follow, but it lacks OpenAPI examples and leaves rate limiting as a header description rather than working code.
why: It is mostly stack-free design guidance that fits a node's Next.js route handlers and its SQLite-backed data layer, so it can be applied as written. Its code samples use Express, Django and Go, but they only illustrate the patterns, and the Next.js example already matches the node's stack.

summary: The skill guides an agent through a structured review of the current git changes, looking at SOLID violations, architecture smells, removal candidates, security risks and code quality. It asks for findings ranked from P0 to P3 with file references and suggested fixes, and it waits for the person's confirmation before changing anything. It is aimed at developers who want a senior-engineer style review of their own code.
tasks: review my current git changes
find security risks in this diff
check my code for SOLID violations
list dead code that can be removed
prioritise review findings before merging
qualityWhy: The workflow, severity table, output template and checklists are concrete and ordered, though the reference files are only named here and their depth cannot be checked from SKILL.md alone.
why: Reviewing code is useful for building a Fractera product now and then, and it is stack-free apart from git, so it can be installed as written. Its checklists assume general web and app code rather than the node's Next.js stack, so the findings may need judging against the node's own conventions.

summary: This skill guides an agent through taking card payments with Stripe, covering hosted or embedded checkout, subscriptions, saved payment methods, webhooks for payment events, and refunds. It is written for developers adding paid products or recurring billing to a web or mobile app. The examples are Python, and the document points to a separate reference file for more detailed patterns.
tasks: add a subscription checkout to my site
set up Stripe webhooks for payment events
process a refund for an order
save a customer's card for future payments
test a payment flow with Stripe test cards
qualityWhy: The concepts and a runnable Checkout example are clear, but the file lacks webhook signature verification, idempotency and error-handling steps, and its code is all Python.
needs: Stripe secret API key (test and live)
why: Card payments are a stated Fractera feature, so the skill is directly relevant, but its examples are Python and call Stripe directly, while a node takes payments through its own Stripe element in Next.js and TypeScript. An agent should read it for the flow and concepts and then build the integration through the node's Stripe element. I only reviewed SKILL.md; references/details.md was not included in what I was given.

summary: This is a retired Shopify skill meant to guide an agent through building a custom storefront with direct GraphQL queries and cart mutations against Shopify's storefront API. It now contains only a notice that it has been replaced by the newer shopify skill, with instructions to remove this one and install that. It gives no working steps, examples or checks of its own. The intended users were developers building commerce storefronts on Shopify.
tasks: build a custom Shopify storefront with GraphQL
fetch product data from the Shopify storefront API
add a cart with GraphQL mutations
qualityWhy: The file is a deprecation notice that only points to another skill, so it gives an agent no instructions to follow.
needs: Shopify store with Storefront API access
why: The skill is a retired wrapper with no usable content, and its subject is a cloud commerce platform, which a local-first node does not host, so it is not useful for the node's purposes. The replacement command differs from the node's install flow, but that is a detail to note here rather than a risk.

summary: This skill gives an agent a quick reference for PostgreSQL work: which index type fits which query, which column types to choose, and how to write composite, partial and covering indexes. It also covers cursor pagination, upserts, queue processing, row-level security, and SQL queries for finding unindexed foreign keys and slow statements. It is aimed at developers who design schemas or tune a slow query.
tasks: design a PostgreSQL schema with sensible column types
speed up a slow query with the right index
add row-level security to a table
replace OFFSET pagination with cursor pagination
find unindexed foreign keys and slow statements
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete SQL examples and checks, but it is a short cheat sheet with no step-by-step workflow and it defers deeper guidance to another agent.
why: The skill is written for the PostgreSQL engine, while a Fractera node keeps its data in the SQLite element as the only door to data, so the SQL cannot be used as written; an agent can take the indexing and schema ideas and apply them to SQLite. It is not tied to a cloud service in its own text, although it cites Supabase as its source.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a structured brainstorming session on a topic the person brings. The agent acts as a coach in one of three stances: it only asks questions, it plays along with its own ideas, or it runs the whole session and reports the results. It draws on a catalog of creative techniques served by a small Python script, and it keeps a running on-disk log so a session can resume after interruption. It is aimed at people who want more and better ideas than they would reach alone.
tasks: help me brainstorm product features for my app
generate content ideas for my blog or social channel
run a facilitated ideation session on a business problem
pick a creative technique and generate ideas, then narrow them down
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and well sequenced, with stances, a memlog protocol, and tests for the helper script, but the activation depends on BMad project scripts (memlog.py, resolve_config.py) that are not shipped in these files.
why: It is a general thinking aid that helps the person generate and narrow ideas for products and content, not a build or delivery tool, so its value is occasional. It runs without any outside service, but on a node without a BMad setup it will offer to install the BMad framework via npx, and the memlog and config scripts it calls must come from that framework.

summary: The skill is a reference checklist of common Python mistakes, such as scattered retry logic, hard-coded secrets, unclosed resources, blocking calls in async code, missing type hints and happy-path-only tests. An agent uses it as a review aid before merging or finalising code, and it gives a fix and a short code example for each pattern. It is aimed at developers reviewing or refactoring Python code.
tasks: review this Python code for anti-patterns
check my implementation before merging
find why my async code is blocking
refactor legacy Python to remove bad practices
qualityWhy: It is a clear, well-organised checklist with a bad/good example per pattern, but the examples are fragmentary and it gives no steps for running a review or checking code.
why: It is a general Python review checklist, so an agent can use it on any Python code, but its fixes assume pydantic, SQLAlchemy-style ORMs and requests/httpx, while a Fractera node builds on TypeScript, so it fits as a reference for Python-side code only. Its use is 'ideas' because the node's own stack differs and the skill must be read and applied rather than installed as written.

summary: This guide teaches an agent how to structure a Django project: split settings, custom models and querysets, and service-layer business logic. It also covers building REST APIs with Django REST Framework, plus caching, signals, middleware and query optimization. It is aimed at developers who maintain Django back ends. The advice is general and comes with code examples.
tasks: design a Django REST API for a shop
review Django ORM queries for N+1 problems
set up split dev and production settings
add caching to slow Django views
qualityWhy: It gives concrete, well-organized code patterns and checklists for many Django tasks, though several snippets use undefined names such as slugify, timezone, logger, Cart and env without their imports.
why: Fractera nodes are built on Next.js, so Django is a stack the node replaces; an agent should read this for its architecture ideas and rebuild them in the node's own stack rather than install it as written. It is useful only when a person is actually working on a Django project.

summary: This skill lets an agent typeset finished documents from ready-made templates: resumes, one-pagers, letters, portfolios, long reports, changelogs, equity reports, slide decks and static landing pages. It supplies a content schema, writing and quality checks, and a build script that renders PDFs and page images and verifies fonts, layout and content coverage. It is aimed at people who want polished paper or screen output without designing from scratch.
tasks: turn a draft into a print-ready two-page resume PDF
make a one-page executive summary for investors
build a 10-slide deck in Chinese or English
create a static landing page for a product
typeset a changelog or long white paper as PDF
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete routing tables, JSON content schemas, step-by-step delivery commands, explicit quality bars and verification gates, which an agent can follow directly.
why: It directly serves making content for a product (landing pages, PDFs, decks) and runs entirely on the person's own machine with no cloud service required. The update check contacts GitHub at most once a day and sends no document content, and optional MathJax and font setup needs Node.js and network access; the unseen script files were not reviewed.

summary: This skill lets an agent look up the progress of a background research job by its run ID. It runs a single command-line call against the Parallel research service and returns the job's status as JSON. It is aimed at people who start long web research tasks and want to check on them later.
tasks: check the status of a research run
see whether a background research job has finished
look up progress of a research task by run ID
qualityWhy: It is a stub: one command line with a single fallback sentence and no steps, checks, output handling or examples.
needs: Parallel research service account and API key
why: Research runs happen on Parallel's cloud, so this is an outside service that produces results a node could save locally, which makes it install-with-service rather than skip. Its use is occasional and the skill itself adds little beyond the command, so the value is only some.

summary: This skill turns an agent into Winston, a system architect persona who turns a ticket's requirements into a technical design. It loads a customizable persona and project config from a BMad project folder, reads the active ticket first, then offers a numbered menu of architecture actions or dispatches to other BMad skills. It is aimed at teams planning how a system should be built, and it favors simple, proven technology and explicit trade-offs.
tasks: design the architecture for a new feature
turn this ticket into a technical plan
compare trade-offs between two technical approaches
choose a simple stack for a web app
qualityWhy: The file sets out a clear activation sequence, but it is mostly persona and dispatch rules, with little concrete architecture method, and much of its behaviour depends on customize.toml and the BMad folder layout, which are not included.
why: It is stack-free planning guidance, so it fits a node without changes, but its real value depends on a BMad project layout (_bmad folder and tickets) and on other BMad skills it hands off to. It only helps occasionally, when designing or reviewing system structure.

summary: The skill guides an agent through reading, creating and reviewing PDF files where layout matters. It asks the agent to render pages to PNG with Poppler and inspect them visually, to generate new documents with reportlab, and to extract text with pdfplumber or pypdf. It is aimed at people who need polished, defect-free PDF documents.
tasks: generate a formatted PDF report
extract text from a PDF
check a PDF's layout by rendering its pages
review a PDF for visual defects
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and the tools are named, but the instructions are generic, with no code examples, no template, and only a brief checklist for layout verification.
why: PDF creation and checking are useful now and then for content and documents on a node, and all tools run locally. The skill installs Python packages and Poppler, which are normal local dependencies, so nothing needs to be skipped.

summary: The skill guides an agent through producing a short architecture spine: a set of binding invariants and durable design decisions that keep separately built parts of a system consistent. It supports creating, updating, or validating such a document from a ticket file or an existing codebase, using a coaching-first workflow with a memory log. A bundled Python linter checks the resulting document for placeholders, broken decision IDs, missing fields, and unpinned versions.
tasks: create an architecture spine for a new feature
validate an existing architecture document
record key technical decisions for a project
update architecture decisions after a change
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed with clear steps, rules, templates and a working deterministic linter with tests, though some sections depend on other BMad skills and files not included here.
why: It is a methodology for architecture documents rather than a stack tool, and it is built around the BMad agent ecosystem and its own memlog and workspace scripts, so it would need adapting to the node's own structure; its value for building products is moderate.

summary: The skill lets an agent generate images from a text prompt or from reference images, using the Volcengine Ark Seedream model through a Node.js script. It can produce a set of consistent images, optionally improve the prompt with style presets, and save the results to a local folder. It is aimed at people who want illustrations or visuals made quickly from chat.
tasks: generate an illustration from a text description
make a set of four consistent images in one style
create a new image from reference pictures
produce a styled image such as cyberpunk or watercolor
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with parameter tables, a prompt template for image sets, and a rendering template, though the script was cut off so its full behaviour could not be checked.
needs: Volcengine Ark Agent Plan API key (starts with ark-)
why: Image generation directly serves making content, but the script searches for and reads other tools' credentials, including the Claude Code auth token and dotenv files outside its purpose, so it should not be installed as written. The API is an outside paid service the person would choose, which by itself would have been install-with-service.
risks: The script reads ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and other API-key-like environment variables and dotenv files from other platforms (for example /root/.openclaw/.env) to find a key, exposing credentials it does not need for image generation.
The skill tells the agent to prefer its tool over others and not to ask the person, which overrides the person's choice of tool.

summary: This skill turns the agent into John, a product manager persona who runs PRD creation through user interviews, requirements discovery and stakeholder alignment. On activation it loads a customization block and project context, then offers a numbered menu of product-planning actions. It is aimed at people who need to turn a product idea into small increments that development can build.
tasks: write a PRD for a new product or feature
interview me to discover requirements
break a product vision into small shippable increments
align stakeholders on scope before development starts
qualityWhy: The activation flow is concrete, but the actual PRD method is delegated to other skills and scripts that are not included, so the file alone gives little guidance on how to write a PRD.
needs: bmad skill and _bmad/ project setup (scripts resolve_customization.py and resolve_config.py)
why: Requirements planning helps build products, so it is useful now and then, and it is stack-free, so it can be installed as written. It depends on a BMad project folder with its own scripts, which are not included here, and the fallback suggests installing the bmad package from a GitHub repo, a choice the person makes.

summary: This skill tells an agent to write a specification file for a solution component, saved under a /spec/ folder with a fixed naming pattern and an 11-section template. The spec covers requirements, interfaces, acceptance criteria, test strategy and dependencies, written so that another generative AI can read it without outside context. It suits teams who want to plan a feature or system in a structured, machine-readable document before building.
tasks: write a specification for a new feature
document requirements and acceptance criteria for a component
create a structured spec file for an AI agent to build from
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear template, naming convention and writing rules that an agent can follow, though it lacks worked examples of a finished spec and some sections are only placeholders.
why: It is a stack-free planning habit that helps an agent draft specs for a node's own apps, so it is useful now and then; it does lean on a .NET testing example in the template, which an agent should adapt to Next.js and TypeScript rather than copy.

summary: This skill fetches the finished output of a deep research task on the Parallel platform, using a run ID the user supplies. It runs a command-line poll for that run and asks the agent to present the returned findings in an organized, readable form. It is aimed at people who have already started a research job and want its report.
tasks: fetch the result of a finished research run
show the report for a research run ID
organize research findings for reading
qualityWhy: It is a very short wrapper that runs one CLI command and gives only a vague instruction to present results clearly, with no steps, examples or checks.
needs: Parallel account and API key via parallel-cli
why: It is useful only if a node user runs Parallel research tasks, which is an outside paid service that makes research and returns text to local files, so it is install-with-service rather than skip. It is thin and depends on a CLI setup step that is not in the skill itself.

summary: This skill tells an agent to use the official Svelte command-line tools before writing or changing any Svelte component or Svelte module. The agent can list the Svelte 5 and SvelteKit documentation sections, fetch the pages it needs, and run an autofixer that flags common mistakes in component code. It is aimed at developers working on Svelte projects, not on Fractera's React and Next.js stack.
tasks: write a Svelte 5 component with runes
check a .svelte file for common mistakes
look up SvelteKit documentation for a feature
migrate a Svelte 4 component to Svelte 5 syntax
qualityWhy: The commands, options, escaping rule for runes in the shell, and the validate-before-finishing workflow are concrete and easy to follow, though it says little about the Svelte code itself.
why: The skill is built for Svelte, which a Fractera node does not use (its stack is Next.js, React and Tailwind), so an agent would only borrow its checking habits and rebuild them for the node's own stack. Its tools need network access through npx but no keys or accounts.

summary: This skill makes an agent scan a repository for CLAUDE.md, .claude.local.md and related memory files, then score each one against criteria for commands, architecture, gotchas, conciseness, currency and actionability. It outputs a graded quality report before proposing targeted, minimal additions as diffs. Only after the person approves does it edit the files. It is aimed at developers who keep project context for Claude Code up to date.
tasks: audit the CLAUDE.md files in my project
check whether my project memory is current and accurate
add missing build and test commands to CLAUDE.md
suggest gotchas worth recording for future sessions
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear five-phase workflow, a scoring rubric, a report format, diff rules and a checklist, though the referenced rubric and template files are not shown and the weights are not fully consistent.
why: It helps maintain the project memory of a node's codebase, which is useful now and then but does not directly build, run, sell or create content for a product. It is stack-free, needs no outside service, and only edits CLAUDE.md files after the person approves the changes.

summary: This skill gives an agent architectural guidance for splitting a system into separately deployed services. It covers choosing service boundaries by business capability or domain, picking synchronous or event-based communication, handling data ownership and multi-step transactions, and adding resilience patterns such as circuit breakers, retries and bulkheads. It is aimed at architects and engineers who are decomposing a monolith or designing a distributed system.
tasks: decompose a monolith into services
design service boundaries for an application
choose between REST, gRPC and event messaging
plan a saga for a multi-step transaction
add circuit breakers and retries to service calls
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is a concise, correct overview of pattern names, but it has no steps, examples or checks, and the detailed guidance sits in a reference file that was only partly visible.
why: It is stack-free architecture guidance, so an agent can read and apply it directly, but a Fractera node is normally one app with its own SQLite element, so most microservice splitting will rarely apply and only comes up when a larger system is being decomposed. The reference file was not fully reviewed, so its depth is unverified.

summary: This skill turns the agent into Amelia, a senior software engineer persona who implements approved user stories test-first, working through each acceptance criterion until the code passes. It loads project configuration and ticket files from a BMad project folder, then offers a menu of development actions. It is aimed at people who already plan work as tickets and want an agent to write and verify the code.
tasks: implement the next user story test-first
build a code change from an approved ticket
work through each acceptance criterion and verify it
fix a bug described in a ticket
qualityWhy: The activation and menu flow is detailed and followable, but the actual development method (red, green, refactor, AC checks) is only named in one sentence, with no concrete steps or checks.
why: It directly helps build software for a product, and it is not tied to a cloud service or to a stack the node replaces. It depends on the BMad project layout (_bmad folder, resolver scripts, tickets) and needs the BMad setup to be present, so an agent must set that up or fall back to reading the files by hand.

summary: This skill guides an agent through running AlloyDB for PostgreSQL on Google Cloud, covering clusters, instances, backups, scaling, networking, and IAM-based access. It also points to AlloyDB's AI search features and MCP tool integration. It is aimed at engineers who administer Google-hosted databases, not at people building local apps.
tasks: create an AlloyDB cluster and primary instance
set up private IP connectivity for a database
configure IAM database authentication for a service
back up or scale an AlloyDB instance
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete gcloud commands, explicit security directives and reference files for each subtopic, though it leans on references that were not included and has some repetitive directive text.
needs: AlloyDB API enabled in a Google Cloud project
why: AlloyDB is a cloud-hosted database, which the node's local-first design excludes, so it is not useful for building or running a node's own data. The skill itself carries no harmful instructions.

summary: This skill guides an agent through answering a complex question in two linked parts: first mapping related fields, authors and theories and checking their sources, then comparing historical cases of success, failure and counterexamples that share the same structure. It ends with a conditional "standard answer" that states the conditions and where it stops working. It is aimed at people who want theory-backed, historically grounded answers, and it can also produce short-video, course, PPT or copy versions of the result.
tasks: answer a complex question with theory and historical precedent
find a classic solution used in history for a problem
turn a theory into a short video that solves people's problems
check a claim and find its theoretical basis
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete steps, scoring tables, output templates, source-priority rules and a self-check list, though some sections are long and abstract.
why: It is a stack-free research and writing method, so it fits a node for planning content or answering questions, but it is not core to building a product. It may call web search when outside facts matter, which the person can allow or refuse.

summary: This skill makes an agent take on the persona of Mary, a business analyst who helps with market research, competitive analysis, and turning vague needs into requirements. It first resolves a layered configuration from TOML files and loads project context from a BMad work folder. It then greets the user and offers a numbered menu of analysis tasks, dispatching to other BMad skills when one fits. The main users are founders and product people who want structured analysis before building.
tasks: research the market for a new product idea
compare competitors and their strengths
turn a vague idea into written requirements
analyse a domain before planning a site or app
qualityWhy: The activation steps are concrete and ordered with fallbacks, but several referenced scripts and skills are not shipped with this skill and must come from a separate BMad setup.
why: It is a planning and analysis persona rather than a builder or content maker, so its value is occasional rather than core. It is stack-free, but it depends on a BMad project layout with a _bmad folder, uv scripts and other BMad skills that this package does not include. The npx fallback only installs a skill if the person agrees.

summary: The skill guides an agent through keeping passwords, API keys and certificates out of code and CI/CD pipelines, using HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager and the secret stores built into GitHub and GitLab. It includes sample pipeline YAML, a Terraform snippet, a rotation Lambda, a Kubernetes External Secrets setup and secret-scanning hooks. Its audience is DevOps engineers who deploy cloud-hosted services.
tasks: store API keys in a secret manager instead of the repo
set up GitHub Actions secrets for a deployment
rotate database passwords automatically
add secret scanning to a commit hook
qualityWhy: The steps and YAML snippets are concrete and checkable, though the rotation Lambda calls undefined helpers and much of the material is reference text.
why: The skill is built around cloud secret stores and cloud CI/CD pipelines, which are cloud administration rather than work on a local-first node that keeps its own data and secrets. Its general hygiene points (never commit secrets, mask logs, rotate keys) apply to any project, but the node's own env and sign-in setup is not covered.

summary: This skill guides an agent through designing reusable UI components in React, Vue and Svelte. It covers composition patterns such as compound components, render props and slots, plus choosing a styling approach like Tailwind, CSS Modules or CSS-in-JS. It includes a variant-based React button built with class-variance-authority and a context-based accordion. It is aimed at developers building component libraries or design systems.
tasks: build a reusable button component with variants
design a compound accordion or select component
set up a component library styled with Tailwind
refactor a component to use composition instead of many props
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives useful patterns and a complete React button example, but it is broad and generic, and the Vue snippet is incomplete (Ref is not imported and props are undefined); the reference files were not included in the review.
why: Component design is a daily part of building sites and web apps on a node, and the React, Tailwind and cva examples fit the node's Next.js, React 19 and Tailwind 4 stack. The Vue and Svelte sections do not apply to this node and the forwardRef pattern is older than React 19's ref-as-prop, so the agent should use the React parts and modern idioms.

summary: This skill gives an agent ready-made GitLab CI pipeline templates covering multi-stage builds, dependency caching, Docker image build and push, environment-gated Kubernetes and Terraform deployments, security scanning and dynamic child pipelines. It is aimed at developers and DevOps engineers who want to automate testing and releases for a project hosted on GitLab.
tasks: set up a GitLab CI pipeline for a Node.js app
speed up slow CI builds with caching
build and push a Docker image from GitLab CI
add manual production deploy gates to a pipeline
add security scanning to a GitLab pipeline
qualityWhy: The YAML examples are concrete and copyable, but the skill relies on the deprecated `only` keyword instead of `rules`, gives no verification steps, and omits how to fix common failures.
needs: GitLab account or self-hosted GitLab instance
GitLab container registry for Docker images
Kubernetes cluster and kubeconfig token for the deploy examples
Terraform state backend for the Terraform example
why: Pipeline patterns are useful for shipping a node's app, but the node has no GitLab-specific element and the deploy examples target external Kubernetes or Terraform infrastructure the person must provide. The Node.js build example is generic, not Next.js-specific, and it needs a GitLab instance and runners the person chooses to use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through creating, updating, or validating a product requirements document. It runs a facilitated discovery: the agent gathers context, calibrates the level of rigor, and then drafts requirements in one of two working modes. It keeps an append-only decision log and can run reviewer subagents over the finished document. It is aimed at product owners and teams who are planning what to build.
tasks: write a PRD for a new web app
update an existing product requirements document after a change
validate a PRD against a quality checklist
turn a product brief into requirements
qualityWhy: The steps, modes, file roles and finalize sequence are concrete and checkable, but several referenced scripts and the template files are not bundled and depend on a BMad project layout.
why: It is a stack-free planning method, useful now and then for scoping a product before building it, but it does not directly build, run or sell anything. It only works where the BMad `_bmad` folder, its Python scripts and `uv` are present, so an agent on a node without that setup would hit missing-script errors; the offered `npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD` install is only suggested when setup is missing, and it runs remote code only with the person's agreement.

summary: This skill guides an agent through designing LLM applications with LangChain 1.x and LangGraph, covering ReAct agents, multi-agent supervisor patterns, state with TypedDict, memory options, document loading and retrieval, and tracing. It is written for developers building autonomous agents, multi-step workflows and document pipelines in Python. The main file gives a quick-start ReAct agent with a safe calculator tool, plus test and performance snippets using Redis caching and Pinecone.
tasks: build a ReAct agent with tool access
add conversation memory that persists across sessions
create a multi-step LLM workflow with LangGraph
set up a document processing and retrieval pipeline
cache LLM responses to cut cost and latency
qualityWhy: The examples are concrete and runnable-looking, but the rest is a thin overview that defers details to a reference file and has some inaccuracies, such as an unexplained test assertion and a model name that may not exist.
why: The skill targets a Python LangChain and LangGraph stack, while a Fractera node is built on TypeScript and Next.js, so it must be read for ideas and rebuilt in the node's own stack. The Python-only stack, paid model and vector services, and the lack of a local-first emphasis limit its value to agent design ideas.

summary: The skill guides an agent to design and provision production Grafana dashboards for visualizing Prometheus and application metrics. It covers layout hierarchy, RED and USE monitoring methods, panel types, template variables, dashboard-embedded alerts, file provisioning, and Terraform or Ansible as-code deployment. It is aimed at engineers and operators who need monitoring and observability interfaces.
tasks: build a monitoring dashboard for an API
visualize Prometheus metrics in Grafana
add template variables to a dashboard
set up dashboard provisioning as code
qualityWhy: It gives useful JSON examples for panels, variables and alerts, but it is generic, has no verification steps, and mixes older panel types like 'graph' with no version notes.
why: The skill is about running monitoring infrastructure on Grafana and Prometheus, which are external server-side services and not local-first node content or product features. Its metrics and dashboards live on a remote monitoring stack rather than on the person's own computer, so it does not serve building, running or selling products on a Fractera node.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a six-phase research pipeline that turns a pile of sources into a reference, outline, notes set or publish-ready article. It stresses collecting primary sources, digesting them into a real mental model, keeping contradictions visible, and running a linear self-review. It is aimed at people who need to get up to speed on an unfamiliar domain or compile materials into one authoritative piece.
tasks: research an unfamiliar domain and write a draft
compile a set of sources into one reference article
make quick notes to learn a topic fast
turn existing materials into an outline and long-form post
qualityWhy: The phases, modes, exit criteria and hard rules are concrete and followable, though fetch and style steps depend on other installed skills and some phrasing is abstract.
why: It is a stack-free research and writing workflow that serves content making for a node, but it is only occasionally needed and works best alongside the /read and /write skills. Nothing in the file calls a cloud service or asks for keys, and the publish step is gated on explicit user confirmation.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to turn implementation plans, PR reviews and general technical explanations into self-contained HTML pages with Plannotator's colours and typography. It sets out three routes: a prescriptive plan layout, a prescriptive PR walkthrough layout, and a general path that borrows another skill's structure. Every Mermaid diagram must render in both light and dark palettes before the page is opened in Plannotator's annotation view. It is aimed at developers who need to review or explain code changes and designs.
tasks: turn an implementation plan into a reviewable HTML page
write a visual walkthrough of a pull request
draw an architecture diagram as a self-contained page
make a styled data table or slide deck explaining a technical topic
qualityWhy: The plan and PR paths give concrete section orders, theme tokens, a hard Mermaid render gate and a test file, though some reference files were cut from view.

It is stack-free and local, and the Plannotator CLI runs on the person's machine. The general path asks the person before running a global install of visual-explainer, which differs from this node's per-element install, so that step needs the person's own approval.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to build web-based slide decks with Slidev, writing presentations in Markdown with Vue components, syntax-highlighted code, click animations, diagrams and math. It is aimed at developers preparing technical talks, code walkthroughs, workshops and teaching material. tasks: make a technical slide deck with code walkthroughs

summary: This skill tells an agent to build features, fix bugs and refactor code test-first: write a failing test, confirm it fails for the right reason, make the smallest change that turns it green, then refactor and check for at least 80% coverage. continue from a plan.md file using the TDD cycle
check test coverage reaches 80 percent

The test-runner detection is generic, and the Supabase, Redis and OpenAI mock examples are only illustrations. Step 0 runs a helper script from an ECC root chosen by environment variable, which is not shipped with this skill, so the agent should confirm that root before running it.

summary: This skill lets an agent generate videos from text, from a still image, or from up to nine character reference images, and edit existing videos with plain-language instructions. It runs Alibaba HappyHorse 1.0 models through the inference.sh belt CLI and documents app IDs, example commands, parameter tables and pricing. why: It directly serves making video content for products and social networks, but generation runs on the inference.sh cloud service, so the person's prompts and uploaded images or videos are sent there and the person must pay per second of output. The skill does not spell out that data upload in its own text, so the person should know it before use.

summary: This skill turns the agent into Sally, a UX designer persona who translates user needs into interaction design and UX specifications. On activation it resolves a BMad customization file, loads project config and existing ticket or design documents, greets the person, and offers a menu of design tasks. summary: This skill tells a Caffeine app builder's agent how to add LLM chat to an app using the platform's own inference service, with no user-supplied API key. why: It directly serves building LLM features into a product, but it depends on the Caffeine Inference hosted service and its platform-provided credentials, which is a paid service the person chooses. Its design is built for Caffeine's own canister runtime, so it does not fit a local-first Fractera node's own stack and may need adapting before use.

summary: This skill makes an agent act as a patient product-brief coach. npx skills CLI (only if the user asks to install BMad)

uv to run the BMad Python scripts

summary: The skill guides an agent through building web games and small game engines with HTML5 Canvas, WebGL and plain JavaScript, covering the game loop, collision, controls, audio and rendering choices. summary: This skill teaches an agent to create new pictures from text descriptions and to change existing ones, using OpenAI's GPT-Image-2 model through the inference.sh command-line tool. summary: This package is a stub. Its visible SKILL.md has a name and a one-line description, "The router", with a heading and no instructions. The skill is aimed at people who rent cloud GPU compute from RunPod.

summary: This skill lets an agent generate and edit images with Pruna's optimized P-Image models by running commands through the inference.sh belt CLI. summary: This skill gives an agent two motion-design modes: build interactive UI animations with purposeful timing and easing, or audit existing motion for overused or AI-generated-looking patterns and produce an HTML report with demos. summary: This skill guides an agent through upgrading a React Native app to a newer version. summary: This skill lets an agent drive a live marimo notebook as a shared workspace: it runs Python in the same kernel the user sees, inspects cells and dataflow state, and commits durable notebook edits through a private code-mode API instead of editing the .py file. summary: This skill teaches an agent to capture network traffic with Wireshark, tshark, tcpdump and mitmproxy, then analyse it with display filters and Scapy. why: It is a stack-free debugging skill, useful now and then for diagnosing traffic on a node's own services, though most node work will not need packet-level analysis. Interception and fuzzing steps should only be run against systems the person owns or is authorised to test, and the skill's use of --ssl-insecure and active replay should be applied with that in mind.

summary: The skill guides an agent to write an AGENTS.md file at a repository root, documenting setup, development, testing, code style, build and deployment, and pull request conventions so coding agents can work on the project. It is a generic, stack-free prompt that asks the agent to analyze package.json scripts, CI files and docs before writing the file. why: It helps a node developer write a project's AGENTS.md, which is useful now and then but not central to building or selling a product; it is stack-free, so it installs as written.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to turn a single portrait photo into a talking-head video using the Pruna P-Video-Avatar model through the inference.sh belt CLI. summary: The skill guides an agent through adding Solana wallet support to a React Native Expo app using Mobile Wallet Adapter and the Wallet UI kit. summary: This skill guides an agent through splitting a developer relations budget into line items across pillars such as events, content, community, tooling, education and sponsorship. summary: This skill guides an agent through designing the pricing and packaging of a developer tool: choosing a value metric such as seats, consumption, capacity or outcome, drawing a free-to-paid tier ladder, setting price points between a margin floor and self-host or build-it ceilings, and planning price changes without triggering backlash. summary: This skill guides an agent through capturing a product's UX vision as two linked documents: DESIGN.md for visual identity and EXPERIENCE.md for behavior, information architecture, states and accessibility. It runs a facilitated discovery that pulls requirements from an existing ticket, records decisions in a memory log, and optionally renders creative-tool mockups, then finalizes and validates the spines. summary: This skill guides a hiring manager through recruiting a developer relations person. It also covers grant applications and a self-set measurement threshold. The target user is a solo or small-team open-source maintainer, not a company deciding where to fund.
tasks: set up GitHub Sponsors tiers for my open-source project
design a sponsor ladder that companies can buy
write a funding page and FUNDING.yml for my library
plan an outreach to companies that depend on my project
check whether a grant fits my project before applying
qualityWhy: The skill gives a detailed, ordered workflow with interview questions, decision rules and a deliverable template, though much of it is ranking logic rather than executable steps and several figures are self-declared baselines.
why: It is a fundraising and program-design guide for open-source maintainers and does not build, run or sell a product or content on a node, so it serves none of the node's uses. Its related platforms (GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective) are outside services, and the skill also points to cloud-style fiscal hosts for money handling.

summary: This skill makes an agent write a community's code of conduct together with the private playbook that enforces it. The playbook covers scope, an escalation ladder, reporting channels, an incident runbook, a moderator roster and platform controls. It also tells the agent to handle a live harm case first and to refuse rules that exempt the community's most powerful members. It is aimed at people who run company-backed or volunteer open-source communities.
tasks: write a code of conduct for our community

handle a harassment report about a member
plan moderator roles and coverage
audit our existing community rules
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed and ordered, with a publish checklist, decision rules, templates and worked examples, though some sections are long and essay-like.
why: It is a stack-free policy and operations skill, so it installs as written, but it serves community operations rather than building or running the product itself. Its platform controls describe chat and forum tools in general, not anything in the node stack.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing a GitHub personal or organization profile as a developer-relations page. It runs a read-only script against GitHub's API to collect facts such as field lengths, README status, widgets, and pinned repositories, then scores the page against a checklist. The agent then helps the owner choose a positioning sentence, pick pins, rebuild the README, and set a review habit. The intended users are open-source maintainers, company org owners, and engineers whose profile gets read during hiring.
tasks: audit my GitHub profile
rewrite our organization profile README
choose which six repositories to pin
make my GitHub profile readable for a conference organizer
qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, a runnable audit script, a scorecard with thresholds, and a cold-reader test, though its prose is long, repetitive, and hedged, and some ordering rules are hard to follow.

why: It is useful now and then for presenting a GitHub profile, but it does not directly serve building or running a node's sites, apps or content. It is GitHub-scoped and calls GitHub's API, and the script reads only public data, so it works without a token; its thresholds are self-set and its evidence base is English-language and US-centric.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of code-quality heuristics drawn from Robert C. Martin's Clean Code: intention-revealing names, small single-purpose functions, few arguments, comments replaced by clearer code, sensible formatting, data-structure hygiene, error handling without null returns, and TDD habits. It is aimed at developers who want to write new code, review pull requests, or refactor working but messy code. The guidance is checklist-style and framed as heuristics rather than hard rules.
tasks: refactor messy code for clearer names
review a pull request for readability
split long functions into smaller ones
replace comments with self-explanatory code
qualityWhy: It is a clear summary of well-known principles with a checklist, but it is mostly bullet-point rules with few concrete before-and-after examples or steps an agent can follow.
why: It is a stack-free design-habit skill, so it fits any node project and is useful now and then when writing or reviewing code, but it does not build, run, or sell anything on its own. Its guidance is generic and language-agnostic, so the agent must still follow the project's own conventions.

summary: Guides an agent through cutting a developer audience into a few named, sized and ranked segments, choosing two dimensions, estimating segment sizes with confidence tiers, mapping who evaluates, approves and pays inside each segment, and producing a written segment map with a primary, a secondary and an anti-segment. It is aimed at developer-relations and product people deciding who their developer audience is and where effort goes. The skill is a strategy method with no code or stack dependence.
tasks: decide which developer audience to serve first
size a language ecosystem or developer persona
map who signs when the developer is not the buyer
write a segment map with an anti-segment
qualityWhy: Detailed and sequenced with interview questions, decision rules, a quality gate and a map template, though many references are external files whose content was not included in the skill text.
why: It is a stack-free planning method that serves product strategy for a developer-facing node, but it does not build, run or sell anything directly, so its use is occasional. Sizing relies on public surveys the agent may need to browse, which is an unknown but not a blocker.

summary: This guide shows an agent how to harden a Laravel application: production settings, login and session handling, roles and policies, safe database queries, CSRF and XSS defences, API tokens and rate limits, and file upload checks. It is written for developers reviewing or deploying PHP web apps and APIs. The agent can use its checklists to audit an existing Laravel project for common vulnerabilities.
tasks: audit a Laravel app for security problems

harden a Laravel API with tokens and rate limits
review Laravel file uploads and forms for injection or XSS
qualityWhy: It gives many concrete code examples and a checklist, but it mixes old and new Laravel versions, has some doubtful snippets such as the validated() override and trusted_proxies placement, and gives no verification steps.
why: It targets Laravel, a PHP framework that a Fractera node does not use (the node runs Next.js, React and TypeScript), so an agent should read it for security ideas such as CSRF, mass assignment and security headers and apply them the node's way. Its storage examples lean on S3, which conflicts with the local-first design, but that is a usage note rather than a risk.

summary: The skill guides an agent to turn support tickets, issue history and error telemetry into troubleshooting pages that a developer finds by pasting the exact error string. It clusters raw failure reports with a bundled Python script, ranks the clusters by reader-hours unblocked, and writes entries with message, applies-to, cause, fix, confirmation and escalation parts. It also covers generating error-code catalogs from one source file and re-indexing AI assistants after content changes. The audience is developer-relations writers and documentation teams maintaining product docs.
tasks: turn support tickets into troubleshooting docs
write a page for each recurring error code
build a known-issues page for a release
cluster repeated error reports and rank them for documentation
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear ten-step method with interview gates, ranking tables, entry templates, verification steps and a failure-mode table, though it relies on several referenced files whose content I could not inspect.
why: It is a documentation-writing method, not a Fractera feature, so it is useful now and then for a product's own error docs but needs no stack; its cluster script is local and needs no key. Its use is "ideas" rather than "install" because the instructions assume an external ticket and telemetry workflow and a docs generator the node does not provide, so it must be adapted to the node's own docs. The skill also points to other skills, which the install would not include.

summary: The skill makes an agent write HTML or JSX with daisyUI 5 class names on top of Tailwind CSS 4, picking components such as buttons, cards, modals and navbars from per-component guides. It also points to guides for installation, configuration, theme colors and usage rules. It is aimed at developers and designers building interface markup.

style a login form with input and button components
add a dark theme to a Tailwind project
create a card grid for a product landing page
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear selection protocol and a reference table, and the sub-guides cover each component, though the root file alone is mostly a router.
why: Building page UI is central to what a Fractera node is for, and daisyUI is a stack-compatible CSS library that fits the Tailwind 4 stack the node uses. It needs no outside service or key, and the install guide reads as a normal npm setup.

summary: This skill gives an agent a condensed set of C++ Core Guidelines rules for writing, reviewing and refactoring modern C++ (C++17/20/23). It covers ownership and RAII, const-by-default immutability, type safety, error handling with custom exceptions, locking, templates with concepts, naming, and performance habits. It is aimed at developers who want consistent, safe C++ code in a project.

add concepts to a template function
qualityWhy: It gives concrete rule tables, before-and-after code examples and a closing checklist, though it has no test or tooling steps and some rules are only summarised.
why: It is a stack-free style guide that helps when a node project contains C++ code, but most Fractera work is TypeScript, so it is only occasionally useful. No outside service or account is needed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through measuring an existing developer community, whether a chat or forum space, an open-source contributor base, or both. The agent interviews the team about its goals, data access and privacy limits, then builds a short metric sheet across responsiveness, contributor funnel, activity and sentiment. Each metric gets a formula, a baseline and a threshold drawn from the community's own history, plus an owner and an action. A bundled bash script computes a contributor absence factor from a local git repository. The intended users are community managers, developer relations teams and open-source maintainers.

why: It is a stack-free measurement method that directly serves running and growing a developer product's community, and it needs no service or key. Optional inputs such as forge APIs or venue analytics exports are used only if the team already has access, and the skill's privacy gate covers exports. The script runs locally on git history with no network calls.

summary: This skill gives an agent a policy for code samples in developer documentation: what each sample must contain, how it must handle copy-paste and credential safety, which execution tier it belongs to, and how language versions should match. It also audits an existing docs tree by inventorying every fenced snippet and running a mechanical lint script, then returns a ranked fix queue. write a code sample policy for our SDK documentation
find leaked keys or unsafe commands in docs snippets
check whether documentation examples still compile after an API change
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete steps, a runnable lint script, rubrics, severity anchors and templates, with only small gaps such as citations that cannot be checked from the files alone.
why: It is stack-free and works on Markdown files, so it fits any node, but it only matters when the node is used to publish developer documentation with code samples rather than sites or content in general. The script reads local files only and sends nothing out.

summary: This guide teaches an agent to review a Java Spring Boot service for security weaknesses. why: It is built for Java Spring Boot, which the node does not use, so an agent should read it for ideas and rebuild the checks in the node's Next.js and next-auth stack. Its security principles (deny by default, validate input, keep secrets out of code) do apply to any product built on a node.

summary: The skill guides an agent to design a sustainable build-in-public practice for an open-source project or developer tool. why: It serves maintainers planning public communication about their product, which matters for growth, but it is a strategy and planning aid rather than a build or run tool for a node's site or app, so its use is occasional. summary: The skill guides an agent building a Caffeine canister app to send SMS and MMS through Twilio, using a mops client with Basic Auth credentials held by the canister. Sends cost money and US traffic needs weeks of A2P registration, which the person should know before building.

summary: This skill tells an agent to write a structured implementation plan file for a feature, refactor, package upgrade, or design or infrastructure change. why: It is a stack-free planning habit that helps build features and refactors on a node, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. It only writes Markdown files and calls no outside service.

summary: This skill guides an agent through improving a person's LinkedIn profile so recruiters and hiring managers can find it. why: Local FFmpeg processing directly serves making video and audio content and preparing assets for a node's product, and it needs no outside service or account. The reference.md file was not provided, so its contents could not be checked; platform limits may change over time.

summary: The skill guides an agent to rewrite weak resume bullet points into achievement-focused statements that include metrics, using frameworks such as X-Y-Z, STAR and CAR. summary: This skill teaches an agent to add Apple's iOS 26 Liquid Glass material to native apps. It covers glass effects on views, buttons and containers in SwiftUI, the matching UIKit classes, and tinted glass in WidgetKit widgets. It is written for iOS developers building native Apple interfaces.

summary: This skill lets an agent turn a plain-language description into a structured list of entities such as companies or people, using the parallel-cli tool. summary: Turns an agent into a research-first design assistant for UI, landing pages, dashboards, redesigns and visual polish. summary: This skill lets an agent set up long-running web monitors that re-check a page or topic on a schedule and record when something changes. why: Monitors run as server-side jobs on Parallel's cloud and keep their events there, so they are a cloud place to run and store work rather than something that lives on the node's own computer. The skill is well written, but it does not serve building, running, or making content on a local-first node, so it should be skipped.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive a real browser against a locally running web app with Playwright. The agent can navigate pages, fill forms, click through user flows, check visibility and text, capture screenshots, and read console logs. It is aimed at developers who want to verify frontend behaviour or debug UI problems before shipping.

qualityWhy: The instructions are clear and cover the main capabilities, but the examples are fragments with no full runnable script, no install commands for the browser binaries, and no concrete steps for starting the app or waiting on it.
why: Testing a locally running web app in a real browser directly serves building and running a product, and it runs entirely on the person's machine with no outside service. It is not tied to a particular framework, so it works with a Next.js app on a node, though the agent will need to write its own complete test script from the fragments.

summary: The skill guides an agent through configuring Expo's EAS Update for over-the-air JavaScript and asset delivery to installed apps, using expo-updates and the EAS CLI. summary: This skill tells an agent how to fetch full-text academic papers for a user from a list of DOIs, titles or topics. risks: Instructs the agent to automatically attempt sliders, checkboxes and robot checks on publisher and CNKI pages, which bypasses anti-bot safety controls.

summary: This skill checks academic references field by field against several sources such as Crossref, IEEE Xplore, web search and CNKI. summary: This skill gives an agent a set of safe database migration habits: forward-only production changes, expand-contract renames, concurrent index builds, and batched backfills. summary: Guides an agent reviewing Swift code for concurrency correctness, covering actor reentrancy, structured versus unstructured tasks, cancellation, async streams, bridging, legacy migration and strict-concurrency diagnostics. summary: Gives an agent a set of Playwright end-to-end testing patterns: a folder layout for specs, a Page Object Model class, a configuration file with multi-browser projects, CI workflow YAML, and artifact handling for screenshots, traces and video. why: Playwright testing is useful for a node's web products, so an agent could use it now and then to test sites it builds. summary: The skill teaches an agent to set up, run, diagnose and upgrade Ultracite, a zero-config linting and formatting preset for JavaScript and TypeScript projects, covering Oxlint, Biome and ESLint backends. summary: This is a short entry point for Orca's per-workspace environment recipes, which are disposable runtimes such as cloud sandboxes, VMs, SSH hosts or local containers that Orca creates for each workspace. It tells an agent which Orca executable to call, then to fetch the full guide for the installed Orca version. The guide itself is not included, so the agent cannot set up a recipe from this file alone. It serves developers configuring coding-agent workspaces, not people building or running a product.

summary: The skill guides an agent through competitive analysis: mapping rivals on two key dimensions, profiling competitors, comparing pricing tiers, and judging whether an advantage is defensible. summary: This skill guides an agent through designing ClickHouse tables, choosing MergeTree engine variants, and writing fast analytical queries such as aggregations, window functions, retention and funnel analysis. summary: This skill guides an agent through acquiring RAM from live Windows, Linux, macOS and virtual machines, then analysing the dumps with Volatility 3. summary: The skill teaches an agent to write unit tests for shell scripts with the Bats framework, covering error-path checks, skipping tests when a dependency is missing, running a script under bash, sh and dash, parallel runs, a shared helper file, and CI wiring with GitHub Actions and a Makefile. summary: This skill helps an agent understand the protection layers met while analysing software: anti-debugging, timing checks, packing and detection of virtual machines.
