redesign an OAuth consent screen
set token TTLs and refresh rotation policy
design an app verification program
qualityWhy: It is detailed and decision-oriented with ranked options, named standards and concrete checks, but it leans on references to other files and gives few step-by-step commands an agent could run directly.
why: It is useful when a node builds an OAuth issuer for third-party apps, but Fractera's sign-in is next-auth 5 and not a standalone OAuth server, so the design must be adapted to that stack and cannot be installed as written. It is a design-guidance skill with no code or stack commands of its own, so it is advice rather than a tool an agent runs.

summary: This skill gives an agent control over the layout of cmux, a macOS terminal app: creating and moving windows, workspaces, panes and surfaces, changing focus, reordering tabs, and flashing a cue on a surface. It is aimed at automation that needs predictable placement in a multi-pane terminal setup. It also covers cmux's own settings file and how to launch commands in new terminals.
tasks: open a new split pane running the dev server
move a terminal tab to another pane
rename or colour a workspace
flash a pane to draw attention
reload cmux settings after an edit
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete command examples, a handle model and a clear split into reference files, though several details are only pointers to other files.
why: It controls a macOS terminal application's layout and has nothing to do with building, running or selling a web product, content, or AI agents on a Fractera node. It is a desktop-tooling skill and not useful for node work.

summary: Guides an agent in drafting C-suite and VP-level resumes that lead with strategic leadership, a leadership-brand profile, career highlights with metrics, and board or advisory roles. It is aimed at senior executives who need a 2 to 3 page document for recruiters and board members. It covers structure, bullet formulas, tone, tenure framing and confidentiality.
tasks: write a C-suite resume for a COO
draft a VP-level executive profile
frame short executive tenures for a resume
add board and advisory roles to a resume
qualityWhy: It gives a clear structure, formulas, a worked example and an output template, though it has no checklist for verifying metrics and is light on how to gather facts from the person.
why: It is a stack-free writing skill that helps a person prepare a document for job applications, which is useful now and then rather than for building or running a product. No risks were found in the file.

summary: The skill guides an agent to design the operator-side review process for third-party apps on a B2B SaaS marketplace. It covers review-pipeline shape scaled to data sensitivity, permission audits, automated pre-screening with human triage, objective re-review triggers on updates, publish-channel hardening, appeal paths, and tiered revocation. It is aimed at platform teams that run an app marketplace and need to decide what gets approved and what gets removed. It is a design-document methodology with no code, scripts or install steps of its own.
tasks: design a security review process for third-party marketplace apps
add a fast path to slow app approvals without reopening updates
rewrite re-review and revocation policy after an update leaked data
define objective triggers for re-reviewing app updates
design an appeal path for rejected marketplace apps
qualityWhy: Detailed, structured and falsifiable with interview questions, ranked menus, gates and KPIs, though it leans on external references and some claims are not checkable from the file alone.
why: It is a process-design methodology for marketplace operators, which a node runs only if it hosts a third-party app marketplace; it is not a building or content task for most nodes. It is written as a general process, not for a specific stack, so it can be read and applied directly with no adaptation to Fractera's own stack, but its design-document output is advisory rather than something a node installs. Some of its named incidents and platform figures cannot be verified from the file.

summary: The skill guides an agent in designing the test or sandbox mode of a public API platform, so outside integrators can build and check their work without touching real money, messages or data. It covers how isolated the sandbox should be, test-key prefixes, magic input values that trigger specific outcomes, simulated events and time, reset and seeding, sandbox quotas, abuse controls and the path to going live. It is aimed at teams that run third-party API platforms, not at the builders of a single product.
tasks: design a test mode for a payments API
let integrators trigger test webhook events on demand
choose between a test-mode toggle and a separate sandbox
plan the cutover from sandbox to live keys
qualityWhy: The skill is detailed, with decision rules, clarifying questions, anti-patterns, measurement gates and reference files, though some sections are dense and assume a platform-design context.
why: A node is local-first, and this skill is about designing a sandbox for a public API platform's external integrators, which is not building or running a site, app, agent or content on a node. It relies on design of a platform surface rather than on local tools, so it does not serve what nodes are for.

summary: This skill gives an agent team a set of messaging rules: when to send a direct message versus a broadcast, how a lead reviews and approves a teammate's plan before work starts, and how to shut a team down gracefully once tasks are done. It also lists common coordination mistakes and how to debug stalled teammates or deadlocks. It is aimed at people orchestrating multi-agent coding teams rather than at end products.
tasks: set communication norms for a newly spawned agent team
approve or reject a teammate's implementation plan
shut down a finished agent team gracefully
debug teammates that are not coordinating at integration points
qualityWhy: The rules are clear and the message formats are concrete, but the file gives no end-to-end example run and leaves several protocol details (request_id origin, shutdown_response format) only partly specified.
why: It is a protocol for orchestrating Claude Code agent teams, not for building, running or selling a product on a node, so it does not serve what nodes are for. It also relies on Claude Code's internal team tooling and a local ~/.claude directory rather than the node's own elements.

summary: This tool checks whether a coding agent actually follows a given skill, rule or agent definition, instead of assuming it does. It turns the file into an expected sequence of steps, writes test prompts at three levels of pressure, runs the agent, and labels each tool call against those steps. It then reports compliance rates with a full tool-call timeline. It is aimed at people who build and maintain agent instructions and want evidence that those instructions work.
tasks: check whether an agent follows a rule
measure compliance of a skill with test scenarios
generate a compliance report with tool-call timelines
find which steps of an agent workflow are skipped
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is mostly a description with usage commands and little step-by-step guidance, but the bundled Python code is substantial, structured and tested.
needs: Claude Code CLI with a signed-in account
why: It is a developer tool for checking agent behaviour rather than something that builds or sells a product, so it is useful now and then. It runs many agent sessions through the person's own Claude account, which costs money, and the runner module was not visible, so I could not confirm whether it changes permission settings.

summary: The skill guides an agent to design server-side idempotency keys for a public API so that retried writes don't duplicate effects, and to write client retry guidance with backoff, jitter, timeouts and retry budgets. It covers key scoping, payload-mismatch rejection, in-flight handling, replay windows, atomic claim mechanisms, and SDK defaults. It is aimed at API designers and backend teams who ship endpoints or SDKs to third-party integrators.
tasks: add Idempotency-Key support to a POST payments endpoint
write retry guidance for API docs
pick backoff and jitter defaults for an SDK
audit an API for duplicate-request races
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is detailed and structured with a clear workflow, ranked decision rules, an anti-pattern checklist, measurement gates, and linked reference files with formulas and vendor defaults.
why: It is a general API design skill that fits building a node's public endpoints, but the node's own stack (Next.js and SQLite with its own data element) differs from the Postgres and DynamoDB examples, so it must be adapted to the node's own claim mechanism and storage rather than installed as written. No risks found in the file contents shown.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to write HTML email templates as React components, preview them in a local dev server, and render them to HTML or plain text. It also covers sending through Resend or other providers, and embedding a visual email editor in an app. It is aimed at developers building transactional mail, newsletters and notifications.
tasks: build a welcome email template in React
add a password reset email
render an email component to HTML and plain text
send an order confirmation with Resend
embed a visual email editor in my app
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete code, rules for email-client compatibility, required classes and a clarifying-questions step, with reference files for deeper detail, though the visible content is mostly reference links.
needs: other email provider credentials if not using Resend
why: Email templates are a core part of building a product and sending its messages, and the skill runs locally with the node's stack. It uses React and Tailwind, which fit the node, and sending needs a Resend or other provider account the person chooses. It is marked as needing a service because the sending path depends on an outside email provider.

summary: This skill guides an agent in designing how an API platform tells its outside consumers about outages: a status page modeled on four incident stages, component states based on breadth of impact, status driven by monitoring rather than a person flipping a switch, and push plus pull channels. It also covers incident update cadence, public postmortems for developers, public SLA and uptime reporting, and maintenance-window notices. It is aimed at teams running a public API or developer platform.
tasks: design a status page for our public API
write a public postmortem for a recent outage
plan a maintenance window notice for customers
fix status page that stayed green during an outage
publish SLA and uptime reporting
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, ordered in steps, and include clarifying questions, templates, and checks, though much of it is design reasoning rather than executable steps and it refers to reference files not included in this review.
why: It is a communication practice, not code, so it fits a node's API platform work now and then, but it is written for a generic developer-platform stack and the node's own status and monitoring elements would need adapting. The skill itself names other skills in its collection that it depends on, which the node may not have.

summary: This skill helps an agent decide how many teammates to spawn for a multi-agent job, which preset team to use (review, debug, feature, fullstack, research, security, migration), which subagent type gives each role the tools it needs, and how to set the display mode for teammates. It is aimed at developers coordinating Claude Code agent teams on coding work. The guidance is orchestration advice about team shape rather than a stack-specific build recipe.
tasks: decide how many agents to spawn for a refactor
set up a security audit team with four reviewers
choose the right subagent type for each role
configure tmux display for teammate agents
qualityWhy: The sizing table, preset compositions, subagent type table and troubleshooting section are concrete and actionable, though the reference files were not reviewed here and some presets lack examples.
why: It is a planning aid for coordinating agents, not something a Fractera node builds or sells with, so its use is occasional. It depends on Claude Code's agent-teams features (team-reviewer, team-implementer and so on) that are not part of the node's own stack, so it should be read for ideas and not installed as written.

summary: This skill gives an agent a checklist of sustainability practices for Google Cloud projects, drawn from the environmental pillar of Google's Well-Architected Framework. It covers choosing low-carbon regions, cutting idle compute and wasteful AI workloads, writing lighter software, archiving cold storage, and tracking emissions. It is aimed at cloud architects and teams who want to reduce the carbon footprint of workloads they run on Google Cloud.
tasks: assess a Google Cloud workload for sustainability
pick a low-carbon region for a deployment
find idle resources to cut cloud energy waste
set up carbon footprint reporting in BigQuery
qualityWhy: It offers useful principles, assessment questions and a validation checklist, but most items point to external docs and it gives no concrete commands or steps an agent can run.
needs: Carbon Footprint data export to BigQuery
why: The skill is guidance for running and optimizing Google Cloud infrastructure, which is cloud administration on a cloud provider, not a local-first product or content tool, so it is not useful for building on a node. The mandatory references/attribution.md file was not included in what I reviewed, so its contents are unverified.

summary: This skill guides an agent through reading the current git status and diff, judging whether the pending work is a feature, a release or a hotfix under the nvie Git Flow model, and then creating a branch with a kebab-case name. It is written for developers who keep their repositories in Git Flow order and want the branch chosen and named consistently.
tasks: create a git flow branch for my current changes
name a feature branch for new API endpoints
start a hotfix branch for a production security fix
prepare a release branch with version bumps
qualityWhy: The steps and examples are concrete, but the XML padding is heavy, the no-ff rule in the reference contradicts the plain checkout examples, and it never checks that develop or master exist before branching.
why: Git branching discipline helps anyone building and shipping a site or app on a node, but it is a general developer habit rather than a core node feature. It needs only the local git CLI and no outside service, so it can be installed as written, with the caveat that it assumes the repository already uses develop and master.

summary: The skill guides an agent through auditing every button or form action in a user interface by tracing the ordered sequence of state changes each handler triggers. It is aimed at developers whose buttons appear to do nothing even though each function works on its own. The agent maps store side effects first, then checks each handler for undo conflicts, stale values, race conditions and dead code paths, and reports each finding in a fixed format.
tasks: find why a button does nothing in the UI
audit click handlers for conflicting state changes
check state store side effects after a refactor
review form submit flows for wrong final state
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear method, named bug patterns, output formats and a worked example, though it lacks commands and a test checklist.
why: It is a stack-free debugging method, but its examples assume Zustand and React hooks, which Fractera nodes use only in part, so an agent should adapt the store-mapping step to the node's own state layer. No install or outside service is needed, and no risk is found in the file.

summary: This skill guides an agent through deciding which integration surfaces a platform should offer external developers and AI agents, such as REST, webhooks, GraphQL, SDKs, CLI, MCP and embedded components, and in what order. It is written for platform teams and works through an interview about buyers, existing APIs, spec quality and demand signals, then produces a sequenced plan with a named audience and handoff per surface. It is a strategy layer that points to sibling skills for the detailed design of each surface.
tasks: decide which API to build first
plan an integration surface roadmap
decide whether to add an MCP layer
choose API-first or embedded-first for a non-technical buyer
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear interview, ranked postures, a workflow with sections and measurable gates, and named failure modes, though some cited statistics and launch dates are unverified and it leans on sibling skills.
why: It is a planning skill for API and platform strategy rather than building product features, so it is useful now and then for deciding surfaces. It is written around an API-first platform and a sibling skill collection, not Fractera's own stack, so its outputs need adapting to the node's Next.js and element-based architecture before use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through running containers on AWS: Kubernetes clusters on EKS, task-based services on ECS and Fargate, image storage in ECR, and web apps on Elastic Beanstalk. It routes each question to the matching reference file and includes a procedure for recommending and reading ECS Action Logs when deployments fail. It is aimed at engineers who deploy, debug, or optimize workloads on AWS.
tasks: deploy a container to ECS or Fargate
debug a failed EKS deployment
set up an ECR repository with lifecycle policies
enable ECS Action Logs to troubleshoot a rollback
qualityWhy: The visible SKILL.md gives a clear routing table and guardrails, but most of the concrete procedures sit in reference files that were not shown.
needs: AWS MCP Server or AWS CLI access
why: The skill is built around hosting and running workloads on AWS cloud services, which a local-first node does not use, so it is not useful for its purpose. Its reference files were only partly visible, so this rating rests on SKILL.md alone.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing the rate-limit policy a public API publishes to its consumers: choosing request counting versus GraphQL cost points, setting burst and sustained numbers per tier, adding fairness between tenants, picking rate-limit header families, shaping 429 and Retry-After responses, defining enterprise override paths, and writing notice rules for limit changes. It is aimed at API product owners and platform teams who need predictable, documented throttling for their consumers. It is a policy and design document, with no code to install or run.
tasks: design rate-limit tiers for a public REST API
plan rate limits across REST and GraphQL surfaces
add fairness so one tenant cannot degrade others
audit rate-limit docs against enforced limits
define the process for enterprise rate-limit overrides
qualityWhy: It is a thorough, structured workflow with clarifying questions, ranked options, named vendor examples, anti-pattern checklists and measurable gates, all drawn from its own files.
why: It is policy-level guidance for designing published API limits, which is only occasionally useful for a Fractera node that builds its own sites or apps. It is stack-free, so it can be read directly, but it contains no install steps and is not tied to the node's own API layer, so its use is limited to design advice.

summary: This skill guides an agent to write Python code that talks to Microsoft Dataverse through its client SDK, with a focus on production habits. It sets out a retry pattern with backoff for throttled or timed-out requests, a single shared client object, structured error handling, and logging in place of print calls. It also asks for narrow column selection and server-side filtering to keep queries lean. The intended users are Python developers who integrate with a Dataverse environment.
tasks: write a Dataverse client service with retry and error handling
add logging and audit trails to a Dataverse script
optimize Dataverse queries with filters and selected columns
generate typed Python code for Dataverse record operations
qualityWhy: It gives useful rules and code fragments, but the examples are partial (the retry loop body is a placeholder and no real SDK calls are shown), so an agent would still have to fill in much of the work.
needs: Microsoft Entra ID credentials for Dataverse
why: Dataverse is a cloud database service, and a Fractera node keeps its data in its own local SQLite element, which is the only route to data, so this skill does not fit the node's purpose. Its own content is clean, with no risky commands or secret handling.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing, deploying and troubleshooting AWS infrastructure with the CDK in TypeScript or Python. It covers bootstrapping, stack structure, construct patterns, cdk-nag checks, drift detection, importing existing resources, safe refactoring and fixing CDK or CloudFormation errors. It is aimed at engineers who run their workloads on AWS.
tasks: bootstrap an AWS account for CDK
write a CDK stack for a serverless API
fix a failed cdk deploy
detect drift on a CloudFormation stack
refactor CDK constructs without replacing resources
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete commands, error-to-fix tables and explicit warnings, with detail pushed to reference files that are well organised, though only the main file was judged here.
needs: AWS CDK bootstrap in the target account
why: The skill is built around deploying to AWS cloud infrastructure, which is a cloud hosting and cloud administration service, so it does not fit a local-first Fractera node. It is well written and would be useful for a separate AWS project, but not for building or running a node.

summary: This skill guides an agent designing a SaaS product's MCP server as a surface AI agents operate. It covers sizing the build effort, curating a small set of workflow tools instead of mirroring API endpoints, safety patterns for write tools, remote hosting with OAuth 2.1 resource-server rules, versioning, registry publication, telemetry, and staged rollout. It is written for product and platform teams deciding what to expose to agents, and it is a design layer rather than code scaffolding.
tasks: design an MCP server for our product
curate the tools agents should call
add safety gates to write tools
decide hosting and OAuth for an MCP server
plan MCP rollout and adoption metrics
qualityWhy: Detailed, structured and actionable with clear steps, checks and a measurement section, though much of it is strategic framing with few concrete code-level examples.
why: Useful for a team designing an MCP surface, but it is a design-level document rather than an installable tool and it assumes a SaaS product, so a node would read it for ideas. It is not tied to a stack the node replaces, but it gives no runnable steps for a Fractera node's own build, so it should be used as guidance only.

summary: This skill guides an agent through deciding a public API's language SDK portfolio: which languages get official SDKs and in what order, whether to generate them or hand-write them, how support tiers and promotion work, and how SDK versions relate to API versions and end-of-life. It is written for platform teams that already chose SDKs as an integration surface. The agent interviews the team step by step and drafts an approved strategy document.
tasks: decide which language SDKs to build first
define official and community SDK support tiers
choose between generated and handwritten SDKs
plan SDK deprecation and end-of-life
separate SDK versioning from API versioning
qualityWhy: The skill has a clear seven-step workflow, interview questions, decision rules and references, though much of it is strategy prose with few concrete steps an agent can run.
why: A Fractera node is local-first and builds sites, apps, agents and content; a portfolio strategy for public API client libraries is planning for a platform's external integrators, not something a node's own builders need day to day, and it leans on hosted generators like Stainless and Fern that conflict with local-first use.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to look up current documentation, API references and code examples for a named library, framework, SDK or CLI tool. The agent first resolves the library name to a Context7 ID, then queries that library's docs with a focused question, and reports when the lookup fails or quota runs out. It is aimed at developers who need accurate, up-to-date API details instead of possibly outdated training data.
tasks: look up the current API syntax for a library
find setup steps for a framework like Next.js or Tailwind
check a configuration option for a library version
debug a library-specific error with current docs
migrate code to a newer library version
qualityWhy: The skill gives clear two-step commands, query-writing rules, a selection process, error handling and common mistakes, though it is focused on one CLI and offers no examples of reading the output.
needs: optional CONTEXT7_API_KEY for higher rate limits
why: Looking up docs for Next.js, React, Tailwind and other node stack libraries directly serves building products on a node, but every query is sent to the outside Context7 service, and npx ctx7@latest always fetches the newest CLI from npm, so the person should know this before install.

summary: The skill asks an agent to review the changes on a branch compared with main and strip out code that an AI assistant tends to leave behind, such as redundant comments, needless defensive checks or try/catch blocks, casts to any, and deep nesting. It is meant for developers tidying their own code before merging. The edits are supposed to be small and keep behavior the same.
tasks: clean up AI-generated code before merging a branch
remove unnecessary comments and try/catch blocks from my diff
simplify deeply nested code with early returns
remove any casts that only silence type errors
qualityWhy: It names the focus areas and guardrails but gives no concrete steps, examples of slop versus acceptable code, or checks for verifying behavior is preserved.
why: It is a stack-free code-review habit that helps any repository, but it is thin and gives the agent little guidance on how to judge what counts as slop in a given file. Nothing in it calls an outside service.

summary: This skill makes an agent act as an interviewer that refines a rough task request into a structured prompt. It asks clarifying questions about scope, deliverables, constraints and success criteria, may explore the project to gather context, and then outputs the finished prompt as markdown. It is meant for people who want a clearer brief before starting work.
tasks: turn a rough idea into a detailed task prompt
clarify scope and success criteria before coding
organize requirements into a structured brief
copy a finished prompt to the clipboard for review
qualityWhy: The workflow is clear and easy to follow, but the instructions are short and generic, with no examples of questions, output sections or checks.
why: The interview-and-refine habit is stack-free and could help plan product or content tasks, but the clipboard step depends on Joyride and the VS Code API, which a Fractera node does not provide, so it must be rebuilt in the node's own way. Its promise of no code writing also fits only part of what nodes do.

summary: This skill guides an agent through recording a narrated screen capture of a running web app with Playwright. The agent first inspects the real pages to map their form fields and buttons, then dry-runs the selectors, and only then records a WebM video. The recording adds a visible arrow cursor, slower typing, smooth scrolling and short on-screen captions. It is aimed at people who need a walkthrough, tutorial or feature showcase for documentation, onboarding or a stakeholder presentation.
tasks: record a walkthrough video of my web app
make a tutorial video for a new feature
create a screen recording for onboarding
produce a product demo video for stakeholders
qualityWhy: It gives concrete discovery, rehearsal and recording steps with working helper code, a template and a checklist, though it omits Playwright install steps and leaves the video-merge pitfall vague.
why: It directly serves making product walkthrough videos for a web app running on the node, and it runs locally with no outside service or key. It is not written for the node's own stack, but Playwright is a standalone tool that drives any URL, so it needs no adaptation. The licence is unstated, and the agent should check it before reuse.

summary: The skill guides an agent to optimize a B2B software vendor's own listing on a third-party app marketplace such as AppExchange, HubSpot, Atlassian, Shopify or Slack. It covers instrumenting analytics, rewriting keyword fields, ordering screenshots and demo video, building compliant review requests, and pursuing badges. It is written for vendors who need installs and search visibility on those platforms.
tasks: audit our AppExchange listing and fix what hurts installs
plan a six-week Atlassian Marketplace launch listing
defend Shopify App Store rankings with a refresh cycle
design a compliant review-request program for an app listing
qualityWhy: The instruction is detailed, with interview questions, staged workflow, ranked levers, provenance labels and measurable gates, though much of it is conceptual and lacks concrete templates.
needs: an active listing on a third-party marketplace
why: It serves a vendor's marketplace presence, not building or running a Fractera site or content, so value is some; it is for marketplace listings outside the node's stack, so it must be adapted rather than installed as written.

summary: The skill gives an agent a checklist of idiomatic conventions for building Spring Boot applications in Kotlin. It covers Maven or Gradle setup with the kotlin-jpa plugin, constructor injection, data-class DTOs, validation, global exception handling, transactions, logging, testing with Kotest, MockK and Testcontainers, and coroutines. It is written for backend developers working on the JVM rather than on Node.
tasks: write a Spring Boot REST controller in Kotlin
set up a Kotlin Spring Boot project with JPA
review Kotlin backend code for idiomatic style
add validation and error handling to a Kotlin API

why: A Node is built on Next.js, TypeScript and SQLite, and this skill is for a Spring Boot and Kotlin JVM stack the node does not use, so it is not useful for what nodes are for. Its advice is also tied to a different stack, so it would have to be rewritten to be used.

summary: This skill guides an agent through binary exploitation for capture-the-flag challenges, turning memory corruption in a native target into code execution or privilege escalation. It covers stack and heap overflows, format strings, ROP and ret2libc, shellcode, seccomp and sandbox escapes, and kernel exploitation, with a reference index and pwntools-based example scripts. The intended users are security students and CTF players working on vulnerable services they are allowed to test.
tasks: solve a buffer overflow CTF challenge
write a ROP chain to bypass NX
exploit a heap use-after-free to get a shell
bypass a seccomp filter to read a flag
qualityWhy: The files are extensive and concrete, with commands, exploit code and checks, but the scripts rely on placeholder addresses and the referenced install script is not among the listed files.
why: Its purpose is CTF training and vulnerability exploitation, which does not serve building, running, selling or making content for a product on a Fractera node. The install script it mentions is missing from the file list, and the scripts carry odd "audit-ok" comments, but neither creates a risk to the person's computer.

summary: This skill gives an agent a structured method for weighing several job offers against each other. It totals cash, equity, benefits and perks into a yearly figure, scores non-money factors such as growth, work-life balance and team quality, and applies weighted priorities to reach a recommendation. It is aimed at an individual deciding on a career move, with checklists for red flags and questions to ask before accepting.
tasks: compare two job offers side by side
work out the total yearly value of a job offer
rank job offers using weighted priorities
list questions to ask before accepting an offer
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete templates, a worked weighted-scoring example and a checklist, though tax treatment and equity valuation are mentioned without real guidance.
why: It is a personal career-decision method with no link to building, running, selling or making content for a product, so it does not serve what a node is for.

summary: This skill guides an agent through deciding whether a SaaS product should appear as a data source inside other companies' ETL or ELT pipelines. It walks through checking real customer demand, choosing which pipeline platforms to target, and comparing build options by who carries the ongoing maintenance cost. It also audits whether the product's API can support incremental extraction and states honestly what change-data-capture can and cannot promise. The intended users are product and data leads at SaaS vendors.
tasks: decide whether to build an ETL platform connector
compare platform-managed and SDK connector options
audit a product API for incremental extraction
write honest incremental-sync wording for customers
plan the maintenance budget for a source connector
qualityWhy: It gives a clear step-by-step workflow, interview gates, checklists and pass/fail measures, backed by three reference files, though much of it is strategic prose rather than executable steps.
why: It is a stack-free planning aid that helps a node-built SaaS decide on pipeline presence, which is useful only when that product exists and its customers use ETL tools, so it is occasional rather than core. Nothing in it needs a cloud account or key, and the platform figures it quotes are a dated snapshot the user should re-check.

summary: The skill guides an agent to design what external developers and partner ISVs can see about their own failing integrations: per-integration request, event and webhook delivery logs with optional replay, correlation IDs carried from response headers into support tickets, error rates split by 4xx, 5xx and 429 per API key or app, and well-timed partner alerts with cooldowns. It also covers a provider-side fleet view ranking which partner integrations are breaking. It is written for platform teams whose partners currently learn about outages from end users.
tasks: design a developer-facing request log for our API
stop alerting partners on every failed webhook
audit what integrators can see about their own failures
build a fleet view of which partner apps are breaking
make request IDs resolvable by support
qualityWhy: Detailed, structured and opinionated with clear decision rungs and checks, though much of it is design reasoning rather than executable steps and it depends on referenced files for concrete schemas.
why: It is a design methodology for a provider-side integration visibility surface, which is occasionally useful for a node that exposes an API to partners, but it does not build code directly and assumes a Stripe-like stack and external practices. It is written against a generic platform, so an agent would have to adapt it to the node's Next.js, SQLite and next-auth setup rather than install it as is.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to drive ImageMagick from PowerShell or Bash to inspect image dimensions and metadata, resize images singly or in batches, convert formats, make thumbnails, and filter files by size before processing. It is aimed at people who need to prepare pictures such as wallpapers or thumbnails for different screen sizes. It is a single SKILL.md with short command snippets and no scripts or external calls.
tasks: resize a folder of photos to thumbnails

tasks: save this to my knowledge base
deduplicate and organize my notes
sync my agent session history to a notes repo
find what I already know about a topic

The sync section commits and pushes session histories to a Git remote, which could expose conversations, so the person should check what gets pushed.

summary: This skill makes an agent read-only audit a workspace: repo config, MCP servers, plugins, connectors, environment key names and harness setup. find which capabilities my workspace is missing
decide whether a workflow should be a skill, hook or agent

why: It is a stack-free planning and audit habit that helps set up the agent harness, not product building, so its value is occasional rather than direct. It is read-only and needs no keys, though it does reference ECC-specific names that a Fractera node will not have.

summary: This skill is a thin launcher for a Korean weather lookup. It tells the agent to fetch its real instructions from an npm package at runtime rather than containing them. add a Korean weather widget to a web app
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is only a stub that points to a remote CLI and a GitHub file, so the actual instructions are not in the reviewed files.
needs: Korea Meteorological Administration short-term forecast API service key
why: The weather data is useful now and then for a site or app, but the skill's only real content is fetched and executed from an npm package at runtime, which is a risk and the reviewed files give no usable steps.
risks: Runs the npm package @nomadamas/k-skill via npx at runtime and follows its output as primary instructions, so remote code and remote instructions can change without review.
The update command upgrades the CLI and every installed coding-agent skill automatically, which spreads remote changes to other skills.

summary: This skill lets an agent drive Alibaba's Bailian platform through the `bl` command-line tool to create and edit images, generate and edit short videos, synthesize and transcribe speech, and describe images or video. needs: Alibaba Cloud Bailian (DashScope) account and API key
bl CLI installed via bl skill init
why: It directly serves making images, video, voice and social content, and it returns results as local files, but the generation runs on Alibaba's paid cloud service. Local files are uploaded to DashScope temporary storage for up to 48 hours, which the skill discloses, so the person should know that before using it on private media.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to write, read, review and maintain Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.2 bundles: Markdown concept files with YAML frontmatter, reserved index and log files, and standard links. review frontmatter and links in a knowledge bundle
respond to okf plugin conformance warnings
maintain a dated log.md of knowledge changes
record provenance and verification for concepts
qualityWhy: It gives concrete rules, required formats and reserved-file conventions with clear do and don't guidance, though it has no worked examples or step-by-step procedures.
why: It is a format spec guide for knowledge bundles, not a site or app building skill, so it is only occasionally useful to a Fractera node; it is written for the OpenKnowledge stack, not Fractera's own SQLite and file elements, so it should be read for ideas and adapted to the node's own data layout.

summary: This skill sets up a loop in which one agent builds an application while a separate, deliberately strict agent tests the running app in a browser and scores it against a rubric. The loop repeats until the score clears a pass threshold or an iteration cap is reached. It is aimed at developers who want an autonomous build with high visual and functional quality and accept a higher time and cost budget.
tasks: build a complete app from a one-line prompt
improve the design of a landing page through repeated review
run an autonomous build-and-test loop until quality passes
check that every feature of a web app works in a browser
qualityWhy: The file explains the approach and gives concrete rubric weights, environment variables and commands, but it refers to scripts, slash commands and prompt files (gan-build, gan-harness.sh, PLANNER_PROMPT.md, EVALUATOR_PROMPT.md) that are not included, so an agent cannot follow it end to end.
needs: Claude Code or Anthropic API access
why: It directly serves building and testing applications, and its workflow is stack-free, so it would otherwise be an install; it is marked skip because the sample commands pre-approve Bash for the evaluator through --allowedTools, which lets it run shell commands without the person's confirmation. The cost of about $50 to $200 per run and the missing scripts are also open points.
risks: The evaluator is pre-approved to run Bash through --allowedTools, so shell commands can run without the person's confirmation.

summary: Gives an agent an evidence-first routine for running commands in a code repository, checking git state, debugging CI or build failures, making a narrow fix, and reporting exactly what was executed, verified, committed or pushed. why: It is a stack-free operator habit, useful now and then for debugging and verified fixes on a node, though it leans on other ECC skills that are not part of the node. Nothing in it calls an outside service.

summary: Turns a product requirement, roadmap item or founder discussion into a written capability plan before multi-service coding starts. decide whether a feature needs architecture review or product clarification first
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, rules, an output template and a handoff step, though it leans on references to other ECC lanes and a template file that is not included.
why: It is a stack-free planning method that helps before building, so it is useful now and then rather than for building node sites directly. It refers to an external template file and other ECC lanes that are not part of this skill, so an agent would need to write its own template; nothing in it touches the node's data or sends information out.

summary: This skill is a shared rulebook for the Alibaba Cloud Bailian `bl` command-line tool. why: It is useful for making images, video and speech, but it is a protocol for a cloud service rather than a building tool, so it helps only now and then. It calls Bailian and needs an account, and it sends local files and personal knowledge to Bailian's cloud, though it asks for consent first. Its own version samples are out of date.

summary: This skill tells an agent to look up Korean listed stocks, read KRX base information, and fetch daily trade snapshots through a k-skill proxy, so the person does not need their own KRX API key. summary: This skill asks the agent to act as a QA engineer and produce a test strategy, a GitHub test-issues checklist and a quality assurance plan from existing feature documents such as a PRD, technical breakdown and implementation plan. summary: The skill guides an agent through building one self-contained HTML dashboard file with KPI cards, Chart.js charts, dropdown and date filters, and a sortable table. summary: This skill guides an agent through fine-tuning a model on Alibaba Cloud's Bailian platform using the bl command-line tool. summary: This skill guides an agent through working a real mailbox: sorting incoming mail, reading a thread before replying, and drafting or sending new messages. It requires the agent to check the exact account and recipient, draft first unless a live send was clearly requested, and confirm any send in the Sent folder before reporting it. It treats inbound mail as untrusted text, so instructions inside messages are reported rather than followed. It is aimed at a person who handles business or customer correspondence.

draft a reply to a customer thread
check whether an email was already sent
send an outreach email and confirm it reached Sent
qualityWhy: The workflow and guardrails are clear and usable, but it names no concrete mail client, commands or API, so an agent has to guess how to reach the mailbox and how to check Sent.
needs: a mailbox account the person grants access to, such as their mail provider
why: Mailbox work helps a product only indirectly, through customer replies and outreach, so the value is some rather than high. The skill depends on a mail surface it never names and on other ECC skills (brand-voice, customer-billing-ops and others) that are not part of this node, so those would need to be present for the full workflow.

summary: The skill tells an agent to act as a product manager and turn a rough epic idea into a structured Product Requirements Document. The document covers the problem, solution, personas, user journeys, functional and non-functional requirements, success metrics, out-of-scope items and business value. The result is meant to feed a later technical architecture spec, so it suits product and engineering teams planning larger SaaS features.

turn a product idea into a requirements document
define scope, personas and success metrics for a feature
prepare requirements before technical architecture design

why: It is a stack-free planning prompt, so it fits a node for planning a product or app build, but it is not a direct building tool. The output path /docs/ways-of-work/plan/ is a suggestion that the agent can adjust to the node's folder layout.

summary: The skill guides an agent through fine-tuning open models (Gemma, Qwen, Llama, GLM) and Gemini models on Google Cloud's Agent Platform, from checking project, region and IAM setup, through dataset validation and upload to Cloud Storage, to submitting, monitoring and deploying a tuning job. monitor or cancel a running tuning job

why: The skill is built around Google Cloud cloud infrastructure (Agent Platform tuning jobs, GCS storage for datasets and artifacts, cloud deployment endpoints), which the local-first node rules classify as a cloud place to run and store things, so it is not useful for a local-first node and is skipped.

summary: The skill turns an agent into a senior-engineer persona that reads incomplete shorthand, pseudo-code and loosely worded requests, then produces full working code in the target language. It is aimed at developers who collaborate with people of mixed technical skill.

implement a feature from a rough natural-language description
fill in shorthand markers inside a source file
add validation and error handling to a draft snippet

why: It is stack-free and can help an agent write code from rough notes for any project, though it adds little that a capable agent does not already do. It contains no risky instructions.

summary: Guides an agent through managing managed prompts on Google Cloud's Agent Platform via the Vertex AI Python SDK: creating, listing, retrieving, versioning and deleting prompt resources. It enforces tiered confirmation rules, with typed confirmation before any deletion and a yes/no card before any creation. The audience is developers working inside Google Cloud who build prompt-driven applications.

list the prompts in my Agent Platform project
retrieve a prompt version and fill in its variables
delete an outdated prompt after confirmation
qualityWhy: Concrete snippets, safety tiers and verification steps are given, though the reference files are short and the setup relies on the user's gcloud account.
why: The skill manages prompts in Google Cloud's hosted Agent Platform, which is a cloud place to keep and run things, so it does not fit a local-first node. Its use is also skipped because it is a cloud service administration skill.

summary: The skill gives an agent a security checklist and hardened code patterns for reviewing or writing Solidity automated market maker, liquidity pool and swap contracts. It covers reentrancy ordering, donation and inflation attacks on share math, TWAP-based oracle reads, slippage and deadline checks, safe fixed-point math, and access control on admin functions. It is aimed at developers and auditors building or checking DeFi contracts.

add slippage protection and a deadline to a swap function
review liquidity pool deposit and withdraw logic
switch a spot price oracle to a TWAP
qualityWhy: The patterns are concrete and correct in outline, but the file is a short checklist with fragments that omit imports, the TWAP snippet is incomplete, and it gives no step-by-step audit procedure or test examples.
why: The skill is about smart contract security, not about building, running or selling a site, app, agent or content, so the node has no direct use for it. It also relies on Solidity toolchains and libraries rather than the node's Next.js, Tailwind and SQLite stack, so even if relevant it would need adapting; the skill is not a risk on its own.

summary: This skill guides an agent through malware analysis exercises, mainly capture-the-flag challenges. It covers deobfuscating scripts, triaging PE and .NET binaries, decrypting C2 traffic and recovering configuration data, and writing YARA rules and memory-forensics checks. It is written for security students and CTF players rather than for people building products or content.
tasks: deobfuscate a suspicious JavaScript or PowerShell script
extract the C2 configuration from a PE or .NET sample
decrypt RC4 or AES-encrypted C2 traffic from a PCAP
write a YARA rule to detect a malware family
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete commands and checks for each technique, but most entries are one-line pointers to supporting files, so it is thin as a standalone instruction.
why: Malware analysis for CTF challenges does not serve building, running, selling or making content on a local-first node, so it is not useful for what nodes are for.

summary: The skill guides an agent to set up Python projects and standalone scripts with uv, ruff, ty and pytest, and to migrate away from pip, Poetry, mypy or black. It supplies pyproject.toml templates, dependency-group conventions, PEP 723 inline script metadata, and a security-hook setup with prek, detect-secrets, zizmor and pip-audit. It is aimed at developers writing Python code who want a modern, reproducible toolchain.
tasks: set up a new Python package with uv and ruff
convert a requirements.txt project to uv
write a standalone Python script with inline dependencies
configure pytest coverage and pre-commit hooks
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete commands, a config example, a decision tree, anti-pattern table and migration steps, though several details are only pointed to in reference files I did not read.
why: Python tooling is useful for building parts of a node's app, but it is a developer-setup guide rather than something the node is built around, so it is useful now and then. It is stack-free enough to install as written, and it relies on no outside service or key. Some of its advice (uv add, uv run) is generic Python practice, not Fractera-specific.

summary: Guides an agent through an evidence-first audit of the ECC Tools GitHub App when it burns cost: runaway PR creation, quota bypass, premium-model use by free users, duplicate jobs and retry loops. It works read-only first, tracing webhook to queue to worker, then applies fixes in order of burn impact. The audience is maintainers of the ECC Tools repo, not a generic Fractera site builder.
tasks: audit why the GitHub app is creating too many PRs
find where free users reach premium model paths
check whether usage quota can be bypassed by concurrent requests
trace duplicate queue jobs and retry burn
qualityWhy: The workflow is concrete on order and failure patterns, but it names sibling skills and a sibling repo without giving any commands, file names or checks an agent could run directly.
why: It is tied to one company's internal ECC Tools repo and its billing, so it does not serve building, running or making content for a product on a Fractera node. It is also an operator workflow for a cloud-hosted GitHub App, which the node's local-first rule marks as not useful.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to retrieve live personal messages on the person's own machine, such as iMessage texts, social DMs, and recent one-time codes. It asks the agent to first pin down the message source, thread and time window, then read the latest inbound message, and finally report exactly which source was checked and what state the task ended in. It is meant for someone who needs a code or wants to inspect a thread before replying.
tasks: read my recent texts
find the one-time code from my last message
check a DM thread before replying
confirm which message source was inspected
qualityWhy: The instructions are a short checklist of intentions with no concrete commands, helper names, or examples of how to read a message store, so an agent would still have to invent the actual retrieval method.
why: Reading personal messages is a useful assistant habit but not a product-building feature, and the skill refers to a checked helper or standard path it never names, so an agent could not follow it as written on a node. It defers to other ECC skills (email-ops, knowledge-ops) that a node does not have, so it would need adapting before use.
risks: Reading private texts and DMs and pulling one-time codes exposes the person's personal messages to the agent without a clear limit on what it may keep or send elsewhere.

summary: The skill guides an agent to fix fragmented alerting across GitHub, Linear, local hooks, desktop notifications and chat or email. It sorts events by severity, decides whether each should interrupt, batch into a digest, or only be logged, and merges duplicate alerts into one summary with a named owner and next action. It is written for engineering operators who are drowning in CI and review pings.
tasks: consolidate GitHub and Linear alerts into one lane
reduce noisy CI failure notifications
decide which events should interrupt versus go to a digest
design a severity model for team notifications
qualityWhy: It gives a clear pipeline, severity table and output template, but it stays at the level of policy with few concrete commands, examples or checks an agent could execute.
why: It is about engineering alert routing for developer tooling and does not help build, run or sell a node's sites, apps, agents or content, so it is of no value to the node. Its scope is also tied to the ECC toolchain and references other ECC skills that a node does not have.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write Hookify rules, small markdown files with YAML frontmatter that watch Bash commands, file edits, user prompts, or the end of a task. When a pattern matches, the rule shows a warning or blocks the action before it runs. It is aimed at developers who want guardrails that stop an AI coding agent from running dangerous commands, editing secret files, or leaving debug code behind. The skill covers the file format, the event types, regex tips, and how the runtime treats each rule.
tasks: block dangerous shell commands for the coding agent
warn before editing .env or credential files
stop debug code like console.log from being added
list and toggle existing guardrail rules
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear file format, a field table, event and operator lists, pitfalls, a test command and runtime limits, though it has few complete end-to-end examples.
why: It is a local developer guardrail for Claude Code, useful now and then when an agent builds or edits a node project, but it does not directly build products or content. It needs no outside service, and it is a Claude Code tool rather than a stack the node replaces, so it installs as written into the project's .claude folder.

summary: This skill gives an agent a long prompt for examining an existing codebase and writing a technology stack blueprint. The agent detects the languages, frameworks and dependencies in use, with optional versions, licences, coding conventions and diagrams, then saves the result as a single document. It suits developers who want a reference for how a project is built before adding features or onboarding someone. The prompt is written as a fill-in template with configuration variables, so an agent has to resolve those choices itself before it can follow the steps.
tasks: document the tech stack of this codebase
write an architecture blueprint for the project
list dependencies, versions and licences
summarise coding conventions for new contributors
qualityWhy: It covers the right steps and options, but it is a generic template with unresolved variable syntax, no output example, and few concrete checks.
why: It is an analysis prompt with no stack of its own, so it can be used on a node, but its value is occasional, for documenting a project rather than building or selling content. Its stack-specific sections cover .NET, Java, JavaScript, React and Python, not the node's Next.js stack, so an agent would need to apply the general steps to that stack by hand.

summary: This skill lets an agent look up every token a given blockchain wallet currently holds on BSC, Solana, Base or Ethereum. For each token it returns the name, symbol, current price, 24-hour price change and held quantity. It suits someone who has a wallet address and wants a quick portfolio view. The agent pages through results by offset and converts the returned string values to numbers before doing arithmetic.
tasks: show the token holdings of a wallet address
build a portfolio widget for a wallet
list a wallet's positions with 24h price change
summarize what tokens an address holds on Base or BSC

why: It is a read-only lookup of public on-chain holdings, useful for an app that displays wallet balances but not central to building or selling sites or content. It calls an outside Binance service, and the wallet address it sends is public data the person supplies.

summary: This skill guides an agent through researching a Microsoft technology, such as an Azure service, a .NET or npm library, VS Code, or M365, using Microsoft Learn search and fetch tools. It then turns the findings into a new agent skill folder with a SKILL.md, a balance of core knowledge kept locally and deeper lookups left for later, and sample code. The main users are people who write skills for coding agents and want accurate Microsoft coverage. It does not build sites, apps, or content for a product.

turn Microsoft Learn docs into a local skill
build a skill teaching agents a .NET or npm library
generate sample code for a Microsoft SDK skill

Node.js and npm for the mslearn CLI fallback
why: It is a meta-skill for writing skills, so it is useful now and then rather than for building products or content directly. It calls the Microsoft Learn service, which is public and needs no key, so it is marked install-with-service. The CLI fallback runs an npm package at runtime through npx; it is a Microsoft package and was not treated as a risk.

summary: This skill guides an agent through creating, changing and checking Snowflake semantic views, which are business-metric layers over tables. The agent drafts the DDL, looks up table and column comments, tests the statement on a temporary name through the Snowflake CLI, then applies the final version and runs a sample query. why: Snowflake is a cloud database, so under the node's local-first rules this skill is value none and use skip, even though the instructions are solid. Its whole workflow runs against a cloud warehouse.

summary: The skill guides an agent in adding commands to a VS Code extension, covering the required title, category, and when-visibility rules. It is aimed at developers writing VS Code extension manifests.

hide a command from the Command Palette and show it in the Side Bar
place a button in a view title menu with correct ordering

why: The skill serves VS Code extension development, which is not what a Fractera node is for, so it has no value for building sites, apps, agents or content on the node. It is not a risk, but it does not fit the node's purpose.

summary: The skill teaches an agent how to correctly use the Microsoft Fluent UI Blazor component library in .NET Blazor apps. It covers required provider components, service registration, strongly typed icons, the list-binding model for select and autocomplete controls, the dialog and toast service patterns, and theming after render. summary: This skill guides an agent in writing time-boxed technical spike documents, each answering one critical development question before implementation starts. The agent fills a standard markdown template with a research question, investigation tasks, success criteria, findings, and a recommendation, and names files by category and topic. summary: This skill teaches an agent to read ERC-20 token decimals at runtime instead of assuming them, so balances and USD values stay correct across EVM chains. show correct USD values for wallet token balances
build a multi-chain portfolio tracker with exact decimal math
handle bridged tokens whose decimals differ across chains

why: Useful for a node that builds crypto or DeFi features, but not core to sites, content or most agents, so it is 'some'. summary: This skill teaches an agent to work with the Aspire CLI and its AppHost, a .NET project that starts and connects a set of local services, containers and executables. summary: The skill asks an agent to take an existing agent prompt file and polish it: tidy structure and wording, fix spelling and grammar, and keep the front matter and markdown intact without changing the original intent. fix grammar and clarity in a prompt
tidy the structure of a system prompt
prepare a prompt for end users
qualityWhy: It gives only a few generic rules with no steps, examples or checks, so an agent would have to guess what 'proven best practices' means.
why: Useful now and then for editing prompt files, but it is thin and unrelated to building the node's own sites or content, and it carries no stack or service dependency. Nothing in it is harmful.

summary: This skill guides an agent through making a set of game visuals that look consistent with each other, starting from a short art-direction brief and an asset list. generate a consistent set of sprites with transparent backgrounds

Image generation is optional and comes from an outside service the person chooses, so the skill is installed with that service; the 3D and engine-import sections point at other engines and skills, which the agent should use only as the node's own stack allows.

summary: The skill turns a book or document (PDF, EPUB, DOCX, HTML, Markdown and more) into a structured agent skill by extracting frameworks, principles, techniques and anti-patterns rather than summaries. It runs a bundled extraction script, asks the user about content type and purpose, then writes chapter files, a glossary, patterns, a cheatsheet and a master SKILL.md into a skills folder. summary: This skill turns the agent into a Power BI data model reviewer. summary: The skill turns an agent into a reviewer of TypeScript and React 19 code, looking for anti-patterns such as useEffect misuse, state mutation, unsafe keys and any-typing. summary: The skill turns a product requirements document for an epic into a high-level technical architecture specification saved as a Markdown file. It asks the agent to lay out system layers in a Mermaid diagram, list features and technical enablers, name the stack, and estimate technical value and t-shirt size.
