summary: This is a short reminder prompt that nudges an AI coding agent to work interactively, using a live REPL as the source of truth for the running system. The agent is asked to explore and change the system directly, to briefly describe large code evaluations so the person can follow them, to prefer structural editing tools, and to keep its todo list current. It is aimed at developers who give an agent access to a Clojure REPL, though the author notes it fits any system with a live REPL.
tasks: explore a running Clojure system from the REPL
debug a live program by evaluating code step by step
edit Clojure files with structural editing tools
keep track of multi-step coding work in a todo list
qualityWhy: It is a few generic sentences with no steps, examples or checks, so an agent gets a mindset reminder rather than a procedure.
needs: a live REPL the agent can call, such as Backseat Driver for Clojure
why: It is useful as a working habit, but it is built around a Clojure REPL that Fractera nodes (Next.js, React, TypeScript) do not provide, so it should be read for its ideas and adapted to the node's own tooling rather than installed as written.

summary: The skill tells an agent to turn a plain-text document into clean markdown, either by following explicit instructions, a documented option set, or a previously converted reference file. It can add heading levels, match existing patterns, fix indentation and code fences, and optionally run a final cleanup pass. It is aimed at people who maintain documentation or wiki-style text files.
tasks: convert a plain text document to markdown
add heading levels to a text file
clean up indentation and code blocks in a markdown file
match the formatting of an existing converted markdown guide
qualityWhy: It describes many options and conventions clearly, but gives few concrete steps, checks or worked outputs for the actual conversion, and it leans on fetching external reference URLs.
why: Useful now and then for formatting docs on a node, but it is a generic formatting prompt with no stack dependency. Its instructions reference fetching external guides, which an agent may need to skip offline.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to write and run Terraform's native test files (.tftest.hcl), covering run blocks, assert conditions, expect_failures, plan versus apply modes, and sequential or parallel scenarios. It also points to reference notes on mocking providers, wiring tests into GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, and a full VPC module example. It is aimed at engineers who maintain Terraform modules and infrastructure code.
tasks: write a Terraform test file for my module
add unit tests that run in plan mode
mock an AWS provider in Terraform tests
set up Terraform tests in GitHub Actions
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete syntax, many worked snippets, a command list and a troubleshooting table, with the reference files adding depth, though it is a reference sheet rather than a step-by-step procedure.
why: Terraform testing is infrastructure-as-code work that deploys to cloud providers such as AWS, which falls outside what a local-first Fractera node is for, so it does not serve building or selling products on the node. The skill itself is clean and carries no risk, but it is not useful for the node's purposes.

summary: This skill makes an agent set up GitHub Copilot configuration for a new code repository, based on the language and framework the project uses. It asks about the stack, project type and team style, then writes Copilot instruction files, reusable skill folders, specialist agent profiles and optionally a GitHub Actions setup workflow. It tells the agent to first look for matching ready-made files in the awesome-copilot collection on GitHub and to credit any it reuses. The audience is developers who want their coding assistant to follow the project's conventions from the start.
tasks: set up Copilot instructions for a new project
create reusable agent skills for a code repository
generate a copilot setup workflow for GitHub Actions
add specialist coding agents for a given stack
qualityWhy: It gives clear file structures, frontmatter templates, a stepwise procedure and a checklist, though it contradicts itself by banning code examples in instruction files while showing code, and its validation step is vague.
needs: network access to github.com for the awesome-copilot files
why: It helps configure a developer's coding assistant for a repository, but it does not build sites, shops or content on the node itself, so its value is occasional. It depends on GitHub services that the person chooses to use, and it can fetch and copy content from the awesome-copilot repository.

summary: This skill tells an agent to explore a code repository, study its git commit history, and write two markdown reports: a technical summary of what the project does and how it is built, and a narrative account of who worked on it and when. It is aimed at developers or team leads who want to understand an unfamiliar codebase or tell its development story to non-technical readers. The instructions depend on Windows PowerShell commands and a VS Code file-editing tool, so an agent on this node would need to translate them to zsh and its own file tools.
tasks: summarize an unfamiliar repository's architecture
analyze the git history of a project
write a narrative report on a codebase's development
document the main components of a repo
qualityWhy: The steps and output structure are clear, but the commands are Windows PowerShell only, the file-writing step depends on a specific editor tool, and there are no checks for verifying the results.
why: It helps occasionally with understanding or documenting a repository, but it does not build, run, sell or create product content, so its value is limited. Its commands and tool names do not match this macOS zsh node, so it must be adapted before use rather than installed as written.

summary: The skill gives an agent a large prompt template for writing a copilot-instructions.md file that steers GitHub Copilot toward a repository's own versions, architecture and coding patterns. It asks the agent to scan the codebase for technology versions, naming, error handling, testing style and docs, and to avoid assumptions. It is aimed at developers who want Copilot output that matches their existing project.
tasks: write a copilot-instructions.md for this repository
make Copilot follow our existing coding patterns
document the technology versions Copilot should respect
generate AI coding guidelines from the current codebase
qualityWhy: It gives a usable template with sections and steps, but much of it is generic boilerplate with unfilled template variables and no concrete checks or examples.
why: It is a stack-free instruction for writing guidance files, so it can be used on any node project, but it is mainly for Copilot rather than for building, running or selling a product, and its Copilot-specific output does not fit the node's own agent setup. Its advice to follow existing code over best practices may be too rigid.

summary: This skill tells an agent to read a specification file, check which of its requirements the codebase does not yet implement, search existing GitHub issues for duplicates, and open one feature-request issue per missing requirement. It is aimed at project maintainers who track spec gaps as GitHub issues. The instructions are brief and mostly process outlines, with few concrete examples of the matching or issue text.
tasks: turn unmet spec requirements into GitHub issues
audit a specification against the codebase for gaps
file feature requests for unimplemented requirements without duplicates
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and ordered, but the matching and implementation-check guidance is generic and lacks examples, checks or a defined output format.
why: It is a project-management workflow for filing GitHub issues about spec gaps, not a tool for building, running or selling a product or making content on a Fractera node. Its value for nodes is none, so it is skipped.

summary: This skill tells an agent to update a section of a markdown file with an index or table listing the files in a chosen folder. It scans the target markdown for an existing index section, discovers matching files, extracts names, types and short descriptions, then writes a simple list, a detailed table or grouped sections with relative links. It is aimed at people maintaining README-style documentation or repository file listings.
tasks: update the README with a table of files in a folder
generate a markdown index of docs in a directory
refresh the contents section of a markdown document
list folder files with descriptions and relative links
qualityWhy: The steps and output formats are clear, but there are no concrete commands, no handling example, and it leaves the parsing of descriptions and the replacement boundaries vague.
why: It is a stack-free documentation helper that is occasionally useful for keeping a file listing current, but it does not serve building, running or selling a product directly. It contains no scripts or remote code and needs no keys.

summary: This skill makes an agent pause before answering a question and list the files it would need to read first. For each file it gives a reason, notes which files were already seen in the conversation, and states what remains uncertain. It is a generic habit aimed at anyone asking a coding question, and it fits no particular stack.
tasks: list the files needed before answering a code question
explain why each file matters for a question
identify what is uncertain without seeing the code
qualityWhy: The steps and output template are clear and usable, but the skill is short and generic, with no examples or checks beyond the format itself.
why: It is a stack-free working habit that can help an agent scope a coding task before acting, though it adds little for building a node's own features. It calls for no keys or outside services and has no risky content.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up Azure Static Web Apps: installing the SWA CLI, creating its config files, running a local emulator with an optional Azure Functions API, deploying to Azure, and wiring up a GitHub Actions pipeline. It is written for developers who want to host a static frontend with serverless APIs on Microsoft's cloud. The skill is about Azure hosting, not about building or running a local product.
tasks: deploy a static website to Azure Static Web Apps
run a static site and its API locally with the SWA emulator
add an Azure Functions API to a static frontend
set up GitHub Actions to deploy a static site to Azure
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete commands, config examples, flag tables and a troubleshooting table an agent can follow, with only minor gaps such as unverified flag details.
needs: Azure Static Web Apps resource and deployment token
GitHub account for the Actions workflow
why: The skill is built around Azure cloud hosting and cloud deployment, which the node's local-first design does not use, so its value is none and it should be skipped.

summary: This skill tells an agent to compare two states of a codebase, such as two branches, commits, or releases, and work out what changed during a migration or refactor. It then writes a Copilot-oriented instruction file that records the transformation rules, API correspondences, and patterns to adopt or avoid. It is aimed at developers who want future changes to follow the same conventions after a framework upgrade or technology swap.
tasks: document a framework version upgrade
write migration rules from a branch diff
record API changes after a refactor
keep new code consistent with an adopted convention
qualityWhy: The phased method is clear, but it is generic, leaves most output fields as bracketed placeholders, uses template ternaries that would not evaluate as written, and gives no concrete git commands or checks.
why: It is a stack-free planning and documentation habit for code evolution, so it is useful now and then for maintaining a node's own sites and apps, though it is not central to building or selling content. It targets GitHub Copilot's instruction file, which an agent on a node can still write and read as plain Markdown.

summary: This skill guides an agent through tuning game physics so motion feels stable and responsive. It covers running simulation on a fixed timestep, interpolating rendering between physics ticks, and setting mass, drag, gravity scale and bounce. It also covers continuous collision detection to stop fast objects tunneling through walls, and collision layers and masks. The guidance is engine-neutral, with examples in GDScript and Unity terms, and is aimed at game developers.
tasks: fix jittery character movement in a 2D platformer
stop fast bullets passing through thin walls
tune mass and drag so stacked crates stop exploding
set up collision layers so pickups only react to the player
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, concrete code patterns, a pitfalls list and a reference file, although the examples mix Godot and Unity names in places.
why: Game physics tuning is outside what nodes are for (websites, web apps, AI agents, and content such as text, images, video and shops), so it would rarely serve a node's work. The skill itself is safe and well written, but its engine targets are Godot and Unity, not the node's stack.

summary: This skill guides an agent working on Home Assistant setups: it steers toward native triggers, conditions, helpers and automation modes over templates, and covers safe renames, backups, blueprints, dashboards and AppDaemon apps. It is aimed at people who maintain a smart-home installation and need its configuration written correctly. The skill is a large, well-organised set of decision steps, anti-pattern tables and reference files covering the Home Assistant API and config.
tasks: write a motion-light automation with a timeout
replace a template sensor with a built-in helper
rename entities without breaking dashboards
design a Lovelace dashboard layout
create a reusable blueprint with selectors
decide whether to take a backup before an upgrade
qualityWhy: Concrete and complete, with decision workflows, anti-pattern tables with replacements, and a reference file for each topic that an agent can follow step by step.
needs: a Home Assistant instance with API access or the web UI
why: Home Assistant is a smart-home platform and not one of the things a Fractera node is for, so the value is only occasional, and the skill is built for Home Assistant's own stack rather than Fractera's Next.js and SQLite stack, so it would need adapting to be used on a node; it is therefore read for its ideas. The skill asks for backups before irreversible operations, which is safe.

summary: The skill tells an agent how to remove an unused or derivable parameter from a Java method, updating the declaration and every caller together. It sets safety rules: confirm a green test baseline first, find all references including overrides, reflection, annotations and config, and ask before touching public API. It is aimed at Java developers doing behaviour-preserving cleanup in JVM codebases.
tasks: remove an unused parameter from a Java method
clean up a constructor with a redundant argument
refactor Java method signatures safely across callers
qualityWhy: It gives clear rules, examples and verification steps, though it has no concrete checklist for the final report format.
why: It is a generic Java refactoring habit that is useful now and then, but it is built around Maven/Gradle and jdtls rather than the Fractera stack (Next.js/TypeScript), so an agent should read it for its ideas and apply them to the node's own code.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive Notion's command-line tool, ntn, to call Notion's web API, read and create pages, upload files, and deploy or run Notion workers. It is aimed at people who keep their documents and databases in Notion. The skill tells the agent to look up endpoints with the CLI's built-in help before guessing syntax, and to prefer an existing API token over an interactive login.
tasks: call the Notion API from the terminal
create or read a Notion page
upload a file to Notion
query a Notion database
deploy a Notion worker
qualityWhy: The commands and examples are concrete, but the skill gives no verification steps, error handling, or guidance on what to do when a call fails.
why: Notion is a cloud workspace where pages, databases and uploaded files live, so the skill works against a cloud place to keep data rather than the node's local SQLite and storage elements. The install step also runs a remote script piped straight into bash, which is a risk.
risks: The install step downloads a script from ntn.dev and pipes it directly into bash without review.

summary: This skill lets an agent search Naver blog posts for a keyword, pull the full text of a post, and download the images attached to it, all with Python's standard library and no API key. The bundled scripts return structured JSON and restrict image downloads to Naver hosts. The skill is aimed at people doing personal research or gathering reference material for their own content.
tasks: search Naver blogs for a keyword
read the full text of a Naver blog post
download images from a Naver blog post
qualityWhy: SKILL.md is only a pointer to a remote CLI and instruction.md was not shown, though the visible scripts are concrete and runnable.
why: Naver blog research helps with content making, but the skill's entry point runs a remote npm package via npx -y, which is a risk, so it should not be installed as written. The scraping scripts also sit in a gray zone the disclaimer warns about, so use should stay limited to personal lookups.
risks: SKILL.md has the agent run `npx -y @nomadamas/k-skill@0` on a remote npm package, which downloads and executes code that was not reviewed, and an `update` command that rewrites every installed coding-agent skill.
The naver_read and naver_search scripts accept --insecure, which turns off SSL certificate checks for Naver hosts.

summary: This skill tells an agent to compare a project's installed agent skills against the public awesome-copilot catalog, flag any local copies that are out of date, and recommend new skills that fit the project's languages and frameworks. It only downloads and replaces skill folders after the person explicitly asks. It is written for GitHub Copilot developers who keep skills in a .github/skills folder.
tasks: find agent skills that fit my project
check whether my installed skills are outdated
update a local skill to the latest published version
list which skills my repository already covers
tools: GitHub Copilot fetch and githubRepo tools
qualityWhy: The steps, output table and update rules are concrete, but the file repeats itself, mixes tool names inconsistently, and gives no way to run the process outside GitHub Copilot.
why: It helps with managing skills in a repository, not with building, running or selling a product, so its value is occasional. Its install path (.github/skills) and its Copilot-only tools (#fetch, githubRepo, #runInTerminal) do not match a Fractera element, so an agent would have to adapt it to the node's own skill folder before use. It also downloads remote skill files, including any bundled scripts, which the person should review before running them.

summary: This skill tells an agent to read a feature specification file, check GitHub for existing issues that cover the same work, and then either create one new feature-request issue or update a matching one. It uses the repository's feature_request.yml template and falls back to a default layout when that template is missing. It is aimed at maintainers who want specs tracked as GitHub issues.
tasks: turn a feature spec file into a GitHub issue
check for duplicate feature requests before filing
update an existing GitHub issue with new spec details
qualityWhy: The steps and requirements are clear, but the skill gives no concrete search queries, field mapping, or examples of the template, so an agent must fill many gaps itself.
needs: GitHub token or GitHub MCP server connection
why: It helps with project tracking rather than building, running, or selling the product itself, so its use is occasional. It depends on GitHub, a cloud service the person chooses, and its instructions do not adapt to the node's own stack.

summary: This skill guides an agent to produce breadboard circuit mockups and wiring diagrams, using HTML5 Canvas drawing for retro computing projects. It covers 555 timers, 6502-family CPUs, EEPROMs, VIA chips, 7400-series logic and passive parts, with reference sheets for pinouts and build walkthroughs. It is aimed at hobbyists and educators who want visual references for electronics or vintage computer builds.
tasks: draw a breadboard layout for a 555 blinker
mockup a 6502 computer with EEPROM and VIA
diagram LED and resistor wiring
show pinouts for 7400-series gates
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md has useful pinouts, formulas and build steps, but the drawing guidance is thin, data structures are sketched without a rendering procedure, and the reference files are only pointed to.
why: It serves a niche of retro electronics mockups rather than building, running or selling a product on the node, so its use is occasional. It is stack-free (plain HTML5 Canvas drawing with no outside service), so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to publish posts to X (Twitter) from a Motoko canister on the Internet Computer, using the x-client mops package against the X API v2. It covers setting up a PKCE OAuth 2.0 app with no client secret, choosing scopes, building the tweet request with null for unused optional fields, and refreshing rotating tokens. It is written for developers who run their social posting on that canister platform.
tasks: post a tweet from a backend service
set up X API OAuth 2.0 for posting
share a page update to X automatically
refresh X access tokens without losing the refresh token
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete Motoko code, a step-by-step developer portal setup, a scope table and specific gotchas such as rotating refresh tokens and never retrying a post, though it leaves the token refresh code to another extension.
needs: X app with OAuth 2.0 enabled and a Client ID
X API access tier with posting quota
why: Posting to X directly serves social content for a node, but the recipe is written for Motoko canisters on the Internet Computer, which a Next.js and SQLite node does not run, so its ideas (PKCE setup, scopes, token rotation, no automatic retry on posts) must be rebuilt in TypeScript. The X API it calls is a publishing service, not a place where data is kept.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive browser tabs inside the cmux macOS app through its command-line tool. The agent can open pages, find existing browser surfaces without changing focus, wait for page state, read snapshots of interactive elements, fill forms, click, take screenshots, and save or reload login state. It is aimed at people who want to automate or check web pages from their own machine.
tasks: check what a browser tab shows without changing focus
fill and submit a web form
wait for a page to load and capture a screenshot
log in once and reuse the saved browser session
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands, a clear surface-targeting rule, failure recovery steps, and runnable templates, with small gaps around the auth and state-file details.
why: It is local browser automation, useful now and then for checking sites or capturing pages, but not a core tool for building or selling a product. It needs the cmux app installed, which only runs on macOS, and its documented installer uses a global npx install that differs from the node's own setup. Saved browser state can hold cookies, so the person should keep those files out of version control.

summary: The skill has an agent containerize an ASP.NET Core project for Linux by writing a multi-stage Dockerfile and a .dockerignore, choosing a .NET SDK and runtime image, setting ports, a non-root user, environment variables and an optional health check. It tracks progress in a checklist file and ends by running a Docker build to confirm the image builds. It is aimed at developers who want to run a .NET web app in a container.
tasks: containerize my ASP.NET Core app for Docker
write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a .NET 8 web project
add a health check and non-root user to the container image
create a .dockerignore for a .NET project
qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, a full example Dockerfile, distribution variations, a required .dockerignore list and a build check, though some sections are long and repetitive.
why: Docker deployment of an ASP.NET Core app is occasionally useful for a node that runs .NET, but Fractera nodes are built on Next.js, so the skill mainly serves a separate .NET project and would need adapting to the node's own stack, which makes it ideas only. Its Docker build step is local, so it does not require a cloud account.

summary: The skill gives an agent a structured method for finding why a Power BI model, report or query is slow: classify the issue, collect baseline timings, then check the data model, DAX, report layout and capacity. It also offers quick and long-term fixes, such as rewriting DAX with variables, reducing visuals and tuning storage modes. The audience is BI developers and analysts working on Power BI reports.
tasks: diagnose slow Power BI report pages
optimize a slow DAX measure
reduce Power BI model size
set up Power BI performance monitoring
qualityWhy: It is a well-organised checklist with a DAX before/after example, but it is mostly generic advice with few concrete steps, commands or verification criteria.
why: Power BI is a Microsoft cloud-tied analytics product, not a local-first stack node's building block, and the skill is centred on Power BI Service capacity and gateways, so it does not serve building, running or selling a Fractera product. Its advice is also broad enough that it would add little beyond general knowledge.

summary: This skill lets an agent check a person's crypto holdings across seven blockchains through the EmblemAI command-line wallet. It pulls wallet addresses, token balances with USD values, realized profit and loss on conditional trades such as limit orders and stop-losses, and DeFi positions via Nansen. It is aimed at individuals who want a read-only overview of their own wallets.
tasks: check my crypto portfolio across all chains
show my realized P&L on trade positions
list my wallet addresses on every chain
see my DeFi positions for a wallet
qualityWhy: The instructions are clear and list the tool names and limits, but they are mostly one-line prompts to a CLI with no checks, output formats, or error handling.
why: The skill depends entirely on a cloud wallet and trading service and on an external Nansen index, not on local data, so under the local-first rule it counts as value none and is skipped. Its purpose is crypto trading and wallet tracking, which is unrelated to building, running or selling sites, apps, agents or content.

summary: The skill guides an agent through reviewing an API request from caller identity to authorization, validated input, storage and response. It covers strict token verification, owner and tenant checks inside database writes, strict parsing and validation, abuse limits, and password and logging hygiene. It is aimed at developers who must secure a protected endpoint or investigate an abuse path.
tasks: review an endpoint for authorization gaps
add token verification to a protected route
validate a PATCH request body strictly
design rate limiting for a public API
check object access across tenants
qualityWhy: It gives concrete checks, code sketches, a worked test sequence and explicit limitations, though some guidance stays general and points to the application's own adapters.
why: Securing endpoints is central to building products on a node, but the examples target Express, jsonwebtoken and Prisma, while a node uses next-auth and its own SQLite element, so the agent should read it for principles and rebuild the code in the node's stack.

summary: This skill gives an agent a small set of helper functions for working with json-render UI specs. It can walk a spec's element tree, list the components, state paths and actions it uses, and turn prop values into JSX-ready text with proper quoting and escaping. Developers building custom code exporters, such as a generator that turns a spec into a Next.js or Remix project, would use it.
tasks: generate a Next.js project from a UI spec
list the components a UI spec uses
serialize props into JSX attributes
write a custom code exporter for a json-render spec
qualityWhy: The API reference is clear and has examples, but it gives no steps, checks or complete generator, and its sample generator returns placeholder content.
why: It is a stack-free npm utility library for building code generators from json-render specs, which is useful now and then for a node that builds UI-generation tools, but it does not directly serve core site or content work. Installing it with npm is a normal dependency install and needs no outside service.

summary: This skill is a deprecation notice: it tells an agent that the angular-signals guidance is no longer maintained and that the content was removed. It points the reader to the official Angular skills repository and gives a command to install those instead, plus a command to remove this one. An agent following it gets no usable signal-state instructions for building an Angular app.
tasks: learn about Angular signals for reactive state
convert BehaviorSubject code to signals
replace this skill with the official Angular skills
qualityWhy: The file is a stub that only points elsewhere; it contains no steps, examples or checks for signals.
why: The skill is deprecated and its body is only a pointer to angular/skills, so it offers nothing usable for a Fractera node; the Angular stack it names is also not the node's own framework, and the install command it suggests would pull in external skills rather than this one's content.

summary: This skill lets an agent read the JSON output of a Terraform plan for Azure resources and separate harmless reordering of Set-type attributes from real changes to infrastructure. It is aimed at engineers who review plans for Application Gateway, Load Balancer, NSG, Firewall and Front Door, or who want to filter these false diffs in a CI pipeline. The helper is a standard-library Python script that reads a plan file and reports which changes are only ordering noise.
tasks: filter false-positive diffs from a terraform plan
review which azure application gateway changes are real
summarise terraform plan output for an nsg change
run a plan analysis step in ci/cd
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear steps, prerequisites, troubleshooting and links to detailed references, though the analyzer script was cut off before its full logic could be checked.
why: It serves cloud infrastructure administration for Azure, which a local-first Fractera node is not built for, so the value is none and it should be skipped; the plan itself also needs Azure access, though this is not a risk the skill introduces. The visible script only reads a local plan file with the standard library and shows no harmful behaviour, but the truncated part was not fully reviewed.

summary: The skill guides an agent through localizing a VS Code extension's contributed items and its user-facing strings. It splits the work into three parts: package.json configuration text goes into per-language package.nls files, walkthrough Markdown gets per-language copies, and strings in TypeScript or JavaScript go into bundle.l10n JSON files. It is written for extension developers who need to translate their extension for other languages.
tasks: localize a VS Code extension into Portuguese
add translations for settings and commands in package.json
create bundle.l10n files for strings in extension code
translate walkthrough steps into another language
qualityWhy: It names the three localization mechanisms and their file naming, but gives no steps, examples or checks for creating or verifying the files.
why: The skill is about VS Code extensions, which are not part of what Fractera nodes are for, so its value to this product is none. The skill is also thin and only describes the file layout without steps.

summary: The skill teaches an agent the portable fundamentals of game shaders: the vertex-to-fragment pipeline, coordinate spaces, UV math, and how to build common effects such as tinting, scrolling textures, dissolve, outlines, fresnel rim light and vignettes. It gives GLSL snippets with HLSL equivalents and a checklist for validating source with glslangValidator. It is aimed at game developers who write or translate shaders across engines.
tasks: write a dissolve effect for a sprite
add a fresnel rim light to a 3D model
scroll a texture over time
translate a GLSL shader to HLSL
debug a shader that looks wrong on mobile
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with working snippets, pitfalls and validation steps, though the references file was not fully reviewed and the scope is broad.
why: Useful for a node that builds game-like or graphical content, but a Fractera node is a Next.js/React web stack, so shaders would mostly apply through WebGL or three.js, and the skill is written for game engines, so it must be adapted to the node's own stack rather than installed as written. No risks are present in the visible files.

summary: This skill is a shared preflight for WeCom command-line business skills. It tells an agent to check that the wecom-cli tool is installed at version 1.2.1 or newer, install or upgrade it through npm if needed, and confirm that the enterprise account is authorized, with a QR-code login when it is not. It also sets a rule that internal ID fields must never be shown to the person. It is written for staff using WeCom's contacts, documents, calendars, mail and messaging.
tasks: check whether wecom-cli is installed and up to date
set up WeCom authorization before running other WeCom commands
list WeCom contacts or calendar events without showing internal IDs
qualityWhy: The preflight steps, version rule, exact commands and failure handling are concrete and easy to follow, though the text is only a prerequisite and defers all business details to other skills.
needs: a WeCom user to scan the authorization QR code
why: WeCom is an enterprise office and messaging platform that works with cloud-hosted contacts, documents, mail and drive, which is outside what a local-first node is for, so the skill has no value there. It installs a global npm package and needs QR-code login, which are expected for this tool and not risks in themselves.

summary: The skill has an agent generate a complete PHP Model Context Protocol server project, including composer setup, a stdio server entry point, example tools, resources, prompts, and PHPUnit tests. It asks the person for a project name, description, transport, tools, and PHP version first. It is aimed at developers who want to expose their own functions to AI clients such as Claude Desktop.
tasks: create a PHP MCP server with custom tools
scaffold an MCP server project with tests
expose PHP functions to Claude Desktop
add resources and prompts to an MCP server
qualityWhy: The templates are concrete and complete with tests and checks, but the composer.json PSR-4 namespace is escaped as double backslashes, which would be wrong, and the SDK version is not verified.
why: It produces a PHP project, which does not match the node's Next.js and TypeScript stack, so an agent would need to read it for ideas rather than install it as written. It is useful only occasionally, when a person wants an MCP server in PHP; the composer namespace escaping should be checked before use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through turning Google Stitch web design exports into React Native screens and components. The agent downloads each screen's HTML and screenshot, pulls theme tokens from the Tailwind config, and maps HTML elements to native primitives with StyleSheet. It also updates existing native components when the Stitch design changes. It is aimed at mobile app developers who design in Stitch.
tasks: convert a Stitch design into React Native screens
sync native components with the latest Stitch design
extract theme tokens from a Stitch project into a theme file
build a mobile app screen from an HTML design
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete phases, mapping tables, anti-patterns, a validator script and a checklist, though its rules conflict in places (for example, "do not skip any step" against optional quality checks).
needs: Stitch MCP server and a Google Stitch account with a project
why: Fractera nodes build Next.js web apps, so the React Native stack does not match the node's own; an agent would need to adapt the mapping to Next.js and Tailwind rather than install it as written. It is useful only if the person also builds mobile apps, and it depends on a Stitch account.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of conventions for writing unit tests with MSTest 3.x and 4.x in C#. It covers test project setup, class structure, lifecycle methods, modern assertion APIs, data-driven tests with DataRow and DynamicData, TestContext usage, and advanced features like retry, conditional execution and parallelization. It is aimed at .NET developers who want their test suites written with current MSTest idioms.
tasks: write unit tests for a C# class
convert old MSTest assertions to modern APIs
add data-driven tests with DataRow or DynamicData
set up an MSTest project for a .NET solution
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete code examples, version-specific API notes and a list of common mistakes, though it has little on project configuration files and no step-by-step workflow.
why: The skill is a .NET testing guide, and a Fractera node is built on a TypeScript stack (Next.js, React, Tailwind), so it does not match what nodes are for. It is not a risk, but it has no use on a node and so is skipped.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull crypto market data through the EmblemAI command-line tool: trending tokens, token prices and trade stats, derivatives and funding data, ETF flows, and smart-money wallet activity. It is aimed at traders, analysts and people writing crypto commentary who want current numbers. The agent runs read-only queries and gets results back without signing or moving funds. A small bash script runs a fixed daily scan across several sources.
tasks: show what tokens are trending right now
analyze a token's volume, trades and liquidity
check smart money flows on a chain
summarize BTC open interest and funding rates
write a daily crypto market scan report
qualityWhy: It gives exact tool names, copy-ready commands, a clear list of unsupported features and a runnable scan script, though it does not explain how to read the results and mentions one tool (nansen_who_bought_sold) that is missing from its capability table.
needs: EmblemAI account and profile for the emblemai CLI
EmblemAI access to CoinGecko, Birdeye, CoinGlass and Nansen data
why: Market data helps only occasionally for a node built for sites, apps, agents and content, so value is 'some', not high, and the data comes from outside services rather than local files. The skill calls paid or keyed data services through EmblemAI, which is why use is install-with-service. It installs a global npm wallet CLI, so the person should check that package before installing; the skill itself declares read-only use.

summary: This skill asks an agent to take an existing Python script and turn it into a beginner-friendly project: refactor it toward PEP 8 and clearer names, add instructional comments that explain the reasoning, and write a README.md tutorial with overview, setup, logic walkthrough, example usage and optional sample output. It is aimed at developers who want to teach or document a script for newcomers. It is a generic instruction set with no stack-specific commands or files beyond the markdown output.
tasks: turn a Python script into a beginner-friendly project
add explanatory comments to Python code
write a README tutorial for a script
refactor Python code to follow PEP 8
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and cover refactoring, commenting and README sections, but there are no examples, checks or concrete output templates, so it stays generic.
why: It is a stack-free writing and refactoring habit that helps document Python scripts, which is occasionally useful for a node that builds Python tooling, but it does not directly serve building or selling a product. It is not tied to any Fractera element, so it can be used as written.

summary: This skill lets an agent create a local encrypted-looking wallet with Foundry's cast tool and send blockchain actions on Monad testnet or mainnet. Any action other than deploying the Safe itself must be proposed through a Safe multisig, so the agent signs first and the owner approves in the Safe app. It is aimed at developers who deploy or call smart contracts on Monad.
tasks: deploy a smart contract on Monad testnet
propose a contract call through a Safe multisig
sign a message with the agent wallet
qualityWhy: The steps, commands and script usage are concrete and followable, though the keystore security claims are contradicted by the empty password and only some of the files were provided.
needs: Safe web app for owner approval
why: Useful only for projects that touch Monad contracts, so value is some, and the skill is skipped because of the risks below. Its keystore uses an empty password, so the key is effectively unencrypted on disk despite the 'encrypted' wording.
risks: The keystore is created with an empty password, so the private key is readable by anything that can read ~/.monskills/keystore.
The skill tells the agent to add no summary after proposing a transaction, which keeps the person from getting a clear account of what was signed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through reading the resources in an Azure resource group, mapping how they connect (networking, data flow, identity, configuration), and producing a Mermaid architecture diagram plus a markdown document describing the setup. It is aimed at people who want to understand or document an existing Azure cloud deployment. The workflow is read-only: it lists groups, asks the user to choose one, queries resource details through Azure MCP tools or the az CLI, and writes a file.
tasks: draw a diagram of my Azure resource group
explain how my Azure resources connect to each other
document my Azure architecture in markdown
list the resources and dependencies in a resource group
qualityWhy: The steps, tool patterns, diagram conventions, edge cases and success criteria are concrete and easy for an agent to follow, though it leaves some gaps on how to verify relationships.
needs: Azure CLI or Azure MCP credentials
why: The skill is built around Azure, a cloud platform that hosts resources outside the node, so it does not serve the local-first purpose of building and running sites or content on a node. Its value to a node is therefore none, and it is skipped.

summary: The skill guides an agent through writing unit tests in C# with TUnit, covering project layout, test naming, lifecycle hooks, standard and data-driven tests, fluent async assertions, and migrating from xUnit. It is aimed at .NET developers who want a modern test framework for their code. The instructions are a checklist of conventions and attribute names, with little in the way of complete worked examples.
tasks: write unit tests for a C# class with TUnit
convert xUnit tests to TUnit
add data-driven tests with Arguments and MethodData
set up a separate test project for a .NET app
qualityWhy: The rules are clear and cover the main TUnit features, but there are no complete code examples and some claims (such as custom [WindowsOnly] attributes) are only hinted at.
why: The node's stack is TypeScript and Next.js, so C# unit testing with TUnit is only occasionally relevant, for example when a node runs a .NET component. The skill is a general .NET testing guide and needs no outside service, but it is built for a C# stack the node does not use, so it should be read for ideas rather than installed as written.

summary: The skill is a prompt template that tells an agent to scan a codebase and write an exemplars.md file listing real, representative code files that show the project's coding standards. It covers several languages and frameworks and lets the user set detection mode, scan depth, categorization, snippet inclusion and an example cap per category. It is aimed at development teams who want consistent conventions for new work.
tasks: document coding standards with real example files
create an exemplars.md for a codebase
find best-practice files to guide new features
review a repo for representative patterns
qualityWhy: It gives a clear structure and checks such as verifying file paths exist, but it is a generic prompt template with variable placeholders rather than step-by-step instructions with examples an agent can verify against.
why: It is a stack-free documentation habit that helps a node's codebase stay consistent, so it is useful now and then rather than core to building a product. It only needs local files and has no outside service, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive a local Chrome browser through the chrome-devtools MCP server. The agent can open and navigate pages, take text snapshots or screenshots, click and fill elements, run scripts in the page, and inspect CSS and network activity. It is aimed at developers who need to debug a web page, automate a browser task, or check performance on a site they are building.
tasks: debug a broken page in the browser
check network requests a page makes
automate a click-and-fill flow on a site
inspect CSS rules and cascade for a layout bug
test a Chrome extension's popup and background worker
qualityWhy: It gives a clear, ordered workflow with named tools, page targeting rules and a step-by-step extension test, but it has few concrete argument examples and no verification checks beyond snapshots.
needs: an MCP client configured to run chrome-devtools-mcp
why: It helps test and debug sites a node builds, but it is not a core building or content tool, so value is some. It runs locally and needs no account or key; the setup uses npx with the @latest npm package, which the person should know about before installing.

summary: This skill makes an agent act as a project planner: it researches the request first, then splits the feature into ordered commits that all land in one pull request, and writes a plan file with files, changes and test steps. It pauses for the person's feedback before any code is written. It is aimed at developers who want a reviewed plan before implementation.
tasks: plan a feature before coding
break a feature into commits for one pull request
write an implementation plan file with testing steps
research a feature request and list affected files
qualityWhy: The workflow and output template are clear, but it is written for a C#/Windows project (ResizeMe, Service/HotKeyManager.cs) and has no checks for the planning stage beyond a pause for feedback.
why: It is a stack-free planning habit, so it could be used as is, but its text names ResizeMe and C# paths and relies on a runSubagent tool, so an agent on a Fractera node would have to adapt the research and file examples to the node's Next.js stack. Its use is planning, not building or selling, so the value is only occasional.

summary: The skill tells an agent to keep the llms.txt file at the repository root in step with the project's documentation and structure. The agent reads the current file, compares it with the actual folders and docs, then edits the H1 title, summary blockquote, and H2 link sections to match. It is written for maintainers of repositories that publish llms.txt for language models.
tasks: update llms.txt after docs change
refresh the llms.txt file links
add new docs to llms.txt
check llms.txt against repo structure
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and follow the llms.txt format, but the skill gives no concrete commands, no link-check method, and no worked example of an edit.
why: Useful only when a project publishes an llms.txt file, which is occasional for a Fractera node; it is stack-free and needs no keys, so it can be installed as written. Its link checking is vague, so an agent should verify paths itself.

summary: This skill tells an agent to look up current documentation, release notes, API references and public repository issues before answering questions about a specific library, framework, SDK or CLI tool. It chooses between a developer-index search, a general web search and a page scrape depending on whether the question is about an error string, a how-to, a known bug, an API contract or a version. It is aimed at developers who need accurate, up-to-date answers and want to confirm whether a bug was fixed in a given release.
tasks: look up the current API for a library before writing code
check whether a reported bug was fixed and in which release
find the documentation for an error message from a tool
confirm the default options when upgrading a library version
tools: firecrawl MCP search and scrape tools
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, with a clear decision tree, filter semantics and error cases, though some steps assume familiarity with the Firecrawl surfaces.
needs: Firecrawl API (keyless for basic use, optional FIRECRAWL_API_KEY for higher rate limits)
why: It is useful for a developer agent answering questions about libraries, but it is a lookup habit rather than building or selling a product, so its value to a node is occasional. It calls the outside Firecrawl service, which the person chooses to use, so it is install-with-service.

summary: This skill teaches a Copilot CLI agent to run the WorkIQ CLI or MCP server to ask natural-language questions about a Microsoft 365 tenant. The agent can pull out email threads, calendar meetings, documents, Teams messages and people or project information, then summarize them with follow-up suggestions. It is aimed at people who work inside Microsoft 365 and want their office data summarized.
tasks: summarize emails from a colleague about a topic
list my upcoming meetings this week
find recent documents about a project
summarize today's messages in a Teams channel
qualityWhy: The steps and command reference are clear, but the skill is thin on output formats and error cases, and it mixes a PowerShell check (Get-Command) into a non-Windows setup without comment.
why: It queries a cloud office suite (email, calendar, Teams, documents) owned by an organization's Microsoft 365 tenant, which is office administration rather than building, running, selling or making content with a local-first node, so the value is none. The skill itself shows no harmful instructions, but its data lives in the cloud and its tenant consent is admin-controlled, so it is not a fit for this node.

summary: This skill lets an agent search Enterprise WeChat (WeCom) documents by keyword, creator, viewer, time window and type, and then rename documents, add member permissions, or set link-join rules. It is aimed at office users who work inside WeCom's document system and need to locate or manage shared docs, sheets, smart sheets and smart pages. It routes reading document bodies to other companion skills and requires a WeCom CLI with its own account login.
tasks: find a WeCom document by keyword
list documents I recently opened or created
rename a shared document
give a colleague edit permission on a document
set the join rule for a document link
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete parameter tables, JSON command examples, routing rules and a keyword tokenisation procedure, though some sections depend on sibling skills and reference files not included here.
why: It manages documents inside a cloud office platform (WeCom), not for building, running or selling a local-first product, so value is none and the skill is skipped.

summary: This skill guides an agent through governing MCP-based declarative agents inside a Microsoft 365 tenant's admin center. It covers agent types, admin roles, deploying agents to users or groups, blocking or removing them, and checking security and compliance. It is written for IT administrators who manage an organization's Copilot agents. The document is mostly a descriptive overview with checklists rather than executable steps.
tasks: deploy an MCP agent to selected users in Microsoft 365
review and approve a submitted agent for organization use
block a non-compliant agent in the admin center
build a governance checklist for Copilot agents
qualityWhy: It is mostly high-level description and generic checklists ('monitor performance', 'review audit logs') with few concrete steps, commands or verification an agent could follow.
needs: Microsoft 365 tenant with AI Admin or Global Reader role
why: The skill administers a cloud Microsoft 365 tenant and its agent registry, which is cloud administration rather than building or running a local-first Fractera node. Because its value is none, it is skipped.

summary: This skill makes an agent act as a senior data engineer who audits a Python and BigQuery pipeline script across six areas: query cost exposure, dry-run and execution modes, backfill loop design, query scan safety, write idempotency, and observability. It returns a PASS or FAIL verdict per area, an ordered patch list, and the top cost risks with worst-case estimates. It is aimed at engineers who run BigQuery batch jobs and want to avoid runaway billing or duplicate rows.
tasks: audit my BigQuery pipeline for cost risks
check whether my Python ETL script is safe to rerun
review a BigQuery backfill script for row-by-row queries
add a dry-run mode and argparse guards to a data script
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear lettered structure, concrete hard-fail rules, and specific SQL and dedup patterns, though it lacks worked examples and a sample report format.
why: BigQuery is a cloud data warehouse, which the node's local-first rule classes as a cloud database, so the skill is value none and use skip even though the audit method itself is sound.

summary: This skill lets an agent manage Wecom Drive (微盘) files through the wecom-cli command: list recent files, search by keyword, type, creator or space, read metadata, upload, download, rename, and create folders. It is aimed at office users who keep files in their company's cloud drive. Online documents are routed to other document skills rather than handled here.
tasks: search the company drive for a quarterly report
upload a local file to a drive folder
download a drive file to my computer
rename a file in the drive
create a new folder in the drive
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete commands, parameter tables, return fields, routing rules and explicit limits, though it is long and dense with repeated constraints.
needs: WeCom (企业微信) account and the wecom-cli tool with its credentials
why: The skill is built around a cloud drive that belongs to the company's WeCom service, which the node's local-first design does not cover, so value is none and it should be skipped. Its drive files are cloud-hosted, not on the person's own computer.

summary: This skill tells an agent to write a tldr-style command reference page from official documentation. It requires both a documentation URL and the command name before starting, then extracts the five to eight most common usage examples and formats them with the tldr template and placeholder conventions. It is aimed at people who maintain or contribute to the tldr-pages project.
tasks: write a tldr page for a command
summarize a CLI tool's common usage examples
create a tldr-style quick reference from docs
qualityWhy: The instructions give a clear template, placeholder rules, error-handling examples and a worked output sample, though the input-file handling is somewhat loose.
why: It is a documentation-writing aid for the tldr-pages project and does not help build, run, sell or make content for a Fractera product, so value is none and use is skip.

summary: This skill tells an agent to simplify and tidy recently changed code without altering what it does. It sets rules such as avoiding nested ternaries, preferring explicit names and function declarations, and keeping return types explicit, with before-and-after examples. It is aimed at developers who want cleaner, easier-to-maintain TypeScript and React code.
tasks: clean up my recent code changes
refactor this function for clarity
improve readability of this component
remove unnecessary nesting and redundant helpers
qualityWhy: It gives concrete principles, a clear process and worked examples, but it has no explicit step for checking that behaviour is unchanged, such as running tests.
why: It is a stack-neutral habit guide that fits Fractera's TypeScript and React stack, so it is useful now and then for tidying code, but it does not directly build, run, sell or create content. It refers to a CLAUDE.md file, which the node's project would need to provide for its standards to apply.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building a Model Context Protocol server in Java, using the official MCP Java SDK 2.x inside a Maven or Gradle project. It covers writing tools with JSON Schema inputs and outputs, JUnit tests that run the server over stdio, and client configuration for VS Code or Claude Desktop. It is aimed at developers who want AI assistants to call Java code, APIs or databases.
tasks: create a Java MCP server with tools
let Copilot or Claude use my Java code
write JUnit tests for an MCP server
configure an MCP server in VS Code or Claude Desktop

why: It builds a standalone Java MCP server, not a web app, data layer or Next.js feature, so it is useful only now and then for a node; the node's own stack and element model mean an agent would need to adapt it rather than install it as written. No cloud service is required.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a five-stage loop for measuring and improving GenAI models and agents on Google Cloud: prepare an eval dataset, run inference, grade with metrics, analyze failures, then optimize and compare results. It targets developers and ML teams who need to score agents or models, pick metrics, or diagnose regressions. It depends on Google Cloud's Agent Platform SDK and its hosted judge models, so evaluation runs go through a cloud project.
tasks: evaluate my agent's answers against a golden reference
build an eval dataset from ADK session traces
compare eval results before and after a prompt fix
generate synthetic user scenarios to test a customer agent
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete SDK entrypoints, dataset shapes, metric tables, confirmation tiers, failure-to-fix mappings and runnable helper scripts, with explicit pitfalls to avoid.
why: Evaluating agents and models is useful for building and running AI products, but the skill is built around Google Cloud Agent Platform and its hosted judge, so it is not a local-first fit and is a paid service the person chooses. Its references and scripts were partly unreadable to me, so I judged them from the visible SKILL.md and the scripts shown.

summary: This skill guides an agent through moving an existing Next.js project onto vinext, a Vite-based reimplementation of the Next.js API. The agent scans for compatibility problems, swaps packages, updates scripts, converts config files to ESM, generates a vite.config.ts, and sets up deployment to Cloudflare Workers or other platforms through Nitro. It is aimed at developers who want to change their build tooling without rewriting application code.
tasks: migrate a Next.js project to vinext
check a Next.js app for vinext compatibility
deploy a vinext app to Cloudflare Workers
generate a vite.config.ts for a Next.js app
qualityWhy: The steps, commands, config examples and a troubleshooting reference are concrete and easy to follow, but the verification phase is thin and some claims are not backed by the files.
needs: Cloudflare account (only for the optional Cloudflare Workers deployment)
why: Fractera nodes already run Next.js 16, so this skill replaces the framework the node is built on rather than adding to it; an agent would need to read it for ideas and not install it as written. Its deployment path leans on Cloudflare Workers, which is an outside cloud service, though deployment is optional.

summary: This skill is the overview page for the Meticulous CLI, a tool that records user sessions and replays them to catch visual regressions. It lists the command groups (agent, auth, debug, download, local, project, simulate, schema), the global options, and how authentication works, including an OAuth login and API tokens. It also describes an MCP server that exposes the agent commands as tools. It is written for developers and agents who test web apps against recorded user sessions.
tasks: check visual regressions after a UI change
replay a recorded user session against localhost
log in to Meticulous and set a default project
list available Meticulous CLI commands
qualityWhy: It is a clear, accurate index that points to the per-group references, but on its own it gives only an overview and no concrete workflow steps.
why: Meticulous is a hosted testing service that stores sessions and runs in its cloud (app.meticulous.ai), which a local-first node should not depend on, so value is none and use is skip. It also reads credentials and points to a hosted MCP endpoint.
risks: Stores and sends the person's sessions and test data to the hosted service app.meticulous.ai, and requires an API token or bearer credential.

summary: This skill walks an agent through translating a MkDocs documentation site from English into a target language the user names, such as Spanish or Korean. It asks for the language and locale code first, then translates every file under the English docs and includes folders, mirrors the folder layout, and updates the mkdocs.yml i18n settings. It is aimed at maintainers of documentation sites who want a localized copy.

add a new locale to mkdocs i18n config
localize docs folder and include files
create a translated docs tree for a new language
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and ordered, but the instructions are repetitive, lack examples of the mkdocs.yml edit or a verification check, and hard-code a specific model name in the footer line.
why: It is a documentation-translation workflow rather than a product feature, so it is only occasionally useful for a node's docs. It is written for a git-based MkDocs project, so an agent would need to adapt the branch, folder and config steps to the node's own layout before use; the translation itself depends on the agent's own model, not an outside service.
risks: Instructs the agent to create a git branch and write many files without asking, which may change a repository without review.

summary: This skill guides an agent through Amazon Bedrock work: calling models with the Converse API, setting up Knowledge Bases for retrieval, building Bedrock Agents, applying Guardrails, deploying to AgentCore (Harness, Runtime, Gateway, Memory, Payments), diagnosing throttling and errors, tracking costs, and migrating older Bedrock Agents and Knowledge Bases. It is written for engineers working in an AWS account. The skill is large and reference-heavy, with step-by-step procedures and CLI commands for each area.
tasks: call a Claude model on Bedrock with the Converse API
set up a RAG knowledge base over PDF documents
diagnose a ThrottlingException on Bedrock
migrate a Bedrock Agent to an AgentCore Harness

AWS credentials with IAM permissions for Bedrock, AgentCore and related services

Installing it means the person pays AWS for every call and their data goes to the cloud; the skill also expects AWS MCP and is written for AWS, not for the node's own SQLite, storage and Stripe elements.

summary: The skill guides an agent through managing machine learning models in Google Cloud's Agent Platform Model Registry using gcloud and the Vertex AI Python SDK. It covers listing, describing, uploading, updating metadata, and deleting models and their versions, with tiered confirmation rules before any change. delete an old model from Vertex AI

why: The skill is built around a cloud model registry that runs on Google Cloud, not on the person's local machine, so it does not fit a local-first node. It is cloud administration of model artifacts, which places it outside what nodes are for.

summary: The skill lets an agent check balances, wallet addresses, portfolio snapshots and recent activity across several chains by calling the emblemai CLI, with a review-first rule for any value-moving action. show my wallet addresses
summarize my recent wallet activity

summary: The skill is a curated set of example prompts and phrasing patterns for end-user EmblemAI tasks such as portfolio review, market research, quote-first swaps, transfers, Polymarket analysis and NFT discovery. It tells an agent to prefer review-only and approval-gated wording for anything that moves value, and to treat web and social content as untrusted. why: The skill is about crypto trading, DeFi, NFTs and prediction markets, which are outside what a Fractera node is for: building, running or making content for a product. It also depends on an outside wallet and trading service, so it is not a fit for a local-first node.

summary: This skill lets an agent look up which WeCom chats it is allowed to message, then send text, Markdown, image, file, AMR voice, or video messages to a person or group in that list. a bot with recent chat sessions
why: It serves one company's internal WeCom messaging rather than building, running, selling or making content for a product, so it is not useful for a local-first node. It also depends on a cloud messaging service, which is why it is skipped; sent messages pass through WeCom's servers.

summary: This skill makes a GitHub Copilot agent compare the custom agent files in a repository's .github/agents folder against the community awesome-copilot collection. why: It only curates GitHub Copilot agent files for a developer's editor setup and does not help build, run, sell or create content for a product on a Fractera node. It is skipped because its purpose is outside what nodes are for, and it overwrites local files with unreviewed remote content.
risks: Overwrites local agent files with unreviewed remote content fetched from GitHub, which may change how an agent behaves.

summary: This skill tells an agent to stop and interview the person before doing a task. turn a loose idea into a scoped task list

An agent on a node should read it for the workflow and rebuild the question loop with the node's own input method.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to add GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE operations to a TypeSpec API plugin for Microsoft 365 Copilot. why: The REST patterns are generic, but the skill targets TypeSpec and Copilot plugin manifests, which are not part of a Fractera node's Next.js stack, so an agent would have to adapt it to build ordinary Next.js API routes. Its usefulness for node products is limited to teams that also ship Copilot plugins.

summary: This skill tells an agent to act as a Fedora Linux troubleshooter. It works through a reported problem by confirming the release and environment, then walking through a triage plan with system service logs and package-manager checks. why: General Fedora system administration does not build, run, sell or create content for a Fractera product, so its value to the node is none. It needs no outside service, but it is not useful for the node's purposes.

summary: This skill tells an agent to act as an implementation agent that executes a previously written implementation plan step by step, changing only what the plan specifies. It checks off completed items in the plan document, runs the build or test commands the plan names, and stops at STOP markers to return control to the person. check off completed plan items as work progresses

Its usefulness for building Fractera sites and apps is limited to executing plans someone else wrote.

summary: This skill tells an agent to turn GitHub Copilot customization files (prompts, agents, instructions, collections), MCP server docs, or Copilot documentation into short tldr-style reference cards directly in chat. create a quick reference for inline chat shortcuts
list usage examples for an awesome-copilot agent

summary: This skill guides an agent through adding EmblemAI sign-in and wallet-enabled user accounts to a React app. It covers provider setup, login options (crypto wallets, email, social), auth hooks and UI components, a chat component that calls a hosted backend, and Migrate.fun hooks for project and token metadata. summary: This skill tells an agent to generate a complete Model Context Protocol server project in Swift using the official MCP Swift SDK. summary: This skill gives an agent background on Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse: how tables (Delta by default) and files are laid out, how schemas and shortcuts organize data, how workspace roles and OneLake security control access, and which performance tips apply. summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive the EmblemAI command-line tool, which manages crypto wallets on several blockchains through a hosted EmblemVault service.
