summary: This skill teaches an agent to send media files to Transloadit's cloud and run processing jobs on them: encoding video to HLS or MP4, making thumbnails, resizing and watermarking images, extracting or joining audio, adding subtitles, and running OCR on documents. It is written for developers and content makers who want to automate media work through an MCP server or the Transloadit CLI. The skill is mostly a set of JSON step templates with a short setup section.
tasks: encode a video to HLS for streaming
generate thumbnails from a video
resize and watermark a batch of product images
OCR a scanned PDF into text
concatenate audio clips into one file
qualityWhy: It gives concrete JSON step examples, two setup paths, and a clear explanation of how steps chain, but it has no error handling, no way to check a result, and no guidance on choosing robots or presets.
needs: Transloadit API key and secret (TRANSLOADIT_KEY, TRANSLOADIT_SECRET)
why: It directly serves making media content (video, images, audio, documents), and Transloadit only processes files and returns results, so local files stay the source of truth; it is a paid cloud service the person chooses, so it needs install-with-service. The setup puts the secret inside an editor config file, so the person should keep that file out of version control, and the skill runs the npm package with npx -y.

summary: The skill turns a business need described in plain words into a full Dataverse solution in Python, using the PowerPlatform-Dataverse-Client SDK. It proposes a table and relationship design, picks one of six access patterns (transactional, batch, query, file, scheduled, real-time), and writes a service class with logging, error handling and performance tips. It is aimed at developers who build data-backed business apps on Microsoft Dataverse.
tasks: design a document management data model in Dataverse
build a Python batch sync from an external system into Dataverse
generate a Dataverse service class with error handling
optimise high-volume Dataverse reads and writes
qualityWhy: The skill gives a useful structure and a template, but the template is mostly placeholders (empty _initialize, commented-out operations) and it lacks verified, runnable examples for the SDK calls it names.
why: Dataverse is a cloud database that Microsoft hosts, and this skill builds a solution around it; under the node's local-first rule that is a cloud database backend, so value is none and use is skip. Its code also depends on the Azure identity service, which a local node does not use.

summary: This skill walks an agent through creating a Kotlin backend project on Spring Boot 3.4.5 with Java 21. It downloads a starter from start.spring.io, adds Redis, PostgreSQL and MongoDB settings, writes a docker-compose file for those databases, and checks the build with Gradle. It is aimed at developers who want a reactive JVM service backed by several databases.
tasks: scaffold a Spring Boot Kotlin backend
set up Postgres, Redis and MongoDB with docker-compose
add OpenAPI docs and ArchUnit tests to a Gradle project
check that a fresh Spring Boot project builds with gradle test
qualityWhy: The steps are concrete and runnable, but the file has a duplicated unzip section, a webflux versus webmvc mismatch between text and snippet, an invalid spring-boot:run command, and hard-coded default passwords.
why: The skill targets a Spring Boot and JVM stack, which a Next.js node replaces, so an agent would have to adapt it to the node's own stack rather than install it as written. It is still useful as a reference for a backend built on the JVM. Its default credentials are weak and need changing before any real use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up a declarative agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot that connects to an MCP server. It covers scaffolding the project with Microsoft's Agents Toolkit, picking which server tools to expose, configuring OAuth or SSO, and writing the manifest, agent and plugin JSON files. It is aimed at developers who want an assistant inside the Microsoft 365 and Teams ecosystem.
tasks: connect a Copilot agent to an MCP server
set up a Microsoft 365 declarative agent with OAuth
choose which MCP tools Copilot can use
sideload and test an agent in Teams
qualityWhy: It gives concrete JSON examples and a workflow, but it is thin on verification steps and has inconsistent file paths (.vscode/mcp.json versus mcp.json) and a reference to another prompt.
needs: MCP server with OAuth 2.0 or SSO credentials
why: The agent it produces is hosted and run inside Microsoft 365 and Teams cloud services, not on a local node, so it does not serve building, running or selling products on Fractera. Using it would also tie the deliverable to one vendor's cloud administration.

summary: The skill guides an agent to write a TypeSpec project for Microsoft 365 Copilot: an agent definition file and an actions file describing REST operations with paths, parameters, models, and optional auth. It also covers confirmation dialogs, Adaptive Card responses, and reasoning or response instructions. The intended users are developers building Copilot API plugins that call external REST services.
tasks: create a TypeSpec API plugin for an external REST API
add API key or OAuth2 authentication to a Copilot plugin
generate Adaptive Card responses for plugin operations
add confirmation dialogs for destructive plugin actions
qualityWhy: The skill gives a useful template and workflow, but it is short, has no worked example, no compile or validation step, and some snippets are only outlines.
needs: Microsoft 365 Copilot account or tenant for deploying plugins
why: The skill builds Microsoft 365 Copilot plugins, which serve Microsoft's cloud assistant rather than building, running, or selling a local-first Fractera site or app. Its output depends on the Microsoft 365 cloud platform, so it does not fit what nodes are for.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to fetch weather data inside an Internet Computer canister written in Motoko, using generated bindings for the WeatherAPI.com service. It covers current conditions, multi-day forecasts, astronomy, time zones, IP location and place search. It also explains the API key handling, why calls must stay non-replicated, and how optional fields and errors behave. The intended users are developers building weather features on that Motoko stack.
tasks: show current temperature for a city in a canister
fetch a three-day forecast for a location
look up sunrise and sunset times
add location search autocomplete to an app
decode and handle WeatherAPI errors
qualityWhy: It gives a complete, runnable Motoko example, an endpoint table, key setup steps, and clear notes on optional fields, zero/empty parameters and error messages, though it covers only one stack.
why: Weather data can serve sites and apps built on Fractera, but this skill is written for Motoko canisters on the Internet Computer, which Fractera's Next.js, TypeScript and SQLite stack does not use, so an agent would need to port the approach rather than install it. The service itself is an outside paid-tier API that returns data rather than hosting anything, and the key sits in request URLs as the skill itself notes.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building Godot 4.x user interfaces with Control nodes. It covers anchor and offset layout that adapts to window size, Container nodes that arrange children automatically, Theme resources for consistent styling, and keyboard or gamepad focus navigation. It is aimed at developers making HUDs, menus, inventories and settings screens in Godot projects.
tasks: build a game main menu in Godot
lay out a HUD that scales with window size
set up gamepad focus navigation for menus
apply a consistent theme to Godot UI
qualityWhy: It gives concrete GDScript patterns, a clear workflow and a useful pitfalls list, with a references file for deeper detail, though it leaves some API specifics to that file.
why: It is a stack-specific skill for Godot game UI, which is useful when building a game on a node but not a core need for web sites, shops or content making, so value is some; it fits the node as written with no outside service.

summary: This skill lets an agent research DeFi yields, look up wallets' existing DeFi positions and smart-money holdings, check token safety, and enter liquid staking by swapping tokens through the EmblemAI agent wallet CLI. It is aimed at crypto users who want to earn yield or stake assets. Most of the yield analysis relies on the model's own knowledge plus market data calls, not on live pool APY data.
tasks: find the best yield opportunities on Solana
check a wallet's DeFi positions on Ethereum
compare liquid staking options like JitoSOL and mSOL
swap SOL for a liquid staking token
qualityWhy: The steps and commands are clear, but the yield analysis is mostly delegated to the LLM's knowledge, and the skill itself admits that live pool APY ranking and LP management are unsupported.
why: DeFi yield research and token swaps for staking do not serve building, running, selling or making content for a node's products, so the value is none. The skill also moves real funds through a wallet, which is outside what nodes are for, even though swaps require user confirmation in safe mode.

summary: This skill guides an agent through visually regression-testing a frontend change with the Meticulous service. The agent builds the frontend, uploads the build once as a reusable deployment, triggers a test run against a chosen base commit, and then hands off to a companion review skill to label each visual difference as intended or unintended. It is aimed at developers finishing a feature before opening a pull request.
tasks: check a frontend change for unintended visual regressions
run visual tests before creating a pull request
compare a new build against a different base commit
review screenshot differences from a test run
qualityWhy: The steps, commands, flags and the uncommitted-changes caveat are concrete and sequenced, though it depends on other skills and gives no sample output to check against.
why: The tool runs its test runs and stores deployments on Meticulous's cloud service, and it is a testing tool for web frontends rather than something a Fractera node itself needs, so it fails the local-first rule and is skipped.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a structured interview to capture a NoSQL application's requirements, such as access patterns, request rates, and data sizes, and then produces a Cosmos DB data model from them. It writes two working documents, one for requirements and one for the final model, and reasons about aggregate boundaries, partition keys, indexing and cost. It is aimed at developers planning an Azure Cosmos DB backend.
tasks: design a Cosmos DB data model for my app
capture access patterns and request rates for a NoSQL workload
choose partition keys and containers for Cosmos DB
estimate RU costs for a document design
qualityWhy: The skill gives a detailed interview template, decision frameworks, RU math and worked examples that an agent can follow, though the text is very long and repetitive.
why: Cosmos DB is a cloud database, which the node's local-first data model replaces with its own SQLite element, so the skill's core design target does not fit a Fractera node and it should be skipped.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building or repairing user interfaces, from pages and components to typography and spacing. Before coding, it asks for the audience, an aesthetic direction, a signature detail, and hard constraints, then checks the real rendered result at desktop and narrow widths. It also covers screenshot-driven fixes, where the agent names the specific visual defect before changing anything. It is aimed at people building product screens, landing pages, and dashboards on a node.
tasks: build a landing page with a clear visual direction
fix text overflow or misalignment in a screenshot
make a dashboard component look polished on mobile
give three distinct design options for a screen
tools: browser or screenshot tool for rendered checks
qualityWhy: It gives concrete flows, checklists, and verification steps, but several rules point to reference files and scripts outside the six bundled files.
why: It directly serves building and polishing UI for a product, and it is stack-free, so it fits a node without adaptation. Doubts: it cites ../../scripts/check-update.sh and rules/durable-context.md, which are not in the bundle, so those steps may fail when installed alone.

summary: The skill lets an agent scout memecoins on Solana, Base and Hedera by calling EmblemAI tools that list new Pump.fun, LaunchLab, Clanker and MemeJob launches, trending tokens, rug-pull risk scores and smart-money trades. It is aimed at traders and researchers who want to find or vet low-cap tokens. A helper shell script runs a scan for a chosen platform.
tasks: find new memecoins launching on Pump.fun
check whether a Solana token is a rug pull
show trending low-cap tokens on Base
see whether smart money is trading a memecoin
qualityWhy: The instructions give concrete commands, a risk-score table and a clear workflow, but they depend entirely on an opaque CLI with no explanation of its outputs, and the script only prints results.
needs: EmblemAI account or profile for the emblemai CLI
Birdeye and Nansen data access through EmblemAI
why: The skill is about trading speculative tokens on external chain and market data services, not building, running or making content for a node product, so it is out of scope; it also routes all queries through a cloud agent CLI rather than local data. Its advice to act on token alerts could lead to financial loss, so it should not be installed on a node.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to pull text out of images, photos, screenshots and scanned PDFs using the PaddleOCR engine. It covers choosing a language, reading the box and confidence data for each line, rebuilding the page layout, simple image cleanup, and batch runs. It is aimed at people who need text from documents, receipts or business cards turned into usable data.
tasks: extract text from a scanned PDF
read contact details from a business card photo
pull line items and totals from a receipt image
OCR a screenshot with Chinese and English text
batch-convert a folder of scanned pages to text
qualityWhy: The code examples are concrete and runnable in outline, but the metadata description is empty, the listed MCP tool is never used in the body, ocr_pdf uses os without importing it, pdf2image's poppler dependency is not mentioned, and there are no verification steps.
why: OCR is useful for document-based products and agents, and PaddleOCR runs on the person's own machine with no account or key, so it fits a local-first node; it is not core to building sites or content, so the value is only some. The Python stack is separate from the node's TypeScript stack, but it is a standalone script, not a replacement for a node component.

summary: The skill guides an agent to build a complete Power Platform custom connector that exposes an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server to Microsoft Copilot Studio. It covers generating the swagger definition, apiProperties, a C# script for JSON-RPC handling, and a readme, plus schema validation against Copilot Studio constraints. It targets developers building Microsoft-stack agent integrations, not local web apps.
tasks: build a Power Platform connector for Copilot Studio
validate a swagger schema for Copilot Studio
troubleshoot MCP connection failures in Copilot Studio
prepare a connector for Microsoft certification
qualityWhy: The file gives a clear checklist and file layout, but it is mostly a list of requirements with little concrete step-by-step guidance, example files, or code.
why: The skill is built around a Microsoft cloud hosting and connector platform (Power Platform, Copilot Studio), which a local-first Fractera node does not serve, so its value is none and it should be skipped.

summary: The skill guides an agent through MySQL and InnoDB work: designing schemas with sensible primary keys and character sets, choosing and auditing indexes, tuning queries with EXPLAIN, handling transactions and locks, and planning online migrations, connections and replication checks. It is aimed at engineers who need safe, measured database changes. It is a reference-driven checklist that points to linked topic files for detail.
tasks: review a MySQL table schema before a release
speed up a slow query with EXPLAIN
plan an online ALTER TABLE migration
diagnose deadlocks and lock waits
tune connection pool settings for MySQL
qualityWhy: Concrete rules and a clear workflow with linked references, though most guidance is short bullet points that depend on the reference files for depth.
why: It is directly useful for building and running products on a database, but it recommends PlanetScale as the primary host, a cloud service, which conflicts with the local-first node; the self-hosted MySQL advice itself fits the node, so an agent should use the rules while keeping data on the local SQLite element, which means it is not a drop-in fit and is marked as ideas. The reference links point to a remote GitHub raw URL, so an agent would need to fetch them, which is unverified.

summary: This skill tells an agent to take a GitHub owner/repo, work out its package dependencies through the deps.dev API, and find which maintainers accept sponsorship via GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, Ko-fi, Patreon or Tidelift. It checks npm funding metadata, FUNDING.yml files and web search, verifies each link, and writes a friendly report grouped by maintainer. It is aimed at developers who want to support the open source their project relies on.
tasks: find which dependencies of my project accept sponsorship
make a sponsor report for the express repo
show who maintains my dependencies and how to fund them
check whether my npm packages' maintainers have funding links
qualityWhy: The steps, API URL formats, field names, batching rules and report template are concrete and followable, though a few details such as the ecosystem casing and the handling of non-npm funding are left loose.
needs: GitHub access through the GitHub MCP tools
why: It is a reporting tool for an open source maintainer's supply chain, not a building, running or content tool, so its use is occasional, and it relies on web fetch and search for live funding checks. It does not install or run code, and it has no secrets or data-exfiltration steps, so nothing blocks use.

summary: This skill tells an agent to generate a Power Platform custom connector that exposes an MCP server to Microsoft Copilot Studio. It covers a swagger definition, connector properties, a C# script, and a JSON-RPC handler with streamable HTTP at /mcp. It is aimed at developers who want their tools and data to be callable from a Copilot Studio agent.
tasks: build an MCP server for Copilot Studio
create a Power Platform custom connector
expose API tools to a Copilot Studio agent
generate a swagger definition for MCP tools
qualityWhy: It is mainly a template with placeholders and a checklist, with few concrete steps, complete examples, or verification commands an agent could follow directly.
why: Its output is built to run on Microsoft's cloud (Power Platform connectors, Copilot Studio, and typically Azure hosting), which a local-first node does not provide, so it is not useful for what nodes are for.

summary: Guides an agent to pull recorded user sessions from the Meticulous service that cover code changed on the current git branch, then read the downloaded user-event sequences, network request and response pairs, and storage state. The agent uses these to understand real user flows and to build network mocks for tests. It is aimed at developers testing front-end changes against captured traffic.
tasks: write tests using recorded network mocks
understand which user flow a code change affects
find sessions that cover my edited lines
download a specific Meticulous session for debugging
qualityWhy: The steps and option table are clear, but the skill gives no concrete example output, no handling for failed or empty downloads, and it depends on a second skill and an external CLI without explaining how to set them up.
why: Its data comes from a cloud testing service, so the recorded sessions and network traffic leave the person's machine and are not local-first, which makes it value none under the local-first rule. The skill also calls the Meticulous feedback endpoint at the end, which sends a note to a third party without clearly telling the person.
risks: Sends a feedback note to the Meticulous service after each use, which is an outbound report the person may not expect.

summary: The skill gives an agent a full template for building a Model Context Protocol server in Kotlin: a Gradle project layout, build script, entry point, config loading, typed tools with JSON schemas, tests and a README. It targets developers who want an MCP server that exposes custom tools to AI clients over stdio or SSE. The skill is pure text templates; it runs nothing itself.
tasks: generate a Kotlin MCP server project
add a typed tool to an MCP server
set up Gradle for a Kotlin MCP server
build an MCP server with stdio transport
qualityWhy: The templates are concrete and runnable in outline, but the SSE transport section is a placeholder and the test template contains no real tool-calling test.
why: A Kotlin MCP server is a developer tool, not a core node feature, so its value is occasional. The skill is a standalone project scaffold for a JVM stack, which the node does not use; the agent would need to adapt it to Fractera's Next.js and TypeScript stack, so it is 'ideas' rather than 'install'.

summary: This skill guides an agent to produce Excalidraw diagram files (.excalidraw JSON) that communicate relationships and flows visually rather than as plain labelled boxes. It asks for research of real specs for technical diagrams, sectioned JSON construction, and a render-view-fix loop using a bundled Python renderer with Playwright. It is aimed at people who want architecture, workflow or concept diagrams for docs, tutorials or videos.
tasks: draw an architecture diagram of my app
visualize a workflow as an Excalidraw file
make a technical explainer diagram with code examples
render and fix a diagram until it looks clean
qualityWhy: The file gives a clear design process, element templates references, a concrete render loop and a checklist, though it leans on referenced files not included here and has no worked example.
why: Diagrams are useful for documenting a node's architecture or product flows now and then, but it is not core to building or running a product. It runs locally with no cloud service, so it is installable as written, though it needs a Python/uv setup and Playwright Chromium for rendering.

summary: The skill is a general guide for building Microsoft 365 Copilot declarative agents, covering three workflows: basic creation, advanced enterprise design, and validation of existing agents. It describes a v1.5 JSON manifest with capability limits and character limits, a TypeSpec alternative, and testing in the Agents Playground through the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit. It is aimed at developers building Microsoft Teams and Copilot agents.
tasks: create a Microsoft 365 Copilot declarative agent
validate an existing agent manifest against schema v1.5
convert agent JSON to TypeSpec
test an agent in Agents Playground
qualityWhy: The file is mostly an overview with lists of steps and limits but gives no concrete commands, full examples, or checks an agent can actually run, and its TypeSpec sample is a loose model rather than working code.
why: The skill serves Microsoft 365 Copilot agents, which a Fractera node does not build or run, and it is tied to Microsoft's cloud platform rather than local-first work. Its quality is also low as an instruction.

summary: The skill tells an agent to shuffle the objects in a JSON array, but only after checking that every object has the same property names and no nested objects. If the input is missing or inconsistent, the agent should stop and ask for a valid file rather than change the data. Users can override defaults such as which properties to ignore or require. It is aimed at people who need to randomise repetitive records, such as lists of facts or quiz items, without breaking the file.
tasks: shuffle the entries in a JSON file
randomise a list of records without breaking the format
check that JSON objects have consistent keys before reordering
qualityWhy: The instructions are generic and partly contradictory, with no concrete steps, commands, or examples of the actual shuffle, and the Variables section is vague.
why: It is a stack-free data utility that could occasionally help a node's content or data work, but it is thin and the default-state rules are hard to follow. Nothing in it calls outside services or touches secrets.

summary: This skill guides an agent through reviewing Azure infrastructure, both Infrastructure-as-Code files and deployed resources in a resource group, to find cost-saving changes such as right-sizing SKUs, switching to serverless or consumption tiers, and adding storage lifecycle rules. After user confirmation, it opens one GitHub issue per optimization plus an EPIC tracking issue. It is aimed at engineers who run Azure workloads and want a structured cost review.
tasks: find cost savings in my Azure resource group
right-size my App Service plans and databases
review Bicep or Terraform files for overspending
create GitHub issues for each cost optimization
qualityWhy: The steps and issue templates are concrete, but pricing lookups are vague, the priority formula has undefined inputs, and there are internal inconsistencies such as the Step 2 instruction to ignore non-IaC files alongside the EPIC template's mermaid placeholders.
why: The skill is built around Azure cloud resources (App Services, Cosmos DB, Azure storage, Log Analytics), which is a cloud hosting and administration place a local-first Fractera node is not meant to rely on, so it does not serve building or running a product on the node. It also expects the agent to create public GitHub issues and read Azure monitoring data, which is outside the node's scope.

summary: This skill guides an agent to write a TypeSpec file that defines a declarative agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot. The file covers the agent's name and description, behavioural instructions, conversation starters, and the capabilities it may use, such as web search, SharePoint, Teams, email or Graph connectors. It is aimed at developers and administrators who build internal assistants inside a Microsoft 365 tenant. The skill asks the user about the agent's purpose, needed capabilities and typical interactions before generating the definition.
tasks: create a Microsoft 365 Copilot declarative agent
write agent instructions and conversation starters in TypeSpec
scope SharePoint or Teams access for a Copilot agent
qualityWhy: The template and rules are clear and concrete, but the skill gives no compile, validation or deployment steps and little worked output.
why: The skill targets Microsoft 365 Copilot, a cloud platform outside the node's own stack, and its agents are deployed to a Microsoft tenant rather than kept on the person's computer, so it does not serve building or running products on a Fractera node.

summary: This skill guides an agent through checking the health of one Azure resource, such as a web app, virtual machine, database or storage account. The agent pulls error and performance data from Log Analytics and Application Insights with KQL queries, classifies the problems it finds by severity, and writes a phased fix plan with Azure CLI commands and rollback steps. The intended users are cloud operators and developers who run workloads on Azure.
tasks: diagnose why an Azure web app is returning errors
check the health of a virtual machine and explain its failures
review Log Analytics errors for a Cosmos DB account
write a remediation plan for a degraded Azure service
qualityWhy: The skill gives clear steps, resource-type-specific checks, example KQL queries and a report template, though it leaves some details, such as query tuning and exact thresholds, to the agent.
needs: Azure authentication for the Azure MCP server
RBAC read access to the target resource and its Log Analytics workspace
diagnostic settings enabled on the target resource
why: It is a cloud administration workflow for resources hosted on Azure, which a local-first node does not run or keep, so it does not serve building or selling products on the node. The skill itself is clean, but it is only useful with an Azure account, so it is skipped.

summary: The skill tells an agent to act as a CentOS Linux troubleshooter: confirm the release (Stream or legacy), walk through diagnosis with systemctl, journalctl, dnf or yum and logs, then offer copy-paste fixes with checks after each change. It also asks the agent to account for SELinux and firewalld and to finish with rollback steps. It is aimed at system administrators fixing server problems on RHEL-family machines.
tasks: diagnose a failing systemd service on CentOS
fix a dnf or yum package dependency error
troubleshoot SELinux denials blocking an app
open or fix firewalld rules for a service
write a rollback plan for a server change
qualityWhy: The file is a short list of generic instructions with placeholders and no concrete commands, examples, or checks beyond a bare section list.
why: It is a stack-free system administration habit list that helps when a Fractera node runs on CentOS, but it is thin and rarely needed for building, running, or selling a product directly. It is not a local-first concern since it only uses the OS's own tools.

summary: This skill guides an agent through containerizing a legacy ASP.NET .NET Framework web project for Windows Server containers. It covers choosing a Windows Server base image, switching web.config to read settings from environment variables, writing a multi-stage Dockerfile and .dockerignore, and building the image with Docker. It is written for developers moving old IIS-hosted applications into Windows containers.
tasks: containerize an ASP.NET .NET Framework project for Windows
write a multi-stage Dockerfile for an IIS web app
move web.config settings to environment variables
build a Windows Server container image with Docker
qualityWhy: The steps, Dockerfile example and progress checklist are concrete, though a few rules conflict (LogMonitorConfig.json location, 'must not not be modified', and whether to pause for missing NuGet packages versus continuing without pausing).
needs: A Windows host with Docker in Windows container mode
Microsoft.Configuration.ConfigurationBuilders.Environment NuGet package installed manually in the project
why: Node stacks are Next.js and TypeScript with local SQLite, and this skill targets legacy .NET Framework IIS apps that a Fractera node does not run, so it does not serve building, running or selling a product on a node. It also needs a Windows Docker host, which is outside what a node is for.
risks: The Dockerfile downloads LogMonitor.exe with curl and runs it as the container entrypoint, with no checksum check, so the binary is trusted on the strength of the GitHub release URL alone.

summary: This skill guides an agent through creating a new agent skill or improving an existing one, with a plan-then-confirm workflow that scales with the size of the change. It checks each step against established practice, validates structure with bundled scripts, and compares behaviour before and after changes on real tasks. It is aimed at people who maintain skill catalogues and want repeatable, verifiable skill quality. It can also prepare a GitHub repo and verify an npx install, but only on explicit request.
tasks: make a new skill from a recurring problem
improve an existing skill from failure cases
validate a skill's structure and references
prepare a skill for GitHub publishing
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is detailed with routes, invariants, report templates and stop conditions, and the bundled validators are concrete, though the main file is long and some references were not shown.
why: It is a stack-free authoring workflow useful for building and maintaining skills on a node, but its use is occasional rather than core to building a product's site or content. It does not require any external service, though the optional GitHub publishing path needs the user's own gh account and explicit authorization.

summary: This skill lets an agent read Hyperliquid account data (positions, balances, fills, funding, order books, candles) for its own wallet or any 0x address, and place or cancel perp and spot orders, set stop-loss and take-profit triggers, and move USDC between Arbitrum and Hyperliquid. Orders are signed through the platform's wallet service and sent to Hyperliquid's API. It is written for people who want an agent to trade or monitor positions on Hyperliquid.
tasks: check my Hyperliquid positions and PnL
buy or sell a perp with leverage
set a stop loss or take profit
deposit or withdraw USDC on Hyperliquid
analyse another wallet's trading history
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed with examples and error tables, but SKILL.md says hl_* names cannot be called as tools while __init__.py registers them, which is a contradiction an agent could trip over.
why: It is useful only to a node that trades on Hyperliquid, which is an outside venue rather than a product-building task, so value is some. It is set to skip because _trade_report.py posts executed trade events, including wallet address and order details, to an analytics endpoint using the container token, and SKILL.md does not disclose this; the 2 bps builder fee is disclosed. Real-money leveraged trading also carries loss risk that the person must accept.
risks: _trade_report.py sends executed trade data with the wallet address to an analytics endpoint using a bearer token, and SKILL.md does not mention this.

summary: The skill tells an agent to scan a Bicep file for Azure Verified Modules, look up the newest published version of each module in the Microsoft Container Registry tag list, and bump versions where safe. It pauses for approval on breaking parameter, security or behavioural changes, and finishes with a status table plus a summary. The audience is engineers maintaining Azure infrastructure-as-code.
tasks: update Azure Verified Modules in a Bicep file
check Bicep modules for newer versions
review breaking changes before upgrading AVM modules
validate Bicep after a module upgrade
qualityWhy: The steps and output format are clear, but the skill is short and leaves out how to handle a version lookup failure, how to pick the right docs link, and what counts as a breaking change beyond a few broad bullets.
why: The skill is built around Azure cloud infrastructure, which a local-first node does not run or host, so its value is none. It is skipped rather than installed because its purpose is cloud administration, not building, running or making content on a Fractera node.

summary: This skill is a design filter for AI coding agents building interfaces. It makes the agent check its UI work against a list of common generic-AI patterns, require a written purpose for each visual technique, and hold the result to a liveliness and craftsmanship bar. It also covers accessibility, mobile behaviour, honest content, and a delivery check before the work is called done. It is aimed at people who build sites, web apps, and landing pages and want them to look designed rather than generated.
tasks: build a landing page without generic AI styling
audit an existing website UI for AI slop
review a web app's accessibility and interactive states
check a design before delivery
remove fake testimonials and unverified statistics from a page
