why: The skill serves occasional research on Korean funding rather than building, running or selling a product, so its value is only some. summary: This skill sets a working style for a coding agent that runs long tasks through subagents, with a fixed set of playbooks for bug fixes, features, refactors, investigations and pull requests. It asks for short, evidence-backed replies, verification against the real artifact, and triage of automated review comments. It is written for developers shipping code, not for end users of a site or app.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to write or revise a short AGENTS.md (and a CLAUDE.md that links to it) for a code repository. The agent inspects lock files, manifests, CI and docs, then lists only non-obvious conventions, file-scoped commands and paths to existing reference docs. summary: The skill gives an agent a prioritized checklist of React and Next.js performance rules, covering request waterfalls, bundle size, server-side data handling, client fetching, re-render control, rendering, and JavaScript micro-optimizations. It is meant for developers writing, reviewing, or refactoring React code who need to speed up pages or cut client CPU use. Each rule comes with short incorrect/correct code examples that an agent can apply directly.
tasks: review a Next.js page for request waterfalls
reduce first-load JavaScript bundle size
remove unnecessary re-renders from a React component
audit Server Actions for authentication and authorization
improve Core Web Vitals such as LCP and INP
qualityWhy: The rules are organized by priority and most include concrete incorrect/correct code examples, though several entries are one-line bullets without examples and the file is a condensed summary that defers to upstream for full detail.
why: It is a stack-based React and Next.js guide that directly serves building and running a web product, and it matches the node's Next.js 16 and React 19 stack without requiring a different framework. Some rules are version-specific (for example, the React Compiler and Activity references), so an agent should check them against the node's versions before applying them.

summary: This skill guides an agent through reading Salesforce debug logs to find the root cause of failures such as governor-limit hits, exceptions, slow queries, and CPU or heap pressure. It ranks each finding by severity and proposes a small, testable fix. It is written for Salesforce developers and administrators working on their own org.
tasks: diagnose a governor limit error from a debug log
find the cause of an Apex exception in a Salesforce log
spot SOQL or DML inside loops in a trace
rank performance problems in a debug log by severity
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, severity levels, an output format and a rules table, but the commands and the scoring rubric sit in reference files that were not included in the review.
needs: Salesforce CLI (sf) authenticated to the org
why: The skill is built entirely around Salesforce Apex and its cloud org, which a local-first Fractera node does not host or use, so it does not serve building, running or selling a product on the node. It is marked skip because its value is none.

summary: The skill guides an agent through keyword research for a website or campaign: checking for cannibalization against existing pages, building a three-tier keyword universe, classifying search intent, scoring opportunities, and seeding topic clusters. It is aimed at SEO practitioners and site owners who want a prioritized target list. The output is a markdown report with tables and a top-five action list.
tasks: build a keyword research list for my website
find which keywords to target for a new campaign
classify search intent for my target terms
prioritize keywords by opportunity score
group keywords into topic clusters
qualityWhy: It gives concrete tiers, classification tables, a scoring formula and an output template, though it leaves the data sources for volume and difficulty unspecified.
needs: keyword volume and difficulty data source
why: Keyword research helps a node's sites and content products, but it is a marketing habit rather than a build tool, and it depends on external search data the agent cannot get locally. Volume and difficulty numbers must come from a paid or third-party source, and the Pro Tip promotes seojuice.com tools.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of recommended settings for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot clusters, with a checklist for production readiness. It tells the agent which defaults to apply, which choices are hard to change after creation, and how to report differences from those defaults when auditing an existing cluster. It is written for engineers who run containerised workloads on Google Cloud. It also covers how to explain node-upgrade disruption honestly, including PodDisruptionBudgets, replicas and surge settings.
tasks: design a production GKE Autopilot cluster
audit an existing cluster against golden path defaults
check a cluster's production readiness before launch
plan node upgrades with minimal disruption
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete defaults, tables, decision rules and guardrails, though the referenced YAML and attribution files were not visible to judge.
why: GKE is a cloud hosting and cloud administration service, so under the local-first rule it is value none and use skip, even though the instructions are sound.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing firmware for small microcontrollers such as STM32 and ESP32. It covers interrupt handlers, FreeRTOS tasks and queues, bare-metal peripheral setup, DMA, power saving, and memory limits. It is aimed at embedded engineers who build devices that run without an operating system or with a lightweight real-time kernel.
tasks: write an interrupt handler for a UART receive
set up a FreeRTOS sensor task with a queue
configure a timer to blink an LED on an STM32
reduce power draw of a battery-powered sensor
qualityWhy: It gives a clear workflow, checklists, and concrete C templates, though a few details such as the timer clock arithmetic are muddled.
why: Fractera nodes build web apps, sites, agents and content on a Next.js stack, and firmware for microcontrollers is outside what a node is for. The skill has no connection to the node's TypeScript stack, so it would not help any node task.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building real-time features with WebSockets or Socket.IO, covering authentication on connect, rooms, broadcasting, presence tracking and client reconnection. It also covers scaling across several server instances with a Redis pub/sub adapter and sticky sessions. The intended users are developers adding live chat, notifications or dashboards to an application.
tasks: add live chat to a website
show which users are online
push live updates to the browser
scale a socket server across several instances
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, a runnable server example with auth and Redis adapter, a reconnection client, and explicit MUST DO and MUST NOT DO rules, with reference files for deeper topics.
why: Real-time messaging and presence are central to building interactive sites and apps on a node, so the value is high. The skill hard-codes Socket.IO, Redis and its own jsonwebtoken auth, while a node uses next-auth for sign-in and its SQLite element as the only data door, so it must be adapted rather than installed as written. Only SKILL.md was reviewed; the reference files were not read.

summary: This skill publishes a locally generated CLI to the printing-press-library GitHub repo by running validation, a live end-to-end test against the real API, packaging, and opening a pull request, with a separate mode for journaling blocked APIs. It targets maintainers of generated command-line tools who want to contribute them to a shared public library. The skill drives git, GitHub CLI and the cli-printing-press binary through a long, tightly specified sequence of steps.
tasks: publish a generated CLI to the public library
open a pull request for a finished API client
record a blocked API in the blocked-apis journal
qualityWhy: The file is very detailed and gives concrete commands, checks and failure handling, but it is cut off in the middle and depends heavily on the library's own conventions.
needs: GitHub account with fork or push access to mvanhorn/printing-press-library
why: It publishes to a public GitHub repository and forks and pushes branches, which is a cloud hosting and sharing workflow outside the local-first node; the node is for building and running its own sites and content, not contributing to an external public library.
risks: Pushes branches and opens pull requests on a public GitHub repository under the user's account, which is publishing outside the local node.

summary: This skill lets an agent fetch Instagram data through the fetcher.sh HTTP API: a profile by @handle, keyword user search, a user's posts, reels, stories, tagged posts, followers and followings, a single post by shortcode, post comments, and feeds for hashtags, locations and audio tracks. It is aimed at marketers, researchers and developers who want social listening, competitor tracking, influencer discovery or Instagram data pipelines without the official Graph API or a headless browser. Each call is a plain GET billed per request, either from prepaid credits or pay-per-call USDC over x402.
tasks: look up an Instagram profile by handle
track posts under a hashtag for social listening
export a competitor's followers or recent posts
find influencers by searching profiles with a keyword
fetch comments on a specific Instagram post
qualityWhy: It gives concrete curl examples, a full endpoint table, authentication options, error codes and a clear reference section, though the detailed reference files were not included for review.
needs: fetcher.sh prepaid API key (bby_live_...) or an x402-compatible USDC wallet
why: It is a paid outside data service that returns Instagram information to local files, so it suits market research and content planning more than building or running a node's own product. Instagram's terms of service may not allow the scraping this implies, and the skill notes that upstream failures are not refunded.

summary: Guides an agent through managing shadcn-svelte components in a Svelte project: adding, updating, debugging and styling UI pieces through the CLI, following enforced rules for forms, composition, icons and Tailwind classes. It is aimed at developers building Svelte interfaces who use the shadcn-svelte component library. The skill reads components.json for project context and points to official docs for component APIs.
tasks: add a dialog or card component to a Svelte project
build a settings form with validation using shadcn-svelte
fix component imports after adding from a registry URL
update installed shadcn-svelte components
style a Svelte UI using semantic theme tokens
qualityWhy: Concrete and well organised, with enforced rules, Incorrect/Correct examples in linked files and a clear workflow, though some detail sits in referenced files that were not fully reviewed here.
why: The node's stack is Next.js with React, so a Svelte component library does not fit the node's own UI stack and the skill must be read for ideas rather than installed as written. Its CLI commands only touch the project's own components and are not risky.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to take a Go command-line tool that a separate generator produced and make it pass its checks before release. It runs build, verification, scorecard, vet and security scans, applies fixes, reports the before-and-after results, and can offer to publish. It is aimed at maintainers of generated CLI tools, not at people building sites, apps or content on a node. The file was cut off at 40,000 characters, so the later sections were not reviewed.
tasks: polish a generated Go CLI before publishing
fix verification failures in a CLI
run a security scan on a Go CLI
check a CLI against the public library before release
qualityWhy: The steps, commands, pass/fail gates and edge cases are concrete and checkable, though the later part of the file was not visible and it depends heavily on one external generator's conventions.
needs: GitHub account for the optional publish step
why: It polishes Go CLI tools made by an external generator, which is not what a Fractera node is for (sites, web apps, agents, or content), and it fetches and builds code over the network, so it is skipped.
risks: If the installed gosec cannot load every package, the skill builds gosec from remote modules with go get and runs it, which executes code fetched from the network.
The optional publish step forks and opens a pull request on a public GitHub repository using the user's global git configuration.

summary: The skill guides an agent to explain a research paper to a reader without specialist background, starting from everyday situations and showing what the study asked, what the authors contributed, and what the evidence does and does not establish. It produces a saved Org-mode reading note plus a separate research record, then runs a bundled validator and an independent reading check. It is aimed at people who want to understand papers, not at reproducing them.
tasks: explain an arXiv paper in plain language
summarize what a research paper contributes and what its evidence shows
write a saved reading note for a paper link or PDF
check whether a paper explanation is understandable to a newcomer
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed with workflows, output files, a validator script, and checks, though the tangled Chinese writing rules and very specific formatting constraints make it heavy to follow.
why: It is useful for understanding papers and writing notes, which fits a node that makes content, but it is not a core building or selling skill. It is stack-free apart from the Bun validator and Emacs read-back check, and it writes notes to ~/Context/ on the person's own computer. Scripts shown are a validator and a legacy-field alias map with no network, secret, or remote-code behaviour.

summary: This skill is a generic guide for handling Asana project work through an assumed MCP server. It covers task lifecycles, automation rule examples, project and sprint templates, custom field setups, workload views, intake forms, and report layouts. It is written for operations and project managers who run their team's work in Asana.
tasks: set up an Asana project template for a feature launch
check team workload and rebalance tasks
create an intake form for incoming work requests
build a weekly project status report
qualityWhy: It is mostly illustrative YAML and ASCII mockups with no concrete API calls, setup steps, or checks, and it relies on an MCP server and tool names it never defines.
needs: Asana API access or the project-mcp server
why: Asana is a cloud project-management service that holds the team's data, not a local build, run, sell, or content tool for a node. Its content is thin and generic, so it would add little even if the value were higher.

summary: This skill guides an agent through planning and auditing pages that are generated in bulk from data such as CSV files, APIs, or database records. It covers checking whether the source data is rich enough, designing page templates that avoid repetitive text, choosing URL patterns, and automating internal links. It also sets quality gates for thin content, canonical tags, sitemaps, and index bloat, so that site owners can publish many pages without search penalties.
tasks: plan programmatic SEO pages from a product or location database
audit generated template pages for thin content
design URL patterns and internal linking for data-driven pages
check a batch of generated pages for duplicate metadata before publishing
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with thresholds, checklists, URL rules, and a scored output format, but they point to a script that is not in the skill folder and mix hard numbers with unsourced enforcement claims.
why: It is a stack-free planning and audit guide that fits building sites and content pages on a node, so it can be installed as written. The metadata check relies on a plugin script that is not included in these files, and some enforcement dates are cited from third-party reports and could be out of date.

summary: The skill guides an agent through creating secrets in AWS Secrets Manager with a fixed procedure covering dedicated KMS keys, automatic rotation, least-privilege IAM, CloudTrail auditing and lifecycle handling. It targets engineers who need production-grade handling of database credentials, API keys, OAuth tokens and custom secrets on AWS. The skill itself is instructions only; its procedure lives in a referenced file that was not inlined here.
tasks: create a database credential secret in AWS Secrets Manager
store an API key securely with KMS encryption
set up automatic rotation for a secret
troubleshoot secret access denied errors
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is a short overview that points to a separate procedure file for the actual steps, and the troubleshooting hints are generic without commands or examples.
needs: AWS account with IAM permissions for Secrets Manager and KMS
why: The skill is built around AWS cloud services for storing secrets, which a local-first Fractera node does not use, so it counts as no value and should be skipped.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to read n8n validation output, separating real errors that must be fixed from warnings and known false positives. It covers the validate-fix loop, validation profiles, auto-sanitization of operator shapes, and when to run or review a workflow after it validates. It is written for people building n8n automation workflows and for the agents that help them.
tasks: interpret n8n validation errors
decide whether a validation warning is a false positive
fix a broken n8n workflow after validation fails
review an existing n8n workflow for hidden issues
test an n8n workflow before deploying it
tools: n8n MCP tools (validate_node, validate_workflow, n8n_autofix_workflow, n8n_test_workflow)
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete error types, profiles, fix steps, examples and a review checklist, though it leans on external files and some sections are long.
why: It is built around n8n, an external workflow automation engine that is not part of a Fractera node's own stack (its own SQLite, Next.js, and Blocks catalogue), so it does not serve building, running or selling sites or content on the node; the n8n dependency is a cloud-style automation service rather than a local-first tool.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to handle file and directory paths in Dart using package:path and package:file instead of raw string operations, so code works on Windows, macOS and Linux alike. It covers joining and splitting paths, safe extension checks, converting paths to POSIX, Git or URI forms, and making file-system code testable with a mockable file system. It is aimed at developers writing or refactoring Dart command-line tools and services.
tasks: refactor string path joins into safe path joins
make Dart file code work on Windows
convert native paths to git or posix paths
make file system code testable with memory file system
extract file extensions and hash filenames
qualityWhy: It gives concrete rules, anti-pattern comparisons, code examples and an audit checklist, with a few gaps such as a slightly odd hashing example and no test steps.
why: It is a stack-free-ish Dart guide that only applies to Dart projects, so it is useful now and then rather than central to building a Fractera product. It needs no outside service and nothing in it asks for secrets, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill gives an agent a local MCP server with 39 tools for reading, creating, converting and analysing PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, plus OCR on scans and images. It suits people who need to turn data into office documents or pull text and tables out of them. The tools run on the person's own files, so nothing has to leave the machine. The instructions are mostly a catalogue of tools with a short setup section.
tasks: extract text and tables from a PDF
build a PowerPoint deck from a markdown outline
fill a Word template with placeholders
convert an Excel sheet to CSV or JSON
run OCR on scanned pages
qualityWhy: It gives a clear tool table and build steps, but it has no worked examples, no checks for output, and a broken link to an implementation plan that is not in the folder.
why: Document and spreadsheet work is occasionally useful for content and product building, but it is not core to running a node. The setup targets Claude Desktop's config file and an MCP server, not a node element, so it would need adapting to the node's own structure. Tesseract.js downloads language data over the network on first use, which the skill does not mention.

summary: This skill guides an agent through configuring, tuning and troubleshooting GKE ComputeClasses, which control which machine families, accelerators, Spot or on-demand capacity an autoscaled pod lands on. It covers priority ladders, CUD-capped spillover, stateful storage, access restriction through admission policies, and a log-tailing script for autoscaler events. The audience is platform engineers running Kubernetes on Google Cloud.
tasks: configure Spot VMs with on-demand fallback on GKE
cap a machine family to match committed use discounts
debug a pod stuck pending with noScaleUp
restrict which namespaces can use a ComputeClass
qualityWhy: The skill is detailed and concrete with rules, field notes, reference files and assets, though it is very long and dense.
needs: Google Cloud account with GKE cluster
why: It is built entirely around Google Kubernetes Engine, a cloud hosting platform, which the node's local-first design treats as out of scope, so it is not for building or running products on the node.

summary: This skill guides an agent through making workloads on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) more resilient. It covers checking whether a cluster is regional, adding Pod Disruption Budgets, configuring liveness, readiness and startup probes, setting graceful shutdown, and spreading pods across zones and nodes. It is aimed at platform and DevOps engineers who run containerized services on Google Cloud. It also points to other skills for generating manifests and for backups.
tasks: add a pod disruption budget to a GKE deployment
configure liveness and readiness probes for a service
spread application pods across zones in a regional cluster
check whether a GKE cluster is highly available
tools: GKE MCP tools (get_cluster, get_k8s_resource, describe_k8s_resource, apply_k8s_manifest, list_k8s_events)
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands, YAML examples, replica and probe guidelines, and clear routing to related skills, though it has no verification steps after changes.
needs: Google Cloud account with a GKE cluster
why: GKE is a cloud hosting and cloud administration service, so under the local-first rule this skill is not useful for a node that keeps its data and runs on the person's own computer. Its guidance is sound for Google Cloud, but a node does not run workloads on GKE.

summary: The skill guides an agent through storage on Google Kubernetes Engine: choosing StorageClasses, creating PersistentVolumeClaims for block disks, shared Filestore volumes, or Cloud Storage buckets, resizing volumes, and planning zonal capacity. It points to other skills for FUSE mounts and storage troubleshooting. It is aimed at engineers running workloads on GKE clusters.
tasks: create a PVC for a database on GKE
set up shared file storage for multiple pods
resize a persistent volume claim
choose a StorageClass for production volumes
qualityWhy: It gives concrete YAML manifests, a resize procedure, and best-practice checks, though some sections assume prior GKE knowledge and the attribution step adds noise.
why: The skill is built around Google Cloud managed infrastructure (GKE, Filestore, Persistent Disk, Cloud Storage buckets), which is a cloud place to run and keep data rather than local storage on the node, so it falls outside what a local-first Fractera node is for.

summary: Guides an agent through writing and fixing React component, hook and page tests with React Testing Library, Vitest or Jest, and MSW for network mocking. It covers query priority, userEvent interaction, async patterns, axe accessibility checks, and when a test belongs in Playwright or Cypress instead. It is aimed at developers who maintain a React front end and want reliable, behavior-focused tests.
tasks: write tests for a React form component
mock API calls in component tests with MSW
test a custom React hook
add accessibility checks to UI tests
decide between component tests and end-to-end tests
qualityWhy: Concrete and well organized, with runnable code samples, commands, coverage config and clear anti-patterns, though a few setup pieces (test-utils providers, theme) are sketched rather than complete.
why: It is a stack-free testing guide for React, so it is directly useful for a node's front-end work, but it assumes Vitest or Jest and TanStack Query, and it references ECC-specific paths and agents that do not exist on a Fractera node, so it should be adapted to the node's Next.js 16 and Jest or Vitest setup rather than installed as written. The skill itself is not a risk.

summary: This skill guides an agent in writing and tuning Salesforce SOQL and SOSL queries. It covers turning plain-language requests into queries, choosing between parent-child traversal, subqueries, aggregates, and SOSL text search, and checking selectivity, field access and governor limits. It also includes Apex selector templates and a hook that validates .soql files and can run query-plan analysis against a live org. It is written for Salesforce developers and administrators.
tasks: write a SOQL query for accounts and their open opportunities
optimize a slow Salesforce query with a non-selective filter
convert a plain-language request into SOSL text search
build a bulkified Apex selector for trigger contexts
qualityWhy: The workflow, query-shape table, rules, output format and reference index are concrete and complete, though the scripted validation is truncated and the material is very Salesforce-specific.
needs: a Salesforce org with sf CLI login for live query-plan analysis
why: Salesforce is a cloud database and backend, which the node rules class as value none, and the skill's queries and live plan checks run against that cloud org rather than local data. It does not fit Fractera's SQLite-based data layer.

summary: This skill makes an agent check UI for accessibility before it ships: text and non-text contrast, keyboard reach and focus visibility, empty, loading and error states, mobile zoom, and cursor and hover affordances. It includes a WCAG contrast calculator that runs as a command-line script or as a small MCP tool, so the agent can verify colour pairs instead of guessing. It is aimed at people building sites and web apps who need their interfaces to work for users with different eyesight, hands and setups.
tasks: check whether this text colour passes WCAG contrast
make the site keyboard accessible
review the UI for accessibility problems
add visible focus styles to buttons and links
add empty, loading and error states to a data view
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with formulas, a verified reference table, a checklist and copy-ready references, though the MCP server file is not described in SKILL.md and some depth is pushed to other files.
why: Accessibility checks for UI directly serve building and selling a web product, and the contrast tool runs locally with no outside service. The guidance is largely stack-agnostic HTML and CSS, so it fits the node's Next.js and Tailwind setup without adaptation.

summary: This skill tells an agent to verify each finished task against the real artifact before declaring it done. The agent should run the feature, read the actual value, or inspect the diff rather than trusting proxies such as file timestamps, self-reports, or a successful compile. It also recommends writing a deterministic check script whose output can be re-run and reviewed.
tasks: verify a finished feature before declaring it done
check that a build or change really works
write a repeatable verification script
confirm the actual output instead of trusting a report
qualityWhy: The principle is clear and actionable, but it is short and generic, with no concrete steps, examples, or checklists for specific artifact types.
why: It is a stack-free working habit that any node agent can use after building pages, APIs or content, so it is useful now and then rather than central. It has no risky instructions and no external service dependency.

summary: This skill guides an agent through planning TikTok content: choosing content pillars, building a weekly calendar, and writing short scripts with a hook, content section and call to action. It also covers hashtag mixes, posting times and frequency, trend spotting, and a weekly performance report template. It is written for marketers and creators who make short vertical videos for a brand or product.
tasks: plan a week of TikTok content
write a 30-second TikTok script with a hook
pick hashtags for a short video
decide the best posting schedule
write a weekly TikTok performance report
qualityWhy: The frameworks and script templates are clear and usable, but the n8n workflows are YAML outlines rather than runnable configs, the MCP tool calls have no parameters or examples, and the posting-time and reach figures are unsourced.
needs: Google Sheets, Airtable or Slack accounts (optional workflow steps)
why: It directly serves making short-video content for a social network, which is what nodes are for. It calls an MCP server, a TikTok account and several paid AI and workflow services, so it is install-with-service; the person chooses which of these to connect.

summary: This skill turns the agent into a Socratic mentor for junior developers and AI newcomers. It answers with guiding questions, graded hints and pseudocode instead of finished solutions, and asks the learner to explain every line they keep. It also covers Copilot-assisted workflows, a debrief template after urgent fixes, and a learning recap at the end of a session.
tasks: explain this code without giving the answer
help me debug this error step by step
teach me a concept like closures or async/await
review my prompt to an AI coding assistant
write a learning recap after a session
qualityWhy: The skill is detailed, with clear protocols, hint levels, templates and success metrics, though much of it is persona framing and some of it is tied to Copilot's commands.
why: It is a stack-free teaching method, so it helps a node's builders learn and debug now and then, but it does not build or sell anything itself. It is written around Copilot slash commands, which the node does not provide, so those parts would be ignored.

summary: This skill guides an agent through designing small, contained interaction moments such as toggles, buttons, loading states, form validation and confirmations. It frames each moment as trigger, rules, feedback and loops/modes, and scores it against an eight-row diagnostic. It is written for designers and front-end developers who want interfaces to feel responsive and polished.
tasks: make the button feedback feel responsive
design a loading state for a form submit
add inline validation feedback to a signup field
audit a toggle switch for clear states
design a confirmation dialog for deletion
qualityWhy: The file gives a clear four-part framework, a scoring rubric, a diagnostic table and common mistakes, though it is mostly conceptual and leans on referenced files for depth.
why: It is a stack-free design framework, useful now and then for UI polish in a node's apps, but it does not build anything directly. No outside service or key is required.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to pull TikTok data from a paid hosted API at tiktok.fetcher.sh using plain HTTP GET calls. It covers keyword post search with sort and date filters, lookups by share URL or ID, profiles by handle, followers and followings, hashtag and sound feeds, location posts, and comment threads. It is aimed at people doing trend tracking, competitor analysis, or social content research without official TikTok API access.
tasks: search TikTok posts by keyword sorted by most liked
find this week's posts under a hashtag
pull a creator's recent posts and follower list
read the comments on a viral TikTok video
list posts that use a specific trending sound
qualityWhy: It gives a complete endpoint table, copy-ready curl examples, auth options, parameter values and error codes, though its promotional tone and reliance on other skill files for payment details leave small gaps.
needs: fetcher.sh prepaid API key (bby_live_...) or a USDC wallet on Base, Polygon, Arbitrum, Monad or Solana for x402 pay-per-call
why: TikTok trend and creator data helps with social content and market research, but it is a niche use for a local-first node, and the data comes from a cloud service the person pays for per call. Full payment and MCP setup depends on the separate fetcher skill, which was not reviewed here.

summary: This skill guides an agent through taking an application and packaging it for Google's managed Kubernetes service for the first time. It covers assessing the app's stack and needs, writing a multi-stage Dockerfile or using buildpacks, pushing the image to a registry, and producing hardened Deployment and Service manifests with health probes and resource limits. It is aimed at engineers moving a service onto Google Cloud infrastructure.
tasks: onboard a Node.js app to GKE
containerize an app with a Dockerfile
write production Kubernetes deployment manifests with probes
push a container image to Artifact Registry and roll it out
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with a checklist, worked Node.js example files and verification commands, though some referenced material and sibling skills are not included in the files reviewed.
why: The skill is built around Google Cloud's hosted Kubernetes service (GKE, Artifact Registry, cloud deployment), which is a cloud hosting place rather than something that runs on the person's own computer, so it is not useful for a local-first node.

summary: The skill interviews a user once about a single website or SEO project and stores the answers as shared project context in OpenSEO. It guides the agent through checking the MCP connection, reading existing context, collecting site scope, goals, positioning, competitors, key pages, and Google Search Console access. It is aimed at site owners and marketers who want a durable SEO brief that other SEO skills can read.
tasks: set up SEO context for my website
save my SEO goals and competitors to the project
connect Google Search Console to my project
record key pages and positioning for my site
qualityWhy: The steps, required fields, MCP tool signatures and output format are concrete and easy for an agent to follow, though it has no example outputs.
needs: Google account connected for Google Search Console (optional)
why: It is a useful setup workflow for SEO projects on OpenSEO, but it is built around the OpenSEO MCP tools rather than the node's own stack, so its value to building and running a Fractera product is limited to SEO planning. It uses an external SEO service and a Google account, which the person chooses to connect.

summary: The skill guides an agent through a deep analysis of a single named competitor's organic search presence, covering ranking keywords, content themes, backlinks and gaps against the user's own site. It requires a configured OpenSEO project, checks saved competitor context and a 30-day research log before spending credits, and writes findings back to the project. The output is a structured report delivered via a separate seo-report skill. It is aimed at SEO practitioners and site owners who want to decide what to learn from, avoid, or outrank.
tasks: analyze a competitor's organic keywords and traffic
find gaps where a competitor is vulnerable
compare my domain against a competitor's search footprint
check whether a competitor's backlinks explain its rankings
qualityWhy: The workflow, required inputs, tool list, guardrails and output sections are concrete and ordered, though it depends on external skills and tools it does not define.

summary: This skill guides an agent through diagnosing why an AWS Lambda function times out. The agent reads the function's configuration, CloudWatch logs and metrics, VPC and networking setup, cold start behaviour, memory limits and downstream calls, then reports likely causes with ranked fixes. It is aimed at developers and operators who run Lambda functions on AWS.
tasks: debug a Lambda function that keeps timing out
find why a Lambda call is slower than its timeout
check CloudWatch logs for Lambda timeout causes
review a Lambda function for timeout-prone code
qualityWhy: The skill points to a reference procedure with concrete AWS CLI commands, a troubleshooting section and a structured report goal, though the main steps live in a separate file I was not shown.
needs: AWS account credentials with Lambda, CloudWatch Logs and CloudWatch Metrics permissions
why: Its whole subject is AWS cloud-hosted Lambda functions, which is a cloud place to run things rather than a local-first tool, so the value is none and it should be skipped on a Fractera node. The reference file was not provided to me, so I could not verify its steps.

summary: The skill guides an agent through SQL work: finding why a query is slow, writing joins, CTEs, window functions and recursive queries, choosing indexes, reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, and designing or migrating schemas across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle. It is written for developers who own a database and want tuned, set-based queries. Reference files cover query patterns, window functions, optimization, schema design and dialect differences.
tasks: optimize a slow SQL query
write a query with window functions or CTEs
interpret an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan
design a database schema with proper keys and indexes
migrate queries between SQL dialects
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, runnable example queries, explicit checks such as no sequential scans and a sub-100ms target, and a list of reference files, though the reference files were not included in the bundle to confirm their depth.
why: Query tuning and schema design for a product's data layer serve directly what a node is for, and it runs against the node's own SQLite element only if the agent adapts the dialect examples; the skill targets PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle rather than SQLite, so the SQL it writes must be checked against SQLite syntax and indexing features before use. It needs no outside service and carries no risk in its files.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to package a local MCP server together with its Node or Python runtime into a single .mcpb file that someone can install by dragging it into a desktop app, without setting up a toolchain. It covers the manifest.json layout and config fields, the server code pattern for reading local files and driving desktop apps, the build and pack steps, and the testing and signing commands. It is mainly for developers who need an MCP server to run on the user's own machine.
tasks: package a local MCP server as an .mcpb file
make a desktop extension that reads local files for Claude
bundle a Node or Python runtime so users need no toolchain
validate, test and sign an MCPB bundle before distribution
qualityWhy: It gives a concrete manifest example, working server code, build and pack commands and a test checklist, though the signing step and some schema details are only pointed to in reference files.
why: A node runs locally and could host local MCP servers, but this skill is aimed at distributing servers to desktop apps rather than building or selling a site, shop or content, so its use is occasional. It is a stack-agnostic packaging guide that does not need the node's stack replaced, so it can be installed as written.

summary: The skill guides an agent through making web content easier for AI answer engines such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude and Google AI Overviews to extract and cite. It covers citation-friendly structure like definitional opening sentences, comparison tables and FAQs, a five-dimension scoring rubric, entity and Organization schema work, and checking that AI crawlers are not blocked in robots.txt. It is written for site owners and marketers who want brand visibility in AI-generated answers.
tasks: audit a page for AI citation readiness
rewrite a section so AI engines can quote it
check robots.txt for blocked AI crawlers
add organization schema and sameAs links for brand entity
plan AI search visibility for a website
qualityWhy: The rubric and content-type guidance are concrete, but many claims are unsourced generalities and the skill gives no executable steps for the node's stack beyond checklists.
why: Useful now and then for a node's site or landing pages, since it is stack-free writing and audit guidance; it contains a promotional Pro Tip for an outside SEO tool, which is not a required service. Several statistics it cites are unsourced and should be checked before use.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building and debugging a LÖVE 11.x game written in Lua. It covers the load/update/draw callback loop, frame-rate-independent movement scaled by delta time, polled and event-based input, and a small screen-state stack for menus and pause overlays. It is aimed at people making 2D games in LÖVE who need the core structure right.
tasks: set up main.lua and conf.lua for a LÖVE game
fix player movement that runs at the wrong speed
add a menu and pause screen to a LÖVE game
debug keyboard input or colors in a LÖVE project
qualityWhy: Concrete code skeletons, a clear workflow, and a useful pitfalls list make it directly actionable, with only a brief reference to the state manager and a thin related-skills section as small gaps.
why: Nodes are for building sites, web apps, AI agents and content, and LÖVE game development is outside those uses, so value is none and the skill is skipped.

summary: This skill helps an agent turn a token name or symbol into one verified contract, check its liquidity, volume, direction and safety, and prepare a sized buy order with slippage and gas estimates. It is written for a person who wants to buy a crypto token safely and avoid copycat tokens. Execution is handed to a separate signing skill only after the person confirms the order card.
tasks: check whether a token is safe to buy before purchasing
resolve a token name to the correct contract address
size a buy order with slippage and gas estimates
confirm a token is the genuine coin and not a copycat
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, with explicit steps, exit gates, field mappings, thresholds and display templates, though the length and heavy cross-referencing make it harder to follow.
needs: gmgn-swap with a trading key and private key for execution
why: Buying crypto tokens is not among the uses a Fractera node serves: building, running, selling or making content for a product. The skill also carries a risk, so it is skipped.
risks: Asks the person to paste their GMGN API key into the chat, so the secret passes through the conversation log.
Hands confirmed orders to a separate skill that signs real on-chain trades with a private key, where a wrong contract or amount causes irreversible loss.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull a command-line tool that someone else published to a shared catalogue on GitHub, and place it into the author's own local workspace in the same form a fresh generator run would produce. It matches the requested name against the catalogue index, backs up any existing local copy, and rewrites the Go module paths back to local names. It then checks that the result builds. The people who would use it are developers maintaining Go CLI tools in the Printing Press generator workflow.
tasks: import a published CLI from the public library
recover a broken local copy of a CLI
prepare a CLI for polishing
back up and replace an existing local CLI
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete, ordered steps, shell scripts, and verification checks, though some safety detail around overwriting is left to the user's confirmation.
needs: GitHub access via the gh CLI
why: It serves only the Printing Press workflow for Go command-line tools and does nothing for building sites, web apps, AI agents or content, so it is not useful for a Fractera node. It is local-first, but its purpose is outside what nodes are for, so it should be skipped.
risks: It builds the fetched command-line tool and runs its doctor command with no review step, so code from the public catalogue executes on the person's computer.

summary: This skill guides an agent through wiring CloudWatch alarms to notifications sent through Amazon SNS. It covers creating an encrypted topic, allowing CloudWatch to publish to it, and adding email, SMS or webhook subscribers. It also includes checks for common failures, such as an unconfirmed email subscription, a badly formatted phone number, or an alarm with actions disabled. The intended users are engineers who run workloads on AWS and want to be alerted when something breaks.
tasks: set up email alerts for a CloudWatch alarm
send SMS notifications when an AWS alarm fires
troubleshoot alarm notifications that never arrive
qualityWhy: The visible SKILL.md is short and useful but defers the actual procedure to a reference file, and the troubleshooting section is brief, so the instructions are only partly visible here.
needs: AWS region with SNS and SMS support
why: The skill administers AWS cloud monitoring, which is a cloud service that runs outside the node's local-first data and files, so it does not serve building or making content on a Fractera node. Its use is skip because the value is none; the reference procedure file was not provided and was not reviewed.

summary: This skill makes an agent review a finished run of the Printing Press, the generator that builds CLIs, and write a retrospective of what went wrong. It scrubs secrets and personal data from the evidence, sorts the problems into Printing Press defects, and files only P1/P2 issues on GitHub after the user confirms. It is written for maintainers of the Printing Press, not for people building or running their own product.
tasks: run a retro on the last printed CLI
file findings against the Printing Press
write a post-mortem of a generator run
scrub and publish retro findings
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is clear, with a phase table, explicit boundaries and a stated done state, though most of the detail sits in phase files I was not shown.
needs: GitHub account with access to the Printing Press repository
why: It improves a generator's own source and files issues against it, so it does not help build, run, sell or create content for a Fractera node product. It also publishes session evidence publicly after scrubbing and user confirmation, which is a designed safeguard but a further reason not to use it on a node.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing a store or product page for search visibility. It checks titles, meta descriptions, headings, images, internal links and content quality, then validates Product structured data against Google's merchant requirements. With an optional paid DataForSEO account, it can also compare live Google Shopping and Amazon prices and sellers, and find gaps between organic rankings and Shopping visibility. It is aimed at shop owners and the people who build their product catalogues.
tasks: audit a product page for SEO problems
validate and improve Product schema for Google rich results
compare competitor prices on Google Shopping for a keyword
find keyword gaps between organic search and Shopping visibility
check whether a store has a UCP commerce profile
qualityWhy: The checklists, scoring tables and output templates are concrete, but every command calls scripts from an external claude-seo plugin that is not included in these files, so the instructions cannot be followed as written.
needs: DataForSEO account and API credentials (optional, for Shopping and Amazon data)
why: Product-page SEO and store structured data serve running and selling from a shop, so the value is high. The live marketplace features need a paid DataForSEO account the person chooses, and the scripts it depends on come from a separate plugin that is not part of these files.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to drive the belt command-line tool, which runs hosted AI apps for image, video and other generation, and to search and manage skills, knowledge entries and MCP connectors. It gives the agent typed, schema-checked commands for checking an app's inputs, pricing and cost, running it with local file paths, and reading results in JSON. It serves people who want to produce media or automate content work from their own project.
tasks: generate a video from a local photo
run an AI image or video app
check the cost of an AI generation before running it
search skills and knowledge entries
connect an MCP connector such as Slack
qualityWhy: The commands and workflows are concrete and copyable, but it has no verification steps or error handling and reads partly as promotion.
needs: belt account created with belt login
belt credits for paid app runs
outside AI app providers reached through belt
why: It directly serves making images, video and content from a local project, but generation runs on a hosted service and knowledge entries are kept in the cloud, so it is not fully local-first. The install options are a package manager or a download the person reviews first. Local files are uploaded automatically to the service, and the plugin setup installs hooks, which the skill says can be turned off.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up WhatsApp Business messaging for a business: Meta account and API access, message templates that need approval, and automated replies. It also covers order and appointment notifications, a support chatbot with menu flows and AI answers, and broadcast campaigns with opt-out handling. It is aimed at customer support and marketing teams running sales or service over WhatsApp.
tasks: set up an automated WhatsApp customer support bot
send order confirmation and shipping notifications on WhatsApp
create a WhatsApp broadcast campaign to opted-in customers
draft WhatsApp message templates for Meta approval
qualityWhy: It gives useful flow designs, template examples and compliance rules, but it is mostly YAML outlines with no working API calls, code or verification steps an agent could follow directly.
needs: Meta Business account with a verified WhatsApp Business API app
WhatsApp Phone Number ID and access token
OpenAI API key for the AI replies
Shopify or another order system for order triggers (optional)
why: It serves a product's customer messaging and notifications, but WhatsApp delivery runs through Meta's cloud API and the AI replies through OpenAI, so customer data leaves the node and the person should be told this. The n8n and whatsapp-mcp references are optional extras that the node does not provide, so an agent would need to build the sending and webhook parts itself.

summary: This guide shows an agent how to add user sign-in to a Next.js App Router project that uses Supabase as its authentication backend. It covers creating browser and server Supabase clients, refreshing sessions and protecting routes in middleware, handling OAuth redirects, and running login, logout and user lookups in server code. It is aimed at developers who want accounts and protected pages in a web app that depends on a hosted Supabase project.
tasks: add login and logout to a Next.js app
protect dashboard routes with middleware
set up Google sign-in with an OAuth callback
get the current user in a server component
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete, mostly complete code for clients, middleware, callback, server actions and checks, with useful caveats, though it is only fragments and depends on details it does not fully spell out.
why: Supabase is a cloud backend for auth and data, which a local-first Fractera node does not use, since sign-in is its own element and data lives in SQLite. The skill would send users' accounts to a cloud service, so it is not suitable for this node.

summary: The skill guides an agent through a structured review of technical debt in a codebase, sorting problems into code, architecture, test, dependency, documentation and infrastructure categories. It then scores each item on impact, risk and effort to rank them. The output is a prioritized list with effort estimates, a business justification per item and a phased plan that fits alongside feature work. It is aimed at engineering leads and developers who maintain a product.
tasks: audit the codebase for technical debt
prioritize a refactoring backlog
plan phased remediation alongside feature work
explain the business case for fixing code health issues
qualityWhy: The categories and scoring formula are clear, but there are no concrete steps for how to find debt, no examples of scored items, and no checks on the output.
why: It is a stack-free planning habit that helps decide what to refactor on any Fractera node, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. The scoring formula is simple and the instructions are generic, so an agent will need to add its own detection steps.

summary: The skill guides an agent through creating an Amazon EC2 virtual server with defaults for security and cost. It covers picking an image and instance size, setting up network placement, creating a least-privilege role, locking down firewall rules, encrypting disks, and tagging resources. It also gives short fixes for capacity errors, instances that stop right after launch, and failed SSH connections. The intended users are people who run their infrastructure on AWS.
tasks: launch a secure EC2 instance on AWS
choose an AMI and instance size for a workload
fix an EC2 instance that terminates immediately
troubleshoot SSH access to a new EC2 server
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is clear and well organised, but most of the procedure sits in a reference file that was not included, and the troubleshooting section is brief.
needs: AWS credentials with EC2 and IAM permissions
why: The skill is cloud hosting and cloud administration on AWS, which a local-first Fractera node does not use, so it is not useful for building or running a product on the node. It has no security problems in the visible files, but the value is none.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to write a custom streaming response for assistant-ui using the assistant-stream package. It covers building responses with a controller that appends text, reasoning, sources, files, and tool calls, and choosing between the Data Stream and Assistant Transport wire formats. It also explains decoding streams yourself and wiring resumable streams with in-memory, Redis, or ioredis stores. It is aimed at developers building chat backends for a product.
tasks: build a custom chat streaming endpoint
decode an incoming assistant stream
add resumable streaming to a chat
debug a tool call that never finishes in the UI
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with code examples, a method table, a chunk and part reference, and a list of common gotchas with fixes, though the reference files were not inspected.
why: It is directly useful for building chat backends, but it targets the assistant-ui and Vercel AI SDK stack rather than Fractera's own stack, so it must be adapted to the node's Next.js, next-auth and SQLite setup. Redis-backed resumable stores are a cloud-style dependency that would need replacing with a local store on a local-first node.

summary: The skill guides an agent to design test strategies and test plans for software. It explains a testing pyramid of unit, integration and end-to-end tests, and gives per-component advice for API endpoints, data pipelines, frontend and infrastructure. It also says what to cover and skip, and asks for a plan with test types, coverage targets and example cases. It is written for developers and teams deciding how to test their work.
tasks: design a test strategy for a web app
write a test plan for a new API
decide what tests we need for a data pipeline
find gaps in existing test coverage
qualityWhy: It gives a short, generic outline with a pyramid and a few bullets but no concrete steps, examples, or checks an agent can follow.
why: It is a stack-free planning habit that helps when a node's builder needs to plan tests for its sites or apps, but it is thin and gives little beyond general testing knowledge. No outside services are involved and no risks were found.

summary: This skill lets an agent run Salesforce Code Analyzer over Apex, Lightning Web Components, Flows and other Salesforce metadata to find security, performance, style and duplication problems. It turns plain requests into scan commands, saves timestamped results, ranks and filters them, explains individual rules, and can apply engine-provided fixes after the person confirms. The intended users are Salesforce developers and teams preparing AppExchange submissions.
tasks: scan my Salesforce code for security issues
check my LWC and JavaScript with ESLint
find duplicate code in my Apex classes
explain why a rule like ApexCRUDViolation is flagged
apply the engine's auto-fixes after I confirm
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, with exact commands, decision tables, mandatory steps, confirmation gates and verification checks, though some script files are truncated and the file set is large.
why: The skill is built around Salesforce metadata and the sf CLI, which a Fractera node does not use; its engines only help with JavaScript and TypeScript linting in a generic way, and it depends on a Salesforce cloud org for some features. Its stack does not match the Next.js and SQLite node, so it does not serve building, running or selling a product there.

summary: This skill walks an agent through diagnosing problems with Amazon S3 Files file systems, such as mounts that fail or hang, access denied errors, changes that do not reach S3, lost+found conflict folders, and slow performance. It guides the agent to check the aws CLI, security groups, IAM roles, KMS keys and VPC DNS settings, and to confirm each step with the person before running write commands. It is aimed at a person who runs AWS infrastructure in the cloud.
tasks: fix an S3 Files mount that times out
debug access denied on an S3 file system
find out why files are not syncing to S3
recover files from the lost+found folder
qualityWhy: The steps are concrete, with commands, tables and explicit safety rules, but several sections are brief and it depends on AWS documentation for detail.
why: The skill is built around a cloud file system and cloud administration, which a local-first node does not serve, so its value is none and it is skipped.

summary: The skill is a deprecation notice: it tells an agent that this Angular HTTP guidance is no longer maintained and points to the official Angular skills repository instead. It gives no concrete steps for fetching data, using resource() or HttpClient, or handling interceptors. It does not help a person building a Fractera site or app beyond redirecting them elsewhere.
tasks: find the current Angular HTTP data fetching guidance
replace this deprecated skill with the official Angular skills
qualityWhy: The file is a stub that only points to another repository and contains no usable instructions.
why: It has no working guidance for the node's stack, and it only redirects to an external repository, so it is not useful to install here. The official replacement is a separate skill and would need its own review.

summary: The skill guides an agent through installing and initializing Google's Mobile Ads SDK in an Android, iOS, or Unity app, after first confirming the platform. It points to a separate platform guide for each, then has the agent add the dependency, set the app identifier, initialize the SDK and verify the result. Once installation works, it asks the user which ad format to integrate next. It is aimed at app developers working with AdMob or Ad Manager.
tasks: set up Google Mobile Ads SDK in my Android app
integrate AdMob into an iOS project
initialize the mobile ads SDK in a Unity game
verify my AdMob integration works
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is a short, ordered checklist that delegates real detail to platform reference files, so it is clear but thin on its own.
needs: app identifier from the ad platform
why: Mobile ad monetization is useful for apps built on a node, but it is a niche integration rather than core building. It calls the Google ads service and needs the person's AdMob account and app ID, so it is install-with-service.

summary: Guides an agent through creating and configuring a PixiJS v8 Application: the async init options, renderer preference, resize and ticker behaviour, opt-in culling, custom application plugins, and correct teardown. It is aimed at developers building 2D graphics, games or interactive canvas pages in the browser.
tasks: set up a PixiJS canvas that fills the window
add a custom plugin to the PixiJS application
run a manual render loop with PixiJS
tear down and re-create a PixiJS app cleanly
qualityWhy: Concrete code examples, a clear lifecycle, and a common-mistakes section, though the reference file is only linked and not inspected here.
why: Canvas and 2D rendering with PixiJS is directly useful for building interactive sites, games and visual content on a local node, and the skill needs no cloud service. Its stack (pixi.js) is not the node's own stack, but it is a rendering library rather than a replacement for the node's framework, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to regenerate an already-published command-line tool from scratch with the current Printing Press generator, while keeping the old research, feature list and manual fixes in view. It checks whether the tool exists locally, pulls it from the public library if needed, and advises whether to reuse or redo the earlier research based on its age. It then hands the job to the main Printing Press workflow with those notes attached. It is aimed at maintainers of generated API clients who want a tool rebuilt rather than patched by hand.
tasks: regenerate the published CLI for an API from scratch
reprint a CLI after a Printing Press upgrade
carry over prior novel features and hand-fixes into a rebuild
decide whether to reuse or redo prior API research
qualityWhy: It gives concrete shell steps, a reconciliation table, thresholds and explicit decision prompts, though some parts defer to other skills and the age thresholds are rules of thumb.
needs: GitHub access to the public printing-press-library repository
why: It regenerates Go command-line clients from API specs and does not build web apps, sites, agents or content, so it does not serve what a Fractera node is for. It also depends on a separate generator binary and a public GitHub library rather than the node's own stack.

summary: The skill guides an agent through writing landing page copy: headlines, subheads, feature and benefit blocks, social proof placeholders, FAQs and CTA text. It starts from a brief about the product, the single action the page drives, and the reader's source, then builds a message hierarchy before drafting sections. It is aimed at marketers and founders who need words for a sales, waitlist, pricing or product page.
tasks: write a homepage hero and CTA for a product
rewrite weak landing page copy
generate headline variants for an A/B test
turn a product description into landing page sections
draft FAQ answers for a sales page
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with a workflow, checks, a worked example and failure modes, though the referenced framework and template files were not provided for review.
why: Writing landing page copy is a direct part of building and selling a product on a node, and the skill is stack-free, so it works as written. Its output is text only, so the agent has no stack dependency to adapt.

summary: The skill guides an agent through profiling and speeding up a PixiJS v8 app, covering frame rate, draw calls and GPU memory. It explains when to destroy objects correctly, recycle them through pools, batch similar sprites, use BitmapText for changing text, cache subtrees as textures, and cull off-screen objects. It is aimed at developers building 2D games, interactive sites and animated graphics on the web.
tasks: fix frame drops in a PixiJS game
reduce draw calls in a scene with many sprites
stop memory leaks when destroying PixiJS apps
make a score counter update without lag
cull off-screen objects in a PixiJS scene
qualityWhy: It gives concrete code patterns, ordered checks and a list of common mistakes, though some sections are reference-style and it has no step-by-step profiling workflow.
why: PixiJS is a 2D rendering library used to build web apps and games on the node, and this skill directly improves their speed and memory use. It is a stack-specific skill for PixiJS, which the node does not replace, so it can be installed as written, and it needs no outside service or key.

summary: This skill guides an agent through checking why the cmux terminal app is misbehaving, covering its command-line link, settings, agent hooks, session restore and notifications. It runs a bundled read-only script first and reads only file presence, sizes and markers, never raw config or secrets. It is aimed at end users who need a health check or a support-safe debug summary. Its subject is the cmux app itself, not the building or hosting of sites, apps or content.
tasks: run a cmux health check
find out why cmux notifications are not showing
check why cmux did not restore my agent sessions
produce a support-safe cmux doctor report
qualityWhy: SKILL.md gives concrete commands, a clear checklist, interpretation rules and safety rules, though the bundled script's contents were not visible to verify.
why: It serves only the cmux terminal app's own troubleshooting, not building, running, selling or making content for a product, so it is skipped for nodes. I could not read scripts/cmux-diagnostics, so its behaviour is judged from SKILL.md alone and the script was not checked.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing a link acquisition campaign for a website: diagnosing which authority dimension is weakest, choosing strategies such as original research, free tools, guest posts and journalist queries, scoring prospects with a weighted link quality formula, and drafting personalised outreach with follow-up limits. It is written for marketers and site owners who want more backlinks. It also refers to an outside SEOJuice product for audits and tracking.
tasks: plan a backlink campaign for my website
score link prospects by quality
write personalised outreach emails for guest posts
find broken link opportunities in my niche
diagnose why my domain authority is weak
qualityWhy: It gives a clear diagnosis step, ranked tactics, a concrete weighted scoring formula and output template, though it has no worked examples and some benchmarks are unsourced.
needs: SEOJuice MCP account for backlink audit (optional)
why: It is a strategy document for marketing rather than a build tool, so it helps a node's owner promote a site occasionally, not daily development. It is marked install-with-service because its pro tip points to a SEOJuice service and tool; the core advice works without it.

summary: The skill turns an agent into a concept dissector that takes any idea or term and examines it from eight angles: history, dialectics, phenomenology, linguistics, formalization, existentialism, aesthetics and meta-reflection. It then folds these views into a single plain-language insight, a formula and an ASCII structure diagram. It is aimed at people who want to deeply understand a concept, and it writes the result as a Markdown note into a local notes folder.
tasks: explain a concept in depth from several angles
dissect a term or idea into its core structure
write a deep learning note about a concept
compress a concept into one insight and a formula
qualityWhy: The eight-dimension procedure and output template are clear, but the instructions are short and leave the depth and quality checks to the agent's judgement.
why: It is a stack-free thinking and writing habit that works on any node, but its use for building or selling products is indirect, so value is some. It writes a local Markdown note with no outside service needed, so use is install.

summary: The skill guides an agent through creating an API Gateway stage for a REST API with CloudWatch access logging, X-Ray tracing, throttling, WAF web ACL association, IAM roles and method-level settings. It targets engineers deploying an AWS-hosted API to environments such as dev, test or production. It also lists troubleshooting steps for missing logs, failed stage creation and WAF false positives.
tasks: create a production stage for my REST API
enable CloudWatch logging and X-Ray tracing on API Gateway
set throttling limits on an API stage
attach a WAF web ACL to an API Gateway stage
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is thin and defers all real steps to a reference file, which I did not receive, so the instructions cannot be fully judged.
needs: AWS account with API Gateway, CloudWatch, WAF and IAM permissions
why: The skill is built entirely around AWS cloud hosting and administration of API Gateway, which is a cloud place to run things rather than a local-first capability, so it does not serve building or making content on a local node. Use is skipped for that reason; the reference file was not among the material provided, so its contents remain unverified.

summary: This skill tells an agent to look up current library and framework documentation through the Context7 MCP tools before writing code or answering setup questions. The agent first resolves the library ID, picks the best match (preferring the requested version and official packages), then queries one concept at a time. It is aimed at developers who need accurate, up-to-date API usage instead of answers from training data.
tasks: look up current Next.js routing docs
write a Prisma query with up-to-date API usage
check the Supabase auth methods
set up Tailwind CSS 4 with current configuration steps
qualityWhy: The steps for resolving a library ID and querying one concept at a time are concrete and easy to follow, but it has no example tool calls, no fallback when resolution finds nothing, and no check that the returned docs match the requested version.
needs: Context7 API key, if the chosen setup requires one
why: It directly helps an agent build sites and apps on the node with accurate library APIs, but it depends on an outside hosted documentation service. Library names and query text, which are drawn from the user's question, are sent to that service, and the skill does not say so. Nothing in the skill touches local data or secrets.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull live search data from the DataForSEO service through an MCP server, covering Google results, keyword volume and difficulty, backlinks, on-page audits and AI-chatbot citations. It is aimed at people planning or checking content and pages for a site or brand. Each lookup is metered, so the skill also tells the agent to estimate and log costs before and after calls.
tasks: check search volume and difficulty for a list of blog keywords
see which domains rank and which sites compete for a topic
review a competitor's backlink profile and top keywords
check whether ChatGPT or other LLMs mention my brand or cite my pages
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete commands, MCP tool names, default parameters, output formats, cost rules and error handling, but it depends on plugin scripts and an install.sh that are not in the package.

summary: This skill grades command-line tools that a generator produced, using a scorecard binary that rates each one across infrastructure and domain-correctness dimensions. summary: This skill reviews the sample output of a command-line tool that was generated by a printing pipeline. why: It only serves the internal printing-press pipeline for generating CLIs, which is not what Fractera nodes are for, and it is marked internal and not user-invocable. Its commands are scoped to its stated purpose, so there is no safety concern.

The node's own SQLite element should hold the ledger, and the skill's rule to keep data and reconciliation under the business owner's control fits that. The skill's own examples name Stripe and other PSPs, but no key or account is required to use it.
