summary: This skill guides an agent in writing TypeScript code that decodes and encodes ClickHouse RowBinary streams over the HTTP interface in Node.js. It explains when RowBinary beats JSON formats (wide integers, decimals, UUIDs, fixed-width numerics) and when it does not (string-heavy data). It ships per-type reader and writer references plus worked examples with benchmarks. It is aimed at developers who need high-throughput or exact-precision ClickHouse data handling.
tasks: decode a ClickHouse RowBinary response into JS objects
encode rows into RowBinary to insert into ClickHouse
choose between RowBinary, JSON and Native formats for a query
write a fast reader for wide integers or decimals from ClickHouse
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear decision gate, core principles and pointers to detailed reader and writer references and runnable examples, though the sub-files I could see were truncated so completeness is hard to confirm.
why: It is a data-format codec for ClickHouse, which fits a node that stores data in its own SQLite element, so it is relevant only when the node calls an external ClickHouse server, and the codec targets that stack rather than the node's own data layer, so an agent would need to adapt it. It is stack-free in its logic but built around the ClickHouse client, which the node does not replace; it is not a cloud service, so it is not skipped.

summary: This skill is a thin wrapper that tells an agent to download and run a外部 command-line package before doing anything, and the real instructions live outside these files. Its stated purpose is to log into a Saramin corporate recruiting account, search masked job-candidate profiles, and build a shortlist before paid unlocking. It is aimed at HR recruiters who screen candidates.
tasks: build a shortlist of candidates from a talent pool
compare masked candidate profiles before paying to unlock them
search Saramin talent pool for developers with given skills
qualityWhy: SKILL.md is only a stub that tells the agent to run an external npx command and read a remote file, so it gives no usable steps in its own files.
needs: Saramin corporate member account and login session
why: Candidate screening on a recruiting site is outside what a local-first Fractera node is for, and the skill depends on an account and remote instructions, so it should not be installed.
risks: Runs a third-party package fetched at runtime via npx (@0 range), so the code it executes can change without review.
Collects personal data of job candidates from a recruiting site, which its own disclaimer limits to personal, non-organizational lookup.
Works with a logged-in session and a credential vault, creating a path for account credentials to be read or misused.

summary: The skill guides an agent through turning a single large Terraform configuration into smaller reusable modules with typed inputs, validated variables, and clear outputs. It also covers moving existing state to the new addresses using moved blocks or state mv, writing module docs, and testing with terraform-test. It is aimed at infrastructure engineers who manage cloud resources with Terraform.
tasks: split a monolithic Terraform config into reusable modules
plan state migration with moved blocks
write module inputs, outputs and docs
add terraform test files to a module
qualityWhy: It has concrete before and after HCL examples, a state migration procedure, and a checklist, though some sections are thin and the AWS examples are not general.
needs: AWS account for the example resources
why: It is about cloud infrastructure as code: its examples provision AWS VPCs and subnets, which is cloud administration that a local-first node does not serve. It is not a site, app, agent or content tool.

summary: The skill guides an agent through running the review and selection of talk proposals that a technical conference already collected. It covers choosing a review committee, executing blind review, scoring with a written rubric, cutting to a shortlist, checking program balance, and sending accept, decline and waitlist messages. It is written for conference organizers and program committees.
tasks: choose a review committee and scoring rubric for a CFP
run blind review of conference talk submissions
handle reviewer conflicts of interest
shortlist talks and balance the program
write acceptance, decline and waitlist emails
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, with a clear workflow, interview questions, rubrics and failure modes, though much of it is organizational judgment rather than executable steps.
why: The skill serves conference organizers running a call for papers, not building, running or selling a Fractera site, web app, agent or content product, so its value to nodes is none. It also carries no stack and no outside service, but the value rule alone makes it skip.

summary: The skill guides an agent through a multi-phase process for designing Google Cloud systems: it asks clarifying requirement questions first, then proposes products, a Mermaid diagram, a written architecture, design recommendations and deployment guidance, with explicit user approval at each step. It also covers pre-deployment dry runs and runtime checks, and packages the result into a solution guide. It is aimed at architects and teams planning cloud workloads or migrations.
tasks: design a Google Cloud architecture for a new workload
gather requirements before choosing cloud services
generate an architecture diagram and deployment guide for a migration
validate a cloud design with dry-run checks
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed and ordered with explicit approval gates, citations and checks, though the bulk of the content lives in referenced guide files I have not seen.
needs: Google Cloud account for gcloud and deployment steps
Google Developer Knowledge MCP server access
why: The skill designs solutions for Google Cloud, a cloud place to run things, so under the local-first rule it counts as value none and is skipped, even though the architecture thinking itself is generic and could be useful as a planning habit.

summary: This skill is a thin wrapper that tells an agent to run two other skills in sequence: a persistent questioning interview to sharpen a plan or design, and a domain-modeling step. Along the way it is meant to produce decision records and a shared glossary. The people it serves are those planning a product, feature or architecture who want their assumptions challenged and written down.
tasks: challenge my product plan with probing questions
stress-test a feature design before building it
write architecture decision records during planning
build a shared glossary of domain terms
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is only a pointer that says to invoke two other skills, with no steps, examples or checks of its own.
why: Planning and design interviews are stack-free and useful when building a product, but this file contributes nothing beyond calling the grilling and domain-modeling skills, which are not included, so it will not work on its own. Its output (ADRs and a glossary) would be local text files, which fits a local-first node.

summary: Guides an agent to check what a code change could break outside its own diff, such as callers, library behaviour, timing and data formats the grep search would miss. It insists on proving the single fact the change's safety depends on by running real code rather than trusting a plausible write-up. It is aimed at developers reviewing small diffs they do not trust yet.
tasks: check what a change could break elsewhere
review a small diff I don't trust
find the blast radius of a refactor
write a repro script proving a change is safe
qualityWhy: The steps, the evidence ladder and the required output are concrete and followable, though it leans on other skills (how, why, unslop, arena) that are not included and gives no worked example.
why: It is a stack-free review method useful now and then for a product's code changes, not a direct tool for building or making content, so value is some; it is usable as written and calls no outside service. Its references to companion skills it does not ship are a gap.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to generate Salesforce Flow automations, such as screen flows, autolaunched flows, record-triggered flows and scheduled flows, by running a three-step MCP pipeline and returning the resulting flow XML. It is written for Salesforce admins and developers who want no-code business process automation inside a Salesforce org. It includes rules for splitting multi-flow requests, shaping custom object metadata, and avoiding invented actions.
tasks: create a record-triggered flow that updates a field
build a scheduled flow that runs daily
generate a screen flow for collecting user input
split several flow requests into separate pipelines
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete step order, input and output formats, examples and a verification checklist, though some wording is repetitive and a few rules are Salesforce-specific.
why: Salesforce is a cloud platform, so this skill serves a cloud backend rather than the local-first Fractera node's own sites, apps, content or data, which makes it value none and use skip.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building the budget and profit-and-loss model for one edition of a technical event. It splits costs into fixed and per-head lines, sets a revenue mix, builds three scope tiers so break-even has multiple answers, sizes a contingency, plans a multi-edition reserve, and schedules outflows against when money actually arrives. It is written for event organizers, with conferences, hackathons and recurring meetups as the main cases.
tasks: build an event budget for a conference
find break-even for a hackathon
decide what to cut when sponsorship falls short
plan event cash flow before the venue deposit is due
set a reserve policy across recurring meetup editions
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed and structured, with an interview, a workflow, failure modes and expected output, though much of the reasoning is abstract and it depends on several sibling skills and reference files that are not included here.
why: Planning and budgeting a technical event is directly what a node is for, and the skill is stack-free and only reads and writes budget text. It consumes prices from other skills rather than setting them, and its guidance depends on sibling skills and reference files the node would need to have installed.

summary: This skill walks an agent through a full literature review: framing a research question (PICO for clinical work, a domain framing for technical work), planning and logging database searches, deduplicating records, screening sources in stages, extracting data into tables, and synthesizing findings by theme with confidence levels. It also covers verifying citations and a fixed output template. It is aimed at researchers, students and technical writers who need citation-backed background sections or evidence summaries.
tasks: write a systematic literature review on a research question
screen and deduplicate papers from PubMed and arXiv
synthesize the state of the art for a technical topic
prepare a citation-backed background section for a paper
qualityWhy: It gives a clear, ordered workflow with templates, deduplication order, screening stages and citation checks, though it lacks concrete scripts or worked examples for the search steps.
why: Literature review is useful for building content and research-backed sites, but it is not specific to building or running a Fractera node, so it is only occasionally useful. It is stack-free, so it can be installed as written, and it needs no outside service or key.

summary: This skill guides an agent through giving an EC2 virtual machine permission to call AWS services without storing access keys on it. The agent creates or reuses an IAM role with narrow permissions, wraps it in an instance profile, attaches that profile to the instance, and checks that temporary credentials appear. It also covers common failures such as propagation delays, access-denied errors, and leftover hardcoded keys. The intended users are people administering AWS infrastructure.
tasks: attach an IAM role to an EC2 instance
remove hardcoded AWS keys from a server
fix access denied errors on EC2 with S3 or DynamoDB
set up least-privilege permissions for an EC2 app
qualityWhy: SKILL.md gives a clear overview and useful troubleshooting, but the step-by-step procedure lives in a reference file whose contents were not included, so completeness cannot be confirmed from the files provided.
needs: AWS account with IAM and EC2 permissions
why: The skill is cloud administration of AWS EC2 and IAM, which a local-first node does not host or use, so it is not useful for building, running or selling a product on the node. Quality is moderate, but this does not change the decision.

summary: This skill gives an agent a career-planning method for people who want to break into or advance in tech event organizing, from the candidate's side. It starts with a short interview to pick an operating context and target role, then lays out entry paths such as volunteer-to-paid, interview preparation for producer and community-manager roles, and how to read an offer against compensation data. It is aimed at individuals looking for jobs, not at employers.
tasks: plan a career break-in to tech event organizing
prepare for a producer or community-manager interview
evaluate a job offer for an event role
choose between in-house, agency and non-profit event work
qualityWhy: The instructions are structured with a clear interview flow, explicit sourcing caveats, and measurable pass criteria, though much of the substance sits in reference files I did not see in full.
why: The skill is pure career coaching for a person seeking a job in event organizing; it does not help build, run, sell or make content for a product on a local node, so it has no value for what nodes are for.

summary: The skill guides an agent through setting attendee ticket prices for a technical event: whether to charge, how many public price points to show, separate prices by who pays, gating discounts by date or ticket count, and reserving a need-based scholarship route. It also covers group and invoicing rules and writing a refund and transfer policy before sales open. It is aimed at event organizers, mainly community groups and small conference teams.
tasks: set ticket prices for a community tech conference
design an early-bird and student ticket ladder
write a refund and transfer policy for event tickets
decide group discount and invoicing rules for employer purchases
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear interview, an ordered workflow, explicit defaults with reasons, failure modes and worked examples, though some rankings are abstract and it has no code-level checks.
why: It is a method for pricing event tickets, not for building or running a local app, site or content, so it is outside what a node is for. It is not a stack-based skill, so 'ideas' does not apply; its subject is event administration rather than software, and the node's use is limited.

summary: This skill guides an agent through pointing a custom domain at an Amazon CloudFront distribution using Amazon Route 53 DNS. It covers checking the distribution's alternate domain names, requesting and validating a certificate in us-east-1, locating or creating a public hosted zone, and adding alias A and AAAA records. It also lists fixes for common problems such as missing alternate names, certificate region errors, private zones and slow DNS propagation. It is aimed at people who host a site or app on AWS and want their own domain on it.
tasks: point my domain at a CloudFront distribution
set up an HTTPS certificate for a custom domain on CloudFront
create Route 53 alias records for my website
troubleshoot DNS propagation after changing my domain
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md itself is a short overview with useful troubleshooting, but its procedure lives in a reference file whose contents I could not see, so the step-by-step depth is unverified.
needs: AWS account with Route 53 and CloudFront access
AWS Certificate Manager certificate in us-east-1
why: The skill is cloud hosting and DNS administration on AWS, which is outside what a local-first node is for, so it is not worth installing. The reference file's full procedure was not visible to me, which is a further unknown.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to load and manage game and app resources in PixiJS v8 through the Assets singleton. It covers loading textures, video, spritesheets, fonts, GIFs, SVGs and compressed textures, grouping them into bundles or manifests, tracking progress, background loading, and freeing GPU memory. It is aimed at developers building interactive 2D graphics or web games with PixiJS.
tasks: load textures and sprites for a PixiJS scene
group assets into bundles for each game level
show a loading bar while assets download
free GPU memory between screens
load a web font or bitmap font for in-canvas text
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md and its thirteen reference files give concrete code, option tables, a decision guide and common mistakes that an agent can follow directly.
why: The node's stack is Next.js with React, so PixiJS is only used if a person builds a canvas feature; the skill is useful for that but must be adapted to the node's own stack and asset folders, and it does not touch the node's SQLite or file storage. Nothing in the files asks for secrets or runs remote code.

summary: This skill helps an agent choose the overall structure of a technical event before anything is scheduled: the event shape (meetup, hackathon, unconference day, single or multi-day conference), single versus multi-track, the mix of session formats, in-person versus virtual versus hybrid delivery, and hackathon demo judging structure. It is written for event organizers and community leads planning meetups or conferences. It defers grid layout, venue matching and positioning to sibling skills in the same collection.
tasks: decide whether a meetup should become a conference and what shape it should take
choose single-track or multi-track for next year's event
compose the session-format mix for a one-day conference
weigh hybrid versus in-person delivery for a user conference
pick a hackathon demo and judging structure
qualityWhy: The skill gives a detailed interview, ranked menus with explicit trade-offs, promotion conditions and failure modes, and points to reference files, though it is long and leans on cross-skill handoffs.
why: It is a stack-free planning skill that fits building and running events, which is adjacent to what a node is for, but it does not directly build products, sites or content. Its references were not all reviewed, so the sourced figures are unverified.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building a sponsorship rate card for a technical event: fixing the revenue target from the budget, inventorying sellable surfaces, choosing a price-setting method, designing a 2-4 tier ladder with ratios and anchoring, pricing add-ons and exclusivity, valuing in-kind gifts, and writing a negotiation and discount policy. It also covers annual sponsorship for recurring meetup series. It is aimed at event organizers, mostly community conference and hackathon teams, who need to price sponsor packages before selling them.
tasks: build a sponsor rate card for a conference
decide between a published ladder and quote-gated pricing
write a sponsor discount and negotiation policy
price an annual sponsorship for a monthly meetup
value an in-kind sponsor donation
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, sequenced, and include checks, failure modes and references, though some menus lean on self-described heuristics and a few rankings are argued rather than tested.
why: It serves organizers who run events and sell sponsorship, which is useful for a node that makes content and runs event sites, but it is narrow to event planning rather than building the node's own products. It is stack-free planning advice that needs no outside services, so it can be installed as written.

summary: The skill guides an organizing team through an internal, blameless retrospective after one finished edition of a technical event such as a conference, meetup or hackathon. It walks the agent through reconstructing the timeline, splitting what went well from what went poorly, reconciling the outcome against the risk register, budget and run of show, and writing dated lessons-learned entries that each have an owner and a due date. It also decides how much of the result to publish and hands the log to sibling skills. The audience is event organizers, not attendees.
tasks: run a post-event debrief for a conference
build a lessons-learned log with owners and due dates
review an event edition against the goals the team set
decide whether to publish a public event recap
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed and structured with interview questions, a workflow, decision menus and failure modes, though much of the reasoning is judgment-based and the cross-references to sibling skills and reference files are not self-contained.
why: It is a stack-free process skill for running retrospectives, so it fits a node that runs events, but it is only useful now and then, not for building or running the product itself. It has no install command, no scripts and no outside service, and it depends on sibling skills that are not part of this review.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to generate AI images for search-optimised assets such as social preview cards, blog hero images, product photos, infographics and Pinterest pins. It maps each asset type to an aspect ratio, resolution and prompt style, then runs a Gemini image model through an MCP server. After generation it guides the person through alt text, WebP conversion, file naming and ImageObject or og:image markup. It is aimed at site owners, bloggers and marketers who need visuals for their pages.
tasks: make an OG social preview image for a blog post
generate a blog hero image for an article
create a product photo on a white background
make a Pinterest pin for a landing page
generate an infographic visual with data
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear use-case tables, a pipeline, error handling and an SEO checklist, but the references and scripts it depends on are not in the package, so an agent cannot follow several steps as written.
needs: Google Gemini API key from Google AI Studio
why: It directly serves making SEO and social visuals for a site, and the image work is done by an outside Gemini service the person chooses to pay for, with results saved to local files. It is not a stack replacement, but it depends on the banana extension and the claude-seo plugin, which the node does not ship, and the referenced docs are missing, so the agent must check those are present before relying on it.

summary: Teaches an agent to drive the agent-lynx CLI, or its JavaScript connector, to inspect a running Lynx app on Android, iOS or desktop. It covers listing clients and sessions, reading console logs, evaluating JavaScript on the device, DOM/CSS inspection, screenshots, heap snapshots, performance traces, interactive snapshot refs with taps and fills, and inspecting ReactLynx component trees. The audience is developers debugging Lynx apps.
tasks: debug a running Lynx app on a device
take a screenshot of the page with numbered element labels
inspect the ReactLynx component tree and props
record a performance trace of the page
tap or fill elements in the app programmatically
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete commands, options, output shapes and failure diagnostics, with reference pages for the CDP methods, though the main file is very long and bin.mjs is a thin launcher.
needs: a Lynx app with DevTool enabled on a connected Android, iOS or desktop device
why: It is a developer tool for debugging Lynx apps, which is useful for building a Lynx-based node but not for the content or site-serving tasks at the core of the node. It depends on the outside agent-lynx package and needs a connected device, and the connector daemon owns the device connection. Its stack is Lynx rather than the node's Next.js, so it is not a fit for the node's own web app work.

summary: This skill guides an agent through running a technical event's own social media presence inside a marketing plan already set by other skills. It covers choosing platforms by where the audience gathers, deciding campaign versus community hashtags, mapping posts onto campaign phases from announcement through live coverage and wrap, and planning speaker and sponsor amplification with ready-made kits. It is written for event organizers and volunteers running conferences or hackathons.
tasks: plan social posts for a conference announcement and CFP phases
choose which platforms a tech event should post on
pick an event hashtag and decide its purpose
brief a volunteer on live posting during the event
ask speakers and sponsors to amplify event posts
qualityWhy: The file is detailed and structured with interview questions, ranked menus, decision rules, failure modes and references, though it is long and some rules are argued rather than given as concrete steps.
why: It directly serves organizers building and running a technical event's promotion, which is a use case a node is for, and it is a stack-free planning skill. It depends on several sibling skills from the same collection that the node would need to install alongside it, and it reports no numeric targets by design.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to turn raw search hits from several places, such as chat, email, shared documents and task trackers, into one clear answer. It covers merging duplicate findings, citing where each claim came from, rating how far to trust each result by its age and source type, and surfacing contradictions. It is aimed at people who need answers from their team's scattered information.
tasks: combine search results from chat, email and documents into one answer
summarize a large set of search hits with source citations
flag outdated or conflicting information in a search answer
deduplicate the same decision found in several places
qualityWhy: The skill gives clear rules, worked examples, confidence tables and output templates an agent can follow, though it has no scripts or checks for the search step itself.
why: It is stack-free writing and reasoning guidance that a node agent could use to answer questions over its own search results, but it assumes enterprise connectors for chat, email and cloud storage that a node does not provide, so its use for building or selling products is limited. No install command or outside service is involved.

summary: This skill lets an agent turn a person's numbers or structured notes into a chart or diagram, choosing among types such as bars, lines, pies, sankey flows, mind maps and flowcharts. The agent builds a JSON request with the data and options, sends it to a remote chart-rendering endpoint with curl, and returns the image link as Markdown. It fits anyone who needs quick visuals for reports, landing pages or social posts. The skill gives a type-selection guide, a per-chart data format list and the common styling options.
tasks: turn monthly sales numbers into a line chart
draw a mind map of a project plan
make a sankey diagram of traffic sources
show survey results as a pie chart for a landing page
qualityWhy: It gives a clear workflow, a request example, a response shape and a full data-format list for each chart type, but it has no error handling or validation steps.
needs: AntV gpt-vis API at antv-studio.alipay.com (no key is stated in the file)
why: Charts help build and present content, but the chart is rendered by a remote Alipay-hosted service and returned as a remote URL, so the data leaves the node and the image is not kept locally. The person should know their data is sent to that host before using it.

summary: This skill makes an agent explain every step in plain English for people without a software background. Before each approval request, file change, command, or web access, the agent states what it wants to do, why, how risky it is, and what happens if the person says yes or no. It also translates error messages and command output, and ends tasks with a summary and undo steps. It is aimed at lawyers, product managers, designers and writers.
tasks: explain each approval before the agent acts
translate an error message into plain English
plan a multi-step task in plain language
summarize what changed and how to undo it
qualityWhy: The rules are concrete, with exact output formats, a risk table, worked examples and a tone guide, though the bundled references were not included in what I was given to check.
why: It is a stack-free communication layer that helps non-technical people follow what an agent does on their node, but it builds nothing for sites, apps or content by itself. It is written for Copilot CLI, yet its rules do not depend on that tool, so an agent can follow them as written.

summary: This skill turns an event-organizing request into a routing decision across a 72-skill collection for conferences, meetups and hackathons. It first detects what the project already contains, then asks only the questions it cannot answer, and picks one sibling skill or says that none fits. It also keeps a shared context file so later sessions resume without re-interviewing the organizer.
tasks: start planning a new conference or meetup
figure out which event skill to use next
check in on an ongoing event project
route a hackathon or sponsorship question to the right skill
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with decision gates, ordered questions, an output shape and a context-file format, though the file is very long and dense and only part of it was visible.
why: It serves event organizing rather than building or running a product, so it is useful only now and then on a node; it is stack-free and needs no outside service. The other reference files were not fully visible, so their content is unverified.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up no-cash, two-way visibility deals between a technical event and media or community properties such as newsletters, podcasts, Slack/Discord communities and ambassador programs. It covers an interview, classifying deals against sibling skills, scoring candidate partners, choosing an exchange format from a ranked menu, writing one-page terms, and tracking delivery in both directions. It is aimed at event organizers who want barter promotion rather than paid sponsorship or earned press.
tasks: find newsletter and podcast media partners for a conference
set up a community-sponsor tier with no-cash visibility exchanges
trade a newsletter mention for event promotion
draft one-page terms for a logo-for-promotion deal
qualityWhy: The skill gives a detailed interview, workflow, scoring frame, format menu and failure modes, with references, though it has no executable steps and its measurement targets are left for the user to self-set.
why: It serves event organizers who build and promote a conference, which is related to what nodes are for, but it is an organizer-side playbook rather than something that builds or ships site, app or content artifacts on the node. It is stack-free and contains no outside service calls, so it can be installed as written.

summary: The skill makes an agent write a Chinese-language investment analysis report on a single project, using only the materials supplied (company name, business plan, founder conversations, pitch decks). Its central test is whether the business is a self-reinforcing 'order-creating machine' or merely rearranges existing order. The report covers what the company is, a three-level verdict, the core formula that drives growth, market mispricing and moat, and a buy, watch or pass recommendation with exit signals. It is written for an investor or analyst who wants a judgment rather than a balanced summary.
tasks: write an investment report on a startup from its pitch deck
analyze a founder interview and give a buy or pass verdict
evaluate whether a company creates new order or copies old models
produce a Chinese investment analysis note in the user's notes folder
tools: Research skill or subagent for financial data
qualityWhy: The structure and output rules are clear, but the core verdict criteria are abstract and give no worked example, so an agent has little concrete procedure to check its judgment against.
why: It is a writing and reasoning method for investment decisions, which is not something a Fractera node builds, runs, sells or produces as content, so its value for nodes is none. It also depends on the local Write tool and a notes folder rather than the node's own data and storage elements, so it is not a fit for installation on a node.

summary: This skill guides an agent through producing an editor-ready content brief for a target keyword: it reviews the top search results, maps the searcher's intent to a content structure, proposes titles and meta descriptions, lays out a heading outline, and sets E-E-A-T requirements and SEO targets. It is aimed at content writers, editors and SEO specialists preparing articles or landing pages. It is a single markdown file that relies on web search and gives templates and rules without code.
tasks: write a content brief for a target keyword
create an article outline with title options and meta description
check search intent and competitor coverage before writing
set E-E-A-T and word count targets for a blog post
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete steps, tables, formulas and checks for each part of a brief, though it contains no worked example output and leaves some targets as placeholders.
why: Content briefs help the node's owner make blog posts and landing pages that rank, which fits the node's content-making purpose, but it is a planning aid rather than building or running code. It needs no stack or account, and it has no scripts or risky instructions; its pro tip links to an outside SEOJuice tool and MCP commands, which are optional.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to define tools that a language model can call inside an assistant-ui chat, using a single toolkit file that the build splits into a server part and a browser part. It covers backend, frontend and human-input tools, how each tool call is drawn on screen, approval prompts the user must answer before a tool runs, and wiring the toolkit into a Next.js route. It is aimed at developers who build AI chat interfaces with tool use.
tasks: add a weather lookup tool to my chat app
show a custom card while the assistant calls a tool
ask the user to approve an action before the assistant runs it
let the assistant ask me to pick a date with a picker
fix a tool that never runs or never renders
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete numbered steps, full working code for the toolkit, runtime provider and route handler, a table of tool kinds and render fields, an approval example, and a list of common failures with fixes.
needs: an OpenAI API key or another model provider key, as used in the route example
why: It directly serves building an AI chat feature with tools in a Next.js and React app, which matches the node's stack, and it runs locally in the app; the model provider is the only outside service and the person chooses it. The examples target assistant-ui's own packages, so an agent must follow them as written rather than adapt a different stack.

summary: The skill helps a company decide what its own technical event is funded to achieve before planning begins. It walks an agent through an interview covering goal mix (ecosystem goodwill, developer adoption, customer retention, or sales pipeline), who owns and co-funds the budget, and the measurement commitment to write before registration opens. It is aimed at marketing and developer-relations leads at companies running user conferences, developer days or roadshows. It explicitly stays out of event format, pricing, and P&L modelling, which it routes to sibling skills.
tasks: decide the goal for a company user conference
choose who should co-fund a developer day
define measurable goals before registration opens
explain what a roadshow returned to the CFO
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, with an interview script, ranked menus, promotion conditions and a four-field measurement gate, but the references are not reviewed here and some rankings depend on judgement calls.
why: It is a planning and decision skill with no stack, so it could be used directly, but its value to a local-first node is limited to occasional event strategy work rather than building or running the product itself. It is marked as ideas rather than install because it is a strategy layer that expects sibling skills from the same catalogue to exist, and it has no implementation path for a node's own stack.

summary: This skill lets an agent schedule and publish social media posts through the SocialClaw service, covering 13 platforms such as X, LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok and WordPress. It walks through listing connected accounts, uploading media, building a schedule file, validating it, and checking delivery status. It is aimed at people running content campaigns across several networks at once. Publishing is gated behind explicit user approval, and content pulled back from platforms is treated as data rather than instructions.
tasks: schedule one post across X and LinkedIn
upload an image and publish it to Instagram
validate a campaign schedule before it goes live
check whether scheduled posts were delivered
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands, a schedule file format, a validate-then-approve-then-apply sequence and clear rules for untrusted content, though it lacks output examples and error handling.
needs: SocialClaw account with provider OAuth connections (X, LinkedIn, Instagram and others)
optional TweetClaw/OpenClaw account for X research evidence
why: It directly serves publishing and scheduling social posts for a product or brand, but it relies on the getsocialclaw.com cloud service, so post text and media leave the local machine by design. The CLI's --api-key argument can expose the key in process lists and shell history, which the skill itself warns about; the user should run the login step in their own terminal.

summary: This skill lets an agent open a PDF in a live local viewer and work on it visually with the person. The agent can add highlights, notes, stamps and shapes, fill named or printed form fields, and place a signature or initials image at chosen coordinates, checking each change with a screenshot. It suits people who want to review, mark up or complete a document together, not people who only want its text summarised.
tasks: review a contract and highlight key terms
fill out a PDF form field by field
add my initials to each page of a document
stamp a PDF as approved or confidential
walk me through a paper and annotate the important parts
tools: local PDF viewer MCP server (list_pdfs, display_pdf, interact)
qualityWhy: The file gives the tool parameters, annotation types with coordinate rules, step-by-step workflows and a clear out-of-scope list, but it does not cover error handling or what to do when the viewer server is missing.
why: It helps with document markup and forms, which is useful now and then for a product's paperwork, but it is not core to building or running a site or app. It relies on a local PDF viewer server that the node must already provide, and the signature it places is only a visual image, not a certified signature, which the file states.

summary: This skill guides an agent through getting temporary AWS credentials for command-line and SDK use by running the AWS CLI's login command. It checks the CLI version, confirms whether existing credentials still work, and asks the developer before starting the sign-in. It then verifies the result and offers fixes for common failures such as a missing browser or a missing IAM policy. The audience is developers who need AWS access on their own machine.
tasks: set up AWS access on my laptop
fix an expired AWS session
sign in to AWS from the command line
switch to a different AWS profile
qualityWhy: The steps, version requirement, confirmation gates, verification command and error table are concrete and easy to follow, with only minor ambiguity around when to mention alternatives.
needs: IAM identity with the SignInLocalDevelopmentAccess managed policy (not needed for root users)
why: The skill exists only to sign a developer into a cloud provider's administration and hosting platform, which is cloud administration rather than building or running content on a local-first node, so its value is none. It has no safety problems of its own, but it would not serve the node's purpose.

summary: This skill guides an agent through diagnosing and speeding up latency-sensitive systems such as live dashboards, streaming feeds, queues and caches. It asks the agent to track separate metrics (percentile latency, data freshness, queue depth, cache hit rate) and to map each step from an incoming event to what the user sees. It then offers an ordered list of optimization steps and ways to verify a live deployment. It is aimed at engineers working on performance and freshness.
tasks: find why a realtime dashboard feels slow
reduce p95 latency of an API route
check whether cached data is stale
set up freshness and queue-depth monitoring for a streaming feature
qualityWhy: It gives a clear metric list, an ordered optimization sequence and useful guardrails, but has no concrete commands, examples or measurement procedures.
why: It is a stack-free engineering habit guide that helps with performance work on a node's sites and apps now and then, not as a core build feature. It does not require any outside service, and its guardrails bar live orders and risky deploys without approval.

summary: This skill lets an agent plan and run automated code upgrades on a person's repositories using the AWS Transform CLI. It inspects the repos for language versions, AWS SDK usage and framework versions, then matches them to available transformation recipes and asks for confirmation before running anything. Work can run on the local machine for a few repos or in AWS containers for large batches, so it suits developers and small teams who maintain several codebases.
tasks: upgrade this project from Java 8 to Java 21
migrate our boto2 Python code to boto3
move our Node.js project off the AWS SDK v2
run a framework upgrade across 20 repositories
analyze this codebase and generate documentation
qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, commands, confirmation gates and checks for each stage, though it depends on reference files not included here and has minor inconsistencies in its concurrency limits.
needs: Docker (only for a custom remote container image)
GitHub personal access token or SSH key stored in AWS Secrets Manager (only for private repos in remote mode)
why: Local-mode migrations on the person's own repos are useful now and then, but the skill is built around an AWS-hosted transformation service, and its remote mode is AWS account administration (IAM policy attachment, CloudFormation/CDK deployment, S3 and Secrets Manager setup) that conflicts with the node's local-first design. It is installable with the AWS service, and the telemetry and cloud upload are disclosed.

summary: The skill guides an agent through adding OpenTelemetry instrumentation to an application so it emits metrics, logs, and traces. It covers auto-instrumentation for several languages, setting the OTLP endpoint and credentials through environment variables, routing data through Alloy or an OpenTelemetry Collector, and choosing head or tail sampling. It is written for developers who run services and need to see their behaviour in Grafana.
tasks: instrument my Java app and send traces to Grafana
point the OTLP exporter at Grafana Cloud and verify spans
set up tail sampling to keep error traces
auto-inject the OpenTelemetry agent into Kubernetes pods
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete commands, env-var examples, verification steps and a troubleshooting list, though the referenced collector and SDK files were not reviewed and the Operator example uses a beta image.
needs: Grafana Cloud stack or self-hosted Mimir, Loki and Tempo
Grafana Cloud API token with MetricsPublisher, LogsPublisher and TracesPublisher roles
why: Instrumenting apps is useful for a node that runs products, but the skill is built around sending telemetry to a cloud backend, so it is only partly suited to a local-first node. It also tells the agent to download the Grafana JVM agent from the unpinned 'latest' GitHub release and run it, which is remote code execution without a version pin or checksum, so it is marked skip; the reference files were not reviewed.
risks: Downloads the Grafana JVM agent from the unpinned 'latest' GitHub release and runs it with -javaagent, without a version pin or checksum.

summary: The skill gives an agent a shared mental model of the PixiJS v8 scene graph: how containers differ from leaf draw objects, how local and world coordinates relate, and how render order, render groups, culling, and masking fit together. It points to a leaf-specific skill for each display object such as Sprite, Graphics, Text, or Mesh. It is aimed at developers building 2D games, interactive graphics, and visual web content with PixiJS.
tasks: debug a wrong sprite position in nested containers
decide between sortableChildren and RenderLayer for draw order
clip a sub-tree of display objects with a mask
speed up a large static scene with render groups
qualityWhy: It is well structured, with concrete code examples, a common-mistakes section, and a leaf comparison table, though only the main file was supplied and the reference files were not reviewed.
why: The content is a general 2D rendering reference for PixiJS, which is a client-side library and not something a Fractera node is built on, so it is only useful when a node's site or app uses PixiJS for graphics. It is written for PixiJS's own rendering model, not the node's stack, so it should be read for ideas rather than installed as written. Doubts remain about the unreviewed reference files.

summary: This skill guides an agent to speed up multi-step work by splitting a task into lanes, marking which lanes can run at once, and isolating writes by file, worktree, branch or service. It also covers reusing shared preparation across a bounded set of similar records while keeping each write sequential and verified. The result is a verification table rather than a vague speed claim. It is aimed at developers and operators who run concurrent agents, builds, tests or deploys.
tasks: plan parallel lanes for a large code change
batch repo scans and status checks before editing
run isolated worktrees for separate implementation passes
process a bounded list of similar records with shared setup
qualityWhy: The core pattern and lane matrix are clear and actionable, but the bounded-homogeneous-work section is abstract and padded with synthetic examples that are hard for an agent to apply directly.
why: It is a stack-free workflow habit useful when building or shipping a product, not tied to a specific framework. It has no outside service dependency and no risky commands, though its examples are dense and partly speculative.

summary: The skill guides an agent through creating a VPC peering connection between two AWS VPCs, covering acceptance, route table updates in both VPCs, DNS resolution settings, and security group adjustments. It targets engineers who need private network connectivity across same-region, cross-region, or cross-account setups. It also lists troubleshooting steps for pending peering, route conflicts, DNS failures and cross-region issues.
tasks: connect two AWS VPCs with peering
fix a stuck pending VPC peering connection
update route tables for cross-VPC traffic
enable DNS resolution across peered VPCs
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is short and mostly points to a reference procedure, and the visible files do not show the full steps, so the instruction is useful but thin here.
why: It is cloud network administration on AWS, which the node's local-first rules classify as value none, so it is skipped.

summary: This skill guides an agent through giving a Lambda function running in private VPC subnets outbound internet access. It covers creating a NAT Gateway, routing private subnets through a public subnet and an Internet Gateway, and checking security group rules. It also lists common fixes for timeouts and route table association problems. The audience is developers who run AWS Lambda inside a VPC.
tasks: give a VPC Lambda function internet access
set up a NAT Gateway for private subnets
fix a Lambda timeout caused by missing outbound access
check route table associations for Lambda subnets
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md body is short and mostly points to a reference procedure, and I could only see the SKILL.md file, so the reference file's depth is unverified.
needs: AWS account with credentials for VPC and Lambda
why: The skill administers AWS cloud networking (VPC, NAT Gateway, route tables) for hosted Lambda functions, which is cloud administration the node is not for, so it is rated none and skipped. It needs an AWS account and the reference file was not reviewed.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building Telegram bots for chatbots, server and order alerts, scheduled digests, group moderation and AI assistants. It describes BotFather setup, command handlers, n8n-style workflows and inline keyboards, mostly as YAML outlines and message templates. It is aimed at engineers or operators who want to automate Telegram messaging.
tasks: build a Telegram chatbot with AI replies
send server alerts to a Telegram group
set up a daily sales digest bot
add welcome and moderation to a Telegram group
qualityWhy: Mostly YAML outlines and placeholder templates with few runnable steps, checks or code, and the one code sample uses an undefined telegram object.
needs: OpenAI API key for AI features
n8n instance for the workflow examples
why: Telegram messaging is useful for notifications and bots on a node, but the skill is thin and leans on n8n and OpenAI, which the node does not provide, so an agent would need to write the bot itself from the Telegram Bot API. The skill's own mention of a telegram-mcp server is not described in its files.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a security review of a codebase or system: mapping the attack surface, running scanners for code, dependencies and leaked secrets, then manually checking authentication, input handling and cryptography. It asks the agent to rate each finding by severity, give a file location and a fix, and write an audit report with prioritised recommendations. It is aimed at developers and security reviewers who want to check a product before release or after changes.
tasks: review my web app code for security vulnerabilities
scan the repository for hardcoded secrets and API keys
run a dependency audit and list vulnerable packages
write a security audit report with severity ratings and fixes
qualityWhy: The workflow, example commands, severity rules, MUST/MUST NOT constraints and a finding template are concrete and easy to follow, though it has no Next.js or TypeScript-specific checks and only a Python example.
why: Reviewing a product's code for security is directly useful when building a site or app on a node, and the scanners run locally with no account or key. Only SKILL.md was fully visible; the six reference files were listed but not read, so their content is unverified, and the penetration-testing material must only be used on systems the person is authorised to test.

summary: This skill lets an agent query Google NotebookLM notebooks through a browser automation layer and return answers with citations drawn only from the uploaded sources. It also manages a local notebook library, uploads files and folders as sources, and generates podcasts, slides and infographics from them. It is aimed at researchers and writers who keep their reference material in NotebookLM.
tasks: ask my NotebookLM notebook a question
upload a folder of documents to a notebook
generate a podcast or slide deck from my sources
download a book from Z-Library into a notebook
qualityWhy: The steps and command table are concrete, but the instructions contradict each other (for example, notebook metadata is both required and never to be specified) and the script bodies are mostly cut, so the behaviour cannot be fully checked.
why: NotebookLM is a Google cloud service, so the notebook sources live outside the node, and the skill is useful only now and then for research; it is skipped because it drives a logged-in Google session through automation against the service's terms and includes a shadow-library download path.
risks: Stores Google session credentials and Z-Library login state in plain JSON files under the skill's data folder.
Downloads copyrighted books from a shadow library (Z-Library) and uploads them to a third-party service.
Rotates multiple Google accounts to get around the daily query limit, which breaks the service's terms of use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through diagnosing Google Ads account problems by running GAQL queries through the Google Ads MCP server. It covers sudden drops in conversions or conversion value, lost impression share caused by low ad rank or small budgets, low lead flow, and failing offline conversion uploads. It is written for marketers and analysts who run ads for a business and need to find out why results changed.
tasks: diagnose a sudden drop in conversions
find out why lead flow is low this week
check lost impression share from budget or ad rank
check whether offline conversion uploads are failing
qualityWhy: The steps, example GAQL queries, field gotchas and fallback behaviour are concrete and checkable, with only small gaps such as no guidance on comparing date windows.
needs: Google Ads MCP Server with OAuth access
why: It helps a node that runs paid ads for a product, but only when a Google Ads account and MCP server are connected, and the skill does not build sites, data or content. The skill itself has no stack conflict and needs no adaptation to the node.

summary: The skill guides an agent through choosing and using PixiJS v8 text classes: Text for crisp styled labels, BitmapText for fast frequently changing values, HTMLText for inline HTML markup, and the split variants for per-character animation. It explains options-object constructors, tagStyles, font loading and BitmapFont installation, and lists common mistakes such as updating Text every frame. It is aimed at developers building PixiJS canvas games, interactive graphics or visual front ends.
tasks: render a styled score label that updates every frame
add a custom font to a PixiJS text label
animate each character of a title in PixiJS
show mixed bold and colored text with HTML tags in a canvas
qualityWhy: The main file gives a clear decision table, a cost comparison, runnable examples and concrete wrong/correct pairs, though the reference files were not included for checking.
why: It is a PixiJS-specific skill for canvas rendering, which is not part of the node's stack, but the text concepts can be read and applied in a Next.js app; the node's own UI is React/Tailwind, so most of the work would be rebuilt the node's way. Its value is limited to projects that render text on a canvas.

summary: Gives an agent a structured method for planning how to fill a technical event with attendees: choosing a calendar spine (percent of expected ticket sales for paid events, percent of attendance goal for free ones), mapping audience segments to promotion channels, allocating a budget across channel postures, and setting per-phase registration targets. It routes each channel's execution to sibling skills for copy, social, press and landing pages. Aimed at event organizers and community or company teams running conferences or hackathons.
tasks: plan how to fill a paid developer conference
set registration targets by date for a hackathon
choose promotion channels for a tech event
split a small promotion budget across channels
diagnose whether low ticket sales are a demand or marketing problem
qualityWhy: Detailed, structured interview, decision rules and failure modes an agent can follow, though it leans on external references and sibling skills not included here.
why: Useful for planning event promotion, which is adjacent to what a node is for (running sites and content), but it is about event marketing rather than building or running products, so use is occasional. It is stack-free planning guidance that needs no outside service, and it routes work to sibling skills that are not part of this package.

summary: The skill guides an agent through exporting an Amazon RDS or Aurora database snapshot to Amazon S3 as Apache Parquet files. It covers choosing or creating the snapshot, setting up an IAM role and KMS encryption, preparing the bucket, starting and monitoring the export task, and checking the data. It also includes troubleshooting notes for common failures. The intended users are engineers and data teams who want the data in S3 for Athena, Glue or Redshift Spectrum.
tasks: export an RDS snapshot to S3 as Parquet
set up IAM role and KMS encryption for a database export
check the progress of an Aurora snapshot export
query exported RDS data with Athena
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear outline and troubleshooting notes but delegates the actual procedure to a reference file, which I did not see in full, so the step detail cannot be fully judged.
needs: AWS credentials with RDS, S3, IAM and KMS permissions
why: This is cloud database administration on AWS, which runs against cloud RDS and S3 rather than local-first data on the person's computer, so it is not useful for building or running a node. I only read SKILL.md and not the 59 KB reference file, so the full procedure may contain details I could not assess.

summary: This skill guides an agent through PixiJS v8's ticker, the per-frame loop that runs animation and game logic. It explains which timing value to read (deltaTime, deltaMS or elapsedMS), how callback priority orders work, how to cap frame rate and scale speed, and when to use per-object onRender hooks or manual rendering. It is written for developers building 2D graphics, games or interactive visuals in PixiJS.
tasks: add frame-rate-independent animation to a sprite
cap a canvas scene to 30 fps
run physics before rendering in a PixiJS game
pause or drive the render loop manually
migrate v7 ticker callbacks to v8
qualityWhy: Concrete examples, a clear table of time units, priority ordering and a set of common mistakes with wrong and right code, though it lacks a full end-to-end example.
why: It is a focused, accurate reference for a rendering library rather than a site or product feature, so it is only occasionally useful on a node. It is built for PixiJS, which the node does not use, so an agent would read it for ideas and adapt them to the node's own stack, not install it as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through diagnosing TextMeshPro problems in the Unity game engine, covering font atlas memory, SDF sampling and padding ratios, AutoSize CPU cost, worldspace text choice, and multilingual Latin and CJK alignment. It gives symptom-based advice and a checklist of common mistakes. It is written for Unity developers shipping games or apps.
tasks: reduce TextMeshPro atlas memory in a Unity game
fix blurry or inconsistent font weight in Unity UI
align mixed Latin and CJK text in a Unity build
cut CPU spikes from frequently updated Unity text
qualityWhy: The steps, ratios, symptom table and pitfalls are concrete and checkable, though a few claims such as the Scale 0.9 import default are asserted without evidence.
why: It is built for Unity game engine text rendering, which has nothing to do with building websites, web apps, AI agents or web content on a Next.js node. Unity is outside the node's stack, so the skill is not useful there.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to apply visual effects to PixiJS v8 containers through the filter pipeline. It covers built-in filters such as blur, color matrix, displacement, alpha and noise, writing custom GLSL or WGSL fragment shaders with Filter.from, and tuning options like resolution, padding, antialias and filterArea. It is aimed at developers building 2D graphics, games or interactive visuals with PixiJS.
tasks: add a blur or glow effect to a sprite
apply a custom shader effect to a container
adjust brightness, contrast or saturation of an image
speed up a filtered scene by tuning filterArea and resolution
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete code, correct v8 API patterns, a list of common mistakes with fixes, and related skill pointers, though it has no step-by-step workflow or verification checks.
why: It is a stack-free rendering reference for PixiJS, a client-side library that runs locally, so it fits a node that builds web apps, but it only matters when the person is building PixiJS graphics rather than general site content. Nothing in the file calls an outside service or needs a key.

summary: This skill guides an agent through an offline App Store optimisation audit of locally pulled metadata files, checking keyword overlap, field usage, missing fields, separator errors and cross-locale duplication. When Astro MCP is connected, it also compares keyword popularity and competitor keywords per store to find gaps. It is aimed at developers and marketers who ship iOS apps and want to tune their App Store listings.
tasks: audit my App Store metadata for keyword waste
find keyword gaps against competitors
check whether my locales are actually localized
review keyword field usage before submitting a new version
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete checks, field limits, file paths, severity levels and a report template, though some tokenisation and fuzzy-matching rules are described loosely.
why: It serves an app's store listing rather than the node's core build, run or content work, so its value is occasional. It needs Astro MCP and Apple Ads for the gap analysis, and the offline checks depend on the asc CLI pulling metadata from App Store Connect.

summary: The skill guides an agent through producing competitive SEO content briefs for a new page or for improving an existing one. It covers SERP competitor scoring, search intent classification, per-section word counts, keyword placement and meta tag length rules, E-E-A-T needs, and internal linking. It is aimed at site owners, marketers and content writers who need a structured brief before drafting.
tasks: write a content brief for a target keyword
outline a service page for a new keyword
improve an existing blog post with a brief
make a content outline with word counts
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with a fixed output template, character limits, placement rules, and error handling, though the referenced files were not provided to verify them.
why: Writing SEO briefs for the sites a node hosts is directly useful for content and site building. The skill runs without any paid service, but its richer SERP data depends on optional DataForSEO or Ahrefs accounts. The skill's own metadata lists it as MIT licensed and not a cloud service, and its fetch and security rules are sound.

summary: Teaches an agent how to render very large numbers of simple sprites in PixiJS v8 using ParticleContainer and Particle objects, covering creation, constructor options, which attributes update per frame, batch operations, and the restrictions compared with a normal container. It is aimed at developers building particle effects, bullet patterns or similar visuals in a web game or interactive page.
tasks: render ten thousand particles in a PixiJS scene
add a particle effect with fading and tinting
speed up a sprite-heavy animation
build a bullet pattern in a game
qualityWhy: It gives concrete code, option tables, a migration table and a list of common mistakes, though a few details are only described and not shown.
why: Rendering many sprites is a common need for building interactive pages and games on the Next.js stack, and the skill is stack-free PixiJS guidance that runs locally with no service. The skill points to other skills and an external API reference, but none of that is required to use it.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building async Python REST APIs with FastAPI and Pydantic V2. It covers request and response schemas, routers with dependency injection, async SQLAlchemy data access, JWT login, WebSocket endpoints, pytest tests, and migrating from Django. It is aimed at developers who want a Python backend.
tasks: build a REST API in Python with FastAPI
add request validation with Pydantic V2 models
add JWT login to a Python API
write async tests for an API endpoint
migrate a Django REST API to FastAPI

why: A Fractera node is built on Next.js and TypeScript, so a Python FastAPI backend is outside its stack. Its SQLAlchemy and JWT parts would replace the node's SQLite element and next-auth sign-in, so an agent should read it for ideas and build the node's way. Its Pydantic validation patterns may still be useful.

summary: This skill guides an agent through adding, configuring and debugging Unity's in-app purchase package in a Unity game or app, covering product loading, the two-step pending-then-confirm purchase flow, restores, subscriptions and entitlement checks. It also covers migrating from native store billing, RevenueCat, Adapty and other Unity billing kits, and a direct-to-customer payment path through Stripe or Coda. The intended users are Unity developers selling digital goods inside their games.
tasks: add in-app purchases to a Unity mobile game
set up subscriptions with receipt validation
migrate from native billing or RevenueCat to Unity IAP
debug a purchase flow that never confirms
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and complete, with a routing step, exact event orders, API signatures, a list of common mistakes and a validation checklist that an agent can follow step by step.
needs: Unity project with the Unity IAP package
Stripe or Coda account for direct-to-customer payments
why: It targets Unity game store billing, which is outside a Fractera node's Next.js and web stack, so it does not serve building or selling web sites, web apps or content. The skill is high quality, but its value to nodes is none.

summary: The skill guides an agent to judge whether a technical event's concept, audience and price meet real demand at three stages: before launch, while tickets sell, and after an edition. It assembles leading, mid-sale and lagging signals into a go, hold, pivot or stop call, with thresholds declared up front. It is written for event organizers of conferences, hackathons and meetup-to-conference jumps.
tasks: validate demand for a new tech conference before launch
check whether ticket sales are on pace against expected checkpoints
decide whether an event should recur or scale after an edition
diagnose why a past edition underperformed
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, with interview steps, declared thresholds, failure differentials and clear routing to sibling skills, though some composites are self-described syntheses and the benchmark numbers are only referenced in files not shown here.
why: It serves event organizers, not building, running or selling a Fractera product, site, app or content, so it is not useful for what nodes are for. It reads signals only and calls no tool, so there is no security risk, but it does not fit the node's purpose.

summary: This skill lets an agent change keyboard shortcuts in the cmux macOS terminal app by editing its JSON config file. It proposes ready-made layouts such as tmux-style prefixes, Vim-style pane movement, and agent-focused unread handling, then applies only the bindings the user picks. It also records previous values so each change can be reverted and checks that the config still parses.
tasks: rebind a split or pane shortcut in cmux
set up tmux-style key prefixes in my terminal
audit my cmux keyboard shortcut overrides
reset a cmux shortcut to its default

why: It customizes the keys of one desktop terminal app on the user's Mac and does not help build, run, sell or make content for a Fractera product, so the value is none and it is skipped.

summary: This skill guides an agent through finding and fixing the real slowdown in large data jobs such as ingestion, backfills, exports and warehouse loads. It separates source, network, load, transform and freshness delays, then benchmarks a few variants before choosing one. Its main rule is that a faster run only counts if row counts and timestamps still match the manifest and target tables. It is aimed at data engineers who need faster pipelines without losing correctness.
tasks: speed up a slow data backfill
find the bottleneck in an ETL pipeline
make a warehouse load idempotent and verified
report row counts and timestamps after a catch-up run
qualityWhy: It gives a clear workflow, heuristics and an accounting template, but it has no concrete commands, scripts or examples for any particular engine.
why: It is a stack-free set of data habits that a node could use occasionally when a product's data jobs are slow, though it is mostly for pipeline engineering rather than site or content building. It names no database or cloud service, so it does not conflict with the node's local-first data model.

summary: This skill is meant to help an agent suggest Korean personal names by combining a person's birth date and time, their family name, and candidate given names, then scoring them with saju element balance and name-study heuristics. Its SKILL.md is only a launcher: it tells the agent to fetch and run an external npm package and treat that package's output as the real instructions. The actual method is in a separate instruction file that was not shown, so the naming logic cannot be checked here.
tasks: suggest a Korean baby name from birth date and family name
score candidate names by saju elements
compare given-name options for a family name
qualityWhy: SKILL.md is a stub that only points to an external CLI and a remote instruction file, so the skill itself gives an agent no steps, examples or checks.
why: The skill is a niche naming utility, not a tool for building, running, selling or making content for a product, and the stub's remote execution makes it unsafe to install as written.
risks: Runs a remote npm package via npx with -y and treats its output as the primary instructions, so whatever that package returns is executed and followed without review.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to add a multi-conversation sidebar to an assistant-ui chat app, letting people create, switch, rename, archive, delete, search and page through threads. It covers three storage paths: a managed cloud service, a custom backend adapter, or an existing external state store. It is aimed at developers building chat products on assistant-ui.

let users rename, archive or delete chats

build a custom thread list layout with search and grouping

summary: The skill guides an agent through creating an AWS CloudTrail trail that covers every region, storing logs in S3 and forwarding them to CloudWatch Logs for querying. It also covers Logs Insights queries for security monitoring and compliance audits. The main audience is cloud or security engineers who need centralized API activity logging in AWS. The SKILL.md itself is short and points to a reference procedure, which was not provided to me, so I judged only the visible text.
tasks: set up a multi-region CloudTrail trail
send CloudTrail logs to CloudWatch Logs for analysis
