decide how companies get on the demo day stage
choose pitch length and format for a demo day
define what the pitch winner receives
qualityWhy: The skill is detailed and structured, with menus, interview questions, dominance checks and explicit gates, though it is heavy on reasoning and light on concrete templates an agent can execute directly.
why: It serves organizing an event rather than building or running a site, app or content on a Fractera node, so it is only occasionally useful; it also leans on sibling skills from another collection and is designed for a conference, not a product stack, so it would need adapting to the node's own workflows.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to create, convert and adjust colours in PixiJS v8 using the Color class. It shows the many accepted input formats (hex, CSS names, RGB and HSL objects, arrays), output conversions, alpha and multiply operations, and reusable buffers for per-frame work. It is aimed at developers building 2D graphics, sprites and tinted visuals in PixiJS.
tasks: convert a hex colour to a number for a sprite tint
tint a sprite with a per-frame colour animation
set alpha and premultiply a fill colour
validate user colour input before use
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete code for each input and output format, common mistakes with fixes, and performance notes, though it has no verification steps.
why: It is a useful reference for PixiJS colour handling, but it targets PixiJS v8 as a library, which a Fractera node would use only if the site or app includes it; it is a stack-specific library reference, so the agent should check that pixi.js fits the node's own stack before adopting it. Its value is limited to canvas or game-style visuals rather than the node's core web stack.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing the on-site day for general attendees at a technical event: check-in and badge pickup, badge privacy and scanning rules, signage and wayfinding, the quiet room, dietary meal distribution, the help desk, and first-timer orientation. It ends with a walkthrough audit of the finished design. It is aimed at event organizers, community-run or vendor-run, who want a plan they can execute and check by walking the venue.
tasks: plan check-in and badge pickup for a conference
decide whether to put a QR code on attendee badges
place the quiet room and signage for a multi-floor venue
arrange distribution of dietary-restricted meals
orient first-time attendees on the day
qualityWhy: Detailed, structured decision menus with explicit defaults, interview questions, workflow steps and a measurement section, though several parts depend on reference files and self-set judgement rather than hard steps.
why: It is a planning skill for physical events, not software, so it is useful to an event organizer but only now and then for a node that builds and runs sites or apps. It is stack-free, so the agent can apply it directly, but it is not a building skill for the node. It depends on sibling skills from another catalogue that are not installed, and it does not touch the node's own elements.

summary: This skill guides an agent through staffing one edition of a technical event with unpaid volunteers. It works from the run of show to a list of posts, sizes the roster from shift arithmetic instead of attendee counts, writes role descriptions with fit criteria, and sets up sign-up, confirmation, briefings, and a replacement protocol. It is written for event organizers who run community or mid-size conferences.
tasks: size the volunteer roster for a conference
write volunteer role descriptions and shift plan
brief volunteers including the code-of-conduct escalation script
set up a replacement protocol for no-show volunteers
qualityWhy: The skill is concrete and detailed, with ordered steps, a sizing formula, measurable checks and reference files, though parts are argued at length and the menus are heavy.
why: It is a stack-free event-staffing process with no link to building, running, selling or making content for a product on a node, so its value for node uses is none and it is skipped. It has no risks beyond normal handling of volunteers' personal data, which the skill itself flags for a retention rule.

summary: This skill guides an agent through reviewing C# code that uses Entity Framework Core for slow or incorrect data access. It covers finding N+1 queries, deferred versus in-memory filtering, tracking choices, index-friendly predicates, keyset pagination, and set-based updates. It is aimed at backend developers working on .NET services, imports, and background jobs.
tasks: review EF Core data access for slow queries
fix N+1 queries in a .NET service
replace offset paging with keyset pagination
check whether EF Core queries can use existing indexes
qualityWhy: It gives a step-by-step review workflow, concrete code examples, explicit verification steps, and clear limits on what source-only review can prove.
why: The skill is written for C# and EF Core, but Fractera nodes use TypeScript with their own SQLite element as the only data door, so an agent should read it for query-optimization principles and apply them in the node's own stack. Its guidance is careful about not applying migrations without approval, and it has no outside service dependency.

summary: This skill tells an agent to prepare a Korean court electronic payment-order application. It gathers the creditor, debtor, claim amount, grounds and evidence through an interview, drafts the application, and prepares a handoff for the official e-court browser steps. Its only content is a wrapper that tells the agent to fetch and run an npm package to get the real instructions.
tasks: prepare a court payment-order application
draft a payment-order claim for an unpaid debt
collect claim details and evidence for an e-court filing
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is only a stub that points to a remote CLI for all real instructions, so it gives an agent no usable steps by itself.
why: A court filing assistant is not for building, running, selling or making content for a product, so its value is none. It also depends on a remote npm package run with npx, which is a risk.
risks: Runs the npm package @nomadamas/k-skill via npx -y at every use, executing remote code that the skill does not pin or review.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing how a hackathon picks its winners. It works out how many judges and teams fit the judging window, weights the categories already named in the brief, and sets the scoring scale and how judge scores are combined. It also covers conflict-of-interest rules for sponsors and judges, a published tie-break order, and how results are announced and challenged. It is aimed at event organizers preparing a jury before the ceremony.
tasks: design a hackathon judging rubric and criteria weights
work out how many judges a team count needs in the judging window
write a tie-break order and conflict-of-interest rule for a hackathon
brief judges and plan the results announcement
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear interview, ordered workflow, worked arithmetic for judge allocation, and explicit validation checks, though its repeated dominance-check wording is dense and some sections run long.
why: Hackathon judging is event-organizing work rather than building or selling a product on the node, so its use is occasional, though it could support a node that hosts an event site. It is stack-free planning guidance that needs no outside services. I only saw SKILL.md; the evals and reference files were not shown to me, so I could not check them for hidden instructions.

summary: This skill lets an agent turn plain-language finance questions, such as asking how a stock has done lately or which sector is strongest, into Tushare data pulls, cleaning, comparisons and short summaries. It covers A-shares, indices, funds, financials, valuation, money flows, announcements and macro data. It is aimed at people doing market research or preparing financial data exports.
tasks: compare recent stock performance and valuation
pull quarterly financial trends for a company
find the strongest sectors and capital inflows
export daily market data to CSV for analysis
qualityWhy: The workflows, default time windows, data-quality checks and error handling are concrete, but the referenced interface document is not included and the two scripts are only basic demos.
needs: Tushare account and TUSHARE_TOKEN from tushare.pro
why: It serves financial research and data export rather than building or running a node product, so its value is occasional. It depends on a third-party data service with a token and point-based permissions, and the agent must check those limits before pulling data.

summary: This skill guides an agent through the speaker experience after a speaker accepts a talk: collecting bios, headshots, A/V and travel details against dated deadlines, naming a single contact, sending a packet, running the tech check and green room, documenting recording consent, and following up after the event. It is written for event organizers, mainly community-run or vendor conferences. It also covers reminder cadence, first-time speaker care and retention of sensitive travel documents.
tasks: send accepted speakers their pre-event packet
collect speaker bios, headshots and A/V needs before a deadline
document recording consent per session format
plan the green room and tech check for speakers
arrange speaker travel or lodging
send post-event thank-you and recording link to speakers
qualityWhy: Detailed, structured and actionable with a clear workflow, interview questions, ranked menus and failure modes, though much of it is judgment-based guidance rather than step-by-step checks.
why: Useful for organizing events on a node that hosts event sites, but it is a stack-free operational playbook used now and then, not a direct build or product feature. Its recording and travel-data sections call for care with personal data, which the node's own storage should handle.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to read, search, send, reply to, forward, download attachments from, and clean up email through the agently-cli command-line tool, after an OAuth login. It is aimed at people who want an agent to handle their day-to-day mailbox work. It also sets two-step confirmation before any write action and treats email content as untrusted input that must not be obeyed as instructions.
tasks: send an email with an attachment
summarise my unread emails
reply to all on a thread
search my inbox for a report and download its attachment
watch for new mail and act on it
qualityWhy: It gives a complete command table, parameter lists, a two-phase confirmation flow, exit-code handling and prompt-injection rules, though the install line is oddly worded and it refers to a CodeBuddy product name.
why: The mailbox is kept on Tencent's cloud mail service and the CLI works against it remotely, which conflicts with the local-first design of a node, so it is not a fit for building or running a product here. Email is communication rather than a product-building tool, and the person's mail data would sit with a third party.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing and tuning Unity audio: clip import settings such as load type, sample rate, compression and forcing 3D sources to mono, plus Audio Mixer group depth and effects. It runs every check and change as C# inside a live Unity Editor through the Unity CLI, and requires the user to review findings and approve changes at explicit checkpoints. It is aimed at game developers reducing audio memory or CPU cost and fixing playback quality problems.
tasks: reduce audio memory in a Unity game
fix a 3D sound that only plays in one ear
cut Audio Mixer CPU cost
set compression and sample rate for mobile builds
qualityWhy: The skill gives ordered steps, checkpoints, verification reads and troubleshooting cases tied to concrete Unity API calls, though some recipes live in separate reference files.
needs: Unity Editor with the Pipeline package
why: The skill is for Unity game projects, which a Fractera node (web apps, sites, AI agents, content) does not serve, so its value is none. It also has no security risk, but the use is skip because value is none.

summary: This skill guides an agent through deciding which accessibility and inclusion provisions a technical event should commit to, including physical, sensory, dietary, economic and digital access. It sizes each provision to the event's funding, venue, audience and effort limits, and drafts the public accessibility declaration and the data-handling posture for accommodation requests. It is aimed at conference and meetup organizers who need to decide what to offer and how to publish it honestly.
tasks: decide which accessibility provisions a conference should offer
write an accessibility page for an event
decide whether to caption talks or use automatic captions
plan childcare or travel grants for attendees
handle an accommodation request for an event
qualityWhy: The skill gives an ordered interview, explicit ranking menus with stated defaults and overrides, concrete failure modes, a workflow and sourced reference files, so an agent can follow it step by step.
why: It is a planning skill for event organizers, not for building or running a Fractera site, app or content; it is not a stack skill, but it serves event planning rather than what nodes are for, so the value is none.

summary: The skill gives an agent a set of n8n-style workflow recipes for Google Calendar and Outlook: a morning schedule digest sent to Slack, meeting prep documents, weekly time-blocking, Calendly-to-calendar booking handling, and weekly calendar analytics. It is aimed at individual workers and managers who want their calendar summarised and organised. Most of the content is YAML pseudocode and report templates rather than executable steps.
tasks: send me a morning digest of today's meetings
block focus time on my calendar next week
prepare a briefing before my next meeting
create a weekly report on how I spend my time in meetings
qualityWhy: It is mostly pseudocode YAML and templates with placeholders; it names no concrete API calls, auth steps or checks an agent could follow to actually build the workflows, and it leans on an MCP server it never explains.
needs: Google Workspace account or Outlook account
why: Calendar digests and time-blocking are useful occasionally for a node's operators, but the skill is about personal productivity rather than building or selling a product, and it depends on several outside SaaS services (Slack, Calendly, HubSpot, Clearbit, LinkedIn) the person must set up. It is written for n8n rather than the node's stack, so an agent would have to adapt it, though the model label and install context keep it usable as-is for a service-backed setup.

summary: This skill guides an agent through creating, editing and checking Salesforce validation rule metadata. It covers the required fields (name, active flag, error formula, error message), the rules for common formula functions such as TEXT, CASE, VALUE and ISPICKVAL, wrapping formulas in CDATA when they contain XML, and the .validationRule-meta.xml file format. It is written for Salesforce administrators and developers.
tasks: create a validation rule for a required field
fix a validation rule formula that fails to deploy
add a condition to an existing validation rule
write a clear error message for a validation rule
qualityWhy: The skill gives a precise specification and a useful list of common formula mistakes, but it has no worked examples, no full XML template and no verification steps.
needs: a Salesforce org and its metadata
why: The skill is built only for Salesforce validation rules, which belong to a cloud CRM platform and not to the Fractera stack of Next.js, SQLite and local files, so it does not serve building, running or selling a product on a node.

summary: This skill guides an agent through Salesforce record work: creating, updating, deleting, importing and exporting data through the sf command-line tool and anonymous Apex. It also covers generating test records with factories, running bulk loads, and cleaning up afterwards. It is written for Salesforce developers and admins who need realistic data for testing or migration. It includes ready-made Apex, CSV and JSON templates, plus a Python pre-flight validator.
tasks: seed test accounts and contacts in a sandbox org
bulk import opportunities from a CSV file
delete test records created by an earlier run
check picklist values and required fields before inserting records
qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, decision tables, failure patterns, a validator and many templates, though the scripts were cut off and some checks are shallow.
needs: a Salesforce org and login through the sf CLI
why: Every operation acts on records in a remote Salesforce org, which is a cloud database and backend, so it does not fit a local-first node. Nothing in the skill targets local data, files or media.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to apply blend modes to PixiJS v8 display objects, covering the built-in GPU modes such as add, multiply, screen and erase, plus a larger set of advanced modes loaded through an extra import. It also explains how to order sibling objects so that draw calls stay low, and it lists common mistakes such as forgetting the advanced-mode import or the back-buffer option. The target reader is a developer building 2D graphics, glow or lighting effects in a PixiJS scene.
tasks: add a glow effect with additive blending
apply multiply shadows to sprites
use overlay or color-burn blend modes in a PixiJS scene
reduce draw calls by reordering blended sprites
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete code, a full mode table, batching advice and a set of wrong-versus-correct examples, though it has no test steps.
why: Blend modes are useful for visual effects in web apps and games on a node, which makes this skill useful now and then; it is written for PixiJS v8 with no cloud dependency, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through installing the assistant-ui chat library with its command-line tool, either as a new project or inside an existing Next.js app. It then helps pick the right runtime adapter for the backend, such as the Vercel AI SDK, LangGraph, Google ADK or an AG-UI server, so a chat interface can talk to an AI agent. It also covers keeping the install current with updates, codemods and diagnostics. It is aimed at developers building AI chat features into a product.
tasks: add a chat interface to an existing Next.js app
connect a chat UI to a LangGraph or Google ADK agent
scaffold a new AI chat project
upgrade assistant-ui to the latest version

optional AssistantCloud account for the cloud persistence templates
optional Clerk account for the cloud-clerk template
why: A chat UI for AI agents directly serves building and running products on a node, and init fits the node's existing Next.js and shadcn stack. It calls outside LLM services and some templates and runtimes depend on cloud services (AssistantCloud, Clerk, Cloudflare Durable Objects, Claude Managed Agents), so the node's local-first data and its own sign-in element should be used instead of those.

summary: This skill acts as a router for AWS networking questions. It reads a request, decides which AWS service area it belongs to (DNS, CDN, hybrid links, VPN, web firewall, or DDoS protection), and hands the work to a more specific skill. It also lists the security controls and logging to remember along the way. It does not configure anything itself, and it is written for engineers running AWS infrastructure.
tasks: route DNS and health-check questions to the right AWS skill
decide between Transit Gateway, Direct Connect and VPN for hybrid connectivity
set up CloudFront with a WAF and DDoS protection
find out which AWS log source shows blocked traffic
qualityWhy: The routing tables, disambiguation concepts and security checklist are clear and specific, but the skill only triages and defers all implementation to other skills, so it gives an agent few steps of its own.
needs: AWS MCP server or AWS CLI credentials
why: AWS networking is cloud infrastructure administration, and a Fractera node is local-first, so this does not serve building, running or selling products on the node. Nothing in it is a security risk to the person's computer.

summary: This skill tells an agent to look up public defense procurement notices on the D2B portal, filtering by notice title, notice type, posting or bid-opening dates, G2B notice number, or issuing agency. In this file, though, the actual procedure is not written out: the SKILL.md only instructs the agent to run an external npm package to fetch the instructions. The skill is aimed at people tracking government bids rather than at building or running a product.
tasks: search defense procurement bid notices by agency
find D2B notices by G2B notice number
list open bid notices by date range
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is a stub that only points to a remote CLI for its real instructions, and the bundled instruction.md was not provided for review.
why: Procurement bid lookup on a national defense portal does not serve building, running, selling or making content for a node, and the skill is a wrapper that defers to an external CLI. The instruction.md and skill.json files were listed but not shown, so their content is unverified.
risks: Runs an npm package fetched at execution time via npx -y, executing remote code without a pinned version.
The update command rewrites every installed coding-agent skill, changing files beyond this one skill.

summary: The skill guides an agent through checking an iOS app's subscriptions and in-app purchases in Apple's App Store Connect against the matching products, entitlements, offerings and packages in RevenueCat. It starts with a read-only audit, then, with approval, creates missing App Store items and maps them into RevenueCat. It is written for mobile developers who sell app subscriptions and want their two catalogs to match before release.
tasks: audit App Store subscriptions against RevenueCat before release
create missing App Store subscriptions and map them to RevenueCat
set up RevenueCat entitlements and offerings from App Store products
find product ID drift between App Store Connect and RevenueCat
qualityWhy: The steps, commands, conditional create/update rules, validation gates and output format are concrete and complete, though the document is long and dense.
needs: App Store Connect account and asc CLI authentication
RevenueCat account with a write-enabled API v2 key
why: The skill only administers cloud catalogs at Apple and RevenueCat, which are cloud services rather than local data, files or media, so it falls under cloud administration and is not useful for building a Fractera node. It is also aimed at iOS apps and their native stack, not the node's own web stack.

summary: This skill lets an agent change Unity sprite metadata such as names, rectangles, borders, pivots, outlines and slices by writing C# snippets and running them through a live Unity Editor. It is aimed at developers working on sprite sheets inside a Unity project. The skill depends on a separate unity-cli skill to connect to the Editor and on the script eval command being available in the catalog. Its instructions cover the compile limits of script eval, such as no using directives and fully qualified type names.
tasks: slice a sprite sheet into a grid
set sprite pivots to bottom center
adjust nine-slice borders on a sprite
rename sprites in a texture importer
add outline geometry to sprites
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow and useful compile pitfalls, but its key steps defer to referenced files and the safety pattern, so the main instructions are thin on their own.
why: The skill is useful for Unity sprite art pipelines but Fractera nodes do not build Unity projects, so it does not serve a node's stack of web apps and content. It is not a cloud service, but it is for a different toolchain than the node's own. Because it does not fit the node and its value is limited, I am marking it skip.

summary: This skill lets an agent hand a bounded coding task to the Google Antigravity CLI (agy) as a background implementer, then review the resulting diff and commit it itself. It explains how to write a self-contained brief, dispatch it through a bundled Node relay script that wraps agy in print mode, poll for a result file, and verify gates and touched files before landing. It is aimed at developers who want to run queues of implementation work through agy while staying the reviewer.
tasks: delegate a coding task to Antigravity
run a queue of refactors through agy
have agy implement a fix and review its diff
resume an agy run with a delta brief
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md and relay script give concrete commands, flags, a result.json contract, permission caveats and a review loop, though the reference files were not fully visible and some sections are long.
needs: Google Antigravity CLI (agy) installed and authenticated
why: It is a coding-workflow tool that drives an external coding agent rather than building or running a Fractera site, app or content, so use is limited to occasional delegated coding; it is marked skip because the relay runs agy with permission-related flags and the skill documents an option to auto-approve tool permissions, and it reads a permission config file that holds user grants.
risks: Documents and can pass --dangerously-skip-permissions, which auto-approves the agent's tool calls if a human opts in.
Relay passes the full brief as a command-line argument, exposing it in the process list.

summary: This skill sets up a Claude Code project so each tool call is checked against a Cedar policy file before it runs, and each completed call writes an Ed25519-signed receipt to a local JSONL file. It walks the agent through installing the plugin and hooks, generating a signing key, writing the policy, and verifying the receipt chain offline. It is aimed at people who need tamper-evident records of agent actions, such as teams in regulated work.
tasks: add an audit trail to Claude Code tool calls
block risky shell commands with a Cedar policy
verify signed receipts of agent actions
set up a signing key for agent receipts
qualityWhy: It gives concrete install commands, a full hook configuration, a working Cedar policy and verification steps, but leaves the policy path as a placeholder and describes its string-matching limits only briefly.
why: It is a local governance tool for the agent's own tool calls, not a direct aid to building or selling a node's sites or content, so its value is occasional. It needs no cloud service or account and keeps receipts and keys on the local machine, and its only dependencies are pinned npm packages and Claude Code hooks. Its Bash permit rules rely on best-effort string matching and allow npm scripts that can run arbitrary code, which the skill itself notes.

summary: This skill lets an agent create new Word documents and edit existing ones by writing Python code with the python-docx library. It covers headings, paragraphs, tables, images, page setup, headers and footers, and simple placeholder filling for templates. It is aimed at people who need reports, letters, or contracts produced from data or templates without opening Word by hand.
tasks: generate a formatted Word report with tables
fill a Word template with placeholder values
write a business letter as a .docx file
add headers and footers to an existing document
qualityWhy: The examples are concrete and runnable, but several snippets are incomplete or missing imports (page-number field, RGBColor, qn, OxmlElement, datetime), the mail merge only covers body paragraphs and not tables, and the frontmatter references an undefined office-mcp server.
why: It is a local Python library with no outside service, so it fits a local-first node, but Word documents are only occasionally useful for building sites and apps. The skill is written for Python rather than the node's TypeScript stack, so an agent would run it as a separate local script; the gaps in the snippets are worth checking before relying on them.

summary: This skill guides an agent to pick the right dotnet test command for a .NET repository, covering classic MSBuild/vstest runners, VSTest mode, bridged Microsoft Testing Platform (MTP) and native MTP on SDK 10+. It explains filter syntax for MSTest, xUnit, NUnit and TUnit, plus TRX, diagnostics, dumps and coverage flags. It is aimed at developers who need an exact, runnable test command for their project.
tasks: run only the integration tests of a .NET project
give the exact dotnet test command with TRX output
run xUnit v3 tests on Microsoft Testing Platform with a filter
collect code coverage for a .NET test project
find the right test runner flags for a classic MSTest repository
qualityWhy: It gives a detailed decision table, workflow, concrete command examples, validation checks and output rules that an agent can follow step by step.
why: It is directly useful for a team building .NET apps on a node, but only when the node hosts .NET projects, which is not the node's main stack; it is a stack-free-to-install CLI helper with no outside services. It reads repository files and may run dotnet commands, all within the stated purpose.

summary: The skill lets an agent search over 200 open icon libraries through the better-icons command-line tool, then fetch an icon as SVG with chosen colour and size, or batch-download search results into a folder. It can also run as an MCP server so AI agents can search, recommend and insert icons into project files. It is aimed at developers who need icons for web or app interfaces.
tasks: find an arrow icon for a navigation menu
download a set of star icons as SVG files
add a home icon to a React component
recommend icons for a checkout page
qualityWhy: The commands and options are clear and there are examples, but the file is short, has no error handling or verification steps, and the MCP section gives only a table and types without setup detail.
why: Icons are a direct need for building sites and apps on a node, and the tool runs locally, with only a public icon API used for lookups and no account or key required. The install step is a global npm or bun install, which is the normal way to add a CLI tool and differs from nothing in the node's stack.

summary: Guides an agent in drafting or revising a pull request body: a summary paragraph, the repository's template sections, and reviewer guidance such as reading order and focus areas. It asks the agent to verify commit-message claims against the code, record decisions with rejected alternatives, and report validation honestly. It is aimed at developers and reviewers working in git repositories.
tasks: write a pull request description
fill in the repository PR template
refresh a PR description after new commits
add a review guide for reviewers
qualityWhy: Detailed, ordered steps with concrete checks, anti-patterns and a self-check, though it leans on referenced files and some guidance is abstract.
why: It is a stack-free writing and review habit that helps any repository workflow, but it serves code collaboration rather than building or selling a product on the node. It only reads git history and uses the gh CLI for read-only PR views, so it is installable as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing a custom Unity Shader Graph node from HLSL code. The agent adds a reflection define and Shader Graph hint tags to a function, then saves it into a ShaderInclude .hlsl asset in a Unity project, asking first before it appends to an existing file. It is aimed at Unity developers and technical artists who need new shader nodes.
tasks: create a custom Shader Graph node from HLSL

add hint tags to a shader function for Shader Graph search
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and the hint requirements are listed, but the SKILL.md is short and depends on a separate hints file without a complete worked example.

why: Unity Shader Graph is a game-engine tool and does not match Fractera's web stack or its content uses such as sites, shops, blogs, and media, so it is not useful for what nodes are for.

summary: Teaches an agent to read, filter, deduplicate and convert SARIF output from static analysis scanners such as CodeQL and Semgrep, with a focus on resolving severity correctly when result levels are inherited from rule metadata. It bundles jq queries, a standard-library Python helper module, and tests with fixtures. It serves developers and security engineers who want to gate CI on scan results or aggregate findings. It does not run scans itself.
tasks: parse a SARIF file from CodeQL
deduplicate alerts across scanner runs
fail CI if there are error-level findings
convert scan results to CSV or HTML
qualityWhy: Concrete and complete, with runnable commands, a correct severity-resolution algorithm tied to the SARIF spec, test fixtures, and explicit pitfalls and checks.
why: Useful for a node that analyses or gates code scan results, but it is a developer-tooling skill and not directly about building or selling a product. It is stack-free apart from optional Python and jq, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to bulk-extract content from a website by crawling its linked pages, optionally limited to one path such as /docs, with a page limit or depth cap. It runs the Firecrawl command-line tool, waits for the job or polls a job ID, and saves the results to a local JSON file. It is aimed at someone who needs many pages from one site, such as documentation or a blog section, collected in one go.
tasks: crawl all the docs pages of a website
collect everything under a section of a site into a local file
check the status of a running site crawl
gather blog posts from a site for content research
qualityWhy: The file gives clear commands, a done-when check and scoping tips, but it leaves out the output format, error handling and how to read the saved pages.
why: It is useful for collecting content from other sites into local files, but it depends on the paid Firecrawl cloud service and needs a logged-in account, which the person must choose to set up. Its usefulness to a node's own products is occasional rather than central.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to place a plain HTML element on top of a PixiJS v8 canvas and keep its position and opacity synced with a display object in the scene graph. It covers the DOMContainer class, anchoring, the pixi.js/dom import for custom builds, visibility and cleanup, and pointer-events handling. It is aimed at developers who need native inputs, iframes, or video inside a canvas-based app.
tasks: overlay a text input on a canvas game
embed a video player over a PixiJS scene
add an HTML panel that follows a sprite
fix a DOM overlay that never appears in a custom build

A grouped switcher lets the person flip between states while working on visuals. When finished, the page and its fixtures are removed in one step. why: It helps when building or checking a Next.js UI component's states, which fits building a product, but it is a dev-workflow habit rather than content or site output. It has no stack-specific install step beyond the node's own Next.js app, so it can be used as written.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull current items from dozens of news, tech, AI, and podcast sources through a Python script, then write a Chinese-language report for each source. collect updates from my own RSS feed list

why: It helps with research and content ideas, not with building or running a site or app, so it is useful only now and then. It needs no API keys or paid services, but Playwright requires a separate Chromium download, and the scripts were not reviewed.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building PowerPoint decks: writing slides as HTML sized 720x405pt and converting them to .pptx with a Node script, or editing existing templates by auditing thumbnails, duplicating and reordering slides, and injecting text from a JSON inventory. why: Making slide decks is a content task that fits a node building and selling products, but it is not central to running a web app, so its use is occasional; it is stack-free in that it produces files locally without any cloud service. The shown scripts only handle local files, though the full html2pptx.js and other scripts were not visible to check them.

summary: This skill makes an agent take one statement, phenomenon or question and push it downward layer by layer, changing the explanatory frame at each step (social, psychological, biological, physical, mathematical, logical) until it reaches a basic root. save a deep-dive thinking note as Markdown

It writes files to a fixed ~/Documents/notes path on the person's own computer, which is local and matches its stated purpose, so the agent should tell the person where the file went.

summary: The skill teaches an agent how to write marimo notebooks as plain Python files with cell-based functions, reactive variable dependencies, and PEP 723 inline dependencies. It covers script versus interactive mode, UI widgets, rendering rules, linting with marimo check, pytest tests, and pointers to reference docs on exports, deployment, caching and widgets. It is aimed at data scientists and developers who build analysis tools, dashboards or interactive demos.
tasks: write a marimo notebook for data exploration
add interactive sliders to a notebook
check a marimo notebook for errors
add pytest tests to a notebook
export a notebook as HTML or PDF
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete examples, good and bad patterns, and commands to check, with further reference files, though some references were not shown and the guidance is spread across many files.
why: It is a stack-free-ish guide for writing marimo notebooks, which is useful for analysis and demos but not core to building or running a Fractera site, app or content pipeline. It is a Python notebook tool, not a Next.js/SQLite stack, so it fits without adaptation, and nothing in it calls an outside service.

summary: This skill gives an agent a reference for backend Node.js work: running TypeScript directly through native type stripping, handling errors and async code, and processing large data with streams. It also covers caching, logging, environment configuration, and diagnosing flaky or hanging tests and slow code paths. It is aimed at developers who build and debug Node server code. An entry-point file routes the agent to one of 16 detailed rule files, and two example files show a graceful HTTP server and its tests.

process a large CSV file with streams

profile and speed up a slow Node endpoint

why: It is general Node.js guidance with no outside service, so it can be installed as written. Its fit is partial, because Fractera nodes run on Next.js, which handles much of the server layer that the raw-http shutdown and streaming rules describe. The agent should apply the advice to the node's own server code, not to Next.js internals.

summary: The skill walks an agent through signing a Fractera node into OKX exchange accounts via an OAuth device flow, or through API-key setup, before any trading, portfolio, earn or bot action. It forces a site choice (global, EEA, US or TR) and a fixed pre-login checklist, and covers status checks, re-login and removing the okx-auth binary. why: It is built around a cloud exchange account and trading service, not around building, running or making content for a local product, so it does not fit a local-first node; it also depends on an external trading platform's credentials.

summary: This skill makes an agent generate a full set of design tokens, as CSS custom properties or a Tailwind config, for a project. It first checks for existing tokens and extends them, then reads a design brief to pick values for colour, spacing, type, layout, motion and breakpoints. It also requires both light and dark palettes that suit the chosen aesthetic. The work is aimed at developers and designers setting up a visual system before building components.

generate a light and dark colour palette from a design brief

extend existing CSS variables with missing dark mode tokens

Its Tailwind step still refers to tailwind.config.js, while Tailwind 4 configures theme values in CSS, so an agent may need to adjust that step; it also points to the /frontend-design skill and a .design brief folder that the node may not have.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to build Lambda functions that run multi-step workflows over long periods, saving progress so work resumes after interruptions. It explains the replay model that such functions depend on, plus rules for steps, waits and callbacks, retries, and compensating actions. why: The skill is built around AWS Lambda, a cloud service for running and administering functions, so under the node's local-first rule it is not useful for building here and is skipped.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to make a PixiJS v8 canvas app usable with screen readers and keyboard. It explains how to turn on the AccessibilitySystem, which places an invisible DOM overlay over accessible containers, and how to set titles, hints, tab order and activation options on each container. add screen reader labels to canvas buttons
set tab order for PixiJS menu items
enable accessibility overlay in a PixiJS app

summary: The skill turns an agent into an English LaTeX paper assistant that works on an existing manuscript: it diagnoses compile failures, checks venue formatting, bibliography and citations, grammar, logic, tables, figures, pseudocode and abstracts, and proposes rewrites for sections, de-AI polish and claim-forward wording. why: It is a stack-free writing and LaTeX aid that fits a document-making node, but it is for academic papers only, so use is occasional rather than central to building products. It runs local scripts and needs no outside service; the optional online bibliography check only runs if the user opts in.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to work with Google Cloud Storage buckets and objects, choosing between an MCP server, the gcloud CLI, the JSON API, or client libraries. It covers creating buckets, uploading and downloading, access control, lifecycle and cost, data protection, transfers, FUSE mounts, and Terraform. why: Cloud Storage is a cloud object store, which a local-first Fractera node is not meant to rely on for its data, files or media, so the skill is value none and skipped.

summary: The skill guides an agent through negotiation preparation and live conversations using tactical empathy, mirroring, labeling, calibrated questions, an accusation audit, Ackerman bargaining and Black Swan discovery. It is aimed at people facing salary talks, vendor pricing, contract terms or objections where both sides need to feel heard. structure counter-offers with the Ackerman method
plan a vendor contract negotiation
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear framework, scoring, tables and copy patterns with worked examples, but its details on some techniques are pushed into a separate reference file.
why: It is a stack-free soft-skill guide, useful for sales, pricing and client conversations on a node that sells products, but not for building the node's code. Its main usefulness is in the operator's own business dealings rather than in the product itself.

summary: This skill guides an agent through creating one isometric line-drawing figure in the Hairline style, which reacts to the pointer and ships as a single self-contained HTML file. qualityWhy: The skill gives an ordered workflow, explicit rules, worked examples and validation commands an agent can follow, though some referenced files were not shown to check.
why: It is a graphics-generation skill that makes standalone HTML figures, which a node could use for page illustrations, but it is built around its own kernel and bench rather than the node's Next.js stack, so it would be read for ideas and rebuilt the node's way. The skill installs a Playwright browser helper outside the folder on first run, which the person should know about.

summary: This skill guides an agent through planning the structural skeleton of a product or site before visual design: site map, navigation model, content hierarchy, user flows, naming, component reuse and URL strategy. It first reads any existing design brief and routing or layout code, then interviews the user with recommended answers, and finally writes an INFORMATION_ARCHITECTURE.md document. why: It is a stack-free planning method that directly serves building a product or site on a node, and it tells the agent to extend existing routing rather than ignore it. Its main gap is that it does not state how to verify the finished IA beyond the template itself.

summary: This skill lets an agent look up official overseas and training trip reports published by Korean election, anti-corruption, and local council sites, and list them with their dates and attachments. It also serves civic transparency research rather than building, running, or selling a product on a node, so value is none.
risks: Runs the npm package @nomadamas/k-skill through npx -y at each step, so remote code executes and its instructions can change without the person seeing them.
The 'update' command rewrites every coding-agent skill install on the machine, not just this one.

summary: This skill lets an agent query OKX's Smart Money data through the okx command-line tool: ranking top crypto traders, looking up a trader's open and closed positions and trade records, and summarising which coins those traders are buying or selling. summary: The skill guides an agent through writing custom Semgrep rules for security bugs and code patterns. It requires reading Semgrep documentation first, writing a test file with ruleid and ok annotations before the rule, inspecting the AST, and iterating until every test passes. why: It helps a developer write code-scanning rules for a product's own codebase, which is useful now and then rather than core to building or running a site. It is stack-free apart from Semgrep, which runs locally, and the workflow needs WebFetch to read Semgrep docs online.

summary: This skill acts as a router for AWS database questions. It sends a request either to a selection procedure for choosing among AWS database services or to a service-specific skill for setup, operations, or cost estimates. why: Every service it covers is a cloud-hosted AWS database, which a local-first node should not depend on, so it is not useful for building or running a Fractera product and is skipped on that basis.

summary: This skill makes an agent scan a codebase for places where shallow modules could be deepened, focusing on recently changed hot spots from git history. It writes a self-contained HTML report with before/after diagrams and a recommendation strength for each candidate, then asks which candidate the person wants to explore. summary: This skill guides an agent through troubleshooting AWS Clean Rooms collaborations when access is denied or custom ML model jobs produce no logs. why: It is a debugging guide for AWS cloud administration, which a local-first node does not use, so it is not useful for building, running or making content on a node. The reference files were not provided, so their completeness is unknown.

summary: This skill guides an agent through upgrading an existing assistant-ui application, first moving the AI SDK and its adapter to compatible versions, then applying version-by-version API migrations for assistant-ui 0.8 through 0.15. It walks through detecting installed package lines, choosing which codemods to run in order, running the bundled upgrade CLI with dry-run previews, and verifying with typecheck, build and chat-path checks. summary: The skill guides an agent through deciding whether AWS Lambda Managed Instances fits a workload, then sizing, configuring, migrating code to, and cutting over to EC2-backed Lambda capacity. It covers cost comparison against standard Lambda, thread-safety review per runtime, IAM and VPC setup, SOCI lazy loading for large container images, and the 90-minute timeout for asynchronous and queue-driven jobs. The audience is cloud engineers running steady, high-volume or long-running AWS workloads.

why: The skill is built entirely around AWS cloud hosting and cloud compute administration (EC2-backed Lambda capacity, VPCs, NAT gateways), which the node's local-first model treats as a cloud place to run things, so it is not useful for building or running a Fractera node.

summary: This skill tells an agent to look through commit history, reverts, review comments and workaround comments to find mistakes that keep recurring in a repo. For each repeated mistake it guides the agent to make the mistake impossible, trying architecture first, then types, then a lint or CI check, then a behavior test, and docs last. why: It is a stack-free engineering process that helps maintain any node project where agents make recurring errors, but it does not build, run, sell or create content directly. Its advice to add lints and CI checks depends on the project's own tooling, which the agent must check before applying it.

summary: The skill tells an agent to create or edit raster images, such as photos, illustrations, sprites, mockups and transparent cutouts, using a built-in image generation tool by default. summary: This skill has an agent audit Lightning Web Component files for Salesforce Lightning Design System (SLDS) compliance. It runs the SLDS linter, runs a bundled Node script that checks CSS, HTML and JS for missing fallbacks, invented hooks, accessibility attribute gaps and code-quality issues, then requires a manual review before giving a scored grade and a production-readiness verdict. summary: The skill guides an agent through lean startup practice: framing each product bet as testable hypotheses, choosing the smallest experiment that could falsify them, and judging results with actionable metrics and explicit pivot-or-persevere criteria. summary: The skill guides an agent to draft business proposals for sales, projects, partnerships, RFP responses, grants and service agreements. summary: This skill guides an agent through adding, searching, fixing and styling shadcn-vue components, which are copied as source code into a Vue project using the CLI. summary: This skill guides an agent through building, changing, auditing, debugging and deploying Salesforce Agentforce agents written in Agent Script, a domain-specific language. It covers design specs, local syntax checks, previewing conversations, testing, and gated publishing. summary: The skill guides an agent through pandas DataFrame work: inspecting dtypes and missing values, vectorized transforms, groupby and pivot aggregations, merges with cardinality checks, time series resampling, and memory reduction on large tables. It is aimed at a developer or analyst who needs reliable tabular data processing in Python. Reference files cover operations, cleaning, aggregation, merging and performance.

tasks: check what kind of WordPress project this repo is
find the test and build commands for a WordPress plugin
detect the WordPress core or Gutenberg version in a checkout

why: Fractera nodes build on Next.js, React and SQLite, not WordPress, so a WordPress repo inspector does not serve what nodes are for. It is also not a risk on its own: the script reads wp-config.php only to report flags as booleans and does not send data anywhere.

summary: The skill asks an agent to review the diff of the current branch against main and strip out signs of AI-written code: needless comments, unusual defensive checks or try/catch blocks, casts to any, and style that doesn't match the surrounding file. It is aimed at developers who want a cleanup pass after generating code. The agent finishes with a short one-to-three sentence report of the changes.

why: It is a stack-free habit that helps any code project, so it fits a node's development work, but it is only occasionally useful and its guidance is vague. Nothing in it calls an outside service or requires a key.

summary: This skill is a deprecation notice for an older Angular directives guide. It tells the agent that the skill is unmaintained, that its previous contents were removed, and that the Angular team's official skills repository should be installed instead. It gives a command to install the replacement and another to remove this one. It offers no concrete directive guidance of its own.

replace an unmaintained Angular skill with the official one

summary: The skill teaches an agent to write, validate and deploy HashiCorp Terraform Stacks configurations, which are HCL files named .tfcomponent.hcl and .tfdeploy.hcl that describe components, providers and deployments across regions or environments. why: Terraform Stacks deploy infrastructure to cloud providers through HCP Terraform, a cloud backend, which the node's local-first design rules out, so the skill serves cloud administration rather than building a Fractera product.

summary: The skill gives an agent a python-pptx based playbook for creating, opening, editing and extracting content from PowerPoint files. It covers slide layouts, text boxes, shapes, images, tables, charts and formatting, with a pitch-deck and sales-report example. why: Slide generation is useful for content makers and presentation work, but it is only occasionally relevant to building a product on a node. It is a stack-free local Python library with no outside service, so it can be installed as written, though the skill mentions MCP tools that a node may not provide.

summary: The skill describes a multi-platform social media publishing workflow covering TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, X, Facebook, Threads and Pinterest. publish a video to TikTok, Instagram and YouTube

summary: This skill guides an agent through the lifecycle of AWS ElastiCache, a managed in-memory service: choosing between Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached, provisioning serverless or node-based caches, wiring up VPC access, TLS and IAM auth, and designing cache keys and TTLs. summary: The skill lets an agent send money from the authenticated Stripe business to another Stripe business identified by a Stripe Profile handle, after reviewing the transfer details. summary: This skill gives an agent a writing standard for technical documents, combining four layers: Diátaxis mode selection, Google developer style sentence rules, STE-style short instruction rules, and Global English clarity rules. It tells the agent to pick one mode per document (tutorial, how-to, reference, or explanation), write short direct sentences, and avoid ambiguity. It refers to an adapter file and the unslop skill, which the agent must also have installed; neither is an outside service, so no keys are needed.

summary: The skill turns an agent into a code security reviewer that scans a project in stages: dependencies first, then secrets and config, then a deep reasoning pass over injection, access control, data handling, cryptography and business logic, followed by cross-file data-flow tracing. why: It audits code for security flaws, which is useful when building a product, but it is a review habit rather than a tool for building, running or selling content, so it is only occasionally needed. It is stack-agnostic and reads local files, so it needs no outside service; the reference files were not supplied, so their detection accuracy is unverified.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building a complete Salesforce Lightning Experience app from a plain-language description. design a management system with related Salesforce objects

why: It produces Salesforce metadata for a cloud CRM platform, which is outside what Fractera nodes are for, and it relies on a cloud service rather than local data. It is not a fit for building, running or selling a product on a local node.

summary: This skill acts as a router for building on the Convex hosted backend. qualityWhy: It is mainly a router whose referenced skills are not included in the folder, though its short list of rules is concrete.

summary: The skill makes an agent review token contracts and the code that accepts arbitrary tokens, checking ERC20 and ERC721 conformity, owner privileges, and a long list of non-standard token behaviours such as fee-on-transfer, rebasing, missing return values and blocklists. needs: an Ethereum RPC endpoint for on-chain queries (optional)
why: It serves security review of Solidity token code, which is useful for a node that builds on-chain products but not for building, running or selling a product's content directly, so value is some. It is Solidity and EVM focused and needs an RPC endpoint for on-chain analysis, so use is install-with-service rather than install.

summary: This skill guides a coding agent to decide when to build a temporary, task-specific harness instead of running steps by hand, and when to promote that harness into a shared skill. why: It is a stack-free process skill, so it fits building and running a node's agent workflows, but it does not produce site, content or product code by itself. Its ECC2 control pane references are unclear on a Fractera node, which an agent should simply skip.

summary: The skill gives an agent a behavior-design framework based on the Fogg Behavior Model (motivation, ability and prompt converging) to diagnose why users sign up but do not stick around. audit friction in a core action

why: It is a stack-free design method that directly serves building and running a product's activation and retention. It does not depend on any outside service, and its guidance applies to any node-built app without adaptation.

summary: This skill guides an agent through moving Salesforce Lightning Web Components from the older SLDS 1 styling system to SLDS 2. It runs the SLDS linter with auto-fix, then works through the remaining violations by hand: swapping hardcoded values and legacy tokens for SLDS 2 styling hooks, renaming overridden SLDS classes, and checking that fallbacks match the original values. Its mandatory npx run of the unpinned @latest linter with --fix also executes whatever package version is current.
risks: The mandatory command runs `npx @salesforce-ux/slds-linter@latest lint --fix`, which downloads and executes an unpinned npm package and rewrites files automatically.

summary: This skill lets an agent sign into a QianWen AI account through a device-code login and then read usage figures, free-tier quotas, pay-as-you-go costs, billing cycles, subscription status and per-request call logs. why: It administers a cloud AI provider's account, billing and quotas rather than helping build, run, sell or create content for a node product, so it falls under cloud quota administration. It is also a cloud service's account tool, which the node rules mark as skip.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building React front ends that talk to a GraphQL server with Apollo Client 4.x. summary: The skill guides an agent through real-time online multiplayer built on Unity Multiplayer Services, focusing on sessions such as rooms, parties and lobbies, plus network topology and matchmaking choices. summary: This skill guides an agent writing React TSX components in a lobe-ui codebase: choosing a styling approach (StyleX first, then createStaticStyles, inline styles, and createStyles as a last resort), picking components from base-ui before the root library, keeping state local, closing popovers on navigation, and applying memoization only when a render boundary is proven. Its advice on state, popovers and memoization transfers well, though.

summary: This skill tells an agent to pull a competitor's active ads from public ad libraries such as Facebook and LinkedIn, save screenshots, and break the messaging down into problems highlighted, use cases, headline and copy patterns, and visual formats. It is aimed at marketers and founders who want inspiration or positioning ideas for their own campaigns. summary: This skill walks an agent through connecting a project to the QianWen (Qwen) model API by setting up an API key, placing it in an environment variable or a local .env file, and checking that it works with a small curl request. The service is paid and chosen by the person, and the key lives in local .env or environment variables. The optional OSS section is cloud file storage, but it is not the skill's main purpose, so the skill is not skipped. The gossamer.py script it mentions is not in the shipped files, so the update-check path is unverified.

summary: The skill guides an agent through a structured review of a smart contract codebase against Trail of Bits development guidelines. It covers generating plain-English documentation and diagrams, checking upgradeability and proxy patterns, reviewing functions, inheritance, events, pitfalls, dependencies and tests, then producing prioritized recommendations. summary: This skill teaches an agent how to measure which code a fuzzing campaign actually reaches, using LLVM coverage tools, gcov/gcovr, or cargo-fuzz's coverage command. It explains how to build instrumented binaries, replay a corpus through them, produce text and HTML reports, and act on the results by adding dictionary entries, seeds, or harness fixes. identify magic value checks blocking the fuzzer
qualityWhy: Concrete and well organised, with build commands, step-by-step workflow, troubleshooting table and tool-specific guidance, though some sections are thin and the Rust HTML script is duplicated.
why: The skill is about fuzzing C, C++ and Rust code, which is a security testing topic and does not serve building, running or selling a product or making content on a local-first node. Its stack (clang, llvm-cov, gcovr, cargo-fuzz) also does not match the node's Next.js and TypeScript stack, so it is not useful to a node, and it is marked skip for that reason.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building React 18+ and Next.js App Router code: components, custom hooks, forms that use React 19 actions, Server Components, and Suspense. summary: Scans Android APK files for Firebase misconfigurations. It then writes text and JSON reports. It is meant for security auditors working on apps they are authorized to test.

summary: This skill guides an agent in writing prompts for AI image generators such as DALL-E, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion. summary: The skill has an agent query the official Hankookilbo remote MCP server without authentication to pull Korean news metadata: front-page headlines, most-read and most-carefully-read articles, latest stories, section picks, topic search, and a daily horoscope. qualityWhy: The provided SKILL.md is a generated stub that only points to an external CLI and the source instruction.md, so the skill's actual steps are not visible in these files.

summary: The skill steers an agent away from the generic AI-generated look when writing HTML, CSS or frontend framework code. It sets rules for sidebars, cards, buttons, shadows, radii, spacing and colour palettes, aiming for calm, Linear- or GitHub-like interfaces. It lists banned patterns such as eyebrow labels, hero strips in dashboards, gradient fills, and KPI card grids. It is aimed at developers and designers who build web UIs.

style a sidebar, cards and buttons in a clean way
qualityWhy: It gives many concrete rules and palettes, but much of it is a list of prohibitions with little step-by-step guidance, some rules conflict (e.g. the 12px radius rule versus the 8-10px button rule), and it has no checks or examples an agent can run.
why: It directly serves building the UI of a product on a node, and it is stack-free, so it fits the node as written. Its contradictions and loose wording mean an agent may apply it inconsistently.

summary: Guides an agent to research and rank companies that could buy a person's product or service, starting from the product's description or codebase. It defines an ideal customer profile, looks for buying signals such as hiring, tech stack or funding, scores each lead, and writes per-lead outreach angles and conversation starters. The output is a scannable report that can be exported to CSV for a CRM. It is aimed at sales, business development and marketing people.
tasks: find 10 companies that would buy my product
build a scored list of sales leads in a region
write outreach strategy for each target account
prepare a CRM-ready prospect list
qualityWhy: The steps and output template are clear, but it gives no concrete search method, data sources, scoring rubric or verification checks, so it stays generic.
why: It is about finding outside companies to sell to, not about building, running or making content for a Fractera product, so it does not serve the node's purposes. Its LinkedIn and company lookups also depend on web search that the skill never specifies.

summary: This skill lets an agent create images from a text description by choosing one of eight image models and calling a small Node script. It adds style words to the prompt, picks an aspect ratio, and returns a result URL, and it can run Midjourney follow-up actions such as upscaling, variations and rerolls. It is aimed at people making visuals for content, products or design work who do not want to manage several image-generation accounts.

make a logo or app icon
create a 16:9 illustration for a blog post
make a quick image draft to iterate on
upscale or vary a Midjourney grid image

needs: hosted image proxy at image-gen-proxy.vercel.app (default, operated by a third party; optional IMAGE_STUDIO_TOKEN)
fal.ai and Legnext.ai, reached through the proxy
why: It directly serves making images for content and products, and the image models are an outside service the person chooses to use, so it is install-with-service. Prompts and results pass through a third-party relay whose operator and privacy terms are not named, and some documented features are missing from the script.

summary: This skill helps an agent find command-line tools for professional software, such as image editors, video editors, 3D modelling programs and audio tools. It explains how to search a public catalog, check which tools a multi-tool workflow (called a matrix) needs, and install only the parts a task requires. The catalog itself is a remote instruction file that the agent is told to consult, so the skill mostly routes the agent to other tools. It is aimed at people who want an agent to run creative or productivity software from the terminal.
tasks: find a command-line tool for editing images
check which tools a video production workflow needs
install only the transcription tool for a task
search the catalog for a 3D modelling CLI
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands, exit codes and install scopes, but most of the real content lives in a remote catalog it points to rather than in the file itself.
why: Discovering CLIs for image, video and audio work is occasionally useful for making content, but most listed tools (office suites, streaming, desktop editors) are outside what a node is for. It is skipped because installing unvetted third-party packages and following an auto-updating remote instruction file carries a risk.
risks: Installs third-party pip packages from a public registry, which runs their code on the person's computer without a review step.
Fetches an auto-updated instruction file from an external CDN that the agent would follow, so its content can change without the person's knowledge.

summary: This skill lets an agent query Binance's public fiat payment data: which fiat currencies, crypto assets and payment methods are offered in a given country, their limits, and indicative prices. It also explains how to build links that send users to Binance buy, sell, deposit or withdraw pages. A separate reference covers authenticated lookups of the user's order and payment history using their own API key and secret.
tasks: check which payment methods can buy BTC with EUR in France
compare the indicative price of ETH in USD across buy and sell
list fiat deposit options for a given country
show my Binance fiat order history
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete endpoints, parameters, response fields, a workflow, and presentation rules, though the authenticated reference was not fully verified here.
why: It serves a crypto exchange's fiat funnel rather than building or running a product, so value is only occasional; the public calls need no key, and the history lookup needs the person's own Binance API key and secret. The skill is built for Binance's own API, so it fits without changes, but its price and link output is advisory and could be stale.

summary: The skill guides an agent in writing fuzzing harnesses for C, C++ and Rust code: the entry function that receives random bytes and routes them into the code under test. It covers turning raw bytes into typed inputs, keeping runs deterministic, avoiding slow or leaking harnesses, and choosing which functions to fuzz together. It is aimed at security-minded developers and maintainers of parsers or libraries.
tasks: write a first fuzz harness for a C++ parser
fix a fuzz target whose crashes will not reproduce
structure fuzz inputs for a Rust API
improve coverage of a libFuzzer campaign
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete code for several fuzzers, a step-by-step process, anti-patterns and a troubleshooting table, though the Go section and some tool guidance are thin.
why: It is a testing technique for C, C++ and Rust code, useful for security work but not for building or running a Fractera site, app or content; it is a general technique rather than a stack for the node, so it is best read for ideas. No risks were found in the file.

summary: The skill walks an agent through a five-day design sprint (Monday to Friday) to test a product idea with real users before any production code is written. It covers mapping the problem, individual sketching, a single decider vote, building a realistic clickable prototype, and interviewing five target customers. It is aimed at product leads and founders facing a costly or stuck product decision.
tasks: plan a design sprint for a new feature
validate a product idea before building it
prototype and test a concept with five users
run a decision workshop to pick one solution
prepare a user interview script for prototype testing
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete day-by-day steps, time-boxes, templates, a scoring rubric and common mistakes, with deeper reference files, though the reference files themselves were not provided for review.
why: It is a method for a product team rather than code, so it is useful now and then for planning what to build, but nothing in it writes to a node's stack; the prototyping steps point at Figma and Keynote, not the node's Next.js and Tailwind stack, so it should be read for its process and applied by hand. No risks found in the visible files.

summary: This file is only a redirect notice saying the technical SEO checker has moved to another repository. It gives no audit steps, checks or commands of its own beyond an install line for the bundled version. An agent reading it learns where the skill now lives, not how to check a site's technical SEO.
tasks: audit a website for technical SEO problems
find the current version of the technical SEO checker skill
qualityWhy: The file is a redirect stub that points to other repositories and contains no instructions an agent could follow.
why: The file contains no usable technical SEO guidance, so it adds nothing to a node. The active bundled version it points to would need its own review before any install.

summary: This skill gives an agent a persistent Playwright session inside a JavaScript REPL to drive a local web app or Electron app, reuse the same page handles across edits, and run functional and visual QA with real user input. It also covers screenshot normalization to CSS pixels and viewport-fit checks. It is aimed at developers debugging UI on their own machine.

run functional and visual QA on an Electron window
check that a page fits the viewport at mobile and desktop sizes
capture CSS-normalized screenshots for coordinate-based clicks

why: It is a testing workflow for local UI debugging, useful now and then when building a site or app on a node, but it is written for the Codex js_repl environment and needs adapting to the node's own agent tooling, so it is read for ideas. It also requires running with sandboxing disabled, which the node should not be set up to do by default.
risks: It requires starting the agent with sandboxing disabled (--sandbox danger-full-access), which removes a safety boundary.

summary: This skill makes an agent review code changes the way Sentry engineers do: look for runtime errors, performance problems, side effects, breaking API changes and security gaps, check test coverage, and flag risky changes for senior review. It also sets a polite, actionable feedback tone and approval rules that avoid blocking PRs over style. It is aimed at developers and reviewers who check pull requests, and it includes short Python and TypeScript examples of common mistakes.
tasks: review a pull request for bugs and security issues
give polite actionable feedback on code changes
check whether a change has adequate test coverage
flag schema or API changes for senior review
qualityWhy: It is a useful checklist with a few examples, but it stays generic and gives no concrete steps, commands or verification procedure an agent could follow.
why: A stack-free review checklist that an agent can use on any Fractera project's changes, though it is thin and mostly applies general review habits rather than node-specific knowledge. Its examples lean toward Python/Django, which does not match the node's TypeScript and Next.js stack, so it is useful only as a general guide.

summary: This skill sets up a Claude Code PreToolUse hook that inspects Bash commands before they run and blocks destructive git operations such as push, hard reset, forced clean and force branch deletion. It asks whether to install for the current project or globally, copies a small shell script into the right hooks folder, merges the hook into the settings file without overwriting other settings, and checks that the hook blocks a test command. It suits developers who want a person-controlled brake on an AI agent's git history changes.
tasks: stop the agent from pushing to remote git
block git reset --hard and clean commands
add git safety hooks to Claude Code
protect uncommitted work from agent git commands
qualityWhy: The steps, settings JSON, script and test command are concrete and easy to follow, but the script fails open when jq is missing and its substring patterns can misfire.
why: It is a local developer safeguard for agents working in git, useful now and then rather than for building or running a product directly, and it needs no outside service. The regex matching is only a guardrail, not a security boundary: it can be bypassed with unusual spacing or flags, and it can block harmless text such as commit messages containing 'git push'.

summary: The skill guides an agent to statically check compiled code for timing side channels: it compiles a source file, inspects the emitted assembly or bytecode for variable-time instructions such as division, and then triages which flagged operations actually touch secret data. It also covers secret-dependent branches, early-exit comparisons of tags and MACs, and secret-indexed table lookups across many languages. The audience is developers and reviewers writing or auditing cryptographic routines.
tasks: check my signing routine for timing leaks
review this crypto code for division on secrets
find early-exit comparisons on authentication tags
audit a key derivation function for constant-time issues
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and complete, with exact analyzer commands, flag tables, per-language coverage limits, triage questions, worked examples and known-answer fixtures.
why: It serves a narrow but real need for anyone writing cryptographic code on a node, such as a signing or encryption element, yet most node work is web and content, so it is only occasionally useful. It is a stack-free static analysis skill that runs locally and needs no outside service, though it depends on local compilers and interpreters being installed.

summary: This skill walks an agent through designing a multi-product agentic data science system on Google Cloud. It starts by gathering requirements and confirming a component breakdown with the user, then picks an agent pattern, maps components to Google Cloud products, and drafts a Mermaid architecture diagram with a solution guide. It then covers deployment prerequisites, Terraform and Agents CLI steps, and validation checks. The intended users are cloud architects and data teams building analytics or ML agents on Google Cloud.
tasks: design a multi-agent data analytics architecture on Google Cloud
draft a Mermaid architecture diagram for an agent-based ML workload
plan deployment of an ADK agent to Cloud Run
write validation checks for an agentic data science deployment
qualityWhy: The workflow is concrete, with phased steps, explicit halt points for user approval, and named docs and templates, though much of the detail depends on external Google documentation that the agent must fetch.
needs: Google Cloud APIs and IAM permissions
why: The skill is built around designing and deploying onto Google Cloud services such as Cloud Run and AlloyDB, which are cloud places to run and keep data, so it does not fit a local-first node. Its output would send the workload to a cloud backend rather than the node's own SQLite and storage elements.

summary: The skill guides an agent through SwiftUI animation work targeting iOS 26 and later: choosing between explicit withAnimation, scoped implicit animations, springs, transitions, PhaseAnimator and KeyframeAnimator choreography, matched geometry and navigation zoom, and SF Symbol effects. summary: Scaffolds course exercise folders for a section and exercise plan, with problem, solution and explainer variants, each holding a readme. fix lint errors in exercise directories

why: It only helps someone authoring a course repository built around the ai-hero-cli lint tool, which is not a product-building, content-for-sale or running-site use on a Fractera node. It is also written for a repository layout that the node does not provide.

summary: This skill guides an agent through scaling workloads on Google Kubernetes Engine: manual replica changes, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler setup on CPU, memory or external metrics, and Vertical Pod Autoscaler in its Off, Initial, Auto and InPlaceOrRecreate modes. It also gives a rightsizing procedure that compares recommendations with actual usage. The audience is operators who run their workloads on Google Cloud.

why: The skill administers cloud-hosted Kubernetes on Google Cloud, which is a cloud place to run workloads, so it does not fit a local-first node and is skipped.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing Terraform code to define cloud infrastructure on AWS, Azure, or GCP. summary: This skill tells an agent to scaffold a small local LangGraph agent in Python, a calculator-style math agent built with the Graph API, by following the official LangGraph quickstart page. summary: This skill sets up a Git pre-commit hook in an existing repository using Husky, so that staged files are formatted with Prettier through lint-staged.
