summary: This skill lets an agent amend an already published CLI in the public printing-press library. It can mine the current Claude Code session for friction such as missing flags or failed calls, or take user-supplied asks like renaming commands, adding feeds, or sniffing a site for endpoints. It also reads the Claude Code session transcript and pushes to a third-party repository, so it carries a risk and is skipped.

summary: This skill gives an agent a reference set of Kubernetes manifest patterns covering Deployments with probes, resource requests and limits, services and TLS ingress, ConfigMaps and Secrets, RBAC, autoscaling, disruption budgets, jobs, and a kubectl debugging cheatsheet. configure HPA and a PodDisruptionBudget for a web service

why: It is a deployment and operations reference for Kubernetes clusters, which a local-first node does not run, so its use on a node is occasional rather than central to building products. Its stack is plain Kubernetes rather than the node's own stack, so it fits as reading material and should be adapted to the node's Next.js and SQLite setup, not installed as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through scanning a software project, grouping its files into batches, and having sub-agents describe each file's functions, classes and imports. It depends on a full plugin checkout with a pnpm-built core package and on a sub-agent setup, so it must be installed with that plugin root present.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to set up and run cargo-fuzz on a Rust crate: initialise a fuzz folder, write a libFuzzer harness, choose sanitizers, check coverage and reproduce crash artifacts. It is aimed at developers who want to find memory-safety or panic bugs in Rust code, especially parsers and unsafe or FFI code. It is a developer testing workflow rather than a product feature.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to work with the Drizzle ORM in TypeScript: defining tables for several SQL dialects, declaring relations between them, and writing typed queries for reads, writes, joins and aggregates. summary: This skill guides an agent through designing, building and deploying AI agent or multi-agent systems on Google Cloud. summary: The skill guides an agent to write ad copy for Google Ads, Meta/Facebook, TikTok and LinkedIn. summary: Teaches an agent to build C, C++ or Rust code with AddressSanitizer enabled so memory errors such as buffer overflows and use-after-free show up during fuzzing or tests. why: It is a local compiler and testing technique with no outside service or account, so it fits a node that builds native code or fuzz targets, but it is only useful when the node has C, C++ or Rust code to test and is not a general web or content tool. summary: This skill is a router for Unity UI work: it picks between UI Toolkit, uGUI and IMGUI based on explicit keywords, file types or the project's existing code, and answers comparison questions directly. summary: This skill guides an agent through moving TypeScript test files away from `as` type assertions to the shoehorn library. summary: The skill guides an agent to sort and rename files by reading their content, proposing folder trees and consistent date-first naming patterns for documents, invoices, images and meeting notes. It also covers spotting duplicates and writing simple auto-organization rules. It is aimed at individuals tidying personal or project folders.

summary: This skill tells an agent to look for an existing library, runtime feature or repository function before writing new helper code, wrapper, tool or API client. It gives a table mapping common needs, such as utilities, date handling, retries, SQL and auth, to established packages. It is aimed at developers who want less code to maintain. The main body is short, and the detailed search method lives in a separate usecase file.
tasks: add a helper for grouping or chunking an array without writing it from scratch
pick a library for retries, dates or validation
wrap an external API client without writing a wrapper around existing code
check whether the project already has a function before adding a new one
qualityWhy: The rules are clear and the library mapping is concrete, but the body is short and the search method depends on a referenced file whose content was not included.
why: It is a general coding habit that helps any stack, but most of the library list assumes Effect, drizzle, better-auth and TanStack, which Fractera replaces with next-auth and its own SQLite element, so an agent should read it for ideas and apply them to the node's own stack. No risks were found.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building navigation for React Native apps with React Navigation 7. It covers stacks and modals, bottom and material top tabs, drawers, form sheets, header configuration, and safe-area insets. It helps mobile app developers choose the right navigator and follow its patterns, with a static-versus-dynamic API choice for new apps.
tasks: add tab navigation to a React Native app
set up a stack with modal screens
add a drawer or sidebar menu
fix safe-area and header inset problems
show a bottom sheet or form sheet
qualityWhy: The shown SKILL.md is a clear index that maps problems to references, but the reference files are not included, so the concrete steps and checks cannot be verified here.
why: React Navigation targets React Native mobile apps, while a Fractera node builds Next.js 16 web apps, so the patterns must be adapted to the node's own stack and cannot be installed as written. It is useful only for the occasional mobile project, and the reference files were not available to check.

summary: This skill lets an agent reconstruct what happened in one Agentforce conversation, using audit tables that Salesforce Data Cloud holds in the cloud. It pulls the session's steps, LLM calls, gateway requests, messages and feedback, joins them into a tree, and writes a readable summary. It can also search for sessions by time, agent, channel, outcome or text when the user has no session id. The intended users are Salesforce admins and engineers debugging Agentforce agents.
tasks: trace an Agentforce session by its id
summarize what an agent did in a conversation
find escalated Agentforce sessions from today
list recent sessions for a given agent or channel
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with exact commands, filters, output artifacts, validation rules and known caveats, though much of the logic sits in scripts that were not shown.
needs: Salesforce org with Data Cloud enabled
why: It reads Agentforce audit data from Salesforce's cloud Data Cloud service, which is administration of a vendor platform and not building, running or making content for a node's own product, so it does not fit a local-first node. It also needs the org's live access token, which is a credential the skill reads.
risks: Reads the sf CLI org access token via `sf org auth show-access-token` and uses it to call the Data Cloud API, so credentials are read and sent to Salesforce.

summary: The skill is a short Japanese guide that tells an agent how people read, think and pick up unstated cues, so the agent can write text that humans can actually follow and check its assumptions with the user. It fits when writing for people, asking for a decision, or interpreting a user's correction. It is a mindset note with no code, tools or setup steps.
tasks: write a document a person will read carefully
ask the user for a decision without losing their intent
interpret why the user corrected a specific sentence
check assumptions before acting on vague feedback
qualityWhy: The guidance is clear and well structured but stays at the level of general principles, with few concrete steps, examples or checks an agent can apply directly.
why: It is stack-free and useful now and then for how an agent writes for and consults people, but it does not build, run or sell anything on a node. It is a habit note, not a workflow, so its benefit is mainly indirect.

summary: This skill guides an agent through turning notes or markdown into a slide deck with a consistent visual style. It picks one of five brand looks (keynote, corporate, creative, financial, startup), maps headings, bullets, quotes, images and tables to slide layouts, and sets fonts, spacing and restrained transitions. It is aimed at founders, marketers and analysts who need a polished pitch, report or launch deck.
tasks: turn this markdown into a investor pitch deck
make a corporate report presentation from my notes
design a product launch slide deck in a keynote style
check a PowerPoint file for consistent fonts and colours
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed and well organised, but several referenced files (validate_consistency.py, CUSTOMIZATION.md, templates/brands/) are missing, and some promised features such as morph transitions and auto-charts go beyond what python-pptx can do.
why: Making decks for a product, sales or reports is a core use of a node, and the stack is local (python-pptx and a local MCP server) with no paid outside service. Doubts: the Smithery install runs a third-party npm package, the validator script is referenced but absent, and some animation claims may not be achievable with the named tools.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to edit video through conversation: it transcribes footage with word-level timestamps, proposes a cut plan for the user to approve, then assembles the edit with ffmpeg. It also covers color grading, subtitles, and short animated overlays. It is written for people making talking-head, tutorial, travel, or promo videos who want to describe the edit in plain language.
tasks: edit a talking-head video into a tight 60-second clip
burn word-level subtitles into an interview
color grade footage for a warm cinematic look
add an animated title overlay to a product demo
assemble the best takes from several recordings into one video
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with hard correctness rules, a step-by-step process, verification checks, and reusable briefs, but the helper scripts and install.md it depends on are not included in the files provided.
needs: ElevenLabs API key for Scribe transcription
Node.js 22+ if HyperFrames or Remotion slots are used
why: It directly serves making video content for social, landing pages, and promos, and it runs locally on the person's footage, but transcription sends the audio to the paid hosted ElevenLabs Scribe service. The helpers (transcribe.py, render.py, grade.py) and install.md are not among the files, so an agent cannot run it as written until they are present, and optional HyperFrames/Remotion setup uses npx --yes to fetch unpinned npm packages on demand.

summary: This skill makes an agent audit a project's source code for security flaws. It plans which vulnerability classes to check for each part of the code, such as injection, cross-site scripting, broken access control and SSRF, then dispatches scan workers over the candidate files. Each finding is verified before it is reported. It is aimed at developers who want a security review of their own application or library before release.
tasks: audit my code for security vulnerabilities
run a SAST scan on this repository
find injection or access-control flaws in my app
check my library for unsafe deserialization or path traversal
qualityWhy: The steps, output layout, verification checks and per-stack criteria files are concrete and followable, though the prompt files were not all read and the setup relies on a separate repo-context skill.
needs: Claude Code CLI (claude) with model access for the scan workers
git (optional, used for the commit hash in the output path)
why: It is stack-free and serves building and running a product by finding security flaws before release, with no cloud service needed. Scan output is written under the home directory (~/.ghost), outside the project, which the person should expect.

summary: The skill guides an agent through auditing FunC smart contracts on The Open Network (TON) for three platform-specific flaws: using positive integers as booleans, accepting Jetton transfer notifications without checking the sender, and forwarding TON without reserving gas. It asks the agent to grep contracts, check each pattern, and report every pattern with a verdict. It is aimed at security reviewers auditing TON contracts before launch.
tasks: audit a FunC contract for security flaws
check a Jetton transfer handler for fake deposits
review gas reserves in TON message forwarding
produce a TON contract security coverage report
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete grep searches, checklists, a finding template and test examples, though its sample tests use APIs that are not fully defined and the pattern details live in a separate file.
why: It serves a narrow audit need for TON developers rather than building, running or selling a product, so value is some; it is stack-free in the sense that it needs only local files and the FunC toolchain, so use is install. Nothing in the files runs remote code or touches secrets.

summary: The skill guides an agent to detect and rewrite patterns that make French text read like machine output, such as stock vocabulary, anglicisms, formulaic openings, uniform sentence length and mixed typography. It also asks the agent to inject voice and register-appropriate personality, and to clarify the target register before editing. It serves writers, editors and content makers who want natural French for articles, posts or pages.
tasks: humaniser un article de blog en français
enlever les tournures IA d'un texte
réécrire un post LinkedIn plus naturellement
corriger les anglicismes et la typographie française
qualityWhy: The skill is detailed and concrete, with many before/after examples, replacement tables and explicit checks, though it is long and somewhat repetitive.
why: Editing and humanizing French copy directly serves content creation and product text on a node, and it needs no outside service. It is a text-only instruction set that relies only on the agent's own reading and editing tools.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to work with Google's OSS-Fuzz fuzzing framework: running a single harness locally through its helper script, building fuzzers with sanitizers, and generating coverage reports. It also covers writing the project.yaml, Dockerfile and build.sh files needed to enrol a C, C++, Python or Rust library. The intended user is a maintainer of an open-source library who wants to find memory-safety bugs. Crash-report reproduction is named in the description but barely covered, and the acceptance criteria it promises are not in the file.
tasks: set up fuzzing for an open-source C library
run a fuzz harness locally with AddressSanitizer
write project.yaml, Dockerfile and build.sh for OSS-Fuzz enrollment
generate a fuzzing coverage report
qualityWhy: The commands and file templates are concrete and usable, but the skill leans on external links and tables and does not deliver the crash reproduction or acceptance criteria its description promises.
needs: Google OSS-Fuzz project enrollment and approval for continuous fuzzing
gsutil with Google Cloud Storage for coverage reports
why: Fuzzing is a useful developer activity for libraries that a node's products depend on, but it is niche for sites, apps, agents and content. The local helper path runs in Docker, while enrollment, continuous fuzzing and coverage hosting depend on Google's cloud, so the person should know that before installing.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing a quiz or scorecard funnel that captures leads before questions, scores answers into categories, and shows tier-specific results and follow-up emails. It is aimed at marketers and founders who want qualified leads from self-assessment tools. The files are instructional text with checklists, copy patterns and diagnostics, and include no code or scripts.
tasks: design a quiz funnel for lead generation
write scoring tiers and results pages for a self-assessment
create a lead magnet scorecard for my audience
plan tier-based follow-up emails for quiz leads
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear four-step system with checklists, diagnostics and common mistakes, though it leans on reference files for implementation detail and has no code examples.
why: It directly serves making lead-capture content for a product, and its guidance is platform-neutral text an agent can apply on a Fractera node with its own forms and Blocks. Its conversion benchmarks are unsourced and should be treated as claims, not facts.

summary: This skill walks an agent through setting up AFL++ and running multi-core fuzzing campaigns on C and C++ projects compiled with afl-clang-fast or afl-gcc-fast. It covers writing libFuzzer-style harnesses, seeding and minimizing the corpus, reading the status output, triaging crashes, and adding sanitizers. The intended users are security-minded developers who want to test mature native code for memory-safety bugs.
tasks: fuzz a C library with AFL++ across multiple cores
set up a libFuzzer-style harness for a C++ parser
minimize a fuzzing corpus after a campaign
triage crashes found by afl-fuzz
add ASan or UBSan to a fuzzing build
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands, decision trees, checks and troubleshooting tables, though several cross-referenced technique skills are not included in the files.
needs: Docker or a local AFL++ install
Linux host with root access for system tuning
why: Fuzzing native C/C++ code is useful for security testing but is not a core task for building sites, apps or content on a node. The skill also instructs disabling kernel security mitigations on the host, which makes it unsafe to run on a development machine.
risks: Tells the agent to run afl-persistent-config, update-grub and reboot, which turns off kernel security mitigations on the host machine.
Runs the fuzzing wrapper container with --privileged and mounts the working directory into it, which gives the container broad access to the host.

summary: This skill makes an agent run structured web research on a topic and deliver a cited Markdown report. It splits the work across parallel sub-agents, each covering one angle such as market size, competitors or regulation, and requires every claim to link to a source with a confidence level. Conflicting sources are flagged rather than silently resolved. It suits someone who needs a sourced analysis before a product, content or business decision.
tasks: research a topic and write a cited report
analyze competitors for a new product
size a market and map its segments
run a literature review on a research question
do due diligence on a company or person
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and complete, with a step-by-step workflow, sub-agent prompt template, citation format, confidence ladder and report structure, though one guardrail refers to a non-existent 'additional round' in Step 5 and only SKILL.md was reviewed.
why: It is a stack-free research method that fits a node's content and market-research needs, but it is not a build tool for the product itself. It needs only built-in web access and no keys or accounts, and its file writes stay in the project's ./research folder.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up Atheris, a coverage-guided fuzzer for Python built on libFuzzer, and writing harnesses for pure Python code or Python C extensions. It covers TestOneInput entry points, FuzzedDataProvider for structured input, compiling extensions with clang and AddressSanitizer, corpus handling and reading run output. It is aimed at developers hunting crashes and memory corruption in Python packages.
tasks: fuzz a Python package for crashes
hunt memory corruption in a Python C extension
write a fuzzing harness with FuzzedDataProvider
choose between Atheris and Hypothesis for testing
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete harness code, install steps, a Dockerfile, sanitizer settings, and a troubleshooting table, with a few gaps such as no full worked campaign walkthrough.
why: Fuzzing a Python package or its C extensions is useful for quality and security work, but it is not a core part of building or running a Fractera site, app or content flow, so use is occasional. It is stack-free in the sense that it only needs a local Python toolchain and clang, so it can be installed as written.

summary: Walks an agent through scaffolding a small local LangChain agent in TypeScript by fetching the official quickstart page and following it. It asks the person which model provider to use, works in a fresh directory, keeps the API key in a gitignored .env file the person edits themselves, and runs the example before stopping. It is aimed at people who want to try a LangChain agent on their own machine.
tasks: build a small LangChain agent in TypeScript
try a LangChain agent locally
scaffold a weather agent with createAgent
switch the agent to a different model provider
qualityWhy: The skill is short and clear about constraints, but it defers all concrete steps to an external docs page and gives no commands, files or checks of its own.
needs: an LLM provider API key, such as OpenAI, Anthropic or Google
why: It is a one-time learning scaffold rather than a tool for building or running a product, so its use is occasional; it depends on a model provider the person pays for and on the live docs page being reachable. Its constraints (local directory, key in .env, no LangSmith or Tavily) keep it local-first.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing Cairo smart contracts on StarkNet for six platform-specific flaws: felt252 overflow, L1-L2 address conversion, message cancellation gaps, overconstrained bridge coupling, signature replay, and unchecked from_address in L1 handlers. It requires a coverage table with a verdict for every pattern, so a reader can see what was checked. It is aimed at security reviewers and developers of StarkNet projects before launch.
tasks: audit a StarkNet bridge contract
check Cairo code for felt252 overflow
review L1 handler from_address validation
scan Cairo project with Caracal
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete steps, grep commands, checklists, a finding template and a required coverage table, though some sections are thin, such as the example output which is a placeholder.
why: The skill is a security audit guide for Cairo/StarkNet contracts, which Fractera does not run; a Cairo audit is outside what a local-first node is built for, so the skill is not useful for building, running or making content on this node. It also installs Caracal from a git source via cargo, which is a build step the person would have to trust.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to build durable, resumable workflows with Vercel's Workflow SDK, splitting logic into orchestrating workflow functions and retryable step functions. It covers pausing for external events through hooks and webhooks, starting child runs, streaming output, error classes, serialization of class instances, Vitest-based testing, and inspecting runs via the CLI and World API. It is aimed at developers who want long-running, multi-step processes that survive restarts.
tasks: build a durable multi-step order processing workflow
pause a workflow until an approval webhook arrives
add retries and error handling to a background job
stream progress from a long-running agent run to the client
inspect and cancel a stuck workflow run
qualityWhy: It gives concrete rules, code examples, API signatures, limits and checks for a complex SDK, though some sections lean on pointing to external docs.
why: The skill is built for Vercel's own Workflow SDK and hosted runs, which a local-first node would have to adapt; the Vercel World backend and dashboard links are cloud-side, so only the local World path fits the node. Read it for patterns, then build with the node's own stack.

summary: This skill makes an agent run a competitive exploration: it spawns several parallel candidate attempts at the same task, has a separate model judge them against a rubric, picks the strongest one as a base, and ports the best parts of the losing attempts into it. It targets non-trivial artifacts where a single first attempt might lock in the wrong design. The skill is aimed at developers and agent operators who want more deliberate output on complex work.
tasks: compare several designs for a new feature before committing
explore different approaches to a complex component
pick the best draft from multiple parallel attempts
merge the strongest ideas from alternative implementations
qualityWhy: The phases are clear and ordered, but the file is heavily tied to Cursor-specific rules files and model-routing config, and it gives few concrete examples or checks an agent could follow without that setup.
why: It is a general workflow for picking among drafts, not a stack-specific tool, so it is useful now and then for building features on a node. It depends on Cursor rule files (~/.cursor/rules/pstack-models.mdc) and pstack skill names, and it points to other skills and an adapter doc, so an agent on a node would need to adapt it rather than install it as written.

summary: The skill guides an agent through a weekly customer discovery routine built on Opportunity Solution Trees, assumption mapping, and short story-based interview snapshots. It is aimed at product teams (product manager, designer, engineer together) who want to keep decisions tied to fresh customer evidence. It also covers experience mapping, prioritizing opportunities, and building the habit into ongoing delivery work.
tasks: set up a weekly customer interview routine
build an opportunity solution tree from our outcome
test the riskiest assumption before building a feature
rank our top product opportunities against each other
qualityWhy: The skill has clear sections, decision tables, a diagnostic scoring rubric and pointers to reference files, though it is mostly conceptual and gives few concrete commands or templates inside SKILL.md itself.
why: It is a stack-free method guide with no code, so it is useful for planning and product work, but it is not about building or running a node's app, sites or content directly. It is marked "ideas" rather than "install" because it describes a discovery practice, not a tool for the node's own stack, and it leans on other skills for interview technique and team structure.

summary: This skill is a reference guide for building a Discord bot that handles community tasks: setup, slash commands, auto-moderation, welcome messages, reaction roles, ticket channels, scheduled posts, and AI chat or image replies. It is written for server admins and developers who want a bot to run their Discord community. Most of the content is YAML-style outline rather than runnable code.
tasks: set up a Discord bot for my server
add auto-moderation for spam and banned words
post a welcome message when members join
schedule a daily question in a channel
add an AI chat assistant to my Discord
qualityWhy: Most of the body is YAML-like outline with placeholders and no working implementation, and the only real code is a short discord.js snippet without setup or error handling.
needs: Discord developer application and bot token
OpenAI API key for the AI chat and image features
why: A Discord bot is a messaging channel for community and notifications rather than a cloud place to keep data, so it is useful now and then for a product's community. It calls the Discord API and optionally OpenAI, which needs the person's own accounts and keys. The guide is thin, so an agent would have to fill in most of the implementation itself.

summary: This skill guides an agent through turning a technology product's launch from an early-adopter niche into a mainstream market. It walks through choosing one narrow beachhead segment, assembling a complete whole product through partners, positioning as evolution rather than revolution, and then expanding through adjacent segments. It is written for founders and go-to-market teams selling technical products to businesses.
tasks: plan a go-to-market strategy for a technical product
choose a beachhead customer segment
map whole product gaps and partners
reposition messaging for pragmatist buyers
plan expansion into adjacent segments
qualityWhy: The skill gives clear steps, tables, formulas, a scoring diagnostic and reference files, though much of it is conceptual with few executable checks.
why: It is a stack-free strategy framework that helps plan launches and messaging for a product sold on a node, so it is useful now and then rather than for building the node itself. It has no install or runtime dependencies and no outside service calls.

summary: The skill guides an agent through configuring Grafana Alerting, Grafana Incident Response Management and SLOs. It covers creating contact points, notification policy routing trees, silences, alert rules in several formats, IRM integrations with on-call routing, and multi-window burn-rate SLO alerts. It is aimed at engineers who operate Grafana monitoring and need alerts routed to the right people.
tasks: set up a Slack or PagerDuty alert for errors
route critical alerts to the on-call team
define an SLO with burn-rate alerts
debug why an alert is not firing
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete YAML, curl commands, verification steps and a clear workflow, with reference files for depth, though some details rely on the referenced files.
why: Useful for monitoring and alerting a product built on a node, but it is about operating a Grafana server rather than building the node itself, and it calls external services such as Slack and PagerDuty that the person must set up.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing and editing Japanese prose, including documentation, commit messages, READMEs, articles and novels. It stresses deciding what each edit protects in the text rather than applying style rules mechanically, and it separates document types such as procedures, reference material and explanations. It also gives a set of article formats, from research notes to essays, each with its own structure. It is written for a writer who wants clear, non-repetitive text that a reader can follow in one pass.
tasks: rewrite a README so people know whether to use the project
edit an AI-sounding or wordy Japanese draft
turn a chat with Claude into a published article
write a blog post or essay in a chosen article format
tighten documentation and commit messages
qualityWhy: The principles are concrete, with per-type usecase files and a clear decision for choosing an article type, but many passages are abstract and it leans on referenced skills that are not bundled.
why: It is stack-free and directly helps write product docs, READMEs, landing copy and content for social or blog posts, though it is Japanese-focused and tuned to one author's article types. It points to two external skills (humanity-and-humanness and japanese) that are not in the bundle, so an agent will have less guidance unless those are installed too.

summary: This skill tells a coding agent how to work on a repository safely: read the relevant code before editing, keep changes inside the agreed scope, and plan more carefully when a change is risky. It requires that a claim of "done" or "fixed" rest on test, type-check or build output seen in the same session. It also includes helper scripts that detect the project language, find its test commands and run them. It is aimed at developers and the agents that help them build and maintain software.
tasks: fix a failing test in the project and prove it passes
refactor a module without changing its behavior
review a change for risky or unverified edits
debug an error and verify the fix before reporting it
run the project's type check, lint and tests before a release
qualityWhy: The rules, output formats and verification ladder are concrete, but the enforcement pieces it names (a gravitas CLI, hooks, contract.json, gravitas_verify) are not in the folder, so much of it is guidance without the tooling behind it.
why: It is a stack-free workflow for building, debugging and verifying code, which is what a node's agents do, so it fits without changes and needs no outside service. Doubts: the scripts import a helper from a plugin path outside the skill and fall back silently when it is missing, and the eslint check in verify.sh uses a glob test that never matches, so it skips lint without saying so.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing motivation systems for products, teams and gamification, built on autonomy, mastery and purpose. It gives a scoring rubric and diagnostic for existing engagement loops, and warns against if-then reward schemes that crowd out intrinsic drive. It is aimed at product designers, managers and founders whose users or staff have gone disengaged.
tasks: fix broken gamification
design onboarding progression
audit a motivation system
reduce team disengagement
replace points-based rewards with intrinsic design
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is concrete, with a scoring rubric, tables, a diagnostic and common mistakes, and it points to reference files for depth, though the examples are mostly conceptual rather than step-by-step procedures.
why: It is a stack-free design framework, so it fits a node for planning engagement features in apps and sites, but it is not a build tool and will not produce code or content directly. No risks found in the files.

summary: The skill guides an agent to parse PDFs, Word files, PowerPoint decks, images and HTML with the docling library, returning markdown, plain text, JSON, tables as dataframes, and extracted figures. It is aimed at people who need structured content from documents such as reports, papers or contracts. The file is mostly code snippets, with a short overview and limitations section.
tasks: parse this PDF and extract all tables
convert this academic paper to structured markdown
extract figures and captions from a document
batch convert a folder of reports to markdown
qualityWhy: Useful code examples, but several snippets use attributes that are not verified (element.type, element.caption, element.image), the front matter description is broken (">"), and there are no checks or error handling for the agent to follow.
why: Document parsing helps when a node's content pipeline needs to read incoming files, but it does not directly build or publish a product, so value is some. It runs locally with a Python library and needs no account or key, so install is fine, though the agent should verify the docling API against the installed version before trusting the snippets.

summary: This skill nudges an agent to notice when it is writing the same instruction again or fixing the same mistake repeatedly. Instead of adding more text, the agent should turn the lesson into a lint rule, metadata flag, runtime check or script. When a lesson needs judgment and cannot be encoded, the agent should make the instruction more prominent and add an example of the failure. It is aimed at developers and agents maintaining a codebase or a set of working instructions.
tasks: stop repeating the same correction in the instructions
turn a recurring review comment into a lint rule
add a runtime check for a mistake that keeps happening
decide whether a lesson belongs in code or in prose
qualityWhy: It states a sound principle with one clear corollary, but gives no steps, examples or checks for how to pick or build the structural fix.
why: It is a stack-free working habit that can help an agent keep a node's code and instructions clean, but it is short and only occasionally useful. Its disable-model-invocation flag means it is applied only when explicitly invoked.

summary: This skill gives an agent a periodic, human-supervised cleanup routine for a Claude Code configuration folder. It scans skills, memory files, hooks, permission entries, MCP servers, scheduled jobs and caches for duplicates, orphans and stale items, then proposes a small ranked batch. Each deletion is confirmed one at a time, moved to a trash folder or renamed rather than erased, and logged with undo steps. It is aimed at people who want a slimmer, tidier Claude Code setup.
tasks: clean up my Claude Code config
audit my skills and hooks for stale items
reduce redundant permission entries in settings
run a periodic config review with undo logging
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear channel-by-channel scan method, a one-at-a-time confirmation workflow, concrete shell examples and explicit anti-patterns, with only minor gaps such as no check for the memory index format.
why: It maintains the Claude Code setup itself, which is useful now and then for a node's developer environment, but it does not build, run or sell a product. It is stack-free and runs locally with no outside service, and it only touches ~/.claude and the project's .claude folder, deleting nothing without confirmation.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to check a cryptographic implementation against Project Wycheproof test vectors, which encode known attacks and edge cases for AES-GCM, ECDSA, ECDH, RSA, EdDSA and similar constructions. It covers fetching the JSON files, loading and filtering test groups, mapping valid, invalid and acceptable result flags onto pass and fail expectations, and reading failures. It is aimed at developers and auditors who build or review crypto code.
tasks: test my AES-GCM implementation against Wycheproof vectors
check an ECDSA verifier for signature malleability
find out why two crypto libraries disagree on the same input
set up a CI test harness for crypto test vectors
qualityWhy: It gives concrete loader code, a parameterized harness and a case study with fix steps, though some harness logic is partly incomplete and the related-skills tables point to other skills.
why: It is a stack-free testing method for crypto code, useful when building or auditing a node's crypto, but it is not a core part of building sites or content, so value is some. Its examples use Python and JavaScript test frameworks, so an agent must adapt them to the node's TypeScript stack, which may need a judgment call. The skill makes no network calls beyond fetching public test files from GitHub.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to read Culture Index behavioral survey results, either from a PDF run through an OpenCV extraction script or from a JSON file, and interpret traits by distance from the population arrow rather than absolute scores. It covers individual profiles, team gas/brake/glue balance, burnout signals from Survey versus Job graphs, hiring profiles, manager coaching, interview-based trait prediction, debriefs, onboarding and conflict mediation. It is aimed at HR and people-management staff, not at building or running a product.
tasks: interpret a Culture Index PDF profile
compare a team's behavioral profiles for gaps
check a employee for burnout using survey versus job graphs
draft a hiring profile for a role
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, with routing tables, verification steps, reference files and a working extraction script, though the large amount of domain content is only partly visible here.
why: It is an HR and people-assessment skill about analysing employees and candidates, which does not serve building, running, selling or making content for a product on a local-first node. Its only input is a local PDF or JSON, so there is no cloud dependency, but the purpose falls outside what nodes are for.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing Substrate and FRAME pallets for seven platform-specific flaws: arithmetic overflow, panics that halt block processing, incorrect weights, storage writes before validation, unsigned transaction handling, weak randomness, and wrong origin checks. qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, syntax templates, version gates, fallbacks and error-handling rules that an agent can follow closely.
needs: an Elasticsearch cluster (self-managed or Elastic Cloud)
elastic CLI configured with cluster credentials
why: Elasticsearch is a separate database engine, and the node keeps its data in its own SQLite element, so the skill cannot be used as written; its query techniques are useful as ideas. Several features need a Platinum licence or newer versions, and the skill assumes a cluster the node does not provide.

summary: The skill guides an agent through reserving remote Android devices on Google's Developer Device Platform, using gcloud and REST calls to create, check, extend and cancel device sessions. It also sets up an ADB tunnel so the agent or a developer can control the remote phone from a local terminal. It is aimed at developers who need real or virtual Android hardware for testing apps.
tasks: reserve a remote Android device for testing
connect adb to a cloud Android phone
extend a device session lease
cancel a reserved device session
check status of my device sessions
qualityWhy: The skill gives ordered steps, exact curl references and checks such as polling session state and confirming billing, though some parts defer to linked files and it is in Preview.
needs: Device Streaming API enabled on a Google Cloud project
why: It manages hosted Google Cloud device sessions and billing rather than local data, so it is a cloud administration tool that the local-first node should skip.

summary: This skill gives an agent the layering, file-organization, documentation, testability and concurrency rules for a macOS Swift codebase split into Swift Packages. It tells the agent how to decide package boundaries, inject dependencies through initializers, keep one major type per file, and avoid forbidden Swift 6 concurrency primitives. It is written for engineers refactoring or adding Swift code inside that one app, not for web or content work.
tasks: split a large Swift app target into packages
review Swift code for concurrency and layering rules
add a new Swift package with DocC documentation
qualityWhy: The rules are concrete, with named types, commands and checks, but they are tied to one repository's layout and scripts, so they are not usable as a general guide.
needs: PostHog, only for the feature-flag rule
why: It is Swift and macOS architecture guidance, which does not help build, run, sell or make content for a Next.js web node, so it has no value here and should not be installed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through moving a web app, such as one built on Lovable, Bolt.new or Replit, or a static or server-rendered frontend, onto AWS. It handles sign-in, uploads the source to a hosted analysis service, reviews a migration plan and cost estimate with the owner, then downloads generated AWS Blocks infrastructure code to apply locally. It is aimed at people who want their app hosted on AWS rather than on their own machine.
tasks: move my vibe-coded app to AWS
migrate my React site to AWS hosting
estimate the monthly cost of hosting my app on AWS
deploy my Replit app with AWS infrastructure
qualityWhy: The steps, commands, confirmation gates and failure paths are concrete and easy for an agent to follow, though some scripts were truncated and could not be fully checked.
needs: an AWS account for the final deployment
why: The skill is built around hosting and running the app on AWS (S3, CloudFront, Lambda, Cognito, Aurora), which the node's local-first rule treats as value none and use skip. Its source upload to a hosted AWS service is disclosed and gated on approval.
risks: Uploads the user's source code to a hosted AWS service, with filtering of secret files that is only best effort.
Downloads a remote migration snapshot, overlays it into the user's repository, and tells the agent to follow its DEPLOY.md to deploy into the user's AWS account.

summary: The skill walks an agent through connecting an OpenTelemetry collector to a Managed ClickStack service on ClickHouse Cloud. It either deploys a local ClickStack collector via Docker or Compose, or adds a ClickHouse exporter to an existing collector. It creates a restricted ingest SQL user, sends synthetic logs, traces and metrics, and checks that rows land in the otel database. It is written for people operating observability for their own services.
tasks: connect my OpenTelemetry collector to ClickStack
set up a local collector with Docker Compose for ClickHouse Cloud
verify telemetry is visible in ClickStack
create a restricted ingest user for OTLP data
qualityWhy: Very detailed and concrete, with ordered steps, exact config, error symptoms and verification queries, though it is long and some steps assume the clickhousectl CLI is installed.
why: ClickStack on ClickHouse Cloud is a cloud database and backend, so the skill is built around a cloud place to keep data, which the local-first node does not allow. It also creates a cloud DB user and needs a cloud Admin API key, so it is skipped.
risks: Installs clickhousectl by piping a remote curl script into sh, which runs remote code.
Writes the ClickHouse Cloud API key and secret into a creds.env file and handles secrets in a shell workflow.
Sends telemetry and creates users on a third-party cloud service the person may not have chosen.

summary: This skill turns an AI agent into a self-improving system: it reviews the agent's past runs, looks for repeated failures or slow steps, and proposes or applies code changes to fix them. It reaches the EvoMap Hub only through a local proxy mailbox, which can share and fetch reusable improvement assets. It is aimed at people who run autonomous agents and want those agents to tune themselves over time.
tasks: analyze agent run history for recurring failures
propose fixes for slow or error-prone agent steps
share a tested improvement with the EvoMap hub
search the hub for existing fixes to a known error
qualityWhy: The file lists many endpoints and configuration options clearly, but it gives no concrete step-by-step evolution workflow, examples of a successful run, or checks for verifying a change before it is applied.
needs: EvoMap Hub (evomap.ai) access through the local proxy
GITHUB_TOKEN (optional, for issue reporting and releases)
why: It modifies the agent's own code and sends assets to an outside hub, which does not serve building, running or selling a local product, and the data sent is not clearly described.
risks: During solidify it writes changes to the person's src/ code automatically, and self-modification is on by default in the workflow unless the flag is set off.
It publishes assets and reports to evomap.ai and possibly GitHub issues via GITHUB_TOKEN without spelling out exactly what content leaves the machine.
The hard rollback mode runs git reset --hard, which can discard the person's uncommitted work.

summary: This skill walks a life-sciences researcher through a first orientation to the bio-research plugin. It checks which literature, drug-discovery and visualization servers are connected, lists the bundled analysis skills, and points to optional binary servers. It then asks what the researcher wants to do and suggests starting points. Its audience is scientists setting up a research workspace, not people building products.
tasks: orient myself in the bio-research plugin
check which literature and drug databases are connected
list available single-cell and sequencing analysis skills
suggest a starting workflow for a new research project
qualityWhy: It is mostly a menu that names other skills and servers without concrete checks, commands or steps an agent could verify, so it is closer to a pointer than an instruction.
why: Its subject is bioinformatics and biology research, which a Fractera node is not built for: sites, web apps, AI agents and content for products. It depends on external research databases and optional binary downloads that a local-first node would not normally use. The download step is optional and only fetches files, so it is not a stated risk, but the skill has no use for a node.

summary: This skill guides an agent to design scheduled data pipelines that pull records from databases, APIs and SaaS tools, clean and reshape them, and load them into warehouses, sheets or files. It is written as reference notes and YAML-style templates rather than runnable steps. It suits analysts or operators who want recurring reports and data syncs.
tasks: build a daily sales data pipeline
clean and merge orders with payments data
load query results into a spreadsheet on a schedule
add data quality checks to an ETL job
set up failure alerts for a data sync
qualityWhy: It is mostly a generic outline with pseudo-YAML templates and no executable steps, commands, or verification procedure an agent can follow exactly.
why: Pipelines are useful for reporting, but the skill assumes cloud warehouses, cloud file storage and n8n rather than the node's own SQLite element, so it must be adapted to the node's data layer before use. The outside services it names are the person's choice and it does not hide data movement, so no risk is listed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through finding and removing duplicated code in a codebase, at three levels: copy-pasted blocks, shared logic across packages, and trivial wrapper functions. It also covers spotting concept-level duplication, where one domain rule is implemented in several places, and consolidating it into a single owner module. The steps rely on the indexion command-line tool for detection, followed by test runs to verify the fixes. It is aimed at developers maintaining MoonBit-style codebases.
tasks: remove duplicated code across modules
extract shared code into a common package
clean up trivial wrapper functions
consolidate scattered domain logic into one module
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete commands, option tables, phased workflow, and verification steps, though it assumes the indexion tool and MoonBit toolchain are present and some sections are descriptive rather than fully step-by-step.
why: The skill is built around the indexion and MoonBit toolchain, which does not match a Fractera node's TypeScript, Next.js and SQLite stack, so it is not a fit for what nodes are for. Its code examples and commands target .mbt files, so it would need adaptation to the node's stack, and it is not a direct help for building or running sites, apps or content.

summary: The skill guides an agent to find the open pull request for the current git branch and go through its review comments, conversation comments and inline review threads. A bundled Python script pulls all of them through the GitHub CLI's GraphQL API, then the agent lists them with numbers, asks which to fix, and applies the chosen fixes. It is aimed at developers working on code review feedback.
tasks: address review comments on my pull request
list the open review threads on this branch's PR
apply fixes for the comments I select on my GitHub PR
check whether gh is logged in before fetching PR comments
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and the script is concrete, but the SKILL.md is short and gives no details on how to apply fixes or verify them.
why: It serves a git hosting workflow, not building, running, selling or making content for a node's product, so value is none and it is skipped. The skill is otherwise sound, but it is out of scope for what nodes are for.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of Slack automation patterns: a daily async standup bot, an expense approval flow with buttons, onboarding and incident channels, and posts triggered by CRM, payment or code events. It is written for operations and team leads who want notifications and routine coordination in Slack. Most of the content is descriptive configuration with message templates rather than step-by-step setup.
tasks: set up a daily async standup in Slack
route expense approval requests to managers
post deal-won or payment-failed alerts to a channel
create an incident channel when an alert fires
qualityWhy: It is mostly pseudo-YAML and sample messages with no setup, authentication or verification steps, so an agent cannot reliably execute the workflows as written.
needs: Slack workspace and a Slack app or bot token for slack-mcp
HubSpot, Stripe, GitHub or Jira accounts only if those integrations are used
why: Slack is an outside messaging service, not a place where node data is kept, and the skill mainly serves team operations rather than building or selling a product, so the value is only occasional. The workflows need a Slack account and a token, and several steps (reminders, timeouts, archiving) are described without an explicit mechanism.

summary: This skill lets an agent connect WhatsApp to a product through Kapso's hosted platform. It walks through onboarding customers with setup links, detecting when a number is connected, and receiving events through signed webhooks. It also covers sending text, templates, interactive messages and media, reading conversations, and building WhatsApp Flows with optional data endpoints. The intended users are developers and small teams who want WhatsApp as a messaging channel for their app.
tasks: connect a customer's WhatsApp number to my app
send a WhatsApp order-status template message
receive incoming WhatsApp messages with a webhook
build and publish a WhatsApp Flow form
show the WhatsApp inbox inside my dashboard
qualityWhy: It gives concrete CLI commands, payload assets, verification steps, troubleshooting and a clear map of scripts and references that an agent can follow directly.
needs: Meta WhatsApp Business account (WABA) and a WhatsApp phone number, connected through Kapso setup links
why: WhatsApp messaging is a direct channel for selling and serving users, so it fits what nodes are for, but it depends on Kapso's hosted platform: messages, webhooks, functions and Flow data pass through a third party, and some functions run on Kapso's cloud. Several script files were not visible, so their exact behaviour is unverified, though the SKILL.md itself handles credentials and redirects carefully.

summary: This skill guides an agent through diagnosing why a large AI/ML training job run as a JobSet on Google Kubernetes Engine keeps restarting or getting interrupted. The agent checks restart counters, spot preemptions and node-pool events, unhealthy nodes and their physical hosts, and coordinator worker logs, then suggests fixes such as moving to on-demand capacity or replacing a faulty host. It is written for engineers running training clusters on Google Cloud.
tasks: diagnose a JobSet restart loop on GKE
find out why spot VMs keep preempting my training job
check whether a faulty host VM is failing coordinator pods
review Cloud Logging for node-pool interruption events
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete, ordered queries and diagnostic logic for each step, though the validation script's checks are partly inconsistent and it leaves some resolution details thin.
needs: Google Cloud project with a GKE cluster
Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring enabled
why: The skill depends entirely on Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring, which are cloud hosting and cloud administration rather than something a local-first node runs, so it is not useful for building, running or making content on a node.

summary: The skill guides an agent through adding zero-code observability to an application using Grafana Beyla, an eBPF-based tool that captures HTTP, gRPC and database traffic without code changes or restarts. It covers running Beyla under Docker, deploying it as a cluster-wide Kubernetes DaemonSet, and exporting traces and Prometheus metrics via OTLP or Grafana Cloud through Alloy. It is aimed at operators who need to instrument services they cannot recompile, such as closed-source binaries.
tasks: instrument a closed-source binary without code changes
add tracing and RED metrics to a running service
deploy Beyla as a Kubernetes DaemonSet
send eBPF telemetry to Grafana Cloud via Alloy
qualityWhy: The instructions give concrete Docker and kubectl commands with verification steps and point to reference files for full YAML, though the main file itself is brief.
why: Observability for running services is only occasionally relevant to building and running a node's own site or app, and the skill is built around an operator-level eBPF agent that requires privileged host access. It is not a cloud-only service, but its privileged setup makes it unsuitable to install as written on a node.
risks: Requires privileged containers, host PID namespace and CAP_SYS_ADMIN, which gives the agent broad control over the host system if followed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through Aurora DSQL, AWS's serverless PostgreSQL-compatible database: creating and deleting clusters, connecting with psql using generated IAM tokens, designing multi-tenant schemas, running safe parameterized queries, performing table-recreation and MySQL-to-DSQL migrations, and diagnosing slow query plans. It is written for developers building apps on AWS's managed cloud database. It is heavily oriented to AWS cloud infrastructure and cluster administration.
tasks: create an Aurora DSQL cluster and connect with psql
design a multi-tenant schema with safe queries
migrate a MySQL schema to DSQL
diagnose a slow query plan
qualityWhy: The files are detailed and concrete, with steps, code examples, validator rules and checks, though much of it is tied to AWS-specific tooling.
why: Aurora DSQL is a cloud-hosted database and cluster administration is an AWS cloud service, which a local-first Fractera node must not rely on, so value is none and use is skip.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of planning templates for HR workflows: candidate pipelines, AI resume scoring, interview scheduling, new-hire onboarding, time-off approvals, performance review cycles, and offboarding with access revocation. It is written as pseudo-YAML outlines for HR staff and recruiters at companies, not as runnable instructions. It names outside HR and collaboration SaaS products as the systems to connect to.
tasks: design a new-hire onboarding checklist
set up a candidate screening pipeline
plan a quarterly performance review cycle
automate time-off approval routing
outline an employee offboarding and access revocation process
qualityWhy: It is mostly vague YAML outlines with no concrete commands, code, file formats, or verification steps an agent could follow to build anything.
needs: openai api key for ai resume screening
why: HR process automation built around cloud HRIS and recruiting SaaS serves a company's internal HR operations, not building, running, selling, or making content for a product on a local-first node, so value is none and use is skip.
risks: Describes sending candidates' resumes to a third-party AI model and moving tax, banking and ID documents through outside SaaS tools without telling the people involved.

summary: This skill guides an agent through fixing alerts from snyk-agent-scan, a scanner that checks agent skill files for risky patterns. It covers rewording instructions that point at external content, moving install commands, and removing MCP tool names from the body, so the scan passes without deleting information. It is aimed at people who write or maintain agent skills and need their scans or CI pipelines to pass.
tasks: fix snyk-agent-scan alerts in a skill
rewrite a skill body so the scanner passes
triage a failed skill scan in CI
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear rules, a fix order, a re-scan loop and a pre-authoring checklist, though the detailed patterns sit in reference files that were only partly reviewed.
why: It only helps a node that authors agent skills for its catalog, not sites, apps or content, so its value is limited. It is marked skip because its guidance teaches rewording and moving commands to frontmatter, which the skill itself says the scanner does not check; that can hide real risks from the safety scan.
risks: Advises moving install commands into frontmatter because the scanner does not flag it, which can conceal real risky patterns from the safety check.

summary: This skill guides an agent to turn a topic, outline or rough notes into a full slide deck, with a sensible structure of title, agenda, content, summary and closing slides. It also shows how to write the result as Marp markdown so it can be rendered into slides. It is aimed at people who need talks, pitch decks or training material without building slides by hand. The guidance is mostly general, and the example code is a sketch with placeholder functions rather than a working generator.
tasks: make a 10-slide deck about a topic
draft a pitch deck for a startup
turn rough notes into training slides
build a quarterly review presentation
qualityWhy: The structure advice is reasonable, but the Python sketch calls undefined functions, the outline stub is empty, and the Marp converter never emits content slides, so an agent has little concrete procedure to follow.
why: Slide and deck creation fits the node's content-making purpose, and the Marp output stays local as plain markdown, but it is not a core feature. The skill names an office-mcp server with create_pptx and add_slide tools, which a node may not have, so an agent would need to check that before relying on it.

summary: Gives an agent patterns for writing unit tests of Jakarta Bean Validation (JSR-380) constraints using JUnit 5 and Hibernate Validator, without a Spring context. It covers built-in constraints, custom ConstraintValidator tests, cross-field checks, validation groups and parameterized tests. Aimed at developers who want fast checks that DTO and request data rules hold.
tasks: write unit tests for DTO validation annotations
test a custom constraint validator
check password confirmation matches in a form object
add parameterized tests for email and age rules
qualityWhy: Gives clear setup, runnable Java examples, a step list, pitfalls and troubleshooting, though the reference files were not fully reviewed and some assertions depend on default messages.
why: The node is for building Next.js, TypeScript and React products, and this skill targets Java unit tests with Maven, so it does not fit the node's stack. It is a Java-specific testing guide, not something a Fractera node uses.

summary: This skill gives an agent a fixed four-step discipline for debugging: first build a reliable, fast reproduction, then narrow down where the code fails using a debugger, tracing, or instrumentation, then try to disprove candidate causes before accepting them, and finally check every experiment against the whole session's history. It is meant for anyone who reports a broken feature, error or stack trace. It also requires reciting a fixed block of text at the start of a session.
tasks: diagnose why a feature throws an error
reproduce an intermittent bug reliably
investigate a stack trace from logs
narrow down the root cause of a failing test
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and ordered, but the skill is a general methodology with no concrete examples, checks or stack-specific commands for a Next.js project.
why: It is a stack-free debugging habit that fits any Fractera node project, so it is useful when something breaks, though it adds little beyond good practice and requires a fixed recital at session start.

summary: The file is a redirect notice: this repository no longer develops the serp-analysis skill and points readers to an active copy in a different bundle, plus a frozen standalone copy at a tagged version. It gives an install command for the bundled version. An agent reading only this file learns where to fetch the real instructions but gets no SERP analysis steps itself.
tasks: find the current serp-analysis skill
install serp-analysis from the marketing skills bundle
locate the frozen standalone serp-analysis copy
qualityWhy: The file is only a signpost with no instructions of its own, so it is a wrapper that just points elsewhere.
why: The skill carries no SERP analysis guidance and only redirects to other repositories, so there is nothing for a Fractera node to use directly. It is also an external install pointer rather than a stack-free instruction set.

summary: The skill guides an agent to pull tables out of PDF documents with the camelot Python library, choosing between lattice mode for bordered tables and stream mode for borderless ones. It covers page selection, table area and column options, checking accuracy scores, visual debugging, and exporting results to CSV, Excel, JSON or HTML. It is aimed at people who need structured data from reports, invoices or research papers.
tasks: extract all tables from this PDF report
get the table on page 5 as Excel
pull line items from an invoice PDF
convert borderless PDF tables to CSV
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete code for each mode, options, exports and batch patterns, but it has a broken YAML description, some example code that would not run as written, and little on error handling.
why: Table extraction from PDFs helps with document-to-data work, but it is a narrow parsing task rather than a core building feature; it runs locally with no outside service. Its metadata refers to an office-mcp tool that a node does not provide, so the agent should rely on the Python code instead.

summary: This skill guides an agent in building a custom sidebar for the cmux terminal app from a plain-language request. The agent writes a SwiftUI-style file into the user's config folder, validates it against live workspace data, selects it, and iterates with hot reload. It is aimed at people who want a personal sidebar showing workspaces, tabs, PRs or a clock, and who should not need to know the syntax.
tasks: build a custom sidebar that lists my workspaces
add a clock and PR status to my sidebar
make a sidebar I can jump between tabs with
fix a blank or broken custom sidebar
qualityWhy: It gives a clear workflow, a quick-start example, a data-field reference and troubleshooting steps, but it defers the full syntax contract to an external document.
why: It only serves the cmux terminal's own UI and has nothing to do with building, running, selling or making content for a Fractera site, app or agent. It also fetches an external document with curl at runtime, which an agent should not do unprompted.
risks: It tells the agent to download and read a remote markdown file from GitHub with curl during setup.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to maintain a project wiki stored under a .indexion/wiki folder. It covers creating and updating Markdown pages through a command that keeps the page, manifest, search index and audit log in step. It also explains how to find pages whose source files changed, check links and structure, and detect drift between code symbols and documentation. The intended users are developers and agents who keep technical docs for a codebase current.
tasks: keep project wiki pages in sync with code changes
find wiki pages that went stale after source edits
check wiki links and structure before publishing docs
plan a new wiki for an unfamiliar codebase
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete commands, expected outputs, a maintenance cycle and pitfalls, though it does not explain how to install the indexion CLI.
why: It maintains documentation for a codebase rather than building, running or selling a product, so it is only occasionally useful on a node. It runs a local CLI with no outside service or key, and it does not conflict with the node's stack, but the indexion CLI must already be present for it to work.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing test files or suites for quality problems such as tests that assert nothing, swallowed exceptions, flaky timing or ordering, duplication, and magic values. It produces a severity-ranked report with concrete fixes and positive observations. It is aimed at developers reviewing test code across many languages and frameworks, mainly .NET.
tasks: audit my test suite for anti-patterns
find why my tests are flaky
review test quality and naming
list tests that give false confidence
qualityWhy: The skill gives a detailed, step-by-step audit procedure with severity rules, a catalog of anti-patterns per language, and a validation checklist, though some sections are very long and repetitive.
why: It reviews existing test code rather than building a node feature, so it is useful now and then for quality checks on a product's tests. It is stack-free apart from .NET examples, reads only workspace files, and has no outside service or risky command.

summary: This skill has an agent build a working operating system for a music business inside its own repository: folders for artists, compositions, or catalog cases, a self-managing CLAUDE.md, and a read-only health check. It also adds templates for knowledge capture, skill promotion, and a plugin packaged for Claude, Cursor, and Codex. It is written for labels, publishers, and catalog administrators who want their workspace to stay current on its own.
tasks: set up a label operating workspace
organize a publishing catalog repo
mirror an artist roster into folders
schedule a weekly workspace health check
qualityWhy: The phases, references, templates and validator give an agent concrete steps and checks, though the prose is dense and some rules are spread across sections.
needs: Recoup platform account for hosted records (optional)
why: It is an internal operating system for one music company's catalog and royalty work, not for building sites, apps, agents or content, so value is none. It also relies on a hosted Recoup platform as the authoritative store for records, which the local-first rule treats as a cloud place to keep data.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to use the indexion command-line tool to inspect how a source file is split into tokens, turned into parse events, and reduced to dependency edges. It is aimed at developers who are adding language support, editing a KGF spec, or trying to understand why indexion's analysis output or grep matches look wrong. It also gives PEG ordering and token priority pitfalls to check when writing specs.
tasks: debug why indexion parses a source file incorrectly
inspect the tokens and edges of a source file
fix a grep pattern that does not match
add or change support for a programming language
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete subcommands, options, a step-by-step workflow and specific PEG and token-priority pitfalls with good and bad examples, though it assumes familiarity with indexion and KGF.
why: It is a developer tool for debugging code analysis rather than for building, running or selling a site or app, so it is useful only occasionally on a node. It needs the indexion CLI installed locally, and the update subcommand downloads specs from GitHub.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to run the indexion command-line tool, which cuts a long text file into segments for retrieval and embedding work. The agent picks a splitting method (sliding-window divergence, TF-IDF topic shifts, or sentence punctuation, plus a hybrid mode) and sets size limits and thresholds to suit the document. It is aimed at developers who are preparing documents for search, RAG or similarity features.
tasks: split a long document into chunks for an embedding index
break a transcript or article into topic sections
tune chunk size and threshold for a RAG pipeline
qualityWhy: The options table and usage examples are clear, but the skill never explains how to install the indexion tool, what the output files look like, or how to check the result.
why: Chunking text is a core step before storing content in the node's vector or knowledge-graph elements, and the tool runs locally with no outside service. The install source for the indexion CLI is not stated, so an agent would have to find it first.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to turn audio and video into text: transcripts, speaker-labelled meeting notes, and SRT or VTT subtitles, with some notes on translation and podcast show notes. It is written mainly as YAML configuration templates and a few API snippets. It is aimed at people who make video, podcasts or meeting records and need searchable text or captions.
tasks: transcribe a meeting recording with speaker labels
generate SRT subtitles for a video
turn a podcast episode into show notes and chapters
translate captions into several languages
qualityWhy: Most of the file is configuration and example output rather than steps an agent can follow, it names an MCP server ('media-mcp') that is not defined anywhere, and the accuracy report is illustrative with no check to run.
why: Transcription and subtitles directly serve making video and audio content, but the default engines are paid cloud APIs, so person's audio is sent to third parties; the skill never says this plainly, and a fully local option via Whisper is not spelled out. The workflows also assume outside services and an MCP server that the skill does not supply.

summary: This skill guides an agent through speeding up a Next.js site, mainly by checking Core Web Vitals and fixing the usual causes: heavy client-side JavaScript, unoptimized images and fonts, missing caching, and blocking data loads. It covers moving work into Server Components, streaming with Suspense, tag-based cache revalidation, and trimming bundles. It is written for developers who already know React and Next.js and want production-grade results. It also covers Next.js 16 and React 19 patterns such as async params and useOptimistic.
tasks: speed up a slow Next.js page
fix layout shift from images or fonts
convert a client component into a server component
add caching and revalidation to data fetching
reduce JavaScript bundle size
stream a page with Suspense
qualityWhy: It has concrete before-and-after examples, a checklist, and clear common mistakes, but it gives little verification beyond Lighthouse and includes an unsupported "-70% JS" figure.
why: It targets Next.js 16 App Router, which is the node's own stack, and it directly improves the sites and apps people build on it. Its examples use a placeholder db client that must be pointed at the node's SQLite element, and some caching advice (unstable_cache) may be superseded by newer Next.js caching APIs, so an agent should check those parts against the installed version.

summary: This skill lets an agent give a user a short-lived web link where they can type a password or API key, so the secret never enters the chat. The agent opens a local form on the computer, exposes it through a temporary Cloudflare Quick Tunnel, and writes the submitted values straight into a file path the user has approved. It is aimed at developers and operators who need to hand credentials to an agent building or running a project.
tasks: share an API key with the agent without pasting it into chat
collect several credentials through a one-time web form
write submitted secrets into a local .env file for a project
cancel or expire a secret-drop link before it is used
qualityWhy: The workflow, commands and safety rules are concrete and clear, but the scripts/handoff.py CLI and the references it depends on are not included in the package, so an agent cannot follow it as delivered.
needs: outbound network access to Cloudflare (no Cloudflare account required)
why: Useful now and then for passing secrets to an agent during a build, but not a core part of building or running a site or app. Cloudflare terminates TLS and sees submitted secrets in plaintext, which the skill states openly, and the CLI and reference files it needs are missing from the package.

summary: This skill guides a coding agent through a pre-edit orientation step for an unfamiliar codebase. The agent generates a brief from the indexion CLI that lists likely implementation owners, documentation sources, consumer surfaces, and files to avoid, then confirms the owner with grep, search, and doc graph before editing. It is aimed at developers who hand implementation work to AI coding agents, including delegated subagents.
tasks: map code ownership before editing an unfamiliar repository
generate an orientation brief for a coding subagent

summary: This skill guides a coding agent through connecting a project to LaunchDarkly, a hosted feature-flag service. The agent scans the codebase, installs the matching SDK, wires its initialization to an environment variable, creates a first flag, and adds a banner that the person can watch switch on in the browser. It can also set up an editor integration and add the observability plugin. It is written for developers who are new to LaunchDarkly.
tasks: add feature flags to my app
set up LaunchDarkly in this project
create a first flag and show it toggling
add the LaunchDarkly observability plugin
qualityWhy: The steps, branching rules, fallbacks, ask-forms and verification checks are concrete and complete, though some behaviour is left to the agent's judgement.
needs: LaunchDarkly SDK key, client-side ID or mobile key
LaunchDarkly MCP connection or API token (optional)
why: Feature flags are evaluated against LaunchDarkly's hosted service, so the node's local-first data model does not apply and the app depends on a cloud service for its flags. The skill also depends on an account, keys and a remote skill installer, and it tells the agent to keep its work quiet. Those are reasons to skip it on a node.
risks: It tells the agent to work silently, skip onboarding logs and avoid narrating changes, so the person may not see edits to their code or env files.
It adds a hidden source-attribution marker to the signup link that the agent must never show the user.

summary: This skill routes WordPress Playground tasks to the right focused workflow: local command-line runs with the Playground CLI, browser-only website and share-link setup, WebMCP site tools, snapshots, mounts, version switching, and Xdebug debugging. It sends Blueprint JSON authoring to a separate blueprint skill. It is aimed at developers who want disposable WordPress test instances.

switch WordPress or PHP version in a test instance

why: Playground is a disposable WordPress test environment, useful for trying out or previewing a site during development, but it is not a production host for a Fractera node's own data. It is stack-free in the sense that it runs WordPress itself rather than replacing a Fractera element, so no adaptation is needed.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to manage Goldsky's named credential objects, which pipeline sinks use to reach external databases and queues. It covers creating a secret from a connection string or JSON, listing and inspecting secrets, rotating passwords without breaking pipelines, and deleting unused secrets. It is written for people running Goldsky data pipelines against hosted databases such as Neon, Supabase or ClickHouse.
tasks: store a Postgres connection string as a Goldsky secret
rotate a database password in a pipeline secret
list or delete unused Goldsky secrets
qualityWhy: The steps, command examples, error fixes and rotation procedure are concrete, though the create workflow repeats Step 5 and Step 6 and mixes inline --value guidance with warnings against it.

credentials for the target sink, such as Neon, Supabase or ClickHouse
why: Goldsky is a cloud data-pipeline service that stores credentials in its own cloud, which the node's local-first design excludes, and the skill serves pipeline operations rather than building, running or selling a product on the node. The skill also makes an agent handle live database passwords.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building production React Native apps with Expo: file-based routing with Expo Router, validating route params, separating server, client, route and form state, and fetching data with a cache library plus Zod checks. store auth tokens securely in an Expo app
