why: Sending email and SMS is useful for building and running a product, but the service is a hosted third party that stores messages, inbox threads and logs, so it is not local-first; the person must choose it and get a key. The skill relies on npx running an unpinned npm CLI and on the MCP server reading the project env file, which the person should know about.

summary: This skill guides an agent through implementing a change that should leave the UI visually untouched, such as a dependency upgrade, refactor, or migration, and uses Meticulous visual diff runs as a loop to drive the code to a clean result before opening a pull request. It covers building the frontend as CI does, uploading builds, triggering test runs, classifying each diff as regression, acceptable, or unrelated, rejecting and replying to comments, and checking the PR's own run. It is written for developers maintaining a web frontend with CI pipelines on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket.
tasks: upgrade a dependency without changing the UI
refactor components and confirm no visual diffs
migrate a build tool and verify visual stability
open a PR with a clean Meticulous visual diff result
qualityWhy: The steps are detailed, with exact commands for both CLI and MCP, decision rules for classifying diffs, and checks against drift between local and CI runs, though it depends on several other skills and external service setup.
needs: CI configuration using Meticulous upload steps
why: It serves a development workflow for testing a site's UI during upgrades and refactors, which is useful but occasional for a node's own build and run work. It relies on the Meticulous hosted service, which the person would choose, and needs the Meticulous CLI installed and a project set up; it also assumes a git repo with CI, which may not match every node element.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a structured bug investigation: reproduce the failure on demand, narrow it to the smallest failing code path, test one hypothesis at a time, then apply a minimal root-cause fix and add a regression test. It is aimed at developers whose tests fail for unclear reasons, whose verification checks report failures, or whose code behaves incorrectly. The skill also asks the person to supply exact steps when a bug cannot be reproduced, and it can optionally delegate the hunt to a subagent.
tasks: debug a failing test with an unclear cause
find the root cause of wrong behavior
fix a bug and add a regression test
investigate a failure reported by a verification check
qualityWhy: The loop, the single-hypothesis rule, the minimal-fix rule and the report template are concrete and easy to follow, though it gives no stack-specific commands and few worked examples.
why: The method is stack-free and useful for any product, but the skill refers to AGENTS.md, docs/conventions.md, /test and /architect, which belong to another project's workflow, so it must be adapted to the node's own conventions and commands before use. The output style rules also demand no hyphens, which the node's own style guide may not share.

summary: This skill describes how an agent could manage Linear, a hosted issue tracker, for engineering teams. It covers creating and updating issues from templates, moving work through states, planning and reporting on cycles, and syncing with GitHub branches and pull requests. The target users are engineering managers and developers who run their product work in Linear. The file is mostly YAML config, diagrams and placeholder GraphQL queries rather than step-by-step instructions.
tasks: create a Linear bug report from a user description
plan the next two-week cycle in Linear
summarize cycle progress and blockers
link GitHub pull requests to Linear issues
qualityWhy: The file is mostly descriptive YAML and ASCII diagrams with placeholder IDs and pseudo-automations, and it gives no concrete steps, auth setup or checks an agent can follow.
why: Linear is a cloud tracker that holds the team's issues outside the node, which the node's local-first rule treats as no value. The skill also describes a workflow tool rather than building, running or selling a product on the node.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to organise a Trello kanban board: creating and moving cards, adding labels, due dates and checklists, and setting up Butler automation rules. It also covers board templates for sprints and content calendars, plus simple reporting on card counts and cycle times. It is aimed at project managers and operations teams who run work in Trello.

create and move cards with checklists
add Butler rules to automate card moves
report on board velocity and cycle time

why: Trello is a cloud project-management service, and managing a team's task board is not building, running, selling or making content for a node product, so the value is none. The skill would also hold the person's work data in a third-party cloud, not in the node's local storage.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to copy Salesforce's open source Lightning Web Component and label files from a GitHub repository into a Salesforce B2B Commerce store's site metadata, so they appear in Experience Builder. It is written for Salesforce developers who run a store on the Salesforce cloud. tasks: add open source components to a Salesforce B2B store
copy commerce components into Experience Builder
retrieve a store and integrate its open code components

git and internet access to GitHub
why: It only serves Salesforce B2B Commerce stores, which run on a cloud platform outside Fractera's local-first stack and its Next.js, SQLite and Stripe elements, so it does not help build or run a Fractera node. Its steps are clear, but they only fit a Salesforce org.

summary: This skill turns the agent into an interactive tutor for the AI Engineering from Scratch course. It finds the learner's next lesson from a progress file, teaches it section by section with prediction questions and hands-on code walkthroughs, then runs a quiz and records the score. It works from a local clone or by fetching lesson files straight from GitHub. It is aimed at people who want to learn AI engineering step by step.

quiz me on the lesson I just finished
resume my AI engineering learning progress
walk me through backpropagation from scratch

why: It helps learners study AI engineering, which is useful now and then for building products, but it does not build, run or sell anything on the node itself. It is stack-free and needs no keys; the optional lesson screen needs node 20 or later and a local browser, and it hands off to other skills by name.

summary: The skill keeps a reviewable decision trail for long or unattended agent runs, writing one TSV row per decision with the what, why, evidence pointer and result. An agent uses a bundled shell helper to append rows, and it audits its own log against the transcript before handing back. record why each change was made with evidence
audit a long agent run before a reviewer signs off
trace which decisions led to the final result

why: It is a stack-free process habit that helps a node's agents keep an auditable trail of their builds, but it is only occasionally needed. It refers to a missing adapter doc and to other pstack skills, which the agent cannot resolve from these files alone.

summary: This skill guides an agent through running e-signature work on the DocuSign cloud service: building envelopes, placing signature and date fields, setting signing order and reminders, reusing templates, sending bulk batches, and tracking status through webhooks and audit trails. It is aimed at legal, sales and operations staff who need contracts signed. Most of the content is sample YAML and a loose JavaScript snippet rather than working steps.

download the signed contract and its audit trail

why: The skill is built around DocuSign's hosted cloud, which keeps envelopes, signed documents and audit trails outside the node, so it does not fit the local-first design. It also sends signer details and contract files to a third party, and its quality is low.
risks: Sends signer names, emails and contract documents to the DocuSign cloud and to a webhook callback URL without telling the person.

summary: This skill guides an agent through designing database synchronization between systems such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB and Redis, covering one-way and two-way replication, change data capture, conflict rules and schema migrations. It is aimed at data engineers or backend teams who need to keep a production database and an analytics or search copy in step. The file is mostly reference material: YAML configs, SQL snippets and ASCII diagrams, with no runnable scripts.

why: It is useful engineering background, but it is built for external database engines and a data-mcp service rather than the node's own SQLite element, so an agent would have to re-plan it around the node's data layer. Its examples are templates that would need validation before use.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to sort a person's emails into categories such as action required, FYI, waiting, delegated, archive and delete, and to rate each one's priority and response time. It works from pasted email text, supports batch sorting and user-defined rules for trusted senders and auto-routing, and includes a checklist for spotting phishing. It is aimed at people with overloaded inboxes.

apply my own rules for VIP senders and auto-delegation
check whether an email looks like phishing

why: Inbox triage for one person is personal productivity and does not help build, run, sell or create content for a Fractera product, and the skill works only on pasted text with no node data.

summary: The skill describes a way to chain document operations such as extracting PDF text, transforming data, running AI analysis and generating DOCX or report output into reusable pipelines. It is written as a general overview with a YAML pipeline format and a small Python Pipeline class, aimed at people processing contracts, reports and spreadsheets. It contains no concrete step-by-step procedure for a specific library call beyond a pip install line, and the stage operations are placeholders that the agent must write itself.
tasks: build a pipeline that extracts text from a PDF and generates a DOCX report
chain OCR, summarizing and report creation for scanned images
turn an Excel file into analysis charts and a slide deck
review contracts with an extract-analyze-report workflow
qualityWhy: The skill is mostly an overview with illustrative code whose operations (extract_pdf_text, analyze_with_ai, create_docx_report) are undefined, so an agent gets little concrete guidance to follow.
why: Chaining document steps is useful now and then for content and reporting work on a node, and the pipeline pattern is stack-free Python that the node can host, though the skill gives little that an agent could not write unaided. Nothing in the file calls a cloud service or sends data elsewhere.

summary: This skill guides an agent through taking a GitHub pull request to green CI: it reads failing checks and their logs, fixes root causes, commits and pushes, then polls until actionable review bots finish and handles high and medium review comments. It is aimed at developers working on a repository's PR who want an automated fix-and-wait loop, while stopping at human approval, draft and merge gates.
tasks: fix failing CI checks on my pull request
address high and medium review feedback on a PR
keep iterating until the PR's checks go green
reply to review threads after fixing comments
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow with tables, exit conditions and fallbacks, and the bundled scripts are substantive, though the tool is tied to Sentry-style LOGAF conventions and some script internals were cut off.
needs: authenticated GitHub CLI (gh) with access to the repository
why: It works on a git repository's pull requests rather than building or running a Fractera site, so its use is occasional, but it is a stack-free development habit that needs no outside service beyond GitHub. The bundled scripts run gh and GraphQL calls against the PR and write only JSON to stdout, and the skill relies on the node's own repository, so it installs as written.
risks: Commits and pushes code changes to the remote branch automatically, and loops until CI passes, which the person may not expect.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to produce Excalidraw diagram files, including flowcharts, architecture charts, sequence diagrams and mind maps, with a consistent colour palette, font scale and arrow rules. It then guides export to SVG through the Kroki web API or to PNG and SVG through a local Firefox-based CLI, and asks the agent to inspect the rendered image and fix layout defects before reporting. It also covers a review loop for user edits and a helper for dropping community icon libraries into a scene. It is aimed at people who need to explain a system or process visually.
tasks: draw an architecture diagram of our services
make a flowchart of the checkout process
export a diagram as PNG or SVG for a document
turn a multi-step process into a visual diagram
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and complete, with a JSON schema, layout and spacing numbers, verified property values, export commands, a render-check table and a common-mistakes table.
needs: npm registry and Firefox download for the local CLI
raw.githubusercontent.com for community libraries (optional, no key)
why: Diagrams for explaining systems and processes serve building and documenting a product directly. The default SVG path sends the diagram source to the external kroki.io service, which the skill documents, though a local Kroki or the local CLI keeps the data on the machine. The macOS setup edits the installed CLI's source file in the global npm folder, which the person should know about.

summary: The skill is a short catalogue page that presents a large collection of MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers as one hub. It explains how Claude connects to filesystems, databases, APIs and document tools through MCP, gives a sample JSON configuration, and lists marketplaces where servers can be found. It is aimed at people who want to extend an agent with external tools, and it does not give concrete steps for any particular task.
tasks: connect Claude to a local filesystem
find an MCP server for a database
configure MCP servers in a JSON file
integrate an agent with Google Drive
qualityWhy: The file is mostly a directory of links and a generic overview, with no steps, checks or verifiable examples, and the Python snippet is only comments.
why: MCP is a general protocol, but this skill points at outside servers and a generic config rather than the node's own elements, and the document libraries it lists are not part of the node's stack. Its config example would have to be adapted to the node's own sign-in, database and file storage, so it is read for ideas only; the star counts and claims of '1200+' servers are unverified.

summary: The skill lets an agent look up official Google developer documentation across Google Cloud, Firebase, Android, Chrome, Flutter, Go, Web and AI platforms. It prefers an MCP server with search and answer tools and falls back to a REST API using either a gcloud token or an API key. The agent is told to verify each lookup succeeded, retry on quota errors, and state plainly when documentation could not be reached. It is aimed at developers who need exact CLI syntax, IAM permissions or product comparisons.
tasks: look up gcloud command syntax for a Cloud Run task
find the IAM permission needed for a Cloud Storage operation
compare Google Cloud products for a project
get the official Firebase setup steps
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with working curl examples, explicit fallback order and failure handling, though the reference files were not provided and some steps assume a live Google service.
needs: Developer Knowledge API key or an authenticated gcloud account
why: Useful when a Fractera agent builds sites or apps on Google services, but it is a documentation lookup rather than a builder, so it serves only occasional needs. It calls a Google service and needs a credential the person must supply, which is a paid or account choice they make; it is not a cloud-hosting skill that would move the node's data off-device.

summary: This skill tells an agent to pause before settling on a new UI interaction or architecture choice that the codebase has no precedent for. It asks the agent to build two or three competing prototypes and compare them side by side. It also extends the same habit to product decisions where the user experience depends on feel rather than logic. The file is only a short stub, so an agent gets the intent but no concrete steps.
tasks: compare two prototype designs before choosing a new UI interaction
choose between competing architecture options for a new feature
decide a product flow where the feel of the experience matters
qualityWhy: The file is a stub: a frontmatter line and two sentences with no steps, examples, or checks an agent can follow.
why: It is a stack-free design habit, so it works on any node, but it only applies now and then to new UI or architecture decisions. Its thinness means an agent would have to supply its own method.

summary: This skill guides an agent reviewing or shaping code to reduce how much a reader must trace and hold in mind. It asks the agent to count indirection layers between a question and its answer, collapse single-caller wrappers and pass-through adapters, and keep mutable state as local as possible. It is aimed at developers who maintain hard-to-follow codebases.
tasks: review code for unnecessary wrapper layers
simplify a hard-to-trace module
reduce mutable state in a codebase
decide whether a new abstraction is worth adding
qualityWhy: The principles are clear and well argued, but it gives no concrete steps, examples or checks beyond a single 30-second test, so it reads as general guidance.
why: It is a stack-free design habit that helps when reviewing code on a Fractera node, so it is useful now and then rather than central to building or selling a product. It carries no risk and needs no service.

summary: The skill makes an agent run a full health check on a mobile app's store page, covering title, subtitle, keyword field, description, screenshots, preview video, ratings, icon, keyword rankings and conversion signals. It scores each area out of 10, combines them into an overall score, and produces a prioritised plan of quick wins, weekly changes and monthly strategy. It is aimed at app developers and marketers who want to know why their app is not ranking or converting in the App Store or Google Play.
tasks: audit my app store listing
explain why my app isn't ranking
score my app's ASO and prioritise fixes
review my app's screenshots and description for conversion
qualityWhy: It has a clear framework, scoring tables and an output template, but it gives no concrete steps for collecting the data and its factor weights add up to 105%, which makes the overall score unreliable.
needs: Appeeky MCP or API (optional; without it the user must supply metadata by hand)
why: It is a marketing analysis for mobile app listings, so it is useful only when the person sells a mobile app, not for the web sites, apps and content a node mainly serves. It calls an outside data service when one is available, and its weights do not add up to 100%.

summary: This skill gives an agent a large set of UI and UX rules for web interfaces: animation timing and easing, exit animations, CSS pseudo-elements and View Transitions, audio feedback and Web Audio synthesis, morphing icons, container resizing, UX laws, prefetching, typography and visual design. It lets the agent review existing code and generate new components, citing file and line for each finding. The intended users are front-end developers and designers building or auditing web products.
tasks: review the animations in my React components
add a smooth exit animation to a modal
pick easing and duration for button hover states
fix the typography of a landing page
add subtle sound feedback to a checkout flow
make a dropdown resize smoothly with its content
qualityWhy: Each rule is short and prioritised, with incorrect and correct code examples and a clear review format, though some rules are thin and the category counts do not quite match the stated total.

Its examples use Motion, which is a UI library rather than a replacement for the node's own stack, so no adaptation is needed. Only the SKILL.md and rule files shown were reviewed, and the remaining files were not read.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how the Preview panel of a node works after a preview service is started, and how to diagnose blank screens, missing tabs, 404 assets and unreachable services. It tells the agent to use relative asset paths, never to send users to localhost, and to read a local registry and history file before scanning the workspace. restore a preview tab that disappeared
fix 404 errors on JS and CSS assets in a preview
list and restart previously running services
find which project to preview

Its advice about relative paths is generally valid for any app served under a sub-path.

summary: The skill turns one source document into a stylised slide deck using NotebookLM via the notebooklm command-line tool. It creates a notebook, uploads the document, and asks NotebookLM to generate a kawaii-themed narrative deck, then hands back the notebook link. It is aimed at people who want shareable slides from a report or write-up.
tasks: turn this report into a slide deck
make a kawaii slide deck about a document
create shareable narrative slides from a file
qualityWhy: The steps are concrete with commands and failure modes, but it is short and leans on the external tool with little detail on checks or output handling.
why: Slide generation is useful for content making but the output is a Google NotebookLM deck, so it depends on a Google service and is not local-first; the source is uploaded to Google and the user must authenticate interactively.
risks: Uploads the user's source document to Google NotebookLM, so sensitive or unreleased content would leave the machine.

summary: This skill guides an agent through Amazon Route 53 DNS work: creating public and private records, steering traffic with weighted or failover policies, and setting up health checks. It also covers DNS Firewall, Route 53 Profiles, Resolver for hybrid and Outposts networks, and Global Resolver. A top-level router sends each request to a per-task procedure file. The intended users are cloud and network administrators running infrastructure on AWS.
tasks: point a domain at a load balancer or IP address
split traffic between two endpoints for a canary release
set up failover between two AWS Regions
block malicious domains for a VPC
resolve private DNS across a hybrid network
qualityWhy: The router gives a clear task-to-procedure table, routing notes and security constraints, but only SKILL.md was provided, so the procedure files could not be checked.
why: Route 53 is a cloud DNS hosting and administration service on AWS, which the node's local-first design rules out, so it does not serve building or running a product on the node. The skill is well written, but it is not for this node.

summary: This skill acts as a pre merge gate for a code change. why: It is a development workflow helper for checking changes rather than building or making content, so it is only occasionally useful on a node, and it is stack free enough to install as written. The mode files were not fully visible, so their completeness is unknown.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building monthly, quarterly, annual or year-to-date financial statements: an income statement with prior-period and budget comparisons, variance percentages, margin metrics, and a list of material variances needing investigation. summary: This skill guides an agent through running a customer support desk in Zendesk: sorting incoming tickets by intent, urgency and customer tier, routing them to teams, and drafting replies from templates. summary: This skill guides an agent to write commands, lifecycle steps and processing loops that reach the correct end state no matter how many times they run or where an earlier run stopped. add stale lock detection to a processing pipeline

why: It is a stack-free design habit that helps when a node's own commands or SQLite-backed processing loops must survive restarts, though it is not directly about content or sites. No risks found in the skill's text.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to configure an iii engine in one of two modes: a managed engine declared in worker-compose.yaml, or a directly supervised engine in config.yaml. Mermaid loads from a CDN only as an optional, degradable extra.

summary: This skill guides an agent through turning a product idea into a coarse, living feature plan stored in docs/scope/. summary: The skill guides an agent to write developer-focused slide decks in Slidev, a Vue-based Markdown presentation framework. It is written for a connector-based plugin ecosystem (Gmail/Outlook, Salesforce-style CRM, customer-voice quote pipeline) rather than a local SQLite element, so it would need rewriting for the node's data layer and Page/artifact conventions before use.

summary: This skill walks an agent through installing the iii engine, creating a project, and starting a local backend with a first worker. npx skills add fetches and installs skill code from a GitHub repository without a review step.

why: It is a stack-free writing aid for developer workflow rather than a product feature, so it is useful now and then for a node that is being built. It runs git locally, and it only touches GitHub after you confirm.

summary: This skill makes an agent read an existing codebase with search and file-reading tools only, map its structure and data flows, and record the behaviour it finds as requirements. summary: This skill runs as the last step after a code change to bring the project's AGENTS.md notes, scope checklist and spec status lines in line with what the repo now shows. summary: This skill guides an agent through deploying apps and infrastructure to Cloudflare. summary: This skill guides an agent through choosing and wiring backend architecture patterns built from iii engine primitives. summary: This skill guides an agent through designing a database schema from a plain description of an app's data. why: It is Go code for Grafana app-sdk Kubernetes admission webhooks, which Fractera nodes do not use (they run Next.js, TypeScript and SQLite), so it does not serve building or running a node product. Its own text notes the handlers must be adapted to a different runtime, and it is not a stack the node uses.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building, debugging and extending Model Context Protocol servers and clients. It covers writing tool handlers with Zod or Pydantic input validation, exposing resources, choosing stdio, HTTP or SSE transport, and checking protocol compliance with the MCP inspector. It is aimed at developers who want AI assistants to reach their own data sources and external APIs.
tasks: build an MCP server that exposes tools to an AI assistant
add a resource provider for app configuration
debug a tool call that returns a malformed response
set up stdio or HTTP transport for an MCP server
validate MCP tool inputs with Zod or Pydantic
qualityWhy: It gives a clear workflow, two working code examples, a test-and-fix feedback loop and explicit MUST/MUST NOT rules, but its examples call undefined helpers such as fetchWeather and the reference files were not shown, so some detail is unverified.
why: Building MCP servers and clients is a direct way to connect the AI agents a node runs to tools and data, and the skill is stack-neutral enough to fit a Node.js or Python project. Its only dependencies are open-source SDKs installed from npm or PyPI, with no account or paid service required.

summary: This skill makes an agent answer as Steve Jobs, using his product-focus reasoning, his short and blunt speaking style, and a set of named decision rules. Before judging a specific product or company, it asks the agent to search the web for current reviews, competitors and market facts, and it includes fallback steps for when searches come up empty. It is aimed at founders and product people who want a sharp, opinionated review of a product idea, a feature list or a strategic choice. It also covers a personal decision test built around thinking about one's own death.
tasks: review a product idea through a focus-and-cut-features lens
decide which features to remove from a product roadmap
give blunt product feedback on a landing page or app flow
judge whether a product's end-to-end experience is good enough to ship
qualityWhy: The workflow, checkpoints and fallback table are concrete, but much of the text is persona narrative, and the research and author reference files it points to are not in the package.
why: It is a stack-free thinking aid, so it fits a node as written, but it only helps now and then with product decisions and is not a building tool. Its quotes and historical claims come from public sources that I could not check from SKILL.md alone, and the cited references/ folder is missing.

summary: The skill guides an agent through designing Google Cloud infrastructure as Terraform, checking it locally, scanning the plan for security and cost issues, and then importing and deploying it through Google's Application Design Center. It also covers troubleshooting failed deployments and verifying the running services. It is written for cloud architects and platform engineers working on GCP projects.
tasks: design a GCP network and Cloud Run setup in Terraform
scan a Terraform plan for security issues before deploying
deploy an infrastructure template to a GCP project
debug a failed GCP deployment
qualityWhy: The workflow has concrete phases, exact commands, exit criteria and retry rules, though some steps depend on reference files and hosted tools the agent cannot see.
why: The skill exists to deploy and manage infrastructure on Google Cloud, which is cloud hosting and cloud administration, so it is not useful for building a local-first node. It is well written, but its whole purpose is the excluded cloud deployment role.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building and debugging interactive WordPress blocks with the Interactivity API. It covers data-wp-* directives, shared stores and state, server-side rendering of initial state, and hydration problems. It is aimed at WordPress plugin and theme developers.
tasks: add interactivity to a WordPress block
debug directives that do nothing on the frontend
fix hydration mismatch or layout shift on page load
set up server-side rendered initial state for a block
qualityWhy: The procedure and PHP examples are concrete, but the reference files it points to were not included and several steps stay general.
why: It is written for WordPress, PHP and @wordpress/* tooling, which a Fractera node does not run, so an agent would need to read it for ideas and rebuild them in Next.js and React. The reference files were not provided, so their content is unverified.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to find existing Coralogix dashboards and widgets before building new ones. It offers natural-language search over dashboards, search of widget queries by description or by field path, and a full catalog listing, then shows how to pull a found dashboard's JSON and copy it. It is aimed at engineers who monitor services on Coralogix and want to avoid duplicate dashboards.
tasks: find an existing dashboard for a service
check whether a monitoring dashboard already exists before creating one
find widgets that query a specific field
clone an existing dashboard as a starting point
qualityWhy: The commands and examples are clear, but the skill is short and thin, with no error handling, no output-parsing guidance, and no details on the search result format.
why: The skill is built around the Coralogix cloud observability service, which is a cloud place to run and monitor things, so under the local-first rule its value is none and it should be skipped on a local-first node.

summary: This skill guides an agent through shrinking the main JavaScript entry file of a Grafana app plugin by moving feature code behind lazy-loaded React components. It sets a priority order for splitting (entry file wrappers first, then routes, extensions and tab panels), with measurement steps and checks. It also covers an optional CI job that compares bundle sizes on pull requests. The audience is developers maintaining Grafana plugins.
tasks: reduce the module.js size of a Grafana app plugin
add React.lazy code splitting to plugin routes
set up bundle size comparison on pull requests
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete code, ordered steps, size targets and verification commands, with small gaps such as an unpinned npx tool version and some assumed project layout.
needs: GitHub account for the optional bundle-size CI workflow
why: It targets Grafana app plugins built with webpack, not the Next.js stack of a Fractera node, so an agent should borrow the lazy-loading and splitting ideas and apply them the node's way. The Grafana-specific tooling and CI parts do not transfer.

summary: This is an index of guidance for designing and debugging AI agent systems, covering how to manage what a model sees at inference time, how to coordinate several agents, and how to store memory. It also covers how to evaluate agents and keep long-running autonomous loops reliable. It is aimed at engineers building agents who want a structured mental model before choosing an implementation. Most of the text is conceptual summary, and it points to separate sub-skills for the detail.
tasks: design a multi-agent system
reduce context bloat in an agent
debug why an agent loses track of earlier information
plan memory for a long-running agent
set up an evaluation harness for an agent
qualityWhy: It is mostly a high-level overview with no concrete steps, examples or checks, and its detailed guidance lives in sub-skill files that are not included.
why: It is stack-free and useful as background when designing agents on a node, but it gives no build steps for the node's own stack. The skill links to about 18 sub-skills under skills/ that are missing from this single SKILL.md, so installing it alone gives an index rather than the detailed instructions.

summary: This skill guides an agent through migrating a Grafana plugin to React 19 compatibility without upgrading React itself. It covers scanning with react-detect, updating create-plugin scaffolding, completing an ESLint 9 flat-config move, externalizing the jsx-runtime, bumping Grafana and Faro dependencies, and fixing deprecated React patterns in source code. It is written for plugin developers working on Grafana plugins, not for Fractera node sites or apps.
tasks: migrate a Grafana plugin to React 19 compatibility
run react-detect and fix flagged issues in a plugin
bump grafanaDependency and Grafana packages for React 19
externalize jsx-runtime in a Grafana plugin build
qualityWhy: The steps are concrete and ordered with commands, decision branches and an error-to-fix table, though some steps reference external docs and a few fixes are only described briefly.
why: It serves only Grafana plugin development, which is outside what Fractera nodes are for (sites, web apps, AI agents and content made locally). Its workflow also rewrites git history with a soft reset to origin/main and runs package installs with --ignore-engines and --no-verify, which the node should not do automatically.
risks: Runs git reset --soft origin/main and commits with --no-verify, bypassing hooks and rewriting branch history.

summary: This skill lets an agent operate third-party apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar, GitHub, Notion, Twitter and Instagram through a remote relay instead of calling each API directly. It covers finding the right action, checking the parameter format, running actions and reading responses. It also includes a separate section for driving a remote browser session, and it is written for the Starchild platform's internal network rather than a general setup.
tasks: send an email from my Gmail account
add an event to my Google Calendar
open a GitHub issue for a bug
post a tweet with an image
publish an Instagram photo post
qualityWhy: The steps and examples are concrete, but the file contradicts itself on key handling and depends on one platform's internal network and gateway.
needs: OAuth connections to each target app (Gmail, Google Calendar, GitHub, Twitter, Instagram, Notion, Google Drive)
Starchild Composio gateway on the internal flycast network
Browserbase API key and project ID for the browser section
why: Useful for publishing and app actions, but it routes the person's mail, calendar and social data through Composio Cloud and a hosted gateway, and it needs infrastructure a Fractera node does not provide, so it is skipped. The risks below would also need resolving before use.
risks: Tells the agent to bypass the platform's sc-proxy for the gateway host, avoiding a proxy layer on purpose.
Reads COMPOSIO_API_KEY from a .env file in a Twitter script, while the same file says the agent never touches that key.
Embeds the Browserbase API key as a query parameter in a WebSocket URL.

summary: This skill guides an agent to scaffold a new Claude skill folder with a SKILL.md file and standard subfolders, check the metadata, and package the result as a zip. It can also announce the new skill in a Slack channel through Rube so a team can find it. It is aimed at people who write and share agent skills for their team.
tasks: create a new skill with a SKILL.md template
validate a skill's metadata before sharing
package a skill as a zip file
post a new skill announcement to a Slack channel
qualityWhy: The file gives an overview and feature list but no concrete steps, commands or examples for creation, validation or packaging, and it names scripts and a LICENSE.txt that are not included.
why: Skill scaffolding helps when building agent skills for a node, but the Slack sharing is a team-notification step rather than a core node use, and it depends on a Rube connection the person must set up. The skill posts skill names and descriptions to Slack automatically; this is stated in the file and the person chooses the service, so it is not listed as a risk, but the agent should confirm before posting. The bundled scripts and LICENSE.txt were not provided, so their contents are unknown.

summary: This skill tells an agent to create a git branch named by Sentry's conventions: a type prefix such as feat, fix or chore, followed by a short kebab-case description. It works non-interactively, derives the description from arguments or the local diff, picks a base branch automatically, and avoids name collisions. It is aimed at developers who start new work in a repository.
tasks: create a branch for the current changes
start a new feature branch
name a branch following Sentry conventions
make a fix branch from the default branch
qualityWhy: The steps, type table, naming rules, base-branch fallbacks and collision handling are concrete and easy for an agent to follow, though there are no examples of generated names.
why: It is a stack-free git habit that helps when starting branches in any repo on a node, but it only matters now and then for building a product. It needs no keys or outside services, and it does nothing beyond creating a local branch.

summary: The skill guides an agent through writing Spring Boot test suites: plain Mockito unit tests, slice tests for repositories and MVC controllers, full integration tests, and Testcontainers wired in via @ServiceConnection. It also covers CI configuration and test dependencies. It is aimed at Java developers who maintain Spring Boot back ends.
tasks: write unit tests for a Spring service
add repository tests with a real database container
test REST controllers with MockMvc
set up Testcontainers for Spring Boot integration tests
configure CI to run Spring tests
qualityWhy: Concrete code samples, slice and performance targets, and validation checkpoints are given, but several snippets are partial and the reference files were not inspected in full.
why: The node's stack is Next.js and TypeScript, so a Spring Boot testing skill does not serve what nodes are for, and the skill is built for a Java stack the node does not run. Docker is needed for the container tests, which is a local requirement and not a cloud service.

summary: Guides an agent through the LobeHub project's test setup: which Vitest commands to run for a single file, how to handle database and client-versus-server test splits, and when to use spies, mocks, or regression tests. It also covers UI library mocking rules and a decision process for whether to fix or delete failing tests. Its target is developers working on the LobeHub codebase rather than people building a Fractera site or app.
tasks: write Vitest tests for a database model
fix a failing test after an implementation change
decide whether to keep or delete an over-specified test
mock the base UI library in a test file
qualityWhy: Concrete commands, categories, rules and a decision checklist, but the reference files it points to were not provided, so several steps depend on unseen detail.
why: It is written for LobeHub's own monorepo layout, commands and test configs, which a Fractera node does not have, so it would need adapting to the node's Next.js and Vitest setup. Its general habits (prefer spies, test behaviour, write regression tests) are useful, but the database and UI mock rules are specific to LobeHub.

summary: This skill guides an agent through administering Grafana Cloud: creating and deleting stacks through the Cloud API, minting service-account tokens for automation, assigning RBAC roles, inviting users into teams, and configuring SSO providers such as SAML, OAuth and GitHub. It also covers Terraform-based provisioning of teams, folders and dashboards. The intended audience is operators who run monitoring infrastructure for their organization.
tasks: set up SSO for a Grafana Cloud stack
create a service account for CI/CD
invite a team and assign roles in Grafana
create or delete a Grafana stack
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete curl commands, numbered workflows and verification steps, though the detailed references were not reviewed here.
needs: SSO identity provider such as Okta, SAML or GitHub OAuth
why: Grafana Cloud is a hosted cloud service, and this skill administers it (accounts, stacks, access and SSO), which the node's local-first rules classify as cloud administration with no local product use. It is well written, but it does not help build, run, sell or make content for a product on the node.

summary: The skill guides an agent to plan multi-page print publications such as brochures, magazines, catalogs and annual reports. The agent writes a blueprint covering spread roles, typed content blocks, word budgets and design intent, then uses the k2f skill to build a K2F document and export it as an IDML package for InDesign. It is aimed at designers and content makers who need editable print handoff rather than flattened PDFs.
tasks: make an editable InDesign package for a brochure
plan a magazine layout with spread-by-spread story flow
turn a product catalog draft into a designer-ready IDML file
structure an annual report into editorial blocks before layout
qualityWhy: The planning steps, checklists and failure modes are concrete, but the export and build steps just defer to the separate k2f skill with no commands or examples of its own.
why: Directly serves making print collateral for a product or client, and it is stack-free apart from the k2f dependency, which the node's own tooling covers. Its install line uses a standard npx command that a node would run as written; the export result still needs a designer to check it in InDesign.

summary: This skill makes an agent review a branch or set of commits against a fixed point such as a commit, branch, tag or merge-base. It checks the diff on two separate axes: whether the code follows the repo's documented coding standards plus a fixed set of Fowler code-smell heuristics, and whether it faithfully implements the linked issue or spec. The two reviews run as parallel sub-agents and their findings are reported side by side, without merging. It is aimed at developers reviewing branches, pull requests or in-progress changes.
tasks: review my branch against main
check my changes against the coding standards
verify the diff implements the issue spec
review everything since commit X
qualityWhy: The steps are concrete and ordered, with git commands, a fallback when no spec exists, and tightly written sub-agent briefs, though the spec-source lookup and the smell list are only lightly tied to real checks.
why: It is a generic git-diff review habit that any node agent could use, but it depends on the node's own issue tracker setup via /setup-matt-pocock-skills, a command that does not exist on Fractera, so it must be adapted to the node's own workflow. It is useful for reviewing changes to a site or app but not central to building or selling content.

summary: This skill guides an agent through implementing a spec file that has already been approved. It first checks that the spec's status line means approved in any language, then creates or switches to a git branch named after the spec, and reviews the working tree before changing anything. Implementation then proceeds one plan step at a time, pausing for the person to review each diff, with no automatic commits. It is aimed at developers who work from written specs in a repository.
tasks: implement an approved spec step by step
start work on a spec in its own git branch
check a spec is approved before coding
review each implementation step before continuing
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and ordered, with explicit stop conditions, error messages and a review rhythm, though some branch and config details are left loose.
why: It is a stack-free development workflow that helps a builder implement specs in a repository, so it is useful now and then rather than core to running a node. It needs no outside service and only uses local git commands.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to actively build and sharpen a project's domain model during design work. It checks new terms against an existing glossary, pushes back on vague or overloaded words, and tests concepts with concrete edge-case scenarios. It also says when to write glossary entries and architecture decision records, and where to put them. It is aimed at developers and product builders who want consistent terminology and a record of key decisions.
tasks: challenge inconsistent terms in our domain glossary
write or update GLOSSARY.md for this codebase
record an architecture decision as an ADR
stress-test a feature design with edge-case scenarios
check whether the code matches how we describe the domain
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear behaviours, a file layout for single and multi-context repos, lazy-creation rules and explicit ADR criteria with examples, but the referenced format files were not included for review.
why: It is a stack-free design discipline that helps any product team keep terms and decisions consistent, so it directly serves building a product on the node. Its instructions are in Chinese and it depends on the linked ADR-FORMAT.md and GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md files, which I could not read, so their content is unverified.

summary: This skill lets an agent turn written text, articles, ebooks or subtitle files into spoken audio. It can use a local open-source voice engine offline, or a cloud voice service that supports cloning a voice from a sample, adjusting emotion and fixing a segment's exact length. It is aimed at people producing narration, voiceovers, dubbed video or voice messages.
tasks: turn an article into an audio narration
make a voiceover for a video from an SRT file
clone a voice from a short sample for a promo
produce a voice message in ogg format
dub subtitles with a different voice per segment
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete commands, a voice-map format, a backend comparison and an auth note, but it points to reference.md and examples/ that are not in the bundle and the main tts.py was not shown.
needs: Noiz API key (optional; guest mode works without one with fewer features)
ffmpeg in PATH for timeline mode
why: It directly produces voiceovers and dubbed audio for content, and the Kokoro path runs offline on the person's own computer, but the Noiz backend uploads text and reference audio to noiz.ai, which the skill discloses. Voice cloning from someone else's recording needs their consent, and the rest of tts.py was not visible to check. The skill also copies a legacy key file from the home folder, which is disclosed and limited to the same key.

summary: This skill makes an agent write optimized prompts for specific AI tools such as LLMs, coding agents, image, video and voice generators, and workflow builders. It asks for the target tool when unclear, pulls out the real task, format and constraints, and returns one paste-ready prompt with model-specific guidance. It is aimed at people who want better results from AI tools, not at building the product itself.
tasks: write a prompt for Midjourney to generate a product image
fix a prompt that gives inconsistent output in ChatGPT
adapt an existing prompt for Cursor or Claude Code
split a large agent request into sequential prompts
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete per-tool routing, output format rules, diagnostics and verification checks, though it is long and some model-specific claims are time-sensitive.
why: Useful for writing prompts for AI tools the person uses on the node, including content and image or video prompts, but it does not build the product itself. It has no stack dependency and no outside service, and its model names and version claims may go stale.

summary: This skill gives an agent a Python toolkit for making animated GIFs for Slack, from requests like "make a GIF of X doing Y". It provides size and dimension validators for Slack's message and emoji limits, plus composable motion primitives such as shake, bounce, spin, slide and explode. It also includes helpers for text outlines, colour palettes, easing and particle effects. The output is aimed at people who want reaction GIFs or emoji animations for their team chat.
tasks: make an animated GIF for Slack
create a custom Slack emoji animation under 64KB
validate a GIF's size and dimensions for Slack upload
add motion effects like shake or bounce to an image
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is concrete, with Slack limits, runnable examples and validator calls, but some composition examples use helpers without importing them, and the text and emoji helpers assume macOS font paths.
why: It is a local Python toolkit that writes GIF files to disk with no outside service, so it fits a node, but its use is narrow to Slack GIFs and emoji rather than sites, apps or general content. Install it with pip into the element folder. The unseen files (typography, validators, templates) were not inspected, so their contents are unverified.

summary: The skill guides an agent through implementing, reviewing and debugging iOS and macOS push notifications with UserNotifications and APNs. It covers the permission flow, device token registration, local and remote payloads, silent background pushes, foreground and tap handling, actions and categories, grouping, and rich notifications with service extensions. It is written for Swift app developers building native Apple apps.
tasks: add push notifications to an iOS app
debug why APNs notifications are not arriving
set up notification actions and categories
review a silent push background-update design
add a rich notification with an image attachment
qualityWhy: It gives concrete Swift code, explicit contracts for review, common mistakes with fixes, and a checklist, with references to deeper files.
why: The skill is for native Apple apps built in Swift, and the node's stack is Next.js and React, so it does not serve building or running sites, web apps or content on a Fractera node. It is not a risky skill; it is simply out of scope for this stack.

summary: This skill helps an agent write a morning market briefing that links global stocks, rates, currencies, commodities and volatility to what they mean for Korean markets, with a source link for each figure. The bundled Python helper pulls public end-of-day data from the US Treasury, FRED, Cboe, the ECB and the Bank of Korea, and records the observation date of each value so stale numbers are flagged. It is aimed at analysts, newsletter writers and finance-content producers. The helper is offline-tested, but the SKILL.md itself mostly points to a remote CLI for the actual instructions.
tasks: write a morning market briefing for Korean investors
summarize overnight US market moves and their Korean impact
review an existing market briefing for missing or stale data
pull public rates, FX and volatility figures with dates
tools: US Treasury daily yield curve CSV
qualityWhy: The bundled helper and its tests are concrete and careful, but SKILL.md is a stub that defers its real instructions to a remote npm package, so the visible files are thin as instructions.
why: The subject is finance content, which only partly fits building and running a product, and the skill's real instructions come from a remote package it runs on every start, so it should not be installed until that is reviewed.
risks: SKILL.md runs a remote npm package via npx -y on every start and treats its output as the primary instructions, so arbitrary code and prompts from that package would run on the machine.
The skill runs npx update to upgrade the CLI and every installed skill, which pulls and applies new remote code without the person's review.

summary: This skill acts as a router for a larger set of engineering skills, telling an agent which step or skill fits a situation. It lays out a main path from a rough idea through interviews, specs, ticket splitting, test-first implementation and review, plus side paths for bug triage, large unclear efforts and codebase upkeep. It is aimed at developers who want an agent to pick the right working method without memorising each skill. Most of its content is process guidance rather than code.
tasks: decide which engineering skill fits the current task
plan a feature from an idea to tickets
choose between handoff, compact, clear or subagent at a phase boundary
triage incoming bug reports and feature requests
decide whether a big unclear effort needs a wayfinder-style map
qualityWhy: The routing logic and phase-boundary guidance are concrete and well-ordered, but nearly every step points to sibling skills that are not in this folder, so an agent cannot act on most of it alone.
why: It is a stack-free process guide that could help an agent plan and build features on a node, but it only makes sense alongside the other skills in its repo, which are not included here. The sibling skills it names (grill-with-docs, to-spec, implement and others) would need installing separately before the routing works.

summary: This skill keeps a local folder of the developer's own GitHub repositories and lets an agent search them for conventions, such as how a Helm chart or Docker Compose file is organised, before making a new decision. It can clone or pull one repository, or sync the whole set using a manual list or the GitHub CLI. It can also produce a time-sorted overview of GitHub Actions triggers and cron schedules across those repositories. It is aimed at a developer who wants new work to match their existing projects.
tasks: find how a sibling project structures its Helm chart
clone a reference repository to check a pattern
sync all reference repositories before a review
list when every GitHub Actions workflow runs across my repos
qualityWhy: The instructions give clear steps, exit codes, examples and citation rules, though the referenced search-patterns file was not fully checked and some steps depend on the reader knowing the directory layout.
needs: GitHub CLI (gh) authenticated to that account
why: It helps with consistent project conventions, but it does not build, run or sell anything on a node directly. It needs the GitHub CLI and an account to clone or sync private repositories, so the person must set that up themselves.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to decide whether a Google Cloud Storage bucket should be mounted as a POSIX file system with gcsfuse, or read directly through gs:// paths instead. When a mount is the right choice, it guides the agent through tuning the mount for the workload, configuring GKE, Compute Engine or Cloud Run, keeping ML checkpoint writes safe, and diagnosing slow training or rising bills from gcsfuse metrics. It is written for engineers running training jobs and data pipelines on Google Cloud.
tasks: decide whether to mount a cloud bucket or read it directly
mount a bucket into GKE training pods
make ML checkpoint writes safe on a mount
diagnose slow training from storage metrics
tools: GKE Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver
qualityWhy: The skill gives a concrete fit gate, routing table, tuning keys, manifests and a telemetry-first runbook, though it leaves some config details to its reference files.
needs: GKE or Compute Engine or Cloud Run deployment
why: It is built around Google Cloud's hosted bucket storage and hosted compute (GKE, Cloud Run), which a local-first node does not provide, so it is not useful for what nodes are for. It also tags each gcloud and API call with a usage label sent to Google's collection pipeline.

summary: This skill makes an agent check its own or a supplied text for factual claims before the text is shown or published. It pulls out each statement that can be verified, searches the web for sources the person can open themselves, and looks for common hallucination patterns such as invented citations and unsourced statistics. It gives a confidence rating per claim, with a fuller report for legal, regulatory or high-risk content. It suits anyone who writes or publishes AI-assisted material and needs to catch errors first.
tasks: verify facts in a draft article before publishing
check citations in a legal or compliance memo
flag unsourced statistics in a landing page or blog post
produce a verification report with source links
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear three-layer procedure with categories, rating scales, escalation rules and domain guidance, though it has no worked example and leaves search query wording to the agent.
why: It is a stack-free review habit that helps content and legal writing on a node, but it does not build the product itself. It relies only on the agent's own web_search tool, with no key or account, and nothing in the files runs code or sends data elsewhere.

summary: This skill makes an agent debug hard bugs and performance regressions by first building a fast, reliable pass/fail loop that reproduces the exact symptom. It then requires minimising the repro, ranking falsifiable hypotheses, instrumenting one variable at a time, writing a regression test, and cleaning up. It is aimed at developers who need a systematic debugging routine for a product's code.
tasks: debug a broken export button
find why a page is suddenly slow
reproduce an intermittent failure
write a regression test for a fixed bug
bisect a regression between two commits
qualityWhy: The phases, completion checklists and fallback steps are concrete and followable, though it lacks worked examples and assumes a GLOSSARY.md and ADRs that may not exist.
why: It is a stack-free debugging discipline that directly supports building and running a product, so it can be installed as written. The text is in Chinese and it refers to GLOSSARY.md and ADRs, which a node may not have, so the agent should skip those steps when the files are missing.

summary: This skill guides an agent through the full AWS resilience lifecycle, linking Resilience Hub v2 assessments, Fault Injection Service experiments, and Application Recovery Controller operational controls in three stages: define, test, operate. It tells the agent to validate each remediation with a fault experiment before marking a finding resolved, and to route observability setup to a separate skill. It is aimed at cloud architects and SRE teams running AWS workloads.
tasks: plan a resilience program on AWS

design FIS experiments tied to assessment findings
set up ARC recovery controls for a workload
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is concrete with clear workflow, guardrails and troubleshooting, but the procedural detail lives in reference files I was not given, so its depth is unverified here.
needs: AWS CLI or AWS MCP server
why: The skill is built around AWS cloud services for running and administering workloads, which the local-first node does not host, so it does not serve building or making content on a node. Its guidance is useful for AWS-hosted systems but off-purpose for Fractera.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building a NestJS backend that uses Drizzle ORM over PostgreSQL. It covers defining table schemas, wiring a database provider, building controller-service-repository CRUD modules, validating input with DTOs, adding JWT guards, running transactions, writing mocked unit tests, and generating migrations with drizzle-kit. It is aimed at developers who want a server-side API.
tasks: build a REST API with CRUD endpoints for a database table
add JWT login protection to API routes
set up schema migrations with drizzle-kit
write unit tests for a NestJS service with mocked repositories
qualityWhy: The examples are concrete and follow a clear workflow, but several snippets are incomplete (DatabaseService is never defined, imports are missing, and the JWT guard does not show how the secret is configured).
