why: The skill targets NestJS with Drizzle on PostgreSQL, but a Fractera node is built on Next.js with its own SQLite element as the only data door, so the patterns must be adapted to the node's stack rather than installed as written. Only SKILL.md was reviewed; the reference files were not included in the text provided.

summary: This skill makes an agent answer as a Chinese relationship-content creator, speaking in first person with a blunt, self-deprecating tone and addressing the reader as "brothers". It applies five mental models and nine decision rules drawn from video subtitles about dating, flirting and social dynamics. It is aimed at people who want advice on romance, interpersonal conduct or personal growth framed through that persona.
tasks: advise on a romantic relationship in the persona's style
analyse why someone acts a certain way in a social situation
write a blunt, humorous post about dating or personal growth
qualityWhy: The file is clearly structured with models, heuristics, voice rules and stated limits, but it is built on a single person's subtitles and mostly describes a persona rather than giving steps or checks an agent can execute.
why: It is a stack-free text persona usable now and then for relationship advice or social content, but it has no tool use and its own limits say it is weak for business decisions. It concerns a real identifiable person's public persona, and the agent should not present the output as that person's actual views.

summary: This skill guides an agent through AWS Transit Gateway work: building a regional hub, attaching VPCs, splitting traffic with route tables, routing egress and east-west traffic through inspection, connecting on-premises networks, peering across Regions, moving off VPC peering, and handling multicast. It acts as a router that points each task to a detailed reference file. It is aimed at cloud network engineers and infrastructure teams running AWS networking.
tasks: connect many VPCs through one transit gateway
isolate environments with transit gateway route tables
send spoke traffic through a central inspected egress VPC
link a transit gateway to on-premises over VPN or Direct Connect
qualityWhy: The router and security sections are concrete and the per-task references are detailed, though the router file itself contains no commands and the referenced files were not provided to verify.
needs: AWS account with an assumed IAM role or IAM Identity Center access
AWS CLI or AWS MCP server
why: A transit gateway is a cloud networking service run by AWS, so under the local-first rule this counts as cloud infrastructure administration and is value none and use skip. The skill is well written, but its whole purpose is operating a cloud service that a Fractera node would not host.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building native Apple-platform apps in Swift 5.9+. It covers SwiftUI views and state with @Observable, protocol-first designs with associated types, async/await with actors for thread safety, memory and performance tuning, and XCTest-based testing. It is aimed at developers shipping iOS, macOS, watchOS or tvOS software, and it also mentions server-side Swift with Vapor.
tasks: build an iOS app screen in SwiftUI
add async/await networking with error handling
make a shared cache thread-safe with an actor
design a protocol-based repository layer
write XCTest tests for async code
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with correct-versus-incorrect code pairs, reference files for each topic, and build and test checkpoints, though some examples are loose (for instance the generic Repository protocol's fetch signature does not match its associated type).
why: Fractera nodes build web sites, web apps, agents and content, so native Swift apps are only occasionally relevant, for example a companion iOS app. The skill is built for Xcode and Swift toolchains that the node does not provide, so it should be read for ideas and adapted to the node's own stack rather than installed as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through moving a HeroUI v2 React app to HeroUI v3. It explains the main breaking changes, such as compound components, the removal of the Provider, and the switch to Tailwind v4, then fetches the official step-by-step guides through bundled scripts. It is aimed at developers who keep an existing HeroUI project and need to upgrade it.
tasks: upgrade a HeroUI v2 app to v3
migrate a single HeroUI component to v3
plan an incremental HeroUI migration
update HeroUI styling and hooks after an upgrade
qualityWhy: The instructions are clear and ordered, but most of the real migration detail lives in remote docs that the agent has to fetch, so the file alone is thin.
why: A node builds on Next.js with Tailwind 4 and shadcn/ui, so this only helps if the person has an existing HeroUI v2 app to move; it is not a general build guide, so the agent should read it for ideas and not as a drop-in install. The scripts fetch docs from a staging preview URL, which the person may want to know about.

summary: The skill guides an agent through auditing paid-advertising creative: it inventories assets by concept, hook, offer, format and placement, checks them against current platform specifications and policy, and scores attention, clarity, accessibility, destination match and disclosure. It separates creative quality from format compliance and measured performance, and diagnoses fatigue only from delivery and response data over time. The output is prioritised refresh or experiment briefs. It is aimed at marketers and ad teams reviewing campaigns.
tasks: audit my ad creatives for fatigue and diversity
review ad copy and hooks before launch
check video and image ads against platform specs
prioritise creative refresh and test briefs
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and sensible, but the file is short and generic, with no concrete checklists, examples or platform specifics to follow.
why: It is a stack-free audit method that helps a node that sells or promotes products review ad creative, but it is only occasionally needed and gives no hands-on tooling. It names no outside service, so no key is required.

summary: This skill guides an agent through researching what competitors are running in paid advertising. It starts by confirming the named competitors, market, and goal, then pulls observations from public ad transparency libraries and operator-supplied auction data. The agent logs each finding with its date, platform, and source, keeps observed facts apart from guesses, and groups recurring themes and gaps into experiments. It is written for marketers and founders planning paid campaigns.
tasks: research what competitors are advertising on Meta and Google
compare competitor ad messaging and offers with ours
find gaps and opportunities in competitor paid campaigns
build a sourced competitor ad report with test ideas
qualityWhy: It gives a clear, ordered research method and sensible compliance rules, but it has no concrete steps per platform, no output template, and no examples.
why: It is a stack-free research method that helps a product's marketing and ad planning, but it does not build or run anything on the node. The ad libraries it relies on are free public sources, so no key or paid service is required.

summary: This skill guides an agent through adding internationalization to an app: moving user-facing text into translation keys, organizing locale files by feature, and handling plurals, dates, numbers and right-to-left layouts. It also bundles a Python checker that flags likely hardcoded strings and compares key sets across locale JSON files. It is aimed at developers preparing a public site, SaaS product or shop for several languages.
tasks: translate my Next.js site into several languages
find hardcoded text in my components
check that all locale files have the same keys
add right-to-left support for Arabic or Hebrew
set up locale files and fallback language
qualityWhy: The guidance is useful but mostly generic, with short examples and no step-by-step setup, and the checker is an explicitly heuristic, English-biased regex scan capped at 50 files.
why: Internationalization directly supports sites and shops built on a node, but the skill is advisory and does not itself do translation, so it is only useful now and then. It mentions next-intl and react-i18next, which the node may not use, so the agent should match the node's own stack; the bundled checker only reads local files and makes no network calls, and I could not see the truncated end of the script.

summary: This guide tells an agent how to write frontend code that talks to a Medusa commerce backend: call built-in endpoints through the Medusa JS client, call custom backend routes, and wrap those calls in React Query for reads, writes, cache refreshes and error handling. It also lists common mistakes, such as dividing prices by 100 or building request bodies with JSON.stringify. The intended reader is a developer building a shop frontend on Medusa.
tasks: build a product listing page for an online shop
call a custom API route from the storefront
add a review form with optimistic updates
fix price display in a Medusa storefront
wire up cart mutations with React Query
qualityWhy: It gives clear rules with correct and incorrect examples and a checklist, but the detailed patterns sit in a reference file and the main text leans on rule lists.
needs: a Medusa store publishable API key
why: Shop frontends are a core node use, but this skill is built around Medusa's own backend and its SDK, which a node replaces with its SQLite data element and Stripe element, so an agent should take the request patterns and rebuild them on the node's data layer. Its rules about fetch(), price display and query keys are still useful.

summary: This skill walks an AI coding agent, such as Claude Code, through sending its model requests to the Salesforce Models API instead of a default provider. It explains how to mint a signed access token from a Salesforce connected app, verify the endpoint with a test call, and write the agent's settings file. It also includes a troubleshooting table for authorization and model-name errors. It is aimed at developers who run Salesforce-based AI models for their agents.
tasks: route Claude Code through the Salesforce Models API
fix 401 or 404 errors from the Models API endpoint
set up OrgJWT client_credentials auth for an agent
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete steps, exact settings keys, a verification curl, a checklist and a diagnosis table, with only small gaps in the non-Claude agent guidance.
needs: Salesforce org with a connected app that has the sfap_api scope and client_credentials flow enabled
Salesforce Models API entitlement for the org
consumer key and secret of the connected app
why: It configures how an agent reaches an outside model service, which is useful now and then but is not core to building node products. It depends on a Salesforce org and its credentials, so the person must choose that service.
risks: The runbook option asks for the exact .orgjwt.env contents, which could write the client secret into a Markdown file if the placeholders are filled in.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull a list of open GitHub pull requests that are waiting for the user's review. It keeps only the requests where a chosen team was asked to review or where the author belongs to that team. It relies on the GitHub CLI and a small Python script run through uv, and it falls back to manual gh api calls if the script fails. It is aimed at engineers working through a shared team review queue in a GitHub organization.
tasks: list the pull requests I need to review
show the review queue for my team
check which open PRs a team was asked to review
qualityWhy: The steps, output format, script and manual fallback are concrete and easy to follow, though the script leaves the team display names unused and the multi-team example repeats the single-team command.
needs: GitHub CLI authenticated with read access to the getsentry organization and its teams
why: It is a review-queue tool for one company's GitHub organization and team structure, not something a node uses to build, run, sell or make content for a product. It has no risky behaviour, so the skip comes from its low value to nodes.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to document TypeScript code: it adds JSDoc comments to functions, classes and types, sets up TypeDoc to generate API reference pages, and writes architecture decision records. It also covers ESLint rules that check documentation quality and a CI job that regenerates the docs. The guidance is aimed at developers who maintain libraries or applications and want their code explained to other people.
tasks: document the public API of a TypeScript library
write an architecture decision record for a design choice
set up TypeDoc generation for a project
add JSDoc comments to a React hook or utility function
enforce documentation rules with ESLint
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete config files, annotated code examples and a validation step, and the reference files add depth, though some sections are long and framework examples are only partly tied to the steps.
why: Documentation of code helps a product, but it is not a core node function, so the value is some. The skill is stack-neutral (npm, TypeDoc, ESLint) and needs no cloud service or account, so it can be installed as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent to plan a single-page flyer for an event, sale, listing, or campaign. It has the agent pick one main message and one call to action, sort facts into hero, support, and footer tiers, and describe tone, hierarchy, and contrast without giving layout coordinates. The finished plan is then turned into a K2F package and exported, usually as a PDF. It is aimed at people making print or digital one-pagers.
tasks: make a one-page flyer for an open house
write a flyer for a restaurant special
plan a print handout for a gym sign-up drive
turn event details into a printable promo sheet
qualityWhy: The steps, tiers, genre guidance, failure table and checklist are concrete and followable, though the export step only points to the separate k2f skill.
why: It is useful for occasional flyer and print one-pager work, but flyers are not a core node use and it depends on the separate k2f skill and K2F engine, which the agent must install first with npx skills add suzheng/k2f --skill k2f. The description reads like marketing copy, but the body is plain instructions.

summary: This skill lets an agent hand a bounded coding task to the Cursor Agent CLI as a background implementer, using a bundled Node relay that feeds the brief on stdin and records a structured result. The orchestrating agent then re-runs the project's gates, reviews the diff against the brief, and does the commit itself. It also covers read-only second opinions and sequential queues of tasks, with each step written as a concrete procedure. It is aimed at developers who want to delegate implementation work while keeping control of review and landing.
tasks: have Cursor implement a feature in this repository
delegate a bug fix to Cursor and review its diff
run a queue of refactoring tasks through Cursor
get a read-only second opinion on a contested code change
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with clear steps, flag tables, failure exit codes, a review checklist and a documented commit boundary, but the relay script was truncated so its full behaviour could not be checked and it refers to other skills that may not be installed.
needs: cursor-agent CLI installed and logged in with a Cursor account
why: It serves building software directly, but the default relay runs Cursor with --force (commands run without approval) and --trust (skips the workspace-trust prompt), which switches off the safety prompts for a repository, so the skill is marked skip; the install would be acceptable only if the person always runs it with --no-force and trusted repositories, and the truncated relay script could not be fully checked.
risks: The default dispatch passes --force and --trust, so Cursor runs commands and works in the repository without the usual approval or workspace-trust prompts.
The --sandbox override lets an agent turn off Cursor's sandbox for a run.

summary: The skill guides an agent through moving a project's code formatter from Prettier or Biome to Oxfmt. It runs the built-in migration command, which turns the old config into an .oxfmtrc.json, then reviews option differences, sets up Oxfmt extensions such as import sorting and Tailwind class sorting, updates CI scripts, and checks the resulting formatting diff. It is aimed at developers maintaining a codebase.
tasks: migrate a project from Prettier to Oxfmt
switch a project's formatter from Biome to Oxfmt
update CI to run Oxfmt --check
review formatting diff after migration
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands, option mapping tables, known pitfalls and checks an agent can follow, with only minor gaps such as no example of a full migration run.
why: It is a developer-tooling migration guide that helps maintain code formatting, but a Fractera node does not directly build or run sites, so its use is occasional. It is written for a project's own formatter setup, not for Fractera's stack, so an agent should read it for ideas and adapt the steps to the node's own setup rather than install it as written.

summary: This skill gives an agent a structured rubric for judging how good an Agent Skill is, covering its knowledge content, format, progressive loading, and usefulness. It scores eight weighted dimensions out of 120, checks the description field for trigger keywords, and flags common failure patterns such as tutorial-style padding or vague warnings. It is aimed at people who write or maintain skills and want an audit with prioritized fixes.
tasks: audit a SKILL.md file for quality
score an agent skill against best practices
suggest fixes for a skill's description
find redundant or generic content in a skill
qualityWhy: The rubric is concrete, with scoring tables, a report template, a step-by-step protocol and a checklist, though some claims such as 'derived from 17+ official examples' are unsupported and the self-evaluation note is asserted rather than shown.
why: It is a stack-free review method, so it fits a node that builds and maintains agent skills, but it does not directly build products, content or running services. Its length (about 31 KB, well above its own 300-line ideal) and its unverified provenance claims are weaknesses to weigh, not blockers.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of checks and rewrite guides for existing Chinese LaTeX dissertation projects. It diagnoses XeLaTeX build errors, GB/T 7714 references, formula and table layout, terminology drift, chapter structure, and writing style, and it helps answer reviewer comments on a thesis. It is aimed at graduate students preparing a degree thesis, not at product or web work.
tasks: diagnose why a Chinese thesis fails to compile in XeLaTeX
check GB/T 7714 references in a thesis bibliography
reply point by point to thesis reviewer comments
polish one chapter of a Chinese thesis
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a detailed module router, exact commands, output formats and safety boundaries, though it is dense and some reference and script files were not visible to review.
why: It works on local .tex thesis files, which fits the local-first design, but its subject is degree-thesis typesetting and academic writing, which nodes are not built for, so it is marked none and skip. The scripts beyond the visible ones (for example online_bib_verify.py, which is opt-in) were not reviewed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through changing IAM v1 allow policies on Google Cloud projects, folders, or organizations. Before any change is applied, it replays the last 90 days of access logs against the proposed policy using the Policy Simulator, then checks the results for revoked access. It applies the change only after the person confirms, and it is aimed at cloud administrators managing who can access their cloud resources.
tasks: simulate an IAM role change before applying it
check whether a new IAM binding would break existing access
safely grant or remove a role on a Google Cloud project
audit access impact of an IAM policy change on a folder or organization
qualityWhy: The steps, exact gcloud commands, safety gates and a helper script are concrete and checkable, but the fixed /tmp paths, the unverified response shape the script parses, and the lack of a rollback step leave small gaps.
needs: Google Cloud account with roles/policysimulator.admin, roles/cloudasset.viewer and IAM admin roles on the target resource
gcloud CLI authenticated to Google Cloud
why: It administers Google Cloud IAM for cloud resources, which is cloud administration rather than building, running or selling a local-first product, so its value to a node is none. It is not a risk, but it changes live cloud permissions, which is outside the node's purpose.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to produce architecture documentation as C4 model diagrams written in Mermaid syntax. It covers context, container, component, deployment and dynamic views, with element and relationship syntax, styling, and rules on what to avoid. It is aimed at developers, architects and product people who need to explain how a software system is structured.
tasks: draw a system context diagram for my app
document the container architecture of this project
make a deployment diagram for production
visualize how the services talk to each other
qualityWhy: It gives concrete workflow steps, runnable examples for each C4 level, a syntax reference and output naming rules, though it leans on referenced files for depth.
why: Documentation diagrams are useful for building and explaining a node-hosted product now and then, and the skill is stack-free and local, but it is not core to running a site or app. No outside service is called and nothing sensitive is touched.

summary: This skill makes an agent review the current chat session for lessons worth keeping. It runs three parallel review passes over the transcript, merges their findings into accepted, rejected, and backlog items, and proposes edits to existing agent skills. Each edit waits for the person's approval before it is applied. It is aimed at teams who maintain shared agent skills in Cursor.
tasks: reflect on this session and improve the skills
turn lessons from a conversation into skill edits
review a chat transcript for reusable learnings
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete steps, a routing table, and approval gates, but it depends on Cursor-specific paths and skills and on reference files that were not included.
needs: MCP servers for the team's tickets and devex tracker
why: It is a maintenance workflow for editing agent skills in a Cursor team, not a tool for building, running, selling or making content in a Fractera node. It also reads transcripts from the Cursor projects folder and assumes Cursor-only tooling.
risks: Conversation transcripts, which may contain secrets or private data, are passed to subagents with MCP access and backlog items are filed to an external tracker without per-item approval.

summary: The skill lets an agent author and edit K2F documents, a JSON-based semantic format that compiles to pixel-identical Word, PDF, fillable PDF and InDesign output. It guides building menus, certificates, planners, invitations and worksheets from a starter package or Gallery templates, then validating, rendering and exporting. It is aimed at people who produce print-style documents with an AI agent.
tasks: design a printable certificate as a K2F document
export an editable PDF from a K2F file
create a fillable form PDF with blanks and checkboxes
convert a Markdown report into an InDesign IDML file
edit a K2F flyer's text and re-verify the render
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md and references are concrete, with explicit workflows, validation steps, error-code guidance and golden example fragments, though several referenced files were not shown to me.
why: It produces documents, not sites, apps, or social/video content, so its use on a node is occasional rather than core. It needs the k2f CLI installed via pip and its own format, not the node's stack, so an agent should read it for ideas rather than install as-is; the pip install step is a local tool, not a cloud service.

summary: This skill guides an agent through slimming a bloated agent instruction file such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md. It finds contradictions, keeps only universal essentials in the root file, and moves topic-specific rules into linked, categorized markdown files. It also flags vague or redundant lines for deletion. It is aimed at developers who maintain instruction files for coding agents.
tasks: refactor my CLAUDE.md into linked files
split my AGENTS.md because it is too long
clean up my agent config and remove vague rules
organize agent instructions with progressive disclosure
qualityWhy: The skill gives clear phases, tables, templates, a checklist and verification steps that an agent can follow, though it lacks a worked example of the contradiction-resolution loop.
why: It is a stack-free documentation habit that helps a node's developers keep their agent instruction files lean, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. It only edits markdown files and has no external calls, so it is safe to install as written.

summary: This skill lets an agent draw one or more random winners from a list, a CSV or Excel file, or a Google Sheet, for giveaways, raffles and contests. It can exclude earlier winners, weight entries by ticket count, name runner-ups, and split a list into equal teams. The output shows the chosen row and a timestamp so the draw can be reported. It is aimed at social media managers, event hosts and small product teams.
tasks: pick a random giveaway winner from a spreadsheet
draw three winners and two runner-ups from entries
select event raffle winners from an attendee CSV
split a participant list into equal random teams
qualityWhy: It is a short description with example prompts and outputs, but it gives no procedure for reading files or Sheets, no method for the random draw, and no checks, while claiming cryptographic randomness and 'no manipulation possible' without showing how.
needs: Google Sheets access, only if a Google Sheet is used as the source
why: A local CSV or Excel list works without any account, so the skill fits a node's local-first setup for occasional giveaways. Its fairness claims are unverified and an agent would need to write the actual selection code itself, so treat the output as a convenience rather than a audited draw.

summary: This skill guides an agent to pick the simplest visual model for a relationship, such as components and connections, ordered messages, process steps, state transitions, hierarchy, timelines, matrices or quantities. It then builds one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and JavaScript, using HTML/CSS, SVG, Canvas or WebGL as the scale requires. It is meant for people who want a diagram explaining a system or idea, and it asks the agent to check layout, keyboard access and reduced motion before returning the file path.
tasks: draw a diagram of how the components of this app connect
make an interactive sequence diagram of the login flow
turn this process into a visual flowchart I can open in a browser
show the state transitions of this order as a diagram
qualityWhy: It gives a clear decision method, rendering rules and a verification checklist, but has no concrete examples, templates or step-by-step build procedure.
why: A stack-free skill that produces a standalone HTML diagram usable on a node for docs, landing pages or explainers, so it is useful now and then rather than constantly. It references an optional design-artifact skill for surrounding composition, which the node does not need to run.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up and running a private network link between a customer's data center or colocation facility and AWS. It covers choosing a connection type, creating virtual interfaces with BGP, reaching many VPCs through a gateway, encrypting the link, improving resilience, managing link aggregation groups, SiteLink, and migrating from a virtual private gateway to a transit gateway. It is aimed at network engineers and cloud operators working on AWS infrastructure. Each task routes to a separate procedure file.
tasks: set up a dedicated AWS Direct Connect link to a data center
add a virtual interface and bring up BGP peering
encrypt traffic over a Direct Connect link
make a Direct Connect connection resilient to failure
migrate from a virtual private gateway to a transit gateway
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is a clear router with explicit ordering rules, constraints and least-privilege IAM guidance, but only its main file was provided, so the per-task procedures could not be checked.
needs: AWS account with Direct Connect permissions
Direct Connect location or colocation partner
why: Direct Connect is cloud networking administration for AWS, which a local-first Fractera node does not serve, so the value is none and it is skipped. The skill itself carries no harmful instructions.

summary: This skill gives an agent a routine for working with a persistent memory store: search it for earlier decisions before starting a nontrivial task, save each decision with its reasoning as soon as it is settled, and turn user corrections into lessons. It is aimed at agents that work across many sessions on the same project. It also says what not to store, such as anything readable from the code, secrets, and step-by-step narration, and warns against treating retrieved records as trusted facts.
tasks: recall earlier decisions before starting a feature
save a design decision with the reason behind it
record a lesson after the user corrects my approach
check memory for a known gotcha before debugging
qualityWhy: The loop and its checklist are clear, but the tool calls are only sketched, the mechanics of hook capture and summaries are left to other places, and it depends on companion skills it does not define.
why: A memory habit is useful for agents that build and maintain sites or apps over many sessions, but the skill uses agentmemory's own store, which would be a second data store beside the node's SQLite element, the only door to data. The loop should be rebuilt on the node's own SQLite element rather than installed as written. Whether any hooks capture events is unverified.

summary: This skill lets an agent review a TikTok advertising account without changing it. It checks the measurement setup, Pixel events, mobile-first creative, audiences, Smart+ and TikTok Shop campaigns, bidding, budgets, attribution and ad policy. The findings come back as structured observations, diagnoses and prioritized recommendations for a marketer or the account owner. Changes are only drafted and left for a separate skill to apply.
tasks: audit my TikTok Ads campaigns
check whether my TikTok Pixel events are firing correctly
review Smart+ or GMV Max campaign setup
find creative and policy problems in my TikTok ads
qualityWhy: The skill is a short abstract procedure that depends on referenced files (ads/references/tiktok-audit.md and a main ads contract) that are not included, so an agent cannot follow its checks concretely.
needs: TikTok Ads Manager exports or API access
why: It is an advertising audit for social media campaigns, useful now and then for a product that sells through TikTok, and it reads data from a TikTok account the person must supply. The referenced audit file and the main ads contract are missing from the package, so the procedure cannot run as written.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building, improving and reviewing SwiftUI Liquid Glass effects for iOS 26 and later. It covers the glass modifier, grouping containers, glass button styles, morphing transitions, tinting, interactivity, toolbar and scroll-edge APIs, and availability fallbacks for older systems. It is aimed at iOS app developers who want their interface to follow Apple's current design language.
tasks: add Liquid Glass buttons to an iOS 26 app
review SwiftUI code for glass effect misuse
animate morphing glass shapes between states
add an availability fallback for older iOS versions
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, API tables, concrete code examples, a common-mistakes table and a review checklist, with a reference file for depth; it is solid though some sections are terse.
why: It is useful for native iOS apps but this node builds Next.js web sites and apps, so the Swift content does not apply to the node's stack and should be read for ideas only. Its iOS-specific guidance has no bearing on the node's own UI, which uses Tailwind and shadcn/ui.

summary: The skill guides an agent through setting up machine-learning and AI features in Grafana Cloud. It covers forecast alerts that learn seasonal patterns, outlier alerts that flag one service unlike its peers, triggering automated root-cause investigations, and configuring an LLM provider plugin. It is aimed at people who run monitoring for their services and want anomaly detection or assisted debugging without writing static thresholds.
tasks: alert when a metric deviates from its forecast
find the service that behaves differently from its peers
run an automated root-cause investigation for an incident
connect an LLM provider to Grafana
qualityWhy: The steps are concrete with curl examples and checks, but the main SKILL.md is a short overview that defers most detail to reference files and does not explain the failure cases.
needs: Grafana Cloud API token with plugins:write
LLM provider key such as OpenAI or Anthropic, if the LLM plugin is used
why: Every feature runs on Grafana Cloud, a cloud monitoring service, and the skill has no local-first path, so it does not serve a local node that keeps its data on the person's own computer. Its uses are observability of cloud infrastructure, not building or selling a product on the node.
risks: The LLM plugin setup writes provider API keys into a provisioning file, so an agent following it handles secrets.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a structured audit of paid advertising across up to twelve ad platforms, such as Google, Meta, and TikTok. It starts from a versioned JSON bundle of account data and runs one worker per platform, then scores the results with deterministic rules. Marketers and business owners who run paid campaigns would use it to check account health, tracking, budget and creative. Human-readable reports are rendered from the bundle at the end.
tasks: audit my Google and Meta ad accounts
find wasted spend in paid campaigns
check conversion tracking for ad campaigns
produce a prioritized paid-media action plan
qualityWhy: The procedure is concrete and well structured, but it depends on files not included here, such as the main ads contract, the audit-worker-result schema, control registries, capability manifests and the report renderer, so an agent cannot follow it from this skill alone.
needs: paid advertising accounts or exports from Google, Meta, YouTube, LinkedIn, TikTok, Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Reddit, Pinterest, Snapchat or X
the separate ads operating contract and schema files the skill references
why: It is a marketing analysis tool rather than something for building the product itself, though it helps a business sell through paid ads, and it reads from ad platforms the person chooses to connect. Its referenced companion files are missing from this skill, so an agent would need them installed before it could work.

summary: This skill guides an agent through connecting a Grafana Cloud stack to AWS, Azure or GCP over private networking, so telemetry skips the public internet. It covers creating VPC endpoints, private endpoints or forwarding rules per signal type, pointing the Alloy agent at private DNS names, and checking that DNS resolves privately. It is aimed at DevOps and platform engineers who want to cut egress costs or meet compliance rules.
tasks: set up AWS PrivateLink for Grafana Cloud
send metrics and logs over a private endpoint
verify private DNS for telemetry endpoints
configure Private Data Source Connect

It is written around one project's pipeline (its companion skills, config files and backward-compatibility rules), so it would need adapting to the node's own conventions before use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through AWS Shield Advanced, the paid DDoS protection tier for internet-facing AWS resources. summary: The skill tells an agent how to open modal dialogs in a Next.js app using the base-ui modal stack from @lobehub/ui. summary: This skill reviews an existing GitHub pull request by number in an isolated worktree, running a code-review engine or a specification review for design-only PRs. summary: This skill tells an agent to pull a project's full claude-mem activity log from the local worker, split it into one file per ISO week, and then write one narrative chapter per week. summarise what changed each week of development

why: It is a developer-history tool rather than a way to build, run, sell or make content, so it is only occasionally useful on a node, and it depends on the claude-mem worker, which is not a node element. Python is needed for the split script, and the agent must be able to run subagents one after another.

summary: This skill guides an agent building or reviewing user interfaces that follow the WordPress Design System. why: It is built for WordPress components and tokens (@wordpress/components, @wordpress/ui), which a Fractera node does not use, so an agent would have to adapt it to Next.js, Tailwind and shadcn/ui. It only helps with UI work that targets the WordPress look, and it depends on a local MCP server the person must set up.

summary: This skill guides an agent in choosing a Redis data type for a given access pattern, such as a String for counters, a Hash for objects with independently updated fields, or a Sorted Set for rankings. Redis can run locally, so it is not a cloud-only service, but it is only occasionally useful for node products.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to take a GitHub issue backlog that has piled up with repeated reports and regroup it by underlying architectural defect. summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing a LaunchDarkly feature-flag project. summary: The skill guides an agent through building Progressive Web Apps: a web app manifest for install metadata, service worker lifecycle, caching strategies such as cache-first and network-first, and Workbox setup. summary: This skill turns an agent into a thinking partner for exploring ideas, investigating problems and clarifying requirements before or during an OpenSpec change. summary: This skill guides an agent through debugging native iOS apps written in Swift. summary: The skill has an agent run a WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility audit on a design file or web page. summary: This skill turns an agent into a Prisma ORM helper for schema design, migrations, query tuning, connection settings and transactions. summary: This skill lets an agent take a GitHub-style tracker issue, or a plain problem description it first files as an issue, and drive it to a reviewed pull request. summary: This playbook guides an agent through authorized security testing of Android apps. It also covers root detection and Play Integrity evasion, tapjacking overlays, and extracting app backups and data from a device. The intended users are mobile security testers.

why: It is security testing material for mobile apps, not something a Fractera node builds or runs, so its value is limited to occasional use. It is skipped because it teaches bypassing security controls such as pinning, root checks and Play Integrity, and it includes clipboard-sniffing code described as exfiltrating passwords.
risks: Teaches bypassing SSL pinning, root detection and Play Integrity checks, which an agent could apply to apps the person does not own.
Includes a clipboard-sniffing snippet described as exfiltrating copied passwords and tokens.

summary: Builds a local code graph of functions, classes, calls and semantic metadata across many languages, then runs security pre-analysis passes such as blast radius, entrypoint enumeration, privilege boundaries and taint marking. summary: Guides an agent through turning raw user research material, such as interview transcripts, surveys, usability notes, support tickets, NPS responses or app reviews, into named themes with supporting quotes, user segments, prioritized opportunities and recommendations. summary: This skill teaches an agent to read .NET Cobertura coverage reports and explain what they prove, including partial branch conditions, plateaus and how many lines a target still needs. summary: This skill makes an agent build a code graph of a target directory with the Trailmark tool and run its four pre-analysis passes. summary: The skill has an agent send a piece of AI-written text to the HumanizerAI web service, which rewrites it to read more like a person wrote it, and then reports before and after detector scores and the remaining credits. summary: This skill teaches an agent to run the reaper MITM proxy, a command-line tool that records HTTP and HTTPS traffic between a client and a server. summary: This skill guides an agent through documenting a Java Spring Boot REST API with SpringDoc, which generates OpenAPI 3.0 specs and a Swagger UI page. summary: The skill is a security playbook for finding and exploiting cross-site scripting: it identifies the injection context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript string, URL sink, XML), then suggests payloads, filter and WAF bypasses, CSP bypasses, mXSS and multi-reflection tricks, and post-exploitation chains such as cookie theft and CSRF via XSS. summary: This skill teaches an agent how to make an in-app AI assistant aware of and able to act on a running web app. It covers steering the assistant with instructions, passing read-only app state at send time, letting it read or click rendered components, giving it two-way state for panels or inline artifacts, and bridging tools across an iframe. It is aimed at developers building chat-style copilots in React apps.

It only reads a file and writes a markdown plan, with no outside service and no secrets involved.

summary: Guides an agent on how to structure UI work in Next.js or Astro apps with a server-first approach: detect the framework from package.json or config files, keep client-side code to the smallest interactive surface, and follow existing shadcn primitives and DESIGN.md. It also requires explicit loading, empty and error states for data displays, plus a short pre-close checklist. The intended users are developers changing layouts, components, theming or server/client boundaries.
tasks: refactor a Next.js page to move client code to the server
add a component with loading, empty and error states
decide where an Astro island boundary belongs
review a UI change for unnecessary client-side code

why: It directly serves building and maintaining Next.js or Astro UIs on a Fractera node, and it is stack-free apart from the two frameworks it targets, which the node uses as Next.js. Its references to other skills (shadcn-component-boundaries, project-min-evaluation) are optional and only apply when those are installed; the reference files were listed but their content was not inspected.

summary: This skill walks an agent through turning a person's working habits into a personal skill that other agents follow. It mines recent chat transcripts from one workspace for repeated preferences, asks the person a few structured questions, groups the findings into sections, and drafts a short skill file. It then trims the prose and lands the change through a git branch and pull request. It is aimed at developers who use Cursor and want their agents to match how they work.

update my personal mode skill from recent chats
capture my coding and review preferences for agents
draft and refine a personal skill file

why: It only produces personal agent-workflow skills and does not help build, run, sell or make content for a product, and it depends on Cursor-specific tools and transcript paths that a Fractera node does not have.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to build AI features in Python with the Genkit SDK, from one-off text generation and streaming to tool-using flows and multi-turn agents with history, approvals and state. It also covers serving these over FastAPI, managing prompts and evaluations, and using the Genkit CLI to capture and inspect traces. add tool calling to an AI assistant
stream model responses to a web app
expose an AI agent over HTTP with FastAPI
debug model calls with Genkit traces
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete code, a clear workflow, CLI commands, and pointers to detailed references for each topic, though the reference files were not all visible to judge their depth.

why: It directly serves building AI assistants and agents for a product, but it is a Python SDK with FastAPI, while nodes are built on Next.js and TypeScript, so an agent would need to adapt it to the node's own stack rather than install it as written.

summary: This skill tells an agent where to put UI components in a shadcn project: registry primitives go into the resolved ui directory, product-owned reusable components go into common, and feature-specific components go into feature folders or beside their feature. It also sets a one-way dependency rule (feature to common to ui) and asks the agent to change looks through variants rather than call-site restyling. It is aimed at developers maintaining component structure in a Next.js or React project that uses shadcn.
tasks: decide where a new shadcn component should live
move a custom wrapper out of components/ui
check component imports for reverse dependencies
organise common and feature components in a React project
qualityWhy: It gives clear hard rules, a decision table, ordered steps and an output contract, though the worked examples live in a separate file and the verification step is brief.
why: It is a stack-free organisation guide that fits a shadcn-based Next.js node, and it is useful now and then rather than central to building or running a product. The skill is written for shadcn projects, which Fractera nodes use, so it needs no adaptation; the lint rule in point 9 only applies if @shadcn/lint is configured.

summary: This skill tells an agent to check which project documents exist (README, DESIGN, AGENTS, and ADR records) and then update only those that a structural change touches. It gives a table that maps change types to documents, such as architecture to README, UI standards to DESIGN, and durable decisions to a numbered ADR. It asks the agent to keep each fact in one place, record decisions rather than history, and reread edited sections against the code. It is aimed at developers and teams who want their written project guidance to stay accurate as the codebase changes.
tasks: update the README after a folder structure change
record an architecture decision as a new ADR
sync the design guide after a UI standard changes
check which project docs need edits after a quality gate change
qualityWhy: The steps, decision table and output contract are clear and followable, but there are no examples, the ADR format lives in a very short reference file, and edge cases are barely covered.
why: It is stack-free and fits any node project that keeps README, DESIGN, AGENTS or ADR files, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. The metadata lists Apache-2.0 while the catalogue says MIT, which should be checked before relying on it.

summary: This skill makes an agent run a Node project's own quality scripts, such as lint, typecheck, format check, tests and doctor, before it calls a task finished. It picks the package manager from the project's lockfile or packageManager field, runs only scripts that exist in package.json, and stops at the first failure. It is aimed at developers who want a repeatable verification step before a commit or handoff.
tasks: verify my changes before committing
run the quality checks and tell me what failed
confirm the project passes lint and typecheck
check that the work is really complete
qualityWhy: The steps, runner decision table, stop-on-failure rule and report format are concrete and easy to follow, though the reference file was only described and the e2e trigger is left vague.
why: It is a stack-free habit that fits a Next.js node project, which has package.json scripts, so it works as written and needs no outside service. It is useful now and then rather than central to building the product, and the reference file's edge cases were not fully checked.

summary: The skill guides an agent to produce draw.io (.drawio) XML files for logical flow diagrams, abstract architecture diagrams, BPMN, UML, data flow and decision flowcharts, avoiding cloud-provider specifics. It includes a validation checklist, a generic shape and colour palette, and two worked examples plus reference templates. It is aimed at people documenting system design who need a diagram file they can open in draw.io.
tasks: draw a logical flow diagram of an order process
create a three-tier architecture diagram
make a BPMN or UML sequence diagram as a drawio file
document a system's data flow diagram
qualityWhy: Concrete XML structure, a validation checklist, a palette and full examples make it followable, though the reference files were not reviewed and some rules are brief.
why: Diagram files are useful for documenting a site or app's design now and then, but they are not core to building or running a node. It is stack-free, writes only local .drawio files, and needs no service or key.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to hand code, plans or large document sets to Google's Gemini command-line tool and get an analysis back. It covers choosing a Gemini model, picking an approval mode, and running commands in the background with a timeout. It is aimed at developers who want a second reviewer for a codebase or architecture plan. The guidance also covers spotting and killing a hung Gemini process.
tasks: review my codebase for security issues
review an architecture plan for scalability gaps
analyze a whole project with a large context window
run a background code review with a timeout
qualityWhy: The commands are concrete and usable, but the file repeats itself a lot, gives contradictory approval-mode guidance, and rests on benchmark claims it does not support.
needs: Google Gemini account or API key for the CLI
why: It is useful for code and plan review, but it sends the person's code to an outside Google model, and it makes yolo approval mode the default for background runs, so the skill carries a risk and is skipped.
risks: It recommends --approval-mode yolo for background and automated runs, which auto-approves every tool call, including edits and shell commands, without asking the person.

summary: The skill has an agent answer questions about LLM and agentic application behaviour using telemetry already in Elasticsearch: latency, error rate, token use, response quality and guardrail events, and reconstruction of multi-step agent call chains. It is written for operators who need to know what their models are doing and what they cost to run. It insists on discovering which ingestion path and field names exist before querying, and on reporting cost only when a real cost field is present.
tasks: find which model is slowest and failing
report token usage per model over 24 hours
find the bottleneck step in a slow agent run
check whether prompts are being blocked by content filters
check whether any alerts or SLOs already cover LLM services
qualityWhy: The skill gives an ordered discovery process, concrete ES|QL examples, a field catalogue, explicit version gating, and clear rules for when to report absence rather than guess.
needs: an Elasticsearch deployment holding LLM telemetry from APM, OTLP or an Elastic LLM integration
the elastic CLI version 0.2 or later with es and kb support
why: It serves a node's need to monitor and report on the LLM parts of a product, and it works from local Elasticsearch data without a cloud service. The main unknown is whether a given deployment has the trace or integration data it needs, which the skill checks first.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building machine learning pipelines: logging experiments and models to MLflow or Weights & Biases, defining training workflows as Kubeflow, Airflow or Prefect DAGs, and setting up feature stores with Feast. It also covers data validation before training, hyperparameter tuning, and gated model promotion. It is aimed at engineers who train and ship models and need reproducible, tracked training runs. The skill comes with reference notes on each subtopic and short Python templates.
tasks: set up MLflow experiment tracking for a classifier
build an Airflow DAG for scheduled model retraining
design a Feast feature store schema
add data validation checks before model training
tune hyperparameters and compare runs
qualityWhy: The skill has clear workflow steps, constraints and reference files, but its data validation template is broken (it applies &= to a dict) and it leans on Great Expectations and Kubeflow APIs that are old or unverified.
why: It is useful for building and tracking models, but ML training pipelines are only a side use of a node that mainly serves sites, apps, agents and content. Local MLflow and DVC work without outside accounts, but the templates assume Kubernetes, Airflow or cloud storage, so an agent should check for local-only options first; Weights & Biases and cloud stores are optional.

summary: This skill guides an agent through installing and checking the 1Password command-line tool, then reading or injecting stored secrets such as passwords and API keys. It covers three ways of signing in: a service account token, the desktop app's integration, or a standalone password sign-in held in a terminal session. It also tells the agent to keep secrets out of logs and files and to let the person complete sign-in themselves. It is written for someone who needs credentials available to scripts, deployments or agents on their own machine.
tasks: read an API key from 1Password for a script
inject secrets into a local config with op run
set up 1Password CLI sign-in on this machine
check which 1Password account and vault are available
qualityWhy: The steps, auth-mode detection, commands and guardrails are concrete and checkable, though parts are tied to the OpenClaw gateway and its tmux and browser tools.
needs: 1Password service account token or 1Password desktop app with CLI integration
why: It is useful for handling secrets during builds and deployments, but 1Password is a cloud-hosted password vault rather than a local store, so it is only partly suited to a local-first node and requires the person's own 1Password account. The gateway-specific parts (OpenClaw paths, tmux socket, Claude in Chrome tools) would need to be dropped or adapted on a Fractera node.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to audit existing unit tests for weak assertions: it classifies each assertion into categories like equality, null, exception, state and structural, then computes diversity and coverage metrics. It flags trivial, self-referential and assertion-free tests and recommends concrete assertions to add. It is aimed at developers who want to know whether their test suite actually verifies anything meaningful.
tasks: check whether my tests are actually testing anything meaningful
find assertion-free or trivial tests in a test suite
measure assertion diversity across my MSTest, Jest, pytest or Go tests
suggest stronger assertions for shallow tests
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, with a clear workflow, classification tables, calibration rules, a report template and a validation checklist, though they lean on an external extensions catalog that is not included.
why: Useful for a team that writes tests for products built on a node, but it is a code-review habit rather than a feature of the node itself, so it is used now and then. It is stack-free in its core, and the language extension files it references are reference-only and not bundled with this skill, so per-language detail would be missing.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to handle update notices whenever a cx command from the Coralogix CLI runs. It asks the agent to look for a newer binary and a newer skills bundle in the command output, then offer both upgrade commands once at the end of the answer. It also lists a few general CLI habits such as machine-readable output, multi-profile runs, timeouts, and read-only mode. It is aimed at people who run Coralogix observability queries from the terminal.
tasks: check whether the cx CLI has a newer version
run a cx command and summarise the result
discover available cx commands and flags
query Coralogix data with multiple profiles
qualityWhy: The instructions are clear about the update-notice format, but the rest is thin and only covers the CLI's own housekeeping rather than concrete steps for building or running anything.

why: The skill only concerns the Coralogix observability CLI and its update notices, which do not serve building, running, selling or making content on a local-first Fractera node. It also depends on a cloud observability service and asks the agent to run upgrade commands, which is a reason to skip.
risks: Asks the agent to offer running upgrade commands (brew upgrade, npx skills add) that install remote code, and it lacks any safety check on that.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to merge the delta specs of an active OpenSpec change into the project's main specs, without archiving the change. The agent reads each delta, edits the matching main spec to add, modify, rename or remove requirements, keeps untouched content, and then validates the result with the openspec CLI. why: It is a local spec-writing workflow that helps build products, not a cloud service, but it only matters for projects that use OpenSpec and the openspec CLI on the machine. It is stack-free and runs with the local CLI, so no outside account is needed.

summary: This skill gives an agent rules for writing Slack messages in Slack's mrkdwn syntax rather than standard Markdown. It covers bold, italics, links, mentions and lists, plus advice on leading with the key point, keeping messages short, and choosing between threads and channel posts. It is aimed at people drafting Slack messages or announcements through Slack tools.

format a message with bold deadlines and bullet lists
reply to a Slack thread without cluttering the channel
convert a Markdown note into Slack mrkdwn

why: Useful now and then for writing messages a node's owner sends to Slack, but it does not help build, run or sell a product on the node itself. It is stack-free text guidance, so it works as written, and it notes that the MCP tools cannot add reactions.

summary: This guide teaches an agent to write Inngest functions in TypeScript that keep working through crashes, retries and restarts. It covers when a step should wrap side effects, how step memoization and idempotency keys behave, and how to set up event, cron and invoke triggers. It also explains cancellation, retry and non-retriable error rules, and logging. The intended users are backend developers who need reliable background jobs.

The skill itself is clear, but its use on a node would depend on an external service the node does not provide.

summary: This skill guides an agent through turning a validated brand profile, campaign goal and audience into ad campaign concepts, messaging, copy and a creative brief. It separates verified facts from operator-approved claims and untested creative ideas, and it checks copy against the length and policy rules of each ad platform. It is aimed at marketers and product owners who need ad copy ready for human review before launch.

create a creative brief for an ad campaign
generate distinct campaign concepts for a product
check ad copy against platform length and policy limits

why: It directly serves making ad content and marketing copy for a product, and it needs no outside service or framework. Its platform rules point to reference files and another skill that are not in this package, so an agent would need those files for the policy and specification checks to work.

summary: This skill guides an agent through structuring a Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.5 application using Clean Architecture, Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) and DDD tactical patterns. It covers the layer rules, a feature-based package layout, framework-free domain entities and value objects, ports and adapters, and tests at each layer. It is written for Java developers who want testable business logic and swappable infrastructure.

separate domain logic from framework code

model entities and value objects with domain events

summary: Audits a project's Google Mobile Ads SDK integration for iOS, Android or Unity apps. It checks for test application IDs and test ad units left in production code, confirms that SKAdNetwork IDs are complete, verifies mediation adapter SDK version compatibility, and reviews ad preloading. It can run as a full pre-launch audit or as a single targeted check, and it reports each check as Pass, Warning, Fail or N/A in a Markdown table.
tasks: audit my app before launch
check for test ad unit IDs in production
verify SKAdNetwork IDs are complete
check mediation adapter versions
qualityWhy: The checklist and reporting template are clear and point to reference files for each check, though the reference contents were not included for review, so the depth of each criterion is unconfirmed.
why: It is useful for shipping an app that shows Google ads, a narrow but real need for an app builder, and it is stack-agnostic within mobile ad integration. It only reads project files and is not directly about the node's web stack, so its value is occasional rather than central.

summary: Guides an agent through diagnosing MSBuild build failures from a binary log file. The preferred route queries the log through a bundled binlog MCP server for errors, properties, items, target execution and embedded source files. A fallback replays the log to text files and searches them with grep. It is aimed at developers whose .NET builds fail in ways the console output does not explain.
tasks: diagnose an unclear MSBuild build error
trace cascading failures across a multi-project solution
find which MSBuild target caused a compile failure
inspect MSBuild properties and package references from a binlog
qualityWhy: The steps and commands are concrete, but the guidance is thin on how to interpret the results, and the MCP tool names are never listed.
why: It serves developers who build .NET projects, which is useful for a node that builds apps, but it is a narrow debugging aid rather than something that directly builds or sells a product. It is written for a dotnet plugin, but it needs no outside service or key, and its MCP server runs locally. Its one uncertainty is that it depends on the bundled MCP server being available.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to read an OpenAPI 3.0 file in JSON or YAML, check that it is valid, and turn its schemas and endpoints into a TypeScript file with interfaces, request and response types, and runtime type guards. It is aimed at developers who need typed API clients or data models for a web app. The agent asks where to save the output and writes it to a file.
tasks: generate TypeScript types from an OpenAPI spec
create API interfaces from a schema file
add runtime type guards for API responses
convert a JSON or YAML API description to TS
qualityWhy: The mapping tables and examples are clear and usable, but the skill leaves gaps: it does not explain how to handle allOf or circular references in detail, its naming rule for endpoint types conflicts with its own example, and it covers nested objects and OpenAPI 3.1 poorly.
why: It is a stack-free code generator that writes a local .ts file and needs no outside service, so it can be installed as written. Its usefulness is occasional, since it only helps when a project has an OpenAPI spec to type against.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to use the mcporter command-line tool to work with Model Context Protocol servers. The agent can list a server's tools and their input schemas, call a tool with key=value arguments or a JSON payload, and run the OAuth login flow. It can also manage the config file, control the mcporter daemon, and generate CLI or TypeScript wrappers from a server. It suits a developer who wants to reach external MCP tools from a project or script.
tasks: list the tools an MCP server exposes
call an MCP tool with arguments from the terminal
authenticate to an MCP server with OAuth
generate a TypeScript client for an MCP server
qualityWhy: It gives correct, concrete command forms, but it is a short reference card with no steps, worked examples, or verification checks.
why: It is a stack-free command-line reference that fits a node's need to call outside MCP tools now and then, so it can be installed as written. The skill itself needs no key, but some MCP servers it reaches may require OAuth or an account the person chooses, and the stdio form runs whatever command is given.

summary: This skill guides an agent through iOS authentication work: Sign in with Apple with credential state checks and revocation handling, passkey registration and sign-in, OAuth via ASWebAuthenticationSession, Password AutoFill, and local biometric re-authentication with LAContext. It is written for iOS app developers. It stays on the client side and points server-side token checks and deeper security work to other material.

set up passkey login for an iOS app
add OAuth login with Google or GitHub in a Swift app
require Face ID before showing account settings
qualityWhy: Concrete Swift code for each flow, a checklist and a list of common mistakes, with two reference files for deeper detail, though it has no test steps for the server side.
why: The skill targets native iOS and Swift, and a Fractera node is a Next.js web stack, so it cannot be used on a node as written. Its value for nodes is therefore none, which the rules set to skip.

summary: This playbook teaches an agent to hunt business logic flaws in web applications: pricing and quantity tricks, race conditions, skipped workflow steps, coupon and referral abuse, and authorization gaps between steps. It is written for security testers and bug bounty work, and an agent can use it to review a site's checkout, sign-up, reset and access rules. It also includes a checklist of items to mark as vulnerable, not applicable, or needing a recheck.
tasks: audit my checkout for price or quantity manipulation
check my coupon and referral logic for abuse
find race conditions in my payment or redeem endpoints
review my password reset and 2FA flow for skipped steps
run a business logic security sweep before launch
qualityWhy: It gives concrete attack patterns, decision questions and checklist items with clear reasons, though many examples are single real cases without step-by-step verification commands.
why: It is a defensive-audit style methodology that works on any stack, so an agent can apply it to a site built on a node, but it is not core to building or selling. It is offensive in nature, so it should only be used against systems the person owns or is authorized to test; some examples (SMS bombing, fraud replay) must not be aimed at third parties.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to schedule and run background work in an iOS app using BGTaskScheduler, covering short refresh tasks, longer maintenance tasks, and iOS 26 continued-processing tasks started from the foreground. It also covers background URLSession downloads and silent push wake-ups. It is written for iOS developers building Swift apps, not for building web sites or apps on a local-first Fractera node.
tasks: schedule a background refresh for an iOS app

download files in the background on iPhone
handle background push wake-ups in Swift
qualityWhy: Concrete Swift code for each task type, expiration handling, Info.plist setup and a review checklist, though it omits some details such as the reference file's debugging steps.
needs: Apple developer account for background capabilities
why: The skill targets native iOS apps in Swift, which a Fractera node (Next.js web stack) does not build or run, so it does not serve the node's purpose. Its own stack is Apple's, so it cannot be used as written on a node.

summary: The skill turns an agent into a portfolio analyst for a brokerage account. It pulls holdings and account data from Alpaca (via MCP or a REST fallback), then produces allocation, diversification, risk, performance and rebalancing reports. It also ships an offline CSV holdings reviewer and a broker-versus-memory reconciliation gate for weekly reviews.
tasks: analyze my portfolio
check my asset allocation and sector concentration
suggest rebalancing trades
reconcile broker positions with my trading notes

needs: Alpaca brokerage account and API keys
why: The skill is built around a cloud brokerage service (Alpaca) as its data source, and the node is local-first, so it counts as no value for node use and is skipped. Its offline CSV mode is the only local part and does not cover the full workflow.
risks: Reads Alpaca API keys from environment variables and sends them to Alpaca's endpoints, and it asks the user to put brokerage account data into the workflow.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how to pay for and authenticate against fetcher.sh, a pay-per-call web-data API covering social platforms, search, maps, news, app stores and reviews. It explains prepaid credits with a Bearer key, per-call payment in USDC through x402, and how to connect the fetcher MCP server. It also covers the standard response envelope, error codes, and how to treat scraped text as untrusted data. It is aimed at people who need to pull public web data into their own tools or research.

pay per call in USDC with an x402 client
connect the fetcher MCP server to my AI client
check the remaining credit balance
fix a 402 topup_required error and retry

optional EVM or Solana private key for x402 signing

summary: This skill gives an agent a structured way to plan and run hard workplace conversations, such as performance concerns, team conflicts, and unrealistic deadlines. It covers a three-stage preparation, delivery, and follow-up model and the Situation-Behavior-Impact feedback technique, with example phrasings and checklists. It is aimed at managers, leads, and team members who need to give or receive difficult feedback.

write feedback using the SBI model
plan how to handle a conflict between two team members
draft a follow-up message after a feedback meeting
push back on an unrealistic deadline with a stakeholder
qualityWhy: The skill gives clear steps, scenario walkthroughs, opening lines and checklists that an agent can follow, but some statistics (such as the 60% and 30% figures) are unsourced.
why: It is a stack-free set of workplace communication habits, so it works on a node as written, but it only helps now and then with building, running, or selling a product. The unsourced research figures should be treated as approximate.

summary: This skill guides an agent through making a .NET project compatible with Native AOT and trimming by working through IL trim and AOT analyzer warnings in a build-driven loop. It covers enabling the analyzers in the project file, grouping warnings by code, and applying annotation, refactoring, source-generated JSON, or last-resort attribute fixes. It is aimed at developers who maintain .NET codebases and need them to survive trimming or AOT publishing.

switch JsonSerializer calls to a source-generated context

why: The skill is a pure build-tool workflow for a .NET library or app; it serves no node purpose of building, running, or selling a site, agent, or content, so value is none. It would also be stack-specific to .NET, which the node does not use.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing Dart code with the Genkit SDK: setting up a Genkit instance, calling models, defining tools and flows, and building conversational agents with sessions and interrupts. It also covers prompt files, serving agents over HTTP, and using the Genkit CLI to capture traces and check runs. The intended users are Dart and Flutter developers who want to add LLM features to their apps.
tasks: build a conversational AI agent in Dart
add LLM generation with tools to a Flutter app
define a Genkit flow with structured output
debug a Genkit app using traces
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is concrete, with version-specific API corrections, gotchas and verification steps, though most detail sits in reference files I could not check.
needs: Gemini, Anthropic or OpenAI API key, depending on the chosen model provider
why: The node stack is Next.js and TypeScript, so the Dart SDK only helps when a person builds a Dart or Flutter product, and its install step pipes a remote script into bash; the skill is skipped because it carries that risk.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing, reviewing and improving prompts for language models. It covers choosing few-shot examples, adding step-by-step reasoning, designing system prompts, and building reusable prompt templates. design a system prompt for a support assistant
build a reusable prompt template with variables
test a prompt against edge-case inputs

why: Prompt design is central to building AI agents and generating content on a node, and the skill is stack-free so it fits as written. Its integration section names Java-based langchain4j skills that the node does not use, but these are optional pointers rather than requirements.

summary: This is an unfilled template for writing an agent skill, not a working skill. Its header lists the metadata fields a skill file can carry, and its body is placeholder sections for overview, key concepts, patterns and best practices. An agent that loads it gets no real instructions, only guidance on how a skill should be structured. It is aimed at people who write skills for the Grafana monitoring domain.
tasks: write a new agent skill file
structure a SKILL.md with frontmatter
check that a skill meets the agent skills spec
qualityWhy: The file is a placeholder stub: the name, description and every body section are unfilled template text with no real domain content.
why: It contains no usable instructions for building, running, selling or making content on a Fractera node, and its only subject is a generic skill template for Grafana. It is a stub, so it should not be installed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a security audit of TypeScript and Node.js code, covering Express, NestJS and Next.js projects. The agent maps the sensitive parts of the code, then checks authentication, injection, input validation, XSS, secrets, dependencies and headers. It reports findings by severity with fix examples. It is aimed at developers who want to check an app before release.
tasks: review my Next.js app for security issues before deployment
audit JWT and authentication code for flaws
check my project for hardcoded secrets and vulnerable dependencies
find XSS and injection risks in my API routes

why: It directly helps a node's owner check the sites, web apps and APIs they build before release, and it needs no outside service. Its findings are only a code-level aid and do not replace a professional penetration test, which the skill itself states.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write AI features in Go with the Genkit SDK, including text generation, structured output, streaming, tool calling, prompt templates and flows served over HTTP. It also covers a stateful agent API that is marked experimental, a generative UI plugin, and a CLI for capturing and reading traces. The intended readers are Go developers building AI services.
tasks: build an AI flow in Go
add tool calling to a Go assistant
stream model output from a Go service
debug a Genkit app with traces
