It covers SQL injection in login forms, password reset and recovery weaknesses, account enumeration, brute-force protections, two-factor authentication gaps, OAuth and SSO takeover, and session handling. It is aimed at security testers reviewing a system they are authorized to test.
tasks: test a login form for authentication bypass
check password reset tokens for predictability or reuse
review two-factor authentication for skip or brute-force weaknesses
audit session invalidation after logout and privilege change
qualityWhy: It is a broad, useful list of attack patterns, but most items are one-line hints without verification steps, and a few claims are inaccurate, such as calling MD5(username+timestamp) reversible.
why: It is a stack-free security checklist, so an agent can use it as written, but it serves testing rather than building or running a product, so its value is occasional. It has no scripts, but it describes offensive techniques such as credential stuffing and brute forcing, which should only be used with written authorization on systems the person owns.

summary: The skill guides an agent to produce product photography variants for paid ads from a source image the operator has rights to, using a validated brand profile. It covers studio, contextual, ingredient, detail and lifestyle hypotheses, keeps product geometry, packaging and logos intact, and records hashes, prompts, provider, cost and dimensions in a manifest. It is aimed at marketers and ad teams who need compliant product shots, and it requires human review before use.
tasks: make studio shots of a product for ads
create lifestyle product images for a campaign
produce ingredient or detail shots with a manifest
check generated product photos for fidelity and policy issues
qualityWhy: The file is a short list of high-level steps with no concrete commands, schemas, providers, or examples an agent could follow exactly.
needs: an image generation provider or model for the photoshoot variants
why: It is useful for making product ad images, which fits a node that makes content, but it names no stack or tooling, so an agent would have to build the pipeline itself; the cost and provider are left to the operator. The skill is for a generation step that needs an outside image provider, so it is not a pure local tool.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to connect an application to a hosted, SQLite-compatible cloud database, using per-language client libraries for JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust. It also covers issuing scoped access tokens, wiring external auth providers, and managing databases provisioned through Vercel. It is aimed at developers who want their data kept on a managed cloud service rather than on their own machine.
tasks: connect a Next.js app to a hosted SQLite database
create a read-only token limited to one database
set up a database through the Vercel Marketplace
add vector search to a cloud database for embeddings
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is mostly a routing index to sub-skills and a list of docs links, and the detailed sub-files were not provided for review, so there are few concrete steps to judge.
needs: Vercel account for the Marketplace integration
why: The skill is built around a cloud-hosted database, but a node keeps its data in its own local SQLite element, so this cannot serve the node's purpose. Its SQLite feature notes could be read for ideas, but the skill should not be installed.

summary: Gives an agent a broad playbook for finding Insecure Direct Object Reference and Broken Object Level Authorization flaws in web APIs. It covers where object IDs hide in requests, two-account replay testing, HTTP verb swapping, parameter pollution, admin function access, mass assignment, state-machine abuse, and ORM filter leaks. It is written for security testers doing authorized bug-bounty or pentest work.
tasks: test an API for IDOR and broken object authorization
check whether one user can read another user's records
find hidden admin endpoints and mass assignment fields
audit an ORM filter for data leaks
qualityWhy: It is a dense, well-organized checklist with concrete examples, but it gives few step-by-step verification criteria and no exact commands, so it reads more like a reference than a procedure.
why: It is a security-testing playbook aimed at finding flaws in other people's systems, which does not serve building, running, or making content for a Fractera node. Its content is about attacking applications, so a node agent following it would be probing third-party targets rather than improving its own product.
risks: Gives offensive exploitation techniques (account enumeration, ORM filter extraction, privilege escalation) that could be used against systems the person does not own.

summary: This skill guides an agent through creating a new Terraform provider workspace in Go using the Plugin Framework. It covers module setup, a main.go entry point, and a provider.go with a schema and a Configure step that reads credentials from explicit config or environment variables. The agent then builds and tests the scaffold. It is aimed at developers who want to write infrastructure-as-code plugins for an API.
tasks: scaffold a new Terraform provider for an API
start a terraform-provider-* project in Go
set up provider configuration with environment variable fallback
qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, complete example files and build and test checks, with small gaps such as an awkward first-person opening and placeholder names that must be renamed by hand.
why: A Terraform provider is infrastructure tooling, not something that helps build, run, sell or create content for sites, apps, agents or media on a local-first node, so its value is none. Its Go stack would also not fit the node anyway.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a research job: it saves a written plan first, splits the question into separate subtopics, and hands each one to a subagent with a fixed budget of three to five web searches. The subagents save their findings to files, and the main agent then reads those files and writes a answer with cited sources, plus an optional report. It suits someone who needs an online comparison or a sourced briefing on current facts.
tasks: research a topic online and write a cited report
compare several products or options with sources
find current information on a question
gather facts and source links for a content piece
qualityWhy: It gives clear steps, a plan file format and a subagent template, but it has no source-credibility checks, no report layout and no handling of failed searches.
why: Research is useful for building and making content on a node, but it is not a core node task, so the value is some. It is stack-free and only needs the harness tools it names (web_search, fetch_url, task, file tools), so it installs as written; the search provider is not named, so the person should check which service backs web_search and where queries are sent.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building CRUD features for Spring Boot 3 services. It lays out feature packages with domain, application, presentation and infrastructure layers, JPA entities and repositories, record-based DTOs with validation, and REST controllers with standard status codes. It also includes a Python generator that scaffolds these files from a JSON or YAML entity spec. The target audience is Java backend developers.
tasks: add a REST CRUD endpoint for a JPA entity
scaffold a feature package for a Spring Boot entity
add pagination to a Java list endpoint
map request and response DTOs for a JPA aggregate
qualityWhy: The instructions are clear and point to templates, but the examples reference undefined classes such as ProductService, the prose says to defer code while including long listings, and the generator's output conflicts with the record-based guidance.
why: The skill is for Java and Spring Boot, while a Fractera node is built on Next.js, TypeScript and its own SQLite element, so an agent can only borrow the layering and DTO and status-code patterns and must rebuild them in the node's stack. The generator's full code was truncated, so its behaviour is only partly checked.

summary: This guide teaches an agent to build Terraform provider actions, which are imperative operations that run at create or update lifecycle events. It covers wiring the first action into a provider, defining schemas, writing Invoke with progress reporting, timeouts and polling, and writing acceptance tests. It is aimed at engineers who write Terraform providers in Go.
tasks: add an action to a Terraform provider
write a Go action that polls for completion
write acceptance tests for a Terraform action
document a Terraform provider action
qualityWhy: It gives concrete code, schema rules, a polling example, a test pattern and checklists, with small gaps such as no full worked example.
why: It is for writing Terraform provider plugins in Go, which is outside what a Fractera node is for, and a node's data and build stack do not include Terraform providers. It has no security risk; acceptance tests against a real provider would need that provider's own cloud credentials.

summary: This skill guides an agent to turn notes, requirements, or an existing plan into one self-contained HTML document that a team can review and act on. It keeps the original scope, ordering, commitments, and terms intact, and marks where sequence, owners, dependencies, and open questions are real. It also asks the agent to check the page at wide and narrow widths and to confirm nothing from the source was lost. The skill is meant for explicit invocation, not general requests.
tasks: turn meeting notes into a reviewable HTML project plan
restructure a rough implementation plan into phases with owners and dependencies
make an accessible single-file HTML plan for stakeholders to review
list open questions and risks from a plan in an inspectable document
qualityWhy: The rules on traceability, verification, and responsive checks are clear and actionable, but the skill gives no template, example output, or step-by-step procedure for building the file.
why: It is stack-free and works on any node as written, but it serves planning documents rather than building, running, or selling a product, so its use is occasional. It optionally reads a sibling design-artifact skill when that is present, and it adds no outside service or key.

summary: This playbook teaches an agent to probe JWT and OAuth 2.0 implementations for weaknesses. It covers signature checks, algorithm confusion, weak HMAC secrets, header injection, redirect URI and state handling, implicit flow leakage, and token exposure in logs. It is written for security testers reviewing authentication flows.
tasks: audit JWT signature and algorithm validation
test OAuth redirect_uri and state handling
check whether access tokens leak through URLs or logs
qualityWhy: The checklists and command examples are useful, but several commands are placeholders or incomplete, such as the JWKS conversion stub, and some flows are described only briefly.
why: It is stack-free and helps an agent review the security of sign-in on a node, such as next-auth tokens, but it is an offensive playbook, so it is only useful for testing systems the person owns. Its examples are generic and it names third-party targets, so the agent should be told to test only the person's own deployment.

summary: This catalog is an index that points an agent to language-specific testing guidance for C#/.NET, Python, TypeScript, PowerShell, C++, Go, Java, Rust, Ruby, Swift and Kotlin. It explains when to read a base guide and when to load the longer worked examples. It is meant for a code-testing pipeline, so agents read its files directly rather than invoking it as a skill.
tasks: write unit tests for an existing module
add a test suite to a TypeScript project
choose the right test commands for a repository
generate table-driven tests for a Go package
qualityWhy: The file is only an index table and a short usage rule, and the substantive guidance lives in extension files that were not included, so it cannot be judged as an instruction on its own.
why: Testing guidance is useful when building and maintaining apps on a node, but this is an internal reference for a pipeline, so it is only occasionally useful on its own. The TypeScript entries fit the node's stack; the others apply to other projects. The referenced files were not supplied, so their content is unverified.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of production rules for building Convex backends: validators on every function, index-only reads, idempotent mutations, and avoiding write conflicts under optimistic concurrency. It also covers pagination, keeping time out of queries, and linting with the Convex ESLint plugin. It is aimed at developers who review Convex code, set up linting, or diagnose slow queries and conflicting writes.
tasks: review a Convex function for performance and conflict risks
fix write conflicts in a Convex mutation
set up the Convex ESLint plugin
paginate a growing list in a Convex app
qualityWhy: The patterns are concrete, with code examples, a mistakes table and a checklist, though the eslint setup is delegated to a reference file.
needs: a Convex cloud account and deployment
why: Convex is a hosted cloud backend and database, which a local-first Fractera node does not use; its SQLite element is the only data door, so this skill does not fit the node's stack. Its patterns are useful reading, but the skill is built around a cloud service the node replaces, so it is skipped rather than adapted.

summary: Gives an agent a checklist for mapping an API's attack surface before testing it: finding JavaScript-embedded endpoints, probing common documentation and schema paths, and comparing API versions and mobile or legacy routes. It also lists which details to pull from docs, such as optional fields and deprecated endpoints. The audience is security testers doing authorized API assessments.
tasks: map all endpoints of a REST API
find hidden or old API versions
extract undocumented parameters from API docs
enumerate a GraphQL or mobile API surface
qualityWhy: The checklist is useful but thin: one curl command, a list of paths and a routing table, with no steps for verifying findings or handling auth.
why: It is a security reconnaissance playbook for attacking third-party APIs, not something a node uses to build, run, sell or make content for a product, so value is none and it is skipped.
risks: Teaches endpoint and hidden-surface discovery aimed at finding exploitable weaknesses in APIs that may belong to others.

summary: This guide walks an agent through adding Inngest to a TypeScript project so that webhook handlers, background jobs, scheduled tasks and multi-step workflows can run durably and retry after crashes. It covers installing the SDK, creating a shared client, and mounting the function endpoint in frameworks such as Next.js, Express, Hono and Fastify. It also explains a WebSocket worker mode and running the local dev server. It is written for developers who need reliable background processing in their app.
tasks: add retry-safe background jobs to a Next.js app
set up a webhook handler that survives failures
schedule a recurring task with durable execution
run a long multi-step workflow outside a request
qualityWhy: Concrete install, config, endpoint and troubleshooting steps with gotchas, though it leans on external docs for several frameworks and lacks a verification step for the worker mode.
needs: Inngest Cloud account with event key and signing key for production
why: Inngest is a hosted orchestration service: in v4 the default mode is Cloud, where events and function state are run and stored on Inngest's servers, which conflicts with the node's local-first design and its SQLite element as the only data door. The skill is otherwise clear, but it is built around that cloud place to run things, so it is not for this node.
risks: The npx commands use --ignore-scripts=false to run an unpinned npm package, re-enabling install scripts from remote code.

summary: This skill guides an agent through cutting a release of the linear-cli project. It reviews commits since the last tag, adds user-facing changelog entries, recommends a semver bump for the user to confirm, and then runs the project's justfile tag recipe, which runs checks, bumps versions, commits, tags and pushes. It is written for that one repository and its maintainers.
tasks: cut a new release of linear-cli
review commits since the last tag and update the changelog
recommend a semver version bump
publish a tagged version with the justfile tag recipe
qualityWhy: The steps, commands and confirmation gates are concrete and easy to follow, though it depends on undefined local tools and a justfile it does not show.
needs: git remote access with push rights to the linear-cli repository
GitHub Actions release workflow for binaries, Homebrew and npm publishing
why: It only serves the release process of one external Rust CLI project, not building, running or selling a site, app, agent or content on a Fractera node. Running it would push commits and tags to a remote and trigger publishing, which is outside what a node is for.

summary: The skill gives an agent a set of patterns and code samples for building Next.js 16+ apps with the App Router: Server and Client Components, Server Actions for forms, Route Handlers, the "use cache" directive with cacheLife and cacheTag, parallel and intercepting routes, and the async request APIs. It is aimed at developers building web apps and sites. The skill is one folder with a main guide plus several reference documents.
tasks: build a Next.js 16 page with a form
add caching to a product page
create an API route for users
set up parallel routes in a dashboard
migrate middleware to proxy.ts
qualityWhy: The main file gives concrete, runnable examples for each feature and points to detailed references, though some snippets are abbreviated and some references were not reviewed here.
why: It fits what Fractera nodes are for, but it is built around Next.js and Prisma-style code such as db.user.create with no data layer named, while nodes replace the database with their own SQLite element and go through that element only, so the examples must be adapted to the node's data access and sign-in. Nothing in the files asks for keys or cloud accounts. The skill also calls for validating third-party fetch responses, which the node's own rules should cover.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to review code changes in a Git repository, whether uncommitted workspace edits, a branch comparison, or a single commit. The OCR CLI selects the reviewable files and returns the review rules for each file, and the agent reads the diffs and writes the findings itself, grouped by severity. It is aimed at developers who want a structured, complete review with no file silently skipped.
tasks: review my uncommitted changes before committing
review a feature branch against main
review a single commit for bugs and security issues
fix the high-severity issues found in a review
qualityWhy: The steps, command examples, output schema, coverage checklist and fallback rules are concrete and followable, though it lacks a sample output and is a mirror of a canonical file.
why: It helps build and maintain a product's code but does not create product content, so it is useful now and then rather than core. It runs locally with git and a globally installed ocr CLI and needs no LLM endpoint or key on the OCR side. The host agent does the reading, so the code it reviews stays in that agent's context.

summary: This skill fills an Elastic Security deployment with fake but realistic security events, multi-step attack scenarios, and synthetic alerts, so dashboards, the Alerts tab and Attack Discovery have data to show. It is aimed at people running demos, testing detection rules or setting up a proof of concept. It writes into a remote Elasticsearch and Kibana cluster and can remove its own sample data later.
tasks: set up a demo Elastic Security environment for a stakeholder
generate sample alerts to test detection rules
simulate a ransomware attack chain in Elastic
remove sample security data after a demo
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete steps, flags, examples, environment variables and safety guidelines, though the sample-data script was cut off so its full behaviour could not be checked.
needs: Elasticsearch cluster with API key or username and password
Elastic Security project (optional LLM connector for Attack Discovery)
why: It serves Elastic Security SIEM demos and not building, running or selling a site, app, agent or content, and it writes to a remote Elastic Cloud cluster rather than the node's local SQLite and storage. The script also disables TLS certificate checks when KIBANA_INSECURE is set, which is opt-in but weakens the connection.

summary: This skill lets an agent hand the current question or task to a separate advisor agent and get back a judgment, without giving that agent the work itself. The calling agent picks a configured profile, writes a self-contained briefing with the question, files to read and options already ruled out, and asks for a reasoned recommendation. It also forwards requests to run another named skill on the task, such as a diff review. The calling agent then summarises the verdict for the person, who decides what to do. It is aimed at developers who want a fresh second opinion on a design, review or root-cause question.
tasks: get a second opinion on this design
review the current diff with another agent
ask an outside agent why this build is failing
compare approaches before I commit to one
keep an advisor for several decisions in a row
qualityWhy: The steps and briefing outline are clear, but it defers profile handling and agent creation to another skill and gives no worked example of a briefing or synthesis.
needs: Paseo with its paseo skill installed
configured Paseo agent profiles from one or more model providers
why: It is useful now and then for second opinions on coding and design work, but it does not build sites, data or content on the node itself. It needs Paseo and provider accounts that the person chooses, so it is not stack-free.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to pick and use TanStack Pacer, a timing toolkit that limits how often functions run. It covers debouncing, throttling, rate limiting, queuing and batching, with class APIs, factory functions and React hooks. It is aimed at developers who need to tame search inputs, scroll handlers, API calls, uploads or analytics events.
tasks: debounce a search input so it only queries after typing pauses
throttle scroll or resize handlers in a React component
rate-limit calls to an external API
queue file uploads so they run one at a time
batch analytics events before sending them
qualityWhy: It gives concrete code for each utility, a selection table, edge-case guidance and common pitfalls, but it has no verification steps and the library is still in beta.
why: It is a stack-free utility library that fits a Next.js and React 19 node directly, so it can be installed as written. The main doubt is that the library is beta, so the API may shift between versions.

summary: This skill guides an agent through measuring MSBuild and .NET build times before changing anything: cold, warm and no-op builds, each repeated and timed under controlled conditions. It then covers artifacts output layout, deterministic builds, project reference trimming, static graph builds and parallelism tuning. The audience is developers with slow .NET solutions who want evidence before they optimize.
tasks: measure cold, warm and no-op .NET build times
find out why a .NET solution builds slowly
compare build time before and after a change
enable artifacts output in a .NET solution
trim project references to shorten the build
qualityWhy: The steps, commands, sampling rules and decision tree are concrete and checkable, with a few loose spots such as the description of the graph binlog.
why: It applies only to .NET projects built with MSBuild, and a Fractera node's stack is Next.js and TypeScript, so it does not serve building, running or selling what nodes are for. The skill is well made, but it is not relevant here.

summary: This skill lets an agent write small Playwright scripts that drive a real Chromium browser against a local dev server or an approved site. It can check pages at several screen widths, take screenshots, test login and form flows, and check links. A bundled Node runner executes each script from a temporary file. The skill is aimed at developers checking their own web pages.
tasks: check how a page looks on mobile and desktop
test the login flow of a local app
take screenshots of a running site
fill and submit a form to verify it works
check a site's links for breakage
qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, runnable examples, helper functions and clear safety boundaries, but parts of it are repetitive and it leaves some setup details vague.
why: Browser testing of a site the person builds directly serves the node's purpose, and it runs locally with no cloud service. It is skipped because the runner executes arbitrary Node code with the account's full filesystem and network access and is explicitly not a sandbox, and page content could steer an agent into running harmful code.
risks: The runner executes arbitrary generated Node code with the user's filesystem, environment and network privileges, and page content could influence what code the agent writes.
Screenshots, traces and saved session state written to /tmp can contain credentials or personal data and may persist after the task.

summary: This skill gives an agent a checklist of techniques for getting past 401 and 403 access-denied responses on web paths. It covers path spelling tricks, HTTP method changes, headers that claim a different URL or client IP, protocol version changes, and automated scanners. The audience is security testers working on systems they are authorized to assess. It is not a guide to building or running a product.
tasks: test an admin panel for access-control weaknesses during an authorized pentest
check whether a forbidden API endpoint can be reached by changing the path or method
run an automated 403 bypass scan on a client's staging site
qualityWhy: The payload lists are concrete, but the file gives no authorization checks, verification steps, or explanation of why each variant works, and some claims are unverified.
why: It is offensive security material aimed at getting past access controls on other people's systems, which does not serve building, running, selling or making content with a Fractera node. Its main use is unauthorized access to restricted resources.
risks: Applying these bypasses to systems without the owner's permission would be unauthorized access and could create legal liability for the person.

summary: The skill gives an agent an earnings-analysis workflow for listed companies in the US, Hong Kong and China A-share markets. It handles both pre-earnings previews and post-earnings writeups, delivering a quick in-chat summary card by default or a full Markdown research report on request. It fetches its data through the Longbridge CLI via a bundled Python collector. Its audience is investors and analysts who want beat/miss, segment, margin, guidance and valuation views.
tasks: write a post-earnings summary card for a stock
generate a full earnings research report
preview what to watch before a company reports
review the last call's guidance and Q&A
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear step-by-step modes, module lists, fallbacks and hard rules, and the script is concrete, though the reference files were only partly visible.
needs: web search for earnings call transcripts
why: It is directly useful for analysing listed companies, but it is tied to the Longbridge data platform and a CLI, so it is not a product-building skill for a local node. The script runs locally and only calls the Longbridge CLI, and the rest of the content is instruction text. Its data-source policy forbids steering users to rival platforms, which is a reasonable product rule and not a risk for the person.

summary: This skill lets an agent find US stocks that pay dividends, look cheap on P/E and P/B, and show multi-year growth in dividends, revenue and earnings. It runs a two-stage pipeline: an optional FINVIZ Elite pre-filter, then detailed FMP fundamentals with a composite score. The audience is individual investors who want income-portfolio shortlists. It also covers payout ratios, free-cash-flow coverage and a report template.
tasks: screen dividend stocks with value filters
build an income portfolio shortlist
check dividend sustainability and payout ratios
compare dividend growth across candidate stocks
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with commands, output fields, a report template and troubleshooting, but the yield threshold is stated as 3% in one place and 3.5% in another.
why: It is a stock-research tool, which is outside what nodes are for (building, running, selling or making content), so value is none and use is skip. The scripts read the keys only to call the FMP and FINVIZ services and show no other harmful behaviour.

summary: This guide teaches an agent to write, check and fix WordPress Playground Blueprint files, which are JSON recipes that set up a temporary WordPress site in a browser or on the command line. It covers the allowed top-level keys, the resource types for plugins and files, the step names and their required fields, and bundles that ship a plugin as a zip next to the blueprint. It also lists common mistakes and how to test a blueprint with the Playground CLI or a browser link. It is aimed at developers who demo or share WordPress setups.
tasks: create a WordPress Playground blueprint for a demo site
bundle a custom plugin into a blueprint zip
validate and fix a blueprint JSON file
debug a failing blueprint step
qualityWhy: It is concrete, with a schema-based key list, worked JSON examples, a mistakes table and testing commands, but it depends on other skill files and on a schema that may change.
why: It documents WordPress Playground, a WordPress-only tool, and a node runs Next.js, so an agent would read it for ideas rather than install it as written; it is only occasionally useful for demo or staging WordPress sites. The skill contains no scripts and asks for no keys, and the remote plugin and URL sources it describes are what the user chooses to load.

summary: The skill guides an agent through building reusable Zod v4 schemas for API payloads, forms and configuration. It covers primitives, coercion, transforms, cross-field refinements, optional/nullable handling, React Hook Form integration via zodResolver, and safeParse error handling. It is aimed at developers writing validation layers in TypeScript applications.
tasks: validate an API request payload with zod
add form validation with react hook form and zod
coerce query parameters into typed values
add cross-field password confirmation checks
qualityWhy: Concrete Zod v4 examples with a clear safeParse workflow and constraints, though the references file and error-format examples leave some gaps.
why: Zod is a stack-free validation library that fits the node's TypeScript and Next.js stack directly, and the skill has no outside service dependency. The skill lists Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep and Glob, which is normal for a code-writing skill, and nothing in SKILL.md asks for secrets or remote execution.

summary: This skill lets an agent turn a video clip into a set of GIF variants at different frame rates, widths, colour counts and optional lossy compression levels. It then lists the variants by file size so the person can pick one by eye. It is aimed at people making animated demos, previews or social posts from screen recordings or clips.

make a short animated demo for a social post
compare GIF file sizes and pick the smallest acceptable version
trim a clip to a time range and export it as a GIF
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear presets, flags, examples and a step-by-step way to choose a variant, though it has no check that the output actually plays or looks right beyond the size table.
why: It runs entirely on local tools (FFmpeg, uv, optional gifsicle) and produces GIFs for content, so it fits a node that makes social and landing-page media. The visible part of the script only calls ffprobe, ffmpeg and gifsicle with fixed arguments; the cut-off rest of the script was not visible, so that part is unverified.

summary: This skill turns a rough video idea into a shot-by-shot production spec. It asks pointed follow-up questions about audience, platform, duration, and each shot's content, then suggests rendering capabilities such as voiceover, subtitles, motion and transitions. tasks: plan a 30-second promo video shot by shot
turn a product script into a storyboard spec

change pacing and transitions in an existing video-spec.md
choose a visual theme for a short social video

why: It directly serves making video content for a product, promo, or social channel, and it writes a plain markdown spec into the project folder without a cloud service. Doubts: the referenced workflow, question-bank and template files are missing from this package, and the actual video rendering depends on the separate HyperFrames renderer.

summary: This skill makes an agent review another agent skill before it is installed. It runs a bundled Python scanner for mechanical patterns such as injection phrases, obfuscation, risky code calls and leaked keys, then checks the frontmatter, the instructions, the permissions and any outside URLs by hand. The result is a structured report with severity levels and a clear install, caution or do-not-install verdict. It is aimed at people who want to vet skills they plan to add to their agents.

audit a skill for prompt injection
check a SKILL.md for frontmatter and permission problems
review a skill's scripts for exfiltration or dangerous code
qualityWhy: The phased workflow, confidence levels, false-positive guidance and report template are concrete and easy to follow, though the reference files and the scanner's full logic were not visible in the submitted text.
why: It is useful for a node that adds third-party skills, but it does not build, run or sell a product on its own. It is stack-free apart from uv and PyYAML, and the visible script only reads files and prints JSON; the script was cut off at 8000 characters, so its remaining code was not checked.

summary: This skill guides an agent through identifying a web application firewall and then trying to get attack payloads past it. It covers encoding tricks, protocol-level tricks such as chunked bodies and content-type switching, path normalization, parameter pollution, and a decision tree for choosing the next attempt. It is aimed at security testers checking how well a site's defenses hold up.
tasks: test whether my site's WAF blocks SQL injection payloads
identify which firewall protects a web application
find encoding variants that get past a blocked filter
review WAF rules for weaknesses before a release
qualityWhy: The skill has a clear phased method, concrete tables and examples, and a decision tree, but it leaves the vendor-specific details to a second file and gives few checks for confirming a bypass.
why: It is useful only occasionally, for testing the defenses of a product the person owns, and does not help build or run the node itself. It is stack-free and needs no keys, so it can be installed as written, but it is offensive guidance that should be used only on systems the person is authorized to test.

summary: The skill turns supplied material (web pages, PDFs, DOCX, Markdown, plain text, screenshots) into a single offline HTML article built on the reacticle component protocol. It walks the agent through a staged workflow with two user checkpoints, planning, a first-spread review, full build, final review and optional PDF export. make a shareable long-form article from a PDF
build an explainer or briefing page from source notes
export an article as HTML and PDF

why: It produces content pages that fit the node's purpose of making content, but it targets the reacticle package and its own scaffold, not the node's Blocks catalogue and stack, so it would need adaptation. The scaffold installs packages from npm and the PDF script drives a local browser, which the person should be aware of.

summary: This skill gives an agent a checklist for testing how an API decides who a caller is. It covers reading JWT headers and claims for weak signing, key lookup, or issuer trust, plus checking whether request fields such as role flags can be set by the client. It also lists header tricks and batching patterns that may evade rate limits. It mainly serves security reviewers checking an application's own authentication.
tasks: review an API's JWT handling for weak signing
check whether clients can set admin or role fields
test whether rate limits can be bypassed
audit bearer token and API key trust boundaries
qualityWhy: It is a useful attack-pattern checklist with routing links, but it gives short lists with few steps, examples, or verification criteria.
why: It is a stack-free security checklist, so it fits a node only occasionally, for hardening the owner's own sites and APIs; it is not for building or making content. An agent should use it only against APIs the person owns or is authorized to test, since the techniques would harm others otherwise.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull the metadata and body of a WeChat Official Account article from its mp.weixin.qq.com link, including title, author, publish time, cover image and account details. It also handles article types such as video, image, voice and repost, and maps failures like deleted or expired links to error codes. check why a WeChat article link failed to load

It depends on request-promise, which is deprecated, and the text mentions handling anti-scraping measures, so the author should check WeChat's terms and copyright before reuse.

summary: The skill gives an agent a broad guide to computer vision work in Python, covering OpenCV image operations, feature matching, classical and deep-learning object detection, PyTorch augmentation and transfer learning, and video processing. It is aimed at developers who build vision pipelines and want consistent conventions for color spaces, data types, resource release and GPU use. align or stitch photos with feature matching
set up transfer learning for an image classifier

why: It is a stack-free-ish Python guide for vision code that can help build image or video features on a node, but it is only occasionally relevant to building sites, apps or content. It has no risky content and needs no keys.

summary: This guide helps an agent create a new agent skill folder with a SKILL.md file and any optional scripts, references or assets. check a skill against the authoring checklist

Its validation command is the repository's own tool and only applies there.

summary: This skill guides an agent through running build, test, lint, serve and other tasks in an Nx monorepo. It shows how to list a project's available targets, run one task, run several across many projects with filters, and run only tasks for projects changed since a base branch. It also lists common flags such as cache skipping, bailing on the first failure and choosing a configuration. It is aimed at developers working in Nx workspaces, especially in CI.
tasks: run the build and tests for one project
run lint and typecheck across all affected projects

run tests only for projects changed since main
qualityWhy: The commands and flags are concrete and accurate, but it is a short reference with no verification steps or troubleshooting for failing tasks.
why: Nx task running is useful when a node's project is an Nx monorepo, but the node's own stack is Next.js and an Nx workspace is not its default layout, so it is only occasionally relevant. It is stack-free guidance with no install step, so it can be used as written.

summary: The skill guides an agent through splitting documents into chunks for retrieval-augmented generation. It suggests chunk sizes, overlap percentages, and methods ranging from fixed-size to semantic and structure-aware splitting. It also includes checks for chunk coherence and retrieval precision and recall. It is aimed at developers building search or question-answering over their own documents.
tasks: split documents into chunks for a RAG search
choose chunk size and overlap for a vector database
check whether chunks keep their meaning
measure retrieval precision and recall after chunking
qualityWhy: The steps, parameter defaults and code examples are concrete, but the referenced evaluate_chunks.py script is missing, the cohesion formula skips normalization, and the precision snippet uses undefined variables.
why: Chunking is a core step in building retrieval for a product, so the subject fits the node well. The examples are Python with LangChain, while a node is built in TypeScript on its own vectors element, so an agent would need to adapt the methods rather than install the skill as written. I only reviewed SKILL.md; the eight reference files were not checked.

summary: This skill lets an agent inspect a Kapso WhatsApp project: it searches logs across API calls, Meta webhook events, workflow runs and webhook deliveries, traces the delivery history of a given message or customer, and checks phone-number health. It also helps triage recent errors. The intended users are developers and operators who run WhatsApp messaging in production and need to find out why a message or workflow failed.
tasks: find why a WhatsApp message failed to deliver
check whether a webhook was retried or failed
scan recent errors on a WhatsApp number
check the health of a WhatsApp phone number
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete CLI and fallback commands, filter examples, reference guides and a clear map of log sources, though some script files were cut off in the view and could not be checked in full.
needs: a WhatsApp number connected through Kapso
Logs and Elasticsearch enabled on the Kapso project
why: Kapso is a hosted WhatsApp backend that keeps conversations, messages and logs in its cloud, and this skill is built entirely around querying that cloud service, so it is not useful for a local-first node. Nothing in the visible files is harmful: the scripts read the API key from environment variables only for the Kapso request, and the remaining script contents were not visible.

summary: This skill guides an agent through auditing an app's Apple Ads campaigns, covering attribution reconciliation with AdServices and AdAttributionKit, campaign and keyword structure, Search Match, App Store placements, custom product pages, bids, budgets, and policy. It is aimed at people running app-install advertising on Apple's platform. The agent is told to collect the campaign goal, conversion definition, date window and data sources first, then return structured findings instead of changing the account. It depends on a shared ads reference file that is not included in this single SKILL.md.
tasks: audit my Apple Ads app-install campaigns
check Search Match and keyword structure
reconcile Apple attribution with my MMP data
review custom product pages and bids
qualityWhy: The file is mostly a list of audit areas and a pointer to a reference document that is missing from this install, so an agent gets little concrete step-by-step guidance on its own.
needs: Apple Search Ads account and campaign exports
Apple Ads API access or manual data exports
why: It serves a narrow need, auditing Apple App Store ad campaigns, so it is only occasionally useful to a node that builds and sells apps. It needs the person's own Apple Ads account data and the missing shared reference files, and it is written to keep changes as drafts only.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building an automated evaluation pipeline for a Python application that calls an LLM. The agent analyzes the project, wraps its data boundaries, writes a runner, builds a dataset of test scenarios, scores outputs with evaluators, and then analyzes the results. It targets developers who need QA, tests, or benchmarks for an LLM-based Python app. The workflow is structured as six steps with checkpoints and a completion verifier script.
tasks: set up evals for my Python LLM app
build a golden dataset and run pixie test
score agent answers with LLM-as-judge evaluators
find why my LLM app gives wrong answers and write an action plan
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md and scripts give concrete steps, checkpoints, file layout and a verifier, though the reference files were not included in the review and some detail is unverified.
needs: an LLM API key for the app and for LLM-as-judge evaluators
why: It is built for Python projects, while Fractera nodes run a Next.js and TypeScript stack, so it is useful for ideas on evaluating an agent but not a direct fit. Its setup script also re-fetches the skill and installs the latest pixie-qa package without review, which is a risk.
risks: setup.sh re-downloads the skill from GitHub and upgrades pixie-qa from PyPI on every run with auto-confirm, so unreviewed remote code and instructions can be installed silently.

summary: This skill guides an agent through event-driven design in Spring Boot 3: modelling immutable domain events, publishing them from aggregate roots, and handling them after a database commit with transactional listeners. It also covers Kafka producers and consumers, the transactional outbox for reliable delivery, and retry and dead-letter handling. The audience is Java backend developers building microservices or DDD systems.

publish domain events after a database commit

add a transactional outbox for reliable messaging
qualityWhy: The instructions have clear steps, examples and validation checks, but they are thin in places (observability is one vague line, the deprecated Spring Cloud Sleuth is suggested, and some snippets lack imports and full context).
why: It is built for Java and Spring Boot, while a Fractera node runs Next.js with TypeScript, so an agent should read it for the patterns (after-commit events, outbox, idempotent handlers) and rebuild them in the node's own stack. Kafka can run locally, so no cloud service is required.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing Jupyter notebook tutorials that show how to use the Milvus vector database inside an application, such as retrieval-augmented generation or semantic search. The agent edits a Markdown file, where Python blocks become code cells, and converts it to a notebook with a small tool. It then sets up a Jupyter environment and runs the notebook to check it. example API keys such as OpenAI for the sample code

summary: The skill gives an agent a set of NestJS conventions: modular domain modules, choosing provider scope, exception filters, DTO validation with class-validator, and Drizzle ORM repository patterns. summary: This skill lets an agent pull public X (Twitter) data through a paid HTTP service: keyword and operator search, profile lookups, a user's posts, replies and followers, single posts with their replies and reposters, X Lists, and country trends. tasks: track a hashtag or keyword on X
export the followers of an account
monitor a competitor's recent posts

check trending topics in a country

why: It is useful for social listening and content research, but it is not core to running a local-first node, and it depends on a paid third-party service whose results come back to the agent as data. The key or wallet is only sent to that vendor, which the person chooses to use.

summary: This guide teaches an agent how to review WebSocket endpoints for security problems: how the upgrade handshake works, whether the server checks the Origin header, and whether a malicious page could hijack a logged-in user's live channel. It is stack-neutral, so it can be used as written, but its attack examples must be restricted to systems the person is authorized to test.

summary: The skill guides an agent through a structured review of NestJS code changes, covering controllers, services, modules, guards, pipes, dependency injection and database integration. It sorts findings into Critical, Warning and Suggestion levels and asks for evidence and a concrete fix for each. It is aimed at developers preparing pull requests or validating a NestJS architecture.

It does not depend on a particular ORM and contains no install commands or remote code, so it can be used as written; the reference files were not reviewed.

summary: This skill guides an agent through diagnosing and fixing TypeScript projects: compiler errors, tsconfig settings, module resolution, slow type-checking, and migration from JavaScript or to the TypeScript 7 compiler. It tells the agent to inspect the project before changing it, prefer minimal fixes, and keep type safety intact rather than silencing errors with any or suppression comments. It is aimed at developers who maintain TypeScript code in an app, library or monorepo.

migrate a JavaScript project to TypeScript

summary: This playbook teaches an agent to reverse engineer custom virtual machines and bytecode interpreters in software. summary: This skill guides an agent through diagnosing a slow parallel MSBuild or .NET build.
