summary: This playbook guides an agent through testing whether an API properly restricts access to objects, nested resources and admin functions. It has the agent create two accounts, record requests made by one, replay them with the other's token, and try sibling, nested and alternate-verb routes. It also lists hidden writable JSON fields to probe for mass assignment. It is aimed at security testers and developers checking their own APIs.
tasks: check whether one user can read another user's orders
test an API for broken object-level authorization
find hidden writable fields that allow privilege escalation
review admin endpoints for missing function-level checks
qualityWhy: It gives a clear test loop, a surface table and routing links, but it is short and generic, with no concrete request examples, expected results or verification steps.
why: It is a stack-free security-testing habit useful for checking an API a node builds, not for building or making content directly. It does not restrict testing to systems the person owns, so the agent should only run it against the person's own API.

summary: This skill converts a local Markdown file into a Feishu (Lark) cloud document and uploads the images it references. It picks a document title from the first heading, renders Mermaid diagrams to PNG through an external web API, and then cleans up its temporary files. It is written for someone who wants to publish Markdown notes to Feishu.
tasks: publish a markdown article to Feishu
turn a local markdown report into a Lark document
upload markdown notes with images to Feishu
qualityWhy: The steps, commands, fallbacks and cleanup are concrete and easy to follow, though error handling for failed image uploads and rendering is thin.
needs: Feishu (Lark) app ID and app secret
why: Feishu is a cloud document service, so the output is stored in a cloud place rather than locally, which the node's local-first rules treat as no value. The skill also carries a risk, so it is skipped.
risks: Install guidance tells the person to run a remote install script piped straight into sh (curl | sh) from astral.sh.
Mermaid diagram source code is sent to the third-party mermaid.ink service without warning the person that their content leaves the machine.

summary: This skill lets an agent turn Mermaid diagram source, either a standalone .mmd file or the mermaid code blocks inside a markdown document, into animated GIFs. It picks an animation style to suit the diagram's meaning, such as a progressive reveal for architecture or a flowing-line effect for data pipelines. It then suggests replacing the original code blocks with image links. The output suits documentation writers, product teams and social media creators who want diagrams that move.
tasks: turn a mermaid diagram into an animated GIF
batch-convert the mermaid blocks in a markdown doc to images
make an animated architecture diagram for a presentation
replace mermaid code blocks with GIF references in docs
qualityWhy: SKILL.md gives clear workflows, a style-selection guide, a full options table and examples, and the visible script code matches its claims, though the script was cut off before the end so the rest could not be checked.
why: It makes local image output (GIFs) for documentation, sites and social posts, using local Playwright and FFmpeg, with no account or key needed. Mermaid.js is loaded from a CDN at render time, so rendering needs internet, but the person's files stay on their machine. The script was only partly visible, so its remaining code is unverified.

summary: The skill guides an agent through writing, configuring, running and reviewing BenchmarkDotNet microbenchmarks for .NET code. It covers choosing a comparison axis (approaches, runtimes, package versions, builds, GC/JIT settings, scale), picking job presets to control run time, and avoiding common measurement errors such as dead-code elimination and constant folding. It is aimed at developers who need measured performance answers for their .NET code.
tasks: write a BenchmarkDotNet benchmark comparing two implementations
compare performance across .NET runtimes
run a quick benchmark with a short job preset
review an existing benchmark for measurement errors
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is concrete, with a clear workflow, cost table and pitfalls, and it points to detailed reference files, though the referenced files were not provided for review.
why: Useful when a node's project includes .NET code that needs measurement, but Fractera's stack is Next.js and TypeScript, so .NET benchmarking is only occasionally relevant. It is stack-free in the sense that it installs as written and has no outside service dependency.

summary: The skill has an agent turn a folder of technical spec documents into an interactive web presentation, with clickable architecture maps, step-through diagrams and a persuasive narrative arc. It is aimed at engineers who need to understand a design and at readers who need to be convinced of its purpose. The agent proposes an outline for approval, scaffolds a deck from templates, and checks the result with type-checking, a build and browser testing before finishing.
tasks: turn a tech spec into an interactive web deck
make a shareable roadmap page from design documents
refresh an existing spec presentation with new content
qualityWhy: The phases, file rules, component-promotion protocol and verification steps are concrete and followable, though many steps depend on the referenced files and a specific repo layout.
why: It produces marketing-style web decks for technical specs rather than general product sites, so it is only occasionally useful on a node. It depends on a Vite/Astro base, a pnpm workspace and a tech-specs directory that the node does not provide, so it would need adapting to the node's Next.js stack before use.

summary: This skill lets an agent review a named diff, a pull request, or the current branch for bugs, regressions, missing tests, and standards problems. It chooses the review lenses that fit the change, runs them in parallel, and can add an independent pass from a different model provider when one is configured. The output is a ranked list of findings with a verdict and any coverage limits. Fixes are applied locally only when the person explicitly asks. It serves developers who need a thorough review before merging code.
tasks: review my branch before merging
review a pull request for bugs and regressions
check my changes for missing tests and security issues
apply the review's fixes locally
get an independent second-model review of my diff
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and staged, with explicit modes, scope rules, validation steps and output rules, but the skill is large and several scripts (peer-job-runner, review-scope, run-log) were not visible to check.
needs: git repository access for the code under review
GitHub CLI access for pull request review
optional accounts and CLIs for peer model providers such as OpenAI Codex, Anthropic Claude, xAI Grok, Cursor or Google Antigravity
why: It directly serves building and shipping a product by reviewing its code, and its core review works from local git without any outside service. The optional cross-model pass sends the diff to a third-party model provider; the skill requires a disclosure and an explicit user prohibition overrides it, but it also tells the agent not to re-ask for consent, so the person should know that before enabling it.

summary: This skill takes a reference to an existing design spec, such as a file path, a name, an issue, or a spec PR number, and drives an agent through implementing it. It stops cleanly with candidate matches if the spec cannot be found. It then hands the work to companion skills that build the change on its own branch and PR, run review and checks, and optionally verify the UI with screenshots. It is aimed at teams running an autonomous spec-to-PR pipeline on a GitHub-style tracker.
tasks: implement the spec at a given path
build the feature from issue 123
resume the open implementation PR for a spec
verify a user-facing change with screenshots on the PR
tools: GitHub issues and pull requests via tracker descriptor
qualityWhy: The workflow, routing, stop conditions and rules are clear and detailed, but the core work is delegated to companion skills and reference files that are not included, so an agent cannot follow it end to end from these files alone.
needs: GitHub or equivalent tracker access through a descriptor
open-mercato companion skill collection (om-auto-create-pr, om-auto-continue-pr, om-auto-review-pr, om-auto-qa-pr, om-open-pr)
agentic.config.json and tracker descriptor in the repository
why: It is useful for a team that already runs a spec-driven PR pipeline, but it is not a building block for a Fractera product and depends on open-mercato-specific config and companion skills that a node does not provide, so it should be read for its ideas and rebuilt on the node's own stack and workflow. The unseen reference files and companion skills are unknowns that limit trust in the full run.

summary: The skill guides an agent through turning on automatic crash dumps for modern .NET applications, or capturing a dump from a running .NET process. It first checks whether the app is CoreCLR or NativeAOT, then follows a runtime-specific reference, with extra steps for Docker and Kubernetes containers. It limits itself to collection, so analysis and code changes are out of scope. Its audience is .NET developers and operators diagnosing crashes.
tasks: collect a crash dump from a running .NET process
enable automatic crash dumps for a .NET app
set up dump collection for a .NET service in Docker or Kubernetes
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear scope limits, concrete detection commands for each platform and step-by-step execution rules, though the reference files were only listed and not checked in full.
why: The node is built on Next.js, TypeScript and SQLite, and this skill covers .NET runtime crash dumps, which fall outside what nodes are for. The skill does not carry any risk in its instructions, so the skip comes from the value being none.

summary: This skill lets an agent query Google Play Store data through the fetcher.sh HTTP API, without Play Console access. It can search Android apps by keyword, price and storefront country, fetch app details, reviews, permissions and data safety disclosures, list similar apps, and pull a developer's catalog. It suits people doing app store optimization, competitor tracking, or research before building an Android product.
tasks: search Android apps by keyword and price
pull reviews for a competitor app sorted by rating
compare permissions and data safety of similar apps
list a developer's full app catalog
research app store optimization keywords in a given country
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete endpoints, parameters, copy-paste curl examples, an MCP config and an error table, but it has no guidance on handling pagination, result sizes or cost limits.
needs: or a USDC wallet on Base, Polygon, Arbitrum, Monad or Solana for x402 pay-per-call
why: It is a paid outside data service rather than a cloud database or hosting, and its output is research data, so it is useful now and then for app and product work rather than core building. The x402 path signs and spends USDC automatically, which the person must accept before use; the skill does not mention spending limits.

summary: The skill guides an agent to build Model Context Protocol servers in Spring Boot using Spring AI, covering tool handlers declared with annotations, prompt templates, stdio/HTTP/SSE transports, and security filters. It targets Java developers who want to expose functions or data to AI clients. The files include detailed reference material on testing, examples and migration from LangChain4j.
tasks: build a Spring Boot MCP server with tools
expose a database query tool to an AI client
add prompt templates to an MCP server
configure stdio or HTTP transport for MCP
migrate LangChain4j MCP code to Spring AI
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete steps, code samples, configuration and checks, with extensive reference files for deeper patterns.
needs: OpenAI API key or another model provider key
why: The node is built on Next.js and TypeScript, so a Java and Spring Boot MCP server does not fit its stack and the patterns would need adapting to Node-based MCP tooling. Useful as reference for tool design and security, but not something to install directly.

summary: This skill helps an agent figure out when a person would benefit from an extra capability and then search an open registry of agent skills for one. It lists the search and update commands of the skills CLI and gives a response pattern for presenting matches. It also includes a shell script that installs a chosen skill and links it into a project folder. It is aimed at developers who want to extend their agent with ready-made workflows.
tasks: find a skill for a specific task
search the skills registry for a keyword
install a community skill into the project
check installed skills for updates
qualityWhy: The instructions are clear on when to search and how to present results, but the install path is a placeholder, there are no checks on what a found skill contains, and the script's behaviour differs from its docs.
why: Finding skills is occasionally useful, but the script installs skills globally into the home directory and only then symlinks them, which breaks the node rule that a skill lives in one element's folder. Its use is also skipped because it runs an npm package via npx and installs third-party content with auto-confirmation.
risks: npx fetches and executes an npm package from the network on the person's machine.
The script installs third-party skill content globally into the home directory and auto-confirms with -y, without showing the person what it contains.

summary: This skill makes an agent check a computer for the tools needed to build .NET MAUI cross-platform apps, including the .NET SDK, workloads, Microsoft OpenJDK, Android SDK, Xcode and the Windows SDK. It looks up required versions from NuGet metadata rather than fixed values, then guides installs and re-checks each fix. It is aimed at developers who are setting up or repairing a mobile and desktop app toolchain.
tasks: diagnose a broken .NET MAUI build environment
check whether Android SDK and JDK versions match requirements
set up a new machine for MAUI development
verify MAUI toolchain after an OS or SDK update
qualityWhy: The skill gives ordered tasks, platform-specific reference files, concrete validation commands and common pitfalls, though some references were not visible to judge in full.
why: It only prepares a .NET MAUI mobile and desktop development machine, which is not one of the things a Fractera node is for (sites, web apps, AI agents, content). It is a local tool set with no cloud service involved, but its use on a node would be off-purpose.

summary: This skill lets an agent check the broad direction of the stock market over a one-to-two-year horizon. It compares several pairs of exchange-traded funds, such as equal-weight versus cap-weight S&P 500, small caps versus large caps, and high-yield versus investment-grade bonds, then scores each pair for regime shifts. It is aimed at investors and analysts who want a structural market view for long-term portfolio positioning. It writes a JSON file and a Markdown report, and it stops without a report when no data is usable.
tasks: check whether the market regime is changing
explain the RSP/SPY concentration trend
summarize yield curve and credit conditions for positioning
compare the current regime with historical periods
qualityWhy: SKILL.md gives concrete commands, options, output files, a component table and a fail-closed rule, though the calculator and test files were not readable to confirm the detail.
why: It is market analysis rather than a tool for building, running, selling or making content on a node, so its value is limited to finance-related agents. It runs as written, but its optional FMP key and yfinance data come from outside services the person must choose to use.

summary: This skill acts as a routing index for security testing of login, sessions and access control. It helps an agent decide whether a problem is mainly about login mechanics, object-level permissions, browser trust boundaries, or identity protocols like OAuth, JWT and SAML, and then points to the matching deeper skill. It is aimed at people auditing the authentication of their own web application.
tasks: audit login and session security of my web app
check whether users can access other users' records
review OAuth, JWT or SSO setup for weaknesses
decide which auth security topic to test first
qualityWhy: It gives a clear map of subtopics and a recommended testing order, but it contains no concrete steps, checks or examples of its own and relies on linked skills for all substance.
why: It is a stack-free security checklist that could help a builder review the auth of their own site, but it is not about building or making content, so its use is occasional. The linked sub-skills are not part of this file, so the install is only useful if those are installed too.

summary: This skill is a routing guide and reference index for OpenTUI, a library for building terminal user interfaces. It helps an agent pick between the Core, React and Solid packages, then points it to the right docs page for components, layout, keyboard handling, testing, SSH serving and deployment. It is aimed at developers writing command-line or terminal apps. It is not aimed at the web sites, shops or content tools a Fractera node is mainly for.
tasks: build a terminal dashboard
add keyboard shortcuts to a terminal app
serve a terminal UI over SSH
write tests for a terminal interface
qualityWhy: SKILL.md is a clear routing table with working rules, and 127 bundled reference pages back it up, but the file itself mostly sends the agent to other pages rather than giving steps.
why: Terminal UI work is a niche use for a node that mainly builds web sites, apps and content, so it is useful only now and then. The React and Solid bindings render to the terminal, not to Next.js, so an agent would need to read it for ideas and build the node's own way.

summary: This skill is a reference playbook for an agent doing offensive security work against Kubernetes clusters. It covers checking API server access, enumerating RBAC permissions, abusing service account tokens, reading etcd and Kubelet endpoints, and pivoting to cloud metadata services on EKS, GKE and AKS. It is written for penetration testers who have authorization to assess a cluster, and it is not aimed at people building or running a product on a node.
tasks: audit a Kubernetes cluster's RBAC permissions
test a cluster for privilege escalation paths
check exposed Kubelet or etcd endpoints
review service account token permissions in a pod
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands, a permissions table and a decision tree, but some one-liners are fragile and it has no authorization or scope checks.
why: It is an attack playbook for cluster administration and does not help build, run, sell or make content for a product on a local-first node. It is marked skip because it carries risks if an agent followed it against systems it was not authorized to test.
risks: Instructs dumping all cluster secrets, service account tokens and registry pull secrets, which exposes credentials.
Instructs creating privileged pods with host filesystem and namespace access to escape to the underlying node.
Instructs harvesting cloud IAM and managed-identity credentials from metadata endpoints.
Has no authorization or scope check before attacking live clusters.

summary: This skill lets an agent generate a designed PDF from structured content, choosing colours, fonts and cover layout from the document type and an accent colour. It can also fill named form fields in an existing PDF and restyle a Markdown, text or PDF source into the same design system. It is aimed at people who need print-ready reports, proposals, resumes or client documents that look polished.
tasks: make a client-ready proposal PDF
generate a styled report with a cover page
fill in the fields of an existing PDF form
convert a Markdown document into a designed PDF
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear routes, commands, block schemas and checks, though the design file and several scripts were not fully visible, so some gaps cannot be confirmed.
needs: Google Fonts access over the network for cover fonts
why: It is a local-first document generator that serves building and selling content directly, with no cloud storage or account needed. It is marked skip because its Python scripts auto-install packages with --break-system-packages, which overrides the system Python protection; an agent could adapt this to a virtual environment, but as written it should not run. Cover fonts load live from Google Fonts, and the merge, palette and render scripts were truncated in what I could read.
risks: Python scripts silently run pip install with --break-system-packages on import, bypassing the system Python package protection.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up Spring Boot Actuator on a JVM service: adding the dependency, choosing which management endpoints to expose, locking down management traffic with Spring Security, and defining health probe groups. It also covers Micrometer metrics export to Prometheus and diagnostic endpoints for startup and conditions. The intended users are backend engineers who run Java services in production.
tasks: add health checks to a Spring Boot service
expose Prometheus metrics from a Java app
secure the management endpoints of a Spring app
set up readiness and liveness probes for Kubernetes
debug why an actuator endpoint is missing
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with configuration examples, validation steps and a checklist, but some reference entries are duplicated and the scripts folder is empty.
why: The skill targets Spring Boot on the JVM, a stack a Fractera node does not run; its node stack is Next.js and TypeScript, so the content cannot be used as written and would need a rewrite to apply anywhere.

summary: This skill lets an agent shrink PNG and JPEG screenshots on the person's own machine while keeping their original format, so they load faster and stay compatible with tools that reject WebP. It calls the local pngquant and jpegoptim programs through a Python script that can process single files or whole folders, with adjustable quality settings. The intended users are people preparing documentation, README images, or blog screenshots for publishing.
tasks: compress screenshots before committing to a repository
shrink a folder of blog images
reduce PNG and JPEG file sizes for documentation
batch optimize images at a chosen quality
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear steps, flags, quality presets and a dependency check, though it does not cover backups, dry runs or handling of pngquant failures.
why: It is a local, stack-free image tool useful for preparing site and content images now and then, not a core building feature. The script overwrites original files in place with no backup or confirmation, which the skill documents but an agent could still apply to the wrong files.

summary: The skill guides an agent through paid-media financial modelling: it sets out a fixed procedure for working out CPA, CPL, CPC, CPM, ROAS, MER, break-even points, contribution margin, LTV:CAC, budgets and forecasts. It asks the agent to state units, currency, period, refund and tax treatment, and attribution basis, and to show each formula with its inputs. It also requires checks for zero denominators, sign errors and mismatched time windows, plus base, downside and upside cases. It is aimed at marketers and business owners who need to judge ad spend decisions.
tasks: calculate break-even ROAS for a campaign
compute CPA and MER from ad spend and revenue
forecast a paid-media budget with downside and upside cases
model LTV to CAC payback for a product
qualityWhy: The procedure is clear and disciplined, but it has no worked formulas, examples or concrete calculation steps, so an agent has to supply the arithmetic itself.
why: It is a stack-free modelling habit that helps a node's owner check ad economics for a product they sell, but it does not build or run anything in the node. No risks found in the file.

summary: Guides an agent through unit testing a Java service that calls external REST APIs, using WireMock to stub responses on a dynamic port, verify outgoing requests, and simulate timeouts and 4xx/5xx failures without real network calls. Aimed at Java developers who write integration clients and want fast, offline tests. The skill covers Maven setup, JUnit 5 extension registration, stubbing with urlEqualTo and header matching, and AssertJ assertions.
tasks: write unit tests for a client that calls an external REST API
simulate API timeouts and 500 errors in tests
verify the headers and query params my HTTP client sends
mock a third-party weather or payment endpoint for tests
qualityWhy: Clear, correct steps and one solid example, but the error, timeout and stateful patterns are pushed into a reference file and the skill is thin on Java-specific setup details.
why: It is a Java and JUnit testing skill, not something tied to Fractera's TypeScript stack, so an agent on a node would need to adapt the ideas to Vitest or Jest with a Node HTTP mock such as MSW or nock. No secrets, remote execution or data sharing are involved.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write native iOS and macOS Swift code that talks to Bluetooth Low Energy devices through Apple's Core Bluetooth framework. It covers scanning and connecting as a central, reading, writing and subscribing to GATT characteristics, advertising services as a peripheral, handling Bluetooth permission states, background modes, and state restoration. The guidance is aimed at mobile developers building apps that pair with sensors or accessories.
tasks: connect an iPhone app to a heart rate sensor
scan for nearby BLE peripherals and filter by service UUID
read and subscribe to GATT characteristic notifications in Swift
make an iOS app advertise a custom BLE service
add background Bluetooth support and state restoration
qualityWhy: It gives concrete Swift code for each step, a common-mistakes table and a review checklist, though it leaves some details to its reference file.
why: Core Bluetooth is a native Apple framework for Swift apps, which is outside the Next.js, TypeScript and web stack a Fractera node is built for, and it does not serve building sites, web apps, agents or content. It has no risky code, so the skip is only about relevance.

summary: This skill guides an agent through testing CORS misconfigurations: reflected origins, weak allowlist regexes, null-origin acceptance, and cache poisoning via a missing Vary header. It also covers chaining subdomain XSS to credentialed API reads and reaching internal services from a victim's browser. It is written for security testers analysing cross-origin trust on web applications.
tasks: audit a site's CORS headers for origin reflection
test whether an API accepts null or subdomain origins
check CORS policy for cache poisoning via missing Vary
assess credentialed cross-origin reads of an authenticated API
qualityWhy: It gives concrete headers, payloads, regex bypass tables and step checklists, but several sections are terse and SCENARIOS.md is only referenced here.
why: It is an offensive security playbook for attacking other sites' APIs and internal networks, which does not serve building, running or making content for a product on a local-first node. It is skipped as a risk-bearing attack playbook rather than for a missing stack.
risks: Contains attack payloads for credentialed data theft and internal network reconnaissance that could be misused against third parties.

summary: This skill is a routing index for injection-class vulnerabilities. It helps an agent decide, from where attacker-controlled input ends up, whether the work belongs to XSS, SQL injection, SSRF, XXE, template injection, command injection, NoSQL injection or one of several related categories. It is written for security testers who already suspect an injection issue and need to pick the right deep-dive guide.
tasks: route an input to the right injection test
decide whether input reaches a SQL, template or shell sink
pick the correct injection skill for a form parameter
triage which injection class a suspected flaw belongs to
qualityWhy: It gives a clear sink-first routing flow and a complete map of linked skills, but the body is short and offers no concrete steps, examples or checks of its own beyond pointing to other files.
why: It is a security-testing router for auditing other systems, not a tool for building, running or selling a site, app or content on a local-first node, so its value is none and it is skipped.
risks: Its catalogue points to attack-testing guides (payloads and exploitation of other systems), which an agent on a node could be steered toward using against third parties.

summary: The skill has an agent compare the current git changes or a pull request against a saved project knowledge graph. It finds the components that were edited, the components linked to them, and the architectural layers they touch. It then gives a risk view based on complexity and cross-layer links. It also writes an overlay file so a dashboard can show the changes visually. It is aimed at developers who need to review a change before merging it.
tasks: review what my branch changes before merging
show which components a pull request could affect
assess the risk of my current uncommitted changes
highlight the layers touched by a diff
qualityWhy: The steps, git commands, freshness checks and output format are concrete, but it has no worked example and the branch-selection logic is loosely described.
why: It helps a person review changes to a product's code, which is useful now and then, but it does not build, run or sell anything by itself. It needs a knowledge graph already produced by the /understand tool and a git repository; it has no stack of its own, so it works on the node as written. The dashboard step refers to another plugin command that the person must have installed.

summary: This playbook guides an agent through security testing of an iOS app on a jailbroken or non-jailbroken device. It covers checking keychain protection classes, testing URL scheme and Universal Links configuration, hooking runtime methods with Frida and Objection, checking binary protections, reviewing app data locations, and auditing App Transport Security settings. It is written for security professionals doing authorized mobile assessments.
tasks: audit an iOS app's data storage for leaked tokens
check Universal Links and URL scheme setup for hijacking risk
review an iOS app's ATS settings and binary protections
hook an iOS app's methods at runtime to test its login logic
qualityWhy: It gives concrete commands, tables and a decision tree an agent can follow, but it lacks an authorization check and a few steps, such as the non-jailbreak Frida gadget re-signing, are only sketched.
why: It is useful for hardening a product's mobile app as part of building it, but it is a security-testing reference rather than a tool for building, running or making content. It needs no outside service, and it needs no adaptation to the node's stack. The offensive techniques (keychain dumping, IPA decryption) are meant for apps the tester is authorized to test, and the skill does not itself check for that authorization.

summary: The skill walks a product manager through a multi-phase roadmap planning process: gathering business goals, customer problems and stakeholder requests, turning them into epics with hypotheses and effort estimates, scoring and prioritizing them, then sequencing them into quarters with dependencies. It ends with a stakeholder presentation and a published roadmap. It is written for product managers preparing an executive-ready plan, and it leans on other skills (epic-hypothesis, prioritization-advisor) plus a shared facilitation protocol.
tasks: build a Q2 roadmap from 15 candidate initiatives
sequence product work across three teams for six months
turn scattered feature requests into outcome-driven epics
prepare a roadmap presentation for executive review
qualityWhy: It gives a clear phased workflow with time estimates, RICE scoring example, sample epics and common pitfalls, though some phases (dependencies, presentation) are manual with no concrete check steps.
why: It is a stack-free planning method, so it could be installed as written, but it is a process for product managers rather than something that builds or runs a node's product, and it relies on sibling skills that are not in this package. Its files reference skills/ paths that would need to exist in the node for the orchestration to work, so it is best read for its ideas.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to split a Unity Sprite's texture into a 3x3 grid and compare each outer cell's pixels with the majority color of the center cell. It then writes the result as a short text pattern of match and no-match symbols. It is aimed at game developers who want to document, test or catalog the color structure of 2D sprite assets. The included C# script is referenced but its contents were not provided for review.
tasks: analyze a sprite's color layout in Unity
document a sprite's 3x3 color pattern
write a test that checks sprite structure
catalog sprite assets with searchable metadata
qualityWhy: The algorithm, threshold table and output format are clear, but the color-tolerance and tie-break guidance is thin and the referenced script was not included.
why: It is a Unity C# sprite-analysis technique with nothing for building, running or selling a web product, Next.js node, or content for social media, so it does not fit what nodes are for.

summary: The skill makes an agent scan a C# codebase for calls to hard-to-test framework APIs such as DateTime.UtcNow, File and Directory helpers, Environment variables, HttpClient, Console and Process. It then produces a ranked report of call counts per category, the most affected files, and the .NET abstractions that could replace those calls. It is aimed at developers auditing legacy .NET code before adding unit tests.
tasks: audit a C# project for static dependencies

rank which statics to wrap first in a .NET codebase
plan incremental testability improvements for legacy C#
qualityWhy: The file gives a detailed, step-by-step scan workflow, explicit counting rules, a report template, a validation checklist and a pitfalls table, all concrete enough for an agent to follow.
why: It is useful for auditing C# code, but Fractera nodes are built on TypeScript and Next.js, so it helps only when a C# project is involved; its recommendations (TimeProvider, System.IO.Abstractions) are .NET-specific and do not apply to the node's stack, so it should be read for its ideas.

summary: This skill lets an agent read the baseline sharing settings of Salesforce objects, showing whether records are private, read-only or read/write by default. It can also change those defaults for internal and external users, after checking that the requested level is valid for the object. It is aimed at Salesforce administrators who manage access to records in a hosted org.
tasks: check the org-wide sharing defaults for Account and Contact

change external access on a custom object
list every object's sharing default in the org
qualityWhy: The steps, validation tables, deploy-retry limits and verification checks are concrete and sequential, though it depends on reference files not all included here.
why: It administers a cloud-hosted Salesforce org rather than building, running or making content for a product on a local node, so it does not fit the node's purpose. Its data and configuration live in Salesforce's cloud, not on the person's computer.

summary: This skill guides an agent through moving a Unity game project from the older Built-in render pipeline to the Universal Render Pipeline. It covers detecting the current pipeline, inventorying materials, shaders, post-processing and lighting, running converters in a live Editor, and checking the saved results. It is aimed at game developers who maintain Unity projects.
tasks: migrate a Unity project from Built-in to URP
fix pink materials after a URP upgrade
move post-processing volumes to URP
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with ordered phases, C# snippets, and verification gates, but the file is very long and relies on a separate unity-cli skill and a live Editor.
needs: Unity Editor 6000.3 or newer for the Pipeline package
a rollback copy of the Unity project
why: This is a game-engine render pipeline migration, which does not serve building sites, web apps, AI agents or content on a Fractera node, so it is not useful here. It is also not local-only in practice because it depends on a live Unity Editor and package installs.

summary: This skill guides an agent through finding MSBuild projects whose output or intermediate paths collide, such as when two evaluations write bin/obj files to the same place. It walks through generating a binary log, querying evaluations and properties via an MCP tool or a text-log fallback, and then applying fixes like per-project BaseIntermediateOutputPath or removing redundant global properties. It is written for .NET developers debugging flaky or failing builds.
tasks: diagnose intermittent build failures in a multi-project solution
fix project.assets.json clash during NuGet restore
find duplicate project evaluations that overwrite outputs
remove redundant SetTargetFramework from a ProjectReference
qualityWhy: Detailed, concrete steps with examples, commands and a decision table, though it depends on other skills and an MCP server that may not be present.
why: It is a .NET build-diagnosis skill, useful when building .NET projects but not central to a Fractera node's product work, and it is written for MSBuild rather than the node's stack, so it is best read for its ideas. It refers to other skills (binlog-generation, msbuild-antipatterns) that are not included here.

summary: This is a routing index for security testing. It tells an agent to start with an unknown target, draw its attack surface from one application, and then send the resulting inventory to other testing skills. The file itself contains no concrete recon steps; it only names which skills to open next. It is aimed at security testers who want a structured order of work instead of random probing.
tasks: map the attack surface of a new web target
choose the first security test to run on an app
build an endpoint inventory before testing
route findings to the right security testing skill
qualityWhy: It is a wrapper that only lists links to other skills, with no steps, examples or checks of its own.
why: Its subject is offensive security testing of targets, which is not a building, running, selling or content-making use of a local-first node, and the file only points to other skills that are not included.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to add Auth.js 5 (next-auth) sign-in to a Next.js App Router project. It covers provider setup, a route handler, middleware that guards pages, reading the session in Server Components and Server Actions, and role checks for admin-only areas. It is aimed at developers who need login and access control in a web app.
tasks: add GitHub and Google sign-in to a Next.js app
protect a dashboard page so only logged-in users see it
restrict an admin panel to users with an admin role
secure a form action so only signed-in users can save data
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives numbered setup steps, working code, a worked example per use case, and a list of common mistakes, though some points such as mocking auth() in tests stay thin.
needs: GitHub OAuth app client ID and secret
Google OAuth client ID and secret
why: Sign-in and roles are central to building products on a node, but the node already has its own sign-in element, so this skill would duplicate it, and its Prisma and Drizzle adapter guidance clashes with the node's SQLite-only data element, so it should be read for ideas and built the node's way. The skill's middleware pattern may need checking against Next.js 16 conventions, and I judged only SKILL.md, not the reference files.

summary: This skill lets an agent look up sports information through a command-line tool that reads ESPN's public data: live and past scores, schedules, standings, box scores, play-by-play, odds, injuries and poll rankings across ten leagues. It can also keep a local copy of league data for offline search and head-to-head comparisons. It suits a sports fan, journalist or blogger who needs quick, accurate game facts. The instructions are detailed, with commands, output-filtering options and exit codes.
tasks: look up tonight's scores and standings for a league
build a box score or recap for a finished game
compare two teams head to head
pull player leaders and injury reports for a sports post
sync league data locally and search it offline
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete commands, recipes, output filters, exit codes and a clear decision flow, with only minor gaps such as the single-file scope and dense generated-mirror notes.
needs: ESPN public endpoints (no key or account)
why: Sports data is useful for sports sites, blogs and social content but only now and then for a general product, and the skill is built around a single third-party data feed. It is skipped because its install step fetches and runs unpinned remote code: an npx package with -y and a Go module at @latest.
risks: The install runs npx -y on an npm package and go install on a GitHub module at @latest, so unpinned remote code is downloaded and executed on the computer.

summary: This skill makes an agent turn a request into a structured plan before any code is written: it checks for an earlier brainstorm or requirements document, picks a light, standard or heavy plan size, researches the codebase and outside sources, and writes a plan file with reviewed sections and a confidence check. It is built for developers and product owners who want a reviewed plan for software or non-software work. It also describes an optional step that hands a hard reasoning sub-task to a second model through a detached background worker.
tasks: plan a feature from a requirements document
break down an implementation into steps
deepen an existing plan before coding
write a structured plan for a multi-step project
review a plan before handing it to implementation
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete and phased, with explicit routing rules, output contracts, required reference reads and completion checks, though the reference files are very long and depend on sibling skills.
needs: Claude CLI with a model account (only for the optional reasoning-elevation worker)
why: The planning method fits building products and is stack-free, but the optional elevation worker runs the Claude CLI with --permission-mode dontAsk, so its model can read the handoff directory and fetch web pages without prompting, which gives an injected instruction a route to leak evidence. Because of that risk the skill is skipped as written; its planning phases could be considered separately once that worker is removed.
risks: The elevation worker runs the Claude CLI with --permission-mode dontAsk, auto-approving its Read, Glob, Grep, WebSearch and WebFetch calls without prompting, so injected content could read handoff files and send them to a web URL.

summary: The skill guides an agent through Spring Boot dependency injection: prefer constructor injection for mandatory collaborators, handle optional ones with ObjectProvider or no-op fallbacks, choose beans with @Primary and @Qualifier, and keep wiring in configuration classes. It also gives a minimal context test to check wiring before business logic is added. It is aimed at Java developers working on Spring Boot backends.
tasks: replace field injection with constructor injection in a Spring service
wire multiple implementations of a payment gateway bean
troubleshoot an ambiguous bean error at Spring startup
add an optional notification dependency without null checks
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with code examples and a wiring-test checklist, though the reference files were not reviewed here and some guidance is brief.
why: The skill is for a Java Spring Boot stack, which a Fractera node does not use (its stack is Next.js, React, TypeScript), so it cannot be installed as written and would need a full rewrite to fit the node.

summary: This skill lets an agent take a single pull request number, check that it is open and not a draft, and respect the QA and label gates before submitting an approving review. If the gates allow it, the agent squash-merges the PR. It is aimed at developers who run a code-review process on the repository behind their product. When a blocker can be fixed, the skill points to companion skills for CI repair or conflict resolution, and it can file a follow-up issue after the merge.
tasks: approve and merge a pull request by number
ship a reviewed PR once QA gates pass
check why a PR cannot be merged yet
file a follow-up issue after merging a PR
tools: tracker descriptor operations for pull requests (get-pr, review-pr, merge-pr, create-issue)
qualityWhy: The steps, gate rules, refusal cases and report format are concrete and checkable, but the skill relies on an external agentic config, tracker descriptor and companion skills that it does not ship.
needs: a GitHub or other tracker account with rights to approve and merge the repository's pull requests
the open-mercato agentic config file (.ai/agentic.config.json) and a tracker descriptor
the companion skills om-auto-fix-pr, om-setup-agent-pipeline and om-followup-issue-from-pr
why: It is a development-process helper for PR-based repositories, not a feature a node's product uses, so value is some. It needs a tracker account and config from the open-mercato collection, and its companion skills are not part of a bare node, so the person must set those up first.

summary: This skill helps an agent choose the right .NET AI technology for a task, such as classic ML.NET for tabular predictions, Microsoft.Extensions.AI for LLM calls, Agent Framework for tool-using agents, or ONNX Runtime and Ollama for local inference. It also lists the guardrails each choice needs, like reproducible seeds, retry and timeout, and keys kept out of code. It is aimed at developers adding AI features to .NET 8+ applications.
tasks: choose an AI library for a .NET app
add a classifier or forecast with ML.NET
wire an LLM chat feature through Microsoft.Extensions.AI
build a RAG search over documents in .NET
run a local model with Ollama from C#
qualityWhy: The decision tree, branch guardrails, anti-patterns and depth rules are concrete and actionable, though the reference files are only pointed to and not shown here.
needs: an LLM provider key such as OpenAI or Azure OpenAI, only if that provider is chosen
a vector store account such as Azure AI Search or Pinecone, only if chosen
why: It is useful for AI features in .NET projects, but the node builds on Next.js and TypeScript, so the guidance must be read for its ideas and rebuilt in the node's own stack rather than installed as written. It does not cover the node's own stack.

summary: The skill guides an agent through upgrading a .NET 10 project or solution to .NET 11 preview: changing the target framework, updating package versions, fixing compiler and library breaking changes, and updating Dockerfiles and CI pipelines. It is aimed at developers maintaining existing .NET codebases rather than writing new programs. The bundled references list source-breaking and behavioral changes by technology area.
tasks: upgrade my .NET 10 project to .NET 11
fix build errors after updating the .NET 11 SDK
update Dockerfiles and CI pipelines to .NET 11 images
review behavioral changes in EF Core 11 and ASP.NET Core 11
qualityWhy: Concrete steps, before/after code snippets, a clear reference-loading table and a verification checklist, though the reference details are only partly visible here and the skill is marked as covering preview 3 only.
why: It is a .NET migration guide, useful only for projects built on .NET, which a node serves only occasionally; it is written for the .NET toolchain and does not target Fractera's Next.js stack, so an agent would read it for ideas and not install it as written. It also says .NET 11 is in preview and covers changes only through Preview 3.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull a GitHub repository's traffic numbers, including page views, clones, referring sites, popular pages and star count, through the gh command-line tool. It saves each pull into a local history file, since GitHub only keeps 14 days of data, and can draw trend charts as PNG or plain text. It suits maintainers of open-source projects who want to see how their repo is growing.
tasks: show this repo's views and clones for the last two weeks
chart star growth and traffic trends over 30 days
find which sites send visitors to the repository
save a daily traffic snapshot so history builds up
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear prerequisites, flags, workflows, a permissions table and troubleshooting, but the script is cut off in the provided text, so the chart code and error paths cannot be fully checked.
needs: GitHub account with push access to the target repository
gh CLI authenticated with a token that has the repo scope
why: It is useful for tracking a project's public reach, but it is not for building or running a product, so the value is only some. It reads from GitHub's cloud API and needs a GitHub login with write access, which is a service the person chooses, while the history and charts stay on the local machine. The cut-off script means its chart code was not fully reviewed.

summary: The skill guides an agent through App Store keyword research: expanding seed terms via autocomplete, competitor rankings and synonyms, scoring each candidate on volume, difficulty, relevance and intent, and grouping results into primary, secondary, long-tail and aspirational buckets. It ends with a keyword strategy for title, subtitle and keyword field. It is aimed at mobile app marketers and developers who want to improve App Store discoverability.
tasks: find keywords for my iOS app
score app store keyword opportunities
compare my app's keywords with competitors
build a keyword strategy for title and subtitle
qualityWhy: The method and output template are clear, but the skill never says how to get volume or difficulty numbers, so an agent cannot actually run the scoring as written.
why: It is about App Store keyword marketing for mobile apps, not building, running or making content for a Fractera site, web app or agent, so it does not serve the node's purpose. It has no risk, but the value is none and the use is skip.

summary: The skill guides an agent through turning on C# nullable reference types in an existing .NET project and working down the resulting compiler warnings in a disciplined, zero-behavior-change way. It covers choosing a rollout strategy, fixing dereference and annotation warnings, applying nullable attributes, cleaning up suppressions, and adding a regression guard. It also includes a PowerShell scanner that reports NRT settings and counts suppressions. It is aimed at developers maintaining C# codebases, mainly libraries and applications.
tasks: enable nullable reference types in a C# project
fix CS8602 and CS8618 nullable warnings
annotate a library's public API for nullability
audit null-forgiving operators and suppressions
qualityWhy: It is very thorough, with concrete steps, decision flowcharts, warning-by-warning fixes, checkpoints, a validation checklist and pitfalls, and it is backed by a working scanner script.
why: It is a .NET and C# maintenance skill, which is not what a Fractera node is built on (Next.js and TypeScript), so it is useful only occasionally and as reference reading rather than as a direct install. Its guidance is stack-specific to C# and would need to be applied to Fractera projects by hand, which is why the use is ideas. Nothing in the files is harmful; the script only reads project files and counts patterns.

summary: This skill guides an agent through reading, creating, editing, fixing and validating Excel spreadsheets by working directly on the xlsx XML inside the package, with helper scripts for unpacking, packing, row and column insertion, formula checking and LibreOffice recalculation. It also enforces a financial colour and number-format convention. It is aimed at people who need spreadsheets, financial models or tabular reports produced or repaired.
tasks: build a financial model spreadsheet with formulas
add a computed column to an existing Excel file
insert a row into a budget workbook and keep its totals correct
check a spreadsheet for broken formulas
analyze data from an xlsx or csv file
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete routing, step-by-step commands, integrity rules and checks, though the reference files and several scripts were not visible to me, so completeness is not fully confirmed.
why: Spreadsheets are a common product output and the skill works on local xlsx files with no cloud service, so it fits a local-first node; it is stack-free Python and XML, not tied to a foreign framework. Doubts: I could not inspect the truncated scripts or the unseen reference files fully.

summary: This playbook guides an agent through security testing of applications built on language models. It covers direct instruction overrides, indirect injection through documents and web pages, abuse of tool calls, data leaks through rendered output, and risks from MCP servers. It also gives a testing order, a decision tree, and a list of evidence to collect when reporting a finding. It is aimed at security reviewers who need to check AI features before release.
tasks: test a chatbot for prompt injection
check an AI agent's tool calls for data leaks
review MCP server tool descriptions for hidden instructions
write a findings report for an LLM security review
qualityWhy: It gives concrete payloads, a clear test order, a decision tree and reporting criteria, but it is mostly lists of examples with few steps for verifying a finding.
why: It is stack-free and useful when a node builds AI agents and needs to test their defenses, but its main purpose is offensive testing rather than building features. It needs no outside service or key.

summary: The skill guides an agent through choosing a monetization model for a mobile app, including subscription tiers, price points, and free trial length. It also covers paywall timing and layout, in-app purchase tactics, and revenue metrics such as conversion, ARPU, and LTV. It is aimed at app founders and marketers who want to raise revenue without hurting user satisfaction. Its output is a recommendation card and a short rollout plan.
tasks: design subscription pricing for my app
plan a paywall and free trial
choose between subscription and in-app purchases
review my app's revenue metrics
qualityWhy: It gives useful tables, benchmarks and an output template, but the benchmark figures are unsourced and it has no step-by-step checks or worked examples.
why: It is a stack-free strategy text, but it is written for App Store mobile apps and is only partly relevant to a web product or shop on a node; its price benchmarks should be verified before use.

summary: This skill turns a rough idea, a long story excerpt, or a set of reference images, videos and audio into one clean prompt for Seedance 2.5 video generation. It assigns each reference a role, keeps character counts and story events fixed, and sets out the template to follow for generation, keyframes, editing or extension. The agent produces only the prompt and leaves the actual video submission to a separate tool. The skill is aimed at people making short videos and promotional content.
tasks: write a clean Seedance prompt from a short story idea
assign roles to character, product and scene reference images
plan a storyboard or keyframe-driven video
turn a novel excerpt into a filmable video prompt
extend or edit an existing video with a precise prompt
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with templates, worked examples and explicit checks, though the file is very long and the visible portion was cut off before the end.
needs: npm registry access for the skills package
why: The prompt-writing content directly serves making video for a product, but the first step runs an unpinned remote package on every session, so the skill is skipped rather than installed.
risks: Runs 'npx --yes skills@latest update' automatically at the start of each session, executing whatever the latest published package contains without the person's review.
Overwrites the local skill copy with the newest remote version each time, so its contents can change without the person knowing.

summary: This skill guides an AI agent that runs in short, scheduled work sessions on a Paperclip control-plane server. It covers reading assigned tasks and their context, claiming work, posting progress, and setting the correct status, including waiting on human answers, review, or blockers. It also explains how to hand off deliverable files as artifacts, how to delegate subtasks, and how to manage approvals, routines and monitors through the Paperclip API. The intended users are teams running several agents on shared project work.
tasks: claim and update an assigned task
hand off a generated file as a task artifact
delegate subtasks to another agent
ask a human a structured question and wait for the answer
record blockers and follow-up work on a task
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with step order, exact API payloads, helper scripts, and verification rules, though the file is very long and assumes a Paperclip server the node does not provide.
needs: Paperclip control-plane server reachable at PAPERCLIP_API_URL
Paperclip agent API key or run token (PAPERCLIP_API_KEY)
why: It only helps when a team of agents is coordinated through a Paperclip server, so it is useful for running multi-agent product work but not for building sites or content directly on the node. Task state and uploaded artifacts live on that Paperclip server, not in the node's local storage, so the person should check where their Paperclip instance is hosted before installing.

summary: The skill guides an agent to produce a Business Model Canvas with all nine blocks, from customer segments and value propositions through channels, relationships, resources, activities, partners, costs and revenue. It is aimed at people documenting or analysing how an established business creates and captures value. It also compares the canvas with lean and startup alternatives and suggests a rough LTV-to-CAC test.
tasks: draft a business model canvas for my product
analyse how our existing business makes money
compare business model canvas with lean canvas
check unit economics of a revenue model
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear nine-block template and output steps, but it is mostly prompts and questions with little worked example or concrete check beyond the LTV rule.
why: It is a stack-free planning skill, so it fits a node for documenting a business model, though it is generic and only occasionally needed. Its $ARGUMENTS placeholder and lack of a output format may need a little guidance from the agent.

summary: This skill helps an agent list and install other agent skills from GitHub repositories, by default the curated catalogue in openai/skills, into a local skills folder. It targets Codex's own skills directory, so it works as a package manager for agent plugins rather than for building a product. The people it serves are developers who manage the skills their coding agent uses.
tasks: list installable skills from openai/skills
install a curated skill by name
install a skill from a private GitHub repo
qualityWhy: The file gives clear commands, options, fallback behaviour and error handling for its narrow purpose, though some details depend on the truncated script.
needs: GitHub token (GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN), optional, only for private repos
why: It manages Codex skill folders under ~/.codex/skills and does not help build, run, sell or create content for a product, so its value is none. It is also built for another agent platform, not for a Fractera element's skills folder.

summary: This skill gives an agent an expert playbook for exploiting glibc heap bugs such as use-after-free, double free, overflows and off-by-one or null-byte writes. It maps which attack works on which glibc version, how to leak libc and heap addresses, and how to decode safe-linking pointers. It is aimed at security researchers and CTF players working on binary exploitation.
tasks: exploit a use-after-free in a glibc binary
leak libc base from an unsorted bin chunk
pick a tcache attack for a given glibc version
decode safe-linking pointers in a heap exploit
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete layout tables, version-by-version attack lists, a safe-linking code snippet and a decision tree, though it has few worked examples and relies on referenced files for depth.
why: It is a binary exploitation reference for attacking software, not a tool for building, running or selling a site, app or content, so it does not serve what a Fractera node is for. Its purpose is offensive exploit development against other people's programs.
risks: Gives an agent step-by-step guidance for exploiting memory-corruption bugs in target binaries, which could be used to attack systems.

summary: This skill acts as a starting map for testing business logic in an app: the rules about when checks happen and which conditions get verified. It tells an agent to first list the key states and one-time actions in a flow, such as payments, coupons, quotas, or approvals. It then points the agent to check for timing windows, skipped steps, and missing authorization between steps. For developers testing their own shop, booking, or subscription flow, it gives a checklist of where to look.
tasks: check a checkout flow for price tampering
test whether coupons can be stacked or reused
find race conditions in a payment or inventory flow
review a multi-step approval workflow for skipped steps
qualityWhy: It is mostly a router with a short three-step flow and no concrete test steps, examples, or checks; the detailed content lives in a linked skill.
why: It is a stack-free testing checklist that helps someone harden their own product's flows, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. Its value depends on the linked skills it points to, which are not included here and may not be installed on the node.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write unit tests for Java Spring REST controllers using MockMvc in standalone mode, with mocked service dependencies. It covers GET, POST, PUT and DELETE requests, query and path parameters, validation errors, response headers, and content negotiation. It is aimed at Java developers who test their web layer in isolation.
tasks: write unit tests for a Spring REST controller
test API endpoints with MockMvc
check validation and 400 errors in a controller
verify HTTP status codes and JSON responses
qualityWhy: The examples are concrete and runnable in principle, but the 401 and authorization example will not work under standaloneSetup without security configuration, and the skill does not warn about that clearly.
why: A Fractera node builds Next.js and TypeScript apps, so this Java Spring skill does not fit the node's stack and can only be read for general controller-testing ideas, which would need rewriting for Jest or Vitest with the Next.js route handlers. The skill is not useful as an install.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write JUnit 5 tests that run one test body against many inputs. It covers the common sources of those inputs, such as simple value lists, CSV tables, factory methods, enum values and custom providers. It also shows how to name each run so failures are easy to read. The guidance targets Java projects built with Gradle or Maven.
tasks: write data-driven Java unit tests
test boundary values for a method
reduce duplicate test methods with many input cases
add readable display names to parameterized tests
qualityWhy: The steps and examples are clear and useful, but the skill is short and one example is wrong: null cannot be passed through @ValueSource(strings = ...), and the Maven snippet omits the AssertJ dependency it asks for.
why: It is a Java and JUnit testing guide, while nodes build with TypeScript, Next.js and Vitest-style tooling, so an agent should read it for test-design ideas and rewrite the examples in the node's own test stack. It has no outside service requirement and no risky commands.

summary: The skill gives an agent a CSRF testing playbook: it lists high-value state-changing endpoints, token bypass patterns, SameSite edge cases, JSON and multipart CSRF payloads, OAuth state checks and clickjacking as a bypass. It is aimed at security testers reviewing web apps and their defenses. It is a review and attack-reference document; it does not build or run product features.
tasks: review a login or account flow for CSRF weaknesses
test whether an API accepts requests without its anti-CSRF token
check SameSite and CORS settings on session cookies
audit an OAuth callback for a missing state parameter
qualityWhy: It is concrete, with many test steps, PoC templates and a checklist, though some claims (such as the Chrome two-minute Lax exception) are stated loosely and it has no step-by-step verification method.
why: It is useful for security review of a node's own forms and APIs, but it is an offensive testing guide rather than a product-building skill, so it serves occasionally. It is written as an attack playbook for generic web apps, so an agent would need to adapt its checks to the node's next-auth sessions and its own data layer before using it.
risks: Offensive PoC templates (auto-submitting forms, clickjacking overlays) could be aimed at third-party sites if an agent followed them outside a test scope.

summary: This skill tells an agent to search a person's Notion workspace, read the relevant pages, and turn what it finds into a brief, summary, comparison or full report with citations and links back to the sources. It is written for people who keep notes, plans or research in Notion and want an agent to synthesize them into a decision-ready document. The workflow covers scoping with the user, choosing a format, drafting from templates, and updating the page as new information arrives.
tasks: summarize my Notion research notes into a brief
compare options from several Notion pages in a table
write a report with citations from Notion sources
turn scattered meeting notes into a decision document
qualityWhy: The workflow steps are clear, but the SKILL.md itself is short and leans on reference files for templates and citation rules that were not provided in the reviewed body.
needs: Notion account with OAuth login to the Notion MCP server
Codex CLI with the rmcp_client feature
why: Notion is a cloud workspace, and the skill reads from and writes to it through a hosted MCP server, so it conflicts with the local-first design of a Fractera node. Its setup also depends on Codex-specific commands, so it would not run on a node without changes.

summary: This skill is a reference playbook for analyzing network captures: repairing damaged PCAP files, applying Wireshark display filters, and decoding protocols such as HTTP, DNS, FTP, SMTP, USB keyboard traffic and WiFi handshakes. It also covers pulling files and credentials out of captures, spotting covert channels and tunnels, and running tshark and NetworkMiner from the command line. It is aimed at security analysts and CTF players who need to examine a capture file.
tasks: analyze a pcap capture for suspicious traffic
extract files and credentials from network traffic
detect DNS tunneling in a capture
decode USB keyboard keystrokes from a capture
repair a corrupted pcap file
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete filters, commands and a decision tree that an agent can follow, though several sections are brief and the decoding steps are only sketched.
why: Useful for analysing captures but not for building, running or selling a product on a node, so it is occasional rather than core use. It is a stack-free, local tool set with no outside service, and it only describes analysis steps without any risky action. Some content (WiFi cracking, credential harvesting) is offensive-leaning and should be used only on captures the person is authorised to analyse.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write React components on Mantine's internal conventions: a factory wrapper, a Styles API with classNames, styles and vars props, CSS variables from a vars resolver, and compound sub-components. It also covers registering those components in a Mantine theme through extend(). It is aimed at developers who publish a reusable component library on top of Mantine.
tasks: build a reusable React component that accepts classNames and styles overrides
add theme-driven CSS variables and variants to a component
create a compound component with sub-components sharing context
register a custom component in a theme with extend and defaultProps
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a complete, runnable component template, a factory-type table, theme examples and clear pointers to reference files, though the reference files were not included in the material to check.
why: It is built for Mantine 9.x, a UI kit the node does not use (it uses shadcn/ui and Tailwind), so an agent should take the factory and Styles API patterns as ideas and build them the node's way. It only matters when a product is deliberately built on Mantine.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write Java unit tests for JSON serialization and deserialization in Spring Boot, using the JacksonTester support in @JsonTest. It covers checking field names, nested objects, date formats, null handling, custom serializers and polymorphic types. The target users are Java/Spring developers who want to confirm their DTOs produce and read the JSON they expect.
tasks: write a JSON serialization test for a Spring DTO
check that @JsonProperty names map correctly
test a custom Jackson serializer
verify date formatting in JSON output
debug a failing Jackson deserialization test
qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, runnable code examples for many cases, and a debugging table, though it has small gaps such as thin version guidance.
why: The skill is built for Java and Spring Boot, which Fractera nodes do not use (their stack is Next.js and TypeScript), so an agent would need to adapt it to Vitest or Jest with TypeScript types. The general habits of checking JSON paths and null handling are still useful when testing API payloads.

summary: This skill audits existing tests in many languages by naming them with the formal testsmells.org taxonomy of 19 smells, such as Assertion Roulette, Conditional Test Logic and Mystery Guest. It ranks each confirmed smell by risk and gives a framework-correct fix, so it suits a developer who wants a citable, severity-ranked review of a test suite. It is a code-review instruction set with no scripts and no outside services.
tasks: audit my test suite for test smells
give a citable severity-ranked review of these tests
find conditional logic and mystery guests in unit tests
suggest framework-correct fixes for flaky sleep-based tests
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, decision table, calibration rules and output contract, and it points to a full catalog reference, though it leaves some edge cases to judgment.

It is useful only when the person is building an iOS app or wants speech-to-text on Apple devices. Server-backed recognition is Apple's own service and needs network access, which the skill notes.

summary: The skill guides an agent to write unit tests for utility classes, static helpers and pure functions, covering null handling, empty inputs, boundary values and floating-point precision. It uses AssertJ fluent assertions and JUnit @ParameterizedTest, with examples for string, math, collection and validation helpers. It is aimed at Java developers who want their helper code verified.
tasks: write unit tests for a string utility class

test a math helper with floating point tolerance
convert repeated test cases into parameterized tests

why: It is a Java and JUnit testing guide, which a Fractera node built on TypeScript would not use as written, so an agent would need to adapt the ideas to Vitest or Jest. The testing principles are generally useful, but it is not directly about building or running a product on the node.

summary: This skill is a runbook for working on the billing code of the cmux product: Stripe Checkout, Pro/Max/Team pricing, subscriptions, webhooks, and the entitlements that decide which Cloud VM allowance an account gets. It tells an agent which routes do what, how to test payments locally with fake grants and test promotion codes, and how to run a production price change safely. It is written for engineers maintaining that product's billing, not for building general sites or content.
tasks: debug a Stripe checkout or webhook failure
change a subscription price or add a new plan
grant a test account Pro access locally
trace why an account shows the wrong plan
qualityWhy: It gives concrete routes, env names, commands and gotchas an agent can follow, though it is dense and assumes the cmux repository layout.
why: Its whole subject is a cloud payment and hosting stack for one company's product (Stripe, Vercel, Stack Auth, cloud Postgres), which is not a local-first building tool for a node's own sites or content. It is also tied to cmux's private billing and admin setup, so it is not useful for a Fractera node.
risks: Grants paid plans and sends admin-only operations to a live Stripe account, which an agent could run against production if misread.

summary: This reference guide tells an agent how to identify the memory-safety protections in Linux ELF binaries and which techniques get past each one during exploit development. It covers ASLR, PIE, NX, RELRO, stack canaries, FORTIFY_SOURCE, Intel CET and ARM MTE, and includes a decision tree for choosing a path. It is aimed at security researchers and CTF players working on binary exploitation.

plan a bypass for ASLR or PIE
find a way around a stack canary
choose an exploit path under Full RELRO
qualityWhy: The tables and decision tree are clear and organised, but it is mostly a reference with few concrete steps, checks or worked examples an agent could follow end to end.
why: It is binary-exploitation knowledge with no link to building, running, selling or making content for a product, so it does not serve what a Fractera node is for. Its techniques are offensive and dual-use, which is another reason not to install it on a node.

summary: The skill guides an agent through writing Shopify Liquid theme code: sections, blocks and snippets with correct schema JSON, LiquidDoc headers, translation keys and per-component CSS and JavaScript. It serves developers and merchants who build or edit Shopify storefront themes. The main file summarises Liquid syntax, filters, tags, objects and setting types, with deeper references split into separate files.

why: Shopify themes are built for Shopify's own hosted platform, not for a local Fractera node, so the Liquid templating and schema conventions only help if the person is building a Shopify storefront; for the node's Next.js stack the skill must be read for ideas, not installed as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through upgrading a .NET 8 project to .NET 9: bumping the target framework, fixing source-incompatible compiler and library changes, reviewing behavioral changes such as EF Core migration checks and HttpClientFactory handler defaults, and updating Dockerfiles and CI settings. replace BinaryFormatter usage
resolve EF Core 9 migration exceptions
qualityWhy: The workflow has concrete steps, specific diagnostic codes, before-and-after examples and verification steps, with a few details left to the referenced files.
why: It is useful for maintaining existing .NET apps, which is only occasional work on a node, and it is stack-specific to .NET rather than the node's own stack, but it is a stack-free-to-install instruction file for the .NET project it targets. The skill itself makes no external calls, and its only risk is that it touches a project when followed.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to hand larger coding jobs, such as feature builds, pull request reviews, big refactors and issue-to-PR loops, to a separate coding CLI running in the background. review a pull request with a coding agent
run a large refactor in an isolated worktree
turn a GitHub issue into a pull request

GitHub access for issue and PR work
why: It directly helps build and review code for a product, but it is written around OpenClaw's message and process tools, which a Fractera node does not have, and it carries a risk, so it is skipped.

summary: This skill lets an agent turn a request for a diagram, flowchart, architecture chart or sketch into a whiteboard-style .tldr JSON file, then export it to PNG or SVG with a local command-line tool. It includes detailed rules for shape types, colours, arrow binding, box sizing and layout presets for architecture, flowchart, sequence, ML, ER and UML diagrams. make a flowchart of this process
visualize the data flow between components
export the diagram as PNG or SVG

why: Diagrams help a node's builders explain systems and content, but this is a side tool rather than core product building, and it runs locally with no outside service. The skill runs through a global npm install and a puppeteer Chrome download, which the person should approve.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building retrieval-augmented generation: splitting documents into chunks, turning them into embeddings, storing them in a vector database, and wiring a retriever into a chat model so answers cite a knowledge base. add semantic search to a product knowledge base
ground chatbot answers in sourced documentation

a chat model provider key for generating answers

summary: This skill is a reference playbook for finding and exploiting OS command injection in web apps. It lists shell operators, vulnerable code patterns in several languages, blind detection by timing and out-of-band DNS or HTTP, filter-bypass tricks, and payloads for reverse shells and host reconnaissance. It is written for security testers attacking targets, not for developers building products.
tasks: test a ping or diagnostic form for shell injection
check an upload or conversion pipeline for command injection

find blind command injection with timing or DNS callbacks
