why: The content is offensive attack material aimed at other systems and does not serve building, running or selling a product on a node, so it is not useful there. It is also skipped because an agent following it could run reverse shells and secret-harvesting commands.
risks: Includes reverse-shell and secret-reading payloads (env, /proc/1/environ, /etc/shadow) that an agent could run against systems it should not access.

summary: The skill is a security-testing playbook for finding path traversal and local file inclusion flaws in web apps. It lists encoding tricks for escaping directories, target files worth reading, PHP wrapper abuse, log and session poisoning paths to code execution, and framework quirks for Java, Tomcat, Nginx and Node.js. It is written for penetration testers and bug bounty hunters who are assessing a target they are authorised to test.

check a download endpoint for arbitrary file read

audit an Nginx alias configuration for traversal

why: It is an offensive security reference about attacking other systems, not a tool for building, running or selling a product on a Fractera node, so value is none. Its exploit payloads and tool lists are a misuse risk on a node that holds the owner's data.
risks: Offensive exploitation payloads (log poisoning to RCE, AJP Ghostcat, iconv CVE-2024-2961) could be used against systems the person does not own.

summary: The skill teaches an agent to verify that requests to a server come from a genuine Apple device running a legitimate copy of an iOS app. It covers DCDevice per-device bits for simple flags such as promo claims and fraud marks, and App Attest for cryptographic key generation, attestation and per-request assertions, with server-side checks. It is aimed at developers protecting sensitive API endpoints from fraud on iOS.
tasks: protect a sensitive API endpoint with App Attest
flag compromised or fraudulent devices
add device verification to an iOS backend
track whether a device has claimed a promo offer
qualityWhy: Concrete Swift code for each phase, a clear server-verification checklist, error handling and a review checklist, with detailed server steps moved to a reference file that was not included in the reviewed material.

Apple DeviceCheck server API credentials for server-side bit and attestation checks
why: The skill is an iOS-only Swift guide, so it has no direct use in a Fractera node's Next.js and TypeScript stack; its attestation and assertion ideas could be adapted to a server built on the node's own stack, and it only applies to an iOS app client, so the value is limited. The server-side parts also depend on the external reference file, which was not reviewed.

summary: The skill guides an agent through writing unit tests for Spring Boot @ExceptionHandler methods and @ControllerAdvice classes. It shows how to build a standalone MockMvc setup, check HTTP status codes, verify JSON error payloads, and test field-level validation errors. It is aimed at Java developers who maintain REST APIs.
tasks: write unit tests for a Spring exception handler
check error response JSON from a REST API
test field-level validation error messages
mock controller advice in MockMvc tests

why: Fractera nodes are a Next.js, TypeScript and SQLite stack, so a Java/Spring testing skill does not serve what the node is for and would need replacing of the whole stack. Its value to a node is none, so it is skipped.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to operate an Obsidian vault through the official obsidian command-line tool: opening, reading, searching, creating, moving and deleting notes, managing daily notes and tasks, and reading or setting properties and links. It also covers developer commands for reloading plugins, checking errors and evaluating code inside the running app. It is aimed at people who keep notes and knowledge bases in Obsidian and want an agent to work on them.
tasks: search my vault for notes about a project
append a task to today's daily note
move an old note into an archive folder
update a note's status property
list unresolved links in my vault

summary: The skill guides an agent through running a Qdrant vector database locally with Docker, then creating collections, storing embeddings with payloads, and running similarity or filtered searches from Java. tasks: set up a local vector database for semantic search
store document embeddings and search them by similarity

summary: This skill teaches an agent to run the Himalaya command-line mail client against an IMAP/SMTP account. The agent can list folders and messages, read and search mail, compose or reply to messages, and move, copy, delete or flag them. It suits someone who wants to handle their email from a terminal, for example to answer customer messages while building or running a product.

reply to a customer email

send an email with an attachment

account login credentials, kept in a password manager or keyring
why: It is a local client for a remote mail server, so it is useful now and then for product support rather than core building, and it needs the person's own mail account. The skill is stack-free and installs with a standard brew formula, and it advises against pasting secrets into chat.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing unit tests for Java object mappers, mainly MapStruct interfaces and hand-written converter classes. It covers checking that generated mapper code exists, null handling, round-trip conversion, nested objects, enum mapping and expression checks. It is aimed at Java backend developers who move data between entities and DTOs.

summary: This skill walks an agent through switching a GitHub Actions repo that publishes to nuget.org from long-lived API keys to OIDC trusted publishing with short-lived tokens. It classifies the packable .NET projects (library, dotnet tool, MCP server, template, application), checks their required properties, guides the owner through creating a nuget.org policy, and writes or migrates a tag-triggered publish workflow. It is aimed at maintainers of .NET packages, not at the building, running or selling of a node's own product.
tasks: set up NuGet trusted publishing for my repo
replace the NuGet API key with OIDC in my publish workflow
create a GitHub Actions workflow that publishes a dotnet tool to nuget.org
check my .csproj files are ready to pack and publish

why: It publishes .NET packages to nuget.org, which is a cloud package registry and not a local-first product workflow, so it does not serve building, running or selling a node's own sites, apps, agents or content. Because value is none, use is skip.

summary: This playbook teaches an agent to test web applications for server-side template injection: spotting when user input is evaluated by a template engine, identifying which engine it is, and building code-execution payloads for engines such as Jinja2, FreeMarker, Twig, ERB and Thymeleaf. It also covers filter bypasses, blind detection, and what to do after code execution, including reading credentials. It is written for security testers and penetration testers.

write a security report on template injection risk

Describes setting up a reverse shell for persistence on a target system.
Includes Flask debugger PIN recovery from host values, with only a one-line authorization caveat.

summary: This skill tells an agent that the ResolveProjectReferences time shown in an MSBuild performance summary is misleading, because it is mostly wall-clock wait for dependent project builds rather than real work. It steers the agent away from optimizing that target and toward the Task Performance Summary, where the true costly tasks such as Csc, ResolveAssemblyReference or Copy show up. find the real bottleneck task in a binlog

read the Task Performance Summary of a .NET build

why: It is a narrow diagnostic habit for .NET build tuning, useful now and then on a dotnet project, and it is stack-free apart from MSBuild, which a Fractera node's dotnet work would use; it depends on the build-perf-diagnostics and build-parallelism skills it names, which are not included here.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to define LangChain4j AI Services as Java interfaces annotated with system and user messages, wiring in chat memory keyed by user, and registering tools for function calling. It prefers built-in abstractions like TimeProvider and IHttpClientFactory, and System.IO.Abstractions for file access, and only generates custom minimal wrappers or an AsyncLocal-based ambient seam when a static API must keep its signatures. why: The skill is a .NET/C# refactoring guide, and the node's stack is Next.js and TypeScript, so it serves none of the node's uses; it is not a risk, only out of scope.

summary: Gives an agent test patterns for Spring Cache annotations (@Cacheable, @CachePut, @CacheEvict) using an in-memory ConcurrentMapCacheManager and Mockito mocks, without a full Spring context. It shows how to check cache hits and misses through repository call counts, verify eviction, check SpEL-based keys, and test conditional caching. summary: This skill guides an agent through testing a GraphQL API for exposed schema information, such as introspection and type probes. It also covers finding hidden or undocumented parameters, checking whether batched requests bypass authorization, and looking for object-level access flaws. It is written for security testers who check an API's authorization gaps.

It is an offensive testing playbook, so it should be applied only to systems the person owns or is authorized to test.

summary: Gives an agent patterns for unit testing Spring Boot @ConfigurationProperties classes without starting a full application context. It covers checking property binding, validation constraints, default values, type conversions such as Duration and DataSize, and profile-specific settings. The guidance is aimed at Java developers working on Spring Boot services.

why: The skill is entirely for Java and Spring Boot, which the node's stack (Next.js, TypeScript, SQLite) does not use, so it cannot be applied as written. It has no risk, but its use is limited to Java projects.

summary: This skill is an index for contributing to the Playwright browser-testing project itself. It points an agent to guides on adding APIs, MCP tools and CLI commands, vendoring npm dependencies, updating the WebKit Safari user-agent, and working on the trace dashboard. It is written for maintainers of the Playwright monorepo, not for people building products.
tasks: add a new API to the Playwright library

summary: Guides an agent through removing the traces of an abandoned design after a mid-branch decision change. It asks for a one-line statement of the new design, limits the sweep to code the decision touched, hunts dead code, shims, old names, history-narrating comments, outdated tests and docs, then rewrites everything so the tree reads as if the current design was there from the start. It is aimed at developers working in git branches and has no connection to building, running or selling sites, apps or content on a Fractera node.
tasks: clean up the old approach after a design change

why: It is a generic developer habit for git repositories and does not serve building, running, selling or making content for a product, so it is not useful on a Fractera node; the skill itself is safe and has no risks.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to unit test Spring application events without starting the full Spring context. It covers mocking ApplicationEventPublisher, capturing published events with ArgumentCaptor, and calling @EventListener methods directly. It also shows how to check async listeners. It is aimed at Java developers who write Spring Boot services.

summary: This skill is a security playbook for finding and exploiting XML External Entity (XXE) injection. It walks an agent through classic file-read payloads, out-of-band exfiltration through attacker-hosted DTDs, blind and error-based variants, XXE-to-SSRF chaining, and XXE hidden inside SOAP, SVG, Office files and SAML. It is written for penetration testers and security researchers who are assessing systems they are authorised to test.
tasks: test an upload endpoint for XXE through an SVG or docx file

bypass a parser that blocks DOCTYPE declarations
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete payloads, target paths, a detection checklist and a routing list to companion material, though it has some gaps such as no authorisation guidance and loose verification steps.
why: It is an offensive security reference for attacking XML parsers, not a tool for building, running or selling a product on a local-first node, so its value is none. It is skipped because it carries a risk: its payloads read secrets such as SSH keys, AWS credentials and environment variables, and it includes out-of-band exfiltration to attacker-controlled hosts.
risks: Contains payloads that read secrets such as /home/USER/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials and /proc/self/environ, and exfiltrate them to attacker-controlled hosts.

summary: Gives an agent a playbook for testing race conditions in web apps: finding one-time, balance, quota and verification operations that use non-atomic check-then-update logic, then firing parallel requests using HTTP/1.1 last-byte sync, HTTP/2 single-packet bursts or Turbo Intruder gates. It is aimed at security testers working on authorized targets, who need to confirm duplicate successes or inconsistent state. The file is a single SKILL.md with decision trees, SQL isolation examples and a CVE reference.
tasks: test a coupon endpoint for double redeem
check whether a transfer API can double-spend a balance
run a parallel burst against a login rate limit
audit a checkout flow for limit-overrun races
qualityWhy: Concrete and well organised, with attack patterns, a decision tree, verification checklists and code examples, though some sections are generic and a few snippets are illustrative rather than runnable.
why: It is a security-testing playbook, useful for hardening a node's own apps against race conditions, but not a feature for building or making content, so value is some rather than high. The stack-free approach fits any node, and it needs no service or key; it targets Burp tooling that is external to the node. Its own note says to test only authorised targets.

summary: Guides a learner through one of four Claude certification tracks in an open-source AI engineering course, acting as an interactive tutor. It sequences lessons, runs the repository's Python labs and tests, quizzes the learner, and tracks progress in a local state file. It also runs diagnostic and mock assessments and assigns remediation from weak domains.

why: It is a study tutor for a Claude certification course, useful occasionally rather than for building or running a product, and it is stack-free apart from the repo's Python labs. It is independent of Anthropic and does not issue credentials. The optional live Messages API mode needs the learner's own ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, which only applies if they choose it.

summary: The skill is a playbook for an agent doing Linux kernel exploitation in CTF or security-research settings. It covers building a test environment in QEMU, classifying kernel bug types, and turning a bug into privilege escalation via commit_creds, modprobe_path overwrite, or kernel ROP. It also covers mitigation bypasses such as KASLR, SMEP, SMAP and KPTI, and the return to userspace after escalation. The audience is security researchers and CTF players, not people building products on a node.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to find out why a page's main content appears slowly, using Chrome DevTools MCP tools to record a load trace, read the LCP breakdown, and identify the LCP element. summary: The skill teaches an agent to work with the iOS Contacts and ContactsUI frameworks in Swift: requesting access, fetching and enumerating contacts with key descriptors, creating, updating and deleting contacts through save requests, and presenting the system contact picker from SwiftUI. summary: This skill lets an agent view and edit Longbridge brokerage watchlist groups, set, list and delete price alerts, and manage community stock lists through the Longbridge CLI. summary: This skill guides an agent through checking a web target for exposed version-control folders such as .git, .svn, .hg and .bzr, plus leaked backups, .env files and .DS_Store. It lists the paths to probe first, explains how to read status codes like 403 versus 404, and names open-source recovery tools for rebuilding exposed repositories. audit a web server for backup and config file leaks
verify exposed source control on an authorized pentest target

It is offensive-leaning and should only be used on systems the owner has authorized, and the referenced recovery tools are external and not part of the skill.

summary: This skill guides an agent through Rust performance work: measure before changing code, rank the likely gains from algorithm down to SIMD, and reach for common fixes such as pre-allocation, fewer clones and better data layout. It is written for engineers tuning Rust programs who need to find hotspots and judge whether an optimization is worth its added complexity. The skill is a set of decision tables and checklists with no executable scripts.

reduce allocations in a hot loop
set up criterion benchmarks
decide whether an optimization is worth the complexity

Its ideas are useful now and then, but it does not serve the node's main work directly.

summary: This skill tells an agent to explain a piece of code or a change so the person actually understands it. The agent first orients itself in the code, then calls two other skills, one for how the thing works and one for why it was built that way, and merges their findings into one plain account. It favours a short definition first, then layers of depth, and builds diagrams step by step when the system has several moving parts. It is aimed at developers who are new to a codebase, about to change it, reviewing it, or debugging it.

walk me through this code change
help me understand why a module is built this way
onboard me to an unfamiliar part of the codebase

why: It is a stack-free teaching habit that helps a person understand existing work, so it is useful now and then rather than daily. It assumes the how, why and unslop skills and the Claude Code adapter doc are installed alongside it, which this package does not provide, so an agent may need those first.

summary: This skill gives an agent a small typed knowledge graph for remembering people, projects, tasks, events and documents, and for linking them together. find what depends on a blocked task
check stored entities against a schema

I could only see part of ontology.py, so the rest of the validation and relation logic is unverified.

summary: This playbook teaches an agent to test web applications for mistakes in how they trust the HTTP Host header. It covers poisoned password reset links, cache poisoning, routing-based SSRF, hidden virtual hosts, and the header and request-format tricks used to get past Host validation. It is written for a security tester checking systems they are authorized to test, and a site owner could use it to audit their own app.
tasks: check my site for host header injection
test whether password reset emails can be poisoned
find hidden virtual hosts on my server
review how my app builds URLs from the Host header
qualityWhy: It is organized with a decision tree, a framework table and concrete request examples, but several claims (such as the port-parsing and connection-state cases) are speculative and it gives few steps for confirming impact.
why: It is a stack-free security reference, so it fits a node owner who wants to audit their own sites, but it is not about building, running or making content, so the value is only occasional. It only describes attacks, so the agent should use it on systems the person owns or is authorized to test.

summary: This skill gives an agent a security-testing playbook for web caches and CDNs. It explains how a shared cache can wrongly store a logged-in user's private page under a static-looking URL, and how unkeyed headers can poison a cached response for everyone. It lists curl-based checks for path confusion, cache hits, and headers, along with basic defenses such as no-store and Vary. It suits someone auditing their own site's caching.
tasks: audit my site for web cache deception
check whether the CDN caches logged-in account pages
test for unkeyed header cache poisoning
harden Cache-Control and Vary headers on sensitive routes
qualityWhy: The attack steps and curl checks are concrete, but the defense section is short, the section numbering repeats, and the companion reference file was not provided for review.
why: It is a stack-free security audit reference that helps harden a node's own sites against cache leaks, so it is useful now and then rather than core to building content. It is offensive-testing knowledge, so it should be applied only to systems the person owns or is authorized to test.

summary: This skill guides an agent through finding subdomains whose DNS records point at cloud, hosting or SaaS resources that no longer exist, so they can be claimed by someone else. audit my domain for subdomain takeover risk

write a remediation plan for stale DNS records

needs: AWS account (only for the S3 claim step)
Heroku account (only for the Heroku claim step)
GitHub account (only for the GitHub Pages claim step)
why: It is a security audit playbook that is useful now and then for checking a site's custom domains, and it needs no node stack. It is not about building or selling a product, and the offensive claim steps should only be run on domains the person owns or is authorized to test.

summary: This skill tells an agent to write very compressed replies that drop articles, filler and pleasantries while keeping code, commands and error text exact. switch to ultra brief answers for this session

summary: The skill guides an agent through building iOS and iPadOS alarms and countdown timers with Apple's AlarmKit, covering authorization, scheduling fixed or weekly alarms, timers, snooze and stop behaviour, observing alarm state, and a widget extension for countdown and paused Live Activity states. why: Removing duplicated code directly serves building and maintaining a product on the node, and the skill is language-agnostic with no sign-in, database or cloud service involved. It relies on the jscpd command-line tool, which the person runs locally.

summary: This skill guides an agent through putting a Next.js app into production: packaging it as a standalone Docker image, wiring a GitHub Actions pipeline that builds and pushes that image, and handling environment variables. why: It directly serves running a product built on Next.js, and the Docker-based approach is not tied to a single cloud. It is skipped because the example passes the Server Actions encryption key as a build argument and ENV, which would store the secret in the pushed image's metadata. The generated-key mistake and the reliance on GHCR and GitHub also need attention before any use.
risks: The Dockerfile and workflow store NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY as an ARG and ENV, so the secret would be baked into a pushed image that others may be able to pull.

It covers npm, pip, RubyGems, Maven, Composer and Docker, with read-only registry lookups, callback-style proof-of-concept patterns, and defensive controls such as scoped packages, lockfiles and private indexes. It is written for security engineers running authorized supply-chain reviews.

audit lockfiles and CI installs for supply-chain drift
qualityWhy: The steps, commands and decision tree are concrete and complete, though the PoC snippets are illustrative and the authorization boundaries are stated mainly in prose.

Its PoC pattern (higher version plus lifecycle hooks that call out to a host) would run code on third-party machines if followed outside a strictly controlled lab, so it is skipped.
risks: Following the PoC workflow would publish packages to public registries under names owned by others, with install-time scripts that run code on victims' machines and call external hosts.
Squatting third-party or unrelated internal package names on public registries could harm those organizations and their users.

summary: This skill guides an agent through setting up AWS SDK for Java 2.x clients, covering how credentials and regions are found, how sync and async HTTP clients are tuned, and how timeouts and retries are set. It also shows how to register clients as Spring Boot beans, handle SDK exceptions at boundaries, and test the setup. It is written for Java developers who connect their applications to AWS services.

why: The skill exists to connect Java code to AWS cloud services, which the node's local-first design excludes, so it is not useful for building or running a product on the node. It is well written, but its core purpose is cloud integration rather than local work.

why: The skill serves Terraform provider development in Go, which is not part of what a Fractera node is for (sites, web apps, AI agents, content), and acceptance tests create real billable infrastructure in a cloud account, so it is skipped.

retry throttled Bedrock calls with exponential backoff

summary: This playbook teaches an agent how to detect and exploit expression language injection in Java systems, covering Spring's SpEL, Struts2 and Confluence's OGNL, and JSP/JSF Java EL. It lists detection probes, command-execution payloads, sandbox-bypass techniques and specific CVE exploit steps. The intended readers are security testers attacking Java applications.

check a Spring Cloud Gateway for SpEL injection

summary: This skill teaches an agent to build messaging on Amazon Web Services using the AWS SDK for Java 2.x. summary: This skill is a reference playbook for turning an arbitrary write primitive, obtained from heap, format-string or out-of-bounds bugs, into code execution. It lists overwrite targets such as GOT entries, glibc hooks, _IO_FILE vtables, exit handlers, TLS destructors, modprobe_path and C++ vtables, and organizes them by glibc version and RELRO level. It is aimed at security researchers and CTF or exploit developers working on binary exploitation, not at people building or running a web product.
tasks: convert an arbitrary write into code execution
pick an overwrite target for a given glibc version
overwrite a GOT entry to call system
forge an exit handler or TLS destructor entry
qualityWhy: It gives a useful version-keyed map of targets, but most sections are conceptual tables and short snippets with few complete, checkable steps.
why: The skill is offensive binary-exploitation material with no connection to building, running or selling a site, app, agent or content on a local-first node, so its value is none and it is skipped.
risks: Provides step-by-step techniques for achieving remote code execution and kernel privilege escalation, which would serve attacks on systems the person does not control.

summary: The skill gives an agent a playbook for hash-related attacks used in CTF challenges and authorized security tests. It covers length extension on Merkle-Damgard hashes, MD5 and SHA-1 collision tools, birthday bounds, HMAC timing leaks, proof-of-work solving, and password-hash cracking. It is mainly aimed at security students and penetration testers, not at building or running a product.
tasks: solve a CTF hash challenge with length extension
check whether an app's MD5 comparison can be bypassed
write a proof-of-work solver for a challenge server
audit password hashing choices in a web app
qualityWhy: The file covers many attacks with concrete commands and tables, but several code samples are incomplete or inaccurate (the MD5 extension stub, the timing attack logic and the PoW hashcat line) and it gives no verification steps.
why: It is a security-attack reference for CTFs and pentests, which does not serve building, running, selling or making content for a product on a local-first node. Its code also contains a timing-attack script that sends many requests to a target URL, which is a risk when run against systems the person does not own.
risks: Contains a script that sends repeated requests to a target URL for HMAC timing recovery, which could be used against systems without authorization.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to write GraphQL queries, mutations, and subscriptions as a client developer. It covers naming, variables, fragments, directives, and avoiding over-fetching, and it tells the agent to read the project's schema before writing anything. It is aimed at developers whose apps talk to a GraphQL API.
tasks: write a GraphQL query for a product list
add a mutation to create a post
organize shared fields into fragments
set up type generation for GraphQL operations
review GraphQL operations for over-fetching
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear rules, concrete good-and-bad examples, and a schema-first workflow, but the reference files were not part of the review and the guide has few verification steps.
why: A Fractera node has no GraphQL layer; its data goes through the SQLite element, so this only helps when a project deliberately exposes or consumes a GraphQL API. The guidance is generic client practice, so an agent would need to adapt it to the node's own data access rather than install it as written.

summary: This skill asks an agent to remove comments from code by spawning a dedicated reviewer subagent that flags unnecessary comments, then vetting its report, fixing the underlying issues, and deleting or encoding constraint comments. It is aimed at developers who want cleaner codebases with fewer explanatory or workaround comments. The instructions depend on several other internal skills and a Claude Code adapter document, so it is tightly bound to a particular agent ecosystem.
tasks: remove unnecessary comments from my diff
clean up comments in these files
review and delete stale code comments
encode constraint comments as lint rules or tests
qualityWhy: The steps are dense and reference many unseen skills and an adapter file, so an agent cannot follow them without those dependencies, though the process itself is coherent.
why: It is a workflow for a code-review ecosystem outside Fractera's stack and depends on skills and subagents the node does not ship, so it is useful for ideas on comment cleanup rather than direct install. No outside service is needed, and the skill contains no risky actions.

summary: Turns a raw pile of notes, fragments or a transcript into an article written one block at a time. The agent first fixes the reader's prerequisites, offers two or three candidate openings for the user to choose from, then grows the article paragraph by paragraph, appending each agreed block to a separate file and pushing back on weak transitions. It is aimed at writers and editors who want their material shaped into prose with deliberate structure.
tasks: turn my raw notes into an article
shape a transcript into a blog post
draft an article paragraph by paragraph from a pile of material
choose the opening and structure for a long-form piece
qualityWhy: The loop, grounding rules, and specific conversational moves are concrete and followable, though it has no example session or output template.
why: It helps write articles for a site or blog, which is occasional use for a node, and it needs no stack or outside service. It is written in Chinese-mixed English and is more a writing method than a build tool, so it is useful now and then rather than core to building a product.

summary: This skill makes an agent review a code change, whether a pull request, a branch, a commit range, or the current uncommitted work. It runs the repository's configured validation commands, then checks the diff for security, breaking changes, data integrity, missing tests, and cross-module impact. The output is a severity-ranked report with an approve or request-changes verdict. It is aimed at developers who want a consistent review before merging.
tasks: review this pull request before merging
check my branch for security and breaking changes
run the validation gate and report failures
list findings by severity with fix suggestions
tools: GitHub pull request tracker (get-pr, get-pr-diff operations)
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear workflow, severity table, verdict rule, and gate rules, though it relies on referenced checklists and companion skills that the node would need.
needs: GitHub or another configured PR tracker account, for PR review mode
why: A review process is useful for any product being built on a node, but the skill is written for Open Mercato's agentic pipeline and expects its config files (.ai/agentic.config.json, SDLC.md) and companion skills. Local diff review works without a PR tracker, while PR mode needs one.

summary: This skill gives an agent a security-testing playbook for prototype pollution in JavaScript, covering both browser and Node/Express code. It explains how attacker-controlled keys such as __proto__ and constructor.prototype can reach shared objects, and how to probe query parsers and JSON bodies for that. It also lists the gadgets that turn pollution into impact, plus a decision tree for triage. It is aimed at security reviewers and developers hardening their own apps.
tasks: check my Express app for prototype pollution
audit deep merge code for __proto__ keys
review query parsing for unsafe object merging
decide whether a prototype pollution finding is exploitable
qualityWhy: It gives concrete probe payloads, observable signals and a triage tree, but it stops short of step-by-step verification or fix guidance.
why: It helps check and harden a node's own JavaScript apps against a specific class of bug, but it is offensive-leaning and only useful now and then, so it is not core to building content or products. It is not tied to a stack the node replaces, and it needs no keys or outside services. Some payloads target RCE gadgets, so it should only be used on authorized targets.

summary: This skill points an agent at a folder of interlinked markdown notes that follows the Karpathy LLM wiki layout and turns it into a knowledge graph. A Python script first maps the wikilinks, headings and index categories. Then LLM subagents add implicit relationships and topic clusters, and a merge step writes the result into a local data folder. It is aimed at people who keep research or documentation wikis and want to see how their notes connect.
tasks: turn my markdown wiki into a knowledge graph
find hidden connections between my wiki articles
map the topics and categories in my notes
generate an interactive dashboard of my knowledge base
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives clear phases, commands, validation rules and a safe cleanup guard, but the article-analyzer subagent definition and the dashboard skill it calls are not included in the files.
why: It runs locally on the person's own markdown files and writes its output to a local folder, so it fits the local-first node; its use for building products is occasional, not core. The article-analyzer subagent and the understand-dashboard companion are referenced but not shipped here, so they are unverified.

summary: Guides an agent through creating .NET projects from dotnet new templates with validated parameters, framework choices matched to the workspace, and adaptation to Central Package Management via Directory.Packages.props. It also covers composing multi-project solutions, installing or uninstalling template packages, and verifying builds afterward. The audience is developers scaffolding new .NET apps, APIs and test projects.
tasks: create a new ASP.NET web API project
scaffold a solution with API, library and test projects
make a new .NET project that uses central package management
install or uninstall a dotnet template package
qualityWhy: Concrete steps, command examples, a parameter table and a validation checklist that an agent can follow, with a few gaps such as the dependence on another skill for smart defaults.
why: Useful for scaffolding .NET projects, but Fractera nodes are built on Next.js and TypeScript, so .NET project creation is only occasionally relevant. Nothing in the file is risky; it only runs standard dotnet CLI commands.

summary: This skill lets an agent work out where and when a photo was taken. It gathers metadata, OCR text and reverse-image-search hits, records clues on a candidate board that a script ranks, and then checks the leading candidates against satellite imagery, street-level panoramas, sun and shadow angles, and terrain skylines. It is aimed at people who want a verified location for a photo, such as geo-guessing content creators or researchers.
tasks: find where a photo was taken
estimate when a photo was taken from sun and shadow angles
match a landscape skyline to terrain
confirm a building's location against street view
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with ordered steps, commands, tiered confidence rules and self-checks, but they depend on many scripts and region packs that were not all visible.
needs: Google Street View (gsv.py, key likely required)
Yandex and Baidu reverse image search
ML model weight downloads on first use
why: It is an investigation tool, not a builder for sites, apps, shops or social posts, so its use is occasional and mainly for content about geolocation. It calls outside services, and photos are sent to Baidu and Yandex reverse image search; the skill discloses this, but the person should know their photo leaves the machine. The skill also asks for a purpose before locating private residences or minors, which matters because it can be used to find where a stranger was.

summary: This skill makes an agent write a developer handoff spec for a finished design, covering layout, design tokens, component props, interaction states, responsive breakpoints, edge cases, motion and accessibility notes. It is aimed at designers and product teams passing screens to engineers. If a Figma link is given, the agent is told to pull measurements and tokens from it; otherwise it works from a text description or screenshot. The output is a fixed markdown template with tables for each section.
tasks: write a developer handoff spec for a landing page
document component states and responsive breakpoints for engineers
list design tokens and motion details for a checkout screen
turn a Figma frame into an implementation spec
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear output template and a checklist of what to cover, but it has few steps, no worked example, and no real procedure for pulling data from Figma.
needs: Figma account or connector (optional, only if a Figma URL is used)
why: It is stack-free and useful when a node is building a product UI, but it is a generic template rather than a tool for building anything on the node. The Figma connector is optional, and the skill refers to a CONNECTORS.md file that is not in the installed folder, so that link will be dead.

summary: Guides an agent to fix a bug by first writing a focused failing regression test, confirming it fails for the right reason, then making the minimal production fix and rerunning the test. It also tells the agent to skip writing a new test when the test path is expensive, unclear, or integration-heavy, and to use a closer manual or scripted check instead. Intended for developers who ask for TDD or have a bug with an obvious cheap local test target.
tasks: fix a bug with a regression test
write a failing test before fixing the code
add a focused test that reproduces a reported bug
verify a bug fix when no cheap test path exists
qualityWhy: Clear, ordered workflow with explicit checks, guardrails and a reporting format, though it gives no concrete commands or examples for a specific test framework.
why: It is a stack-free debugging habit that fits any codebase, so it is useful for building and maintaining a node's own features, but it only applies to bugs with a cheap local test path and adds no direct product or content output. Nothing in the file asks for secrets, runs remote code, or changes permissions.

summary: This skill lets an agent read production error data from Sentry using the Sentry command-line tool, without changing anything. It lists unresolved issues, shows issue and event details, and can request AI-generated root-cause explanations and fix plans. It is aimed at developers who want to check recent production errors and health of their app.
tasks: list the top open production errors from the last 24 hours
explain the root cause of a Sentry issue
show the events and details for an error ID
summarize recent production health from Sentry
qualityWhy: The instructions give concrete commands, defaults, output rules and fallbacks, though they lack a worked example of the expected output format and error handling.
why: It helps monitor a product's production errors, which is useful now and then rather than for building content, and it relies on the Sentry hosted service that the person would choose and authenticate with. The skill is read-only and its install command is the standard Sentry CLI installer.
risks: The install step pipes a remote script from cli.sentry.dev straight into bash, so the person should check it before running.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how DNS rebinding works: a hostname's IP is changed between lookups so that a victim's browser, which still treats the page as same-origin, can read responses from internal services. It walks through TTL and browser-cache behaviour, several attack variants, the kinds of internal targets involved, a few tools, and how the technique differs from server-side SSRF. The intended audience is security testers who need to check whether an application's origin or network defences hold up.
tasks: test whether an web app's origin checks can be bypassed with DNS rebinding
check if internal admin panels are reachable from a victim's browser
review a site's defences against DNS rebinding and Host header checks
decide whether a fetch-based feature needs SSRF or rebinding hardening
qualityWhy: It is concrete and organised with a decision tree and checklist, but some tool flags and technical claims (such as the multi-A-record fallback behaviour) are unverified and should be checked before use.
needs: rbndr.us or a self-run DNS server (optional, for rebinding infrastructure)
why: It is an offensive security playbook, so its value to a node is limited to security testing of the person's own apps, not building, running or selling products; an agent should use it only against systems the person is authorised to test. It is stack-free, so no adaptation is needed, but the cloud metadata and internal-service payloads are dual-use and deserve caution.

summary: Guides an agent through a codemod-style migration of direct C# static calls such as DateTime.UtcNow, File.* and Environment.* to an already-available abstraction like TimeProvider, IFileSystem or an existing reader, with constructor injection and a scoped AsyncLocal seam for static classes. It is aimed at developers who want to make .NET code testable without changing its behaviour. The skill stresses preserving DateTimeKind, the number and order of reads, and verifying builds and tests.
tasks: migrate DateTime.UtcNow calls to TimeProvider
replace File.ReadAllText with IFileSystem in a project
make a static utility class testable with an ambient seam
update tests to use FakeTimeProvider
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete mapping tables, explicit DateTimeKind rules, a complete AsyncLocal code example, step-by-step verification and a validation checklist, which an agent can follow directly.
why: It serves developers building .NET products rather than the Fractera node's own TypeScript stack, so it is useful only for C# projects on a node, and it needs no outside service. Its scope is narrow and it works only on C# code, which limits its use on a node built around Next.js.

summary: This skill lets an agent take a written plan, a spec file, or a clear build request and carry it through to working, tested code in a git repository. It breaks the work into units, runs each one in its own isolated workspace, and checks the results before reporting. It can also hand the implementation to another AI coding tool and resume an interrupted run. The people it serves are developers and product builders who want a feature finished without rewriting the plan.
tasks: implement a feature from a written plan
build a change from a clear spec file
resume an interrupted implementation run
finish a batch of coding tasks and verify them locally
qualityWhy: The instructions are detailed, staged and checkable, with explicit commit, verification and recovery rules, though the scripts were not fully visible and the reference files are very long.
needs: Optional accounts or API keys for the other AI coding tools it can route work to (Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, Antigravity)
why: It directly serves building a product, but it runs an npm package through npx at runtime and copies a user's Antigravity OAuth token into a scratch folder, so it should not be installed as written.
risks: Runs the npm package acpx through npx at runtime, which downloads and executes remote code.
Copies the user's Antigravity OAuth token file into a private scratch directory, which reads a secret.

summary: This skill is a reference playbook for security assessment of machine learning systems. It walks an agent through model supply chain risks such as pickle-based code execution in model files, adversarial example attacks, training data poisoning, model extraction, privacy attacks like membership inference, and risks in autonomous agents. It is written for security reviewers who test ML systems and need a checklist of attack categories and tools.
tasks: audit a model file for pickle code execution risk
assess an image classifier against adversarial examples
review an ML pipeline for training data poisoning
check an autonomous agent's tool permissions for abuse
qualityWhy: The skill is a broad, well-organized overview with tables and decision tree, but it gives mostly conceptual sketches and pseudocode rather than runnable steps, checks, or concrete procedures.
why: It is a security assessment reference rather than a tool for building or running a product, so its use on a node is occasional, and it is written for attacking and auditing third-party ML systems, which a node builder would need to apply to their own stack. Its material is generic and it points to other skills for depth, so an agent would read it for ideas rather than install it as written.

summary: This skill gives an agent an offensive playbook for attacking local network protocols: ARP spoofing, LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS poisoning, WPAD abuse, DHCPv6 takeover, VLAN hopping, STP manipulation, DNS spoofing, IPv6 router spoofing and IDS evasion. It is aimed at penetration testers who want to capture credentials, reroute traffic or move laterally in a Windows domain. It contains concrete commands and a decision tree for choosing an attack. It does not address building, running or publishing software or content.
tasks: capture network credentials on a local segment
test a corporate network for poisoning weaknesses
relay NTLM authentication to a domain controller
evade an intrusion detection system during a scan
qualityWhy: The commands are concrete and the decision tree is useful, but several examples use placeholders, verification steps are missing, and some sections (such as Kaminsky) are only described in a sentence.
why: The skill serves offensive network testing, not building, running or selling sites, apps, agents or content on a local-first node, so its value is none. Following it would mean intercepting and attacking traffic on networks, which is only lawful with explicit authorization and could harm third parties if the person lacks that permission.
risks: Following the playbook could intercept credentials and redirect traffic on networks the person does not own or have written permission to test.

summary: This skill makes an agent check a code change's user interface in a real browser. It works out which screens the diff affects, writes a scoped test scenario, drives the app through a configured browser provider, and saves screenshots with a pass/fail report. With a tracker and PR number it can also post the evidence as a PR comment, and in local mode it leaves the artifacts folder as the result. It is aimed at developers and QA reviewers who ship web UI changes.
tasks: QA a pull request's UI change in a real browser
capture screenshots and a pass/fail report for a web change
post visual QA evidence on a pull request
check the changed screens of the current worktree before merge
qualityWhy: It gives a clear step-by-step workflow with explicit safety rules, report schemas and verdict logic, but several referenced files and companion skills are not included, so parts can only be judged from SKILL.md.
needs: a tracker such as a Git hosting service, for PR mode
the om-prepare-test-env, om-auto-review-pr and related companion skills
why: It is useful for checking UI changes in web apps, but it depends on an Open Mercato pipeline (its own companion skills, .ai descriptors and labels) that a Fractera node does not have, so it would need adapting before use. The workflow is local-first and does not require a cloud service of its own.

summary: This skill makes an agent run an open-ended interview that collects loose writing material, such as sharp sentences, vignettes, quotes, and half-formed thoughts, without imposing any outline or structure yet. The agent appends each captured piece to one markdown file the person chooses, re-reading the file before each write so their edits survive. It is aimed at writers and content makers who want to gather raw material before shaping an article.
tasks: collect raw ideas for an article
brainstorm a blog post without an outline
capture quotes and observations into a draft file
find a leading word for a recurring idea
qualityWhy: The file format, write rules and fragment types are concrete, but it gives no example session, no end condition, and its description mixes Chinese and English, leaving the steps thin.
why: It is stack-free and directly serves writing articles and social or blog content, so an agent can use it as written by appending to a file the person picks. The skill is mostly prose guidance, so the output quality depends on the agent's interview skill.

summary: This playbook teaches an agent how to pull sensitive page content, such as CSRF tokens, pre-filled form values and hidden fields, out of a page when HTML injection works but JavaScript is blocked. It explains how unclosed tags with URL attributes make the browser send that content to an outside server, and which vectors suit each Content Security Policy setup. It is written for security testers probing web applications, not for building or making content.
tasks: test a site for HTML injection when CSP blocks scripts
check whether a page leaks CSRF tokens through injected markup
assess which exfiltration vector a strict CSP still allows
qualityWhy: It gives concrete payloads, a decision tree, browser differences and limitations, though some browser claims such as the Chrome version and the window.name behaviour are stated without checks.
why: It is an offensive attack playbook for taking data from other people's pages, which does not serve building, running, selling or making content on a node, so it is skipped rather than installed. Its use against third-party sites would expose their users' data, which is the main concern, but the skill itself contains no scripts or commands that would harm the person's own computer.

summary: This skill lets an agent connect to a Superwall paywall editor that is open in a browser and call its editing tools, such as changing text, styles and layout. It is meant for developers of mobile apps who need paywall screens and do not want to build them in code. The skill itself is marked legacy: it tells agents to use the newer code-based framework for new screens and to migrate existing editor paywalls with a CLI command. Its main job is to attach, discover tools, edit, and release a session through a shell script.
tasks: edit an existing paywall in the visual editor
review a paywall before migrating it
change text and styles in a Superwall paywall
qualityWhy: The instructions give concrete commands, a discovery-first workflow, orchestration rules and error handling, though much of the file redirects to other skills and references.
needs: Superwall editor pairing code or browser session
why: Superwall is a cloud service for app paywalls, and the skill drives its hosted browser editor through a remote relay, so it falls outside the local-first uses a node serves. The skill is also legacy and tells agents to use another skill for new screens.
risks: The script searches several .env files, including one in the home directory, for SUPERWALL_API_KEY and sends that key as a bearer token to a remote service.

summary: This skill is a reference playbook of DeFi attack patterns: flash loan exploits, price oracle manipulation (spot versus TWAP), MEV techniques such as sandwich and JIT liquidity, precision loss in vault share math, governance attacks, bridge weaknesses, and token standard edge cases. It helps a security reviewer or auditor, or an agent working on a DeFi codebase, reason about how a protocol could be attacked and what defenses to check for. It is analysis material only and contains no executable code or install steps.
tasks: audit a lending protocol for oracle manipulation risk
review a vault contract for first depositor inflation attack
check a governance contract for flash loan voting attacks
assess a bridge design for signature and replay weaknesses
qualityWhy: It is a well-organized, concrete playbook with flow diagrams, code snippets and a decision tree, though it lacks step-by-step verification procedures and is mostly reference text.
why: A node builds sites, apps and agents, so DeFi security analysis is useful only if the person is building a DeFi product; it is reference material rather than something that builds or runs a product. It targets Solidity and on-chain stacks, which the node does not provide, so an agent should read it for ideas rather than install it as written.

summary: This skill lets an agent apply build-speed changes that a developer has already approved for an Xcode project, such as build settings, script phase guards, source-level compile fixes, and Swift package restructuring. It makes one change at a time, checks that the project still builds, and then reruns a benchmark to measure clean and incremental build times. Its audience is iOS and macOS developers who want faster Xcode builds.
tasks: speed up a slow Xcode build
apply approved build settings changes to an iOS project
re-benchmark clean and incremental builds after a fix
restructure Swift packages to reduce rebuild scope
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete steps, a benchmark command, reference files with before/after patterns, and clear rules for judging regressions, though the benchmark script was cut off in what I could read.
why: The node builds websites, web apps, AI agents and content, and this skill only serves native Xcode and iOS projects, so it does not fit the node's purpose. It is also tied to Xcode and macOS tooling that a Fractera node does not provide.

summary: This skill tells an agent to generate a complete NestJS feature module for an entity: a Drizzle table, a service with create, read, update and soft-delete queries, a controller, Zod-validated DTOs and Jest tests. It is written for backend developers who want a server-side CRUD API quickly. The generator is a Python script that fills in TypeScript templates. Its output targets a monorepo layout and PostgreSQL or Cloudflare D1, not a local SQLite file.
tasks: generate a user CRUD module in NestJS
create a product API with Drizzle and Zod validation
add a new entity with REST endpoints and unit tests
qualityWhy: The steps and templates are concrete, but the templates have real bugs: the DTO file declares a type and a class with the same name, the count is taken from the row array length, the D1 import path looks wrong, and several placeholders are left unfilled.
needs: a PostgreSQL or Cloudflare D1 database account
why: The generated code is built on PostgreSQL (pg-core) and Cloudflare D1, which are cloud databases, so it conflicts with the node's local SQLite element and the rule that data stays on the person's computer. It also targets NestJS, which the node does not use. The rest of the generator script (about 12 KB, truncated at 8 KB in what I saw) was not fully reviewed.

summary: This skill helps a maintainer of a git repository write the release notes for a new version. It gathers the pull requests merged since the last release, sorts each one into a section with an emoji, and works out who should be credited, including when someone else's work was carried forward or merged into a larger branch. It then drafts a CHANGELOG.md entry and hands the edit to a companion skill that opens a docs-only pull request. The draft leaves the highlights paragraph for a human to write.
tasks: draft a changelog entry for the next release
list merged pull requests since the last version
credit the right contributors in release notes
open a docs pull request with the changelog update
tools: GitHub CLI (via the repo's tracker descriptor)
qualityWhy: The workflow, category table, credit rules, verification pass, and report formats are concrete and checkable, but it depends on a companion skill and repo config files that are not included.
needs: GitHub account with read and write access to the repository
why: It is useful for shipping a versioned app or product, but only if the project works through pull requests and a tracker, which is not central to building sites or making content on a node. It is written for an Open Mercato repo pipeline and needs its companion skill and config, so it must be adapted to the node before use. It also applies a skip-qa label to its own pull request, which is a review-process choice the maintainer should know about.

summary: This skill guides an agent to draw a single, very simple cute character for use as a visual identity, such as an animal, robot, or object with a friendly face. It fixes a small palette of two character colours and one background colour, places the character in the lower-left corner, and keeps the shape bold enough to read at 32 × 32 pixels. Before generating, the agent proposes three directions and six candidates for the person to approve. It then produces the images with a top-tier image model and reports each result with its label, path and prompt. The intended users are people building a product, brand or social presence who need a mascot image.
tasks: design a cute mascot character for my app
make six simple character logo candidates
create a friendly animal avatar for a brand
generate a square character image for a landing page
qualityWhy: The skill is concrete, with a full prompt skeleton, a complexity budget, a fixed workflow and labelling rules, though it has some overlapping rules and no detail on how the image APIs are called.
needs: an image generation API key for GPT Image 2, Seedance 5.0 Pro, Nano Banana Pro or Nano Banana 2
why: It directly serves making visual content for a product, but it needs an outside image model the person must choose and pay for, and the generated files come back to local storage. The skill tells the agent to ask for approval before generating and to avoid fallback to SVG, so the person keeps control of the spend.

summary: The skill guides an agent through analysing RAM dumps with Volatility 2 and 3: acquiring memory from Linux, Windows and virtual machines, identifying the operating system, and running plugins to find hidden processes, injected code, network connections, credentials, extracted files and registry or command-history evidence. It is written for malware analysts, incident responders and CTF players. A cheatsheet file maps Vol2 commands to their Vol3 equivalents.
tasks: analyze a memory dump for malware
find hidden processes in a RAM image
extract credentials from a memory capture
detect code injection in a memory dump
build an incident response timeline from memory
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete commands for each step, a decision tree and red-flag indicators, though it lacks expected output examples and some plugin names are stated without verification.
why: Memory forensics is a security-investigation skill and does not help build, run, sell or create content for a Fractera product, so its value is none. Its instructions also involve dumping memory and extracting hashes and plaintext credentials from full machine images, which is a risk on a local node.
risks: Teaches extracting SAM hashes, LSA secrets and plaintext credentials from memory dumps, which could expose the person's own or others' passwords if followed on the wrong machine.

summary: This skill lets an agent measure how stock prices move together. It can find peers that track a given ticker, compare two tickers with correlation, beta and spread, group several tickers into a correlation matrix, and track how correlation shifts over time or in market downturns. It draws its price history from Yahoo Finance through yfinance. It is aimed at investors and financial researchers, not at people building products or content.
tasks: find stocks that move with a given ticker
compare correlation and beta between two stocks
build a correlation matrix for a group of stocks
track rolling correlation between two tickers
qualityWhy: The instructions are concrete, with runnable functions, routing rules, defaults and presentation templates, though a few details are left to the reader, such as the scipy fallback and the screener step.
needs: Yahoo Finance public price data (no key required)
why: Stock correlation research does not serve building sites, apps, agents or content for a product, so the node has no use for it. It depends on yfinance, an unofficial client that is not affiliated with Yahoo, which makes its data source fragile.

summary: This skill teaches an agent how PHP's loose comparison (`==`) can be abused when code compares passwords, tokens or HMAC values without strict typing. It covers magic hashes that start with `0e`, array and null tricks, and CTF-style input tricks, and it tells the agent to verify behavior against the target PHP version. It is aimed at security reviewers and testers working on authorized PHP targets.
tasks: audit PHP login code for loose comparison bugs
check whether an HMAC or token check can be bypassed
explain why md5 magic hashes compare equal in PHP
review legacy PHP code for missing hash_equals
qualityWhy: The skill is concrete and has examples and a routing table, but it contains some inaccurate claims, such as strcmp with arrays returning NULL in PHP 8, and its decision tree is hard to follow.
why: It is an offensive security reference for legacy PHP and does not help build, run, sell or create content for a Next.js, TypeScript or Fractera product. The node's stack has no PHP auth paths to test, so there is no use case here.

summary: This playbook guides an agent through testing whether user-controlled XSLT stylesheets or transform endpoints can be abused. It covers identifying the XSLT processor, probing for XXE and file reads via document(), checking EXSLT file-write behaviour, and assessing PHP, Java and .NET extension exposure. It is aimed at security reviewers and developers auditing their own XML-to-HTML pipelines.

check whether an XML converter leaks local files
identify which XSLT processor a server runs
test a report generator for SSRF through document()
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete probe stylesheets, a fingerprinting method, a decision tree and related-skill routing, though several extension sections are conceptual and lack verification steps.
why: It is a security-testing reference rather than a building, hosting or content tool, so it is only occasionally useful to a node owner auditing their own XSLT endpoints. It is stack-neutral and needs no outside service, but its payloads (command execution, webshell writes) must only be used on systems the person is authorised to test, which the skill itself states.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to use Bun as a single toolkit for JavaScript and TypeScript work: running files without a compile step, installing and managing packages, writing and running tests, and bundling code. It includes a command cheat sheet, config examples for bunfig.toml, guidance on choosing between hoisted and isolated installs and between watch and hot reload, a list of common pitfalls, and a pre-submit checklist. It is aimed at developers who build and test apps and need a faster replacement for Node and npm tooling.
tasks: set up a new TypeScript project with bun
run and test a TypeScript script
bundle an app for the browser
speed up dependency installs in a monorepo
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete commands, config examples, gotchas and a checklist an agent can follow, though some performance claims and version notes are unsourced and it is generic rather than tied to any stack.
why: It is useful developer tooling for scripts, tests and builds, but it does not directly serve content or product features on a Fractera node. Its Node-replacement framing may clash with the node's Next.js 16 stack, where Next.js itself may still need Node, so an agent should check that Bun-based commands work with the project before relying on them.

summary: This skill gives an agent a security-testing playbook for email header injection. It covers how user input placed into SMTP headers (subject, from name, recipient) can add Bcc, Cc, Reply-To or body content, along with the encoding variants to try. It also explains SPF, DKIM and DMARC weaknesses and mail-client rendering risks, and it is written for someone probing contact forms, password-reset mails and email APIs.
tasks: test a contact form for email header injection
check a domain's SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for weaknesses
review how an email API builds SMTP headers from user input
qualityWhy: It is concrete, with payload tables, vulnerable code patterns, a decision tree and a testing sequence, but it has no defensive fixes and some claims are stated without caveats.
why: It is stack-free and can help test a node's own contact forms and mail code, but it is an offensive playbook for phishing, spoofing and mail-client exfiltration, so it only fits systems the person owns and is authorised to test. Its content is not a risk to the person's own computer, so it is not flagged as one.

summary: This skill guides an agent through exporting Blender scenes to web-ready glTF/GLB files using Blender's Python API. It covers batch conversion of .blend files, reducing polygon counts and texture sizes, generating simplified LOD copies, and loading the results in Three.js, React Three Fiber or Babylon.js. reduce polygon count of a 3D model for the web
generate LOD levels for a 3D asset

why: It runs entirely on local Blender with local files and calls no outside service, so it fits a local-first node; its use is niche, and it needs Blender installed on the computer. The listed assets/export_template.blend and shader_library are not among the files, and the bake example is incomplete.

summary: This skill guides an agent through moving .NET test projects from xUnit.net v2 to xunit.v3, covering package renames, central package management, the choice between VSTest and Microsoft Testing Platform runners, and source fixes such as async void tests, attribute signature changes and custom Fact or BeforeAfterTest subclasses. fix xunit v3 breaking changes in test code
keep VSTest or MTP runner when upgrading xunit
convert SkippableFact to Assert.SkipWhen

why: It is a .NET test-maintenance skill, useful occasionally for test projects but not for building the node's own product features. It is written for a generic .NET solution with NuGet feeds and dotnet tooling, so an agent on a node would apply it to a separate .NET test project rather than the Next.js stack, which makes 'ideas' the honest label.

summary: This skill gives an agent a playbook for moving from one compromised Linux host to others on the same network. It covers hijacking SSH agent sockets, finding private keys and stored passwords, adding its own keys to authorized_keys, tunnelling traffic through pivot hosts, abusing D-Bus and systemd, and reusing active sudo sessions. It is written for offensive security work against systems the agent is attacking.
tasks: pivot from a compromised Linux host to other internal hosts
harvest SSH keys and stored credentials on a Linux machine
set up port forwarding through a compromised host
escalate privileges by reusing sudo sessions or abusing systemd
qualityWhy: The commands are concrete and it has a decision tree, but it refers to a missing section (§4.3) and depends on an external tool without setup steps.
why: It is an attack playbook for moving between machines without authorization, which has no use for building, running or selling a node's sites, apps or content. It also carries real risks, so it should not be installed.
risks: Harvests private keys, shadow hashes and stored passwords from the host and other users' home directories.
Injects attacker SSH keys into authorized_keys on other hosts, creating unauthorized access.
Installs a systemd unit containing a reverse shell to a remote address, which is a persistent backdoor.
Hijacks other users' SSH agents and sudo sessions to act as them without their knowledge.

summary: This skill tells an agent how to ingest documents, raw notes, folders, web links, images and chat exports into an Obsidian wiki as distilled, cross-linked pages. It covers manifest-based change detection, batch planning for large folders, git repo sources, academic paper handling with figures, optional QMD search refresh, and provenance markers. It is aimed at people maintaining a personal or team knowledge base.

process my _raw drafts into proper pages
add this web page to the knowledge base
distill a chat export into wiki topics
ingest a research paper with its figures

why: It is a knowledge-base skill, not a site, app, or content-making tool for a product, so value is only occasional use. It depends on the obsidian-wiki CLI, the llm-wiki skill and an Obsidian vault layout, which a Fractera node does not provide, so it must be adapted to the node's own SQLite and storage elements rather than installed as written.

summary: This skill tells an agent to write and review code with a clean-architecture and domain-driven mindset. It asks the agent to reuse existing libraries before writing custom helpers, keep business logic apart from UI and database code, use domain-specific names instead of generic ones like utils, and keep functions and files short. It is aimed at developers who want a code review or design checklist on any software task.
tasks: review code structure before merging
design the module layout for a new feature
refactor a long function into smaller parts
decide whether to build a helper or use a library
check code for naming and separation problems

why: It is a stack-free set of coding habits that helps with building any product, so an agent can use it as written. Its description is very broad, so it may trigger on unrelated tasks, and its limits are guidance rather than checks.

summary: The skill is a reference playbook for an agent that finds itself inside a Docker container, LXC or Kubernetes pod and wants to reach the host. It walks through detecting the container, escaping through privileged mode, dangerous capabilities, the Docker socket, cgroup v1 release_agent, namespace sharing, known runtime CVEs and risky pod specs. It is written for security testers doing authorized penetration work, not for building products.
tasks: check whether a shell is running inside a container
escape a privileged Docker container to the host
assess Kubernetes pod escape paths
enumerate container capabilities and mounts
qualityWhy: It gives many concrete commands and a decision tree, but several sections are thin or placeholders, such as the shellcode injection stub and the runc CVE section with no working steps.
why: The skill is offensive escape tooling aimed at breaking out of a host, which does not serve building, running or selling a product on a local-first node, so the value is none and the use is skip. It also carries a risk because following it would run host-escape and privilege-escalation techniques on the person's machine.
risks: Gives step-by-step host escape and privilege escalation techniques (privileged mount, nsenter, release_agent, Docker socket abuse) that could compromise a machine if followed outside an authorized test.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing an article beat by beat from a raw material file, in a choose-your-own-adventure style. The agent first agrees prerequisites with the user, offers candidate starting beats, appends only the chosen beat, re-reads the file, and offers next beats that each only rely on concepts already introduced. It is aimed at writers turning a pile of notes into a structured piece.

write an article one beat at a time with user choices
plan an article's reading path and introduce concepts in order
qualityWhy: The process is clear and well structured, but it is abstract and has no concrete examples of beat output, file format, or checks an agent can follow.
why: It is a stack-free writing method that helps with making written content, though it is only occasionally useful for building a node's pages or blog; nothing in it calls outside services or needs keys.

summary: This skill guides an agent through checking whether a code change matches its OpenSpec planning artifacts (specs, tasks, design) before the change is archived. The agent reads task checkboxes, searches the codebase for implementation of each requirement and scenario, and reports issues ranked as critical, warning, or suggestion. It is written for developers who use the OpenSpec workflow to plan and track changes.
tasks: verify my change is complete before archiving
check implementation against the spec requirements
review whether tasks and scenarios are covered by code
run an openspec verify on this change
qualityWhy: The instructions are very detailed, with explicit steps, edge cases, report formats and decision rules for skipped checks, leaving little room for the agent to guess.
why: It is a stack-free process skill for checking planning artifacts against code, so it fits a node's development workflow now and then, but it does not build or sell anything itself and depends on the OpenSpec CLI being present. It has no outside service or secret requirements.

summary: This skill gives an agent a step-by-step method for identifying and breaking old-style ciphers in puzzle challenges. It starts by checking the character set and index of coincidence, then covers frequency analysis, Caesar shifts, Vigenere key recovery, affine, Hill, transposition, Bacon, Polybius and Playfair ciphers, and XOR. It includes Python snippets and a list of online and command-line solvers. The intended users are security students and capture-the-flag players.
tasks: decode a Vigenere-encrypted puzzle message
identify the cipher used in an unknown ciphertext
break a Caesar or substitution cipher with frequency analysis
recover an XOR key from captured bytes
qualityWhy: The skill has a clear identification workflow and runnable snippets, but it contains real errors, such as a Bacon table with duplicate keys, a Kasiski routine that does not check its output, and a Hill-cipher matrix setup that is likely wrong.
why: It is built for capture-the-flag puzzles and security study, which does not serve building, running, selling or making content for a node product. Its code also has bugs that would need fixing before use.

summary: This skill makes an agent read an existing test suite, work out what each test is for, and give it one or more standard trait labels such as positive, negative, boundary, or critical-path. It then produces a distribution report showing how the suite splits across these traits. For .NET, pytest, JUnit and similar frameworks it can also add the tag attributes to source files and check that the project still compiles. For frameworks without an agreed tag syntax, it only reports the mapping and leaves the source unchanged.

tag all tests with positive and negative categories
report how test coverage is distributed by test type
check that the project still builds after adding test tags
qualityWhy: The instructions give a concrete taxonomy, per-framework attribute syntax, explicit audit versus edit modes, and build and discovery checks, though the text is long and repeats itself in places.
why: It helps keep a test suite organised, which is useful now and then, but a Fractera node's own stack is Next.js and TypeScript, and the skill's auto-edit support covers other ecosystems such as .NET, pytest and JUnit. For Jest or Vitest, which a node would likely use, it is report-only. Nothing in it needs an outside service or key.

summary: This skill lets an agent turn the native backtrace of an Android tombstone from a .NET MAUI, Xamarin or Mono app into named functions with source files and line numbers. llvm-symbolizer from the Android NDK or LLVM 14+

summary: This skill gives an agent a catalogue of techniques for getting past Linux access controls during a post-exploitation phase. Clears audit and login logs and disables auditd, hiding the agent's actions from the person.
Teaches the agent to evade and switch off security controls on the machine.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to route traffic from a compromised machine into an internal network the attacker cannot reach directly. Its audience is offensive security work on hosts someone has already broken into.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building a Coralogix monitoring dashboard for one service. summary: This skill guides an agent through building Python functions for AWS Lambda, comparing the Chalice framework with plain handler code. summary: The skill guides an agent through moving a .NET test solution from VSTest to Microsoft.Testing.Platform. It covers enabling the MTP runner for MSTest, NUnit, xUnit v2 and v3, choosing the dotnet test integration mode by SDK version, translating VSTest arguments such as filters, logger, coverage and blame, and updating CI pipelines. It is written for .NET developers and build engineers maintaining test projects.
