needs: Tigris storage access key and secret
why: Every building block is a cloud bucket on Tigris, a cloud file store, which a local-first node cannot host, so the skill is skipped even though the instructions are well written. The skill also needs a cloud account and keys for its core functions to run.

summary: Gives an agent a local trading-journal layer: it turns screener outputs and manually entered broker fills into thesis records, tracks each idea from idea through entry, open position, partial trims and close, flags theses due for review, and writes postmortems with P&L and MAE/MFE. It is aimed at traders and investors who keep a record of their own positions. The files show a mature CLI with fail-closed validation, schema checks, atomic writes and tests covering equity and futures positions.
tasks: register a stock idea from a screener output
record an already-open broker position
check which theses are due for review
write a postmortem for a closed trade
show win rate and average P&L across closed theses

why: The skill is a trading journal for investment positions, which is not what a node is for: building, running or selling sites, apps, agents or content. It is also a local-first state layer, so it does not need a cloud service to work, but its purpose is outside the node's uses.

summary: The skill guides an agent through setting up, reading and improving mobile app analytics. It covers which free and paid tools to use, the key acquisition, engagement, retention and revenue metrics with their formulas and benchmarks, a core event naming plan, and dashboard layouts. It is written for app founders and marketers who want data-driven decisions about their app's performance.
tasks: set up an analytics tracking plan for my app
explain what my App Store Connect numbers mean
design a funnel dashboard for downloads and purchases
define the core in-app events to track
qualityWhy: It is organised and gives useful formulas, benchmarks and an event list, but it has no concrete implementation steps, code, or checks an agent can follow, so it reads more like a reference sheet.
why: It is a stack-free measurement guide that helps plan metrics and events, which is occasionally useful for a node building apps, but it does not build or run anything on the node itself. Several of the tools it names are paid or cloud services, and the agent would only use them if the person chooses to; no risk was found in the file.

summary: This skill lets an agent search academic literature through the Semantic Scholar API, covering keyword and boolean searches, exact title lookups, author profiles, citation tracing, and paper recommendations. It runs everything through one Python helper with built-in rate limiting and retries, then formats the results as tables, details, and BibTeX or Markdown exports. The intended users are researchers and writers doing literature discovery or citation checks.
tasks: find recent papers on a research topic
list who cited a specific paper and how
find papers similar to a known work
look up a researcher's publications
export a reference list as BibTeX
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives a clear four-phase workflow, decision tables, checkpoints, worked examples and a troubleshooting table, though the helper module was truncated so some behaviour could not be verified.
why: It is useful for research lookups but not for building or running a product, and the Semantic Scholar service is only a search source rather than a place to keep data. It is skipped because the prelude falls back to importing s2.py from the current working directory, so an untrusted folder's s2.py would run as code.
risks: The prelude searches the current directory for s2.py and imports it, so a planted s2.py in an untrusted folder would execute.

summary: This skill guides an agent through generating and critiquing improvement ideas grounded in a codebase or topic before any one idea is picked for development. It runs parallel grounding agents, decomposes the topic into axes, dispatches divergent ideation frames, filters the candidates with explicit rejection reasons, and writes a ranked artifact. It is aimed at developers and teams deciding which directions are worth exploring next.
tasks: brainstorm improvement ideas for my codebase
generate and rank feature ideas before planning
find surprising directions for a product area
critique and shortlist candidate ideas

why: It is useful for product ideation but is built around the Compound Engineering plugin's own artifact layout, config files and subagent conventions, so it would need adapting to the node's stack and paths rather than being installed as written. Its dispatch of generic subagents and temp-directory scratch space are not described in enough detail here to confirm they fit the node.

summary: This skill lets an agent run Graham-style and Buffett-style value investing checks on listed stocks. It can score a single company for net-asset and cheapness criteria, or check business moat and financial health, and it can screen a whole index or market for candidates. It is aimed at individual investors and analysts who want ranked stock lists with a stated margin of safety. Market data comes from the Longbridge CLI, with an MCP fallback and web search only for gaps.
tasks: screen net-net stocks with Graham NCAV rules
score a company's economic moat like Buffett would
find quality compounders using ROE and free cash flow filters
check the margin of safety before buying a stock

risks: Its error-handling path has the agent run a shell installer that downloads and executes the Longbridge CLI, and that script is not reviewed here.

summary: This skill lets an agent read Reddit without logging in, by fetching public listings in JSON form. It can list hot, new, top or rising posts from a subreddit, search posts across Reddit or within one community, open a single thread with its top comments, and show subreddit or user profile details. It suits someone researching discussions, trends or audience opinions for a product or piece of content.
tasks: find the most discussed posts in a subreddit this week
search Reddit for opinions on a product or topic
read the top comments on a Reddit thread

why: It is useful for research into Reddit discussions rather than for building or running a product, so the value is some. It calls Reddit's public API, so it is install-with-service; the claimed 100 requests per minute limit and unauthenticated access are unverified and Reddit's access rules change over time.

summary: This skill guides an agent through checking an Android project's Gradle files and R8 keep rules, then measuring which rules keep the most classes, fields and methods from being shrunk or obfuscated. It produces a scored report that flags redundant, package-wide and subsumed rules, with remediation advice. why: The skill serves Android app builds, which are outside what a Fractera node is for (sites, web apps, AI agents and content), so its value here is none. It is an Android-only tool that would need the node's own stack replaced, and it is not a risk.

summary: This skill guides an agent through checking whether Swift Package Manager dependencies, build plugins, and module layout slow down Xcode builds for native iOS or macOS apps. It has the agent confirm which local packages are really linked to targets, flag branch-pinned dependencies, and look for circular or oversized modules. summary: This skill guides an agent through timing Xcode builds of an iOS or macOS app: clean builds, zero-change builds, and optional edit-and-rebuild loops, with repeatable settings. summary: This skill guides an agent through planning a launch for a new app or major update, from an eight-week countdown to a month after release. summary: This skill guides an agent through planning a complex Blazor page before coding it. summary: This skill guides an agent through US tax planning for dividend income. It sorts each holding's payouts into likely qualified, likely ordinary, or needs-verification, checks the holding period against the required minimum days, and suggests whether to hold each asset in a taxable or tax-advantaged account. A bundled Python script turns a holdings file into a Markdown and CSV planning sheet. It is aimed at individual income investors and their advisers.

generate an annual dividend tax planning memo
qualityWhy: The workflow, classification thresholds, input contract and tests are concrete and checkable, though it leans on references for much of the tax detail.
why: It serves a personal investor's tax planning, not building, running, selling or making content for a product, so it does not fit what a node is for. The script runs locally with no outside service, but that does not change the value verdict.

summary: This skill makes an agent run an unattended improvement loop on a codebase. The agent first asks the person for a goal, a command that produces a number, the files it may touch, and any limits. It then makes one small change per experiment, commits it, measures it, and keeps or reverts the change, logging each run to a TSV file. It suits developers who want a measurable metric pushed up or down without watching every step.
tasks: optimize a slow function until the benchmark improves
run automatic experiments to raise test coverage
reduce bundle size by trying changes and measuring each one
tune build time with an automated experiment log
qualityWhy: The skill gives clear phases, a TSV format, a loop with decision rules and reporting steps, but it leaves gaps such as how to handle a dirty working tree and which files to stage.
why: The method is stack-free and useful now and then for performance tuning, but the loop uses 'git add' without naming files and then 'git reset --hard HEAD~1', which can commit and then discard unrelated uncommitted work, so it should not be installed as written.
risks: Runs 'git add' and 'git reset --hard HEAD~1' with no file list, so unrelated uncommitted changes can be committed and then discarded.

summary: This skill tells an agent to create a new repository on GitHub with the gh command-line tool, then clone it to the local machine. It defaults to a public repository with a README and switches to private only when asked. It is aimed at a developer who wants a fresh code repository started quickly from the terminal.
tasks: create a new GitHub repository
clone a new repo to my computer
start a fresh public or private repo with a README
qualityWhy: The steps and commands are concrete, but the skill is very short and has no checks for login state, name conflicts, or clone errors, and it hardcodes one account name.
needs: gh CLI authenticated to that account
why: Creating and cloning a GitHub repository is cloud repository administration, which the node's local-first design treats as not useful, so it is skipped. It also hardcodes the account zc277584121, so it would not fit another user.
risks: Creates a public GitHub repository by default without asking the person to confirm visibility.

summary: This skill makes an agent close out a project's knowledge after development: it checks that code, running behaviour, docs, agent rule files, permitted memory and leftover workspace files all describe the same current state. It gives a light five-step path for solo projects and a fuller path with a staged report for projects that have release or multi-project workflows. It is written for developers and project owners who want the next session or teammate to start from one accurate answer. It also restricts writes to the current project, keeps memory read-only unless explicitly authorised, and requires confirmation before anything is deleted.

list leftover plan and backup files for deletion review

why: It is a stack-free documentation and governance habit that a node project can use now and then to keep its CLAUDE.md and docs accurate, but it does not directly help build, run, sell or create content. It needs no outside service, and its own script only lists metadata and never reads file contents.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building full-stack applications, covering project layering, config and environment handling, error handling, database access, frontend API clients, auth flows, file uploads, real-time features and production hardening. summary: Guides an agent through designing the lifecycle of Rust resources: when they are created, used and cleaned up, and who owns that cleanup. It is marked 'ideas' because it is built around Rust and the node's own stack is TypeScript/Next.js, so it should be read for its ideas rather than installed as written.

summary: This skill guides an agent through domain modeling in Rust. summary: This skill guides an agent to build a written company profile from public sources such as executive interviews, earnings calls, product blogs and engineering posts. why: It is a stack-free engineering method that fits building and maintaining products on a node, and it works with any language since it is about process rather than a framework. Its examples lean on jest and pytest, which a node can use directly; the reference files were not all reviewed, so their depth is assumed from the SKILL.md.

summary: This guide teaches an agent how to write, review and repair JavaScript interop inside Blazor .NET components. It covers collocated module files, when interop is safe to run during the component lifecycle, batching calls in both directions, typed wrapper classes, and disposing of JS references. It is aimed at developers who build Blazor apps and need their browser code connected to C#.
tasks: add JavaScript interop to a Blazor component
review Blazor JS interop for lifecycle bugs
call .NET methods from JavaScript callbacks
fix memory leaks in Blazor JS module disposal
qualityWhy: The guide is concrete and complete, with working code samples, a lifecycle rule set, a disposal pattern, and a checklist and mistakes table an agent can apply directly.
why: It is written for Blazor and .NET, which are not the Next.js, React and TypeScript stack that Fractera nodes use, so it does not serve building, running or selling on a node. Nothing in it is risky; it is simply for a different framework.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of plain-language analogies and mental models for Rust's core ideas: ownership, moving values, borrowing, lifetimes and smart pointers. It also lists common wrong beliefs and how to correct them, and maps compiler error codes to better ways of thinking. It is aimed at people learning Rust or moving to it from other languages. The main file includes simple memory diagrams.
tasks: explain Rust ownership with a simple analogy
help me understand why the borrow checker rejects my code
compare Rust's model with Java or Python memory handling
explain what E0502 or E0382 means in plain words
qualityWhy: The file is well organised, with tables, misconception fixes and diagrams, but it has little runnable code, no worked examples, and many links to sibling skills (m01–m15, unsafe-checker) that are not in this package.
why: Rust concepts serve no part of what a Fractera node is for, since the node's stack is TypeScript, Next.js and React, so this is a general language-learning guide with no product use. The patterns/thinking-in-rust.md file was listed but not provided, so I could not check it.

summary: This skill is a long philosophical guide to architecture: it asks the agent to start from the problem domain, map systems and external dependencies, surface constraints such as politics, budget and compliance, and split AI work into bounded, verifiable tasks. It also covers a 'loyalty' principle of sticking with chosen patterns and a spec-driven development outline with constitution, blueprint and task levels. It is aimed at people leading software design decisions, but it is almost entirely mindset and process with no concrete commands, code or stack-specific steps.
tasks: review an architecture decision before committing to it
map dependencies and failure modes for a multi-service system
split a large feature into bounded tasks for an AI agent
decide whether a new framework or AI tool is worth adopting
qualityWhy: It is useful as a thinking framework but mostly generic and abstract, with few steps, examples or checks an agent can concretely apply, and the SKILL.md alone is very long relative to its actionable content.
why: It is stack-free and can help planning and design discussions on a node, though it does not build or run anything itself and its tool-evaluation lists name outside products that the node would not use by default. The skill's own files were not inspected beyond SKILL.md, so the CHECKLIST, EXAMPLES and REFERENCE contents are unknown.

summary: This skill guides an agent through Apple's App Store editorial featuring process, covering what editors look for such as design quality, Apple technology adoption, rating, and stability. It gives a checklist for featuring readiness, a pitch structure and email template for the self-nomination form, and advice on timing pitches and planning In-App Events. It is written for app developers who want Apple to feature their iOS app.
tasks: get my app featured on the App Store
draft a pitch email to Apple editorial
plan In-App Events for the Today tab
score my app's featuring readiness
qualityWhy: The skill is clear and well organised with checklists and a template, but it is mostly generic marketing advice with no concrete steps tied to measurable thresholds or tooling beyond a single form link.
why: It is a stack-free marketing and strategy skill that helps a developer seek App Store featuring, which is useful now and then rather than for building the product itself. It names no outside service or key, and its claims about editorial criteria are unverified opinion.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to rewrite web pages so AI answer engines like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and AI Overviews can quote them. It gives rules for short self-contained answers, dated claims with sources, FAQ blocks with structured data, and a scoring pass for extraction readiness. It is aimed at people who publish sites, landing pages and blogs and want AI search visibility.
tasks: optimize a landing page for AI citations
write 15 FAQs with FAQPage schema
add evidence panels with sources and dates to a product page
score a blog post for AI extraction readiness
qualityWhy: SKILL.md gives a clear overview, checklist and test protocol, but the detailed templates live in prd.md and several claims (such as the 95% freshness figure and the 115% visibility gain) are unsourced.
why: It directly helps build and write content for sites and landing pages, and it needs no outside service or stack, so it can be used as written. The statistics it quotes should be treated as unverified, and I judged only SKILL.md, not the other four files in full.

summary: This skill guides an agent through a git commit-and-push cycle without opening a pull request. It can create a branch, review the diff for stray files, stage only the relevant files, commit with a sign-off line, and push to origin. It is aimed at developers who want their changes on the remote quickly.
tasks: commit my changes and push to origin
push this work to a new branch without opening a PR
review the diff and commit only the relevant files
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and ordered, but the skill is short, has no checks beyond status and diff, and gives no guidance on conflicts or failed pushes.
needs: git remote access to origin with the person's own credentials
why: It is a generic git workflow, useful now and then for a node's code, but it is not tied to building or running a product. It hardcodes another person's name and email as the commit author and forbids any mention of AI in commit messages, so an agent on someone else's node would commit under a stranger's identity and hide AI involvement from reviewers.
risks: Hardcodes a third person's name and email as the commit author, misattributing every commit made on the node.
Forbids mentioning AI or automated generation in commit messages, concealing that changes were made by an agent from the repository's reviewers.

summary: This skill guides an agent through moving an existing codebase off Exa, Tavily, Perplexity, or Firecrawl web-search and scraping calls onto Parallel's search, extract, chat, and task APIs. It covers request construction, response consumers, dependencies, environment variables, and tests, and it sorts capabilities that have no Parallel equivalent, such as crawling, browser sessions, or embeddings, into a block-or-keep decision. A bundled stdlib Python scanner inventories leftover provider usage in a repository. The guidance is written for developers and agents maintaining apps that fetch web data.
tasks: migrate our Tavily search calls to Parallel
replace Exa search in the Next.js app
audit the repo for leftover Perplexity usage
finish a half-done Firecrawl-to-Parallel migration
qualityWhy: It gives concrete steps, a per-call decision table, invariants, verification commands and a completion gate that an agent can follow exactly.
why: It is useful only for node apps that already call Exa, Tavily, Perplexity, or Firecrawl; it is a migration guide, not a general build aid. Parallel is an outside paid search service that returns results to local files, so it qualifies as install-with-service. The skill itself is framework-agnostic and needs no adaptation to the node's stack.

summary: The skill guides an agent through Apple CloudKit and iCloud sync work in iOS and macOS apps: container and database setup, record CRUD, queries, subscriptions, CKSyncEngine, SwiftData cloud sync, key-value storage, iCloud Drive files, error classification and conflict merging. It is aimed at Swift developers building native Apple apps that keep user data in sync across their devices. It is a reference for Apple-platform code, not for the Fractera web stack.
tasks: add iCloud sync to an iOS app
resolve CloudKit record conflicts
review SwiftData CloudKit model setup
handle CKError retry and quota cases
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md is concrete and complete, with workflow steps, code samples for each API, a CKError strategy table, a conflict-resolution example and a review checklist.
needs: Apple Developer account with iCloud and CloudKit enabled
why: The skill is built for Swift and Apple's cloud, and CloudKit is a cloud database and backend, which a local-first Fractera node does not use; it is not useful for the node's web stack.

summary: This skill makes an agent pull stock market data from Yahoo Finance through the yfinance Python library and assemble a pre-earnings briefing. The briefing covers the report date and timing, consensus EPS and revenue estimates, the recent beat/miss record, analyst ratings and price targets, and the points the market is likely to focus on. It is written for investors and analysts who want to know what the street expects before a company reports.
tasks: prepare a briefing before a company's earnings report
check consensus EPS and revenue estimates for a ticker
summarize analyst ratings and price targets
review a company's recent beat/miss history
qualityWhy: The steps, data-source table, output sections and caveats are concrete and easy to follow, though it has few explicit error-handling steps for missing or malformed Yahoo data.
needs: Yahoo Finance data via yfinance (no API key required)
why: Stock earnings previews are financial research, not building, running, selling or making content for a product, so the skill does not serve what a node is for. The data comes from a Yahoo Finance service rather than local files, which also does not fit a local-first node.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull a Binance AI analysis report for a chosen coin, such as BTC, ETH or SOL, and print its text. It can also fetch the latest flash news from TheBlockBeats, with optional page and size settings. It suits someone who wants crypto market commentary or headlines to read, or to base posts on.
tasks: get an AI market analysis report for BTC
summarise the latest blockchain news
check what is happening with ETH today
gather crypto headlines for a social post
qualityWhy: The instructions are a few shell commands with no output examples, error handling, or checks, and the news script has a bug that leaves an unset PAYLOAD in its curl call.
needs: Binance public web API (no key required)
why: Crypto news and market commentary are useful now and then for content or research, but they are not core to building or running a product. Both sources are outside services called without a key, and the Binance report is requested in Chinese by default. The news script sends an empty POST body from an unset variable, so it may behave oddly, and the endpoints are undocumented and could change.

summary: This skill lets an agent fetch the spoken-word transcript of a YouTube video from a URL or video ID. It returns plain text by default, or lines prefixed with timestamps on request. It is aimed at people who want to read, quote, or reuse what is said in a video. The bundled script prints the transcript to the terminal, and the agent is expected to save it to a file itself.
tasks: get the transcript of a YouTube video
turn a YouTube video's captions into readable paragraphs
list a talk's transcript with timestamps
summarize a YouTube interview from its transcript
qualityWhy: The steps and supported URL formats are clear and the script is short and readable, but the instructions contradict themselves on editing the transcript and promise a default output file the script never writes.
why: Transcripts help with research, content repurposing and writing, but they are not a core product-building feature. It needs internet access to YouTube and no key, and the library relies on YouTube's unofficial caption access, which may break or conflict with YouTube's terms.

summary: This skill guides an agent through early product discovery for a brand-new product idea. The agent reads any supplied research, optionally searches the market, and then generates five feature ideas each from product manager, designer and engineer viewpoints. It then ranks the best ideas by core value, speed to validate and differentiation, and lists assumptions to test for each. It is aimed at founders and product teams exploring a startup concept.
tasks: brainstorm features for a new startup idea
generate product ideas from PM, designer and engineer views
prioritize early product feature ideas
list assumptions to test for a new product concept
qualityWhy: The steps are clear and usable, but the skill is short and generic, with no templates, examples or checks beyond the basic ranking criteria.
why: It is a stack-free ideation habit that helps when planning what to build on a node, though it is not about building or running the stack itself; it only uses web search if the agent has it, and its output is a markdown document, not code.

summary: This skill guides an agent through choosing and integrating Rust crates: picking a standard library for needs like serialization, async, HTTP, database, CLI and logging, weighing maintenance and API stability before adding a dependency. It also covers language interop (bindgen, cbindgen, PyO3, napi-rs, wasm-bindgen), Cargo features and workspaces, and common compiler errors such as E0433 and E0603. It is aimed at Rust developers.
tasks: choose a Rust crate for a job
fix a missing crate or private item compile error
set up Cargo features or a workspace
wrap a C library or build a Python extension in Rust
qualityWhy: Useful and clearly organized as a decision guide, but thin: mostly tables and short lists with few concrete steps, examples or checks an agent can follow.
why: It helps only when the node's own elements are Rust-based, which they are not: the node's stack is Next.js and TypeScript, so the Rust crate advice (tokio, axum, sqlx, diesel) would have to be read for ideas and rebuilt in the node's own way. The auto-injected grep of Cargo.toml adds nothing for a TypeScript node.

summary: This skill guides an agent that is designing how an application reports and recovers from errors. It helps sort errors by who sees them (end users, developers, operations staff), by whether they can be retried, and by what context to attach for debugging. It offers a Rust error-enum sketch, a retry-with-backoff pattern, and a table of common mistakes. It is written for Rust codebases and is most useful to developers building services or libraries.
tasks: design an error type hierarchy for an API
decide which failures should be retried
add retry with exponential backoff to a flaky call
hide internal errors from end users
qualityWhy: The categorisation tables and checklists are clear, but the code examples are thin and the retry sample would not compile as written (missing Duration import, invalid `impl Future` in a closure return type).
why: The error-design thinking applies to any stack, but the skill is built around Rust crates (thiserror, anyhow, tokio-retry) that a Fractera node, which runs TypeScript and Next.js, does not use, so an agent should adapt the ideas rather than copy the code. Its cross-references to other skills (m06, m07, domain-*) may not be present in the catalogue.

summary: This playbook teaches an agent to exploit a Java character-narrowing flaw, where a 16-bit char is silently cut to an 8-bit byte, so attack strings pass a web application firewall and reach the backend in their original form. It covers SQL injection, deserialization, file upload, path traversal, CRLF and mail header injection, and lists payload tables and affected Java components. The intended users are security testers and attackers, not people building or running a product.
tasks: test a Java site's WAF for SQL injection bypass
check a Java file upload form for filename parsing flaws
probe a Java backend for header or CRLF injection
qualityWhy: The file gives concrete steps, payload tables and per-component recipes, but many CVE and version claims are unverified and it is written partly as directives to the agent.
why: It is an attack playbook for exploiting third-party Java services, not a tool for building, running, selling or making content for a node product. Following it could attack systems the person does not own and expose them to legal harm, so it should not be installed.
risks: Guides an agent to bypass WAFs and exploit third-party systems, including webshell upload and phishing, which could expose the person to legal harm.

summary: This skill guides an agent through writing AWS infrastructure as TypeScript code with the CDK framework. It covers organizing apps and stacks, choosing between low-level and high-level constructs, and building serverless or VPC-based setups with safe IAM and encryption defaults. It also describes a check loop of synth, tests, diff and deploy, aimed at developers who provision cloud infrastructure on AWS.
tasks: set up a CDK app for a serverless API
review a cdk diff before deploying
write assertion tests for a CDK stack
design a VPC network for AWS
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete steps, code samples, a validation loop with checkpoints and a test example, though the referenced files were not reviewed here.
needs: cdk bootstrap run in each account and region
why: It is cloud infrastructure administration for AWS, and the node keeps data and runs locally, so it is not useful for building, running or selling a local-first product. Deploying with it would move the product's resources onto a cloud account the person does not control in this model.

summary: This skill lets an agent drive a real iPhone or iPad through WebDriverAgent using the Midscene CLI, working from screenshots and natural-language commands rather than accessibility labels. It covers connecting to a device, launching apps or links, performing multi-step actions, asserting what is on screen, recording transient UI, and producing reports. It is aimed at people testing or operating iOS apps and checking how they look on a device.
tasks: test my iOS app on an iPhone
check the login screen on an iPad

verify a toast appears after tapping Submit on iOS

needs: a vision-capable model API key such as Gemini, Qwen or Doubao set in MIDSCENE_MODEL_API_KEY
WebDriverAgent running on the iOS device
why: It tests and drives phones and tablets rather than building or hosting a node's own product, so its use is occasional QA rather than core building. It sends screenshots to the chosen external vision model, which the person configures, and it is not tied to the node's stack.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building a ChatGPT app, which pairs an MCP server with a widget UI that renders inside ChatGPT. It covers choosing an app type, planning the tools and their annotations, and wiring the widget through the MCP Apps bridge with optional window.openai extras. summary: This skill lets an agent score the quality of agent skill folders in a project, combining fixed structural checks with a separate language-model review. It produces a weighted score, a list of improvements for weak skills, and Markdown and JSON reports. It suits maintainers who gate merges on a score threshold or who need a repeatable review of their own skill library.

generate an LLM review prompt for a skill
merge an LLM review with automatic checks into one score
list improvements for a low-scoring skill

summary: This skill teaches an agent to build web APIs and small apps with the Hono framework: routing, middleware, request validation, JSX, streaming, and a typed RPC client. It also tells the agent to verify changes with the Hono CLI, which runs the app in-process with app.request(), so no dev server is needed. The main audience is developers who want a lightweight TypeScript API framework, especially one that targets Cloudflare Workers.

Its verification CLI depends on the pre-release @hono/cli@next package, and much of the binding guidance assumes Cloudflare Workers, which a local-first node does not use.

summary: This skill helps an agent check how trading signals performed after their holding period. It compares each signal's predicted direction with 5-day and 20-day returns, sorts outcomes into true positives, false positives, regime mismatches and similar groups, and writes summary reports. The results can then suggest weight changes for a signal-aggregation tool and entries for a skill-improvement backlog. The intended users are traders and quant researchers reviewing their signal quality.

classify signal outcomes as true or false positives
generate weight feedback for a signal aggregator
build a backlog of skill improvements from signal errors
qualityWhy: The instructions give concrete CLI commands, input and output formats, classification rules and a test suite, though some steps assume other skills' output files exist.

why: The skill is for analysing trading performance, which is not building, running, selling or making content for a product, so it does not fit what a Fractera node is for. Its price data comes from a cloud market-data API, and it would be skipped in any case for that reason.

summary: This is a deprecated alias skill. When an agent is told to run it by name, it prints a rename notice, hands the refresh work to the ce-compound skill with mode:refresh and the same arguments, then prints the notice again at the end. It is meant for people with old prompts or scheduled jobs that still use the old name. It does no refresh work of its own.

keep a scheduled learnings refresh running after the rename
audit stored learnings for a directory or module

why: It is a deprecated pointer to ce-compound and has no content for building, running or selling a product on a local node; installing it adds nothing that ce-compound does not already provide.

summary: The skill tells an agent to find and read official Slack platform documentation from docs.slack.dev. It uses a public search endpoint scoped by category, then fetches each page as clean markdown so answers cite the live docs rather than memory. It serves developers building Slack apps who ask conceptual or how-to questions.

No secrets or outside accounts are needed.

summary: The skill walks an agent through full Sentry error monitoring and performance setup for server-side JavaScript on Node.js, Bun and Deno. It covers installing the SDK, writing an instrument file loaded before app code, wiring framework error handlers for Express, Fastify, Koa, Hapi and Connect, and optional features like logs, profiling, metrics, cron monitoring and AI monitoring. It is aimed at developers who run backend services and want crash and slowdown visibility.

monitor scheduled jobs with Sentry crons
configure Sentry logging for a Node.js backend

summary: This skill makes an agent study an existing codebase to find the conventions the team already follows, such as module layout, validation style and error formats. summary: This skill lets an agent look up live and historical market data for stocks in Hong Kong, the US, mainland China A-shares and Singapore through the Longbridge CLI. It covers quotes, candlestick charts, order books, trade ticks, capital flow, sentiment indexes, trading hours, exchange rates and IPO calendars, plus ADR premium and FX carry analysis. It is written for investors and analysts who want fast, read-only market answers.

pull daily candlestick data for a ticker

summary: This guide teaches an agent to write, route, configure and test Netlify serverless functions in TypeScript, JavaScript or Go. It covers HTTP handlers, custom URL paths, streaming responses, long background jobs, cron schedules, and reacting to deploy, identity and form events. It is aimed at developers who host their backend endpoints on Netlify.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to search and export the user's own past coding-agent sessions (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Aider and many others) through a local CLI that builds a local index. summary: This skill guides an agent through making interactive Blazor components behave correctly when the server prerenders them as static HTML first. It covers avoiding duplicate data loads and UI flicker by persisting state with the PersistentState attribute or the PersistentComponentState service, turning prerendering off per component or app-wide, excluding pages from interactive routing so they keep HttpContext, and detecting prerender versus interactive at runtime. summary: Guides an agent through finding memory leaks in JavaScript and Node.js apps by taking, comparing and inspecting heap snapshots through Chrome DevTools MCP memory tools. It requires the server to run with a memory-debugging flag, then walks through capture, diff, retainer tracing and common leak categories. The target users are developers debugging high memory use or out-of-memory crashes in browser or server code.

explain why objects are still retained after navigation
diagnose out-of-memory errors in a Node.js server
qualityWhy: Concrete workflow with named tools, steps and filters, plus a reference file of common leaks, though it lacks explicit success criteria and sample outputs.

why: Debugging memory is useful for building and running a node's web or server apps, but only now and then; it is stack-free debugging guidance that fits the node's JavaScript stack directly.

summary: The skill runs one fixed four-role review of a proposal: a product manager, architect, developer and QA engineer each answer the same topic from their lens, and the agent then writes a synthesis that names where the roles agree and where they conflict. It is meant for someone shaping a feature or initiative before any code is written. It reads an optional project-context file through the file tools and treats its contents as untrusted data.
tasks: review a feature proposal from PM, architect, developer and QA views

onboard a new initiative with first concerns per role
surface blocking concerns before implementation
qualityWhy: The skill gives a clear workflow with a prompt template, output format, trust boundary for the context file, synthesis rules and anti-patterns, with only small gaps such as no example session.

It depends on the agent supporting parallel subagents, which the node's agent setup should provide, and it writes nothing to files unless the user asks.

summary: This skill gives an agent a set of conventions for writing custom MSBuild targets in .NET projects. why: The skill covers MSBuild for .NET projects, which is not the Next.js, TypeScript and SQLite stack a Fractera node runs on, so it does not serve building or running a node's sites or content. Nothing in it is risky, but it has no use on a node.

summary: This skill tells an agent to create a branch, review and stage only the relevant changes, commit with a sign-off, push, and open a pull request against an upstream repository using the GitHub CLI. It can also, when the person has merge rights and asks, merge the PR and reset local branches to the upstream main branch. It is aimed at developers who contribute to someone else's repository.

a git remote named official pointing to the upstream repo
why: It is a developer contribution workflow, useful now and then but not for building, running or selling a product on a node, and it carries risks that stop installation. It hard-codes a commit author and sign-off for a named third person and tells the agent to run a hard reset that can discard local work.
risks: Hard-codes commits to be authored and signed off as a specific named person, which the node's owner would need to change or agree to.
Runs git reset --hard against the upstream branch, which can permanently discard uncommitted local work without asking.

summary: The skill has an agent hand a bounded coding task to the Mistral Vibe CLI running headlessly, using a bundled Node relay script that captures the run into a result file. review and land Vibe's diff

why: It is a coding-workflow skill rather than something that makes content or serves a product directly, so its value is occasional. It depends on the Mistral Vibe CLI and its own loop; the node has no such CLI, so it would need adapting to the node's own tooling, which makes it an ideas-only fit.
risks: The --full-access mode disables Vibe's tool approvals and permits arbitrary shell execution under the user account, so an agent could run unreviewed commands if the person authorizes it carelessly.
The brief is passed as a command-line argument, so its contents are visible in the process list to other users on a shared machine.

summary: This skill helps an agent improve an LLM prompt by pulling its real behaviour from Arize: it finds the prompt inside exported trace spans, gathers error signals, eval scores and annotations, and then rewrites the prompt and checks it with a new experiment. Every step runs through the ax command-line tool against an Arize workspace.

LLM provider credentials for experiments, managed through Arize AI integrations

The generic prompt-writing advice would be useful on a node, but the whole workflow depends on Arize's cloud data.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to set up a local, Docker-backed Postgres for development using the clickhousectl command-line tool, including psql access. summary: This skill guides an agent through photo picking, camera capture, image display and media permissions in iOS apps written in Swift. It covers SwiftUI PhotosPicker usage, PHPicker-style media filtering, AVCaptureSession lifecycle, permission handling with Info.plist keys, and downsampling large images. summary: This skill teaches an agent to call the Valyu web service for searching across web, academic, medical, financial and news sources, extracting clean text from URLs, getting cited AI answers, and running longer deep-research reports. summary: This skill lets an agent split a local video, or a timestamped subtitle file, into chapters, topics or steps, then render a separate navigation-bar MP4 that shows the current section and overall progress. The skill is documented in Chinese and its reference files and Swift helper were only partly visible, so the agent should verify the scripts before relying on them.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to lay out a .NET application in four projects (Domain, Application, Infrastructure, Api) with dependencies pointing inward. why: It is written for C#/.NET with EF Core and Mediator, which a Fractera node (Next.js, TypeScript, SQLite element) does not use, so an agent should take the layering and use-case ideas and rebuild them in TypeScript rather than install it as is. It is useful only when a person picks a .NET stack for a product.

summary: This skill lets an agent take a public GitHub repository, create a fork of it under a fixed account, and clone that fork to the local machine. summary: This skill has an agent collect a person's GitHub activity from the current week and turn it into a short English list for a weekly report. why: It helps with writing status reports rather than building or running a product on the node, so its value is occasional. It reads the GitHub API with the person's own gh login, which is a service they choose to use, and the account name is hardcoded to one user, so it would need editing for anyone else.

summary: This skill guides an agent to turn vague product ideas into short, problem-focused product requirement documents that align engineering, design and product teams. why: It is a stack-free writing and planning aid, useful now and then for a product on the node, though it is mostly guidance and quotes rather than an executable workflow; the references folder is large and was not reviewed in full.

summary: This skill guides an agent through building, styling, debugging, optimizing and deploying Streamlit apps written in Python. summary: The skill guides an agent to write, review and polish posts for Sentry's engineering blog, covering voice, banned phrases, opening lines, reader-question structure, headings, SEO for developer queries, and title and closing rules. summary: This skill lets an agent write a short, personalized sales email or a three-touch follow-up sequence for a named prospect. summary: This skill guides an agent through diagnosing why the Chrome DevTools MCP server fails to connect or start, such as errors in list_pages, new_page or navigate_page. No risk found: it only reads config, runs help and log commands, and searches public issues.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to find the stock visual and copy patterns that make a web project look machine-generated, such as default gradients, generic fonts, glowing status dots and formulaic marketing lines. summary: This skill guides an agent to read how a person is writing and to adjust its reply to match. summary: This skill lets an agent pull analyst earnings and revenue estimates for a stock from Yahoo Finance via the yfinance library, then analyse how those estimates are moving. why: It is a financial-research skill rather than a tool for building, running or selling a product, so its use on a node is occasional. It is stack-free apart from a Python library that runs locally, and Yahoo data is read-only and not stored by the skill; the disclaimers and caveats are already in the file.

summary: This skill runs a short pre-mortem before an agent starts building a product or feature. why: It is a stack-free planning habit that helps decide what to build and validate on a node, not a tool for building or running content itself, so its value is occasional. It has no scripts, no keys and no network calls.

summary: This skill walks an agent through installing a .NET SDK into a project-local .dotnet folder, pinning a version, and pointing global.json at it so the system-wide install stays untouched. summary: This skill lets an agent check a developer's GitHub notifications and the recent open issues and pull requests across a fixed list of repositories. why: It is a read-only developer utility that does not build, run, or sell a product on the node, so its use is occasional, and it is tied to a fixed list of another organization's repositories that would need replacing. The date syntax needs adjusting on macOS before it works.

summary: This skill tells an agent to bring a local main or master branch up to date with a remote. For a fork it fetches the official upstream, hard-resets local main to it, and force-pushes the result to origin. For a project with only origin it fetches and pulls. It finishes by showing the last few commits so the person can confirm the sync worked. It is written for developers managing git repositories.
tasks: sync my fork's main branch with upstream
update local main to the latest origin code
pull the newest main branch changes
check the last commits after syncing

git push --force-with-lease rewrites the remote main history on origin, which can break others' clones and lose commits.

summary: This skill lets an agent fetch the public Hormuz Strait Monitor dashboard and report on the strait's current state: whether it is open, restricted or closed, ship transits, oil prices, stranded vessels, insurance risk, cargo throughput, tanker rates and diplomatic news. summary: The skill teaches an agent how to search a Slack workspace for messages, files, channels and people using four search tools, including modifiers for channel, sender, date and content type. It covers test function layout, TestCase and TestStep fields, modern ConfigStateChecks with custom StateCheck implementations, plan checks, import verification, sweepers, and scenario patterns such as basic, update, disappears, validation and regression. It is aimed at provider developers who test infrastructure resources, not at people building websites or apps on a node.
tasks: write acceptance tests for a Terraform provider resource
add import verification to provider tests
debug a failing terraform-plugin-testing step
structure regression tests for a provider bug fix
qualityWhy: The SKILL.md gives concrete Go code for each pattern, a field reference table and a clear test lifecycle, with reference files for deeper detail, though it leaves some helper code undefined.
why: The skill serves authoring tests for Terraform providers, which is infrastructure tooling and not something a node is for, so it does not fit building, running or selling a product; its stack (Go, terraform-plugin-testing) is also outside the node's stack. The files contain no risky behaviour.

summary: This skill gives an agent a morning briefing routine for a sales or account owner: it pulls today's meetings with account context, flags opportunities closing within two weeks, lists waiting customer emails, and proposes the top three actions for the day. It is written to work against connected calendar, CRM, email, transcript and chat tools, and falls back to uploaded spreadsheets or pasted exports when none are connected. The output is a briefing view with a link to the source of every line.
tasks: prepare my daily briefing
what's on my plate today
list today's meetings with account context
show opportunities closing in the next two weeks
summarize customer emails waiting for a reply
qualityWhy: The steps, tier model, link rules and fallbacks are concrete and complete, though it depends heavily on connector behaviour that is only described in general terms.
why: It is a sales-team workflow rather than a tool for building or running a product, so it is only occasionally useful on a Fractera node; it also assumes an external CRM and Microsoft or Google connectors, which the node does not provide, so it would need adapting to the node's own SQLite data and elements. Read it for the briefing structure and link discipline rather than installing it as written.

summary: This skill makes an agent scan a Markdown knowledge base, find pages that mention each other's names or topics without linking, and insert [[wikilinks]] or a Related section. It scores each candidate by strength, records the relationship type in frontmatter, and writes a report. It is aimed at people maintaining an Obsidian-style wiki after importing or adding many notes. It also covers promoting loose misc pages and refreshing a search index afterwards.
tasks: add missing links between notes in my wiki
connect orphan pages after importing notes
find unlinked mentions in my Obsidian vault
build a cross-reference report for my knowledge base
qualityWhy: The steps, scoring table and report format are concrete, but it depends on an unshipped llm-wiki framework file and contradicts itself by reading every page in full while warning against blind full reads.
why: It serves knowledge-base upkeep, which is only tangential to building sites, apps, agents or content on a node, and it assumes the obsidian-wiki and llm-wiki stack, so it should be read for its ideas and rebuilt the node's way. Its pre-write step runs git add -A and commits every untracked file in the vault when the vault is a standalone repository, without asking first, which could sweep sensitive files into history.

summary: This skill lets an agent pull existing LLM trace data out of the Arize observability service using the ax command-line tool. It can fetch traces, individual spans, or whole conversation sessions by ID, and browse projects with a sample-first approach. It helps developers see what their LLM app is doing and trace errors or behaviour regressions back to specific spans.
tasks: export traces for an LLM app
debug failing LLM traces
download a conversation session by ID
find error spans in production traces
qualityWhy: The skill gives concrete, runnable commands, filter syntax, time-window rules, escalation rules and a troubleshooting table, though it is long and partly repetitive.
why: Arize is a cloud service that keeps the trace data, so it is a cloud place to store the person's data rather than a local-first tool, which makes the value none and the use skip. The skill has no security risks of its own.

summary: This skill teaches an agent to design editable motion graphics in the Tesseract CLI, including full-frame animated scenes, kinetic typography, diagrams, and lower thirds or overlays placed over supplied footage. It asks the agent to plan the visual idea and rhythm first, then build native layers and animation, check the saved result with filmstrip frames, and deliver a portable project file plus a rendered preview. Music waveform review and small local sound accents are included, and transparent overlays can be exported as ProRes with alpha. design an animated diagram for a product explainer

why: It directly serves making motion content and overlays for products and social posts, and it runs locally through the Tesseract CLI with FFmpeg. Installation details and the exact CLI source were not fully visible, and CLI telemetry is opt-out only, which the skill says it respects.
